Battlerite is good. It's better than good, it's great. Honestly, stop reading this and drop the $20!
I'm a long time League player and the idea of battle arenas, really interested me since I started a few years ago. However, I've never liked many of them. Played the now dead Strife, Messed around with HotS and Overwatch, I've got accounts in Awesomenaust and Brawlhala. None of them really clicked like LoL did for me.
Until now of course. Battlerite has a lot going for it, it's fast, there are few objectives to fight over, but enough to make those fights intense (and not a slog like with tower destruction mechanics or minion farming). The fact that you can 2v2 or 3v3 means you don't need to find too many friends to have good games.
The community seems nice and helpful if you have noob questions. The characters feel familiar but different enough that they are distinct. Every fight is tense and coming back to win after losing a couple rounds feels really, really good.
I do have issues, like the ranking in this game feels weird. I've been told it was explained some place, but I haven't really looked. Basically, I'll play a game and win, lose 2 points or have a teamamte disconnect and lose 13 points. Other times I lose and gain points.
But you know, other than MMR stuff, perfect game. Ten tens out of ten.

Hollow Knight is a masterpiece. I haven't enjoyed a game like I enjoyed this game in a very long time. I wasn't much of a platformer type person until this game. I was pleasantly surprised.
Pros:
Beautiful game- The environments are masterfully hand-drawn and pleasing to the eyes. The areas in this game range from dark and dreary to bright and beautiful. The music in this game is also wonderful.
Rewarding gameplay- This game has one difficulty. And that's all it needs. The combat is very crisp and tight, and the monsters have variety in their attacks. Although the game is challenging, it rewards the player. I've felt pure joy after defeating bosses in this game. There's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. There's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t mechanics that make you wonder, "Is that my fault or the games'?"
Size- The game is huge for the genre. I've spent hours upon hours just exploring the maps and finding neat things spread across the game. My first playthrough of the game was around 17 hours, and my completion percentage was 55%. The game is huge. There's so much to do in Hollow Knight.
Combat & Others- The combat in this game is crisp and tight. You have complete control over what your character does. There are two basic ways of combat; spellcasting and swordsmanship. Throughout the game you get different charms and power-ups that can change the way you play. The monsters in Hollow Knight have variety. You don't feel like you're being attacked by the same mob over and over again.
Level Design- Playing through the game, I had a blast going through the levels. The platforming was enjoyable. Throughout the levels there may be hidden things that you can pick-up or attack. However, you are going to have to search for them because they are not clearly marked. The levels in general were fantastic. They was a lot of variety in the ways the maps were laid out.
Openended-ness: The game is almost entirely non-linear. You can explore just about every map in any order you choose. It leaves a lot for the player to choose. You're not forced to do any map in any certain order.
Cons:
Honestly, not much. You may encounter times where you have no idea where you are in a map, but that wasn't too much of a bother for me. I felt like it was just immersive. The fast travel stations in Hollow Knight are also spread thin in some areas, so you'll have to expect a lot of walking and dashing.
I highly recommend this game for anyone. The combat may be challenging, but it's also rewarding. It's also a good starter game to get into this genre.

Assassin's Creed fans know what to expect from the franchise. An engaging story, interesting characters, big-budget cut scenes, cutting edge graphics, great music and lots of taking liberties with history. In this story we meet the famous pirate Captain Kidd early in the game and I look forward to seeing who else turns up. Also of course is the stealth-optional gameplay methodology with a character who can easily swashbuckle through droves of enemies. The challenge comes instead, of course, from jumping puzzles and mastering the in-game economy.
At first, ACIV feels all too familar. You play as Edward Kenway, Haytham's grandfather and a Welsh pirate who rather auspiciously finds himself in the guise of a member of a secret society. Of course this is framed by the common narrative of the Animus. This time you are a faceless Abstergo employee, tasked with playing through Edward's life to start an entertainment franchise. The rather meta nature of this is a nice touch.
The familiarity fades away when you take Edward's ship out for her maiden voyage. The early stages reminiscent of Ezio's tales feel like al less interesting verison of what you've played before, but this is not the meat of the gameplay. You will find rather quickly that the naval missions from AC3 have been heavily expanded on, and even after the hundredth time, boarding an enemy vessel is a highly satisfying experience. Edward soon has his own fleet of ships, their trade missions similar to those in AC3. The naval combat has also been simplified, making it much easier to take on multiple ships at once - and you will want to do so in order to upgrade your own ship as much as possible. Most of the game is spent navigating between land masses in your ship with the city exploration taking a much smaller role in what is now a much larger world.
The pros: Everything you expect from an Assassin's Creed title. The Bahamas come alive and look absolutely amazing. The voice acting is top notch and the character designs tastefully toe the line between historic authenticity and whimsical fantasy. The story is intriguing and engaging, though like that of its predecessors, can be difficult to follow with so many distractions. It is easy to spend an entire session searching for treasures and other tokens or collectibles and forget all about what is going on in the main storyline. Plenty of side missions and challenges.
The cons: Edward inexplicably has all the talents and abilities of an Assassin without ever receiving any training, which shatters suspension of disbelief almost immediately and presents a rather gaping plot hole. Edward's two swords style feels rather forced and awkward, no doubt a result of the popularity of "dual-wielding," a fictional invention with no place in history. I find myself using the hidden blade instead most of the time.
As in Assassin's Creed 3, the gambling is a waste of time. The AI is infallible and never makes a bad move, so you can only lose or stalemate.
PC Gamers have a tenuous relationship with Ubisoft. The CEO has gone on public record stating he believes all pc gamers are pirates, a statement that is of course patently ridiculous. In any case, as a result of Ubisoft's virulently anti-consumer behavior, there are no special pc options and we basically get a bare bones console port. However, 1440p and 60 fps are both supported, albeit with some qualifications. For example, if your fps should drop to 59, the game auto caps to 30. No refresh rates higher than 60ms are supported.
UPlay is, as ever, an obnoxious and unnecessary DRM disguised as a gaming platform. It has never prevented me from playing the game though. So while it is an annoyance, it is not a dealbreaker. Due to poor pc optimization, even high end systems will have trouble keeping 60 fps.
Overall it is a great game with little left to be desired. PC enthusiasts will be a little disappointed in the lack of options, but the game still looks miles better than its console counterparts and will keep you busy for many hours.

This is one of my favorite metroidvania games of all time.
The art style is lovingly done and the music ranges from haunting to calming, to exciting. The UI is simple with easy to learn controls and while I played excusively on an xbox 360 controller, I have heard that keyboard is acceptable. Regardless, most if not all buttons can be remapped for both setups. The in-game menu can be annoying at times as switching between, say, inventory and map takes a tad too long, and since there are 4 screens in the menu, switching between them can be tiresome.
The game starts off by giving you control of this cute little guy who wields a nail as a weapon. Initially you have a very limited moveset with almost no abilities besides jump, attack, and interacting with objects and NPCs. Eventually the player will encounter dozens of characters and hundreds of different enemies and bosses, and be given access to a large variety of abilities and areas. Some enemies, items, and abilities are hard-sought and/or require a tough battles to get through. Most rewards feel justly won, with higher difficulty areas and enemies barring access to high value items or abilities.
You will need to explore every nook and cranny to find everything the game has to offer. Like old metroidvania games, secrets will be hidden in walls, underground, and in the ceiling. Taking from the soulsborne series, you will find some NPCs accessible in certain areas at certain times. Also taking from the soulsborne series is the idea that most areas should be accessible early on, even if the area has a high difficulty, and there are very rarely plots barriers preventing you from moving somewhere you haven't been yet. My first playthrough had me missing a decent number of the areas in the game, due to me trying to go for "plot" points. The game gives little direction and it's up to you for the most part to decide how to proceed and in what order.
A large complaint of the game is that the map does not fill in on it's own and requires purchasing one from an NPC, in addition to no icon showing your character's placement on the map even once it's purchased. (There is an item you can get relatively early that allows you to see your character's icon, but it takes up points that should probably be spent on something more pragmatic, like abilities or some such. Despite these complaints from some, I feel that this is a key part of the game and keeps with the theme.
The game has an overall theme of personal accountability. You must keep track of where you are in time and space or else lose an ability slot to equip a map's character icon. Dying will spawn you at the last bench you rested at with half of your max  soul/mana and all your currency gone. Getting back to where you died will allow you to recover your true max soul/mana and all the currency you were carrying. If you die a second time before reaching that spot, all the currency you had before the first death will be lost, with the new currency recovery being set to whatever you were carrying in between the first death and the second. In essence, soulsborne.
The difficulty makes the substantial gains even more rewarding. The exploration feels fairly unrestrictive and can be done in almost any order. The story is vague at times and is up to interpretation to some degree. There are multiple endings and each one feels rewarding for the amount of work you put into them. Some areas will take your breath away, and others will make you feel anxious. Some of you will breeze through portions of the game only to become incredibly frustrated with a specific boss, or challenge. You can play the game your way and tailor the experience to your playstyle.
As I write this, it's on sale for less than $10 US and it's worth a hell of a lot more than that. Please give yourself the pleasure of trying this fantastic experience.

As many of my friends well know, I have a game called Dungeon Defenders. You may not know what this is about, but I'll give u the short version. It is a third-person, tower defence game, and the objective is to protect crystals that are shown to u at the beginning of the match. You place down towers and traps for the ogres, orcs, goblins and dark elves to be killed from. You must create a character of your liking, the classes you can choose from are Apprentice (wizard), Squire (knight), Huntress (archer/gunwoman) and Monk (martial artist). Each class has a unique kind of tower that it can place down, I won't tell u what they are, caus that will spoil it ;). Make sure the class you pick suits you, because all your progress is saved onto that character. You may solo the levels, or you may team up with some friends or even just some randoms. The game is abit old and there are not many people playing it now, but coming out in Spring 2014 is Dungeon Defenders 2, so if you want to get a hang of the game so you can get a good headstart with Dungeon Defenders 2, this is your kind of game. There are also some DLC's for the game if you want some extra characters to play as. I definetly reccomend this game to whoever likes a mixture of third-person/first-person and tower defence.

I've been very pleasantly surprised. After the festering pile of dog vomit that was AC3, I held off on buying AC4 until it went on a deep discount sale.
This game takes the fun stuff that worked from AC2, and basically kicks AC3 out the door, except for the ship combat aspects.
No more interminable and pointless wilderness maps with no fast travel points.  There are a ton of maps to explore, all of various sizes (from the 200 meter maps you can sprint across in a few seconds to the 1km maps with multiple fast travel spots). The story is just 'ok'. Most of the time it feels like there's some portion missing, but the stuff that's presented is tolerable. The gameplay is exactly the same as it has been for 5 years.
Over all, is it worth the current price of 40$ for the plain (or 60 for deluxe) then adding all the DLC for another 30$...?
No.  It really is just another annual interpretation of the same game they've been pushing for years. If you can get it on sale, everything for 30-40$, then it's a great deal. But 70-90 for all the content? Forget it.

It's a fairly average Assassin's Creed game for a good portion of it; namely, all the ground segments. You have a fairly standard assortment of weapons (smoke bombs, up to four pistols, swords, hidden blades, and three kinds of darts), and, while fun, is nothing special.
Then you get a ship. And then much pirate-based fun was had.
The sailing feels awesome. Naval combat, while still a bit basic, is suprisingly good fun. Ramming enemies is satisfying. Using the swivel guns is satisfying. The shanties are nice to listen to whilst sailing about, and it's quite fun to take advantage of, and avoid, the stormy weather. The thick clouds of white smoke that you get in naval combat do their job quite well. It takes a little bit to get to the ship portion, but it is oh-so-satisfying when it is gotten to.
There are also other water-based sections that I won't spoil, but they are quite satisfying to go through, if tense.
Overall, a good game. Also, makes me wish for a sequel or spiritual successor to Sid Meyer's Pirates with this sort of perspective available.

Black Flag is going to be the last Assassin's Creed I buy and I've liked the series since the original (Yeah, I actually like that game). Why you ask? I mean after all I've played more than 50 hours of this game, I clearly didn't hate it. There's a lot to like here, the pirating is fun, especially because there's been barely any good pirate games ever since the remake of Sid Meier's Pirates and that was ten years ago. Edward Kenway is a likable protagonist that doesn't give a crap about ancient aliens brought to you by the History Channel, he just wants the British and Spanish to donate to his retirement fund by giving him all their sugar and rum. It's also a atmospheric game with some nice exploration, finding everything will definitely keep you busy.
The thing is though is that the game is still plagued with frustrations, that while they don't straight up ruin the game, prevent it from becoming truly great. This mainly comes through the old Assassin's Creed gameplay of platforming and combat. Black Flag is jank as hell when it comes to platforming. Assassin's Creed always had a bit of clunky platforming at times but this is noticeably worse. Coming off of Shadow of Mordor proves this to me even more, Mordor was utterly smooth while in Black Flag it wasn't uncommon for the controls to sh*t themselves causing me to plunge to my death. The combat is also worse than the Ezio trilogy due to the sh*tty camera which was way too zoomed in which allows enemies to cheap shot you off screen. Enemies also have too good priority, being able to see you and hit you before you react sometimes. The future plot is at an absolute nadir here with an obnoxious metaplot that’s far more annoying than Desmond’s stuff ever was and I always thought he was the worst part of the series. (Though I never played 3)
All this goes to show that Assassin's Creed really isn’t improving and I assume 3 has ruined the series from here on out. But ultimately do I recommend this game? Yes, I do. Despite all the problems it’s a solid sendoff for the series seeing is that Unity and Rogue clearly aren’t helping to prevent the series' downward spiral. It’s definitely worth your time if you’ve liked the series up till this point and/or want a new pirate game.

Of course I'd heard that this is a great game. What it showed me, though, is how tired I am of Assassin's Creed story... This could be a superb game in its own right and the more AC games I see, the more I think they all could be completely separate - like Far Cry, that is just a set of mechanics in different settings. On the other hand, Ubisoft seems to be going towards one set of mechanics for all their titles. Anyway, I expected an AC game with ships and instead I got Sid Meier's Pirates!, Assassin's Creed style! How could I be complaining?
That it is about assassins vs templars everyone knows. Same with the Animus part. But this time it's the Caribbean Islands - THE setting for a pirate game. And we get to meet some people we know from history. The story is interesting but, I feel, a little forced with the assassin story. Let's just say that suspension of disbelief is frequently required when following the main story. The characters are great and "colorful" - they're mostly pirates, after all. Edward is likable and charismatic. Being a sailor and a pirate, it's not that surprising that he can pull off all those acrobatic feats, can fight well, etc.
It could as well be the next Pirates! game. We spend a lot of the game on the ship, traveling to locations around the Caribbean, accompanied by shanties that we collect around the world, in sun and in storms, fighting other ships, boarding, attacking forts, diving and harpooning, visiting tiny islands to look for treasure chests. The map is big, but there is fast travel possible if needed. Side missions are varied enough and fighting bigger ships can be a welcome challenge. Captured ships can also be added to Kenway's fleet, which is basically a kind of daily management minigame, where we can send the ships to different missions for growing amounts of money, that take growing amounts of real time.
The downsides for me are imprecise controls - the standard for AC games. I found myself frequently jumping on or off of somethig when I didn't want to. And, on occasion, Edward keeps jumping on a wall and doesn't catch on anything even though he's just a little step to the side, or will be jumping on a wall in front of him even though I'm holding a completely different direction. Let's face it - walking is slow. Running, though, means automatically freerunning, so instead of going through a door or passage, I'll be half way to the roof before I manage to stop. And interacting with objects is possible only from a specific side within a specific distance. I was constantly swearing at chests or at a swivel gun that can be used during boarding. Walking to it is slow and if I run I either stop too far from it to interact or jump onto it.
I also didn't find the out-of-Animus part of the story engaging in any way. These scenes are mostly a distraction and not much more. Similar, for me. are the focused scenes when assassinating major characters. I loved them in AC2 - they seemed seamless, could be happening in Ezzio's head when he was paying last respects to his targets while holding them. In this case, though, Edward is walking around and talking with the person, asking questions. It seems out of place, disconnected.
All in all, I love the game, even though it's frustrating at times, because all the other time it is pure fun.

I'm part of the small minority that don't think this game is the best in the series. In fact, I don't even think it should be called Assassin's Creed. Black Flag feels like Ubisoft started to create a pirate game, and then halfway through decided that it should be an Assassin's Creed game instead, so they tacked on a few Templar related elements. I've played Asssassin's Creed 1, 2, Brotherhood, Revalations, and 3 before this one. So I am familiar with the lore of the game and what I enjoyed in the series. For me the wheels came off with the terrible protagonist Conor in 3. Assassin's Creed 3 and 4 both feel disjointed to me, and disconnected from the Assassin roots. Somehow the games have become less and less about finding out about the history of the Assassin's and their struggle with the Templars, and more about individual characters that just fall into the organization by chance.
The game looks fine, the naval warfare from 3 is back and has been expanded upon greatly - so much so that it makes out a giant chunk of the game so if you didn't enjoy that aspect give this a skip - and combat works well enough, but for me this game is just missing something. Like the core of the game somehow went lost in translation. I don't much care for Conor or Edward, and the stealth element has been almost completely removed from this game as well as (to a lesser extent) its predecessor. In many cases you will be faced with scenario where stealth either isn't possible, or you don't have time to deal with it. The game encourages full frontal attacks in which you endlessly counter attack until heaps of bodies surround you.
Perhaps if this was a completely separate game with a different story line I could have enjoyed it, but as an Assasin's Creed game I have to say that I'm disappointed, especially given the extremely hyperbolic reviews I've read. 6/10.

TL;DR Version: It's an f'in awesome game, but works best if you only do one playthrough of it.
Pros:
Amazing melee combat

-The ability to clean your sword is awesome, as I haven't seen it in any other game before.
Pretty dang realistic physics and gibbing
-Another one of my obsessions, this game definitely fits my expectations of what a hack n' slash game should have in terms of body physics and dismembering.
Awesome references and humor
-The goriest games should always have the funniest dialogue.
-Also, the only time I heard "reaction" dialogue repeated was when Lo Wang "hurt his wang", so to speak.
Pretty nice story and soundtrack
-I've never been good at judging such things, so that's about as much as I can say.
-Nice upgrade system
-Good graphics
-Lots of hidden things
-Survival mode's pretty cool
-Unlike other games, if you have full ammo and try to reload it will actually show him checking his weapons instead of not doing anything like most FPS'
Cons:
VV Major problem w/ the Game VV
-After playing through the entire game, upgrading yourself and your weapons, it's basically all pointless since you can't go back and replay levels with your gear.
-While it does make sense that the weapons might be to OP, this isn't a multiplayer game, so there's no one who would find it  "unfair".
-Also, how can you get every upgrade in the game if, when you start at the beginning to get more karma points or ki crystals, your upgrades, the entire reason you wanted to replay the game, are gone?!!?
Otherwise, there's just these minor problems;
-cutscenes often glitch or won't animate properly
-I played through the entire game without actually using any of the extra powers besides the regeneration one, so it's not like getting them in the first place is really necessary
-Inconsistent fall damage
-The stereotypical "video game weakspot" bull enemies are so d@mn hard to kill I once had to throw shurikens at one in order to kill it because I had literally ran out of ammo in every other gun trying to hit it's back.
-While still fun, having to frequently fight a wave or two of enemies can get boring
-No markers to tell you where to go
-According to the end scene (where you can see yourself/Lo Wang,) Lo Wang apparently shaved off every hair on his body (i.e. he's too damn bald!)
-Not enough wang puns
Overall a great game, and I'll probably keep it one my computer for a while, but it still has very low replay-ability due to the whole "weapons-and-gear-not-saving" thing I mentioned earlier.

Wow. I can't remember the last time that i hated a game so much that i decided to spread the word about its awfulness.
RaceRoom is the absolutely worst racing experience of a life-time. I love the racing genre and i've played them all. This is one of those games that has tons of potential but is ruined by its incredibly boring core game-play and the details of its design-choices. However, it doesn't stop there.
From the clunky, bloated and confusing UI to the hopelessly boring "challenges" of learning the tracks to the rear-wheel driven impossible-to-steer cars you get to drive in your very first race (!), i have never before come across a game in which there were so many different things that i disliked right away. It's as if the developers want to scare you away from the idea of a free racing game and/or donate this product to scientists who are doing patience-research on modern man. It wouldn't surprise me if the developers themselves are scientists who have no idea what fun is in a video game. The multi-player button is greyed out and thus inaccessible, possibly because you're expected to finish all the "challenges" first. Something i would guarantee that 90% of all those who try the game never will. There's no AI to race against, but only single ghosts of times to beat. So who cares about beating a ghost when you get absolutely nothing for it at the end of a race, nor have any fun whatsoever during the race?
RaceRoom is a remarkable monument to what happens when you go too far with making something that used to be fun into a professional "experience". Valve are frankly risking the credibilty of Steam to put this "game" into the racing genre. It belongs in the software section along with 3DMark and Folding@Home. It's chores. It's so complex it becomes stupid. It's a huge waste of time as nobody but the most desperately unemployed people in countries no longer with a functioning welfare system looking to win one of the sponsored tournaments to sell the winnings to pay their rent and heating bill will be able to stand for longer than a week. I can't even see the most serious professional race-car drivers enjoying this. There is no fun-factor whatsoever.
If you ended up being disappointed with Gran Turismo 5, stay away from RaceRoom. It's even more boring than you could ever imagine. Simbin Studios have made a shameful hit on the entire racing genre this day.
I you'd like fun mixed into the formula of a free multi-player racer, try something like Trackmania Nations.

Where to start? For a bit of context, I have not yet played AC: Rogue or Unity.
For those who don't know, you play as a pirate, and a lot of the assassin-themed gameplay prevalent in the previous titles has taken a backseat to the updated naval combat mechanics from AC3. And honestly, it's for the better. You'll still be doing the classic free-running and assassinating, but the focus generally seems to have moved to good ol' plundering and looting on the high seas with your very own ship: the Jackdaw.
The sailing mechanics, while not completely realistic, are a lot of fun and have a surprising amount of player feedback for an Assassin's Creed game. After you severely damage enemy ships with the impressive range of weaponry equipped on the Jackdaw, you'll be given an opportunity to board it. This brings up a short sequence of mini-objectives that have an atmosphere oozing with piratey goodness: swinging from ropes, blasting soldiers with broadside cannons and an amazing soundtrack; which feel absolutely exhilarating at times.
Successfully taking over ships gives you materials that can be used to help upgrade the Jackdaw. Cloth, wood and metal are each used in reasonably balanced upgrade trees that lead through a satisfying and addictive progression system. And yes, it is addictive. I spent many hours gathering the materials required to max out my mortar so I could demolish some of the game's many naval bases easily. For the first time ever in an Assassin's Creed game, I actually wanted to collect money to buy things.
Now, onto the story. You play as Edward Kenway, a greedy pirate looking to make a quick buck after acquiring an Assassin's uniform (and also the grandfather of AC3's Connor). Ed is easily the best protagonist in the series to date, and I'd even go as far to say he's more fun than Ezio. He just doesn't give a damn about anything, especially early in the game. This is a refreshing perspective and one of the many great things with the story. The dialogue is also great; it's filled with plenty of pirate slang and less "WHERE IS CHARLES LEE?!" There's also a great host of supporting characters, which I would say is probably a first for the franchise.
Unfortunately, the story still has problems. The modern-day Animus stuff is still here, and although it's been (thankfully) toned down a great deal, it still butchers the pacing and immersion. I used to enjoy the modern-day story, but after the horrendously bad ending of AC3, I just don't give a damn anymore and I'm sure many other people would be more than happy to see it just go away forever and focus on the historical time periods. Besides that, Black Flag seems to have some trouble spelling out specific details that are important to the plot, leaving some sequences a bit of a mess because things are poorly explained and/or illogical. It baffles me that they still haven't figured out a way to make a 2 year time-skip not feel like a 2-hour time-skip. A simple "Two years later" screen will fix this issue, Ubisoft!
Otherwise, the story is quite good by Assassin's Creed standards. Memorable characters with solid voice acting are the real appeal here.
As great as the naval combat is, it certainly feels held back be being an Assassin's Creed game. Namely due to the fact that the awkward free-running mechanics and♥♥♥♥♥♥poor combat are largely unchanged from AC3. It's always infuriating when the shoddy controls make Edward run up the side of a wall instead of around a corner thanks to a minute level of imprecision, and even worse when you try to jump down to a slightly lower ledge but instead leap off the building like a suicidal maniac. And the combat? Let's just say that they desperately need to update this. It's essentially a glorified quick-time event where enemies line up in a single file and dive into your sword like a bunch of lemmings. Even the naval combat, despite being generally very good, suffers from being too easy and a bit shallow.
Regardless, these issues are tolerable. There's plenty of fun to be had in the Caribbean, which by the way, is absolutely gorgeous. The city of Havana in particular rivals Florence and Venice from AC2 as one of the most stunning locations yet. The map is also cluttered with a daunting amount of side missions. Most of these feel a bit samey, but they do offer some unique challenges, such as attempting to decipher a crudely drawn treasure map. Aside from the naval combat sequences (which make up at least 50% of the game), most of the missions are what you'd expect from an Assassin's Creed game; kill such-and-such, jump in that bale of hay, and follow the paranoid Templar for five minutes (unfortunately, it feels like Black Flag has a higher number of those tedious tailing missions than previous iterations). Which a few glaring exceptions, the optional objectives are much more reasonable and enjoyable this time around. No more "swim across the river without getting wet" crap.
I had a few bugs and frame-rate issues, but thankfully it seems much more stable than AC3, which was ludicrously unpolished. This is definitely a step in the right direction for a series that's becoming stale. I really wish they'd improve the awkward controls at the very least, and make a fully-fledged pirate game unrelated to the Assassin's Creed brand.

This is a great game, but it's just not my type.
Pros:
-The game itself is great. It's a metroidvania style game and really fits into that genre well. It's mechanically well made and handles pretty responsively, which is necessary in these sorts of games.
-The music is fantastic, and I'm considerign buyign the soundtrack.
-Figuring out enemy patterns is fairly engaging, and combined with the soulsborne style run-back-to-where-you-died-to-reclaim-your-currency-while-in-a-weakened-state mechanic really does make you feel like you just need to "git gud."
-The ability to regain health after a few attacks provides interesting risk-benefit and allows the player to continue going on in level for longer peroids of time once they learn enemy attack patterns
-Charms are nice for adjusting playstyle based on personal preferences or situational need.
-Story is engaging enough, mainly because you're trying to piece together what is going on in this strange, alien world and (I suppose) what your place in it is.
Cons:
-Checkpoints are often pretty far away. Now, I made the soulsborne  comparison a few lines ago, but it's a little different here. There are fewer good shortcuts, and even then you can take damage or die taking them. Given that you can only take 5 hits in the early game before needing to find a way to heal, corpse runs are pretty stressful.
-This also makes exploration a bit hard. At least as far in the game that I got, there is no efficient way to travel other than the transport you get access to pretty deep in a zone, so if you wanted to explore or check out the areas you missed earlier, it's going to be a trek to get back to them, to the point that it almost feels like it's not worth it and that you should just come back at endgame.
-Finally, it's just not for me. I bought the game hoping that I would enjoy it, but it just didn't pan out that way. I would just play and advance the story, all the while waiting for it to start getting fun. Eventually, I just decided that if I'm not having fun 6 hours in, it's not going to be fun for a while if at all, so I just dropped it. The game itself is great, hence the "like" but I just don't like it.

Where to start? For a bit of context, I have not yet played AC: Rogue or Unity.
For those who don't know, you play as a pirate, and a lot of the assassin-themed gameplay prevalent in the previous titles has taken a backseat to the updated naval combat mechanics from AC3. And honestly, it's for the better. You'll still be doing the classic free-running and assassinating, but the focus generally seems to have moved to good ol' plundering and looting on the high seas with your very own ship: the Jackdaw.
The sailing mechanics, while not completely realistic, are a lot of fun and have a surprising amount of player feedback for an Assassin's Creed game. After you severely damage enemy ships with the impressive range of weaponry equipped on the Jackdaw, you'll be given an opportunity to board it. This brings up a short sequence of mini-objectives that have an atmosphere oozing with piratey goodness: swinging from ropes, blasting soldiers with broadside cannons and an amazing soundtrack; which feel absolutely exhilarating at times.
Successfully taking over ships gives you materials that can be used to help upgrade the Jackdaw. Cloth, wood and metal are each used in reasonably balanced upgrade trees that lead through a satisfying and addictive progression system. And yes, it is addictive. I spent many hours gathering the materials required to max out my mortar so I could demolish some of the game's many naval bases easily. For the first time ever in an Assassin's Creed game, I actually wanted to collect money to buy things.
Now, onto the story. You play as Edward Kenway, a greedy pirate looking to make a quick buck after acquiring an Assassin's uniform (and also the grandfather of AC3's Connor). Ed is easily the best protagonist in the series to date, and I'd even go as far to say he's more fun than Ezio. He just doesn't give a damn about anything, especially early in the game. This is a refreshing perspective and one of the many great things with the story. The dialogue is also great; it's filled with plenty of pirate slang and less "WHERE IS CHARLES LEE?!" There's also a great host of supporting characters, which I would say is probably a first for the franchise.
Unfortunately, the story still has problems. The modern-day Animus stuff is still here, and although it's been (thankfully) toned down a great deal, it still butchers the pacing and immersion. I used to enjoy the modern-day story, but after the horrendously bad ending of AC3, I just don't give a damn anymore and I'm sure many other people would be more than happy to see it just go away forever and focus on the historical time periods. Besides that, Black Flag seems to have some trouble spelling out specific details that are important to the plot, leaving some sequences a bit of a mess because things are poorly explained and/or illogical. It baffles me that they still haven't figured out a way to make a 2 year time-skip not feel like a 2-hour time-skip. A simple "Two years later" screen will fix this issue, Ubisoft!
Otherwise, the story is quite good by Assassin's Creed standards. Memorable characters with solid voice acting are the real appeal here.
As great as the naval combat is, it certainly feels held back be being an Assassin's Creed game. Namely due to the fact that the awkward free-running mechanics and♥♥♥♥♥♥poor combat are largely unchanged from AC3. It's always infuriating when the shoddy controls make Edward run up the side of a wall instead of around a corner thanks to a minute level of imprecision, and even worse when you try to jump down to a slightly lower ledge but instead leap off the building like a suicidal maniac. And the combat? Let's just say that they desperately need to update this. It's essentially a glorified quick-time event where enemies line up in a single file and dive into your sword like a bunch of lemmings. Even the naval combat, despite being generally very good, suffers from being too easy and a bit shallow.
Regardless, these issues are tolerable. There's plenty of fun to be had in the Caribbean, which by the way, is absolutely gorgeous. The city of Havana in particular rivals Florence and Venice from AC2 as one of the most stunning locations yet. The map is also cluttered with a daunting amount of side missions. Most of these feel a bit samey, but they do offer some unique challenges, such as attempting to decipher a crudely drawn treasure map. Aside from the naval combat sequences (which make up at least 50% of the game), most of the missions are what you'd expect from an Assassin's Creed game; kill such-and-such, jump in that bale of hay, and follow the paranoid Templar for five minutes (unfortunately, it feels like Black Flag has a higher number of those tedious tailing missions than previous iterations). Which a few glaring exceptions, the optional objectives are much more reasonable and enjoyable this time around. No more "swim across the river without getting wet" crap.
I had a few bugs and frame-rate issues, but thankfully it seems much more stable than AC3, which was ludicrously unpolished. This is definitely a step in the right direction for a series that's becoming stale. I really wish they'd improve the awkward controls at the very least, and make a fully-fledged pirate game unrelated to the Assassin's Creed brand.

Gameplay is tight, fluid, and simple. Your repitoire of moves does grow somewhat with certain items collected, but not by a huge amount--which is a good thing.
Boss fights are challenging, usually fair, and quite varied. Enemy variety is good, as well. The environments are gorgeous and immersive.
It's not without its flaws, though. Exploration can be a pain, since the map system can be extremely frustrating and downright extortionist (you have to buy the map for each area, but first you need to find the mapmaker for each area. You don't get a marker showing where you are on a map unless you have a charm equipped, which takes up one of your precious charm slots for something that should be an inherent feature. You have to buy each and every "icon" that the map would normally be populated by--such as hot springs, vendors, fast travel stations, etc--and they aren't cheap. You even have to buy an item that allows you to fill in the incomplete area maps with your own exploration!). Additionally, since save points can be sparse (especially in certain areas) and fast travel stations even rarer, exploration can be very tedious at times, since you can end up exploring lots of areas to a dead end before you discover an item that actually gives you the ability you need to progress in other areas.
Charms are not very well balanced. Some charms are borderline useless, either because they take up far too many charm slots for the benefit they provide, or the benefit they provide is gimped by its own limitations (such as a charm that gives you a shield while you charge up your heal, but if the shield is hit, your heal is interrupted, and the shield itself can only take four hits before breaking, requiring you to repair it at a bench). Some charms give benefits that feel like they should be basic features or inherent upgrades that you can find, such as a charm that automatically collects the scattered geo that appears when you kill enemies--not having this charm equipped makes collecting geo after killing every enemy a tedious chore. A charm that gives your melee attacks bonus damage when you're at 1 hit point costs twice as many charm slots as a charm that automatically hits all nearby enemies when you get hit. A charm that lets you dash more frequently is useful, but not nearly as useful as a charm that doubles your melee range, especially since the former doesn't have any real utility beyond getting from place to place faster.
Expect lots of backtracking and traversing areas you've already thoroughly explored if you aren't familiar enough with the game to speedrun it. Use of a complete map (from a third-party source/guide) is recommended to save time, if you are turned off by this.
The game also has plenty of frustrating elements that seem poorly thought out, some of which I've mentioned above. One such element is that there is a way to recover your lost shade (which you drop after dying, containing all of your geo) without having to go and kill it wherever it is--very useful if you die in a platforming section which contains plenty of difficult enemies, making killing your shade basically impossible or suicidal--but in order to use this option, you have to use a one-use key item that costs a ton of geo (which is what you already lost to need this in the first place). You can find another of these keys relatively easily not too far into the game, but you also need this key to unlock a vital area in the same region, which allows you to progress further in the game. Additionally, since fast travel points are few and far between, chances are that you died very far away from one, making the task of using this mechanic a LONG, tedious chore. There's a bank you can discover and use, but the game gives no indication that the thing is a scam until the banker just up and disappears once you've put enough geo into it, and finding the banker and retrieving your stolen geo takes time and most likely a guide (and another one of those one-use keys).
In order to get the true ending and true final boss fight, you have to complete the White Palace, which is a true platforming hell of epic proportions that is guaranteed to make your want to rip out your hair in frustration.
Lastly, in order to even fight the true final boss, you have to beat the normal final boss beforehand. Every. Single. Time. Talk about needless tedium.
Still, don't let these flaws turn you away--overall, Hollow Knight is a fantastic game, and you won't regret buying it.

I have greatly enjoyed my time with Hollow Knight.  I didn't really play any metroidvania games growing up, and I have never really been able to get into the genre.  Hollow Knight flipped the script on that.  I have been loving the exploration of the vast open world, the wit and speed testing platforming, and the exacto knife precise combat experience.
The art and sound direction coupled with the solid (if VERY soulsian) world building have created one of the best exploration experiences I have ever had in gaming. Exploring this world has been a treat, especially considering how well the gating is done and how natural it feels to recieve new movement abilities and backtrack throughougt the level.  I love the unique map system as well.  Blindly traveling through new zones as you try to find the cartographer always puts me on the edge of my seat and brings out the cautious player in me, and really makes it feel awesome when you can start mapping a zone out and discovering all of its secrets.  One thing I would love to have would be pins that I could place on the map to remind me of things i want to explore again later.
I am not a very good twitch platformer.  That being said I found the platforming in Hollow Knight to be solid.  Most of the more challenging puzzels are for optional collectables, so I was often able to leave a puzzel that was frustrating me and come back when I had more/better movement abilities.  The ability to put down a part of the game that was bothering me was a godsend.  I feel like there is always enough to do and to explore that I could put a challenge down and come back to it later with better stats, equipment, and movement.
Combat has been great for me.  I really like how mobile and flowing fights are.  Very rarely (or against very weak enemies) do I find myself simply hacking away in hopes of taking out the opponent.  This coming from the guy who tank and spanked his way through all of the Dark Souls games doing as little dodging and movement as possible.
On the whole I think Hollow Knight is on my shortlist for Game of the Year.

The game is simple in terms of play. You pick a character, then you go into a match with one to two other teammates, be they friends or random players.
Each character has specific strengths and playstyles, and how you utilize these abilities with your teammates is vital as to whether or not you win or lose the match.
The matches are relatively short, working on a best of five win condition with each battle lasting roughly 5 minutes at the most. Each battle, everyone is also given one additional perk to their abilities. The perks can be that of more utility in a spell, more damage, or more support for your teammates.
The only downside I feel to this game is that some partner pairings aren't really ideal when you have randoms in your group, as you may have two characters who don't necessarily synergize. The team can still work, but when matched up against opponents who have a better composition, it can be a bit difficult to outplay them based on the composition alone.
This game is very reminiscent of Diablo 2's PvP, and does a good job to mimic it. If you want to re-live that kind of combat without having to worry about making a build and actually grinding, this is an exceptional game for it. It's quick, easy to learn, and has a lot of room for simply out-doing your opponent on skill alone.

I don't really like Assassin's Creed games. I played about 1/3 of the first game before I got bored of the repetitive gameplay. The Creed games are not really my cup of tea. And that's why I
like Black Flag: it's as much AC as it is Sid Meier's Pirates.
The sailing part is really where the heart of the game is for me. Even while being repetitive as well it never gets old  seeing the soothing crystal blue waters of the Caribbean slide past while dolphins jump out of the water across the bow and your pirate crew starts singing another shanty (that you collected yourself a few moments earlier). Or seeing the water wash over the deck as you avoid water spouts and freak waves while lightning sets the horizon alight. Or finally crippling an enemy frigate and getting near it's starboard side, ready to board, al the while avoiding the mortar fire of a nearby fort.
And the Assassination missions? Well, they are not all bad, although many are very easy, because protagonist Edward has superhuman fighting skills. And the climbing animations are always nice to look at. And you can fire guns and a blowpipe, which are satisfyingly effective.
The game is big. Much stuff to do besides sinking ships: harpooning whales, finding hiden treasures, diving to shipwrecks... I didn't really care for the story or the characters that much and the meta-story in the present day is equally uninspiring, but I do like that the typical pirate clichés are avoided and the dialogs at least sound appropriate to the era. The lore you collect is often nice to read as well, so props to Ubisoft for having eye for details. Now if they would only pull the plug out of Uplay...
Concluding: Black Flag might not be the game AC fans waited for (is Unity that game?) but if you want a fine pirate adventure game, beautifully rendered with high production values, then get this, you won't be disappointed.

An absolute hidden gem of a game that surprised me with each and every aspect of it's design.
I was not expecting this much depth out of the story or mechanics; specifically in the upgrade/skill system. While the game does have certain old school FPS sensibilities (collecting ammo/health, finding secrets, unlocking doors to progress) it does not neglect the narrative and totally sucked me into the story with decent writing and top-notch voice acting and all that made me want to continue playing the game for more than just the gameplay.
The gameplay (which even on it's own) is amazing and the visceral feeling of gunning down, blowing up and, most importantly, slicing up enemies is truly a delight. Especially especially using the katana which (in my humble opinion) is the best melee weapon I've ever used in a game so far.
The fact that the developers have taken the time and effort to include many many gore-y animations for when you go on a rampage shows they know what makes for a satisfying experience. As for the other weapons: all of them are wonderfully designed with alternate firemodes each and are generally a joy to use in their own ways; after all these are some of the Painkiller devs we're talking about.
Finally, the cherry on top for me would be the sense of humor and the (non-pandering) pop-culture references which really make you feel at home with everything from Star Wars to Taxi Driver. Everything just has a fun-loving and playful feel to it.
So, yeah, I haven't covered everything, but seriously watch the trailers and download the demo (yeah.. remember those?) and then seriously consider purchasing this little slice of gold.

AC:4 stands out from previous AC installments from its near-perfect execution of naval warfare and exploration. However, AC:4’s heavy use of naval warfare/exploration detracted from the traditional AC your-in-a-historical-time/place-have-fun feeling. AC:4 is an important game in the franchise as it serves as epilogue for the series’ lead protagonist Desmond Miles. Although AC:4 showed that it can make a character feel real through hidden messages, it severely lacked the depth previous AC games had involving the lead protagonist outside of the animus. Inside of the animus AC:4 showed it had some ideas on developing a more compelling character then it ever had before. Which it did by breaking the traditional AC linear character progression by adding an internal character development not solely based on impersonal events.
For a veteran of the AC franchise the feeling of a half-baked AC game will be ever present in its external-animus storyline culminating in a somber and anti-climactic ending. But it’s still a

This is not a good game.  I was truly shocked after hearing so many positive reviews about how this is an exhilerating shooter.  It's not.  Not even close.
In short, Shadow Warrior is A ONE TRICK PONY.
Gameplay consists of running into large arena areas, or occasionally streets or tunnels that restrict your movement a bit more, and then waves of THE SAME breeds of demons materialize from thin air or the walls to chase after you or shoot slow-moving projectiles at you.  The player generally has to run backwards in circles to avoid enemies while picking them off one at a time.  This is fun for about the first 1-2 hours, mostly in part to the outstanding sword mechanics.  But it quickly becomes apparent there is very little variety.  The game can't be exhilerating when its just so ♥♥♥♥ing predictable when and how every fight is going to take place.  The game needed more enemy types that attack you in different ways and more interesting environments that force you to adapt your tactics in every fight.  It needed more surprises to force you to think on your feet!  Not just portals opening and melee demons pouring through in hordes.  That's how you make an exhilerating FPS.  Oh, and the level design?  I've heard praise for how solid it is.  No, it's pretty linear.  Occasionally you have a choice between going left or going right but there's no element of exploration.  Secrets have very little value and barely qualify as secrets at all because they can usually be detected very easily since they are rarely off the path.  And again, I'll say it once more, very little difference in each fighting area.  A large arena for you to run circles or backwards in as you gradually wear the horde down.  So mindnumbingly repetitive.  You might think 'oh, an old school 100/100 health system, thats cool', no, because that's rendered completely meaningless because you can regenerate a minimum of 65% of your health AT ANY TIME.  MORE if you upgrade that skill!  This whole game is a DECEPTION.  It's not a "classic" FPS, its not even a GOOD FPS.
The postives of the game are swordplay, gunplay, graphics, and humor.  The swordplay is easily the best part of the game.  You can do special moves, weave in and out of danger, and make really satisfying kills.  The guns are also fun, punchy, upgradable, and interesting.  Unfortunately this is all futile because the player is bombarded with the same enemies in identical situations over and over.  Graphics are solid.  The humor is juvenille but the protagonist and his companion are witty.

This is the best game of its type that I've ever played.
It is slick, beautifully animated and above all extremely varied. Each area has new and charming enemies and secrets - a wasp that arches its back and spears at you in a straight line, then a beetle knight with a shield and a short sword, then a harmless jellyfish that releases a deadly homing explosion when struck. The soundtrack and foley are excellent - a deep cavern feels very different to a desolate and rain soaked fountain. Traversal and combat both felt great: challenging, but fair. There are loads of things to find and do that a less generous game would not have included.
My only real gripe is that the fast travel systems are a little limited. Some backtracking can be very rewarding when you finally return triumphant to a pit or cliff you couldn't conquer on your first pass, but other times it was just retreading the same ground. I found myself quitting to menu to fast return to a bench after I had found the item I was after, as the game lacks a homeward bone analog.
If you have a controller and some time, I highly recommend this game.

This is a great game, but it's just not my type.
Pros:
-The game itself is great. It's a metroidvania style game and really fits into that genre well. It's mechanically well made and handles pretty responsively, which is necessary in these sorts of games.
-The music is fantastic, and I'm considerign buyign the soundtrack.
-Figuring out enemy patterns is fairly engaging, and combined with the soulsborne style run-back-to-where-you-died-to-reclaim-your-currency-while-in-a-weakened-state mechanic really does make you feel like you just need to "git gud."
-The ability to regain health after a few attacks provides interesting risk-benefit and allows the player to continue going on in level for longer peroids of time once they learn enemy attack patterns
-Charms are nice for adjusting playstyle based on personal preferences or situational need.
-Story is engaging enough, mainly because you're trying to piece together what is going on in this strange, alien world and (I suppose) what your place in it is.
Cons:
-Checkpoints are often pretty far away. Now, I made the soulsborne  comparison a few lines ago, but it's a little different here. There are fewer good shortcuts, and even then you can take damage or die taking them. Given that you can only take 5 hits in the early game before needing to find a way to heal, corpse runs are pretty stressful.
-This also makes exploration a bit hard. At least as far in the game that I got, there is no efficient way to travel other than the transport you get access to pretty deep in a zone, so if you wanted to explore or check out the areas you missed earlier, it's going to be a trek to get back to them, to the point that it almost feels like it's not worth it and that you should just come back at endgame.
-Finally, it's just not for me. I bought the game hoping that I would enjoy it, but it just didn't pan out that way. I would just play and advance the story, all the while waiting for it to start getting fun. Eventually, I just decided that if I'm not having fun 6 hours in, it's not going to be fun for a while if at all, so I just dropped it. The game itself is great, hence the "like" but I just don't like it.

I am going to be very honest here. I really thought it lost its touch after the first 6 or so minutes. I love everything corny and 80's about it to death, but once he traveled back in time, the pacing of the entire movie just became so slow and off-beat that so much of the humor and crazy, zany appeal the movie had became lost. My guess is that they promised a 30-minute short film, but had a script that wasn't long enough and just had to extend sections of it to take up more time. For example, the big Nazi fight scene at the end felt really drawn-out, unneccesarily long, and without much really happening. There's also the very long argument about mustaches which contributes nothing to the movie and isn't actually that funny, and there is a surprisingly long amount of time that characters just spend staring. At each other, at lazor raptors, or just staring. These are just examples.

I am conflicted about this game. On the one hand, there are so many aspects of it that make it extremely exciting and fun to play. There are certain improvements over previous games that make this a great step forward. On the other hand, however, there are so many random glitches, complications, and ridiculous lack of foresight in mission design that it becomes so terrible to play through.
To start with the improvements, let's just say that the game is, in many ways, much more enjoyable. The addition of naval combat, fun little mini-games (hunting is improved with the addition of fishing, table top games to kill time (even if the AI is ridiculously ill-equipped to compete against), etc), expansion of some weapons, and the addition of not requiring the purchase of random "treasure maps" to be able to find trunks and collectible items. These improvements do, in many ways, add a lot of replayability to the series which was lacking before. Of course, the setting itself is quite enjoyable and the characters are interesting enough to make the story worthwhile. In so many ways this game is fantastic, but unfortunately, there are so many complications and problems that make these improvements not as wonderful as they should be.
I am not sure if there are just problems with the PC version of this game or not, but there are countless random bugs and glitches that make this game lose some of its appeal. One of the first things I noticed was the distortion of enemies during assassinations. The majority of times that I would do hidden knife assassinations (or even with swords) by walking/running up to an enemy, the enemy would randomly turn into a graphical version of the old Stretch Armstrong toys: their body and limbs would randomly warp way out of proportion in a goofy looking ragdoll animation, as if each limb had it's own rule of physics it was adhering to whilst still keeping the body in tact.
There are other random graphical glitches (such as freezing facial features: during one play through Edward's lips were stuck wide open like a snarl, and his face looked furious. It was frozen like this through every cut scene and even in-game play until I restarted the game) that are annoying. Yet aside from the graphical glitches there are various gameplay glitches: not being able to climb up the rest of a wall until you move over 1 inch because it acts as if the way is being blocked, even when you're just trying to climb up the top part of a cliff or house. Glitches during fighting where you randomly can't block or you randomly attack a character that you obviously weren't aiming for, often times ruining your whole chain attack. Of course these are annoying and unfortunately a lot more present than I was expecting them to be, especially this long after the games release.
Gameplay mechanics are also annoying at times. AC has had a long history, at least for me, of having frustrating parkour mechanics. I can't recall how many times in previous games where I died because Ezio (or in this case, Edward) would randomly launch off from the top of a huge cathedral because it registered my controls as a means of saying "you know that ledge right off to the right of me? Yeah, let's just jump under that for no reason and fall to our demise". Or of course, randomly climbing up things when you are just trying to run around them. Or not being able to climb up things because you haven't aimed at it in the exact perfect position that the game expects you to. When the freerunning mechanics work, they can be fluid and wonderful, but sadly they do not always work.
Fighting mechanics are also annoying. I feel like the chain kills in this game are way longer and drawn out than any previous game. By the time you do one or two chain kills, you end up taking so long in the execution that your chain is broken by those around you because they got tired of waiting for their turn. I am surprised that I have managed to get longer chains in this game at all, because the process is so long and drawn out that I often times can barely kill 2 guys in a row before any interruption. Of course, the further in the game you get you start fighting more and more of the ever-annoying characters that can't be out-right attacked without some sort of disruption of their defence. Meaning the further in the game you get, the even harder it becomes to chain attack. Add to this the aforementioned random attacking pattern of Edward and you get a blur of confusion and frustration.
Aside from that though, I have found the missions to be completely annoying. The first 3 hours of missions are basically "follow this person. Follow this boat. Make sure you don't get caught, but here's 5000 people to follow right behind and on the side of your target to make sure it's 'interesting'. Also, let's make the follow time unbareable so that you are just hoping you don't get caught right before the end in order to have to endure it all over again." Even the missions that aren't "follow" missions are ridiculous. Currently I stuck on a "stealth" mission where you can't get caught. But the way they set up the level and the massive amount of enemies they have strewn throughout the level make it ridiculously difficult. By the time I almost make it to the next checkpoint, I reach a terrible level design where the slightest mistake causes me to get caught again, leaving me to redo the whole ridiculous "stealth" all over again. Of course this is made further frustrating by being unable to "kill" the enemies, and not having yet recieved any help from non-lethal ranged weapons. You literally have to try and sneak past a million assassins with only being able to do close-range non-lethal take downs, even when lots of the enemies in your visual range are at a distance. It is beyond frustrating and a testament to where the mission set-up is so boring that they are trying to make it "interesting" by adding a level of challenge to it. Unfortunately the challenge isn't in the mission, but in the lack of gameplay mechanics and tools to make it accessible.
There are a number of other aspects of the game that are frustrating and I feel could have been much more well polished. Which is unfortunate, because the game in many aspects is absolutely amazing. When I'm sticking to doing side missions and just having fun with naval warfare and improving my ship, I am having a wonderful time. But as soon as I start working on missions and dealing with frustrating and boring level designs, I have to take a break. Add to that the random weird glitches and lack of control and this game is unfortunately, one that I can barely recommend.
It deserves to be recommended, and I do recommend it for people to try it out and experience some of the awesome aspects that this game has. But, if I were to try and recommend it based on its overall performance and gameplay, I would have to say look elsewhere. If glitches were fixed and gameplay was more accessible, this game would easily be the most amazing in the series. Unfortunately technical issues and unimaginative missions make this game only interesting in the areas that are supposed to be added enjoyability, and not the full source of enjoyment.

This is not a good game.  I was truly shocked after hearing so many positive reviews about how this is an exhilerating shooter.  It's not.  Not even close.
In short, Shadow Warrior is A ONE TRICK PONY.
Gameplay consists of running into large arena areas, or occasionally streets or tunnels that restrict your movement a bit more, and then waves of THE SAME breeds of demons materialize from thin air or the walls to chase after you or shoot slow-moving projectiles at you.  The player generally has to run backwards in circles to avoid enemies while picking them off one at a time.  This is fun for about the first 1-2 hours, mostly in part to the outstanding sword mechanics.  But it quickly becomes apparent there is very little variety.  The game can't be exhilerating when its just so ♥♥♥♥ing predictable when and how every fight is going to take place.  The game needed more enemy types that attack you in different ways and more interesting environments that force you to adapt your tactics in every fight.  It needed more surprises to force you to think on your feet!  Not just portals opening and melee demons pouring through in hordes.  That's how you make an exhilerating FPS.  Oh, and the level design?  I've heard praise for how solid it is.  No, it's pretty linear.  Occasionally you have a choice between going left or going right but there's no element of exploration.  Secrets have very little value and barely qualify as secrets at all because they can usually be detected very easily since they are rarely off the path.  And again, I'll say it once more, very little difference in each fighting area.  A large arena for you to run circles or backwards in as you gradually wear the horde down.  So mindnumbingly repetitive.  You might think 'oh, an old school 100/100 health system, thats cool', no, because that's rendered completely meaningless because you can regenerate a minimum of 65% of your health AT ANY TIME.  MORE if you upgrade that skill!  This whole game is a DECEPTION.  It's not a "classic" FPS, its not even a GOOD FPS.
The postives of the game are swordplay, gunplay, graphics, and humor.  The swordplay is easily the best part of the game.  You can do special moves, weave in and out of danger, and make really satisfying kills.  The guns are also fun, punchy, upgradable, and interesting.  Unfortunately this is all futile because the player is bombarded with the same enemies in identical situations over and over.  Graphics are solid.  The humor is juvenille but the protagonist and his companion are witty.

Developed and published by indie developers Galactic Cafe, The Stanley Parable is a HD remake of the original Stanley Parable, published as a mod for Half Life 2 in 2011. The game could be described as a "walking simulator," but where many "walking simulator" genre games fail and end up trying to be more than they really are, The Stanley Parable knows its limits, its intentions and what players expect of it, both subverting and playing with the tropes associated with games of its genre. I highly recommend downloading the free demo, which gives a small sneak peak into what to expect from what is/isn't the game known as The Stanley Parable.
Describing what The Stanley Parable is about would risk ruining the impact the game has for the player. The Stanley Parable is a game that must be played and experienced firsthand to have the impact that it has. It takes the players expectations of what to expect in a game and subverts them, challenging and them.
The Stanley Parable has a story, but at the same time doesn't have a story. You play as Stanley, but you won't play as Stanley. Stanley's job as employee 427 is to press buttons on a computer. One day, his computer goes blank. Not knowing what to do, Stanley starts to explore his office building, where all of his co-workers have suddenly vanished. This happens in the game, but also doesn't happen in the game. There are no true answers in The Stanley Parable.
The player has many choices to make throughout The Stanley Parable, yet there are no choices to make. The game has multiple endings, but there is no ending. Any other game trying to tackle the subject/s The Stanley Parable does would come off as pretentious, but The Stanley Parable is anything but. It is very aware of what it is and does what it does extremely well, in no small part to the excellent narrator, voiced by Kevan Brighting, of whom without the game couldn't possibly stand without his impeccable voice acting.
Recommending The Stanley Parable as a purchase is a tough thing. It is certainly not a game for everyone, and describing it further would ruin the entire experience. Anything but a blind playthrough would not have the impact it should have. It is a somewhat short experience, but then again, is as long as you want it to be. Simply put, it is an experience that must be played.

UPDATE: It's now out of Early Access and F2P. The update is "It's still amazing and unique and the best MOBA that's not a MOBA." I appreciate the intense skill-based combat even more now; there's simply no alternative for me. I can not go back to actual MOBAs with all the RNG and endless memorization of 100 different heroes and 500 different item builds. Battlerite isn't really a MOBA, but if it was, it would be the least frustrating, most skill based, and best solo-queue MOBA. But it's not a MOBA; it's something better*. (*Unless you really like MOBAs, in which case, never mind.)
Original Early Access review below:
______________
It feels like a mixture of a MOBA, the best of WOW pvp, a dual-stick shooter, and a pinch of fighting game.. and it's awesome. It's familiar, but there's nothing quite like it.
It looks like a MOBA at first glance, but it's only a MOBA if you take the acronym literally. It is a "Multiplayer Online Battle Arena", with emphasis on "arena". Your team fights to the death, with no respawning, and the best out of 5 rounds wins. Unlike MOBAs, there are no towers, no creeps, no leveling up, no "feeding" or "farming", no wards or couriers, and no list of a thousand items and "builds" to memorize.
Basically it looks like a MOBA on the surface, but it's missing literally all of that annoying "MOBA" stuff.
I've played several MOBAs (LOL, DOTA 2, and even HOTS), but as much as I enjoyed the combat mechanics and teamfights, these games can also be extremely frustrating and anti-fun. But for me, Battlerite is the meat without the fat:
In it's current state, the gameplay is extremely polished and one of the most intense video game experiences I've had. If I had to summarize this game with one word, it would be "intense". You're always a few hits from victory or defeat. It's just one long teamfight until the next round, or until you're left to 1v1 the last enemy while your fallen comrade(s) watch on the edge of their seat(s). It's also extremely watchable (go watch on Twitch if you're curious), and easy to see what's going on.
If you're looking for a negative, it's basically
. The menus, out-of-game progression, "skins" (just recolors basically), etc, all look like they were just thrown together to make the game functional for early-access. They really need to work on this stuff if they want the wide audience that this game deserves.
Battlerite is made to be a competitive game with an E-sports scene, and I would love to see it be able to compete with the "heavy hitters" out there. They don't have the money of Blizzard or Riot, but they have a great game.. good enough for a few thousand of the players to take the time to write a review very much like this one, because that's the most that we can do.

A must buy for metroidvania fans.
The graphics and artwork are superb, managing to make a rotting world of bugs both cute and endearing.  There is a deliberate melancholy tone to the graphics and music, which oddly enough I find more relaxing than depressing.  The style simultaneously reminds me of Tim Burton and Edmund McMillen, an excellent blend that makes you fall in love with the world.
The sound effects are absolutely stellar, not just completing the game but drastically improving it.  From the murmuring gibberish of the characters, to the delightful *thud* when falling from great heights, to the sounds of clutter being destroyed and hitting the ground as you attack it, everything in this game sounds superb.  I am really impressed by the sound work.
The controls are very tight, and the game feels very responsive.  All animations are quick, you never feel like the controls or game design is holding you back.  You can attack in four directions by holding the dpad, including while you are in the air.  Attacking pushes you and the enemy back slightly, unless the enemy is enormous.  This means you can do some ducktales-esque attacks where you bounce yourself off an enemy by attacking downward while midair.  I love that, it was fun when I was a kid and it is still fun now.
The game does not do everything perfectly, however.  In a bizarre choice you must use one of your character customization slots (charms, in this game) to actually see yourself on a map.  If you want your character to be at full strength, you need to manually pore over the maps to figure out where you are - and they are not detailed enough to make this easy.  Save points (benches) can be far apart, and far from where you died when you just want to get back into the action.  In an effort to increase the punishment of death, you lose all your currency and part of your maximum mana (soul vessels).  You can retrieve it by reaching where you died and defeating your shade (who seems like a complete pushover).  My understanding is that if you do not reach and defeat your shade before dying again, you permanantly lose all your currency, and will not regain your max mana until you defeat your new shade.
I take issue with all of these things for the same reason - they are deliberate attempts to waste the players time.  Wasting a players time is a recent and absurd trend among games that want to be "difficult."  A difficult boss doesn't become less difficult if you can reattempt him right after dying.  Losing your items from dying does not make the game more difficult, it just makes it more grindy.  This old "corpse-run" concept is from games like Everquest and Diablo, where it is intended to get players working together.  In single player games it is just bad game design.
Fortunately, though, those few problems do not take away from the brilliant whole.  This game is excellent, a load of fun, and something you need to play if you are looking for a Metroidvania.  The only other metroidvania near this level of quality on PC is Ori and the Blind Forest.  Though I would say Hollow Knight is not quite as good as Ori, Hollow Knight has far better combat.  Hollow Knight is also cheaper while being much longer.  If you like exploring-focused metroidvanias, pick up Ori first.  If you like combat-focused metroidvanias, pick up Hollow Knight first.  If you like metroidvanias at all, though, you owe it to yourself to play both of them.

A strong contender for best Metroid game of the decade, right up there with Axiom Verge and AM2R.
Hollow Knight takes the classic Metroidvania formula of "get item, open pathway" and puts it on steroids. After the first few hours of the game, the familiar linearity of its predecessors (including Super Metroid) is thrown out in favor of having multiple possible objectives for players to pursue in any order. It's precisely this lack of rigidity that makes Hollow Knight so fun to play through. You'll come across areas where you need new abilities to unlock something, but between the time you find that item and return you may end up on the other side of the map fighting multiple bosses and exploring totally different areas, and the whole process feels like an organic exploration of the game world.
This game also borrows from Dark Souls in a way that makes exploration feel appropriately risky and challenging: dying creates a Shade which you must return to and kill in order to retrieve your lost money and regain your full magic meter.
Pros:
1. Tight Combat
2. Great atmospheric music
3. Bosses are well designed, challenging, and many are optional or secret.
4. Almost every progression item affects movement or combat in a fundamental way (wings, dash, projectile, etc.)
5. Multiple Endings
6. HAND DRAWN GAME HOLY CRAP
7. First Playthrough is a meaty campaign (took me 17.5 hours and I had about 70% completeion before I actually unlocked the final boss of the simplest ending).

Cons:
1. Checkpointing and Fast Travel Points are too spread out for the map size (may be fixed in a free content update coming in July)
2. You probably haven't bought this game yet if you're still reading this.
