"The Stanley Parable" is one of the most unique, thought-provoking and humorous titles that has ever graced gaming with it's presence. Every single, minute detail in the presentation of this experience speaks volumes to how much it has to offer. At a first glance it seems like a short walking-simulator, but deep within itself it manages to entertain, provoke and teach many things, if one is willing to invest time and attention in it.
Those are the three most key words I'd use to describe this masterpiece. It's entertaining, as it contains many, many interpretations of "the story" (or lack there of) and, from a purely gamer standpoint, it's amusing to simply explore the small, but rich world of Stanley.
Provoking it indeed is, as with almost every single varriation of it's formula, "The Stanley Parable" has something to say. A existencial comment on many, many subjects, that manage to be light-spirited through clever written humor. If one is willing to look at what Stanley and his Office represent, the adventures they go on together and what the content of those adventures mean as a symbol, one can spend much time pondering the ideas behind everything. And everything is absolutely, brilliantly polished.
Last, but certainly not least: the game teaches. The game teaches about many things, if one is willing to hear it. It's a astounding lesson in game design, with significant notes on how a simple gameplay mechanic can be used in multiple, different ways to achieve interest and evade monotony. But above and beyond this, "The Stanley Parable" teaches a lot about risk taking and consequence. That every action has a reasult, that the concepts of "wrong" and "right" are merely concepts and that ultimately, though a obvious path may seem painted, one can always stray from it, whenever he has the strenght to face the trial of his actions later on.
The end is never the end in this marvelous gem, but the true "ending" starts with the "Quit" button. And that's the most important lesson that is taught. And I mean this in the best possible way.
If you play it and you get it, you will see what I mean.
I've firmly recommend The Stanley Parable. It's something everyone - and I do mean everyone - needs to see.
Notice I've not used the term "game" at all in this review. This is intentional, as "The Stanley Parable" aspires and achieves being something much more special and grand.

At first glance many are going to compare this to popular MOBAs but with a lack of "lane phase" and item diversity / build diversity. Numerically speaking, this is easily the most sparce game of it's type I have played - And that's a good thing.
Honestly when there are only 1-2 valid build paths or skill orders in your MOBA is there really any value in the 300 items, 20 talents, and rune pages? I'd say not. It's just baggage that you're obligated to carry around with you from game to game.
Battlerite's non-cosmetic customization comes down to perks which you can select one of three of per round. Each rounds choices are exclusive and unique to each champion. One might buff healing off of your auto attacks. One might add a knockback to your disengage. Simple tweaks to fit your playstyle and opposition.  These choises are what I find interesting. Choices that can be changed on a per-match basis reactively based on how your opponenets are playing.
Playing a healer and getting focused? Pickup some more disengage.
Not getting focused? Lower some healing CDs or enhance a damaging skill.
Skip the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t memorization of what build is best this week and get down to what's actually fun.
The meat of this game feels incredibly solid. Not once have I felt as if lag was the culprit of a death or missed skillshot.
Did I mention /everything/ is a skillshot?  When there are no auto-attacks or 20k gold advantages everything comes down to raw skill in the moment. There are still leavers/ragers - but it's amazing how little they sting when you can instantly forefit and be back in another match in 30 seconds.
This is all the best parts of the MOBA genre condesnsed down into bite-seized sessions full of outplay and skill.

What can I say about Hollow Knight? Hollow Knight is a dark and non-linear 2D platformer with an amazing soundtrack, intuitive controls, and lots of content to play through. As far as Indie games are concerned, this game has the feel of a game produced by a AAA studio and all the right elements to make it fun for hours and hours on end.
What I like about this game:
- Soundtrack is great at setting the mood
- Flows extremely well with default controller inputs
- Puzzles are area-specific, and aren't too difficult to solve
- Completion takes multiple passes through areas after obtaining various items and abilities
What I dislike about the game:
- Starting out, recovery from healing is a bit slow (improves with charms later on)
- Some bosses are far more difficult than others
- Sometimes finding a rest bench near a boss doesn't happen and the walk of shame can get frustrating
Overall, I'm enjoying the hell out of Hollow Knight, and would recommend this to anyone that enjoys single-player 2D platformers. Also, as the developers suggest on the opening screens of the game, a controller is going to make your life a whole lot easier since the default mapping is truly intuitive.

+ A good mix of simple Combat with smooth Platforming.
One does not make you want to stop doing the another. Which is usually an issue with Metroidvania games because you have to do both of them.
+ Artstyle and Lore complements the Challenge and Exploration of the gameplay.
Basically the dark atmosphere fits the gameplay. You venture into the unknown, looking for new challenges while discovering good looking places.
+ Navigation is fun.
It is easy to use the map, the rooms are shaped very nicely so it is usually not difficult to remember which room is which one.
+ The Challenge is there.
But simply comparing the gameplay to Dark Souls just because it is hard is not right. Dark Souls actively makes you try to find a weakness in the enemies movement, you can't just go in. This game makes you depend on your motor skills and the Bosses don't neccessarily have an "opening". You can win a fight for fighting well as the game does not punish you as much when you make a mistake. You don't fall off a cliff and die instantly.
o The Dark Souls feel
The game is made to feel like Dark Souls. It is dark, challenging, has NPC's that give lore away. Sure. It is obvious so it is not even something to mention. But nobody actually bothers to tell what is different about it. It is more lighthearted in the way it looks and plays. Very cartoonish, NPCs are not all downers and they are mostly very cute. Gameplay-wise it feels way faster as you're not afraid of punishment. You actually explore places zipping around instead of looking for an ambush all day crawling through the kingdom.
o There is some lore there. But it feels like it "tries" to be a thing like Souls.
There is the corrupting Infection much like the Abyss in Dark Souls. Souls are a source of power for some reason. You can interact with Dreams. It is nice that these concepts are there, they are cool, they bring depth to the world, but there is little explanation to why they are there. Unlike how Dark and Abyss are opposed to the Fire in Souls, Hollow Knight throws more characters and concepts, quotes/flashbacks from the past. It makes it harder to keep track of which are related. Why are you Hollow? Why do you fill yourself with soul and dreams? Why is there concepts of Light and Dark in this game? What is "The Infection" ? It feels like they are only there to be an allegory and not that much related to the game. The idea is not refined enough. The light and dark could still be there without making it too up in the nose. The whole "pale being" thing is overly played while there is some meat in the dreams and soul part left untouched.
But it is a game about some fallen bug kingdom where different kinds of bugs are united. They have some silly language. It tries to be fun and it succeeds. It is really nice those weird concepts are there in the first place. So there is not much reason to complain about what is there, it is more about there is not enough of it.
- The game has a true ending.
To get to that you should work a little more which kinda felt like a "grind" even though it is technically is not.
It repeats some bosses in a "harder" mode, it makes you go through a platforming gauntlet. It is really not that much of an issue, but it surely slows the pace of the game down by removing the "exploration" aspect.
- The economy of the game is kinda weird.
If you die twice in a row without recieving your shade (similar to Souls again) you lose all your money. But there is not much to spend your money on anyway. It is sort of an empty threat and not a big deal unlike the game makes it seems to be.
- Backtracking is sometimes a hassle.
Some of the Stag Stations (simply fast travel points) are not useful enough. Although it is fun to move around, sometimes walking to that one place you wanted to check out seems like some busywork when you already know there is not much interest on your way.

I picked Dungeon Defenders up during the holiday sale and had hoped it would be another decent tower defense game.  Ever since the Starcraft & Warcraft III (Cube Defense) days these kinds of titles have been able to deliver a lot of depth and strategy for relatively simple mechanics. Sadly, Dungeon Defenders failed in most of those aspects and felt a lot more like a cheap iPad knockoff of a good game.  The game has an arbitrary item drop system that constantly requires futzing with upgrades and switching between weapons - the RPGness of this title was disappointing to say the least. No tower mazing. Uninteresting weapons. Repetitive gameplay. Worst of all is the autoaim feature, which redirects shots in completely unanticipated ways - no option or mod exists to disable (WHY?). The game runs on the Unreal Engine 3, and it does look nice, so there's that. Play Sanctum 2 for a much better executed TD in a similar theme. If you want something hardcore just skip to Defense Grid for a proper TD. 4/10 for a very mediocre tower defense title.

Team Cherry’s Kickstarter project Hollow Knight is by far the best game I played in recent years. It takes the core elements the Dark Souls games are loved for, like the reduced yet very atmospheric world building or the challenging but rewarding approach on gameplay, and combines it with a simplistic modern take on the castlevania genre.
Like most Castelvania style games Hollow Knight can feel a little overwhelming and demotivating at the beginning but after you get a sense of the world and your objectives, it's a blast to explore. Finding health and stamina upgrades as well as charms and notches (skill tree system) feels important because the game is actually challenging. The charms system is similar to rings in Dark Souls whereas every charm has unique passive effects and the notches determine the amount of charms you can wear. The effects range from improving the attack speed to completely changing some skills which makes experimenting with different charms depending on the situation / encounter fun. I just wish there were some more reliable combinations during endgame.
Controls are tight and spot on, they allow very fast and precise gameplay. casting different spells instantly, quickly dodging attacks using walljumps... all of that is possible with ease. Sadly the nail arts (special melee attacks) feal a little out of place because they need to be charged for a short moment which you won't have in most fights.
The art and sound is phenomenal, from the extremely well crafted world, characters and their animations everything feels like it was made with an incredible sense for detail and a very focused artistic vision. While the world is dark and gloomy, the game knows that it is about little cute looking bugs which is perfectly reflected in animation, dialog and sound design without destroying the depressing mood. These two contrary elements are hold together through the epic soundtrack by Christopher Larkin.
Which brings me to the final point I want to tackle. Yes the game is announced for Nintendo’s Switch and it looks like a perfect fit for that, but please don’t wait for it. The first playthrough gains so much from beeing played with headphones and a bigger screen. Listening to the incredible soundtrack setting the mood while exploring the depressing depths of Hollownest, creates a fealing you won’t get while waiting on a station for your bus to arrive. Please just buy it already and get up to 50 hours of playtime for a bargain (especially during steam sale).

***IMPORTANT NOTE: Most if not all negative reviews are from salty players who think the game is unbalanced. However, it really is actually fantastically balanced, and to prove it you need look no further than the highest ranked players, who all play an extremely wide variety of characters. In any ranked, any composition, and every hero, is viable. It's literally 100% skill reliant***
I've been playing this game since early access. Long story short, I love it. I used to be really into Overwatch and League of Legends, both of which are FANTASTIC games, but are also ridiculously team reliant and insanely tilting at times. Of course that is going to some degree be true of any online game one plays.
But that being said the short, fast paced bite sized format that is Battlerite is much more palatable. Bad teammates mean the game is over pretty quick and you can move on in about five minutes or less. But even good, intense matches don't play out anymore than 10-15 tops. So far the game is very balanced, every champion feels very fun to play and viable. The game HEAVILY rewards single champion mastery because you always que as the champion YOU want to play. There is both ranked and casual mode, as well as a practice arena where you can try out any champion as well as different builds, so it's not that hard at all to spend hours upon hours practicing and refinning your mastery of a champion's kit.
The best part though is there exists no semblence of pay 2 win, all purchases are cosmetic or to unlock new playable characters. Battlerites, which are champion specific perks that unlock buffs or modify abilities are available equally to all players to mix and match at will. Plus the devs have done a fantastic job putting out new cosmetics and starting awesome events, so yeah I might've dropped a little money already.
TL;DR Battlerite is a fun, fast paced and VERY well executed arena fighter game with lots of solo carry potential and heavily rewarding individual mastery.

This game is touted for it's viceral combat and gameplay, and it has that, in spades.
Combat is really enjoyable, and there is an RPG element to it, as you progress through the game, you can choose what abilities / weapons to unlock as you go, and you get rewarded for killing many enemies in a variety of ways... burning, expoding, beheading, killing while stunned, Killing while airborn, and nailing to the wall to name a few. These aspects are really well done, as there are a few things that require combos, and unlocking them gradually really gives you a chance to get used to each ability, and it's key press combo... rather than being swamped with too much all at once, it gives you new abilities and weapons in little bits. This is the genius of this game, in that it keeps the variety by giving you new ways to evicerate, just as the combat would otherwise become tedious, a new enemy, and a new way to rip their limbs asunder.
These are some of the things that the game are known for, but clearly those reviewers never played this game through, as it's real drawcard, is the storyline. Yes, in a game where the action stops for nothing, they nailed the killing and dismemberment, sure... but this game actually has a great story.
Not really a spoiler, more of a "this is what's going on so that you understand how the story is being revealed to you" but I'll spoiler tag if for you anyway;
[/spoiler] When you kill a whisperer, (which is created from an ancients' memories) you gain the memories that were used to created it, that's why you get a cut scene when you kill it. Also, for some reason, you do kill the last whisperer, but it never shows is, although to do get to see the story it reveals.[/spoiler]
The story is original, emotional, powerfully told, and truely draws you into the game, leaving you wanting to continue on to find out what happens next. Make sure you get to the end, as it's definatley worth it, then remember to come back here and comment.

Also, they better contextualize the "chase this collectable before it blows away" stuff by actually giving you a reason to want to grab it
Also, finding treasure maps that you could follow to find buried treasure was a fun thematic addition!
Cons:
Uplay
Menus can be a little overwhelming to navigate through
Abstergo/Animus stuff is dumb, distracting, and breaks the feel and flow of the game as a whole
Uplay
Opening chests and looting bodies is still finicky and slow
Combat is simplistic and way too easy
Uplay
Also, and this is my main gripe with the game, the free-running engine is starting to show it's age, and hasn't had any real improvements from previous games
Removing the "A" button from free-running and make it so you only have to hold RT to climb stuff was a dumb idea, and you'll be grabbing onto things and climbing atop small ledges without meaning to when you're just trying to run normally. Previous games had it to where if you held RT, you'd run, but you wouldn't actually grab onto stuff unless you held "A" with RT. It was intuitive and it made sense. They needlessly sreamlined it, and it's a little to sticky.

The Stanely Parable is my favorite game of all time. It is a game about choices. The themes in it are thought provoking. It indirectly questions wether or not we really have choices or if it is all just a predetermined path, this question looks like it is about the game at first, but when you explore it further you realize that it is really asking this about life. The story line conveys this theme perfectly. The game is from the perspective of a man named Stanley. While at work one day Stanley realizes that he is alone. Stanley goes on a adventure to find an answer. Everything he does is dictated by the narrator, a voice in his head. The narration is wonderful and is the cherry on top of this game. As Stanley and the Narrator go on their adventures they explore different aspects of both of the characters personalities.  There are many different endings to this game. As you wander to each ending Stanley has apiphanies as more and more is revealed by the narrator. When you reach an ending the game starts over and everyhting returns to as it started because the end is never the end. Each playthrough takes about ten mins depending on what ending you get. This game has a lot of easter eggs hidden within each ending which makes the game repayable to some extent. I have put many hours in the game, which is probably far more than needed, but I would say that there are still parts of the game I haven't discovered. I will still be putting more hours in this game, which is good, but it is probably mostly due to my extreme liking of the game. To tell you much more would be to spoil the game. I warn you, do not read to much into this game before playing it, it really is best to know little to nothing when starting this game, so wait to read about it until after you have played for a little while. Go right now, buy the game, I know you will not regret it. This game no doubt is worth it.

My GOTY for 2017, above anything else. Always really loved Metroidvanias, but there aren't great ones that often. This is one of those great ones.
Really expansive world with branching paths, some of which you can skip entirely, but personally, I wanted to scour every last inch.
The controls feel good on mouse & keyboard, further aided by having complete key remapping as desired. Never felt like a bad movement was the game's fault.
Paired with a fairly cool 'charm' system where you choose some upgrades you find to fit within a certain capacity. My favorite part of the charms is you can put in a charm that doesn't fit in the capacity but take double damage for it, a cool risk vs reward dynamic.
The bosses are pretty unique and have a lot of personality, some scary, some quite lovable.
All in all the world of Hollow Knight draws me and has me wanting more. Thankfully, DLC is planned for it! Not that it feels incomplete as is, not at all.
As for cons... uh, I guess the fact it's a Metroidvania, if you're not into that kind of thing?
The main path isn't too hard, but some of the optional paths may be reasonably hard for some, I've heard a lot of complaints about White Palace in particular, though personally I liked it. But it is of note that area is kind of like super meat boy, which may also not be everyone's thing. That said, it's an optional area just for true ending.
And I guess finally, the fact it has you roam, typically falls into Metroidvania category but still worth note: you can wander aimlessly at parts, so mileage may vary on how much you like exploring for exploring's sake.
It's one of a few games that I'll absolutely give a 10/10 unreservedly. Criminally cheap for quality too, even more so with sales. If you think you might like it, I recommend giving it a shot!

The Stanley Parable. A game where you decide between two options, again and again. That's the simple explanation.
In The Stanley Parable, you play as a man called Stanley, working as a button-pusher at a company. One day Stanley finds himself in his office, with only one thing different than all the other days; no one else has shown up. Stanley therefore begins to walk around in the company offices, guided by the narrator. You can either choose to follow the narrator's own story of Stanley, or deviate from what he tells Stanley to do, which leads to many funny situations and many different endings. I will not tell you concrete examples, as it will ruin the game for you. The rest you have to discover for yourself!

Battlerite is a multiplayer online game where you battle in an area.
It is not a MOBA similar to League of Legends, Dota 2, Smite, etc.
It is an arena fighter using different characters (Currently 15 as of 10/2/2016)
The game is easy to get in to with a low skill floor, but hard to master with a high skill cap.
The game is not Pay2Win, and the only thing you can use your credits you earn and chests you open is to get cosmetic items and poses for each of the characters which doesn't affect gameplay at all.
There are no runes or masteries like in league, but there are different talents you can put a point into as the game goes on.
Every round you can select 1 of 3 talents for your character.
I have currently bought the game (20 USD) and purchased 5 Golden Chests (Around 7.49 USD) and I have to say I have enjoyed the game so far.
If you love playing League of Legends, Dota 2, and especially Smite, I think you'd love this game too.
PROS:
Easy to get into
Great artwork
Fun characters (No static, boring kits)
Fun arena combat
Not Pay2Win
Practice where you can try out all the characters
CONS:
No Unranked and Ranked (Every game will affect your rating)
Costumes are lacking
Way too many Icons in chests

Overall Rating: 7/10
Shadow Warrior is a very good FPS, combining solid gunplay with great melee combat. The heavy melee focus sets it apart from similar games like Serious Sam or the Painkiller series, while you try to keep your distance from enemies in most shooters, here you will seek close contact much more often.
The levels are large and despite there being only one linear path to actually progress, there is always lots of secrets and pick-ups hidden in dark corners. Some might complain, that the lack of a mini-map or any kind of quest-marker makes it hard to know where to go sometimes, even when losing your way chances are high that you find at least something helpful or funny along the way.
Fun is something the game emphasizes a lot, the story is light, but the dialogs present range from cheeky to hilarious. There are three main settings, and the graphics are still great, especially the lighting is impressive throughout. Some bad textures and a couple of boring industrial areas in the second act dimish the overall good visual impression.
The only real downside to the game is the lack of enemy variety, since Shadow Warrior follows in Painkiller and Serious Sam’s footsteps of offering large scale battles and seemingly endless waves of enemies, there should be more enemy types to mix things up a bit better. As a result it is recommended to play this game not in long sessions but one or two levels a day. This way it keeps fresh and entertaining.
Pro:
- fantastic swordplay
- good variety of useful guns
- Full of pop-culture jokes
- solid upgrade system
- beautiful lighting and settings
Cons:
- not enough enemy variety
- some boring levels
- easy to get lost in the larger levels

This game is a must-have.
Hollownest is a joy to explore - all the areas are uniquely beautiful and there are hidden rewards everywhere. You can find money, badges (which give boosts that can significantly affect gameplay), powerups (that unlock new areas and give new moves in combat), NPCs, story fragments, and more!
The controls feel natural and have a perfect mix of precision and responsiveness. I used a controller to play this game, and recommend the same.
The combat is thrilling: It generally takes 2-4 hits to kill any enemy, and 4 hits to die yourself. You can heal yourself, if you can find an opening, but it takes charge gained by damaging enemies, and you are vulnerable while you heal. The enemies always give a warning just before they attack, so avoiding being hit is possible, if you know what to look for. If you die, your money falls where you died and can be recovered if you don't die again.
Each new enemy is interesting and unique - no two enemies have the same set of attacks. You won't find any reskins or pallet swaps here.
The story is a bit of an enigma: the history of Hollownest and yourself is revealed gradually and non-intrusively, in a way that often leaves you with more questions than answers.
Playtime is around 20hrs.
This game is definitely worth $10 (summer sale). Just this week the first (free) content pack was released, and the devs are planning a DLC that will add a completely new storyline.

After 700 hours, I guess I can give a review.  This is a fun game and well worth the Humble Bundle or other means to pick it up.

***IMPORTANT NOTE: Most if not all negative reviews are from salty players who think the game is unbalanced. However, it really is actually fantastically balanced, and to prove it you need look no further than the highest ranked players, who all play an extremely wide variety of characters. In any ranked, any composition, and every hero, is viable. It's literally 100% skill reliant***
I've been playing this game since early access. Long story short, I love it. I used to be really into Overwatch and League of Legends, both of which are FANTASTIC games, but are also ridiculously team reliant and insanely tilting at times. Of course that is going to some degree be true of any online game one plays.
But that being said the short, fast paced bite sized format that is Battlerite is much more palatable. Bad teammates mean the game is over pretty quick and you can move on in about five minutes or less. But even good, intense matches don't play out anymore than 10-15 tops. So far the game is very balanced, every champion feels very fun to play and viable. The game HEAVILY rewards single champion mastery because you always que as the champion YOU want to play. There is both ranked and casual mode, as well as a practice arena where you can try out any champion as well as different builds, so it's not that hard at all to spend hours upon hours practicing and refinning your mastery of a champion's kit.
The best part though is there exists no semblence of pay 2 win, all purchases are cosmetic or to unlock new playable characters. Battlerites, which are champion specific perks that unlock buffs or modify abilities are available equally to all players to mix and match at will. Plus the devs have done a fantastic job putting out new cosmetics and starting awesome events, so yeah I might've dropped a little money already.
TL;DR Battlerite is a fun, fast paced and VERY well executed arena fighter game with lots of solo carry potential and heavily rewarding individual mastery.
Exactly what this genre needs, easy to play, insanely chaotic. Worth.

ArmA 2: Operation Arrowhead is the standalone DLC (Downloadable Content) Pack for ArmA 2, A Military Simulator by Czech developer Bohemia Interactive. ArmA 2: OA is the only standalone DLC pack for ArmA 2. Multiple other DLC packs play part in Takistan, Including the BAF (British Armed Forces) DLC and PMC (Private Military Contractors) DLC.
The Map(s):
ArmA 2: OA is set in the fictional Middle-Eastern country of Takistan. Takistan has many towns, villages and cities to explore, with two airfields on either end of the map. The map of Zargabad, A Small desert city in the middle of nowhere, quite small compared to Chernarus or Takistan, but the city is hugh compared to Takistan's largest, Rasman. Zargabad also comes with an airfield and a few buildings here and there. the PMC and BAF DLCs use this map as well.
The Gameplay:
ArmA 2, as a military simulator has many aspects involved in succeeding. To me, and many others, the most important is Teamwork. You have to work as a team to get things done in this game, and I love that consept. It is very slow paced, very tactical, and aimed at people that don't like to get things done rambo-style. Movement is extremely fiddly with the inability to walk through clearly enterable spaces and breaking your legs on the oddest of places. The game is fairly old, however, coming in at a 2010 release, a year after the original ArmA 2.
Graphics/Voice Acting:
Graphics and Voice Acting are quite shameful, but the game is old and developed by a Czech developer making an english game, and the quality is tolerable.
The Multiplayer:
The ArmA Multiplayer is quite easily where the most fun is to be had. With excessive mods and gamemodes developed plus the original gamemodes implemented to play with your friends, i've spent 99% of my OA Experience on the Multiplayer. My most enjoyable moments on the multiplayer moments were on Takistan Life: Revolution servers. TLR, as it is abbreviated to, is a Roleplay Mission File for OA.
My Issue(s):
My only Issue with OA is the fact that when update 1.63 was released, it wiped out an extremely large fraction of all multiplayer servers. I took this as a sign of BI telling us to go to ArmA 3, which is quite rude. Luckily, servers are popping back up here and there, which is a very good sign.
Summary:
Overall, All ArmA games are amazing in my opinion, but ArmA 2: OA gets the cake. Congratulations to Bohemia Interactive for making such an enjoyable, but serious game and I hope this review was found helpful.

Overall Rating: 7/10
Shadow Warrior is a very good FPS, combining solid gunplay with great melee combat. The heavy melee focus sets it apart from similar games like Serious Sam or the Painkiller series, while you try to keep your distance from enemies in most shooters, here you will seek close contact much more often.
The levels are large and despite there being only one linear path to actually progress, there is always lots of secrets and pick-ups hidden in dark corners. Some might complain, that the lack of a mini-map or any kind of quest-marker makes it hard to know where to go sometimes, even when losing your way chances are high that you find at least something helpful or funny along the way.
Fun is something the game emphasizes a lot, the story is light, but the dialogs present range from cheeky to hilarious. There are three main settings, and the graphics are still great, especially the lighting is impressive throughout. Some bad textures and a couple of boring industrial areas in the second act dimish the overall good visual impression.
The only real downside to the game is the lack of enemy variety, since Shadow Warrior follows in Painkiller and Serious Sam’s footsteps of offering large scale battles and seemingly endless waves of enemies, there should be more enemy types to mix things up a bit better. As a result it is recommended to play this game not in long sessions but one or two levels a day. This way it keeps fresh and entertaining.
Pro:
- fantastic swordplay
- good variety of useful guns
- Full of pop-culture jokes
- solid upgrade system
- beautiful lighting and settings
Cons:
- not enough enemy variety
- some boring levels
- easy to get lost in the larger levels

This is the reason I created my group, Dungeon Defenders Hardcore, for players that care about having fun with the game, not just reaching level 100 ASAP. What then? You know?

Something like a mix of WOW Arena and late game MOBA teamfights.
At first glance many are going to compare this to popular MOBAs but with a lack of "lane phase" and item diversity / build diversity. Numerically speaking, this is easily the most sparce game of it's type I have played - And that's a good thing.
Honestly when there are only 1-2 valid build paths or skill orders in your MOBA is there really any value in the 300 items, 20 talents, and rune pages? I'd say not. It's just baggage that you're obligated to carry around with you from game to game.
Battlerite's non-cosmetic customization comes down to perks which you can select one of three of per round. Each rounds choices are exclusive and unique to each champion. One might buff healing off of your auto attacks. One might add a knockback to your disengage. Simple tweaks to fit your playstyle and opposition.  These choises are what I find interesting. Choices that can be changed on a per-match basis reactively based on how your opponenets are playing.
Playing a healer and getting focused? Pickup some more disengage.
Not getting focused? Lower some healing CDs or enhance a damaging skill.
Skip the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t memorization of what build is best this week and get down to what's actually fun.
The meat of this game feels incredibly solid. Not once have I felt as if lag was the culprit of a death or missed skillshot.
Did I mention /everything/ is a skillshot?  When there are no auto-attacks or 20k gold advantages everything comes down to raw skill in the moment. There are still leavers/ragers - but it's amazing how little they sting when you can instantly forefit and be back in another match in 30 seconds.
This is all the best parts of the MOBA genre condesnsed down into bite-seized sessions full of outplay and skill.

This was amazingly fun with a full group of 4 people when I first started it.  Very fun way to handle the tower defense genre.  There is your standard mage with towers, but also interesting ideas like monk with damage/debuff bubbles, archer using traps for support type defense, and a tanky type knight using walls and ballista.  You can increase either your obstacles' effectiveness, your actual hero effectiveness, or a mix of the two.
It got too difficult to keep up with much of the harder content without getting some amazing gear, which was only obtainable very briefly via some hardcore exploitation.  By the time we got to that point in the content, there was no legit way to get the gear yourself without trading for exorbitant prices.  Was fun while it lasted, and definitely worth some time just to get through the original/non-DLC part of the game to level up and try it out.  Even more so if you've got a group of buddies.
Have not played in a long time so some of the negative aspects may already be addressed by now, but at this point I'm not likely to return.

The Stanley Parable is good fun if you enjoyed the eerie-funny atmosphere of Portal 1 and 2, which is probably one of this game's biggest influences. By coupling you with a cheery narrator who directs you where to go, while you often have a choice of whether to listen to him or not, the experience feels more like an experiment you're part of than a game. There's a lot of good laughs and a slight bit of heavy-handedness as the game seems to try and tell you that the only way to win it is to not play it.
The game is essentially a constantly looping experience where small or big details may change on their own or because of your choices. The unfortunate thing is that after a while, you get bored of trying and failing to elicit new responses, and the game experience just kind of peters out. That also means there's not really any replayability and there's about an hour and a half of enjoyment there.. Still, it's fun while it lasts.

I find that each time I try and write a review about this game, I just can't. I want to somehow express my love for this game so that you, the reader can understand what I'm trying to convey. Let me start off with the first thing you'll see, the price.
For 15$ this game has more content than most 40$ games, it's a steal ffs. But another thing you'll see above the price is the word Metroidvania, which means there WILL be backtracking. So is that bad? Well, no because if that's a con then so is having to explore the entire sprawling map (you don't actually have to explore all of it) that the developers have hand-freaking-drawn. The fact that it's hand drawn is not a selling point, but instead a way for the player to understand the love and time Team Cherry (the developers) put into this game. I would make a comparison to Dark Souls around here, but this game goes above and beyond what Dark Souls came out to be, for me at least. The soundtrack is proof that music sets the tone for the fights, areas, as well as emotions of the player. The combination of music, atmosphere and gameplay is unbelivably well put together, so much so that it's a shame that some people gave this game below an 8/10.
This game rewards the quick, the clever, and the inqusitive. The games not completely impossible if you're not good at the combat, but an aspect of playing games is to improve in them so that will come with time, if needed. The customization of abillity's is another way to change the outcome of fights and the system is done pretty well. The amount of secrets in this game is plenty, but justified if the player can notice the inconsistency of the terrain. And each area is filled with sprawling and converging paths with tons of enjoyable npc's.
The game is beautiful and if I haven't sold you on it, sorry it's my fault. But you should still buy this game.

I'd recommend Battlerite if you're looking for a pure PVP Moba-style arena game. Games are short and to the point. You don't have to worry about spending 45-60 minutes with an extremely toxic team. Arenas are 2v2 and 3v3, so it makes for smaller, more personal games.

True arena style gameplay
Fast paced
Games are first to 3, not too short but not too long
MOBA-like combat without the traditional MOBA characteristics
No NPCs to interfere (minions, bosses, etc.)
All characters unlocked for founders
All items are cosmetic
No "in game" items, just skill power-ups (battlerites)
Things I don't like:
Forced ranked play
Combined 2v2 and 3v3 MMR (I'd rather these be separate)
Total win rates are AI wins + pvp wins combined (I'd rather these be separate)
Cannot sort in character selection screen (this may come later)
Maps are pretty much the same, could use some variation

***IMPORTANT NOTE: Most if not all negative reviews are from salty players who think the game is unbalanced. However, it really is actually fantastically balanced, and to prove it you need look no further than the highest ranked players, who all play an extremely wide variety of characters. In any ranked, any composition, and every hero, is viable. It's literally 100% skill reliant***
I've been playing this game since early access. Long story short, I love it. I used to be really into Overwatch and League of Legends, both of which are FANTASTIC games, but are also ridiculously team reliant and insanely tilting at times. Of course that is going to some degree be true of any online game one plays.
But that being said the short, fast paced bite sized format that is Battlerite is much more palatable. Bad teammates mean the game is over pretty quick and you can move on in about five minutes or less. But even good, intense matches don't play out anymore than 10-15 tops. So far the game is very balanced, every champion feels very fun to play and viable. The game HEAVILY rewards single champion mastery because you always que as the champion YOU want to play. There is both ranked and casual mode, as well as a practice arena where you can try out any champion as well as different builds, so it's not that hard at all to spend hours upon hours practicing and refinning your mastery of a champion's kit.
The best part though is there exists no semblence of pay 2 win, all purchases are cosmetic or to unlock new playable characters. Battlerites, which are champion specific perks that unlock buffs or modify abilities are available equally to all players to mix and match at will. Plus the devs have done a fantastic job putting out new cosmetics and starting awesome events, so yeah I might've dropped a little money already.
TL;DR Battlerite is a fun, fast paced and VERY well executed arena fighter game with lots of solo carry potential and heavily rewarding individual mastery.

Because UPlay.

Today UPlay doesn't work for me (trust me, I tried all the usual stuff as reinstall and so on..) and I know it's not Steams fault and all that is because a thing I don't like, I don't want and I don't use.
It's my fault. I broke my own rule.
For a long time I don't buy games, that requires 3rd party stuff. I never had use for them, didn't create even more accounts, avatars or profiles. And I never will. Also I'm an old fart so I remember those days, when if you bought a game, it wasn't "right to use it for period of time on specific service", it was actually _YOURS_.  Thats why I love GOG and Indie developers so much.
Steam is a different story, but it's a sevice that I CHOSE to use. Also I honestly think it tries to improve itself and I get the feeling Valve loves gamers, do not treat them like enemies that must be punished in advance, because "pirates".
Do I recommend this game?
Of course I won't hate it just for what happened to me. But in order to help you with your decision, all I can say is:  "Please, take a few seconds and think about WHAT and WHO do you support".

A very addicting interactive tower defense strategy game that is almost sure to get you hooked. The story is somewhat poor, but what really makes this game is the gameplay itself. The story uses countless cliches and predictable plot events that make it rather drab, however the unique gameplay makes up for it. Figuring out where to place towers, what towers to place, and when to intervene with your hero abilities is key in this game. The maps are all really different and have lush well developed environments with almost no bugs. This means you always have to be thinking about your strategy, as your tower placement will be different for every level.
From my experience with encouraging others to play this game, you either a) love it and get very addicted to it for a while or b) can't get into the game/hate it. I have spent countless hours on this game and would highly recommend it to anyone who likes strategy and/or tower defense games. The multiplayer is very well-implemented- playing with your buddies is as easy as inviting them to your lobby. You can make private lobbies where only you can be in them and nobody can join your game, invite only lobbies, or totally public lobbies. Most of the time it is very easy to find some people to help you get that elusive challenge or beat that incredibly difficult level.
The game has a great forums community over at
I would recommend posting there if you have further inquiries about the game. The games market is really flawed though, as hacking this game is exceedingly easy, even with VAC protection. I would not recommend getting into the market as you will most likely end up being scammed. The community has great events and is very welcoming making it hard to get mixed in with the wrong crowds.
overall I would give it an 8.5/10.

There aren't many games that have cast a longer shadow over the industry than Dark Souls, and much like what you'll find lurking within them it's been a bit of a curse. Too many indie games have been overtuned to provide a similarly punishing experience, narratives have been undercooked to mimic the subtle storytelling, and action has been slowed to a crawl to imitate the methodical combat. But some titles have taken the right bits of inspiration and mixed them with their own brew of mechanics, and from just such a concoction you will find Hollow Knight. And in many ways, the mix Team Cherry has come up with is a richer taste than what inspired it.
Hollow Knight is the tale of a little bug in a big, dark, scary world of bugs. It's bugs all the way down, you see; the kingdom of Hallownest was once a great and powerful society, spread across deep warrens beneath the surface. But something went wrong long ago and the kingdom fell silent. Now only the tiny hamlet of Dirtmouth remains to mark its location, though recently bugs have found themselves drawn to the lost kingdom in search of something. You will follow them down there, meet them, battle them and the unknown denizens, and change the fate of the cursed kingdom forever.
Pretty heavy stuff, right? Hollow Knight gets that, and that's one of its first and most prominent achievements. The tone this title strikes is both unique and flawless, an unexpected mix of charm, despair, humor, and dread. You've probably noticed already that your little dude is absolutely adorable, nipping along with his little white mask and nail. The other bugs nice enough to speak to you are often just as cute, but sometimes have sinister edges to them, or in a few cases are downright creepy. Friendly critters may crack jokes or help you out, while others relay ominous portends or warn you of the many dangers in and around Hallownest.
This balance carries on to the environments in a big way. The game world is massive for a metroidvania, and each area has a distinct style and atmosphere that hits all the right notes to evoke powerful reactions. From the first area of dark caves and ruins you may end up in a lush grotto of vines and creatures, a pleasant change until you realize the water is acidic and every bush may hide terrible dangers. Or you could descend into the caverns of potent fungi, with mysterious, bulbous foes that must be approached with great caution. Later journeys take you to decaying cities, silent graveyards, bustling coliseums, desolate wastes, and two of the most horrifyingly oppressive places I have ever visited in a video game. I'm not kidding here, Hollow Knight has topped titles from Half-life to SOMA in crafting locations that give me relentless anxiety.
Another achievement worth mentioning is how Hollow Knight can craft such an atmosphere without hobbling the player in how they approach it. Part of the Dark Souls experience is trundling around at a slow jog, fighting battles and dodging traps at a measured pace. Team Cherry wisely elected to ignore this aspect of their inspiration, instead making your little knight swift, nimble, and refreshingly responsive. The controls here are tight, allowing you to execute your dashes and sword swings with ease as you dance around bugs both great and small, airborne and grounded, armed and fanged. At no point was I frustrated with the pace at which I could move about, and the fluid motion made the elaborate and creative battles against bosses and larger enemies all the more enjoyable.
As a metroidvania there's a wealth of hidden items and powers to scrounge up across the world as well. Some are common pieces of the genre like health and magic upgrades, weapon skills and wall climbing and such. But even here there are unique implementations, like one of your earliest powers being essentially unlimited horizontal flight. Uncovering this treasure so early on feels incredibly liberating and exciting, but also reveals to you just how important verticality is to the game. You can further augment your movement and combat with charms that can extend your sword reach, change how you move when hit or attacking, or grant you all sorts of additional effects. I will admit a little disappointment here at how essential some charms are over others and how the limited slots for them tend to keep me from experimenting much, though.
I suppose I could gripe about a few other annoyances, like the rare bug I get where my charged attacks don't work, or how spread out the fast travel is. That latter one is a bit of a pain in truth, because the stations used for fast travel tend to be quite far from points of interest. You certainly won't be relying on them as much as you would Castlevania warp rooms or Dark Souls bonfire warps. The map is another aspect that could be a drag, but honestly I love it. You don't fill in new areas of the map until you reach a save point, and to get a map at all you have to locate an amateur cartographer in each area. He tends to be near one of the logical entrances and has audio and visual cues to lead you to him, so there's a bit of tension in each new locale as you seek him out.
It's details like the map that make me love the game more, really. Hallownest isn't just a maze to run around, it's a functioning world with its own rules and requirements. The things Hollow Knight asks you to do are never unreasonable and fit with the dark and unusual tone of the places you visit. Nothing is out of place here, and it all works in concert to immerse you in this strange world of bugs and mysticism. The characters and locations are far more memorable to me than those of similar games, in large part because they can be funny or creepy or adorable and still fill their role in a seamless narrative. There's a lot to unpack about Hallownest, but instead of just resting on riddles this game makes you WANT to puzzle it out.
On top of everything that Hollow Knight does right, it looks and sounds absolutely breathtaking. The hand-drawn aesthetic gives the enemies and environments an extra spark of life, complimenting the strong lines and flat colors with impressive animated details. The environments in particular are labors of love that bring together careful linework, bold lighting, and rich particle effects to make them feel deep and authentic. And the sound design does just as well, with appropriately subtle, melancholy melodies and impactful effects. There's so much going on here that it baffles me how it could all work together so perfectly and yet it does, on and on for easily 20 hours or more. Hollow Knight does what few games manage to do, take clear inspiration from classics and find its own way to surpass them.

I haven't played Assassin's Creed since the first title.
I happened to be one of the unlucky few who got a locked game from release day, with the game freezing and save corrupting when you get to the first assassination. I think it was a demo.
No matter, I sold that game and never touched the titles again. Until now.
Assassin's Creed 2 didn't catch my eye enough for a buy, and the next Khorne knows how many games based on Ezio I also stayed away from.
It was a personal preference, nothing about them interested me.
Assassin's Creed 3 came around, and it was different. I didn't buy it until after playing this game.
Enter Assassin's Creed IV - Black Flag
YOU'RE A PIRATE! AND YOU'RE NOT A JACK SPARROW CLONE!!?!??!
What is this heresy?
This heresy is possibly one of the best hack and slashes (Behind Dynasty Warriors, my childhood game)
And it allows me to do the one thing I had for the most part only been able to do in RTS games - Naval combat.
Breakdown (It's alright).
Story - I saw a lot of reviews complaining about the story, but then again, most people who complain about stories probably couldn't tell a well written Broadway from a Hollywood blockbuster.
At first, I was going to say the story was often slow. I didn't realize how well they had worked the story for this reaction.
At the beginning of the game, you're a Pirate, being a Pirate. Which involves killing people, stealing their identities, and sneaking into their meetings only to be discovered because at the end of the day, you're still a pirate.
This point is driven home throughout the beginning and middle of the story, and occasionally at the end.
Near the middle of the story, if you're anything like me, you're going to start getting tired of Captain Kenway's sh!t, reflecting what he himself is actually feeling, if you're smart enough to follow the story.
When the climax finally hits and Kenway gets his books together for the finals, things start becoming exceedingly emotional. If you fail to be effected by the ending sequence, then your morals will be in need of severe re-attaching.
The story gets a 9/10 for it's masterful writing and execution, with 1 point deducted because of what happens in the prison escape sequence.
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Gameplay -
Animations - Perhaps one of the most disappointing things was probably one of the smallest in the game - Weapon animations. When you press X, or whatever button on the keyboard it is for you to pull your weapons you, you should do a flourish. Instead you literally shrug. I know that there was supposed to be an animation there, because of the sound the swords make. It's a fast, sharp sound, air being cut. But you just shrug. That's so incredibly lazy, especially since it was never addressed. Other than that the animations are smooth and silky, with the brutal executions taking the forefront, as expected. Animations 7/10 - That lack of a flourish really bothers me.
Weapon Selection - Is lacking. Having played Assassin's Creed 3, and seeing -all- of the weapons offered to our Native grandchild, and comparing it to 5 or 6 models of rapier that Kenway gets. Well... Disappointing. A bow and pistols for the Native Grandchild, just pistols for Kenway. Disappointing. The lack of a usable rifle or atleast carbine would help spice the game up a little, as it sits the weapon selection is without a doubt the single most horrendous part of this game.
Weapon Selection/Variety - 3/10
Ship combat - Is without a doubt where this game shines. There's no real way for me to explain it without being an expert, so just take my rating for it.
Ship Combat - 9/10
Open World - Seamless and lacking lag, with my framerate rarely dropping.
Explain to me again why you'd ever want to use fast travel?
Open World - 9/10
Soundtrack - For the most part, the classical pieces in this game are very fitting and don't seem to intrude too much on the gameplay, instead adding a theme to it. But please give me a patch where my crew never stops singing. The shanties are the most catchy thing ever.
Soundtrack - 10/10
Adewale - Deserves his own rating section. And I think we should go ahead and add him to the list of "best sidekicks ever brought into games".
Adewale - 8/10
Dialogue - Is very impressive from my standpoint, making me grin and laugh and with the references fitting well within the time-period.
Dialogue - 9/10
Blackbeard 10/10
Revenge of Queen Anne 10/10

Note: this review was written before the F2P, launch it has largely improved and most points in this review still hold true
Since the classic MOBAs (Dota2&LoL) hit the gaming scene, I was really hooked by the action based team-fights, I loved the skill-shots and the dodging, but really disliked everything else, Battlerite satisfies this hunger for epic team-fights and indepth combat. Those are achieved by picking one of  over 17 unique characters, which you bring to a small arena in a 2v2 or 3v3 death match. In a best of 5, lasting between 5 to 12 minutes, thereby removing the long time commitment and with it a lot of frustration.
Exactly like the classic MOBAs, this game is played top-down and uses the fog of war really well, thus giving you, the player a lot of vision (more than dota2), to easily hit your abilities. Every character has a set of skills, but this game has more skills, in fact 9 skills per character. Usually one of these skills is a dodge skill, creating a lot of epic moments in 1v2 or 1v3 combacks. Although there are four powerful skills, that require energy, which is gained by using abilities and collecting energy on the map. One of skills often referred to as the Ultimate ability requires 100% energy, while the other skills requires only 25% of the energy, so a player always has to think about whether they want to wait for the Ultimate or if they rather use a skill now to get an advantage over the enemy.
What I really like about the abilities is that the majority of them have some kind of debuff effect on the enemy or buff effect on you, by that giving every player great utility winning 1v2 fights. This utility can be further enhanced by the Battlerite upgrades you gain at the beginning of every round, but there are also some heal and damage options.
So in conclusion the game is great. If the game is more fleshed out. I think this game will be worth playing once it's out as a Free-To-Play game. Or if you really want to try out the great gameplay and want to play with non-free-to-players, just get it now, the gameplay is already so good and satisfying.

This 3-D tower defense strategy game has enormous replayability (as back in the day I logged over 1000 in-game hours) especially if you get sucked into grinding for ever better end-game gear. There is a ton of DLC, and if you have a good time with the base game then the DLC will likely extend your playability for quite a while -- go to the forums for some advice on which DLC you might consider buying, as it's possible that you're not far enough through the game to do some of the content.
Dungeon Defenders has a pretty stalwart community, very helpful game forums (which if you ever get stuck will be happy to help you), and Trendy Entertainment is even releasing a sequel that has a multiplayer segment that looks to be a MOBA... interesting.
The classes are quite varied and balanced, and one of the more interesting aspects is that an excellent end-game defense typically relies on multiple classes working together -- even if that means you yourself have 4 characters, and run around switching between them (or even play two at the same time, through local-coop or excellent multitasking).
In addition, the stark difference between having a character focused on tower stats and a character focused on attack skills and abilities, means you'll certainly need to have at least 2 characters once the going gets tougher.
Once you get to the higher difficulties, the game feels very MMO... in that you grind for superior equipment to be able to survive harder maps... to grind for even better equipment... etc. Once you have a decent grasp of the map layouts and your tower abilities, the game can eventually become stale and repetitive in this manner.
Even though they add new content every once in a while, if your stats are up to snuff, a new map shouldn't be too difficult to conquer if you can decipher a proper layout and strategy. And then you decide to do the same map again... or choose to move on to other games as I eventually did.
There is a small but quite hardcore community, with active hi-end trading and forums. There is also fairly rampant hacking, as all information as you play the game is stored totally locally. So as soon as you start trading, expect to get much better gear for not that much currency... potentially leapfrogging you past a ton of fun that could be had due to your cheap, overpowered gear.
There is a sub-section of the official forums where you can ask whether or not gear is hacked (i.e. the stats are in-bounds of the game) but if someone knows the game well enough, they can very easily make top-tier "legitimate-looking" gear that is totally indistinguishable from properly earned gear. This makes the trading and economy of the game essentially useless, and ultra-rare "event" items that potentially sell for lots of currency have essentially have a pedigree or paper-trail to show they were obtained legitimately, or else they are assumed to be hacked.
In any case, it's a fun game both solo or with friends, and potentially offers a ton of 3-D action and tower defense gameplay, character customization / stat gearing, etc. Just don't immediately ask for cheap gear and ruin the game by being too powerful beyond your current area -- the fun is in the challenge.

Shadow Warrior is a in many aspects successful reimagining of the 3D Realms classic from 1997. In this review I will describe how it holds up in comparison and try to cut right to the chase.
The level design isn't quite as open and doesn't offer as many secrets as the original, but you can tell that Flying Wild Hog put a lot of love and work into this project. The combat is extremely fun and satisfying, especially the different katana moves. The weapons are varied, fun to use and none of them feel unneccessary or even useless. The story is fairly cheesy, so I guess you could say they nailed this aspect. Shadow Warrior and a serious story don't mix as far as I'm concerned. The voice acting is great, even though I miss Lo Wang's original voice. The quips are hit and miss, but overall quite funny. What really impresses me about this game is that it feels like an almost perfect blend of "retro" and modern game design. Many developers have aspired to do that and most of them failed. Flying Wild Hog managed to pull it off, which deserves much respect.
I've spent about 21 hours on Shadow Warrior and enjoyed it a lot. I'm planning to replay it at some point.
Bottom line: If you aren't offended by strong video game violence and dark, sometimes childish humor, you will have a great time with this game!

Note: this review was written before the F2P, launch it has largely improved and most points in this review still hold true
Since the classic MOBAs (Dota2&LoL) hit the gaming scene, I was really hooked by the action based team-fights, I loved the skill-shots and the dodging, but really disliked everything else, Battlerite satisfies this hunger for epic team-fights and indepth combat. Those are achieved by picking one of  over 17 unique characters, which you bring to a small arena in a 2v2 or 3v3 death match. In a best of 5, lasting between 5 to 12 minutes, thereby removing the long time commitment and with it a lot of frustration.
Exactly like the classic MOBAs, this game is played top-down and uses the fog of war really well, thus giving you, the player a lot of vision (more than dota2), to easily hit your abilities. Every character has a set of skills, but this game has more skills, in fact 9 skills per character. Usually one of these skills is a dodge skill, creating a lot of epic moments in 1v2 or 1v3 combacks. Although there are four powerful skills, that require energy, which is gained by using abilities and collecting energy on the map. One of skills often referred to as the Ultimate ability requires 100% energy, while the other skills requires only 25% of the energy, so a player always has to think about whether they want to wait for the Ultimate or if they rather use a skill now to get an advantage over the enemy.
What I really like about the abilities is that the majority of them have some kind of debuff effect on the enemy or buff effect on you, by that giving every player great utility winning 1v2 fights. This utility can be further enhanced by the Battlerite upgrades you gain at the beginning of every round, but there are also some heal and damage options.
So in conclusion the game is great. If the game is more fleshed out. I think this game will be worth playing once it's out as a Free-To-Play game. Or if you really want to try out the great gameplay and want to play with non-free-to-players, just get it now, the gameplay is already so good and satisfying.

My favorite in the series so far, yet the most disappointing as well. With all the yearly iterations we've gone through you would think that some of the core mechanics might have been smoothed out by now. This isn't the case. The engine still favors style over refinement, with animations constantly getting in the way of controls. Your character still annoyingly attempts to climb literally every single thing in the environment, making chase missions an exercise in frustration.
The sailing portion of the game is easily the most entertaining but it too is not without its problems. The ship controls just fine and all of the various weapons are fun and easy to use. Where it breaks down is when you have to board the enemy ship. Your crew is basically used as a timer, if you run out of crew then you desynchronize. While I never found this to be an issue, the crew is ultimitely a liability for an entirely different reason. The only thing they seem to do is crowd the deck which makes fighting the enemy sailors a frustrating chore. Your own crew will regularly hit you, get in your way, or interrupt your combo (making you restart it over and over again) which makes these battles needlessly aggravating.
The only other problem with the game comes when you are forced to leave the Animus. You have to walk around a modern office building, talk to your boss, and spy on your coworkers. Sound fun? Yeah, it's actually worse than you might think. Has anyone ever really cared about the story outside the Animus? Beside being incredibly obnoxious these scenes are also completely unskippable (at least on a first playthrough, not sure if you might skip them in subsequent plays) and feature characters that really add nothing to the game. It's like you go out to a go-kart track and after every lap you have to file someone's taxes. All you really want to do is go back to buckling swashes and yo-ho-hoing as fast as possible.
Those issues aside it is a very fun game. The combat is still great when it works, the stealth is solid, the atmosphere is the best in the series and really, who doesn't want to be a pirate?

A good game, a solid metroidvania on the whole, but deeply flawed in a really weird lopsided sort of way. Feels overall like something one group of very good developers made, and made absolutely perfect, and then for some unknown reason was handed off to another, different group of developers who didn't know what they were doing in a deliberate effort to ruin it as much as possible--not an effort that succeeded, but one that's visibly present. Not that I know anything about how it was actually developed, but that's the best description I have for what kind of a flawed but good game this is. There are just a lot of design choices of the form "make something good and then go back and partially mess up that good thing so it's not as good."
In more detail: First off, the game has a map system which is serviceable--not perfect, it fails to show some areas entirely and likes to show some twisting mazy corridor areas as a big blob, but it's good enough to get by most of the time--but then for some stupid reason you can't just HAVE a map, oh no, someone thought it was a good idea to have to find a guy in an area with NO map before you can have a map, and the ability to see where you are on the map requires taking up an equip slot, which is positively absurd.
The game has a set of upgrades that feel like a lot of fun to use, but some basically mandatory upgrades like "collect money without having to chase after it like someone dropped three gallons of tiny bouncy balls all over the high school gymnasium" and the aforementioned "just see where you are on the map" take up equip slots, which there are already not enough of in the game.
Dying leaves behind a thing you have to go back to where you died and kill to get your money back, which WOULD be somewhat reasonable if you could just CHOOSE to reload instead of having to go all the way back to where you were to get your money back, but for some stupid reason the game saves when you die, which means the only way to choose to reload is to back up your save first and copy it back over the one that saves when you die, a step that has no business being necessary for a player who'd rather reload and lose some progress than go to the trouble of chasing it down. There's a way to "summon" the thing to fight to a safer area instead of chasing after it, but not only does that require going all the way back up to town and having spent an expensive and/or hard to find item to unlock it, but it also costs the use of items which are in limited supply and not all that easy to find, so it's not really a good compromise against the "game saving when it shouldn't" problem.
There are a lot of fun, challenging but not absurd bosses and action sequences throughout the game, but there's a sizable back of it just chock full of garbage. If you want the good ending or some measure of completion, that requires some fights that are just plain impossible without cheating, which all fit the mold of "what if we took an existing boss and made it do double damage and move too fast for a human to react to?" And there's a sidequest of "go from one end of the map to the other without taking any hits" (this is NOT the kind of game where that's a reasonable request), and similar to the problem with dying and reloading, if you take a hit during said quest then the game saves, which means this also requires making a backup and copying it back over to not lose your progress across the map up to a given save point. The kicker is that the very LAST ROOM of said sidequest is the kind of place where the game can just decide that your position wasn't perfect enough and drop you onto spikes anyway, despite giving it pretty much the same input as a "correct" move sequence.
Platforming is mostly good, but spikes behave strangely. All other damage sources just hit the player, and respect the "invulnerability dash" you get later on in the game. Spikes don't respect invulnerability, and magically warp the player to a random platform--sometimes forward, sometimes backwards. This made no sense to me until reaching a section of the game (again, a section which is MANDATORY for getting anything but the "you suck" ending) which is really just a completely unrelated flash puzzle platformer someone thought it'd be a good idea to shoehorn into a game belonging to an entirely different genre. It's actually not bad on the balance, it only overstays its welcome a little bit, but it's a section where the majority of the game's mechanics, like having a health system, are functionally meaningless, and its existence seems to be the sole reason for spikes to behave the weird way they do compared to all other damage in the game.
The world is huge, with lots of stuff to explore and see. Also, the game is very open in this way: I was able to buy something from a shopkeep very early into the game (after beating just the first boss, but I think it's possible before even that) which granted me access to areas intended for way later into the game, including stumbling into a portion of story I think was intended for at least five or six bosses in. I saw nearly the entire map before going back to about a mid-game section to get a movement ability which is usable in a huge number of areas. There are a few "how was I supposed to know that was there?" collectibles but on the whole I really liked how everything is laid out.
The story is needlessly depressing, because why wouldn't it be? 90% of the sideplots involving even marginally friendly characters end with those characters dying, while generally mean or unpleasant characters live forever. Obviously the player character dies or "dies" at the end too, because why would anyone ever want to have any kind of positivity to a game's plot or ending? If you work really hard (do all the difficult stuff I mentioned above) and fight a boss whose intended strategy for beating seems to be "use cheat engine" then one particular side character lives and I guess we're supposed to care about her, even though I never really did.
During all the latter portion of the game's more unfair battle sequences, it becomes increasingly clear that some parts of the controls only respond when they want to. You can push the attack button, HEAR the sound of an attack and still not attack because the game decided you were going to get damaged instead. Pushing the dodge button to get away from or "invulnerable dodge" your way through an attack sometimes just does nothing and you get hit anyway. I've on more than one occasion seen that I was falling toward spikes, pushed the jump button to execute a double jump and NOT hit the spikes, and then despite making both the sound AND animation of a double jump, the game decides "no, you hit those spikes you didn't really hit and I'm gonna magically warp you to some other platform anyway". I don't really even know exactly why it acts this way, the controls usually feel consistent, but it feels like the game is cheating every time it happens.
I had fun for some of it, but I don't think I'll be inclined to play this game again for a very long time, if ever. Also, the game unlocked a permadeath mode on beating the game the first time, despite this belonging to a genre where permadeath makes even less sense than usual.
If it sounds like most of this review is complaining, even though I say I recommend the game, it's because I feel like it had the potential to be--and at some point WAS--something better. That disappointment bleeds through and it's easier somehow to come up with good words for what was wrong than what was right. On the balance I really do like the game and I want to see its makers succeed. So I do recommend getting it, especially if some of my complaints sound like positives to you.

Unity surprised me by accurately showing Arno dropping through the ground and into the white abyss that exists under the real Paris, even to this day. Finally, there is the non-issue of pop-in... Stanley sat down at his computer.
He decided to browse the steam store. More specifically, his wishlist.
Stanley clicked on his wishlist, and saw what was at the top.
"The Stanley Parable".
"What an odd title," he thought to himself. "Perhaps I should consider buying it."
After careful contemplation, he bought the game, and installed it.
"Ah, a wonderful new game for me to enjoy" he thought.
Stanley began to play the game.
He followed the instructions carefully. Then he began to wonder.
"What if... I turned left?" he pondered.
Alas, Stanley followed the path he was told to follow, a puppet in the hands of a voice in his head.
But still, he couldn't help but think; "What would have happened?"
Stanley stopped. He thought it was a bizarre little game.
This didn't stop him though, Stanley being the energetic little man he is.
He opened steam and browsed his library.
Stanley began to write a review.
"Stanley sat down at his computer..."

Choice. It is all about choice. Our choices make a difference. The differences make us all unique. We are defined by our choices. This is particularly true when thinking about computer games. We choose which games to play. We choose how to play the games. Our choices are aided by narrative tools. Nothing can go wrong. Everything will be fine.
.
The Stanley Parable is a game that is playing with the concept of choices in computer games. It is a first-person exploration game where we enter the story as Stanley. He is employee 427 in a large company. His work consists of sitting in room 427 looking at a computer screen which is instructing him which buttons to press on his keyboard, and how long to keep those buttons pressed. Suddenly he realises that his screen is blank, and it seems that all his colleagues have suddenly disappeared. Stanley starts looking for them around the offices and the corridors, accompanied by a narrator commentating on his actions.
The Stanley Parable is a deeply pretentious game pretending to be whimsical or, much more probable, a fundamentally whimsical game pretending to be pretentious. I like this kind of ambivalence, underlined by the narrator’s continual balancing on the line between nonsense and thoughtfulness. The gameplay itself is simple, consisting of moving around and interacting with objects, but that is not the point here. The point is to reflect on the concept of choice. Or, maybe, just to enjoy the game as a slightly interactive story with some clever commentary.
I had fun playing the game. I am just trying to hide it behind some pseudo-pretentious drivel.

After playing the game for few days, I can say the game is really good. Mostly...
The world is huge and full of events, different activities like assassinations, templar hunting or general combat mix with trading, treasure hunts, animal hunting and managing your own trade fleet. Now the bad parts:
- Uplay - one of the worst inventions in history of gaming. Artificial "social network" that causes only problems. I won't go on with the ranting about uplay, suffice to say I genuinely hate it.
- Glitches - sometimes the ships vanish. I was trying to capture a Galleon which... Dissapeared leaving only cannons and some decorations hanging in the air and few people floating in the water. Had to reload and - of course - lost the perfect score I got by avoiding combat everywhere.
- Your ship sometimes vanishes leaving bottomless hole in the ocean. Looks funny, but gets quite annoying when you see it n'th time.
- MOUSE ACCELERATION! this is horrible. I really don't know why so many games come with this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and even worse - you can't disable it at all. This is the worst thing in the entire game that borders a game breaking bug for me. You want to look around quickly during naval combat? You're out of luck. You want to look around while looking for cover quickly? Too bad. You simply want to admire the white whale event? Why don't you stare at the sail of your own ship while the wale goes away. The list goes on.
The bright side - aside from the mouse acceleration and occasional graphical glitches, the game is great.

I really really enjoyed this game. Mainly for the playing pirates part. You have awesome ship battles and can sail around the ocean looking for treasure, upgrading your ship, capturing other ships to add to your fleet, taking strongholds. I didn't like the stealth part too much. You're on the one hand completely overpowered, but on the other hand, the controls are pretty annoying. Running and "Free running" are the same button. That means that sometimes you want to run up to stab a guy before guards get close but you'll end up running up the side of a wall and falling back down by accident. The loot body, pick up body, drop off a ledge, sheath your weapon, and counter button are also all mapped to the same button. This means sometimes you want to move a body real fast but instead hang off a ledge. Sometimes you want to be in counter stance in a sword fight but end up putting your swords away. The other side of this is that other than fighting the controls, no fight is really challenging. The guard AI also forgets where you were really fast. But the sailing the ocean on a pirate ship is so fun it makes it all worth it.
