While it's not as good as the trailers would tell you, but it's certainly not bad at all. As usual, the game looks great. I guess there's not much to add if you're familiar with the rest of the series.
It's hasn't improved. In fact, it changed a little bit for the worse; it's not as spectacular as it used to be and feels kind of clumsy to control. The good part is you can have up to 4 preloaded pistols, so at least thát helps decrease reloading. Either way, you really should use all your tools in this game, they're totally OP compared to the lack of fighting skills.
I guess it's because you play some stinking peasant turned pirate, rather than a trained assassin. Which is actually a nice change; being no part of either templar or assassin but getting in too deep to avoid the crossfire. The story does unfold quite nicely.
The new things in this game are obviously the ship battles, a gimmick from the last game. Well, not too surprising since they went with a pirate theme. Most of the game is either at sea, or in ports. A lovely addition to the sea travel are the shanties; a few drunks singing a song makes the trip more enjoyable, so it pays off to search for a few.
The fun and yet frustrating part is boarding a ship to capture it. Somehow the controls suddenly go more wonky than usual when climbing the sails. Especially when there's a few waves moving the ship. And the decks always feel way too small with the amount of people getting in your way. But most of the boardings look really cool and are fun to do for a while.
Then there's a whole new creature to hunt for: the White Whale, and his nautical buddies. Although whaling is basically just chucking spears at the beast untill it stops flopping, it's pretty cool. Ahab himself would be proud. And the sharks do put up quite a fight.
Oh, and another wonderful thing they added is underwater levels. Because we all know how much people love underwater levels. They actually look quite magical. The screenshots hardly do them justice.
Outside of the Animus there's a few computers to hack, and obviously a less action-packed part of the story going on. Strangely enough you seem to be an Abstergo employee this time around...
Although they really should've included all the DLC's if they wanted to ask such a high price for it, oh well, I bought it anyway when it was on a sale, I blame the pirate theme, ARRR. I guess I can't complain, all in all, it's an entertaining game, pretty much worth what I paid for it. This damn franchise tricks me into buying it anyway.

The Stanley Parable is very in love with itself.
As what I can only describe as an abstract rumination on contemporary game design, Galactic Café’s The Stanley Parable is, from its opening moments, confident to the point of near irreverence. I suppose it’s understandable to a degree, as The Stanley Parable is undeniably witty and unconventional, with a quirky charm and dry self-awareness. It is so overwhelmingly eccentric that it can begin to feel as if not playing along with it and laughing at every joke is an act of disrespect, such is the perception The Stanley Parable cultivates within moments of leaving the main menu to venture forth into a cornucopia of contextually appropriate satire and bizarre dark humor.
The Stanley Parable gives off such a sense of self-prescribed brilliance that I feel both dumbfounded and maybe even a little angry at just how much I dislike it. I get the joke and admire its delivery, but when approached from any angle but the one the game so strongly attempts to cultivate, The Stanley Parable feels like little more than a few intelligent observations on modern game design strung along by a series of amusing, yet immensely inconsistent and inscrutable scenes with no conclusions to be found.
I understand that the lack of closure is part of the point. I can find a certain poetic appreciation for the circular design of the game, and as a lesson in abstract game design The Stanley Parable certainly gets marks for trying. But then it tries some more, and eventually (which is to say sometime within the first 20 minutes of play) I became rather weary of hearing the same joke play out as I raged a supposedly hilarious war with the narrator over increasingly innocuous choices.
There is such an abundance of creativity to be admired within The Stanley Parable, one would think that even in worst case scenarios everyone will be able to find something to like buried in its labyrinth of compounding decisions. But by design each disconnected moment is compiled with the next, creating a sequence of random and oddly directed scenes for which the primary goal is to disorient the player as they continue bumbling through a game with no rules and a rather antagonistic sense of progression.
The Stanley Parable without a doubt knows what it’s doing. The script is tight, the pacing smooth, and the overall concept worthy of praise. And yet I found myself despising every moment I spent with the game. The more I tried to peel back its layers to find the game I had seen praised to the ends of the earth and back, the more I was confronted with the same shallow and narcissistic experience that only became more meandering and unfulfilling the longer I stuck with it. I suppose it was fitting that I eventually arrived in a museum dedicated to the game itself; an internal monument to a project which clearly recognizes its own genius even as I struggle to understand the appeal.

Arma II is riddled with bugs and problems. It's an incredibly demanding game, even on modern machines. It hogs your CPU and can crash for literally no reason at all. If you're playing with other people (as you should) you'll likely spend hours standing around doing nothing, then get shot in the first few seconds of a firefight and spend the next five minutes staring at a black screen until the death screen pops up because you bled out.
You'll drive down a dirt road at a snails pace watching for IEDs, only to get blown up by one you didn't see hidden in a bush. Then you'll drive down the same road, again, and when you arrive at you area of operation you'll take a bullet to the head and die instantly.
Sometimes you'll have to sit around on a hilltop looking at enemies for 30 minutes while you wait for your fireteam leader to radio the squad leader, who then has to radio command, who then has to radio back questions, which are relayed to your fireteam leader, who answer them back to the squad leader, who radios back to command, who radios back to squad leader permission to engage, who sends back to your fireteam leader, who then tells you you can engage. And that's if everyone is listening to each other. More likely you'll sit around for thirty minutes while the fireteam leader tries to contact the squad leader who doesn't even have their radio on.
Occasionally you'll gear up for a halo jump or fastrope operation, gather everyone on the tarmac, load up into the helicopter, wait for the pilot to discuss drop zone with your officers, then after fifteen minutes of flying your screen will go black with the sound of a surface to air missle blowing a hole through the cockpit.
Believe me when I say Arma II has been the most fun and engaging video game I've ever played and if I could only have one game for the rest of my life it would be this.

Hollow Knight has been a favorite of mine for one main factor: simplicity. While most games I encounter these days like to showcase flashy and intricate mechanics, Hollow Knight starts the player with only a few core mechanics: jump, slash, and heal. Even with such few options, the game still feels like it has everything it needs, only adding a few spells and movement enhancements. The few options still yield a sense of control with the character, in that the "jump" button will cause the character to jump higher the longer it is held, and the "slash" button uses all four orthagonal directions.
Aside from the mechanics, the art style was particularly captivating to me. Again following a simplistic design, I personally found certain areas and enemies to be interesting and pretty. Along with a solid soundtrack, everything comes together for a well made and "finished" game.
The real fun of the game comes in the many and frequent boss fights throughout the game. Each boss has its own special set of moves, and the player has to learn to read each bosses actions and learn how to dodge and counterattack each one. While some bosses are more predictable going into the fight and easier to learn, some bosses had taken longer periods of time to finally defeat. Content aside from those bosses are fine in that it's not overbearing on the lore and side quests, but still is available to the player if they are interested.
There are downsides I see to this game. One is that the game requires backtracking a lot, and in such a large map with many parts, those portions of the game can seem tedious. I personally enjoyed the exploring bits of the game, but at times the running around seemed extensive and annoying. The other is that the game doesn't prompt where to go next, and so the player could be stuck trying to find the next piece before they can advance in the story. Some may enjoy the lack of direction, while others may not enjoy trying to find the very edges of unexplored rooms and getting lost in the process.
Overall, the game seems simplistic while still feeling like it has substantial and interesting content to it. Parts between major bosses and sections of the game can be tedious in how much backtracking and exploring needs to be done, but the freedom to roam and explore can also be a positive side to it. I highly recommend Hollow Knight

- Off the bat NPC's are not stale and generic and always seem to have an "air" of good design about them.

It truly is hard to put this game into words. At first it may seem like a simple game, you walk, go where you are told, and finish the game. It now seems to be a fun little game, with some silly moments, biting insults, and multiple endings. But as you play the game even more, you start to notice even more things. I'm only about 13 hours into the game, but I feel that I've already gained an understanding of how great this game is - and I'm only more excited when I read this game's description to see how much quality content this game holds. The combat feels incredibly fluid and is fun to try to perfect, even when backtracking through areas or exploring areas that aren't a challenge anymore. The fights train you for the boss battles, which have been some of my favorite in any game that I have played in my life.
See, these aren't your average "hit it a few times and it dies" or "drain its health meter quickly before it attacks you" bosses. These are long and drawn out boss battles that will make you feel like a fighting god who can wield magic, can sustain a long fight, and artfully dodges attacks. They have tended to require a few attempts, though the player may be able to beat some of the earlier ones on the first attempt (the window of time in which the game allows the player to do this gradually lessens throughout the course of the game).
I'm also very satisfied with the way that my time has been distributed. Though it is a Metroidvania-style game, I only got truly lost a few times, and even then it was resolved after a while. While I was lost, I was at least able to farm enemies and get better at the game - and I learned that it's a good idea to get a map. Navigation in the game is clear enough with signs and maps that it tends not to be frustrating (it's about as bad in this regard as it is in Ori and the Blind Forest), but it remains ambiguous enough for secret bosses, areas, and powers to be discovered. It's structured in a way that, after a few hours in the game, the player feels like he/she has a compelling choice of what things to do and where to go.
Aesthetically, Hollow Knight is unique. The soundtrack (which I plan to listen to beyond the game itself) and the art are masterful in tandem. The games areas start dully, but gradually grow to feel more unique. The music ranges from ambient to creepy to heart-pumping and invigorating to fit the experience.
All in all, don't spoil the game for yourself unless you're truly frustrated. As a full experience, it feels rewarding in its own way to be able to fight and navigate through the depths of Hallownest, as well as to be able to stomach the full scope of Team Cherry's game, which, only partway through the game, already feels fullfilled. Perhaps it'll take the spot of my favorite indie game over TowerFall Ascension.
TL;DR Play Hollow Knight if you like single player games that are about more than gameplay and high graphics

Shadow Warrior was a delightful surprise. A perfunctory examination indicates little promise; it looks and sounds like a pile of cliche: "ninja fights army of demons." On closer inspection however, Shadow Warrior is much more. I understand it's meant to be a callback to older shooters like Duke Nukem or Quake, titles which I never got to experience. Yet even without nostalgia, this game enthralled me despite its faults.
The gameplay has little variation; occaisional half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥puzzles always give way to more fighting, but thankfully that combat is far too fun to deride. The whimsically gratuitous carnage from carving through demon hordes with a spirit-laser firing katana is indescribably fun, and the initially lack-luster firearms can be upgraded to satisfying levels of destruction.
While the storyline may be thin and unclear, the characters are engaging satires of modern cliches. Lo Wang and his questionable name make for healthy banter rather than the usual silence gravely grunts of self-insertion oriented shooters.
Altogether Shadow Warrior is a must-play for any shooter fan, so long as one doesn't mind the occaisional slightly racist Wang pun.

It truly is hard to put this game into words. At first it may seem like a simple game, you walk, go where you are told, and finish the game. But after a bit of playing, you start to find new ways to play the game, and find it to be much larger than you first imagined. It now seems to be a fun little game, with some silly moments, biting insults, and multiple endings. But as you play the game even more, you start to notice even more things. Like that as you were playing the game, the game was playing you. Every decision you make is manipulated by the game. From the first time you escaped, to your rebellious decision to take the door on the right, to every playthrough after that. You don't play this game, the game plays you.
Eventually you notice something amazing. This isn't even a game. The name states that. It's something much greater than just a game, it's a parable. A parable is a story told to teach a moral lesson. I think this game makes a great parable. But, what lesson does it teach? You'll have to play to find out.

I don't always buy games. But when I do, I make sure they're good ones. And Shadow Warrior is definitely one of them. After watching YouTube sensations TotalBiscuit and Jesse Cox play and give their glowing impressions on it, I knew this was something I could get into.
What really sets Shadow Warrior apart from other FPS is its katana swordplay. Every slash and scission bisects objects and beings in a way that is both appropriate and well animated. And it is just as effective as your arsenal of firearms, if not more so--meaning you can get up close and personal with the katana all the time if you really want to. And that's what I like the most about the gameplay: you as a player have a choice on how you want to upgrade weapons and skills. Will you build yourself around guns, swordplay, or a bit of both? That's up to you.
However, what speaks to me most about any game like Shadow Warrior is its attention to detail. For example, the first level has a garden rendering cherry blossoms, rock surfaces, waterfalls, and bamboo forests with spectacular fidelity. And apart from a few dark industrial-themed environments, that kind of quality eye candy never lets up all the way to the end. And the details don't stop with the graphics. Voice acting is witty, modern, and enjoyable. It is never cringeworthy. And the music is absolutely top notch, capable of evoking scale and drama during boss fights, as well as calm and tension before combating an enemy horde in the areas leading up to it.
A game that delivers both mechanically and viscerally while being pleasantly enjoyable to the easily squeemish is a win in my books. I would highly recommend Shadow Warrior to everyone.

WOW! there is absolutely no word to describe this game it's just absolutely fantastic. Set during the early 18th century Caribbean during the Golden Age of Piracy, the story follows notorious pirate Edward Kenway, the grandfather of Assassin's Creed III's protagonist Ratonhnhaké:ton, who stumbles upon the conflict that's waged by the Assassins and Templars.
Unlike most of the previous games, gameplay elements focus more on ship-based exploration in the open world map, while still also retaining the series' third-person land-based exploration, melee combat, and stealth system. Multiplayer also returns, albeit with only land-based modes and settings.
Assassin's Creed IV has three new main cities; Havana, Kingston, and Nassau, which is currently residing under the Spanish, British, and pirate influence, respectively. Assassin's Creed IV has a much more open world feel, with missions that are very similar to those found in Assassin's Creed, as well as fewer restrictions for you.
The world opens up much sooner in the game, as opposed to Assassin's Creed III, which had very scripted missions and did not give the player freedom to explore until the game was well into its first act. You will encounter jungles, forts, ruins, and small villages.
The world is built to allow you to have much more freedom. Assassin's Creed IV also features 50 other individual locations including atolls, sea forts, Mayan ruins, sugar plantations and underwater shipwrecks to explore, with a 60/40 balance between land and naval exploration.
A new aspect in the game is the Jackdaw, the ship that the notorious pirate Edward Kenway captains. The Jackdaw is upgradeable throughout the game, and it is very easily accessible to you when needed. In addition, a new underwater component has also been added. You now have access to a spyglass, which allows for the examination of distant ships, along with all of their cargo and their current strength.
Overall I give this game a solid 10/10 it is by far the best Assassin's Creed game I've played. I really recommend this game because I am 100% sure that Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag will not disappoint you in anyway at all!.

I don't have a witty saying, no "10/10 would _____ again". All I can tell you is I did not enjoy this game.
I've read numerous reviews from users here on Steam, others on youtube, and various game sites. How can so many people enjoy something and I walk away with this feeling of "meh"?
I think it comes down to expectations. I think most people at one point, bought this game because they heard from someone else it's just so good, it can't be explained you just have to play it yourself. Expectations can sometimes be so high that a game can't possibly deliver the imaginary bar you've set.
When I play a game, any game, I derive enjoyment out of the psychology of the developers. To me, playing a game is a silent conversation between two people. The developer says "What do you think about this bit here?" and the answer silently comes across my face as I play the game. Those moments are what I look for, when I can feel the developer speaking directly to me. So in truth this game should be directly up my alley, precisely what I'm looking for, only this time the conversation is much louder with an accent.
Instead, I found myself just walking around. Bored. There is a certain aspect of completionism, where you could keep track of every single branching path. You could conceivably backtrack to every moment you had to make a decision and take the other path. I just couldn't be bothered to. There wasn't a hook. I like the narrator's voice but that can't ever be enough to make a game fun to play. The fun was supposed to be the player experiencing the branches the game had to offer. Finding yourself overthinking and trying to out-think the developers. I think that's where it is. I think that's why I didn't like this game.
I never wanted to argue with the developers. I just wanted a conversation.

Shadow Warrior was a delightful surprise. A perfunctory examination indicates little promise; it looks and sounds like a pile of cliche: "ninja fights army of demons." On closer inspection however, Shadow Warrior is much more. I understand it's meant to be a callback to older shooters like Duke Nukem or Quake, titles which I never got to experience. Yet even without nostalgia, this game enthralled me despite its faults.
The gameplay has little variation; occaisional half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥puzzles always give way to more fighting, but thankfully that combat is far too fun to deride. The whimsically gratuitous carnage from carving through demon hordes with a spirit-laser firing katana is indescribably fun, and the initially lack-luster firearms can be upgraded to satisfying levels of destruction.
While the storyline may be thin and unclear, the characters are engaging satires of modern cliches. Lo Wang and his questionable name make for healthy banter rather than the usual silence gravely grunts of self-insertion oriented shooters.
Altogether Shadow Warrior is a must-play for any shooter fan, so long as one doesn't mind the occaisional slightly racist Wang pun.

Seriously: This is a very good, story-driven shooter in the vein of ye olden days. It starts off (and keeps being) very wacky, with a not-so-subtle 80s-to-90s action movie vibe (quiffs and one-liners galore), but - without going into spoilerish details - turns into something almost dramatic, and sad in the end.
The gameplay is fast and furious, but not unfair. Ok, sometimes you might get squiched in a cavalcade of demons, but even if push comes to shove, the auto-save system kicks in and you don't lose much progress. Of note are the chapters, or levels: It's not the tunnelvision you might be used from current shooters, but rather something with actual thought in the design. There are no quest markers, no "You are going the wrong way". Sometimes you have to backtrack, sometimes the way seems obvious, but there are always hidden, or not so hidden, secrets to be found off the track.
(What I played: Finished the game on normal mode, found some secrets, but not all of them.)

I don't always buy games. But when I do, I make sure they're good ones. And Shadow Warrior is definitely one of them. After watching YouTube sensations TotalBiscuit and Jesse Cox play and give their glowing impressions on it, I knew this was something I could get into.
What really sets Shadow Warrior apart from other FPS is its katana swordplay. Every slash and scission bisects objects and beings in a way that is both appropriate and well animated. And it is just as effective as your arsenal of firearms, if not more so--meaning you can get up close and personal with the katana all the time if you really want to. And that's what I like the most about the gameplay: you as a player have a choice on how you want to upgrade weapons and skills. Will you build yourself around guns, swordplay, or a bit of both? That's up to you.
However, what speaks to me most about any game like Shadow Warrior is its attention to detail. For example, the first level has a garden rendering cherry blossoms, rock surfaces, waterfalls, and bamboo forests with spectacular fidelity. And apart from a few dark industrial-themed environments, that kind of quality eye candy never lets up all the way to the end. And the details don't stop with the graphics. Voice acting is witty, modern, and enjoyable. It is never cringeworthy. And the music is absolutely top notch, capable of evoking scale and drama during boss fights, as well as calm and tension before combating an enemy horde in the areas leading up to it.
A game that delivers both mechanically and viscerally while being pleasantly enjoyable to the easily squeemish is a win in my books. I would highly recommend Shadow Warrior to everyone.

Let me tell you some things about this game:
+Offers a lengthy adventure (I completed 100% in 28 hours and there is still more I could do if I wish)

+The controls are very fine tuned and it always feels like it was my fault if I died and not simply poor game design
+The bosses are sick AF and they all have really cool moves / patterns / styles to them
+The game manages to never feel linear at all, it has no direct markers telling you where to go it simply throws you into the world (Hallownest it is called) and leaves the exploring up to you
+The Soundtrack is bomb. These indie company hits lately always offer a memorable and groovy soundtrack and this game is no different. It offers a few solid themes for many of the fight scenes as well as beautiful atmospheric soundtracks which fit the areas so nicely
+Oh and did I mention the game looks beautiful? Go check images of this game right now like the area "The City of Tears" and just marvel at the amount of detail put into the scenery. For a game this big the art style and attention to detail is truly impressive

Hollow Knight has been a favorite of mine for one main factor: simplicity. While most games I encounter these days like to showcase flashy and intricate mechanics, Hollow Knight starts the player with only a few core mechanics: jump, slash, and heal. Even with such few options, the game still feels like it has everything it needs, only adding a few spells and movement enhancements. The few options still yield a sense of control with the character, in that the "jump" button will cause the character to jump higher the longer it is held, and the "slash" button uses all four orthagonal directions.
Aside from the mechanics, the art style was particularly captivating to me. Again following a simplistic design, I personally found certain areas and enemies to be interesting and pretty. Along with a solid soundtrack, everything comes together for a well made and "finished" game.
The real fun of the game comes in the many and frequent boss fights throughout the game. Each boss has its own special set of moves, and the player has to learn to read each bosses actions and learn how to dodge and counterattack each one. While some bosses are more predictable going into the fight and easier to learn, some bosses had taken longer periods of time to finally defeat. Content aside from those bosses are fine in that it's not overbearing on the lore and side quests, but still is available to the player if they are interested.
There are downsides I see to this game. One is that the game requires backtracking a lot, and in such a large map with many parts, those portions of the game can seem tedious. I personally enjoyed the exploring bits of the game, but at times the running around seemed extensive and annoying. The other is that the game doesn't prompt where to go next, and so the player could be stuck trying to find the next piece before they can advance in the story. Some may enjoy the lack of direction, while others may not enjoy trying to find the very edges of unexplored rooms and getting lost in the process.
Overall, the game seems simplistic while still feeling like it has substantial and interesting content to it. Parts between major bosses and sections of the game can be tedious in how much backtracking and exploring needs to be done, but the freedom to roam and explore can also be a positive side to it. I highly recommend Hollow Knight

Hello random internet people, and awesome people that I love so much that rate my reviews down without an explanation as to why (no, really - I love you guys!). Welcome to my review of
! As always, you can skip to the bottom for a summary, if you really don't feel like reading.
"Admiral Larino, you recommended this game! That means you really liked it, right?" - That's most certainly right little voice from within my head (I thought you moved to Virginia...)! I liked this game for a number of reasons, and I'm going to make sure I explain them as best as I can in this review!
This game tries to blend the awesomeness that shooters used to be before they were made with screaming 12-year-olds in mind, with the technological advantages that exist in modern day game development.
That means not only throwing logic and that oh-so-molded false sense of "realism" out the window, but also dragging it to the very top of the empire state building, slashing it to bits with a katana, and then roundhouse kicking the bits off the skyscraper so you can watch them plummet to the pavement below!
In fact, that fairly accurately summarizes what this game is all about! Replace the empire state building with Asian-styled environments, and logic and realism with demons, and you have this game!
puts you in control of Lo Wang. If Duke Nukem were Chinese, this would be the result. Cheesy one-liners, wielding rocket launchers with a single hand, and carelessly rushing into battle against hordes of demons are all characteristics of this game's antagonist, much like you would expect.
The game has a story, but it's not really anything you're likely going to pay much attention to. It's not really that deep, and it doesn't matter, because the gameplay was the primary focus, which is, without argument, the strongest point of this game!
The gameplay offers you three different methods of unleashing havoc upon enemies - melee attacks, Ki attacks, and your vast array of firearms.
Melee is probably the best part of the game - Spinning around and killing enemies in a circle around you, dashing at high speed and impaling an enemy, and hacking your way through a swarm never ceases to be entertaining.
Then we have the Ki abilities - They're great, they really are, but I personally never really saw much use for them. These include hurling enemies into the air, shielding yourself, and regenerating your health. In a way, it does give off a slight "Bioshock" feel if you really use these.
Finally, the guns. The guns aren't particularly interesting, really, as they're about what you'd expect. That's not to say it can't be fun to unleash havoc with dual SMGs, or my favorite "gun": the crossbow. However... The guns just don't feel like they're really making a huge impact on the enemies most of the time, and in a way, most of them feel sort of like an afterthought, that's really my only gripe with them.
On the bright side with the guns, however, each and every one of them has three upgrades, all three of which change the appearance of the gun! I LOVED this concept when I first saw it in Bioshock, and it's still awesome in this game! It should also be noted that you can also upgrade your skills and ki abilities.
Also, you may have read "health regeneration" and thought "Oh great... one of those.", but you're wrong! the Health regeneration ability only brings you up to a certain amount, and you can still very easily die. There are skills to make your katana's chi-attacks replenish your health, but on higher difficulties, you'll still face a hefty challenge.
I've heard some people claim this game hurls endless swarms of enemies at you toward the end - Let me just say that those people are lying, because after beating the game, I can say that this isn't true. The game does have some fairly long battles toward the end, with plenty of waves, but there is never a case where you're just constantly spammed with enemies until you make your way through an area. In fact, in some cases, I kind of wished that the waves had been a bit more intense.
"But Larino, you said this game lives up to the classics! How does it do that?" - Well little voice in my head, it does that in a number of ways!
For one, the game introduces something I've been dying to see for awhile now in modern day shooters - bosses that actually look and feel like bosses from back when big monstrous freaks being shot down was official daily hobby #1 of shooter game antagonists. The bosses in this game are huge, and look awesome.
But there's a downside to the bosses - There's only three in total, and the very first one was honestly the most exciting with the landscape and the whole scene going on as fire feels like it's everywhere and I frantically fire at this giant armored brute. That's not to say the second fight was bad, but the second one just felt a little simplistic with the fact that the scenery really wasn't that exciting, and there didn't seem to be any epic battle music like the first one had. The final boss, on the other hand... was very underwhelming. I won't spoil it, but just don't expect much.
But that point aside, we have the next thing I loved that brings me back to the classics - Secrets galore! There's hidden stuff all over the levels. Some of the secrets are better placed than others, however. In fact, some secrets I sort of just stumbled upon by casually walking along what I thought was the main progression path, while others were in very creative and interesting spots.
Overall, the game does a good job of trying to bring back some of the glory of the classics. There's a few things that could have been done better, like the guns and the latter two bosses. However, for the variety of upgrade options, the fun and chaotic battles you can have, and the vast number of secrets you can find in this game, I highly recommend it to anyone who likes classic shooters, and wants to see something even remotely close to that done with modern day video game development technology.

Over the years, shooters have made enemies more complex, included RPG elements, attempted epic tales and had moments where it directly addresses the player. These elements collectively drag down the flow and leave a mess of a game behind, which is unfortunately in this case Shadow Warrior.
Shadow Warrior tries to be a competent shooter and succeeds in that regard but is bogged down by far too much to be worth the effort. At first glance there seems to be a variety of weapons and skills, which can be tailored to the way one wants to play. But the variety comes across rather dull with the tedious weapon upgrade system and the woefully small amount of enemies you actually end up fighting. The enemy behaviour is mediocre at best and downright annoying at worst. Some of the skills and upgrades and completely useless make no sense in context, and a majority of the weapons are not as powerful as we've come to expect, the flamethrower and crossbow in particular.
Moving on from what Shadow Warrior is about, we come to what it's not; the story. In a game that already has a flow so broken, why it felt it needs to have overlong stylised cutscenes and such a heavy focus on the characters, it ends up having many of them with odd behavior and no motivation, with the protaganist being my primary example here. None of the "witty" remarks made by Lo Wang or his pocket demon are funny, with the humour coming from the fortune cookies you pick up, which are secret items in themselves and have to be sought after to be found.
Speaking of secret items, there are phrases, names, and even sections of the game which reference other games, which breaks the immersion when you notice how out of place they are. As a close reletive to the Duke Nukem games, I can see how this practice would come about, however it obviously didn't learn from Duke Not Finished on how those references aren't funny. Most jarring of all are the arcade cabinets.The aesthetic does feel rather inconsistent at times, although the environments move fluidly from city to docks and underworld to mountains. In addition to that, the levels themselves are breathtaking near the end of the game with the second boss fight being the most memorable part of the game.
Overall, I'm giving this game a thumbs down. The fun and memorable moments of the game are soured by the long and dreary sections between them and the irritating gameplay which just doesn't feel worth the effort. It's not a terrible game, more of a disappointment due to my excitement prior to playing it. For the base asking price, you'll be getting more irritation than it's worth, which is never a good thing.

Let me tell you some things about this game:
+Offers a lengthy adventure (I completed 100% in 28 hours and there is still more I could do if I wish)
+The combat is so tight! Not only are the mechanics themselves simple and crisp but they are also super deep with things like charms which you can equip to give certain abilities and other classic staples in these types of games like a dash / double jump / wall jump
+The controls are very fine tuned and it always feels like it was my fault if I died and not simply poor game design
+The bosses are sick AF and they all have really cool moves / patterns / styles to them
+The game manages to never feel linear at all, it has no direct markers telling you where to go it simply throws you into the world (Hallownest it is called) and leaves the exploring up to you
+The Soundtrack is bomb. These indie company hits lately always offer a memorable and groovy soundtrack and this game is no different. It offers a few solid themes for many of the fight scenes as well as beautiful atmospheric soundtracks which fit the areas so nicely
+Oh and did I mention the game looks beautiful? Go check images of this game right now like the area "The City of Tears" and just marvel at the amount of detail put into the scenery. For a game this big the art style and attention to detail is truly impressive

Hello random internet people, and awesome people that I love so much that rate my reviews down without an explanation as to why (no, really - I love you guys!). Welcome to my review of
! As always, you can skip to the bottom for a summary, if you really don't feel like reading.
"Admiral Larino, you recommended this game! That means you really liked it, right?" - That's most certainly right little voice from within my head (I thought you moved to Virginia...)! I liked this game for a number of reasons, and I'm going to make sure I explain them as best as I can in this review!
This game tries to blend the awesomeness that shooters used to be before they were made with screaming 12-year-olds in mind, with the technological advantages that exist in modern day game development.
That means not only throwing logic and that oh-so-molded false sense of "realism" out the window, but also dragging it to the very top of the empire state building, slashing it to bits with a katana, and then roundhouse kicking the bits off the skyscraper so you can watch them plummet to the pavement below!
In fact, that fairly accurately summarizes what this game is all about! Replace the empire state building with Asian-styled environments, and logic and realism with demons, and you have this game!
puts you in control of Lo Wang. If Duke Nukem were Chinese, this would be the result. Cheesy one-liners, wielding rocket launchers with a single hand, and carelessly rushing into battle against hordes of demons are all characteristics of this game's antagonist, much like you would expect.
The game has a story, but it's not really anything you're likely going to pay much attention to. It's not really that deep, and it doesn't matter, because the gameplay was the primary focus, which is, without argument, the strongest point of this game!
The gameplay offers you three different methods of unleashing havoc upon enemies - melee attacks, Ki attacks, and your vast array of firearms.
Melee is probably the best part of the game - Spinning around and killing enemies in a circle around you, dashing at high speed and impaling an enemy, and hacking your way through a swarm never ceases to be entertaining.
Then we have the Ki abilities - They're great, they really are, but I personally never really saw much use for them. These include hurling enemies into the air, shielding yourself, and regenerating your health. In a way, it does give off a slight "Bioshock" feel if you really use these.
Finally, the guns. The guns aren't particularly interesting, really, as they're about what you'd expect. That's not to say it can't be fun to unleash havoc with dual SMGs, or my favorite "gun": the crossbow. However... The guns just don't feel like they're really making a huge impact on the enemies most of the time, and in a way, most of them feel sort of like an afterthought, that's really my only gripe with them.
On the bright side with the guns, however, each and every one of them has three upgrades, all three of which change the appearance of the gun! I LOVED this concept when I first saw it in Bioshock, and it's still awesome in this game! It should also be noted that you can also upgrade your skills and ki abilities.
Also, you may have read "health regeneration" and thought "Oh great... one of those.", but you're wrong! the Health regeneration ability only brings you up to a certain amount, and you can still very easily die. There are skills to make your katana's chi-attacks replenish your health, but on higher difficulties, you'll still face a hefty challenge.
I've heard some people claim this game hurls endless swarms of enemies at you toward the end - Let me just say that those people are lying, because after beating the game, I can say that this isn't true. The game does have some fairly long battles toward the end, with plenty of waves, but there is never a case where you're just constantly spammed with enemies until you make your way through an area. In fact, in some cases, I kind of wished that the waves had been a bit more intense.
"But Larino, you said this game lives up to the classics! How does it do that?" - Well little voice in my head, it does that in a number of ways!
For one, the game introduces something I've been dying to see for awhile now in modern day shooters - bosses that actually look and feel like bosses from back when big monstrous freaks being shot down was official daily hobby #1 of shooter game antagonists. The bosses in this game are huge, and look awesome.
But there's a downside to the bosses - There's only three in total, and the very first one was honestly the most exciting with the landscape and the whole scene going on as fire feels like it's everywhere and I frantically fire at this giant armored brute. That's not to say the second fight was bad, but the second one just felt a little simplistic with the fact that the scenery really wasn't that exciting, and there didn't seem to be any epic battle music like the first one had. The final boss, on the other hand... was very underwhelming. I won't spoil it, but just don't expect much.
But that point aside, we have the next thing I loved that brings me back to the classics - Secrets galore! There's hidden stuff all over the levels. Some of the secrets are better placed than others, however. In fact, some secrets I sort of just stumbled upon by casually walking along what I thought was the main progression path, while others were in very creative and interesting spots.
Overall, the game does a good job of trying to bring back some of the glory of the classics. There's a few things that could have been done better, like the guns and the latter two bosses. However, for the variety of upgrade options, the fun and chaotic battles you can have, and the vast number of secrets you can find in this game, I highly recommend it to anyone who likes classic shooters, and wants to see something even remotely close to that done with modern day video game development technology.

Over the years, shooters have made enemies more complex, included RPG elements, attempted epic tales and had moments where it directly addresses the player. These elements collectively drag down the flow and leave a mess of a game behind, which is unfortunately in this case Shadow Warrior.
Shadow Warrior tries to be a competent shooter and succeeds in that regard but is bogged down by far too much to be worth the effort. At first glance there seems to be a variety of weapons and skills, which can be tailored to the way one wants to play. But the variety comes across rather dull with the tedious weapon upgrade system and the woefully small amount of enemies you actually end up fighting. The enemy behaviour is mediocre at best and downright annoying at worst. Some of the skills and upgrades and completely useless make no sense in context, and a majority of the weapons are not as powerful as we've come to expect, the flamethrower and crossbow in particular.
Moving on from what Shadow Warrior is about, we come to what it's not; the story. In a game that already has a flow so broken, why it felt it needs to have overlong stylised cutscenes and such a heavy focus on the characters, it ends up having many of them with odd behavior and no motivation, with the protaganist being my primary example here. None of the "witty" remarks made by Lo Wang or his pocket demon are funny, with the humour coming from the fortune cookies you pick up, which are secret items in themselves and have to be sought after to be found.
Speaking of secret items, there are phrases, names, and even sections of the game which reference other games, which breaks the immersion when you notice how out of place they are. As a close reletive to the Duke Nukem games, I can see how this practice would come about, however it obviously didn't learn from Duke Not Finished on how those references aren't funny. Most jarring of all are the arcade cabinets.The aesthetic does feel rather inconsistent at times, although the environments move fluidly from city to docks and underworld to mountains. In addition to that, the levels themselves are breathtaking near the end of the game with the second boss fight being the most memorable part of the game.
Overall, I'm giving this game a thumbs down. The fun and memorable moments of the game are soured by the long and dreary sections between them and the irritating gameplay which just doesn't feel worth the effort. It's not a terrible game, more of a disappointment due to my excitement prior to playing it. For the base asking price, you'll be getting more irritation than it's worth, which is never a good thing.

Game is incredible! If you are a fan of metroidvanias buy it. It is only $15. The amount of content here is astounding. An average playthrough takes 20-30 hours. Seriously one of, if not my favorite game of 2017.
- Atmosphere and music are wonderful. Soundtrack is memorable. Each area in Hollow Nest feels different and masterfully designed. It was an absolute blast to explore the depths. The world is huge and allows the player to choose their path. Get ready to do some backtracking!
- Beautiful hand drawn art style. The cutscenes and characters designs are cute yet creepy. There are tons of enemies and inventive bosses (130+ enemies and 30+ bosses).
- Tight controls with plenty of abilities to find. The sense of progression is great. You become stronger and more confident as you play. You can also equip charms that give you unique traits.
- Challenging! (think Dark Souls) You will die a lot on boss fights. Learning enemies attack patterns are key to winning these fights. Only one boss felt unfair.

In conclusion, Hollow Knight offers a solid experience through and through. It is an outstanding value for $15. Without any exaggeration, it is one of the best Metroidvania games ever made and one of the most prominent titles this year.

So, Hollow Knight.
First, I'll go through the things I didn't like about the game. I'll start by talking about the exploration aspect. Even though the world is vast, near the end of the game you realise that all the areas, behind all their specific mechanics and art, are all rather similar. There are some areas such as the Ancient Basin, Kingdom's Edge and Howling Cliffs that just feel a bit unfinished, and the best exploration done is limited to discovering a new area, meaning most of it is done in that small section of mid-game after passing through the Fungal Wastes, where you have the option to go wherever you want.
As for bosses, there are a couple of areas which I felt needed a boss such as the Hive and Deepnest, but even some of the areas with actual bosses didn't really feel that brilliant. The main offenders for me were Nosk and Marmu. If you've fought Marmu you'll know what I mean, but for Nosk I just felt like most of the fight you're trying to cheese him down, sitting, healing in the corner where he can't catch you. Still fun, just not as fun as the other bosses. Radiance wasn't that fun but this is mostly because I had trouble with lag and its attacks are quite luck-based.
On the subject of combat, there are a couple of quibbles I have, notably my issues with charms and the lack of diversity, especially early on. For the beginning of the game they're just various helpers, and it's only towards mid-end game that they start developping into full builds with different playstyles. I think it would be better if there were builds right from the start, and it went super-deep later on. I also think it would be quite fun if there was more depth to the sword skills (cyclone slash, dash slash and great slash) as at the moment it's simply a matter of holding down the attack button when there's nothing to hit. This is also a thing with how you unlock the dash and doublejump later into the game, but much less so. I also think the parry mechanic is a bit crap, but I don't really have any better ideas.
My main issue with the game, however, is the changing difficulty of enemies and stat upgrades. Come on guys. This is supposed to be a game about exploration, and fighting things in the order you want, so I think that all areas after the Crossroads and Greenpath should be of roughly equal difficulty, and that that stupid nailmaster should shove his hammer where the Radiance don't shine because what's the point in a game about exploration where you have stat upgrades, so if you pass an early area with a level 3 nail it's a complete breeze, no challenge involved. Also how if you go to difficult areas early on it's simply not balanced.
So what did I like about the game? EVERYTHING ELSE.
The bosses are fantastic, the music and art direction fit so perfectly, the story, even though it feels a bit unfinished, is told brilliantly, the controls and general movement and combat mechanics make you feel like you're in complete control of your character, and make that impact known to the player. The healing system is one of the best I've ever seen in a game, and there are very, VERY few moments where I feel bored or like the game has cheated me. I never got annoyed with a boss, thinking it wasn't my fault I lost (except laggy radiance), and all the backtracking was fine.
If I've made it look at all like I dislike this game in any way (apart from stat upgrades), then you'd be SEVERELY wrong. I absolutely adore this game. This game is easily in my top 5 games of all time and is standing for top 3. If we're only including platformers, then it's an easy #1. This game is purely amazing in every way I can think of (again apart from stat upgrades), and I'm basically just scraping the bottom of the barrel for things I don't like about it.
The only thing I truly got annoyed about was the stupid stat upgrades and difference in difficulty of areas, as I feel like this goes completely against what they set out to achieve, (mind you throughout the game I thought the difficulty was good, I just thought I should have the right to go explore the hive immediately after the fungal wastes and not be looked down upon by the developers) and I love everything else about the game.
So in short, do you like platformers? Do you like fantastic art direction and soundtrack? Do you like cool story? If you like at least zero of the above, GO GET THIS GAME!

Battlerite condenses MOBAs down to teamfights. This can be great, like a rocket league version of dota. You jump in, casual or competitive, play quick rounds with all action and no frills, no items to memorize, no hundred+ heroes to recognize. There's no RNG, no gimmicks, just the same team fights, over and over and over.
Which leads to the one potential downside: It's JUST teamfights. Like a movie, even a 5 minute one, it cannot be ALL climax. There must be some build up, otherwise even the best moment lacks memorability. In the same way that losses are merely fleeting pinpricks on your ego, wins are as well.
I still think Battlerite is fantastic. It accomplishes what it sets out to do with AAA polish, even in early access. I worry though, that despite having gameplay depth, it will have trouble having lasting appeal without resorting to adding new heroes every month like every other MOBA. This however, is a troublesome flaw with their design, not their execution, which is more than I can say for many games today.

It featuers a pleathora of weapons like rocket launchers, machine guns, and the most fun weapon in my opinion, the katana. Cons

The number one issue with this game though, is the instant death triggers. falling in water, falling a semi high height, these deaths are incredibly frustrating and can make the game really unenjoyable to play.
Overall. a wonderful game that I whole heartedly reccommed to any FPS/Adventure fan.

Similar to Serious Sam I first had to get a feeling of the game. Being a good looking, widely new interpreted version of the old game, it first feels...awkward. I tried to figure out the sword, and tried to figure out the guns, being frustrated, until I realized, this game isnt about finding the right time and spot to hit and shoot.
Just hit and shoot your enemy.
This game is all about speed and awareness.
You are some kind of master assassin, who has to claim some mysterious sword from a japanese crime clan. Very fast you will be confronted with magic, CHI, KI, demons and a lot of other mythical crap.
While in most games, your melee weapon is a more a tool than a weapon, this game is refreshing different.
around 3/4 of the combat I could solve with the sword, the guns are for special tasks. Taking out bigger enemys, comanding and summoning units, flying ones or laying down massive AOE into an enemy group.
Weapons like the Pistol and the SMG feeling totally useless in most of the fights are actually impressive against big single targets and mostly used for the massive bossfights.
Everything is upgradable. While finding money everywhere, you can upgrade your weapons, making them stronger, faster and more precise. Also every weapon gets a alternate fire mode, which always is a great fun.
Then you have a great set of abilitys you can unlock from faster movement, damage to using demon skulls as a weapon, healing yourself and big energy blasts.
The combat system is mostly based on your movement, aim and the right use of your abilitys.
The story being a little bit confusing and irrelevant, the dialogues are great work. Even while my second playthrough, I still listening to everything, and dont skipping any cutscene.
The game is a great piece of classic FPS in new grafics and I hope there will be more.

The combat starts out not feeling great, but with a few charms it quickly becomes incredible. My only real gripe is that getting knocked back when you hit an enemy feels terrible, but it only takes a couple hours to get a charm that removes that completely. As you gain combat abilities, going back through old areas becomes a joy. Crushing enemies and moving around them with acrobatic ease.
It's worth noting that this game is LONG. Much longer than most modern metroidvanias. The world map is enormous, and searching out every secret would easily take 40 hours.
Highly recommended.

I went into this game expecting a 6-8 hour romp through Cute Bug World. I would have been content with this. Instead, however, it took me 24 hours to finish the game (not even 100% (but close)) and Cute Bug World was significantly darker than I expected.
The game itself doesn't do anything groundbreaking. There's nothing wildly unique about it, aside from being the only game I've played that's entirely about bugs since A Bug's Life on PS1. This is fine because it doesn't need to be innovative to be very good. The enemy design is incredibly varied (I honestly can't believe how many enemy types are in this game), and most of the bosses are very fun. The difficulty is very balanced too; I don't think I ever felt that something was far too easy or too hard, though some optional challenges are a little obnoxious.
The game is visually and audibly gorgeous. The graphics are so varied and so consistently great that I can't believe this game was ever released. I honestly can't remember much of the music even though the game's soundtrack gets a lot of praise, but I think that's because the music was designed to be background music more than anything. (UPDATE: I LISTENED TO IT ON ITS OWN AND YEAH IT'S PRETTY GOOD) The ambient sound effects, though, are incredible, and really build the atmosphere. I've entered areas and immediately exited them because I hadn't found a checkpoint in a while and was too spooked to continue.
My biggest gripe is probably with the game's plot, lore, worldbuilding ,etc.. Not because it's bad; it's not. It's great. But, and I'm loathe to say this, it's like Dark Souls. It's really Dark Souls! Ridiculously Dark Souls. If you've played Dark Souls with even a basic understanding of what was going on in that game, not too far into Hollow Knight will you say "isn't this just Dark Souls?" Aside from the plot itself, the way it and the characters are presented is also very similar to Dark Souls. I honestly like this, but geez, it's just too Dark Souls.
Despite being too Dark Souls, I cannot recommend Hollow Knight enough. It's definitely one of the best games of its genre.

Taking inspiration from succesful games is great. Making a 2D ripoff of great games is not. They really ought to be paying Hidetaka Miyazaki royalties for this. Dungeon Defenders adds a new twist to tower defense with a mishmash of RPG, action, and tower defense gameplay elements making for a worthwhile investment. There is plenty of content to keep players busy – whether it be working their way through the campaign and tackling challenges. It’s not with its setbacks, though, with the less-than-exciting combat system and loot that feels more like a chore than a reward system.
Tower defense sits at the heart of Dungeon Defenders. The player takes on the role of a Squire, Apprentice, Huntress, or Monk using traps, barricades and magic to defend the castle from an army of evil creatures these would-be child heroes have mistakenly unleashed. Each level plays out in an arena with several entry points for enemies to spawn from. It is the player’s job to analyze the level map and exploit choke points with barricades and traps to prevent enemies from destroying the Eternia crystal at the center of the map. The game is played from the third-person perspective, requiring characters to traverse the map to set up towers while battling enemies along the way.
Enemies are varied and numerous, requiring different strategies to counter their abilities. Hulking orcs will devastate defenses, mages heal enemy units, and suicidal kobolds rush towers with dynamite strapped to their backs. Minibosses in the form of giant ogres made us rethink our tower placement in several situations and the major bosses present the biggest challenges in the game.
Dungeon Defenders has all of the workings of the standard RPG fused into the tower defense gameplay. Player classes have unique abilities, armor, weapon types, and towers. Killing enemies, conquering campaign levels, and completing challenges earns experience which unlocks abilities and towers as well as more powerful items. Character and tower attributes can be upgraded with points earned upon leveling through a somewhat confusing menu system – improving maximum health, damage, casting speed, and movement speed, among others.
All of these features add a great deal of replayability to the game – as does the multiplayer. Once we worked through the levels and beefed up one character, we wanted to level up a complementary character to make proper use of the character swap feature and get the upper hand on some of the more difficult challenges. Setting up spiked barricades as the Squire and switching to the Apprentice to place projectile throwing magic towers makes for a devastating combination. It feels great to level up a character, unlock the advanced towers, and add them to your defense strategy. Playing with a friend or three adds a new dimension in strategy as we were required to actively communicate in tower placement, mana distribution, and repair efforts to hold back the onslaught. The real fun comes in joining a party of friends to tackle the hardest challenges and picking up epic loot.
Unfortunately the action aspect of gameplay falls short. The combat became stale very quickly. Although the characters have special abilities like the Squire’s spin attack or the Huntress’ invisibility, we rarely found a need to use them. Enemies were easily dispatched with well-placed towers and planning trap layouts and developing strategies was fun, but jumping into the fray was not – especially with the melee characters. Combat essentially involves mashing on the one attack button and maybe throwing in a special ability for kicks. Neither feels particularly effective and leaves the combat feeling shallow.
Another problem we had with Dungeon Defenders was the loot. Items can be found in treasure chests and is also dropped by enemies. Picking up epic new armor or weapons and equipping them to benefit from their attribute bonuses is a strong motivator to up the difficulty on the challenges, but the problem lies in having to sort through piles and piles of useless loot at the end of a wave. Checking each dropped item’s stats to compare to our equipped set slowed the game down considerably since all of the loot is spread across the map and it takes at least a few seconds to inspect an item. While we could just run through the map and throw everything into our item box to review later, having fewer, more useful drops would have kept loot gathering from becoming such a chore.
Dungeon Defenders is a worthwhile addition to your game library with plenty of content for the price. Although the combat falls short, the tower defense gameplay, RPG elements, and the challenging game modes will have fans of tower defense delighted.

I want to like Hollow Knight, but I can't.
Aesthetically, musically, it's on point. The combat is nothing to sneeze at too, with some fine bosses. The polish in Hollow Knight is absolutely incredible for an indie game at this price point.
But so damn much of this game bogs down in the travelling. Too few save points, too few fast travel points. It feels like some of the worst parts of the original Dark Souls where runbacks, or even backtracks to explore other opportunities involve so much tedious hiking over terrain you've already cleared that it becomes disspiriting. Every boss fight or spike maze failure feels like it means 20 screens of sleepwalking with no real threat to get back to where you died. Heaven forbid you vaguely remember a path you might be able to tackle with a new power. Or remember a merchant squirreled away somewhere you finally have enough cash to shop at. You just have to route through half the world to get there. I sincerely hope you remembered those prices accurately.*
In the end, the game just felt like a chore, an obligation. That I was just slogging through this boring crap because I was pot-committed and that's what you're supposed to do in a Metroidvania. I can put up with a lot of dumb design in a Metroidvania (I played all three DS Castlevanias after all.) but I just can't take what Hollow Knight asks me to swallow to get to the good parts.
As a side note, the charm system is an incredibly cool idea: X equipment slots, and Y charms that each take Z slots, each granting you different abilities... Unfortunately, those abilities end up usually being crap like "Show yourself on the map" or "Auto-gather all the loot," so you can't even stack fun abilities because you're too busy filling those slots with the "Make the game less of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥quot; near-mandatory options.
Aesthetically, the game owes a lot to Dark Souls, including a completely unnecessary aping of the "get your cash from your dead body" mechanic which only serves to make runbacks both boring AND stressful. As such they substitute a lot of "dead people acting sad" for actual storytelling, but they still manage to be above the average Souls yarn. It is possible the game was meant to not give you a reliable map and ask you to travel by memory, like Dark Souls 1 did. But I can't see it. The game's levels twist and wind back in and around themselves, and very few rooms have any real personality beyond their tileset (And the tilesets are no slouch, mind you...). The only people going through this game by memory are speedrunners on their sixth clear.
Anyway, long story short, an excellent game worn completely thin by just being too damn boring and making getting anywhere or doing anything cool a slog.

The Stanley Parable delivers near-perfect writing and design with its impressively original theme and narrative. Its main star is the overwhelmingly impeccable performance by the excellent disembodied narrator, who couldn't possibly do a better job of making the ambiance feel just right.
The game offers a splendid sense of discovery throughout its entirety despite the player having very little to actually do or interact with. Yet there is no possible fair comparison to games like
, which arguably shares some obvious similarities. It is not a linear experience, though its path branches are definitely finite; the overall experience feels much superior and warrants several playthroughs.
There are some good moments when I laughed out loud or felt impressed by the especially nice developer touches, such as the hilarity in obtaining the 430 achievement and the well-thought museum section. The game is definitely self-conscious without ever being arrogant, ensuring a pleasant though short experience.
However, it ultimately fails to deliver a proper and satisfying conclusion, and lacks any way to track progress. Such downsides are minimal and The Stanley Parable remains highly recommended.

This is the first game in ages that feels like it has the same sort of exploration as Symphony of the Night. You're not just clearing out an area and getting one movement upgrade and moving on. There are tons of connections between areas and unlockable shortcuts. It is truly non-linear, you can find bosses and abilities in very different orders just by wandering into them.
The combat starts out not feeling great, but with a few charms it quickly becomes incredible. My only real gripe is that getting knocked back when you hit an enemy feels terrible, but it only takes a couple hours to get a charm that removes that completely. As you gain combat abilities, going back through old areas becomes a joy. Crushing enemies and moving around them with acrobatic ease.
It's worth noting that this game is LONG. Much longer than most modern metroidvanias. The world map is enormous, and searching out every secret would easily take 40 hours.
Highly recommended.

It's a great game. Even better than I expected. I somewhere read "what duke nukem forever should have been". I tend to agree on that.
For one, it encapsulates all that made the old shooters fun: massive amounts of enemies, weapons that are fun to use and a good mixture of humor. That latter deserves extra mentioning, as the main storyline is actually quite heavy-handed and ridden with family-tragedy. However, with Lo Wang (that's your character), Hoji (your guide) and the fortune cookies doing all the humor part, it actually has a decent narrative overall.
I do have to mention that it's quite clear that this is from the same developers who made Hard reset. Levels are rather linear and have plenty of explosive things in it that can trigger chain reactions (even bikes tend to explode in an extreme way). The visuals may be better and offer more variety, it is clearly on the same engine. Not that I'm complaining: hard reset was a decent game and this one is even better.
Why? Because the upgrade system is more fleshed out, weapons are more fun and the ammo, fortune cookies and easter eggs (like the bunnies) make levels feel less empty.
The katana deserves extra mentioning. Even though this is technically a shooter, the katana is actually a very good weapon. The disadvantage of having to be so close is countered by the extra abilities you can learn from it (as well as it playing part in the plot). While not usefull on bosses, I often switched to this weapon to just start slashing away. It's fun...and deservedly so. :-)
What more to mention? Well...oriental theme, decent music, good variety in levels...I can recommend it. It doesn't automatically heal you, but you have a heal spell you can keep using. In any case: if you like oldskool shooters, you really should try this game. It's worth it. :-)

Hollow Knight has been a pleasant surprise as far as an impulse pickup goes. The aesthetics are gorgeous, the environments ooze atmosphere, and the music is absolutely stunning. The high level of polish and amount of content is just fantastic for a $15 dollar indie game. The best way to describe the game would be a light-hearted dark fantasy metroidvania about bugs. If you're at all interested, look at the promotional material. It should be enough to show you what you're in for.
Once you're much later in the game, simply moving around is a treat, not to mention all the goodies you can find by reexploring areas. There's also plenty of room for you to do things "out of order" if you manage to write down some notes or smack some walls. The game feels responsive and fair. If you're ever having trouble, consider exploring a different area. There's plenty of unique charms to help customize your loadout when needed.
However, that isn't to say the game is without flaws. The game came to a crawling halt to me about 10 hours in, which I'd say for most players would be around the half way point in terms of progression. Depending on how you progressed, the amount of backtracking you'll end up doing becomes tedious, and because fast travel is only available at certain locations, often far away from key NPCs or shortcuts, you can find that you spend huge chunks of time navigating places you've already seen a dozen time, ignoring enemies along the way. I know this is a staple of metroidvanias, but there's no doubt some quality of life issues in moving around the world quickly.
The biggest offense in my book is the boss design. None of the bosses are memorable in any way outside of their character designs. Most bosses have three moves unless they're a major boss, and those moves are often recycled. I can't tell you how many bosses have a combination of a slash, a dash move, a teleport and dive move, and a projectile for their kit. I would have much rather seen half the number of bosses with a much larger move set. Hell, some bosses have one move. One! It's a shame that what feels like should be the highlight of the game was lost to a lack of imagination and resources.
I have high hopes for the future of Hollow Knight and any DLC that may come our way. Team Cherry obviously have an eye for quality in the aesthetics department, I just hope they can realize the value of quality of life, and the importance of climactic boss battles in their future endeavors.
You owe it to yourself to check out of the game if it at all seems interesting.

This is probably the best metroidvania game I've played since symphony of the night. The game play is deliberately simple, but very polished.  The game is also heavily combat focused with  mostly light platforming.  It very much feels like a dark souls  game in this regard. The game also has  a nice sense of progression and player growth, but still manages to retain its difficult throughout. You never become too overpowered and even the most basic enemies can take you down if your not careful. The badge system provides a nice level of player costimization and  the game encourages experimentation. The game is also massive in both length and map size, providing well over 30 hours of game play if you get all the collectibles.  The score is  fantastic and  captures the overall feel of the hollow knight world perfectly.  The story is sparse but also intriguing allowing for interpretation.
I only had few minor gripes with this game, the most annoying of which being the map system. I'm not sure what they were thinking with this,  but having to buy every individual part  of the map individually, including player marker and location markers, seems unnecessarily tedious.  Another issue is  that too many badge slots are used up with utility items  that are practically essential for first  time play throughs; the compass being the most egregious example. My final complaint would  be that the road to the true ending is slightly underwhelming.  Without spoiling  anything, there is an area that becomes extremely platforming focused, which feels out of place in the game. It isn't horrible, but it feels generic  considering the laborious process required to gain access to this area.  Would have much rather perfered some story elements and lore progression.
In conclusion the game is fantastic and with the current game length to price ratio your paying approximately 50 cents per an hour of game play, which is  a steal! If ur a fan casltevania and dark souls  than  buy and support this game!

A fun game to dig into if you are looking for a new tower defense game. Although the graphics are not incredible, the design of each unit and hero character is very unique, which helps for distinguishing whether you need to intervene in your defense (if you are not in towers-only mode, of course). It is very accessible for casual gamers, although some heroes are more frustrating to play with at lower levels than others. The amount of modding that can be done to this game is surprising, though there are separate modes for playing with and without mods.
The game is peppered with DLC though, including massively overpowered DLC heroes. These heroes includes the EV, who can take down ogres (the toughest non-bosses) by layering photon lasers (damages enemies as they cross the laser) next to each other and the Summoner, who can produce units that does not consume the standard defense units, but a separate minion unit system (effectively doubling the amount of defenses that can be produced when in a group). The balance issues do not seem to be a focus for Trendy Ent., since they are focused on developing their free-to-play Dungeon Defenders 2. Also, the leveling system for heroes turns into a grind for the best gears to complement your hero's best defensive structures, only partially alleviated by player-ran shops to purchase greatly desired gears at incredibly high prices.
My biggest disappointments were the simplistic combat animations that don't convey any sense of strength behind the attacks and the lack of synergies between heroes. Although defenses do synergize to an extent, there is no depth to it.
