: "Stanley was fascinated about reading reviews. On this particular day, a new review showed up on his news feed. Stanley got excited. Without hesitation, Stanley began to read it."
: "Sorry, I said, without hesitation, Stanley began to read it."
: "Ahem. Without hesitation, Stanley began to read it."
: "STOP IGNORING ME!"
The Stanley Parable is an odd one partly because it is, in essence, a first-person walking simulator with minimal “gameplay” in it.  So, does it qualify as a game? Not in the traditional sense, that is certain. So what is the catch then?
Unlike other walking simulators you would find around, The Stanley Parable's gimmick is its narrative-driven "gameplay", so to speak. Taking the role of Stanley Parable, you find yourself alone at your desk in the office until one day when the computer screen turns blank and all your colleagues mysteriously vanish. At this point, you begin to follow The Narrator’s voice which “guides” you through the complex by narrating what Stanley would have done in the first place.
But this is where the game shines and, arguably, distinguishes itself from other dull walking simulators. If you remember how games nowadays (maybe even in the past) boast about how they provide the player with choices and consequences which in reality are all just an illusion, then The Stanley Parable showcases and criticises the nature of those narrative constructions in video games. You are given various opportunities to not do what the voice tells you to do which leads to a range of interesting, but twisted events and endings - some are peculiar, some are rather sad and others are hilarious. During each ending though, the playthrough resets and takes you right back from the start where from there on it is up to you to do whatever you want, once again. Whilst this might seem weird, maybe even underwhelming since you begin to think that you just completed the “game”, in fact it is all a continuation. Each reset is a new experience where at least one thing is different from the previous playthrough. As much as I would like to discuss these events and endings, they should be left for the player to experience without spoiling anything. So, the"game"  indirectly encourages the player to break the flow of the narrative and does it in a very smart way, indeed.
It all comes down to the level design which was well thought out. At times, it even starts playing with your mind. It makes you question yourself: Are you in control? Or is the “game”? What if it is neither? Heck, it even mocks both you and itself, including The Narrator. The hidden story behind all this is rather deep once you uncover it. What it tries to achieve here is unprecedented. Additional praises include The Narrator’s voice acting which is excellent and the soundtrack that fits perfectly with the mood of the “game”. Visually, it looks similar to any recent Source game. It has a nice colour pallet and some of its aesthetics resemble something from Aperture Science. In truth, The Stanley Parable does many things right, it seems, making it very hard to criticise it for any flaws or to even be nitpicky. The most obvious observation would be that it is a very short “game” of up to four or five hours if you go for all its endings, I would say. It is even possible to complete it in about five minutes if you follow The Narrator’s instructions. However, based on its scope, I believe it has the right length and does not over stay its welcome. More would have definitely made it actually repetitive.
In conclusion, at the end of the day, I personally found the experience enjoyable and perhaps that is enough to warrant a recommendation. It is a not a traditional game, and I would even say that it is not a game. It acts almost like an interactive playground for the player to experiment various ways to break the narration. But it is uniquely designed, intelligently written and amusing at times. Yes, very creative. Actually, it might as well have the best narrative as far as I am concerned. Personally, I could not find any traditional faults with it, aside from having almost no "gameplay", if that counts. I will admit that this might be the first and only non-game which I really enjoyed. So if you are looking for a traditional game, then do not get The Stanley Parable. You will be disappointed. However, I strongly recommend it for its one-of-a-kind experience which should not be missed nor ignored.
One advice though: Do get it on a sale. I believe ten pounds, or your regional equivalent, is a tad too much for its amount of content, even if it is exceptional. Maybe that is its only flaw actually.

Hollow Knight is a can't miss title.
With elements from a range of popular and adored sources, Hollow Knight is simplistic in its appeal.
Thrust into a world with a goal, but not a motive, the player traverses and appreciates the story, the lore, and the world as they deem appropriate. Characters are unique, with individual voices that speak in gibberish only to establish a sense of personality, and the dialogue itself is engaging.
No review of Hollow Knight will be complete without boasting of the phenomenal OST. Every zone has a unique visual and audible personality.
The gameplay is simple. Swing. Jump. Heal.
A platformer with some combat, and power-ups, is nothing new, and that's part of the appeal. A quality "MetroidVania" isn't easy to reproduce. As the hero explores, they gian access to tremendous new capabilities that unlock paths visble, but inaccessible before, and entire areas that have no bearing on completion.
The story and aethetics of the game itself are dark, and forboding, with a lot of inspiration seeming taken from the Dark Souls franchise.
Hollow Knight is a strong easly contender in 2017 for Game of the Year, and is in my personal favorite games of all time. No praises I could sing would be an accurate enough glowing recommendation.

But so damn much of this game bogs down in the travelling. Too few save points, too few fast travel points. It feels like some of the worst parts of the original Dark Souls where runbacks, or even backtracks to explore other opportunities involve so much tedious hiking over terrain you've already cleared that it becomes disspiriting. Every boss fight or spike maze failure feels like it means 20 screens of sleepwalking with no real threat to get back to where you died. Heaven forbid you vaguely remember a path you might be able to tackle with a new power. Or remember a merchant squirreled away somewhere you finally have enough cash to shop at. You just have to route through half the world to get there. I sincerely hope you remembered those prices accurately.*
In the end, the game just felt like a chore, an obligation. That I was just slogging through this boring crap because I was pot-committed and that's what you're supposed to do in a Metroidvania. I can put up with a lot of dumb design in a Metroidvania (I played all three DS Castlevanias after all.) but I just can't take what Hollow Knight asks me to swallow to get to the good parts.
As a side note, the charm system is an incredibly cool idea: X equipment slots, and Y charms that each take Z slots, each granting you different abilities... Unfortunately, those abilities end up usually being crap like "Show yourself on the map" or "Auto-gather all the loot," so you can't even stack fun abilities because you're too busy filling those slots with the "Make the game less of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥quot; near-mandatory options.
Aesthetically, the game owes a lot to Dark Souls, including a completely unnecessary aping of the "get your cash from your dead body" mechanic which only serves to make runbacks both boring AND stressful. As such they substitute a lot of "dead people acting sad" for actual storytelling, but they still manage to be above the average Souls yarn. It is possible the game was meant to not give you a reliable map and ask you to travel by memory, like Dark Souls 1 did. But I can't see it. The game's levels twist and wind back in and around themselves, and very few rooms have any real personality beyond their tileset (And the tilesets are no slouch, mind you...). The only people going through this game by memory are speedrunners on their sixth clear.
Anyway, long story short, an excellent game worn completely thin by just being too damn boring and making getting anywhere or doing anything cool a slog.

Now THIS is how you reboot a franchise - not the awful mess that was Duke Nukem's most recent outing. The 2 core characters and the fast paced shooting from the original Shadow Warrior returns in this genuinely funny and entertaining piece. New Lo Wang is younger and not an old guy / ridiculious asian stereotype (other than a bit of the 'Engrish' accent). If you look for the many little secrets that are always stashed away in the old school shooters, you can even find little throwback areas to the original game and most of them even use the old school textures.
All the weapons feel distinctly different and handle great, the katana is fantastic and few things come close to a good killing spree with it. You can use money you find laying around the levels to upgrade weapons which lets you upgrade the weapons you enjoy. Each weapon has 3 upgrades with 1 being fairly more expensive but more powerful than the nice little bonuses the other upgrades usually give - these powerful upgrades include dual weilding PDW's, cowboy style revolver shooting, or shooting all the barrels on the shotgun at once. They are nice way to make the weapons feel different from their counterparts and feel reasonably stronger as the game progresses.
There's an also an XP system that rewards fighting with varied weapons, accuracy and quick killing to spend on upgradeable perks that provide new techniques, enhances your current abilities or provides little stat bonuses such as increased health or more ammo on pick ups.
Also out in the world to find are crystals which you use to unlock and upgrade Ki powers. These are helpful but nothing too fantastic. But the combination of weapon and ability upgrades allow you to focus on your playstyle - I focused on upgrading the pistol and PDW first while buffing up my healing ability and survivability and it helped ALOT with boss fights and large swarms of enemies.
The nice thing about this over the original aside from the combat improvements, is the story. Last time it was basically Zilla bad, kill him. This time around we have 2 antagonists, a strange (and damn funny) ally, and a bit of a mystery as to why events are happening. It manages to make Lo Wang much more likeable - he's still a smart aleck♥♥♥♥♥kicker, but with a slightly more human and genuine personality.
My only two complaints are:
(1) I wish there was just a tiny bit more enemy and boss variety. Off the top of my head you got 2 kinds of basic demons, 2 kinds of gross lady demons, some weak flying ones, 2 kinds with shields, yakuza thugs, big buff demons, a lurpy demon that revives weak ones, big pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ones with a weak spot on the back, and ones that blow up. About a dozen types - which to be fair is more than the original game. As for bosses they consist of a large arena style room where you shoot a weakspot until a vital point is exposed. A couple have a little puzzle or trick but nothing that stood out as vastly different. There's constant supplies dropping on the perimiter of the boss rooms too, so don't expect to die on a boss unless you're playing a harder difficulty.
(2) The zoom mechanic on guns is just plain yucky. Rather than hold the right mouse button the standard button is the X key which felt akward to hold and move at the same time. The RMB was reserved for alternate firing on weapons. I was able to deal with this buy putting the alternate input for the zoom as one of the extra buttons on the side of my mouse.
Whether on sale or even for the full 40$ it's a pretty solid package worth playing. As someone who absolutetly destroyed the first game, on normal difficulty it took about 8 hours to clear. But it's worth playing through again on the harder difficulties to unlock even more stuff and find more secrets.

The Stanley Parable delivers near-perfect writing and design with its impressively original theme and narrative. Its main star is the overwhelmingly impeccable performance by the excellent disembodied narrator, who couldn't possibly do a better job of making the ambiance feel just right.
The game offers a splendid sense of discovery throughout its entirety despite the player having very little to actually do or interact with. Yet there is no possible fair comparison to games like
, which arguably shares some obvious similarities. It is not a linear experience, though its path branches are definitely finite; the overall experience feels much superior and warrants several playthroughs.
There are some good moments when I laughed out loud or felt impressed by the especially nice developer touches, such as the hilarity in obtaining the 430 achievement and the well-thought museum section. The game is definitely self-conscious without ever being arrogant, ensuring a pleasant though short experience.
However, it ultimately fails to deliver a proper and satisfying conclusion, and lacks any way to track progress. Such downsides are minimal and The Stanley Parable remains highly recommended.

As far as The Stanley Parable's gameplay goes, it's pretty much a walking simulator. Its controls are: walk forward, backwards, sidestep to the left or to the right, look around and turn, jump, crouch, and occasionally press buttons. So what exactly makes it a game?
The answer is: its unique stories. The Stanley Parable is one of those games that test your own sentiment of importance as an independent player and challenges your own freedom in the face of the video game narrative in an era where games are either "too linear" or "too open without any real content".
Through your choices, you will discover very different experiences of the game, and the amount of attention to details at each and every turn is simply amazing. The narrator of the game ends up evolving from a simple voiceover to a real character, existing alongside you, much like GLaDOS from Portal, except with somewhat less murderous intentions.
It is a very hard task to say more about the game without spoiling it, or ruining the experience a player would have with it, so I can only recommend that you pick it up now, and spare a couple of hours of your day to genuinely get into it, then think about what you've just played.

*THIS IS A REVIEW FOR ARMA II* Steam won't let me review Arma II telling me I need at least 5 minutes recorded in game... For some reason Steam doesn't recognize my game even though everything works properly! So anyways, here it goes:
Arma II, one of the greatest military simulations in the market, second only to Arma III itself. This game, made by Bohemia Interactive, presents itself with very good graphics (if your machine can handle the game properly), a nice set of scenarios for you to complete, cool campaigns (at least 2 from the vanilla game), a fantastic soundtrack and, of course, lots of fun modes for multiplayer.
The game comes also with an Editor which allows you to create both singleplayer missions and multiplayer missions as you see fit. This brings the longevity of the game to a whole new level if we don't count available public servers, allowing you to show your friends how a great military tactitian you are by creating realistic and engaging mission.
The voice acting, though, seems a little bit off. The voice acting during the campaign is just great and at all aspects immersive, but this game lacks non story proper voice acting. You end up telling your fellow squad mates to go to a certain grid and the voice of your character is suddenly different from the one you just heard in the cutscene not to mention it changes with certain words.
On the ther hand the realism of weapons shooting, vehicle handling, aircraft controls and massive war scenarios commanding is at the very top compared with any other game. Here, you'll find the true feeling of being in a war! You hear enemy fire and don't know where it comes from, so you suddenly think the next bullet is coming to you and quickly get down on the floor or find cover behind a wall or an armored vehicle whilst your heart pumps all the adrenaline to your body (this is much more true in multiplayer, either co-op or PvP). Another cool realistic aspect concerns the "get to know the terrain first" meaning that you often find a group of enemies somewhere and despite the urge to start shooting at them you should just get down, grab your binoculars and watch that bearing like your life depends on it (which it kinda does in-game).
The amount of coordination required with the people you play with is, again, realistic and very fun. Having to give accurate enemy bearings to your team, reporting enemy movements, locating enemy vehicles and reporting grids using the Voice over Net makes the game feel so immersive that you even feel you're there yourself.
In general, this is not a common arcade first person shooter like Call of Duty or Battlefield. No, this is something much more war immersive, realistic and, if you like the genre, very addictive in the good way. My personal rating for this game is a smooth 8/10 and in spite of all the good things it has, I don't give it a higher rating because there's, of course, Arma III and some aspects like the voice acting that feel like immersion breaking.
"Make Arma, not war."

I went into this game expecting a 6-8 hour romp through Cute Bug World. I would have been content with this. Instead, however, it took me 24 hours to finish the game (not even 100% (but close)) and Cute Bug World was significantly darker than I expected.
The game itself doesn't do anything groundbreaking. There's nothing wildly unique about it, aside from being the only game I've played that's entirely about bugs since A Bug's Life on PS1. This is fine because it doesn't need to be innovative to be very good. The enemy design is incredibly varied (I honestly can't believe how many enemy types are in this game), and most of the bosses are very fun. The difficulty is very balanced too; I don't think I ever felt that something was far too easy or too hard, though some optional challenges are a little obnoxious.
The game is visually and audibly gorgeous. The graphics are so varied and so consistently great that I can't believe this game was ever released. I honestly can't remember much of the music even though the game's soundtrack gets a lot of praise, but I think that's because the music was designed to be background music more than anything. (UPDATE: I LISTENED TO IT ON ITS OWN AND YEAH IT'S PRETTY GOOD) The ambient sound effects, though, are incredible, and really build the atmosphere. I've entered areas and immediately exited them because I hadn't found a checkpoint in a while and was too spooked to continue.
My biggest gripe is probably with the game's plot, lore, worldbuilding ,etc.. Not because it's bad; it's not. It's great. But, and I'm loathe to say this, it's like Dark Souls. It's really Dark Souls! Ridiculously Dark Souls. If you've played Dark Souls with even a basic understanding of what was going on in that game, not too far into Hollow Knight will you say "isn't this just Dark Souls?" Aside from the plot itself, the way it and the characters are presented is also very similar to Dark Souls. I honestly like this, but geez, it's just too Dark Souls.
Despite being too Dark Souls, I cannot recommend Hollow Knight enough. It's definitely one of the best games of its genre.

: "Stanley was fascinated about reading reviews. On this particular day, a new review showed up on his news feed. Stanley got excited. Without hesitation, Stanley began to read it."
: "Sorry, I said, without hesitation, Stanley began to read it."
: "Ahem. Without hesitation, Stanley began to read it."
: "STOP IGNORING ME!"
The Stanley Parable is an odd one partly because it is, in essence, a first-person walking simulator with minimal “gameplay” in it.  So, does it qualify as a game? Not in the traditional sense, that is certain. So what is the catch then?
Unlike other walking simulators you would find around, The Stanley Parable's gimmick is its narrative-driven "gameplay", so to speak. Taking the role of Stanley Parable, you find yourself alone at your desk in the office until one day when the computer screen turns blank and all your colleagues mysteriously vanish. At this point, you begin to follow The Narrator’s voice which “guides” you through the complex by narrating what Stanley would have done in the first place.
But this is where the game shines and, arguably, distinguishes itself from other dull walking simulators. If you remember how games nowadays (maybe even in the past) boast about how they provide the player with choices and consequences which in reality are all just an illusion, then The Stanley Parable showcases and criticises the nature of those narrative constructions in video games. You are given various opportunities to not do what the voice tells you to do which leads to a range of interesting, but twisted events and endings - some are peculiar, some are rather sad and others are hilarious. During each ending though, the playthrough resets and takes you right back from the start where from there on it is up to you to do whatever you want, once again. Whilst this might seem weird, maybe even underwhelming since you begin to think that you just completed the “game”, in fact it is all a continuation. Each reset is a new experience where at least one thing is different from the previous playthrough. As much as I would like to discuss these events and endings, they should be left for the player to experience without spoiling anything. So, the"game"  indirectly encourages the player to break the flow of the narrative and does it in a very smart way, indeed.
It all comes down to the level design which was well thought out. At times, it even starts playing with your mind. It makes you question yourself: Are you in control? Or is the “game”? What if it is neither? Heck, it even mocks both you and itself, including The Narrator. The hidden story behind all this is rather deep once you uncover it. What it tries to achieve here is unprecedented. Additional praises include The Narrator’s voice acting which is excellent and the soundtrack that fits perfectly with the mood of the “game”. Visually, it looks similar to any recent Source game. It has a nice colour pallet and some of its aesthetics resemble something from Aperture Science. In truth, The Stanley Parable does many things right, it seems, making it very hard to criticise it for any flaws or to even be nitpicky. The most obvious observation would be that it is a very short “game” of up to four or five hours if you go for all its endings, I would say. It is even possible to complete it in about five minutes if you follow The Narrator’s instructions. However, based on its scope, I believe it has the right length and does not over stay its welcome. More would have definitely made it actually repetitive.
In conclusion, at the end of the day, I personally found the experience enjoyable and perhaps that is enough to warrant a recommendation. It is a not a traditional game, and I would even say that it is not a game. It acts almost like an interactive playground for the player to experiment various ways to break the narration. But it is uniquely designed, intelligently written and amusing at times. Yes, very creative. Actually, it might as well have the best narrative as far as I am concerned. Personally, I could not find any traditional faults with it, aside from having almost no "gameplay", if that counts. I will admit that this might be the first and only non-game which I really enjoyed. So if you are looking for a traditional game, then do not get The Stanley Parable. You will be disappointed. However, I strongly recommend it for its one-of-a-kind experience which should not be missed nor ignored.
One advice though: Do get it on a sale. I believe ten pounds, or your regional equivalent, is a tad too much for its amount of content, even if it is exceptional. Maybe that is its only flaw actually.

Shadow Warrior is a must buy for anyone who likes FPS games in the slightest
Story: You play as Lo Wang, who comes off as a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but is incredibly entertaining and has a lot of great one liners. Throughout most of the game, you are accompanied by an entertaining, wisecracking demon sidekick named Hoji. The plot revolves around a demonic invasion occuring as you attempt to track down 3 parts to a legendary sword known as the "Nobitsura Kage". There is a lot of offbeat humor, but nothing is ever gross-out like Duke Nukem Forever. On top of it, the game dips into some pretty heavy story elements, especially near the ending. I don't want to spoil anything, but there is a good but not great story in this game, which is surprising considering the hack and slash gameplay.
Controls: You can play with a gamepad, but I got through just fine with K+M. Performing special moves involves tapping a movement key twice and then one of the mouse buttons, which may feel wonky for some people at first. However, the controls are great overall, and chaining abilities was totally natural for me. There is a "dash" mechanic that allows you to slide around like a mech in Titanfall or in COD: AW. The dash mechanic is great and makes the combat feel fast and fluid. However, be careful not to dash down stairs, or you may dash into midair and then fall 20 feet to a painful landing.
Gameplay: The best part of the game. The game borrows many elements from older FPS games, such as non-regenerating health (although you unlock a skill that allows manual regeneration early on) and no limits on carried weapons. There are a lot of weapons that you will remember from typical FPS games, like an SMG, a  shotgun, a crossbrow, a rocket launcher, and others. You can buy some cool upgrades for them such as dual-wielding SMG and explosive crossbow bolts. However, my favorite weapon in the game is the Katana. It is extremely fun and effective, allowing you to slice through demons with ease. You can perform a bunch of cool manuevers with it, such as launch a slicing projectile through the air, deliver a powerful blow which regenerates your health, or spin around and lop the heads off of everyone around you. There are 3 main upgrade systems in the game: one for weapons, one for passive improvements, and one for powerful magic abilities. The upgrade trees are fairly small but a nice feature, giving you a good sense of progression. One of the problems with the gameplay is how repetitive it can be at times. Many combat sections can feel tedious, especially when flying enemies are introduced. However, this is still a very fun game that you should see through to the end.
There is decent enemy variety, but one of the enemy types can be very annoying. He has a ridiculous amount of health and only one weak point, on his back. Fights against him aren't very fun, which is unfortunate as he is fought frequently near the end of the game. There are 3 boss fights, all of which are quite fun, as you are up against a much larger enemy, making you feel all the more powerful when you bring them down. The final boss was a bit of a letdown, but it's good to see a game with proper, epic boss battles.
Graphics: Textures can look a little rough, but most of the environments, especially early game ones, are great. Beautiful Japanese gardens, a bamboo forest, and a mountaintop castle bathed in red sunset are particular highlights. However, for a good portion of the game you are traversing through docks and the corridor of a ship in some cramped, ugly environments. If only they could be as beautiful as the rest of the game.
Length: It took me 10 hours to beat this game on normal difficulty setting. It should take the average gameer 12-15 hours to beat this game on normal, not counting new game + or harder difficulty settings. Overall a great length for a fairly cheap game.
Overall, Shadow Warrior is a must buy. There are some rough edges, but the product overall is of amazing quality. Anyone who likes FPS games should get this game, now. Don't wait.

As far as The Stanley Parable's gameplay goes, it's pretty much a walking simulator. Its controls are: walk forward, backwards, sidestep to the left or to the right, look around and turn, jump, crouch, and occasionally press buttons. So what exactly makes it a game?
The answer is: its unique stories. The Stanley Parable is one of those games that test your own sentiment of importance as an independent player and challenges your own freedom in the face of the video game narrative in an era where games are either "too linear" or "too open without any real content".
Through your choices, you will discover very different experiences of the game, and the amount of attention to details at each and every turn is simply amazing. The narrator of the game ends up evolving from a simple voiceover to a real character, existing alongside you, much like GLaDOS from Portal, except with somewhat less murderous intentions.
It is a very hard task to say more about the game without spoiling it, or ruining the experience a player would have with it, so I can only recommend that you pick it up now, and spare a couple of hours of your day to genuinely get into it, then think about what you've just played.

Shadow Warrior is a must buy for anyone who likes FPS games in the slightest
Story: You play as Lo Wang, who comes off as a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but is incredibly entertaining and has a lot of great one liners. Throughout most of the game, you are accompanied by an entertaining, wisecracking demon sidekick named Hoji. The plot revolves around a demonic invasion occuring as you attempt to track down 3 parts to a legendary sword known as the "Nobitsura Kage". There is a lot of offbeat humor, but nothing is ever gross-out like Duke Nukem Forever. On top of it, the game dips into some pretty heavy story elements, especially near the ending. I don't want to spoil anything, but there is a good but not great story in this game, which is surprising considering the hack and slash gameplay.
Controls: You can play with a gamepad, but I got through just fine with K+M. Performing special moves involves tapping a movement key twice and then one of the mouse buttons, which may feel wonky for some people at first. However, the controls are great overall, and chaining abilities was totally natural for me. There is a "dash" mechanic that allows you to slide around like a mech in Titanfall or in COD: AW. The dash mechanic is great and makes the combat feel fast and fluid. However, be careful not to dash down stairs, or you may dash into midair and then fall 20 feet to a painful landing.
Gameplay: The best part of the game. The game borrows many elements from older FPS games, such as non-regenerating health (although you unlock a skill that allows manual regeneration early on) and no limits on carried weapons. There are a lot of weapons that you will remember from typical FPS games, like an SMG, a  shotgun, a crossbrow, a rocket launcher, and others. You can buy some cool upgrades for them such as dual-wielding SMG and explosive crossbow bolts. However, my favorite weapon in the game is the Katana. It is extremely fun and effective, allowing you to slice through demons with ease. You can perform a bunch of cool manuevers with it, such as launch a slicing projectile through the air, deliver a powerful blow which regenerates your health, or spin around and lop the heads off of everyone around you. There are 3 main upgrade systems in the game: one for weapons, one for passive improvements, and one for powerful magic abilities. The upgrade trees are fairly small but a nice feature, giving you a good sense of progression. One of the problems with the gameplay is how repetitive it can be at times. Many combat sections can feel tedious, especially when flying enemies are introduced. However, this is still a very fun game that you should see through to the end.
There is decent enemy variety, but one of the enemy types can be very annoying. He has a ridiculous amount of health and only one weak point, on his back. Fights against him aren't very fun, which is unfortunate as he is fought frequently near the end of the game. There are 3 boss fights, all of which are quite fun, as you are up against a much larger enemy, making you feel all the more powerful when you bring them down. The final boss was a bit of a letdown, but it's good to see a game with proper, epic boss battles.
Graphics: Textures can look a little rough, but most of the environments, especially early game ones, are great. Beautiful Japanese gardens, a bamboo forest, and a mountaintop castle bathed in red sunset are particular highlights. However, for a good portion of the game you are traversing through docks and the corridor of a ship in some cramped, ugly environments. If only they could be as beautiful as the rest of the game.
Length: It took me 10 hours to beat this game on normal difficulty setting. It should take the average gameer 12-15 hours to beat this game on normal, not counting new game + or harder difficulty settings. Overall a great length for a fairly cheap game.
Overall, Shadow Warrior is a must buy. There are some rough edges, but the product overall is of amazing quality. Anyone who likes FPS games should get this game, now. Don't wait.

A grand old revitalization of a 1997 Classic. Lo Wang is back, and with slightly less racist jokes this time.
Piting the player against an army of demons and gunmen alike, Shadow Warrior retains exactly what made the original good, while improving upon what it didn't.
Pros:
Lo Wang- A cocky, 80's action movie-style hero. Wang is back to kick♥♥♥♥♥ lob limbs, and toss the occasional one-liner. While some may not find his lack of racist jokes appealing, he seems to be the perfect balance between old and new, and bald.
Combat- As your first weapon is (of course) a katana, you'll find most enemies will go down faster than a bowling ball down an elevator shaft simply swinging your lethal piece of steel at them. Bullets work when you need some distance, but each slash and the flying limbs that accompany it can't be matched.
Exploration- Much as linearity has become second highest on the "Hate list" (aside from microtransactions), SW proves that exploration is not only fun, but rewarding. Most "Secrets" (over 100 of them) are found simply by looking around, and contain either money or karma for upgrades. Good feature.
Visuals- While visuals may not make a game, FWH did a fantastic job of making the enviroment feel real. Each map is eye-candy in and of itself, but wait until everything is dead before taking it in, it'll cost ya.
Difficulty- Rarely is difficulty a pro in a game, but SW proves to know exactly where the sweet spot is. Enemies don't down you in a single hit, but they also don't chip away at your health like scraping off paint with a fork. Enemies do about as much damage as you'd imagine they do. Harder difficulties however maintain the same level of difficulty you'd expect from most games.
Cons:
Wave Rooms- Oh boy, this fun trope that games seem to love adopting. This game has a few (maybe 3 or 4 in total) rooms that simply throw tougher and tougher mobs at you. Can they be handled? Yes. Is it kinda silly in a game about exploration? Also yes.
Only-one-way Enemies- I know I'm cherrypicking; but having enemies that can only be taken down by only one weapon in a game that gives you 9 different weapons, limiting the options seems kinda weird. Especially since the few enemies that do adhere to this are the hardest ones, nice.
I'll try to avoid giving this game a number, mostly because I think that's just plain stupid. But I will say I'd recommend this game. Now go out, and show them who's the bigger Wang.

To me, Hollow Knight has been an incredible experience in all departments; the aesthetics, music, gameplay, mechanics, story and lore- everything was a joy to experience firsthand with no prior knowledge. If you enjoy 2d metroidvania games, or just the adventure of exploring a vast connected world, then you should buy this game. It's worth 14.99, EASY. There's your tl:dr, but if you want more, then allow me to continue...
Hollow Knight's aesthetic is very interesting especially within the backgrounds to the many rooms in the game's maps. The backgrounds look very much like they are simple drawings brought to life, but they still are briming with detail and uniquness from each other. They are not simple tile sprites, copy and pasted around like in classic Metroid games, but all carry a distinct personality based on which room they are in, what purpose the room serves, what is present and so on. This makes the eventual backtracks easier as each room can be distinquished with ease.
Backing this up is the game's absolutely incredible soundtrack, which always fits within their respective areas. Area music is soft, ambient and at times straight up sad and somber, fitting in with the running theme of desolation and ruin the game carries. Boss tracks are always themed perfectly to their owners, from a musical tale of honor, justice and respect, to a depressing, 'I'm so sorry about this' atmosphere which haunts you after the fight is long ended.
There's honestly not much more to say here. You can see the screenshots, and if you want an example of the music then here is a link. Just be aware that there may be spoilers in the comments:
. I warned you. I take no credit for any spoils.
As many other reviewers have likely mentioned, this game has a very intriguing and mysterious story and atmosphere, but I can do one better. I can explain why the story is so good,
It all boils down to the famous saying of SHOW don't TELL. While the story does mainly required dialogue to get you to the end, it its sparce, and large plot points and lore will only be uncovered by where you go, and what you do and see. Heck, the whole game builds up the encounter with the final boss, and yet when you fight, they say NOTHING. No evil monologue, no throw away dialogue, not even a true explaination. And yet, everything is in place for you to work it out for yourself. Even in the best ending, the game throws you a partialy finished puzzle label 'Story' and says "We already know what happened, you played the game, YOU work out what it means". The game sets up the basic premises, then leaves you to work it out for yourself, and a a result you feel like you are actually contributing to the game, instead of simply being told that what you did was important in some way. Of course it doen't mean the story itself is bad or unimportant, it's just that those things are spoilers, and I'm trying hard to avoid those dang things. They're very high in cholesterol. Quite bad for your health.
Now then, the game's mechanics. Oh boy, dis gonna be gud. The game mainly plays as you would expect from the term '2d metroidvania'. Platforming, fighting, exploring, upgrading, backtracking, more platforming (now with upgrades), more upgrading, more fighting (now with upgrades), backtracking to where you were before backtracking (retracking?), explor... OK you get it. However, there are many neat features added to add some spice here and there. Like other metroidvania style games, saving only happens at sparcely located areas across the map; however, these locations are also the only way to fill out your maps, and even then you need to by an area map and quill first. As a result, it is entirely possible to complete the game essentially blind, it you so choose. About half the areas are totally optional, as you can take other paths to your destination, and there is a lot of items that simply aren't required as rewards from these places. Although, my favourite of these is SO good that i'm going to dedicate a whole paragraph to it:
Death. A bit anticlimactic huh? Well let me explain. You may have seen other reviews mention Dark Souls at some point; well in Hollow Knight, when you die you are sent back to the last save bench you used, your special attack meter is locked to half size and your Geo (money) is taken from you. "So what? You back to where you died, grab the money then continue like nothing happened?" NO. When you return to the room where you died (due to spoilery story reasons) a Shade of yourself is there, and NOT HAPPY to see you. This enemy needs to be defeated to undo the effects of death, and acually SCALES WITH YOU. Every 2 hitpoints you have gives it 1 hitpoint, every special attack you have it can use, and it can attack in all directions like you. Oh, and it can fly too. This is pure genius, as it's the game's way of saying "Look, you have max health, awesome specials and powerful attacks. You shouldn't be dying as often, so now I'll punish you for it".
As great as this game is, it is not perfect in every way. Some of the negatives include the following:
- Backtracking through the really large map
- Most of the games equipable charms feel pretty weak compared to others
- There is a lot of backtracking
- The game never really gives you a direction or a path, so progress feels really slow sometimes
- Seriously, the backtracking
- If you lose your Geo, there is no easy way to win it back without grinding
- The backtracking- There is on mission where walk from one end of the map to the other without fasttraveling or getting hit and you only have one shot at it.
- One of the end-game optional areas can F**k right off, as it is pure agrrivating platforming with few ways to heal.
Obviously others will have other gripes but those were some of mine.
However, in all I'd say this game is still worth every cent (or pound. or euro. or yen. or whatever), and you should give it a try at some point.

in my pickup truck, with two of my freedom fighting comrades, heading to Loy Manara. My team, the Indepenents, are currently fighting for control of Takistani towns and villages all over the map. We were aiming to stamp out the OPFOR and the BLUFOR.

With my binoculars I spotted and convoy of OPFOR veichles and they were heading straight up the road to ME. I scrambled my men to disembark my shoddy pickup truck and ordered them to take advantageous posistions. We were going to ambush these idiots. They'll never know what hit 'em. Hidden behind rocks, my lowly farmers with AKs got ready.
The OPFOR BRDM-2 rumbled straight past me and my men, I had been waiting to see the beast's ugly rear and when I got sight of it I readied my RPG. BOOOOOM. Direct hit! ARMAII: Operation Arrowhead has lead to some of the most heart-pounding, gut wrenching and satisfying situations I've ever experienced in a game. Something I never thought would happen in a Military Simulation. The multiplayer is the best part of it, nothing quite beats jumping on with your friends and playing the Takistani guerillas just to roleplay the Taliban. We plant down IEDs and detonate them as a US convoy drives past. We also do the opposite, we play the US Army and jump into Blackhawks and parachute into enemy terrority before delivering American 'Freedom' in the shape of ALOT of bullets.
Graphics still hold up to this day thankfully so the game is a joy to look at as well as being a joy to play. The controls are clunky which admittely is an issue they fixed in ARMA III. There is almost unlimited replayability due to how different the scenarios play out each time, and also thanks to the hundreds of mods on the internet. It's well worth a check, even if you don't think you're into the whole realism part. Just play it with paitience and it's brilliance will shine through. Well worth a purchase.

Story is rather straight forward that could have been a lot better. There are some witty humor thrown into the mix. Wang and Hoji are the primary characters of the game. Your encouraged to explore the levels to find money and other thing that will earn you points to upgrade and learn new abilities. There isn't much objectives to do on these levels other than trying to shoot and slash your way through the next chapter. Overall the game is enjoyable and feels satifysing but at times can feel repetitive.

I will mostly be nitpicking because I like this game so much (no spoiler). The characters and art are adorable, and the controls are fluid and tight. Atmospheric music and a hero who's truly the only one there who can save the whole world.
That being said, the bosses are a bit overhyped. It's great fun, but it does emphasize the whole 'grind till you recognise the pattern' routine. Bit of RNG every now and then, but not overdone. It can get a bit annoying at times because you basically have to be like a sinusodial wave, strict and close in phase with the boss movements. Yeah you have different spells, but you will most likely find you use mainly 1 (2 at a stretch) or just heal in a boss fight.
Customization based on charms (which also look adorable) is either boss based, or like LoL masteries- you're only gonna find a handful meta and useful, whether they make you feel like a noob or a genius. My most used one is the one that puts your hero's icon on the map becauseI get lost and it looks cute.
Achievement based game (I know it's an opinionated thing if you like it or not, I don't really have time to grind all of it), for that sweet 100% is going to hurt you. Especially if you choose to try the game's 2nd unlocked difficulty- which blocks a certain special ability that changes your fightstyle in the late game, and well, if you watched Dunkey's video on difficulty in video games, it'll give you an idea what you're in for, will the challenge be fun, or exhausting?
It's a great game nonetheless in today's collection of hand drawn or platformer games. Please give it a try if you want an enjoyable, soul-sucking experience.
P.S 'soul sucking'- I haven't found 1 person who didn't get annoyed fighting that jackass. Still my favorite boss of the lot, but damn, you have been warned.

Not really sure how I'm even going to begin to start reviewing this game, as I have so many things I'd like to say about it. This is the most fun I've had on a game for a very long time (not to say that other games that I play aren't fun, rather, that this game is incredibly fun).
(Scroll to bottom for tl;dr review)
You play as the humourous, katana-wielding badass that is Lo Wang, who starts out on a quest to retrieve a sword for his master. Along the way, you bump into a demon called Hoji, who befriends you and follows you round for the rest of the game. There's lots of funny banter between the two of them, as well as the funny remarks Lo Wang makes throughout the game, which leads me to the first point.. the humour. The humour in the game is fantastic. "Wang" is incorporated into much of what Lo Wang says, usually with subtle innuendos like "You want some Wang?" when fighting enemies. Fortune cookies scattered throughout the game often have something humourous to say; it's always amusing to pick them up and read the witty humour. A few of my favourites are:
"Having sex is like playing bridge. If you don't have a good partner, you'd better have a great hand."
"He who takes advice from a cookie is sure to crumble."
"Cardboard belt is a waist of paper."
"That's what Ki said."
"All your cookie are belong to us."
"The good news: You're not paranoid. The badnews: Everyone is actually trying to kill you."
"Don't sweat the petty things and don't pet the sweaty things. - George Carlin"
"You will stop procrastinating. Later."
Unless you've played the game, you're probably wondering what the reference to Ki is (mentioned above). Ki is a form of energy used in the game, that allows you to perform many special actions, with or without your katana. Throughout the game, you will occasionally collect Ki crystals, that grant you new powers, and also allow you to upgrade them. These powers include healing, blocking, and immobilising your enemies by thrusting them up into the air, or knocking them down. They're simple to execute too: double tap a movement key, and hold the right mouse button to perform. The key binds are simple in this game. Being left-handed, I like to use the arrow keys and the right-hand part of the keyboard, and not have to worry about too many keybinds. Despite this, you are still able to perform everything with ease, from Ki powers to katana techniques, to the alternate fire option for your weapons. Ah yes, weapons...
The katana is incredibly fun to use. As well as just having your standard 'hack and slash' option, you also have access to various katana techniques, purchased with karma points (see next paragraph). These include powerful thrusts, spinning attacks, and long-ranged attacks. The special techniques with the katana are accessed the same way as with Ki powers, except by holding the left mouse button instead. As if the game wasn't fun enough with a katana, you also carry a huge arsenal of weapons around with you (moreso the further you progress). Most weapons have an alternate fire mode (accessed by holding the right mouse button), which can be bought with the money you collect in game, which gives you even more weapons to enjoy. There are also plenty of passive upgrades for your weapons, such as laser sights, increased magazines and weapon damage, etc. If those weapons are still too mainstream for you, occasionally you'll be able to use demon hearts (damages enemies in close proximity) and demon heads (fires a freakin' laser)! I recommend getting the 'Headhunter I' skill early on to have access to demon heads.
Karma is another essential part of the game. When you kill enemies (or drink a bowl of demon blood), you will obtain Karma, and occasionally receive a Karma point, which allows you to further upgrade Lo Wang. Most of the upgrades that can be purchased with Karma points are passive, such as improved maximum health, stamina (and its regeneration), finding more money/ammunition, and such. It is also where you can learn new katana techniques, and learn the ability to use demons' heads as weapons (Headhunter I).
Perhaps after mentioning all the great weapons and abilities you have at your disposal, I should probably talk about some of the enemies you are likely to face. There's plenty of the standard demons which will run towards and attack you in melee range (if they get the chance), as well airbourne enemies, and some enemies which require a more tactical approach to defeat. Which reminds me, at some points in the game, you get access to a minigun turret to take down lots of airbourne enemies! Yes, it's incredibly fun, though it would be nice if the fun lasted a little longer.
The level design is great, offering room for a little exploration, as well being fairly simple to follow the path to the current objective, with key doors and objects being highlighted in yellow. It's unlikely that you'll ever be short of health or ammunition, as you'll find plenty in boxes and cupboards as you travel around. You may occasionally come across hidden statuettes, which are pretty cool, but don't offer much other than looking fabulous and being worth a considerable amount of money (a bit similar to the Sokolov paintings, if you've played Dishonored). The graphics in the game are beautiful; you get to experience everything from temples, to forests, to snowy mountains.
There is some element of story in the game, as Lo Wang and Hoji both have objectives that they wish to fulfill, although  if you're looking for a story-rich game, Shadow Warrior probably won't tick that box. It is a hack 'n' slash / shoot 'em up game after all, if my review hadn't already implied that. I feel that more could've been done with the ending, though I'm not sure what I was supposed to expect anyway.
Unless you're new to video games in general, I'd recommend playing the game on either 'Hard' or 'Insane'. I wussed out and played the game on Normal, and although it was still incredibly fun, I felt like I wans't being pushed sufficiently to utilise everything at my disposal. There were also plenty of medkits still lying around for me to use, and my ammo was usually near-full on every weapon most of the time. I did notice that the game was pushing me more towards the end, though in hindsight, I think it would've been much more satisfying for me to complete the game on the 'Hard' difficulty. I'm definitely going to go back and try and complete the game on 'Insane' at some point!
TL;DR
If you love...
> Banter, witty humour, and 'Wang' jokes
> Witty fortune cookies
> Using a katana to slash things up
> Upgrades and special powers for your katana to slash things up even harder
> A large arsenal of weapons with loads of ammo at your disposal
> A ton of upgrades and alternate fire modes for your weapons
> Special powers
> Using demon heads to fire lasers at enemies
> Simple keybinds
> Beautiful environments (including forests, mountains, and Japanese temples)
...then you should definitely buy this game! :D

Shadow warrior is well worth a check out. Based on its old school predassesor, Shadow Warrior lives up to its name. Blending a mix of katana combat, and first person shooter action, there are many ways you can deal with baddies. Some of the most satisfying first person melee combat I've ever seen comes from this game, partly because of the various options one has. You have the regular M1 does a simple slash, M2 does a charge attack that appears in most games of this nature. However on top of that you have 3 special moves, allowing for a nice diversity in the way you attack. And boy does it feel good to slice and dice a demon into peices. On top of these 5 katana attacks, you have 4 other moves that can be done alongside any of your guns. The guns are fun and satisfying to use. You also have a  fast dash, which makes can transform combat into fast paced fun. Slashing one person, quickly dashing back, shooting something to explode and then dashing foward to eviscerate 5 enemies with ypur sword and watching them drop to the ground in bits is exhilirating. And Shadow Warrior rewards you for variation. Perfection in combat gets you five stars, something not easily ascertainable. This is based out of a 5 star system, which rewards you with "Karma Points" which in turn you can use to better oneself. And boy is there a lot to upgrade. You can upgrade all of your weapons at any time with money you find in each level, a perk system which also gives you skills, such as mobility, improved healing, sword mastery etc. along with those 4 special moves. These skills you'll find nessecary as different "types"  of enemies begin to appear.  In most  cases one must tackle each new situation in a different way. In the end Shadow Warrior's combat is fun, and intuitive, but if find myself constantly using the katana, because it is overall the best weapon, and yeilds the most satisfying results. But at the same time other weapons have their uses. I feel as though the devs. did so on purpose, to make the katana to feel as though it was your main weapon. Even if i got a new weapon id always find myself going back to the katana. Moving on, Shadow Warrior in some places is absolutely stunning. Many of the environments have their own distinctive look, and are very vibrant and colorful. I, personally, enjoy all of the cherry blossoms and japanese theming that appear at many times throughout the game. I never found myself while playing shadow warrior thinking "This game looks bad." Granted i had to optimize my system a bit, however at the end I still found it to look great (But keep in mind thats just me, im sure others dont have that same problem) . And hidden in these stunning environments are many secrets, and bonuses to find along with sarcastic fortune cookies. I dont have that many qualms with Shadow Warrior. I loved all the cheesey one liners, and the actual plot (which i dont feel like going into because this review is long enough) had no major plot holes, and wasnt necessarily terrible. In fact I quite enjoyed it. But at some points when running through a level, i found it hard to find the actual objective, but this was only one level, for the most part i never had this trouble. On the whole Shadow Warrior is a fantastic game that left me wanting alot more. I'd suggest having it in your steam library, i know im glad i purchased it.

Some of the gags would be written and performed well, but they'd have trouble holding up in terms of overarching theme, scene composition, and sufficient depth of the characters. There'd always be a sense of disappointment when you realized the gags were obviously written before the characters. As example, I'd point to

What

I cannot recommend this game enough. Gorgeous and immersive, Hollow Knight feels like a fusion of Dark Souls and Metroid wrapped up in a cute insectoid package that tugs at the heartstrings just as often as it amuses.
Hollow Knight's expansive game world constantly surprises you with its size and depth, and the few areas that Team Cherry clearly didn't have time to complete don't detract from the experience in the least. The game's sound design is incredible, and works with the writing and visuals to create an impressive level of atmosphere. Deepnest kept me genuinely unnerved all the way up to its final boss, despite being a 2D game with cartoony visuals - I wish I hadn't played that section in the dark. The slowly-emerging story is an intriguing one, and our main character's voiceless faceless mask still communicates more character than most AAA-heroes ever manage.
The slow but steady acquisition of power-ups makes progression hugely satisfying, and the level and enemy design keep areas distinct and memorable - useful for backtracking. The Charm system is initially a little restrictive, but soon opens up for you to play with, although sadly there are enough "no brainer" choices that you'll probably just leave your favourites slotted in forever. The bosses always look great, and while some may be less enjoyable than others, the best (Hornet, Mantis Lords) more than make up for the worst, and teach you how to fight in a way that reminds me of Gascoigne's impact in Bloodborne.
It took me 60 hours to 100% Hollow Knight, and it was worth every second of play. I'll be heading back down into Hallownest soon - the opportunities for sequence-breaking and playing around are intriguing, and Hornet (BEST) seems like she'll be a playable character at some point.

Hollowknight is a member of the metroidvania genre that could very well be counted among the best of its kind.
Going for the more "unimportant" aspects first:
The graphic style is a feast for the eyes and the soundtrack makes for great music for roleplaying sessions or just for atmosphere on a rainy day. The first few times you open the game and start your journey, the intro theme and the asthetics will make for a very welcoming experience.
The most important thing to say about Hollow Knight though: The controls, the combat especially the traversial through the quite large world can only be described as CRISP. Extremely responsive, great feedback on combat hits and traveling through the zones feels very quick and powerful.
If I were to find negative things to say about Hollow Knight, the only things coming to mind are that
a) sometimes one can be "stuck" searching for the next thing to do because the map is (propably intentionally) vague at times
b) the "advanced" combat moves that can be learned feel rather useless. The standard strike is all you'll ever really need and use except for some rare and special encounters where the special moves at most can save you some time.
All in all, Hollow Knight is a MUST for fans of the metrodvania genre.

I am kind of unsure how I feel about this game, so I recommend this game, but if I had written this review yesterday I would not have. It comes down to some design choices that I found annoying.
To start with some technical parts of the game.
It is a two dimensional combat-puzzle action-adventure game.
The graphical stye is of a hand-drawn style, which is well done, the animations are smooth.
Controller is, given by the game and my opinion, the best input device for the contol system.
The game has a permadeath but is first unlocked after completion of a non-permadeath playthough.
The game works by the game design choice that the protagonist arquire upgrades that allow you to go back to previous location and discover new areas, objects and npcs.
The "base" story of the game is simple: The protagonist is a mute bug armed only with a nail (a sword) and have to fight though hundred of enemies and find the path leading to the secrets that are hidden deep inside an old kingdom that have fallen long before the game happens.
The lore of this place is told by "stones" and npcs that is found around the old kingdom, "journal updates" from killing enemies, and some few "flashbacks".
The plot used is based on the common fantasy plot method with some, very, few changes to this.
The lore is loose in a way similar to games like the Dark Soul Series and such, hence much is left open for the player to consider.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Different aspect of the game and what I think about them
Positive:
- Beatiful graphical style.
- Great sound tract and audio design.
- Interesting lore and why of telling it.
- Possible to some extent to change the playstyle using charms.
- Lots of hidden areas and objects.
- Possible to affect the side-stories that are some of the npcs.
- Not all npcs have a good ending.
Neutral:
- Multiple endings. Multiple endings can be archived in a single playthough. Kind of nice, but also meaning that an ending to a playthough do not feel like a "ending" to a playthough. Though one of the endings require a separate playthough as the others lock it out.
- Repetitive method of dealing with enemies. Most enemies just require to hit them to kill them without much movement. There are some enemies that require the player to dodge their attact or hitting a non "shielded" side.
Negative:
- The spells that is related to the tilting of the left stick on a controller are not equal bound for the four direction that the spells are chosen by. The "up" direction is much wider then the other direction.
- I have noticed that there are some artificiel constrains in the movement in the form of some few delays on when specific movement systems can be used, which is slightly ignoring.
- There is an area late game that feels out of place compared the rest of the game. The rest of the game focus on a mix of (a little) puzzles and combat, while this one area focus purely on jumping/movement puzzles. The above mention point of the movement system is quite noticble here.
- Some few puzzles rely on enemy placement to get past, however, the enemies are allowed to move allowed and some times their placement can not be seen before starting the puzzle, meaning that some puzzles rely on luck.
- Some bosses can be trivialised by using specific charms.
- The attack hitbox of an enemy is the entire sprite, not just the weapon or when under an attact "animation". Just something I have never liked in any games.
- Some locations just lack challenges in the form of either difficult enemies or hard puzzles.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
I have enjoyed this game throughout most of my playthrough (took around 33 hours to complete with 97 % completion), however, just some of the negative points really annoyed me when they applied and one of them (the area I felt was out of place) kind of felt it was designed in such a way to just extend the length of the game (I am not saying this was the design choise, but it is how I felt when playing though it) as it was not really hard, just a single mistake meant having to go though a lot of puzzles again.
Some of the bosses were quite hard and challenging to fight, but I found the possibility of trivialising most bosses in the game kind of a wierd design choise.
Overall I would say that this is the kind of games that people who like some challenge and "dark" lore, story, and plot could fine interesting. However, some design choices can make the game stessing and annoying at times.

Black Flags is a AC game and has bugs because Ubisoft. If you are having a V sync issues or stuttering with constant drops to 30fps there is a fix and it gives you alittle more performance as well. You can either use the best method by pressing windows key+L to lock windows then unlock go back into game which gives you about 10% performance boost and runs smooth as butter or run the game as admin with Vsync and triple buffering conrtolled by the gpu but you will still get some frame drops here and there but it fixes the drops to 30fps. Another issue you may get is freezing for a few seconds while sailing. This is a glitch caused by FXAA so don't use it. Also SMAA blurs the water while moving. I recomend using your gpu pannel for AA or MSAA. Now to my review.

Black Flag is not a normal Creed game. Mostly because its amazing, and no game with an "animus" in the story should be called amazing. The other AC games are good don't get me wrong I like them alot; but, not GTA, Fallout, Elder Scrolls, Witcher good. Black Flag is nearly just that. The mechanics in the game are polished and open exluding a few bugs. The graphics are top notch for 2013 as well and with SweetFx and 4k it holds up great . The naval combat is a blast :p, and the melee combat is great. My only gripe is it is restricted to typicall AC themes. I.E. don't be killing civilians, no taking someone elses ship and building that one up, limited to what weapons you can hold on to. I am a pirate so I should be swashbuckling stabby cut throat ♥♥♥♥♥ mongering drunkard fun. The story is ok, but sometimes unbearably in accurate how they portray real pirates(simular to ACIII with its horrible geography and historic figures), and they are just there to move the plot. Black Beard is NOTHING like he was in real life. This is a 6,5"+ 280 pound+ man who left his crew to die by grounding the Queen Annes Revenge to keep the money for himself. Ubisoft portrays him as average size, fairly nice, inept at piracy and loyal person. Don't even get me started on Black Bart.The whole animus thing is bearley a discussion and is still needless. They could have just made it you are a pirate, go and pirate things. No need for the same old story of made up blah blah in historical localations, but the open world lets you forget about that. Though you can never get a new ship or are able to capture one which is a real shame. Though you can upgrade the ship.
With the world being so big and grand, and your crew singing while you sail its easy to get sucked in. (songs like Leave Her Johnny, Drunken Sailor and Fathom the Bowel I find myself singing at times to some odd looks from people) The mini games are a lot of fun and at times. I just like to play a game of checkers while listening to the "live band" who will play period music.(and each region gets their own songs based on the inhabitants. Like an English settlement will play old English and Irish songs like All for My Grog) Another gripe I do have for this game is its a bear to run. Most are lucky to see 30FPS@high res Ultra. I modded it and it tends to run around 45-50fps at 1080p with high on everything but shadows with an i7, 2gb nVidia, and 16gigs ram. So make sure you can run it if you are on a lower end machine or laptop. A 980ti will muscle it at 1440p at 60fps with sweet fx, but the gameworks features will need to be off because its gameworks. To maintain 60 100% of the time I need to drop a few setting down to very high even on a 980ti. For a 1080ti 4k is easily attainable but you will need to ajust your settings.  No joke this is one of the most stressful games to run with all of it's PC features. Black Flag is the one of two games of the series that was developed on PC then ported.(ACIII bring the other) Which is odd it still has bugs given it was made for PC. Since it was developed for PC it has a wide array of graphic options with many different setting to them. I guess none of this is surprising seeing how with ACIII Ubi forgot to add a resolution option in game!
This is a game I would highly recommend to people who even hate the series, because this pirate game shouldn't of bothered with the name Assassins Creed #. No it is to good! This is just Black Flag to me, and Black Flag is great!!!!!!!!! Oh and for some reason I always seem to play this when I've had a few. It just makes the debauchery better I think.

Undoubtedly, one of the best shooters I have played in ages. If not THE best.
Of the many first person shooters I have played in the last several years, only a handful of them reach that balance, timelessness, uniqueness, and most importantly fun factor to them, that stand out amongst my memory. This game not only exceeds in each of those aspects, but it takes what makes fun about the best of the best of first person shooters and, to put it in layman's terms, makes them its ♥♥♥♥♥!
The top shooters that come to mind that I've had fond memories of were Timesplitters: Future Perfect, F.E.A.R. 2, Duke Nukem, and Serious Sam. Shadow Warrior is a renaissance of those games, giving you a wide range of weapons that are vast and have that perfect amount of kick, sound, and bass to them that give the bloody slices and shots to the demons and monsters all the more awarding and incredibly satisfying feel. This game encourages you to run, gun, and slice your way through hoardes of the shadow beings, with enemies dropping health, and the upgrades and strategies needed to kick every♥♥♥♥♥needed.
Sure, this game has guns, but the swordplay. My god, the swordplay. Very rarely do I play, let alone encounter a game, with such amazing and exhilarating sword combat quite like this. It's one thing for a game like Metal Gear Rising to allow you to cut what you will. But there's just something about witnessing the bloody and gory brutality and dismemberment of your unfortunate foes in such over the top fashion, that it feels as though I'm in a game directed by Quentin Tarantino. And that puts a smile on my face.
The visuals are simply stunning. The game has a strong personality that is complemented by the environments, locations, and just the sheer scope and feel to the game. Whoever says this game looks okay, is obviously blind, and closeted in their own bias opinion, for this game has more life and color to it than the monochromatic, military shooter that the so called "gamers" only play based on graphics before gameplay. Shadow Warrior on the otherhand strikes a perfect balance between style AND substance.
In terms of story, the game keeps the intrigue inline with its great one liners and humor delivered by Lo Wang, tied in with the tragic backstory that he gets wrapped up in. And it certainly left an emotional impact me, even months after finishing it. Soundtrack is also phenomenal. The thumping and rhythmic intensity of the drums complimenting amongst the instruments coupled with the ambience and sounds of the various landscapes are both endearing and indubitably atmospheric. In addition, this game is incredibly lenghty, a rarity in modern first person shooters.
By now as you're reading this, you may ask yourself, do I like this game? No.
I love this game.
I bought this game a while ago for 75% off, but at any price it is absolutely worth it. If there was any game that's superior from its visual asthetics, to its deep and enthralling gameplay, it is Shadow Warrior.
I normally don't give games a score, but in this case, I give this game a 10 on the Wang-O-Meter.

For those who enjoy an old school Duke Nukem or DOOM game, you will like this one as it has the same sort of gameplay feel, except you also use a katana as well.  There are even easter eggs that give tribute to the old game style.    Anyway, onto the review.
Story:    This is an interesting one.   It starts off as a simple story with one guy doing his usual business but then demons appear and well thats where things get crazy.   Through out the game, there are tons of hilarious moments, but there are moments of serious story plot that happen in the form of flash backs.   These flashbacks are what makes the ending, all the better.  I won't say what happens of course, but once you've seen all of the cutscenes, the ending will not only make sense, but give you a feel as well.   I did not see it coming but it made the whole story aspect of the game, absolutly amazing.    In short, the game does a great job at keeping things light, but when it gets serious, it makes you stop and think.
Gameplay:    Well, this is interesting because there are a lot of different weapons to use and upgrade.  You have things from the katana, to firearms like pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, etc.   They have other oddball ones that involves a demon heart and head o.O    For those who own games like Saints Row 4, Serious Sam 3, and others, you get exclusive melee weapons that will take place of your katana.  For saint Row 4, you get a giant purple horse cck so um, yeah......enjoy.    In terms of mechanics, its jsut like how DOOM is, big powerful weapons that create an overkill and destroy things, in a messy way.
Visuals:    Beautiful backgrounds and great graphic details.  This game is a bit more demanding than others, and I think someone said that it was partially due to it being a 32-bit game, but I may be wrong.   There are various settings that can be used and tweaked so that it will run for most people.   The Japanese themed maps and buildings, are gorious and make me really want to fly to Japan and see the country side.  Some day, some day.
Music:   Not a whole lot of music per se , but when there is music being played, its just like the visuals, beautiful.  Very often, it is traditional sounding music, which fits the game, and it is also so relaxing.   I think the soundtrack is available to purchase, so that is well worth the extra buck or two.
Overall:    Whenever this game goes on sale like it did recently, it is a steal of a deal.  There is just so much value in it and the gameplay time is easily 10 hours or so, just basic play though.   The arts are great, the game mechanics are there, the plot is there, and the humor is there.   I highly recommend this to anyone who liks hack and slash games or big gun games or likes humor mixed with blood and guts.

While the ship mechanics are new, it is not what I am referring to. It's like they keep making maps that they sell as full games, when in reality they could just a easy have been DLC. I do wish they come up with something different. Every game is at their base the same, climb up, hide in secret spot, stand on top of something, dive into a bush (or similar), hide in crowds etc.. I have already played the next episode (Unity) and yet again they will use the same mechanics. That said, the story is why at least I play these games for, and they have all been good so far. Not the best (or even the most original) but really quite good. And this is no different. I also enjoy playing in different ages, and this is another reason why I like these games. Undoubtedly, one of the best shooters I have played in ages. If not THE best.
Of the many first person shooters I have played in the last several years, only a handful of them reach that balance, timelessness, uniqueness, and most importantly fun factor to them, that stand out amongst my memory. This game not only exceeds in each of those aspects, but it takes what makes fun about the best of the best of first person shooters and, to put it in layman's terms, makes them its ♥♥♥♥♥!
The top shooters that come to mind that I've had fond memories of were Timesplitters: Future Perfect, F.E.A.R. 2, Duke Nukem, and Serious Sam. Shadow Warrior is a renaissance of those games, giving you a wide range of weapons that are vast and have that perfect amount of kick, sound, and bass to them that give the bloody slices and shots to the demons and monsters all the more awarding and incredibly satisfying feel. This game encourages you to run, gun, and slice your way through hoardes of the shadow beings, with enemies dropping health, and the upgrades and strategies needed to kick every♥♥♥♥♥needed.
Sure, this game has guns, but the swordplay. My god, the swordplay. Very rarely do I play, let alone encounter a game, with such amazing and exhilarating sword combat quite like this. It's one thing for a game like Metal Gear Rising to allow you to cut what you will. But there's just something about witnessing the bloody and gory brutality and dismemberment of your unfortunate foes in such over the top fashion, that it feels as though I'm in a game directed by Quentin Tarantino. And that puts a smile on my face.
The visuals are simply stunning. The game has a strong personality that is complemented by the environments, locations, and just the sheer scope and feel to the game. Whoever says this game looks okay, is obviously blind, and closeted in their own bias opinion, for this game has more life and color to it than the monochromatic, military shooter that the so called "gamers" only play based on graphics before gameplay. Shadow Warrior on the otherhand strikes a perfect balance between style AND substance.
In terms of story, the game keeps the intrigue inline with its great one liners and humor delivered by Lo Wang, tied in with the tragic backstory that he gets wrapped up in. And it certainly left an emotional impact me, even months after finishing it. Soundtrack is also phenomenal. The thumping and rhythmic intensity of the drums complimenting amongst the instruments coupled with the ambience and sounds of the various landscapes are both endearing and indubitably atmospheric. In addition, this game is incredibly lenghty, a rarity in modern first person shooters.
By now as you're reading this, you may ask yourself, do I like this game? No.
I love this game.
I bought this game a while ago for 75% off, but at any price it is absolutely worth it. If there was any game that's superior from its visual asthetics, to its deep and enthralling gameplay, it is Shadow Warrior.
I normally don't give games a score, but in this case, I give this game a 10 on the Wang-O-Meter.
