The Assassin's Creed series was never my type of games. I actually never really all enjoyed the series with the exception of the first.
BUT THIS IS AN EFFING PIRATE SIMULATOR (or as close to one as you can get). While the game never takes away the copy paste element of ALL the other Assassin's Creed games, this one has a much more tollerable experience... if you like pirates and simulated games. Black flag has stunning realism in the ocean sailing. There are strangely fun events to partake in and loads of ships to sink, destroy, or board. While you do still do the traditional island hunting, stalking, hawk diving, assasinating of traditional Assasin's Creed games, it's a bit more free roam. Therefore, it will not force you to continue the story line if you just want to kill some whales and blow up ships. Upgrades for your ships, and crafting elements are apparent in this one.
I'd say Black Flag is one of the best, top notch Assassin's Creed games released so far. On PC, expect some framerate dips if you aren't running a brand new $1000 rig, but it's not unplayable. Expect some frustrations with controlling your charecter without a controller as well. I'd strongly reccommend a PC controller for this game. It will make movement on land (with all the traditional Assassin's Creed's mechanics) and sailing your ship far easier.
None the less, Assassin's fans will have a different viewpoint than myself. As not-so-much a cult follower of the series, to another Assassin's fan, get it. To a non-Assassin's fan like myself, it's worth at least finding a friend that has it to try it. You may be impressed. Perhaps you'll get it on sale, never beat the game, and roam the ocean like I do. I'm pretty pleased with the sailing myself. Then again, I always wanted to be a pirate. RRRGGG!!!

For those who enjoy an old school Duke Nukem or DOOM game, you will like this one as it has the same sort of gameplay feel, except you also use a katana as well.  There are even easter eggs that give tribute to the old game style.    Anyway, onto the review.
Story:    This is an interesting one.   It starts off as a simple story with one guy doing his usual business but then demons appear and well thats where things get crazy.   Through out the game, there are tons of hilarious moments, but there are moments of serious story plot that happen in the form of flash backs.   These flashbacks are what makes the ending, all the better.  I won't say what happens of course, but once you've seen all of the cutscenes, the ending will not only make sense, but give you a feel as well.   I did not see it coming but it made the whole story aspect of the game, absolutly amazing.    In short, the game does a great job at keeping things light, but when it gets serious, it makes you stop and think.
Gameplay:    Well, this is interesting because there are a lot of different weapons to use and upgrade.  You have things from the katana, to firearms like pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, etc.   They have other oddball ones that involves a demon heart and head o.O    For those who own games like Saints Row 4, Serious Sam 3, and others, you get exclusive melee weapons that will take place of your katana.  For saint Row 4, you get a giant purple horse cck so um, yeah......enjoy.    In terms of mechanics, its jsut like how DOOM is, big powerful weapons that create an overkill and destroy things, in a messy way.
Visuals:    Beautiful backgrounds and great graphic details.  This game is a bit more demanding than others, and I think someone said that it was partially due to it being a 32-bit game, but I may be wrong.   There are various settings that can be used and tweaked so that it will run for most people.   The Japanese themed maps and buildings, are gorious and make me really want to fly to Japan and see the country side.  Some day, some day.
Music:   Not a whole lot of music per se , but when there is music being played, its just like the visuals, beautiful.  Very often, it is traditional sounding music, which fits the game, and it is also so relaxing.   I think the soundtrack is available to purchase, so that is well worth the extra buck or two.
Overall:    Whenever this game goes on sale like it did recently, it is a steal of a deal.  There is just so much value in it and the gameplay time is easily 10 hours or so, just basic play though.   The arts are great, the game mechanics are there, the plot is there, and the humor is there.   I highly recommend this to anyone who liks hack and slash games or big gun games or likes humor mixed with blood and guts.

This game is simply incredible,and more people need to know about it!It successfully creats that feeling of the FPS's of old,in that you have to look around for medkits,armor,you can carry all your weapons at once...I usually hate magic pockets in any game for the fact that it makes you overpowered,but that is not the case in this game.You will need to use down to the last round of all your weapons very often!The weapons,while they start very basic and takes a little bit to get a reliable gun,are all upgradable and have alternate firing modes.All that being said,the focus here is on the katana:this game has the best melee combat Ive ever seen in a FPS game.Its very fast,gory,empowering and brutally satisfactory!You also get experience and collect stuff that allows you to upgrade your character as well,getting new sword skills,more health,improved chance to find ammo or money,magic blasts,the ability to collect and use as a weapons enemy's hearts and heads(very powerful!),and a lot more!
It is also a very funny game,with some great one-liners at the perfect moment.The character banter between the wise-cracking protagonist Lo-Wang and his spiritual companion is also great.The story is definitely better than in most FPS's these days,and took me by surprise as I realized I was enthralled by it,anxious to find out more and more about this story that starts so light,but gets very serious and surprising towards the last third of the game.
Fortunately,the flaws of the game are very few: sometimes the level design can be a little confusing,it annoyed me that almost every container throughout a country was the exact same,the encounters with giant enemies are boring.Also,it could be a little shorter,but that being said,at least that makes sure you are getting your money's worth duration-wise,so I dont know if I really consider that a flaw.

BGM - I was on a huge military ship with a whole 10 other people at attention for our CO's "big speech", and there was some horrid constant guitar riff in the background that literally made me want to die.
Voice acting - the commander of your Force Recon Marine squad has the voice of a 1950's friendly gas pump attendant, and the attitude to match it. Along with everyone sounding as stereotypically posh white as possible calling me "Coops", that made the little bit I played of the game torturous.
Military "Realism" - the biggest joke of this game.  I go to the boot camp section, since it is my first time playing, and im met with my pump attendant of a commander who says "Gee Coops, what would you like to work on today? Wanna shoot some targets? Run an obstacle course? Or just hang around?" Uhmm.. what kind of commanding officer, MUCH LESS A MARINE, would you hear say that? Answer: none.  Then back to the boat with the horrid guitar riff, standing at attention for this entire ship, for the speech that we are INVADING A RUSSIAN SUB-NATION, are about 10 people. wtf??  Also, when you sight in, you dont get to use the scope on your gun, no no, you get taken back to 2001 with the Medal of Honor: Frontline zoom-down-the-side-of-the-rifle bit.  You basically run and sprint as if your legs are stiff and you move by slamming from one side to the other.  And even with my sensitivity nearly all the way down, "Coops" apparently has an effing swivel for a head, as the slightest move of the mouse can send you in a 180 turn.  And with that slight segway into controls, we move on.
Controls - Second biggest joke of the game.  Motion blur and X-axis movement is INSANELY too much.  ENTER is default for action... ENTER. So to open a door or ANYTHING, you have to either pull hand off mouse, or move from your movement keys.   F is switch weapons.. not 1,2,3,4, not wheel scroll.. but F.  Thank God youu still move with WASD. Only good controls of the game.
Interface - there are like, 30-ish boot camp levels. the main menu is set up almost like Unreal 1, or even the Conflict: Desert Storm games, and even those are more military "realistic" than this garbage.
TL;DR - The game has decent graphics, but that's about it.  Too many loading screens for what it is, being called "Coops" is suck, stupid combat mechanics, and outlandish controls abound.  Basically, this game has "realism" for people that have absolutely no idea what they're talking about.  I'm tight when it comes to money, so I bought the complete pack when it was on sale, and i STILL don't think it was worth the 20 bucks I paid.  Save yourself the trouble (unless you're a hipster for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t), and just buy a Call of Duty or Battlefield game.  Either are more fun and "realistic" than this crap.

It's becoming a bit of a repetitive thing with regard to my game interest if you browse my library and list of reviews - Metroidvania; but, who cares?! To me, Metroidvania games encapsulate the very things gamers and casuals alike want in their experience. Exploration, discovery, tough-as-nails bosses, scarce but effective storyline, and just plain fun. Hollow Knight does a superb job in capturing everything great about these types of games - it really is a game that does the genre justice.
If someone were to ask me what my favorite game of all-time is, I would smirkingly respond, "That's a stupid question." This would be my logical response, as specifying one game to be hyperbolically better than any other game in any genre would be preposterous. However, my gut, knee-jerk response would be Super Metroid. Then, I would tip my hat for runner-up to SOTN.
Is Hollow Knight better than my all-time best game? No.
Here's why. And, I'm not being biased by nostalgia here, as I never owned an SNES when it came out. As a matter of fact, I just played the game for the first time about 2 years ago off the Virtual Store - Wii U – roughly 20 years after its original release. So, I’m saying this after playing it at 4:3 with pixelated graphics on a 55” flat 1080p screen, emulated by Nintendo’s virtual offering. Super Metroid is special. It has all of the things previously mentioned. The difference between Super Metroid and a similar style game like Hollow Knight is that Super Metroid does all of the things above…but effortlessly. Except for the opening scene (and the closing scene), there's no dialogue / monologue. You don't purchase anything. Unless I looked through the literature, I really wouldn't even know the controls. It brilliantly engages the player into a world that allows learning and progressing through the very fabric of the game. No area feels out of place. The graphics, although 16-bit, are integral to the ominous tone of the desolate planet on which Samus explores. Of course, the technology in the mid-90's was limited to that level of commercial graphics, but, again, that's what makes the game so special. It's a Field of Dreams meets Shawshank Redemption meets Goodfellas...it’s a perfect storm (not the movie - that one was just ok).
Hollow Knight pays great homage to Super Metroid. There are other games in the genre that don't; so, that says a lot. Is it pioneering like SM? No...for the reasons above. Super Metroid is lightning in a bottle. Hollow Knight is thunder, rain, clouds, wind...it has all the ingredients. It just doesn't have that special cohesion like Super Metroid - some intentional - some serendipitous.
I won't do pros and cons. I will say that Hollow Knight offers all the things someone would want from a Metroidvania, and it does it better than most (if not, all) other successors. The graphics are good - very good. The controls are quite adequate - responsive to what the game requires of you. The bosses are tough - very tough - especially one certain Failed Champion. I will say the AI in this game is brilliant - frustratingly brilliant. Do enemies have movesets that you can memorize? Absolutely. Are you fighting the same pattern every time? Absolutely NOT! The game adjusts so well to your position, your jump and move trajectory, and your attack pattern, that it feels ridiculously organic...it almost feels like it's a PVP opponent - especially with the aforementioned Dream Boss. Story? It's there. It doesn't hand-hold. But, it tries to be a lot of different games with a common Metroidvania thread. So, the story, is not the main draw. The musical score is fantastical, as it should be.
Should you buy this game? Yes. For $15US, I logged 33 hours with 65% completion - beating the main story. So, there's 35% of the content of the game that I have yet to uncover. And, I don't hesitate in saying I would go back and play the whole thing again.
Addendum: After completing the main game and writing the review, I embarked upon some of the other 35% of the stuff I missed. Holy crap...this game has a ton of content! And, I have to say, this side content contains some of the most difficult platforming, guantlet fights and alternate-version bosses you will encounter. The platforming and guantlet level (one in particular) actually made me improve in other games. This is truly a gem!

Now before I get on with this review I just want to say a few things so here it goes. Firstly I love the idea of this game, its a really easy to pick up, cheap adrenaline rush. That being said there are a few kinks that really need to be worked out if this game wants to fall into the category of a AAA title and really emerge as a competitive balanced game.
Also, this is just a side note and kind of unrealistic hope, but it would be cool just to see a few more game options. As it is now there is 2v2 TDM, 3v3 TDM, 2v2 AI, and practice modes. Mabey introduce some objective game modes in the future with multiple respawns (I.E. Domination, Capture the Flag) instead of sudden death 2v2/3v3.
My Review-
I'm not recommending this game right now for a few reasons but the major reason is balancing.
The balance in this game is totally off. For instance the two classes that are extremely good in an average players hands are Pearl and Poloma. Trust me when I tell you, these to classes are over-powered. I play melee classes. I always play melee classes. But I picked up Pearl and Poloma after getting destroyed for 1 round each was hitting around 400 DPS (on my first game each) and healing for around 200 per round.
Those numbers are crazy for a first time user. In the right hands these classes are very very hard to beat.
Now I don't recommend this product, not because of over powered classes, but insteand I don't recommend this game because every ranged class is over powered. Classes like Rook, Bakko, Freya just simply are not competitive. This is the trend that absolutely every MMO/MOBA game falls into. Ranged classes reign king and melee classes get stomped.
Now don't get me wrong, Rook for instance is a very capable fighter. If you are a master at Rook you will be okay. Same goes for Bakko and Freya and Croak. But if youre a master Poloma, Iva, Pearl, Jade (esspecially Jade),Lucie(Maybe not so much Lucie), Ashka, etc you will win encounters 8/9 out of 10 times. It's simply because the abilities centered around ranged classes are just too good for melee. They have an extensive arsenal of fleeing abilities and ranged attacks that are equal to or better than melee classes. Jade is a prime example of this. In the right hands, I will never gap close and hit a good Jade player with a class like Rook or Bakko, (Shifu is an exception if played extremely well), and that due to the fact that they have an arsenal of abilities that inflict stuns and are fleeing abilities that they can spam.
My suggestion is this, make all ranged, auto attacks stationary attacks (I.E. you can't move while attacking with LMB or RMB) and increase the range of melee LMB and RMB attacks. It is this simple. As it is now, if you miss a gap closing ability (which is extremely easy because gap closing melees need charged up and are easily recognizable  ) you're ruined.
And this is my point really, melee classes are too difficult to Master in comparison to Ranged. this makes Ranged OP for casual players.
Then once mastered , Good to great players will beat a Master melee.
Other reasons i don't recommend the game :
Casual players will get stomped right now.
Gets boring honestly. Win or Lose, every MOBA/Multi game gets boring after a little while because the question arises "Why am I playing this?" At first you answer, "maybe I will be really good and can enter tournaments and stuff and win money". Once those dreams are crushed or the class(es) you like never become the next meta, theres no real reason to continue on unfortunately and 99.5% of us will have this happend *sad face*
You've gotta run with a team if you want to preform in the higher Grades (rank).
This game has adopted the new standard typical microtransaction system of random chance lock boxes to get cosmetic items. Not terrible but it really just adds to the cookie cutter Multiplayer/MOBA atmosphere. And I'm positive this will branch off into other things as well, as long as it stays cosmetic its not a huge turn off but these things can branch off in a huge variety of ways so we will have to wait and see where this goes.
TL;DR Ranged Classes follow the typical MOBA/MMO style of being dominant over Melee Classes. The game needs balancing reworks before I can recommend this game. It is purely pvp so until the balance the game properly, stay away. I'm sure in a few months that will happen.

I cannot recommend this game enough. Gorgeous and immersive, Hollow Knight feels like a fusion of Dark Souls and Metroid wrapped up in a cute insectoid package that tugs at the heartstrings just as often as it amuses.
Hollow Knight's expansive game world constantly surprises you with its size and depth, and the few areas that Team Cherry clearly didn't have time to complete don't detract from the experience in the least. The game's sound design is incredible, and works with the writing and visuals to create an impressive level of atmosphere. Deepnest kept me genuinely unnerved all the way up to its final boss, despite being a 2D game with cartoony visuals - I wish I hadn't played that section in the dark. The slowly-emerging story is an intriguing one, and our main character's voiceless faceless mask still communicates more character than most AAA-heroes ever manage.
The slow but steady acquisition of power-ups makes progression hugely satisfying, and the level and enemy design keep areas distinct and memorable - useful for backtracking. The Charm system is initially a little restrictive, but soon opens up for you to play with, although sadly there are enough "no brainer" choices that you'll probably just leave your favourites slotted in forever. The bosses always look great, and while some may be less enjoyable than others, the best (Hornet, Mantis Lords) more than make up for the worst, and teach you how to fight in a way that reminds me of Gascoigne's impact in Bloodborne.
It took me 60 hours to 100% Hollow Knight, and it was worth every second of play. I'll be heading back down into Hallownest soon - the opportunities for sequence-breaking and playing around are intriguing, and Hornet (BEST) seems like she'll be a playable character at some point.

This is one of those games that I actually tell myself I’m so glad that I played. The concept of this game is great to me.
You play as Stanley. A man who works in a mundane job pushing buttons all day. Orders come through to his screen to push buttons and he does as told. One day, Stanley realises no orders are coming through, and that no one else is in the office. He gets up to see what’s going on.
That’s where we come in! You navigate Stanley around a very seemingly linear office, and quickly discover that you have a narrator dictating everything that you do, before you do it. Of course, leaving you room to either play out what he says, or go against it. You come to various paths and crossroads and are given the choice to either do what you’re told or not.
What I love about this game is how it plays on pure human curiosity. If you go one way, you usually wonder… but what would happen if I went the other way? There is many endings to the game, and as the narrator goes on with his story, you wonder what is true. If anything you’re being told is true, what the real story to the game is or if there even is one. It gets you thinking, and I love a game that’ll make me think!
I enjoyed this game very much. I have an odd “fear”, kind of, of missing or losing things. So being given a game with many paths, endings and different things to find, admittedly I did OCD over it a bit and actually went as far as drawing myself a map (Don’t judge me). But it was a lot of fun! I had a great time playing this game and think it is something anyone could enjoy.
The graphics are nice. I wasn’t aware before, but this game actually started as a Half-Life 2 mod. As a standalone game I think it did really well for itself.
The characters are amazing. I love both Stanley, the narrator and the odd “relationship” they have with each other (Even though Stanley never speaks). The voice casting for the narrator is on point, I honestly couldn’t imagine the character any other way. He’s well-spoken and has a great charm about him. The narrator in ways kind of “trolls” you a bit with how he tries to keep you on track or how he reacts when you go against him. But he’s a great character and that is important for a game so dependent on that character being entertaining.
The humour in this game was something I did enjoy quite a bit. The way things are done and played out I was quite impressed with.
In terms of achievements, a few can be a little tedious, but in ways you ain’t even mad. As said before the game can “troll” you at times and it does so even more through the achievements. I would say that it’s still easy to 100%, but there is a few that you kind of need to “cheat” to achievement. For example, an achievement titled “Go outside”, your task being to “not play The Stanley Parable for 5 years”. Which, come on!
All in all, I love this game and really think you should give it a try. If you like a good bit of humour and like your curiosity being tempted I think this game is a good one for that.
TL ; DR : A great and unique game that tests your curiosity and gets you thinking. It has many endings to offer and generally is fun, definitely try it!

I haven't played many metroidvanias, but I enjoy 2D games and this was reccomended based on its Bloodborne/Souls style atmosphere and I'm pretty happy I got this. It certainly has that feel and aesthetic in places, and also uses a similar aspect that gives you the chance to retrieve your stuff upon death, via backtracking to where you died and defeating your shade.
The environments in this game are beautiful and the soundtrack is just amazing. The world is quite large and progression is very non-linear, I managed to find myself in the Deepnest of all places very early on and missed some early areas and boss fights until very late in the game, because bosses can be fought in almost any order and many are even optional. The difficulty is also set pretty high, especially if you find yourself in an area or fight you are unprepared for and suddenly end up questioning your life decisions leading up to that point. On occassion it got frustrating to the point where I felt compelled to stop playing for a while, especially due to the constant humiliating backtracking to retry a boss since there's no save stations nearby or when the environmental obstacles become reminiscent of something I'd expect to see in Super Meat Boy. Still, the atmosphere and sense of wonder I felt from delving into the depths of this game inevitably pulled me back in and my gripes are comparitively few compared to the positives that Hollow Knight has to offer.
Also fortunately the most difficult parts of the game are optional and can be skipped if going for the normal ending, which can be achieved by pretty much anyone playing this provided they don't neglect a basic level of preparation, since the game is so non-linear you can always revisit areas later after upgrading your character and finding the right equip combos. Or if you love a challenge. are a souls/platformer vet or simply a masochist the optional content has got you covered too as some zones and bosses will just continue to kick your♥♥♥♥♥until you finally make a breakthrough.
I would reccommend this if you are a fan of Metroidvanias or side scrollers, if you like non-linearity and want to be challenged, or if the idea of exploring a strange and confusing world full of amazing, wondrous and sometimes surprising things while sort of trying to fit the pieces together sounds appealling to you. If not, you may still want to consider checking this one out, it definitely has great value and well worth the cheap price.

This is one of the best games of 2017.  The visuals are absolutely gorgeous, and a ethereal soundtrack thorough create a calm, lonely atmosphere very reminiscent at times of Super Metroid.  The controls are tight and combat is fluid, but deliberate.  The amount of content is staggering for a $15 game, especially if you're a completionist.  It took me about 25 hours to complete the game with above 90% completion (I'm still searching for those last few mask shards and charms) and was worth every second.  I never felt lost or without direction and was always working towards something (even if I didn't know exactly what that something was).
The only negatives I can give this game is there are parts of the map that backtracking to can get slightly tedious, which mostly becomes a problem for completionist runs.  In addition to that, there's an option section including some rather brutal, almost Super Meat Boy-esque platforming, which became very frustrating very quickly and really struck me as coming out of nowhere.  Almost the entire rest of the game is more heavy on the action than the platforming, platforming being more of a means to the action and exploration.  There are a couple challenge or almost puzzly platforming sections strewn throughout, but nothing that made me die repeatedly in frustration.   Fortunately, as I said this is an optional section and overall is very doable with perserverance.
If you're a fan of metroidvanias, you'd be doing yourself a disservice to not pick this one up.  It has tight controls, is gorgeous to look at, and is packed to the brim with content (and there's a free patch coming that will introduce even more content).
10/10

It's becoming a bit of a repetitive thing with regard to my game interest if you browse my library and list of reviews - Metroidvania; but, who cares?! To me, Metroidvania games encapsulate the very things gamers and casuals alike want in their experience. Exploration, discovery, tough-as-nails bosses, scarce but effective storyline, and just plain fun. Hollow Knight does a superb job in capturing everything great about these types of games - it really is a game that does the genre justice.
If someone were to ask me what my favorite game of all-time is, I would smirkingly respond, "That's a stupid question." This would be my logical response, as specifying one game to be hyperbolically better than any other game in any genre would be preposterous. However, my gut, knee-jerk response would be Super Metroid. Then, I would tip my hat for runner-up to SOTN.
Is Hollow Knight better than my all-time best game? No.
Here's why. And, I'm not being biased by nostalgia here, as I never owned an SNES when it came out. As a matter of fact, I just played the game for the first time about 2 years ago off the Virtual Store - Wii U – roughly 20 years after its original release. So, I’m saying this after playing it at 4:3 with pixelated graphics on a 55” flat 1080p screen, emulated by Nintendo’s virtual offering. Super Metroid is special. It has all of the things previously mentioned. The difference between Super Metroid and a similar style game like Hollow Knight is that Super Metroid does all of the things above…but effortlessly. Except for the opening scene (and the closing scene), there's no dialogue / monologue. You don't purchase anything. Unless I looked through the literature, I really wouldn't even know the controls. It brilliantly engages the player into a world that allows learning and progressing through the very fabric of the game. No area feels out of place. The graphics, although 16-bit, are integral to the ominous tone of the desolate planet on which Samus explores. Of course, the technology in the mid-90's was limited to that level of commercial graphics, but, again, that's what makes the game so special. It's a Field of Dreams meets Shawshank Redemption meets Goodfellas...it’s a perfect storm (not the movie - that one was just ok).
Hollow Knight pays great homage to Super Metroid. There are other games in the genre that don't; so, that says a lot. Is it pioneering like SM? No...for the reasons above. Super Metroid is lightning in a bottle. Hollow Knight is thunder, rain, clouds, wind...it has all the ingredients. It just doesn't have that special cohesion like Super Metroid - some intentional - some serendipitous.
I won't do pros and cons. I will say that Hollow Knight offers all the things someone would want from a Metroidvania, and it does it better than most (if not, all) other successors. The graphics are good - very good. The controls are quite adequate - responsive to what the game requires of you. The bosses are tough - very tough - especially one certain Failed Champion. I will say the AI in this game is brilliant - frustratingly brilliant. Do enemies have movesets that you can memorize? Absolutely. Are you fighting the same pattern every time? Absolutely NOT! The game adjusts so well to your position, your jump and move trajectory, and your attack pattern, that it feels ridiculously organic...it almost feels like it's a PVP opponent - especially with the aforementioned Dream Boss. Story? It's there. It doesn't hand-hold. But, it tries to be a lot of different games with a common Metroidvania thread. So, the story, is not the main draw. The musical score is fantastical, as it should be.
Should you buy this game? Yes. For $15US, I logged 33 hours with 65% completion - beating the main story. So, there's 35% of the content of the game that I have yet to uncover. And, I don't hesitate in saying I would go back and play the whole thing again.
Addendum: After completing the main game and writing the review, I embarked upon some of the other 35% of the stuff I missed. Holy crap...this game has a ton of content! And, I have to say, this side content contains some of the most difficult platforming, guantlet fights and alternate-version bosses you will encounter. The platforming and guantlet level (one in particular) actually made me improve in other games. This is truly a gem!

When a game starts with the main character driving down a road singing along to Stan Bush's "You've got the touch" blasting on his radio you know the game is going to be awesome and the rest of the game does not disappoint.
From the get-go you're treated to gorgeous Japanese-themed landscapes (and music) and this continues on throughout the game, making this one of the most stunning games I've ever played. It's also really funny as the main character, Lo Wang (yeah, have fun with that one :P) is knowingly over-the-top and regularly cracks jokes and puns when he's not busy slicing apart demons and blowing them up with his incredibly lethal arsenal of weapons.
And this brings me to a very important point: this game is not for the squemish! Enemies that include both human beings and demons are blown apart, utterly dismembered, lit on fire and the level of brutality displayed on screen is downright shocking at first.
The gameplay itself is a lot of fun as you accumulate an increasingly deadly array of weaponry that feel powerful, precise and versatile as each gun has an alternate firing mode that can be unlocked. You also, surpringly for a FPS, wield a katana and can learn some kick♥♥♥♥♥combos and abilties à la Kill Bill that allow you to carve up the opposition in a delightfully graceful manner :D
I also really enjoyed the design of the upgrade system as the menu sports traditional Japanese art illustrations to demonstrate your skill-ups, and a 3D rotating model of your character meditating topless in a circle of candles where each new demonic ability that you learn is reflected as a beautiful tatoo that gets etched on a different part of your skin.
Lastly, the story is quite entertaining and deep as it incorporates elements of revenge, redemption, friendship, love and betrayal. A large part of the story is told via art cutscenes which are absolutely beautiful as well as through Lo Wang's and Hoji's regular conversations and entertaining banter as their bromance blossoms (see what I did there? :P). It's also worth noting that the voice acting is excellent.
The one shortcoming to this game is its length imho. I found that parts of it felt overly long at times and could have benefited from some trimming but it's a minor point.

A game like no other, and really brings the nostalgic feel of old school shooters and hack n' slash. Haven't played the original Shadow Warrior, though I have played old school shooters like doom and such so I anticipate its the same (please correct me if I'm wrong).
You are Lo Wang, a seemingly hard-skin individual able to withstand tons of bullets and giant demons in suit of armors with ease. With an arsenal of badarsey weaponry, you will go through a a journey slaying humans and demons alike in a campaign length of about 8 - 15 hours.
The pros. Oh boy. This game really hits you in the head with its old school combat. With drawbacks to the original with fanservice, references and... naked anime girls? The game comes in with 3 skill-tree like interfaces, called Powers, Skills, and Weapons (though the weapons are more like upgrades) which are- in my opinion pretty cool and can make one's user experience easier (please see cons). You will hack and slash (or gun your way through, but to be honest, no one ever uses guns.. right? I hope.) through a multitude of enemy types. Lo Wang, the protagonist, throughout the game undergoes pretty evident character development, going from a brat and dumb to a pro and awesome. The environments are also VERY well made IMO, able to maneuver quickly and efficiently without much obstacles in your way (unless its a corridor then might as well use your guns and dual-akimbo that crud).
Cons, eh. Like I said before, Powers, Skills and Weapons will make one's user experience much, and I mean, MUCH easier. I really do NOT recommend playing this game on Normal or easier as that will ruin the classic "Shadow Warrior" experience. Besides, old school-like games are mean't to be played with a challenge, no doubt about that. Furthermore, I have two REALLY glaring problems for this game that I think I should address (in my opinion). The first being the enemies themselves. Even though I said that as a Pro point, they really recycled and reused the enemies A LOT. Every few chapters will have 1 new enemy and you will barely need to change your tactics at all. The boss fights are really cool at first, but it kinda disappointed me when every single boss is literally the same "shoot dem armurz and u winz", and to me, most bosses had the same skill sets with different animations (though the last boss fight when you had the Kage sword was pretty damn cool). Second major problem is the map layout and backtracking. As a Pro, the map design (like I said before) is really well made for combat situations. However, the devs seemed to have slacked off about 3/4 into the game. With the map so huge with no sense of direction, I found myself walking back and forth to realize I had to destroy a third statue 2 areas away where I came from in order to progress to the 3rd area I was in. The map flow was ideal for me at the beginning of the game, but it fell off at one point and it just felt damn lazy and it was very boring for me, not to mention that they even reused some parts of the map in other chapters as well.
Even so, I do recommend this game. I wholeheartedly feel that, despite the cons, you will have loads of fun for the dozen of hours you will accumulate. Though, I suggest waiting for a price drop (as I got this for only 10 bucks) as I don't think the amount of content in this game is enough to satisfy that price range now (max 30 dollars imo) but they
include the Viscera Cleanup Detail version for free if you purchase this game.
*NOTE: Everything is in my opinion, so pls no judgey

This is a very enjoyable game.
You play as Lo Wang (insert male reproductive organ jokes here), a hired thug for Zilla, an immensely powerful businessman, and your mission is to retrieve (by monetary means or by force) an ancient sword from another businessman. During the “negotiations” things went awry, and a demon apocalypse is let loose on this world. You, your demonic sidekick, and an ancient sword, are now all that can set things right.
It is difficult to tie this game down as either a hack and slasher, or a shooter. Your first weapon is your sword, but then you have a series of ranged weapons, from a revolver to a rocket launcher, all of which you can upgrade with in game collected money. You can also unlock and upgrade “Ki” based powers, such as healing and stuns, and skills, such as katana skills or passive health perks.
The game takes you from a Japanese city scape, to the docks, to an icy fortress, to the domain of the ancients. The sceneries are all carrying signs from this demonic apocalypse, with mutilated bodies strewn everywhere, destroyed vehicles, and demonic altars or effigies.
While the gameplay is deliciously visceral (you are a walking talking abattoir of demons), the humour is one of its greatest strengths. It is seldom that a game can make you actively chuckle or blurt out a laugh. The banter from Lo Wang to the player is well appreciated, and the general dialogue between characters itself keeps this trend very well. Though I want to recommend this game... I just can't. It is close, if Steam had a "Meh" choice in between yes and no I'd choose it. Basically it breaks down like this:
The Good: It is a pirate game.
The Bad: It is an Assassin's Creed game.
It is very clear they intended to make a nice pirate game where you got to play boats, plunder cargo, murder dudes, and generally have a good time. A modern incarnation of the classic Sid Meyer’s Pirates game. However Ubisoft decided that we wouldn’t buy something if it wasn’t in an existing series and so tried to shoehorn it in to the Assassin’s Creed universe and glomed on a buch of stuff that makes it worse.
The result is you have lots of fun when the game lets you. When it lets you off the leash and you get to go play with your ship, it's great. However that gets interfered with regularly for Assassin's Creed garbage including the dreaded "Follow the guy but don’t get too close!" missions, which now you get to do in your ship as well. You are continually having to deal with annoying missions to forward the story and get to play more.
Also the PC port has horrible optimization. I have a 5930K and a 980GTX and it still struggles to maintain 1080 @ 60fps with details turned up. Give me a break. I mean it looks good, but it should run far better, it is just more Ubisoft laziness on the optimization front.
So while I don't hate it, I wouldn’t recommend it. If it goes on sale for a real cheap price, then sure maybe get it. However get yourself a trainer for it too, so that when you get frustrated with the stupid AC stuff you can just cheat your way by it and get back to being a pirate.
It's sad, because without the AC content, this would be a pretty amazing game. As it is, the annoyance dampens the fun factor a whole lot.

A game like no other, and really brings the nostalgic feel of old school shooters and hack n' slash. Haven't played the original Shadow Warrior, though I have played old school shooters like doom and such so I anticipate its the same (please correct me if I'm wrong).
You are Lo Wang, a seemingly hard-skin individual able to withstand tons of bullets and giant demons in suit of armors with ease. With an arsenal of badarsey weaponry, you will go through a a journey slaying humans and demons alike in a campaign length of about 8 - 15 hours.
The pros. Oh boy. This game really hits you in the head with its old school combat. With drawbacks to the original with fanservice, references and... naked anime girls? The game comes in with 3 skill-tree like interfaces, called Powers, Skills, and Weapons (though the weapons are more like upgrades) which are- in my opinion pretty cool and can make one's user experience easier (please see cons). You will hack and slash (or gun your way through, but to be honest, no one ever uses guns.. right? I hope.) through a multitude of enemy types. Lo Wang, the protagonist, throughout the game undergoes pretty evident character development, going from a brat and dumb to a pro and awesome. The environments are also VERY well made IMO, able to maneuver quickly and efficiently without much obstacles in your way (unless its a corridor then might as well use your guns and dual-akimbo that crud).
Cons, eh. Like I said before, Powers, Skills and Weapons will make one's user experience much, and I mean, MUCH easier. I really do NOT recommend playing this game on Normal or easier as that will ruin the classic "Shadow Warrior" experience. Besides, old school-like games are mean't to be played with a challenge, no doubt about that. Furthermore, I have two REALLY glaring problems for this game that I think I should address (in my opinion). The first being the enemies themselves. Even though I said that as a Pro point, they really recycled and reused the enemies A LOT. Every few chapters will have 1 new enemy and you will barely need to change your tactics at all. The boss fights are really cool at first, but it kinda disappointed me when every single boss is literally the same "shoot dem armurz and u winz", and to me, most bosses had the same skill sets with different animations (though the last boss fight when you had the Kage sword was pretty damn cool). Second major problem is the map layout and backtracking. As a Pro, the map design (like I said before) is really well made for combat situations. However, the devs seemed to have slacked off about 3/4 into the game. With the map so huge with no sense of direction, I found myself walking back and forth to realize I had to destroy a third statue 2 areas away where I came from in order to progress to the 3rd area I was in. The map flow was ideal for me at the beginning of the game, but it fell off at one point and it just felt damn lazy and it was very boring for me, not to mention that they even reused some parts of the map in other chapters as well.
Even so, I do recommend this game. I wholeheartedly feel that, despite the cons, you will have loads of fun for the dozen of hours you will accumulate. Though, I suggest waiting for a price drop (as I got this for only 10 bucks) as I don't think the amount of content in this game is enough to satisfy that price range now (max 30 dollars imo) but they
include the Viscera Cleanup Detail version for free if you purchase this game.

This is a very enjoyable game.
You play as Lo Wang (insert male reproductive organ jokes here), a hired thug for Zilla, an immensely powerful businessman, and your mission is to retrieve (by monetary means or by force) an ancient sword from another businessman. During the “negotiations” things went awry, and a demon apocalypse is let loose on this world. You, your demonic sidekick, and an ancient sword, are now all that can set things right.
It is difficult to tie this game down as either a hack and slasher, or a shooter. Your first weapon is your sword, but then you have a series of ranged weapons, from a revolver to a rocket launcher, all of which you can upgrade with in game collected money. You can also unlock and upgrade “Ki” based powers, such as healing and stuns, and skills, such as katana skills or passive health perks.
The game takes you from a Japanese city scape, to the docks, to an icy fortress, to the domain of the ancients. The sceneries are all carrying signs from this demonic apocalypse, with mutilated bodies strewn everywhere, destroyed vehicles, and demonic altars or effigies.
While the gameplay is deliciously visceral (you are a walking talking abattoir of demons), the humour is one of its greatest strengths. It is seldom that a game can make you actively chuckle or blurt out a laugh. The banter from Lo Wang to the player is well appreciated, and the general dialogue between characters itself keeps this trend very well. Even during serious moments the characters retain their personality.
The story, or rather reason behind the demonic breakout, is a bit convoluted; but never fear, the gameplay more than makes up for any short comings. Although, admittedly you will find yourself thinking, “why am I doing this again?”, but then you just make another demon go splash.
My only complaint would be the linearness of the game’s levels. Once you’ve finished with a section, you’ll never be able to revisit the area. This makes hunting for secrets and loot difficult, as you’d have to replay levels in order to find all secrets.

Wow.
Thank you Devolver Digital, for making a game that almost made me want to shed manly tears...
Regardless of wether or not you liked the original Shadow Warrior from 1997, I was not expecting a game like this to be made from a re-imagining of said game. This is how re-imaginings should be done. Tasteful amounts of nostolgic reference to the source material, with a ton of polish and thought put into it.
Sure, things have changed from the original, but a lot of complaints people have don't seem that bad in the long run. The levels are much more linear, but I found myself getting lost and backtracking a heck of a lot less than the original. There were fewer enemy types, but half of them were not cheap re-skins. Sure there were less weapons, but the ones present had way more battle application than a lot of the weak guns from the original that I never used. The katana combat is more than a melee weapon now, it is the weapon able to tip combat against the hordes of enemies this series is so well known for in your favor. Things have changed, modernized, but not for the worse, for the better.
The mood has changed significantly too. As opposed to being a snarky killer spewing Engrish as you murder Japanese stereotypes, the story in this remake was handled with some grace and effort, and manages to do the impossible: respectfully incorperate Japanese mythos, art, and culture in a game built entirely around a beserk shogun♥♥♥♥♥♥joke killing demons. The humor is still present, the fortunes, the one-liners, the rabbits doing the nasty, but it is all presented in a more subtle way (with the exception of the retro easter egg areas of course). Everything gels pretty well. The combat, story, soundtrack, acting, and visuals are all very consistent and feel like they belong. Whereas the original couldn't shake the feeling of being a Duke Nukem mod, Shadow Warrior can be played with or without knowledge of the original games that spawned it. This is a sign of a good remake.
So, in the end, Shadow Warrior is worth playing if you enjoy the gameplay of retro shooters, but wished they could be a little more polished. Whether or not you think it is worth full price is up to you, but you should certainly give it a try before you discount it as just another remake.

Shadow Warrior is not your typical shooter, in fact it's not even very close to the game its remaking (aside from a few weapons, and the main character).  Does this mean Shadow Warrior is crap? Absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing Not.
In Shadow Warrior you play Japanese/Chinese Assassin Lo Wang, who, armed a katana, cuts down gangsters and demons with ease. As Lo Wang, you enter a pact with a demon?/god called Hoji, who helps you find the three parts of the Nobitsura Kage. All in all, the story, whilst not the greatest, still can keep you interested enough to see it to the end.
Shadow Warrior does get the gameplay right, offering a fair variety in weapons, and allowing for quite a bit customisation as far as your playstyle goes. This customisation comes in three varieties: spending Karma earned through fighting to upgrade passive abilities, spending Money to upgrade your weapons, and spending Ki Crystals to upgrade your active abilities, such as a more powerful shockwave, or a faster heal.
The actual combat allows for experimentation, and using the sword is an absolute blast, as you can feel the impact as you cleave through enemies. The powers also give a dynamic edge to combat and gives you plenty of options even if you want to just play with the katana. The other weapons arent bad either; once you've spent some money to upgrade them they actually come into their own, standing as an alternative to the katana devastation. In the gameplay department, Shadow Warrior doesnt dissapoint.
Graphically, Shadow Warrior uses plenty of lighting effects to its fullest advantage, and it really makes the game feel special at times, especially when you're in the Shadow Realm. Artistically, the designs borrow from a  traditional chinese art aesthetic but with some twists, and it really makes the game feel unique. Music and sounds are also fairly well done, and overall (despite some lower textured/polygon models on some of the characters) Shadow Warrior is a great looking game.
If you enjoy shooters with personality, that give you a lot of different options in tackling combat, and is visually appealing, you can't go wrong with Shadow Warrior, it simply is one of the best and underrated games of 2013.

Such a beautiful, fun and immersive world held back by the gameplay and story. First, I have to say that this game runs terribly, regardless of the graphical settings. Checking the frame rate while running the game, going from absolute highest settings to absolute lowest gives a bonus of only four or five fps, with intensive moments like large naval battles still slogging along in almost slideshow-like quality. This isn't anything wrong with my system, I far, far exceed even recommended hardware requirements, the game simply runs poorly. Quickly googling the Digital Foundry analysis will show that this is not something unique to myself or the other reviewers criticizing the performance, this game is simply running on a poorly-designed, horribly outdated engine, an issue only compounded by the rush-job optimization that clearly took place on pc, with consoles given higher priority than the pc version (ah Ubisoft, it's almost like throwing thousands of employees from studios around the world in two-year development cycles to meet annual release schedules doesn't make for the highest quality software, or something like that). That's not to say the console version, which I also own, runs any better. The ps4 edition, which Digital Foundry says runs the best, still slogs along anytime something intense happens (a leap of faith, naval combat, etc.), but the lower quality textures, minimal AA and reduced field of view on the consoles makes for less stuttering in general, so when you casually walk through a crowded street it's less likely to stutter. So if someone doesn't yet know how the game performs and actually reads this very late review, be warned that the console version, though inferior in several ways, sadly performs more smoothly than the pc version, regardless of hardware capabilities.
The story is boring, every time I got shoehorned into yet another "Follow Person X" mission so the game can progress the story I felt like shooting myself in the face. Even worse is the painfully uninsteresting modern day story, but I won't speak too much about that since some people may honestly want to follow the story for these games. Just know it's not good. The boring story and outdated game design included to tell this story brings up my other point, the low quality gameplay. Don't get me wrong, the naval combat is amazing and I absolutely love fighting monster ships, boarding them and then using my ill-gotten cargo to further upgrade my own ship. The naval aspect does of course get monotonous, anytime one sole aspect of a game is supposed to carry the gameplay you're going to get bored at some point, but all in all it's incredibly fun. The land missions, however, are where the game falls into the exact same traps as every other game in the series. Five years ago, when AC 2 came out and revolutionized the series, the uninspired combat, unresponsive and muddy controls, and the general lack of variety in things to do were overshadowed by the scale of the world, the unexpected quality of the story and the overabundance of side-quests to keep you running from rooftop to rooftop when you felt you needed a break from the story. I think everyone will agree that this is something Ubisoft does right, they continue to absolutely jam their games full of extra content. The issue is that they haven't yet found a way to do anything different with these diversions, in fact they've actually moved backwards in some regards. The big new addition, the hunting side-quests clearly taken from Far Cry 3, has been watered down to be more kid-friendly, negatively affecting the enjoyment of it. There's no real danger aside from harpooning hilariously oversized sharks that can sink your little rowboat, there's no weight to your killing of the animals (clearly an attempt to avert criticism in a game that doesn't gear towards the Far Cry 3 demographic), and it begins to suffer from the series's tediousness when you begin chasing after animals only to get too close to a climb-able object and have your character suddenly climb it despite the object being off at a sharp angle and your character facing away from it, with your control input being in the direction away from the object and towards the animal.
The game is so incredibly buggy, unpolished and downright frustrating to play, especially when they force you into a mission where you must remain undetected and you must not kill anyone, that I feel like I'd only recommend it to someone who knows exactly what they're getting into, and even then I'd recommend it only at a steep discount. After the terrible abortion of a game that is Freedom Cry, I swore I'd never give Ubisoft my money again. Then, during a trade, the only thing to bring the trade to parity is, of course, another Ubisoft game, so here I am playing this game when I swore not to. I just can't, in good conscience, recommend this game to someone looking for casual fun, or even a long-time fan of the series, at anything more than ten dollars, and even then it's a bit of a stretch in my opinion. There's so many other, good games to play for cheaper that the idea of supporting Ubisoft's terrible approach to game design and general business philosophy just seems kind of ludicrous to me. I know it's en vogue to hate on the "Big Three" AAA developers (Ubi, Activision, and EA) and that is most certainly something I don't participate in, but if Ubisoft hasn't shown me they aren't worthy of their asking price then I must be blind. Even in such a lazy, iterative series, this game stands out to me for its stark contrasts. The game's beauty marred by its poor performance, the game's fun naval aspects marred by its terribly outdated land sequences and unresponsive controls, and the game's highly interesting setting completely decimated by uninspired characters and an incredibly disinteresting plot.
So tl;dr- I say no, avoid this if you don't already have it. The game just isn't worth it. The ps4 version runs smoother but still suffers stuttering and slowdown, and the graphics won't be as nice as on pc. If you absolutely must own this game, wait until Unity and Rogue come out and there's a nice sale on the game for less than ten bucks. It's just not worth more.
As an aside, if anyone actually reads this and has the game, if you're getting an issue where the screen freezes when you get near naval forts but the hud continues to work (so you can steer your ship away from the naval fort using the hud to unfreeze your screen), apparently turning ON volumetric fog fixes this for some unknown reason. As someone who spends a lot of his free time writing code for fun, I'd love to see what's going on in the minds of the senior developers when they build an AC game. Some of the design decisions are just incredibly bad.

This is one of the best games of 2017.  The visuals are absolutely gorgeous, and a ethereal soundtrack thorough create a calm, lonely atmosphere very reminiscent at times of Super Metroid.  The controls are tight and combat is fluid, but deliberate.  The amount of content is staggering for a $15 game, especially if you're a completionist.  It took me about 25 hours to complete the game with above 90% completion (I'm still searching for those last few mask shards and charms) and was worth every second.  I never felt lost or without direction and was always working towards something (even if I didn't know exactly what that something was).
The only negatives I can give this game is there are parts of the map that backtracking to can get slightly tedious, which mostly becomes a problem for completionist runs.  In addition to that, there's an option section including some rather brutal, almost Super Meat Boy-esque platforming, which became very frustrating very quickly and really struck me as coming out of nowhere.  Almost the entire rest of the game is more heavy on the action than the platforming, platforming being more of a means to the action and exploration.  There are a couple challenge or almost puzzly platforming sections strewn throughout, but nothing that made me die repeatedly in frustration.   Fortunately, as I said this is an optional section and overall is very doable with perserverance.
If you're a fan of metroidvanias, you'd be doing yourself a disservice to not pick this one up.  It has tight controls, is gorgeous to look at, and is packed to the brim with content (and there's a free patch coming that will introduce even more content).

If you're looking for something fast-paced, something that requires instinct over intution, and something that allows you to jump, then look elsewhere. If you're looking for something clever to pass away a few hours -- perhaps the entirety of a Tuesday (hint, hint), then look no further.
Oh, one last thing: Be sure to play the demo, first. It's a different experience and story from the main game.

It's a first person smash em' up type game where your main weapon of choice will be your sword and as well as guns that are acquired throughout the game (launchers, pistols, machine guns, crossbows, demon heads you know the usual). The game play is addicting to those who like mindless violence and like seeing how well they are rated on their violent tendencies. There are three type of upgrade categories : one which uses money to upgrade physical weapons (dual pistols, dual machine guns, crossbow tips with explosive bolts, mini nukes as your rocket launcher), the second which uses ki to upgrade luck and mental factors of the protagonist, and the third which uses karma to upgrade sword abilities or stamina. Thanks to this upgrade system the mindless violence isn't so mindless as you actually have to use your mind to think which perks would actually benefit you. Enemies vary in shapes and sizes (small and big demons) but are all kill-able. Sometimes it's annoying as heck as some parts can become quite hard, but there's always a way to win.
The graphics are as best as they come. They do not hinder, stall, or skip in any way. Cinematics are just as good. Don't expect any graphical errors here unless you have a problem with your computer.
What happens after your done this game though? Well not much. You can run through it again but I had my fun with it and my friends are now enjoying it off my library. It was a fun game nothing against it, just wish I had more reason to go back to it.

I haven't played many metroidvanias, but I enjoy 2D games and this was reccomended based on its Bloodborne/Souls style atmosphere and I'm pretty happy I got this. It certainly has that feel and aesthetic in places, and also uses a similar aspect that gives you the chance to retrieve your stuff upon death, via backtracking to where you died and defeating your shade.
The environments in this game are beautiful and the soundtrack is just amazing. The world is quite large and progression is very non-linear, I managed to find myself in the Deepnest of all places very early on and missed some early areas and boss fights until very late in the game, because bosses can be fought in almost any order and many are even optional. The difficulty is also set pretty high, especially if you find yourself in an area or fight you are unprepared for and suddenly end up questioning your life decisions leading up to that point. On occassion it got frustrating to the point where I felt compelled to stop playing for a while, especially due to the constant humiliating backtracking to retry a boss since there's no save stations nearby or when the environmental obstacles become reminiscent of something I'd expect to see in Super Meat Boy. Still, the atmosphere and sense of wonder I felt from delving into the depths of this game inevitably pulled me back in and my gripes are comparitively few compared to the positives that Hollow Knight has to offer.
Also fortunately the most difficult parts of the game are optional and can be skipped if going for the normal ending, which can be achieved by pretty much anyone playing this provided they don't neglect a basic level of preparation, since the game is so non-linear you can always revisit areas later after upgrading your character and finding the right equip combos. Or if you love a challenge. are a souls/platformer vet or simply a masochist the optional content has got you covered too as some zones and bosses will just continue to kick your♥♥♥♥♥until you finally make a breakthrough.
I would reccommend this if you are a fan of Metroidvanias or side scrollers, if you like non-linearity and want to be challenged, or if the idea of exploring a strange and confusing world full of amazing, wondrous and sometimes surprising things while sort of trying to fit the pieces together sounds appealling to you. If not, you may still want to consider checking this one out, it definitely has great value and well worth the cheap price.

TLDR – The Stanley Parable is an extremely short game if you just follow the instructions, but it’s carried by the narration and the allure of alternate paths. The game is tagged as an “exploration game” so think of it as Portal without the puzzles, just wandering through rooms guided by a disembodied voice.
You play Stanley, a nondescript corporate drone who just follows directions all day long in an office job, until one day the directions stop coming and you need to find out why. To do this, you navigate the halls of your seemingly abandoned office building and discover what’s been going on behind the scenes as you slaved away day in and day out.
The game is played in first person perspective with no frills or features. You just walk around listening to the narrator talk about what you’re doing and what you’re supposed to do next. I’ll admit, half the time I spent playing this game was to get the Steam achievements, which are actually pretty easy to unlock. If you just follow the directions of the narrator, you can reach the game’s end in less than 10 minutes. However, if you want to experience all that the game has to offer, you’ll need to deliberately do things differently than the narrator describes. For example if the narrator says “Stanley took the door on the left” you go right, etc.
Pros:
+A soothing narrative style, similar to Bastion, with some meta humor thrown in. The game is all about finding all possible routes, most of them pretty obvious.
+Short game with easy Steam achievements.
Cons:
-The game was like 2 gigabytes to download and you can finish it in about 10 minutes…
-If you prefer action games, this isn’t for you. You just walk around listening to the narrator in a completely abandoned building.
Overall, if you just want a game to spend an hour on, you can give Stanley Parable a try. But be aware that it’s not an action game, just wandering around hearing the story, similar to a point and click game (in first person).

If you're looking for something fast-paced, something that requires instinct over intution, and something that allows you to jump, then look elsewhere. If you're looking for something clever to pass away a few hours -- perhaps the entirety of a Tuesday (hint, hint), then look no further.
Oh, one last thing: Be sure to play the demo, first. It's a different experience and story from the main game.

The other reviews don't lie, it's pretty good. So good, that I am about to start my second and third playthroughs (Spoilers: One of the playthroughs will be a bit different) but I am looking to 100% both instances. I can't recommend it enough.
Breakdown:
+Imagine if all Metroidvania games came together to hone their craft to perfection. You Jump, Dodge, slash, smash, and spellcast your way through the world and the tight, fleshed-out controls are truly marvelous, never feeling like they get in the way. There are some pretty crazy movement combos that I have pulled of mid-bossfight in order to save myself from a bad situation.
+An Immense, varied world that combines some of the best platforming I've ever played with some of the best fighting I could imagine in a souls-like game. The most important part of the game is movement, and tying it in with combat is a marvel in iteself. You can get lost without a map, but fast-travel and linkage between settings are adequate to keep the game flowing and there were very few times I was left honestly wishing that something was set up differently.
+/-This game is quite difficult, your results may vary, but I loved almost every minute of it (see below)
-There's at least one boss fight that is probably pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I was only able to beat it due to dumb luck because skill doesn't help after a point
-No health bars on bosses seems like a design oversight, as there's no way to tell if you are close to beating something. There were multiple times where I was left wondering if I was even dealing relevant damage to a few bosses.
+Look at the screenshots. They're beautiful. Add in a few overlays, some animation, and a wonderful parallax and you have quite likely the best-looking game of this year, I would even stretch to say ever.
+The music is incredible. The world exudes a haunting atmosphere, and the complement with the music just compounds on itself to create this solemn, breathing locale of mystery.
+The world itself is put together nicely, and while open-ended requires backtracking and upgrades to fully navigate. It's a maze that is wonderful to get lost in, and the progression is logical and fun.
-If you don't buy the maps, odds are you won't be able to progress in the game.
+The mystery of the land and your character's story is extremely compelling. I am not normally a huge fan of these types of stories (there's almost no narrative exposition, but rather complete environmental control
but this game hit all the right notes to leave me with a sense of what was happening while drawing me in to complete more. I have heard there are multiple endings, and I am looking forward to it immensely.
+The main questline was ominous and foreboding, and when I reached each seal's lair I was truly frightened.
-
+Very rarely does a game come along that can grip me in such a way, hold my attention so well, and challenge me enough to warrant a reaction like this. This is, so far, my GOTY and I can't really see that changing any time soon. A masterpiece, I can not believe how truly wonderful this game turned out to be.
I was playing for 25+ hours at the time of this review, had beaten the game immediately prior, and only had 51% completion. There is a LOT to do. I would pay $30-60 for this game easily, so for $15 it is definitely worth it.
Overall, this game is a must-have. I am bound to complete it to 100% multiple times on steam, and then even more when it releases for the Nintendo Switch. This is a Top-10 game for me pretty easily.

Being a big fan of the original classic game, this looked like a no-brainer purchase. I wasn't disappointed. The graphics are fantastic, the gameplay is addicting, the action intense (and sometimes quite infuriating), the voice acting perfectly done, the humor excellent and a superb soundtrack. I like that it basically takes place in the late 80s. This is indicated by the big brick cellphone Lo Wang uses in his car during the prologue cinematic and that he is listening to (as well as singing along with) the great Stan Bush song "The Touch" from "The Transformers Animated Movie" (1986). Wang is accompanied throughout the game by a friendly demon-ish spirit, Hoji, that attaches to him via a mask on his leg and only reappears visually during cinematic scenes. I say demon-ish in that he isn't a monster. His appearance is more like a jester with a dull one-color patchwork outfit sewn together and his mask is harlequin-like in design. Their conversations are always interesting and often funny. There is so much to like about this new revision of the game. One of the little bits I love is when you get into a really big fight, and you are hacking and slashing down enemies all around you, part of the way into it or near the end, Lo Wang will laugh out loud at the craziness of the situation or say some funny line. BTW, be sure to shoot all the rabbits you see, but also be prepared to take on the hardcore dark hare that appears every so often. It's sort of a nod to the killer rabbit from "Monty Python and the Holy Grail" film.
Another fun thing the developers did is give random nods to the original game via hidden areas that use the same graphics as back then. It really is impressive to see how much computer animation has come when you can look at them side by side in places like this. You go from blocky, flat, low-tech graphics to near photo realism.
I used to be big into game soundtracks, but fell out for many, many years. This game has drawn me back in. I'm actually listening to the soundtrack right now as I type this review (which comes with the collector's edition of the game, though I had to balance the songs volume wise in my audio editor. Their base levels were way too high. Reminded me of the great "Black Mesa Source" game soundtrack). You will really enjoy the music in this game. I don't usually give reviews, but this game is so good I felt I needed to. Below are the key things I feel make this game great.
Difficulty - The challenge of this game is perfectly set in a way that will chalenge you, but not be so hard that it makes you rage quit every time (I might have once or twice, but moving on haha...). The variation in the combat styles of each new monster you come across really keeps you from getting bored throughout the whole story. When you first meet a new monster you will have a hard time with it, but as soon as you master it's attack patterns then you have a severe advantage going forward.
Variety - As you progress through the story you get upgrades, new spells,  and on top of that you get to choose between different power ups that can change how you play the game. This keeps things fresh.
Graphics/gameplay - Everything is so smooth while playing and the art style looks fantastic. Not much else to say about that.
Price - I can't believe this game is only $15. I have already spent over 11 hours on it and I have plenty more to do before I finish!

Being a big fan of the original classic game, this looked like a no-brainer purchase. I wasn't disappointed. The graphics are fantastic, the gameplay is addicting, the action intense (and sometimes quite infuriating), the voice acting perfectly done, the humor excellent and a superb soundtrack. I like that it basically takes place in the late 80s. This is indicated by the big brick cellphone Lo Wang uses in his car during the prologue cinematic and that he is listening to (as well as singing along with) the great Stan Bush song "The Touch" from "The Transformers Animated Movie" (1986). Wang is accompanied throughout the game by a friendly demon-ish spirit, Hoji, that attaches to him via a mask on his leg and only reappears visually during cinematic scenes. I say demon-ish in that he isn't a monster. His appearance is more like a jester with a dull one-color patchwork outfit sewn together and his mask is harlequin-like in design. Their conversations are always interesting and often funny. There is so much to like about this new revision of the game. One of the little bits I love is when you get into a really big fight, and you are hacking and slashing down enemies all around you, part of the way into it or near the end, Lo Wang will laugh out loud at the craziness of the situation or say some funny line. BTW, be sure to shoot all the rabbits you see, but also be prepared to take on the hardcore dark hare that appears every so often. It's sort of a nod to the killer rabbit from "Monty Python and the Holy Grail" film.
Another fun thing the developers did is give random nods to the original game via hidden areas that use the same graphics as back then. It really is impressive to see how much computer animation has come when you can look at them side by side in places like this. You go from blocky, flat, low-tech graphics to near photo realism.

Hollow Knight succeeds our Castlevanias, our Metroids, and continues the trend of telling the industry that yes -- people like hard games.
You won't find anything revolutionary here if you've been a fan of the Metroidvania genre, but what you will encounter is a wonderfully polished experience with beautiful environments, stark themes, and an elegant, melee-focused combat system. Gameplay functions by exploring in a 2D environment through set rooms with enemies carefully placed for unique combat encounters. The best part is that it's tailored as a story experience -- so if you're tired of the inflation of rogue-lites, this is a nice change of pace that alludes to a Dark Souls-esque world.
Starting this game was uncomfortable due to the insane amount of content and size of the map. The most daunting part about these type of games are remembering to backtrack to earlier areas when new abilities are given to traverse a previously impossible obstacle. However, the map is informative enough to help even the most direction-deficient players (that's me). I completed this game in 47 hours with a 99% completion -- all without a single guide on the internet.

There is a lot to say about Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag. You have a vast open world, in which you can travel by foot or by sea. You can either be stealth or brutal in your tactics. You can be the Devil of the Seven Seas or a vigilante of the nations and inspire freedom to your crew.
The graphics are absolutely amazing. I've always admired water textures in video games and other than Skyrim; this has been the best I've seen by far. The sails of the ships and the gusts of wind that push them across the watery abyss. The environmental hazards of the sea; rouge waves and cyclones that rip apart everything in its path. The smallest island to the largest populated city. This game has a realistic and unique quality.
The Gameplay is excellent. The Pirate story line is something that someone can only imagine. Sure, they have movies, other pirate games, etc. But I never have felt the true pirate experience. The Assassin, Edward Kenway, is an amazing addition to the Creed Line. The battles on Land are just as expected as an Assassin's Creed game, but with new tools, outfits and other additions. The Ship Battles are an amazing feature. There's a lot you can choose from to fix it up how you like. Some of the things you love, must be found or conquered to be added upon your ship.
The Present Day story line was rather interesting. Some of it made sense and the rest of it did not. It's pretty expected to be confused about it, because you have no idea who you're character is. Sample 17 is the bloodline from Subject 17. So, as far as it is concerned. The character you are in control of, does not have any connection to the bloodline. You are just going back into Subject 17's ancestral line. Hopefully something will have mention in Unity's Present Day.
The mulitplayer I couldn't really get into. I think it's fun to play with other people, but I don't think they have mastered this quality in their industry yet. They still have some things they need to work on for multiplayer that will appeal and increase their community and fanbase. With Unity on its way, I do believe Co-Op is their greatest option for the moment, until they can figure out what to fix in their multiplayer services.
All in All. Best Assassin's Creed since Altair. 5/5 Singleplayer, 2/5 Online Experience.

On top of that, nightmare mode is such a cliff that you are pretty much forced to buy the summoner and EV dlcs in order to progress through it, as well as farm for hours in order to get decent items. The big flaw in the game is that it relies on RGN; the items rely on stats that are randomly generated. And instead of fixing this system, the devs decided to just give you more items so hopefully you eventually get a lucky drop. Most of the items generated are either missing key stats, or have negative values on them thus reducing your chances of getting anything decent.
The trading community is slowly dying if not dead, since most good players decided to move onto better games.
So like I said, I enjoyed the first few hours pre nightmare, but after that it just isn't worth your time or money.
