Hollow Knight is the love child of Dark Souls and Castlevania. It also had a wild fling with Metroid series that results in a fantastic game. If you like platforming mixed with combat and exploration, then you will love this game.
As for the graphics of the game, the graphics are all drawn by hand and look amazing. Some areas are simply beautiful, and I would love to see this style in future games.
The characters are charming enough, I do reccomend hitting them with a special item to peer into their dreams and getting a bit more story though. They're all unique and contribute to the world in some way, either through a service, or simply lore building. The bosses in particular are well designed with different styles of fighting. Hornet being the most fun in my opinion.
The music is on point as well. It's very Dark Souls, and sets the tone well for certain important areas, but it's upbeat enough to enable me to slash away at the bosses with a smile. Some areas do have background noise that can disrupt the music, but it's fixed by simply turning the effects volume down.
I will mention my biggest complaint though. If you want the true ending, then be prepared to suffer. Without spoiling too much, this involves an area called the White Palace. It is not a palace any sane King or Queen would like. It is a death trap, filled to the brim with saws, spikes, and spears. Several sections require near pixel perfect precision and it took multiple rage quits to complete. I HIGHLY reccomend looking for a guide on youtube that details how to skip a few of the sections in this area. Now, if you're a fan of Super Meat Boy, then prepare to blow a load onto your keyboard upon reaching this point. Finally, the final boss does suffer from a frame rate issue currently. This was a mild complaint, and was fixed once I turned down the particle effects. Honestly this could be attributed to my computer more than anything.
Do I reccomend the game? Yes, 100%. It is a fantastic game with a story that will leave you wanting more. It's well designed with a perfect upgrade/progression system and is filled with tight combat, good, challenging platforming in most cases, and characters that are easily likeable. A good soundtrack accompanies it all, and the world is massive, filled with secrets and rewards for those willing to look. I eagerly await DLC for this, and whatever project the Dev team might have in mind afterwards.

Short Review:
An extremely well cured fps with lots of old school elements, such as simple minding shooting and lots of enemies, as well as some new mechanics, like upgrades, skills and even a healing spell. Despite being very linear and repetitive, it delivers to you what shooters nowadays forgot: mindless and exciting action!
Long Review:
Alongside Serious Sam BFE and maybe Bioshock (whichever you prefer), Shadow warrior is one of the best old school shooters of the last year and despite having two major flaws, the game is absolutely a blast to play through.
While the story is surprisingly well told, even though not a main point of the game itself, and having both old school mechanis as well as new, the game is fast paced, filled with action, lots of different ways to complete the game and, most importantly for a fps, it's lots of fun.
Like I said, the story is very good even though not the focus but the main character is very likeable and your companion is...quite amusing. While you'll never see your main antagonist until later the game is still engaging since the story slowly unfolds itself thanks to splendidly made cutscenes in a sort of 2.5D that really are a beauty: I honestly loved to watch them, and they were great: you can see how much passion it was put into this game but the details and the cure of each level.
The gameplay is fast paced, well made and extremely fun: unlike common shooters, you can also use your sword and I can safely say, it's one of the strongest weapons in the game (minus the range, of course) and it can do a lot of different skills that actually are useful! The thrust is still the best, but it's just fun to experiment with each skill and weapons.
For the weapons themselves, you have a good variety and if I have to pick a bad weapon, it's probably the flame thrower: it's not very good until you upgrade it to launch bombs, but even then you'll get a rocket launcher later...
Each weapon can be upgraded individually and each are visually different when upgraded and are very strong, with most a secondary fire (which is usually needed to be bought first). I honestly can't say which is better since I kept switching weapons all the time: the action requires you to often switch weapons to the one you need the most, so I was never bored when it came to combat!
In addition, the places are so well made, detailed, and some of them have even little easter eggs for those who played the original game. Thumbs up for that!
Alas, my biggest problems with this games are two, and they are really...REALLY big in my opinion.
1) It's extremely repetitive:  despite you can fight the enemies in various way and you -have- always variation, the fights are often the same and...yes you can easily win most of them by using one or two weapons. All the time. There is a lot of variation in weapons, skills and whatnot but how could they make the combat so dull and repetitive at the same time? I played in normal and the fights were not so hard and they were easily won by using the sword. Sure, some fights require you to actually switch weapons often, but that's probably a very big minority of it. That is also why I kept quitting the game: I just got bored too fast.
2) It's linear: for being an old school shooter, the game is extremely linear and except for few shortcuts and hidden secrets, you really go through one single road. It's not small but at the same time you just cannot move as you please: you need to follow a road in order to go further, unlike the old school shooters where the exploration of a level was just part of the game itself. Amazing level design, but still too close to the general fps mind: long corridors with enemies to shoot.
So if you ever wanted a good shooting game that isn't "realistic" and just wants you to shoot stuff? This game is for you.
Just want some mindless gore and some swordplay? Then this game is for you.
Just love some Wang? Then this game is for you.

Hollow Knight is a one of a kind masterpiece.
That's very simply put. Let me elaborate. While I don't have a lot of experience with metroidvanias as most of the commenters here, the game gripped my heart from the very start with its theme, music, and art style. A fallen kingdom of insects shouldn't evoke solemnity or awe, but Team Cherry's game manages this and somehow makes me feel sorry for the crawlies trying to kill me. The music, the scattered lore, the enemies and the environment mesh together into a cohesive whole greater than the sum of its parts. Hollow Knight is an experience that I doubt I could ever relive in the same form.
The combat forms most of this game. If you're a skilled gamer, the fights should not pose that much trouble for you, but otherwise - prepare to die a lot. Hollow Knight rewards perserverance and pattern memorization, the latter of which seems to be easier in a 2d environment. The fights are satisfying, and behind each tough enemy there's some kind of reward, whether it is a collectible or something that modifies the gameplay. Throughout your journey you collect "charms" which help you alter your playstyle in the way that suits you.
Hollow Knight is not a story-heavy game, but if you try you can guess what happened from the bits and pieces you find and hear from the NPCs, some of whom have journeys of their own to take care of, and their side-arcs can be pleasant interludes between all the fighting. Although, the most defining traits of NPCs in this game aren't their stories, they're their voices. Humming, more accurately. I found that in the eeriness of the underground, a familiar tone was incredibly uplifting.
At one point in the game you get an option of peeking into the minds of your enemies, that usually taking the form of a snippet from their thoughts, after which the story takes a more harrowing turn.
I adored Hollow Knight, yet there were some things I found frustrating, mostly the huge amount of walking back and forth. Fast travel is flavorfully implemented, but there's not enough of it in the game I think.
Anyway, if you appreciate good 2D games and can withstand the frustration of bosses killing you over and over again, I absolutely recommend buying this game.

Tower defense mixed with third person hack and slash.  Awesome game over all.
The game is great for at least 40 hours of game play if not more even if you aren't being obessive about upgrades and loot drops.  I ended up playing this single player a great deal of time when I first got it and even before I burned out I played mostly single player, that being said it's great fun to get a group of friends together and run over hoards of goblins and making strategies that fail, bearly work, or are overly powerful.  Expirmentation and variation are great.
The early game and mid game are great for casual gamers.  Some thing to pick up and go.  Hammer out the easy/normal/hard difficulties for fun, leveling up characters and weapons has a fairly decent curve and is enjoyable for most skill levels.  It can be a heck of a challenge for those who try to jump into hard content from a low level or a smooth ride for those who just progress naturally.
The late game is a bit tedious... I'm talking after you beat the normal difficulties and normal maps.  When you get into the advanced content it gets to be a giant pain in the butt to grind for good weapons and armor, trading is a nightmare and the amount of mana to upgrade anything is absolutly insane.  Playing with people at the higher levels is also very aggrivating.  The late game was designed to be very hard, and it is.  It's also for only for the stout hearted.
All of that being said I highly recommend picking up this game on sale or not.  If you like tower defense or hack n' slash you'll probably like this game.  The late game shouldn't put you off because you can easily put in 40 hours or more before you get to late game content if you're just looking for a game to enjoy.

First of all, let me start by saying I am a HUGE fan of the Holy Build Engine Trinity (Duke3D, Shadow Warrior & Blood). When I heard they were re-imagining Shadow Warrior, I got totally excited at the thought, but that thought soon faded out after I thought about how most things like this turn out. Whether it's movies or video games, re-establishments of classic franchises seldom work out.
To say that Shadow Warrior turned out good would be a massive understatement. It's fantastic.
The game LOOKS phenomenal. It runs very fluidly with little to no slow-down on even the highest settings on my machine. The visuals and environments are clearly extremely inspired by the original game's art style, and couldn't possibly have been nailed harder than Flying Wild Hog nailed them here.
The soundtrack and effects are pretty good, with quality voice acting to back it up. The jokes do get a bit lame at times, and both Hoji and Wang can get a bit annoying after awhile, but hey that's the campy goodness we came to know and love from the masterful Build engine franchises.
The controls are smooth (I'm using keyboard/mouse, as I do with most any FPS) and not frustrating at all.
I really feel that FWH really brought home the gold here with melee fighting and gun combat here. The combo system and vast list of special moves and alternate fire modes are really something special.
The upgrade system is also incredibly deep. You actually get to spec Lo Wang here on multiple levels, and they will directly affect the way you play the game.
I'm not totally finished with the campaign yet, but the story is surprisingly good as well. I'm actually not skipping videos and following along. So it's at least good enough to keep me interested, which is saying much more than I can for a lot of shooters I've played in the past.
Overall, the game is well worth the 40 dollar full price-tag they put on it, but it's a steal if you can get it on sale, ESPECIALLY right now at 10 bucks.
You just can't go wrong with this one. One of the best games I've played all year, and an instant classic right up there with the original.

Okay, first admission:
Take my thoughts here with a grain of salt, because there could be parts later on that redeem the bit I'm reviewing.
However, within that window, I was pretty sure this was worth returning, in my case.  Thing is, you can still go ahead and try it yourself, and it may very well be your style.  It's certainly not
, but I found it to offer nothing I couldn't find within Ori and the Blind Forest, and it lacks (in my experience) the kind of vivid, living world that made me want so very much to explore and return to Ori.  On one hand, there is
to be a certain deadness, and it achieves that feel from what I can tell (again I only got the first little bit of gameplay in), but on the other hand when I started noticing how much my choice of path started to branch...well, I started dreading having to retrace steps and return to places, which isn't such a good sign.  I really didn't feel compelled to explore further.  There are ways for a world to feel like it is dying, without the experience of the game being without life - for instance, Ori's world is suffering but it still felt like a world.
As an additional note, the sound design in general seemed a bit flat, ultimately not feeling like it was part of the experience, but rather something happening next to it.  This bit is hard to explain.  So yeah, very subjective review, you could still at the very least give this game a try and see if it suits you within the return window.

Hollow Knight is a fantastic, timeless game. It's the best I've played in many years.
The story is well crafted and executed, the dialogue is superb, the art is stunning, and the music ties it all together. The gameplay is challenging and rewarding. I felt every detail was polished. I never came across a mechanic that I felt wasn't right. When I died—and I died often—I was never angry at the game. It always felt fair.
Team Cherry created something that will stand the test of time. I have several games that I replay every few years. (Classics like Chrono Trigger and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.) Hollow Knight will be one of these games. They've created an instant feeling of nostalgia, even though I'd never before played the game.
Hollow Knight is stable on my Macbook Pro. Most of the games I play on Mac, especially those built by small teams, crash once every few hours. I've come to accept it as given that I will be booted back to my desktop several times a day and I always just hope it isn't at the worst times. Hollow Knight never crashed—not once. I ran into only two bugs during my entire play through. Both bugs have been fixed in the most recent update. I have not experienced any performance issues.
Play this game, and support these developers.

Okay, so I randomly stumbled across this game while looking for something single player to keep myself entertained with.
I noticed from the trailer that it was you, with a katana, going absolutely ham on a bunch of demons. Cool I thought, I like games with swords and hacking things, lets give it a try.
Little did I know what I was going into.
The main character, Wang, ifs a fairly likable protaganist. Even if he makes a few too many♥♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, but a protaganist with a sense of humor is always more welcome that super gritty, super serious protaganist.
The storyline, unlike most games today, is far from lacking a story line, while it does get a little dissifult to follow mid to late game, but thats what I get for skipping cutscenes I suppose. It certainly doesn't dawdle around filling your screen with pointless exposition, it gets right into things from the get-go. You have a katana that's looking pretty bloodthirsty, so why make it wait right?
The swordplay is what stuck out for me. Main reason I bought this game, obviously.
Now, imagine you're watching Kill Bill Vol 1, but instead of watching Uma Thurman hack up the crazy 88, you're actually in control of a Japanese man with an arsenal of various weapons, katana attacks and phallus jokes. And instead of the crazy 88, it's a variety of demons. That's the kind of visceral, satisfying hack, chop and slice combat that made me look forward to the next demon encounter.
The grahics. I know graphics dont exactly "Make a game better", but in this game it really does.
If you have a computer that can max this game, do it. If you don't, go out and buy a computer that can.
I lost count of the amount of times I turned a corner to see an awe-worthy view, sitting there for a moment or two admiring it and then screenshotting it. The suburban Japanese streets, to temples in a forest, to mountain fortresses, everything is so visually satisfying.

The problem with reviewing The Stanley Parable is that it is a game that is much easier to write about than it is to make a video about; in The Stanley Parable you spend most of your time running around an office complex, and so it is difficult to put together enough compelling footage for a five-minute video. The Stanley Parable is much more interesting than I make it sound, but any video-review is nevertheless going to be featuring some sweet corridor action.
In its first astonishing innovation, The Stanley Parable casts you as Stanley, an office worker who one day notices that everyone in his office has disappeared. Aside from a sociopathic failure to notice the world around him, Stanley is also seemingly afflicted with schizophrenia, his adventure narrated by the only other character in the game, called the Narrator, in The Stanley Parable’s second dizzying innovation, an omnipotent being who comments upon Stanley’s actions as you play through the game.
Before I continue with this review, I shall pause for a disclaimer: there is no way of talking about The Stanley Parable without sounding pretentious and wanky. Words like ‘deconstruction’ and ‘interrogate’ and ‘neck-beard’ circle like crows over any writing concerning this game, but the very act of my pointing this fact out lets me get as pretentious as I like so game on.
Now that elephant in the room has been acknowledged, I realise that I have been less than accurate in describing the game and we are only in our fourth paragraph. Though you may play from the viewpoint of Stanley, you never play as him. How could you, you madman, you are sitting comfortably at home with Stanley dangling at the end of your puppet-strings. Stanley has a life, and a wife, and something else ending in –ife, and you fling him from irresponsibly-designed freight lifts, you monster!
You, the player, are the third and final character, and the game spends a significant amount of time musing on the relationship between players and their avatars, which is rather jolly in a beard-stroke-y way. ‘Choice’, narrative, and even the idea of an ‘ending’ in narrative entertainment are The Stanley Parable’s subject matter, and the game does a very good job discussing these themes in a way that is both entertaining and lucid; the whole idea of ‘a’ story in entertainment is commented upon with the introduction of the patented The Stanley Parable Adventure Line™ and some raucous music and the game does a good job of balancing what could be quite a dull subject with amusing and entertaining moments; humour and wit oozes from every line of dialogue and witty whiteboard doodle, the Narrator character deserves to join the pantheon of video game characters alongside GLADoS and Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite, and you, as if you weren’t already frantically fumbling for your debit card, get to play Portal and Minecraft in a glorious fourth-wall-smash-y sequence. The environments are well designed (as should be expected really, as the developers wrote an ending in which you can explore the prototype designs for Stanley’s office) and you are always aware of the choices you have made to reach one of the game’s endings, and as a result you know what choices to make next to reach a new ending.
While The Stanley Parable is certainly not without its amusing and entertaining moments, they are just that really, moments, interspersed with some top-drawer dialogue undoubtedly, involving what can quite quickly become tedious corridor marathons. The question I asked myself most often as I enjoyed The Stanley Parable’s four-hour run time was ‘Where is the game?’ There are almost none of the activities we have become accustomed to in the last 25 years of videogame development, and the designers have made this decision very deliberately; you do not shoot anyone, there is no HUD display, and, Witcher fans revolt, you can’t have awkward videogame sex with anyone. There are, however, no fetch-quests or escort missions. In fact, absence and lack-ofs are a large part of The Stanley Parable experience; the game will not end, despite my polite requests after hour four of tearing up and down corridors, and while the player is presented with ‘choice’ almost constantly, this choice is proved to be illusory. You will restart the game once you realise that the choice you have made is leading you toward an ending you have already experienced, but the writing makes you understand that even restarting the game is a choice in itself.
As an ostensible purveyor of videos and articles that criticise videogames as both art and products for entertainment, I must ask whether I would recommend The Stanley Parable to anyone not interested in the murky waters of videogame narrative. It would undoubtedly give one plenty of street cred to display The Stanley Parable’s achievements in your Steam profile, but as a piece of entertainment that has at best three or four hours of content is paying full price worth it if you are not writing a PhD on videogame narrative?
The Stanley Parable is an essay in the form of a computer game, but crucially it knows what it is doing, and, ultimately, is there any better way of illustrating and analysing the characteristics of our chosen medium than through the use of the medium itself? All of the criticisms I have of the game are pre-empted by the game, and to pursue them further would make me seem rather petty and stubborn. While some may argue otherwise, for me the game’s problems are ultimately diffused by it referring to them before I have even noticed, and as such I am left with no choice but to declare The Stanley Parable the perfect videogame, and, in tribute to a game with nineteen endings and so simultaneously no endings at all, refuse to give my review its own logical conc-

Hollow Knight is a one of a kind masterpiece.
That's very simply put. Let me elaborate. While I don't have a lot of experience with metroidvanias as most of the commenters here, the game gripped my heart from the very start with its theme, music, and art style. A fallen kingdom of insects shouldn't evoke solemnity or awe, but Team Cherry's game manages this and somehow makes me feel sorry for the crawlies trying to kill me. The music, the scattered lore, the enemies and the environment mesh together into a cohesive whole greater than the sum of its parts. Hollow Knight is an experience that I doubt I could ever relive in the same form.
The combat forms most of this game. If you're a skilled gamer, the fights should not pose that much trouble for you, but otherwise - prepare to die a lot. Hollow Knight rewards perserverance and pattern memorization, the latter of which seems to be easier in a 2d environment. The fights are satisfying, and behind each tough enemy there's some kind of reward, whether it is a collectible or something that modifies the gameplay. Throughout your journey you collect "charms" which help you alter your playstyle in the way that suits you.
Hollow Knight is not a story-heavy game, but if you try you can guess what happened from the bits and pieces you find and hear from the NPCs, some of whom have journeys of their own to take care of, and their side-arcs can be pleasant interludes between all the fighting. Although, the most defining traits of NPCs in this game aren't their stories, they're their voices. Humming, more accurately. I found that in the eeriness of the underground, a familiar tone was incredibly uplifting.
At one point in the game you get an option of peeking into the minds of your enemies, that usually taking the form of a snippet from their thoughts, after which the story takes a more harrowing turn.
I adored Hollow Knight, yet there were some things I found frustrating, mostly the huge amount of walking back and forth. Fast travel is flavorfully implemented, but there's not enough of it in the game I think.
Anyway, if you appreciate good 2D games and can withstand the frustration of bosses killing you over and over again, I absolutely recommend buying this game.

First and foremost, let me simply say this is by far the best Assassin's Creed game I've played, and perhaps one of the best games I've ever played.
The most obvious thing it has going on for itself is its refinement. Not to say it is a game that should be played with a cup of tea while exchanging pleasanteries about the dire condition of the human race, but "refined" is really what defines this game. It is the cumulation of many years of experimentation with multiple Assassin's Creed games into one refined episode.
Not only is the usual parkour gameplay still as fun to play around with as it ever was, but it is now enriched with a thrilling pirate exploration inherited straight from AC III, as well as a certain amount of much improved mechanics from this latter game (hunting, I am looking straight at you).
Altogether, this would already make for a pretty damn great AC game. Who doesn't just want to take a ship's wheel and roam the seas to explore and plunder, right? Who doesn't just love neat parkour mechanics in a beautiful carribean landscape?
Yet that is only scratching the surface of what AC Black Flag has to offer. For where AC trully shines is its story-telling. While by essence the AC story-telling is very compelling and addictive, with its inventive re-exploration of historical events and figures mixed with a character-driven plot and modern sci-fi elements, I never really found that any single game really stood out for having a very well-written and especially memorable story of its own. Sure, Ezio had an interesting story-arch, but it altogether felt too cliché, too "good guy driven by revenge" for it to really be memorable. Even Connor was interesting, but too calm and yet brutal to be really appealing.
Yet here, with Edward Kenway, it feels like Ubisoft finally found the ideal character to tell its story through--which is highly ironic, considering he is the first main character to be mostly very uninterested in the Assassins' cause. But maybe that is his true strength. Edward Kenway is a man whose goals are simple, yet understandable--riches, love...and who will do what it takes to achieve the,. He is daring, and for once truly charming, not simply sold to you as a charming boy like Ezio was early on. Perhaps it *is* because he is a true bad boy--not simply a good looking italian nobility boy--that his path to understanding and redemption is all the more touching. His story, rich in highs and lows, will surely not leave you unmoved; and that's also largely due to the array of brilliant side characters, far more interesting than in any game. As the story goes on, you'll be surprised to find that you genuinely care for them. And then the emotional rollercoaster will go on as the story unfolds, and successes are followed by betrayals and losses.
All in all, this Black Flag is a masterpiece, not just in gameplay, but also in story-telling. The best entry in the Assassin's Creed series, and definitely a game worth playing, whether you are familiar with the series or not.

Without a doubt, the best FPS I've ever played. Now, I'm not very good at FPS games and don't play them too much, so take that with a grain of salt. I'm more of a hack-n'-slash fan. And when using the katana, this game honestly feels like a first-person hack-n'-slash. The melee combat is that good. You will likely find yourself using the katana in 90% of scenarios, only switching to guns for large enemies, flying enemies, and mobs, because it's just that fun to use.
However, the gunplay is nothing to sneeze at. The aiming feels incredibly precise, and each weapon has two methods of firing. There's not many things more satisfying than mowing down a group of demons with dual SMGs, and bullets feel like they have weight behind them.
The RPG elements add a nice flair to the game. From looking at the forums, it seems like everyone has a different idea of what's important to upgrade, which means the RPG elements are doing their job of building Lo Wang around your playstyle.
The story is pretty nice, as well. Lo Wang is simply a middleman for his boss, and tries to buy a katana from a martial artist. When he refuses to sell, Wang attempts to take it by force, and soon gets in over his head.
My only real criticism that dampened the experience was that some of the mini-bosses were incredibly annoying. There is a particular type of enemy with a weak spot on their back that drove me insane...you'll know which one I'm talking about when you reach it.
Outside of that, I doubt any FPS will top this one in my book anytime soon.

Amazing game, as a Bloodline Champions veteran returning to the same studios follow up this game captures the spirit and essence (being the general champions/heroes alogn with the core mechanics) of Bloodline Champions but stream lined with better match making, removal of the convluted medalian system and the absurd paywall from before. I'm 55 hours into the game thus far into my review and still entertained. While the art style takes a more league of legends and dota inspired approach juxtopose to the old tribal diablo style theme the characters retain their themes. Granted some of your old favorites may have been reborn as a new hero concept they are still recognizable. The rooster is planned to vastly expand which only makes the game seam more promising in the long run.
This game is essentially a fighting game that uses RTS style controls (eagle eye top down camera with mouse movements and keyboard hot keys). While the control scheme will be reminiscent of a MOBA this game is more akin to wow PVP where PVE, farming, lanes and bases are exlcuded. The sole purpose is to kill your opponents and survive yourself.
The game play is smooth, fast and fluid. Net code differers depending on region and your internet but has been solid for myself and friends who play.
The only major flaw I can think of atm besides missing featueres and a few random bugs I've encountered during play (0 hp orb) are some balance issues. However as the game is in very early access with several patches from the alpha and beta having mended this problem to a much more playable state it's not of major concern. The balance is rather good with some tweaking needed but as far as competative PVP games go with the companies history for balancing BLC this is something that slowly alters over time.
The benefits vastly out weigh the negatives, this game is well worth the 20$ price tag for early access and unquestionably worth playing even if it was released as Free to Play in it's current state with unlocks. Highly reccomended  in my honest opinion.

Phenomenol metroidvania, mixed with bits and pieces of the Souls series.
Honestly, many people have reviewed this game much better than I could, so look up reviews from people you trust.  I'm jotting down my two cents here, but there are plenty of others who have way more time and have gone in to much more detail.
This game was a huge surprise, for me.  I expected a short, fun distraction from my usual gaming; instead, I'm 13 hours in and have barely scratched the surface.  I'm experiencing this game much the same way I experienced Castlevania: Symphony of the Night - I keep thinking I'm nearing the end, and then something new shows up to expand my worldview.
There are some minor complaints I have:
- The shadow (equivalent to the Souls series' bloodstain) isn't always at your last stable location.  What made the bloodstain system so good in the Souls games is that you only had to make it to the same place you made it last time in order to recover your souls.  It was a way to reward people who were consistent.  Hollow Knight does not place those shadows in the last stable location, so sometimes you have to progress *farther* in order to recover your shadow.
- Controls are sometimes a little unresponsive.  Most of the time, this happens when I've shot across the screen and hit a wall, and I'm in a wall slide position, but I can't jump yet.  I'll be able to jump and start climbing the wall as soon as I start sliding down the wall, but there are some cases where I'm very close to spikes or the edge of the wall, and I need to jump before I start sliding. A half second or so of "you're not sliding yet but you can start jumping" would solve that.  Or input buffering.
- There are many places that require you to bounce on invincible enemies using your down attack to cross nearly impassable areas.  If you happen to swing your sword a bit late and take damage from the enemy, it usually means you also lost control of your hopping and fell into whatever impassable object (spikes, acid lake, whatever) is below you.  This means you end up taking damage twice - once from the enemy, once from the impassable object.  If the game were to send you back *without* dealing additional damage when you land on impassable terrain while still in invincible frames, it would feel a lot more fair in those parts.

I really wanted to like this game, and I know a lot of people enjoy it. However, there is not a lot of substance here, it's very short, and you could simply watch the various "endings" on a Wikia or YouTube page to get the whole gist of the "game". I appreciate they tried to do "something different", but the execution of the concept fell flat for me. On the plus side, the voice acting was suberb, and there some funny moments. After playing the game, I wish I would have just watched the online videos instead.

This standalone title was released as an addendum to Arma 2. I will try to remain unbiased in this review despite the fact that i am a long time fan of the original OFP and Armed Assault series. This particular chapter of the series epitomises the milsim genre and is the quintessential PC game for people who enjoy working in unison with other players to undertake large virtual military operations on a massive scale, incorporating unique game mechanics resulting in an unwonted interdenomination of varied archetypal game genres   . The game has a great modding community and as such is full of brilliant addons and extra units made by the mod community who use the games Editor mode to stage scenarios for the units they choose to to revolve the scenario around . Ever since Steam added the Workshop feature as a tool for finding and installing addons, its become easier to apply them to the steam version of Arma 2 OA, bypassing the somewhat arduous process of adding downloaded content to their affiliated folders in the games main directory as was the norm before.. Addon content for this game is made by a large active community whos work has been invaluable in making this one of the most comprehensive and realistic combat experiences available to PC gamers and simulation fans worldwide. Activities online ( the best way to experience arma in many ways) range from the casual coop game to the hardcore realistic milsim depending on the servers difficulty settings and rules of engagement..( some clans will go as far as to simulate colloquial jargon used by real soldiers while operating in the field, for added effect and pratical comms ) all milsim'ers will love. Remember Operation flashpoint? It all started in 2001 when Codemasters and Bohemia worked together to create the first ( atleast for me ) truly varied and open, beutifully rendered, 3d world with a fantastic physics engine and Mission editor buildt in to boot. Ahead of its time with its coverage and combination of multiple iconic game genres such as air combat sims, sea and ground based vehicle combat sims as well as  being a solid ground troop FPS with something with the earmarks of a traditional RTS, in giving you the ability to command your troops from an eagle eye point of view while using the games command menu system. It soon became known for its excellent coop online gameplay and paved the way for future incarnations of the Real Virtuality engine. OFP was the predecessor and inspiration for the much later released Arma series wich brought with it a following of the same experienced modders and mission makers behind most of the addons produced for OFP. It all adds up to be one of my favorite games to date hands down. Highly recommended for milsim fans, but not so much for the casual fps player as its complexity can be a bit overwhelming i suppose. Not to mention it's very idiosyncratic, occasionally gamebreaking bugs of the sui generis sort. ( Arma vets facetiously joke about the fact that ''Its just not Arma without all the yardstick bugs'' that have become canonical to the Real Virtuality engine and officiate still today, much to many newcomers and long time players dismay..as if the games complexity wasnt daunting enough already). That said, if your the patient/forgiving type and/or have been subject to the many game breaking save-state corrupting crashes and early bugs of previous titles, chances are youll waver it as a passing early-release symptom and wait for patches and fixes that are usually right around the corner, like a veteran of the series will inevitably do in stride, and still like the game for its intrinsic advantages and pro's, that do, in my opinion, outweigh the cons. ( because arma 2s main campaign was a mess of framerate complications, bugs and other problems. The much anticipated coop campaign mode was broken and unplayable too..,However these are predominantly release date bugs that bohemia frequently releases/released patches to ultimately fix or at least alleviate to the point where said bugs are no longer an issue. If you decide to try any of the Arma games, get ready for a unique experience that for many surpasses the threshhold of standard PC gaming into a world of simulated conflict and war where death means failing your squad members and your every action as a member of a team or on solo campaign missions where you may find yourself out of ammo and running through thick forests hiding from looming Hinds and prowling T-72s all endowed with an astute and accurate AI. It must be said that the single player campaign in OA and in featured a movie like story that would change according to your ability to acclimate quickly to different and often unexpected situations. Its a hard game, especially when playing it with the difficulty settings raised to 'realistic levels' One shot to an unprotected vital body part and you die.  episodically This is player versus CPU unit based online gaming at its best and is surpassed by no other milsim title for its ability to get players submerged in a complex, ambient world where conflict is the theme and victory is a hard earned commodity. Combined operations and teamwork are key to success.

This game is a blast to play.  The run-and-gun (or run-and-sword) gameplay has the perfect feel of old-school mobility combined with modern visuals and mechanics.  There are several sword techniques, magical powers, and guns to use, and the tactical combination of these elements with environmental damage to exploit makes each monster encounter genuinely fun to play.  The environments and levels are beautiful, ranging from expansive temple grounds to claustrophobic industrial complexes, and are almost as gratifying to explore as they are to cover in demon giblets.  The guns feel weighty and powerful, while remaining situational and specialized enough that no one firearm feels overpowered.
Of course, the star of the show is the katana, which you will learn to use to great effect to slice demons into bite-sized chunks.
Overall, the game is fast, brutal, and even has some bits of humor to it (the protagonist's remarks are good enough to be amusing, and luckily not so frequent as to become annoying).  This game effectively captures the spirit and much of the gameplay of late 90's masterpieces like Duke Nukem 3D.
TL;DR: If you like Painkiller, Hard Reset, or run-and-gun gameplay, this game does it fantastically.

Granted some of your old favorites may have been reborn as a new hero concept they are still recognizable. This game is essentially a fighting game that uses RTS style controls (eagle eye top down camera with mouse movements and keyboard hot keys). While the control scheme will be reminiscent of a MOBA this game is more akin to wow PVP where PVE, farming, lanes and bases are exlcuded. The sole purpose is to kill your opponents and survive yourself.
The game play is smooth, fast and fluid. Net code differers depending on region and your internet but has been solid for myself and friends who play.
The only major flaw I can think of atm besides missing featueres and a few random bugs I've encountered during play (0 hp orb) are some balance issues. However as the game is in very early access with several patches from the alpha and beta having mended this problem to a much more playable state it's not of major concern. The balance is rather good with some tweaking needed but as far as competative PVP games go with the companies history for balancing BLC this is something that slowly alters over time.
The benefits vastly out weigh the negatives, this game is well worth the 20$ price tag for early access and unquestionably worth playing even if it was released as Free to Play in it's current state with unlocks. Highly reccomended  in my honest opinion.

First Bought this game on the PS3 and enjoyed it totally, but found out that the mods were pretty much only on PC so I decided to get a copy on the PC and don't regret it. Picking it up on sale on the humble store is a must to get all the dlc in one package. Now for the gameplay it is a tower defense that can be easy or hard depending on how you make it. Life is always easier with friends, but it doesn't mean you can't play solo easily because the game allows you to switch heroes mid wave and make use of all you heroes towers albeit having separate mana pools.
There is one downside I encountered immediately when I started playing though and it was the TrendyNet feature that while cool I didn't choose to start playing multiplayer until I had already created a character locally meaning I had to create an entirely new one. Also you have to be connected to Trendynet to obtain the steam achievements which is a problem too. This is all solved by private games on the Trendynet server though.
Despite these little things I do enjoy the game's fantastic design that keeps you in the action at all times trying to support your towers whether through repairs or a carefully placed blast of magic.
Overall I do enjoy this game myself and am a fan of the tower defense genre so I recommend it to anyone else who likes them and wants to boost their collection.

I found hollow knight over all to be well worth the 15 dollars I paid to play it. I was a bit surprised at first expecting something closer to a 2D souls like salt and sanctuary, but the game itself is far closer to a Castlevania game such as Symphony of the night. It standard Roam around a map marking places you can't reach yet and getting new abilities to reach them going back for rewards/progression kind of deal.
I want to start with the cons of this game for me. The game in my opinion got worse the longer I played it. Small issues really add up the longer you go. First it doesn't have a good travel system at all. There are a few set stag stations you can travel to, but there are not that many of them and the placements kinda sucks. You will spend a good twenty percent of your game just running from place to place very slowly. As the game expands and you need to back track (Especially at the end for cleaning up things or ending hunting) you gonna get bored and wishing it had a faster system. Especially if you get to a surprise boss giving you trouble cause you can only change your equipment at a rest station. So if you wish to change your gear to fighting stats over exploration and such you have to back track all the way to last rest point and then go thru the whole stage again to get to the boss. The constant eating of your time really can put a damper on wanting to go check every nock and cranny.
I would also argue the rewards kinda suck in this game. The basic health/soul pool upgrades whic you expect in a metroidvania, but in general most of the time you won't find anything but Geo the games currency which you will run out of uses for SUPER fast. I finished the game with 22k just sitting in my pocket with nothing to use it on. You also can get charms the games version if equipment, but many of them you will not ever use and will just sit there. I used the same charms for almost the entirity of the game very rarely changing anything.
Lastly and this I could see as a more personal compliant as others might like this, but the gameplay at the last few hours goes really wonky and I did not like it at all. The game is mostly a 2d hack slash with some minor platforming elements for the first 90% of the game. Then at the very end it changes into a hardcore platformer. You will be reminded of super meat boy almost instantly. This was a jarring change of pace and I didn't care for it mainly as it was not done as well as a game like Super Meat boy where you die and you can rush back in again. In this game if you run out of life you get shoved all the way back to a rest spot to run thru again just to try to get to the section that gives you trouble. This just eats up way sooo much time and gets grindy and annoying really fast.
So what about the Pro's well there are a lot of them! The game is gorgeous to watch. The hand drawn style is really unique and you go thru soo many different types of areas you get to really enjoy it in tons of different atmospheres. Speaking of Atmosphere the music is great as well. It is perfect of helping to set the mood in many different areas and situations and I even caught myself humming one tune myself while not playing.
Combat is also tight and fun. Simple to start with but you get enough to help spice it up to last the game though the platforming controls are definitely solid, but not great.  The enemies you fight will give you enough variety to make you rethink your strategies and adjust to them which is a bit trial and error when you learn their patterns, but can be extremely satisfying when you get into a good rhythm and it just clicks and feels good. Normal enemies are also done fairly well. You do have your standard hit as you run by enemies, but I found lots of fun enemies that would make me stop and give me pause to think about how to approach. They are sprinkled thru so your first time thru a zone is thrilling and exciting as the gameplay can keep you on your toes with unique attack styles of enemies.
The last thing I really want to praise for this game is the freedom you get to enjoy while playing. I was a bit worried early on as I kept stumbling into new place after new place not feeling like I knew much of what was going on, but even as I continued everything just sorta fell into place. I constantly got that old metroid/vania feel of "Ohhh with this I can get there!" at the few points you recieve a upgrade of that kind.  There are some lame bosses of course, but when you get to those good ones they completely got me excited.
In the end I would suggest this game to anyone who likes metroid/vania style games. It has good atmosphere, music, solid combat, exploration, and for the price you easily get your cash out of this game. Even with the irritations the game built up as it went on didn't stop me from beating it around 90% completion. I doubt I'll ever play it again, but it was a great trip this first time around.

However, within that window, I was pretty sure this was worth returning, in my case.  Thing is, you can still go ahead and try it yourself, and it may very well be your style.  It's certainly not
, but I found it to offer nothing I couldn't find within Ori and the Blind Forest, and it lacks (in my experience) the kind of vivid, living world that made me want so very much to explore and return to Ori.  On one hand, there is
to be a certain deadness, and it achieves that feel from what I can tell (again I only got the first little bit of gameplay in), but on the other hand when I started noticing how much my choice of path started to branch...well, I started dreading having to retrace steps and return to places, which isn't such a good sign.  I really didn't feel compelled to explore further.  There are ways for a world to feel like it is dying, without the experience of the game being without life - for instance, Ori's world is suffering but it still felt like a world.
As an additional note, the sound design in general seemed a bit flat, ultimately not feeling like it was part of the experience, but rather something happening next to it.  This bit is hard to explain.  So yeah, very subjective review, you could still at the very least give this game a try and see if it suits you within the return window.

Hollow Knight is a fantastic, timeless game. It's the best I've played in many years.
The story is well crafted and executed, the dialogue is superb, the art is stunning, and the music ties it all together. The gameplay is challenging and rewarding. I felt every detail was polished. I never came across a mechanic that I felt wasn't right. When I died—and I died often—I was never angry at the game. It always felt fair.
Team Cherry created something that will stand the test of time. I have several games that I replay every few years. (Classics like Chrono Trigger and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.) Hollow Knight will be one of these games. They've created an instant feeling of nostalgia, even though I'd never before played the game.
Hollow Knight is stable on my Macbook Pro. Most of the games I play on Mac, especially those built by small teams, crash once every few hours. I've come to accept it as given that I will be booted back to my desktop several times a day and I always just hope it isn't at the worst times. Hollow Knight never crashed—not once. I ran into only two bugs during my entire play through. Both bugs have been fixed in the most recent update. I have not experienced any performance issues.
Play this game, and support these developers.

This game was by far the best new FPS to come out in 2013 and a shining example on how to reboot an old game.
Featuring the best melee combat mechanics in an FPS I've seen since Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast and a satisfying arsenal of upgradable weapons and powers, you play through 17 chapters full of enemy hordes while following a surprisingly solid storyline. If you're tired of tropes of contemporary FPSes and yearn for the old days, then this is the game for you.
The gameplay through out the game was solid.  Granted, the big arena style battles against hordes of enemies can get a bit repetitive, particularly on the higher difficulty settings where you might end up having to repeat the same sections after dying a number of times. Though it was the boss battles that I was slightly put-off by,  as they were essentiallly all pattern-repeating bullet sponges, significantly less fun to fight than the hordes of low-level minions and mini-bosses.
There were a couple graphical optimization issues on launch. Most noticably, the animation on some of the cutscenes were rather janky. A few patches have been released since then, I'm not sure if any of the graphical issues I encountered still remain as I haven't played the game again since I finished it last year.
As an aside, I've noticed similarities between this and another new FPS based on an old series: Wolfenstein: The New Order, in that both games try to be revivals of old-school FPS gameplay albiet with some new features, but also seem to deconstruct the concept of the traditional FPS hero through the story.

This game is essentially a fighting game that uses RTS style controls (eagle eye top down camera with mouse movements and keyboard hot keys). While the control scheme will be reminiscent of a MOBA this game is more akin to wow PVP where PVE, farming, lanes and bases are exlcuded. The sole purpose is to kill your opponents and survive yourself.
The game play is smooth, fast and fluid. Net code differers depending on region and your internet but has been solid for myself and friends who play.
The only major flaw I can think of atm besides missing featueres and a few random bugs I've encountered during play (0 hp orb) are some balance issues. However as the game is in very early access with several patches from the alpha and beta having mended this problem to a much more playable state it's not of major concern. The balance is rather good with some tweaking needed but as far as competative PVP games go with the companies history for balancing BLC this is something that slowly alters over time.
The benefits vastly out weigh the negatives, this game is well worth the 20$ price tag for early access and unquestionably worth playing even if it was released as Free to Play in it's current state with unlocks. Highly reccomended  in my honest opinion.

A pretty good surprise for the price I got it (10€). However I wouldn't recommend it at full price since the game has some problems that hold it back a lot. First, I didn't play the original Shadow Warrior, so for all the nostalgic, you can already skip this review, I probably don't want the same thing as you do.
So, to sum up this game in one sentence, Shadow Warrior: cut them all! That game asks you to use a lot a sword, it's the best weapon in the game and you have skills and attacks to unlock with it. You also use sometimes some guns, but they feel so weak because it needs so many amos just to kill one thing and they sound quite bad, seriously, guns are used mainly for ennemies attacking from the air. On the plus side, the sword feels so good. It's powerful, you cut the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of ennemies and turn them into a pile of remains with blood everywhere, so satisfaying. The game isn't too long and doesn't feel too short. However the story is meh, the story is just a way to make you kill stuff without thinking why you do that.
The game is looking quite good, but on my hardware I had some performence issues (i5 3570k/GTX770), I needed to turn off some options like the mirrors, particle, and physics and even that way, I had sometimes huge frame drops. That was still playable anyway but still. The musics were okay, nothing felt wrong on that side. The game has some good humors too, like begining the game with Stan Bush music calld The Touch.
Is the gameplay good? The swordplay is satisfaying yes, but overall the gameplay gets repetitive a lot. It's mainly due to the linear gameplay that keeps the same layout. You run, cut some demons, do your objectives, cut some more demons, grease and repeat. Talking about demons, you spent most of your time killing them. That's a choice yeah but I would have prefered the game being more focused on fighting humans on sword battle. Besides the variety of demons is non existant. You'll be fighting the same kind of demons during the whole game. And the boss battles that could have been awesome are just bad. It's just about shooting them on one blinking spot and then shoot some more in the revealed weak spot. And that's the same way to kill them for ALL of those bosses.
Overall, that game isn't terrible, I've played way worse than this but for a game sold for 35 bucks on Steam, I expected something less repetitive, even if I got it for 10 bucks. Is it fun? For those unfamiliar with the game, I will try to educate them without really spoiling anything. In its roots, The Stanley Parable is about making decisions, and how those decisions are meaningless. You play as Stanley, a desk worker at an office building, who finds his co-workers to all be inexplicalby absent from work. Other than the titular silent character, the only other character in the game is a narrator who tells you what to do next. How you choose to follow his directions is the story. Despite your decisions being ultimately meaningless, they do affect the narrator on some level. In there lies the story (or stories). Are these stories worth experiencing? Are they worth your $15? Who's to say? Do whatever the hell you want.

Now THIS is how you modernize a classic FPS.
Totalbiscut's best FPS of 2013 and better than Half-Life 3, Shadow Warrior 2013 takes an old game and remakes it as a prequel out of it. You play as Lo Wang, an asinine, wisecracking hitman with a sword who is tasked with retrieving another blade by the name of the Nobitsura Kage. But the deal goes sour and you must fight your way through waves of enemies to reach it. Once you do, however, a trickster spirit who is also a wiseass joke cracking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, inturrupts Lo Wang before he can retrieve the sword and knocks him unconsious.
After he wakes in a bamboo cage, Wang soon escapes to find that demons are running amok and must fight his way through them using various firearms and powerful swordplay. Lo Wang takes a spill not very long after fighting demons and is critically injured inside of a burning building and the trickster spirit comes out to taunt him.
The spirit agrees to help Lo Wang as he is clearly a skilled fighter and has no tangible body of his own to do things, and enables Wang to use his qi (pronounced CHEE) to use several powers. The first of which is a basic healing spell.
This is where it is a mix of old and new. There is no passively regenerating health outside of brink of death raising up to a small amount of HP after a fight, actively healing yourself with the healing spell, and health packs. Health packs mainly serve as a buff, raising your HP above a normal maximum of 100. Being able to heal yourself, even though a slow and limited heal that slows your movement speed as you do it, solves the dilemma of having to power through the majority of a level with 1-2HP and constantly die from that fact. I'm looking at you, majority of Half Life.
Jumping is fairly limited. In the original shadow warrior you were jumping around all over the map at blitzing speeds and were climbing onto big sections of the level to jump across. It was almost a platformer in that regard. Shadow Warrior 2013 isn't like that. Most sections of the level are fairly flat, especially where you fight demons in. And you'll be fighting demons for the majority of the game. And a lot of them are pretty similar. There's only about ten to eleven main enemy types thoughout the entire game, and you're going to be fighting a lot of them at any given time. And a lot of them are fairly bullet spongey without the correct upgrades for your weapons. (the first thing you should unlock for the crossbow is the secondary attack, which is pretty great.) The game does rewards you though for varying up your playstyle and fighting enemies with various weapons. It's actually kind of hard to 5 star a fight.
Lo Wang finds new weapons as he goes on his journey, from a humble revolver all the way up to demon head lasers and rocket launchers, the shadow warrior isn't shy about using any and all weaponry available to him. And all of them are pretty powerful. The revolver has a chance to instant kill on a headshot, the PDW can have double the firerate by having two guns at once, and the sword is a blast to use in combat.
And the secrets. There's a ton of them, and I can almost guarantee you won't find all of them on your first playthrough. Some are even secret areas tucked away that look like they're from a shooter from the 90s. Specifically, the classic shadow warrior. I found the dark forest and a few other hidden zones in levels myself.
If you like older shooter games, and want an actually great representation of the fact that you can remake an old game and it be amazing, Devolver's Shadow Warrior (2013) is a must buy.

Hollow Knight is probably one of the best games I have played in a very long time. It is a Metroidvania style game with Dark Souls-esk implementation. The way which the world is built is beautiful and polished. Although dark in essence, it's characters and animation styles give you a joyful experience with much thought and care put into their development. The level design is impeccable, rewarding players who explore it's maze-like composition. Many times I found myself thinking, "Oh, it's a secret door, probably just gives me some loot." only to find that I found an entirely new area with a new aesthetic and exploration potential.
Combat is skill based, meaning that you have to change your characters position or attack angle in order to defeat enemies. Although most enemies are relatively easy to the typical Metroidvania player, some are very challenging and require you to study their animation patterns in order to achieve victory (especially for boss battles). The combat get's more intricate throughout the game as you gain new abilities and upgrades. The game also has a currency system for things called "Geo's" which the player can use to buy charms (which gives your character a unique passive buff) or map upgrades (such as getting the legends for vendors and benches). Although in the late game your geo begins to accumulate without anything to spend on, the experience in the early and late game kept me enticed, making me want to spend them at the earliest opportunity.
This game definitely got many influences from Dark Souls. For instance, when the player dies they spawn at the last bench they rested at (similar to bonfires) and lose all their Geo's until they go back to the death location and retrieve their "soul". The game also describes it's lore through exploration (finding NPC's and unique items), architecture (Statues, art styles, etc.), and a very unique mechanic which I won't spoil here.
The music in the game is very atmospheric. Although it is well done, they aren't quite memorable (however good enough songs to put in the background while working on a certain Skyrim Mod :P). Animation and art is beautiful across the board. It was extremely surprising to hear that only one animation artist did this entire game, only making the achievement that much more amazing!
The only large complaint I have about the game is the map mechanic and completing the game 100%. For a game this large and puzzle-like, not having a map until you find a particular character in each region makes it tough to explore when you first encounter a zone (contradicting the game's premise of exploration, and actually making it somewhat a chore). Although after finding the mapmaker for a zone, that zone becomes overwhelmingly more enjoyable to explore. In regards to 100%'ing the game, it is hard to tell where each small object is (even when you look online at a 100% completed map). Since the game doesn't keep a record of whether you picked up a certain item at a certain location, you have to remember whether you have been there before and hope you aren't mistaken. Even with these minor flaws, the game's positives overwhelming brush them aside.
Hollow Knight is among one of the best games I have ever played. It's world is so well thought out and intricate that it keeps me entertained the whole way through. For a game which costs only 14.99$, I've gotten 48 hours worth of content over the last month (an amazing deal for a game priced at 25% the typical AAA game). That's even keeping in mind that there is a secondary mode after beating the game which allows you to replay it, but through a harder difficulty which I haven't gotten around to yet (similar to New Game+ in Dark Souls). This game, I advise all my friends to buy and try. At the worst your spending 15$, or you can even refund it on Steam if you don't exceed 2 hours of gameplay, but in my opinion it is a game worth buying and playing (hopefully all the through). Team Cherry has created what I consider a masterpiece and one which I hope will gain more support and recognition through the years to come.

The best thing you can say about Shadow Warrior is that Flying Wild Hog team have come out victorious from a very steep challenge. Remaking one of 3D Realms cult games while introducing a combat system which mixes FPS weapons, swords and magic powers is quite an achievement. Many studios have tried in the past to spice up the usual monotony of FPS encounters and failed horribly.
Sensitive with its classic roots, the game offers many secrets to discover in each level, very well known weapons like the shotgun or the rocket launcher. On top of that funny dialogues and situations help to ease the tension of the combats. In the 90's many FPS didn't take themselves too seriously so reliving some of that careless attitude is welcome here.
Another aspect which has been faithful to the classic FPS is the difficulty, prepare yourself to die a lot. This game is tough as nails, however, given the range of possibilities in combat  you will find yourself retrying the last encounter trying to find a better combination of weapons and powers that works better with your enemies. Actually, it makes it more satisfying when you finally wipe out a hellish horde of foes.
Technically the game runs great at 60 fps (some tinkering may be needed, look in the Steam Forums), offering lush sceneries with breathtaking landscapes.
In conclussion, Shadow Warrior remains throughout the game faithful to its classical roots while offering a very intense and rich combat. It has been one of most entertaining FPS I have played in years.

The makers of Hard Rest (Flying Wild Hog) are responsible for this excellent re imagining of Shadow Warrior. I played very little of the original Shadow Warrior, but it is basically an asian duke-nukem. Maze like level layouts, funny one liners, puzzles, culture references, all that sorta♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now the reboot here is a lot different. The levels are less maze like and more straight forward, like newer fps games. There is some backtracking once and awhile, but in my opinion I didn't mind it. You can carry all of the guns you get and there are secrets and you fight hordes of enemies, no cover shooting at all. Health packs and everything too. Some minor character elements are still there but with a lot that was added to it. There is still some funny one liners and such, dont worry. Also they added a good story with good writing. Now the first part to cover is the gameplay.
The gameplay consists of navigating Japenese inspired levels, doing small objects, and shooting and slicing up hordes of enemies. You have your health and stamina bar. Sprinting and a sort of ninja/dodge/dash with a press of the shift key and either (w a s d). The main focus in this game is the melee combat, which is amazing. A mix of light and heavy attacks, with double presses of either (w a s d). It is a very fluid and satisfying combat system all the way to the end. The enemies also slice up into little gibs, its cool as hell! The guns in the start are a tad underwhelming in the beginning, but it takes upgrades for those guns to make them more enjoyable. There is an upgrade system as well. One tier for powers, another for guns, and a last one for skills. The powers are a double tap (w a s d) right mouse button mechanic, for example self healing or using a force push ability. These use Ki crystals to upgrade by the way. Guns are for what you expect, upgrading your pistol, machine gun, cross bow and other guns with money. Skills are a mix of katana abilities and buffs for health, and killing demons and such, skills upgrade with karma, which you get by fighting enemies and secret karma stashes.
The graphics are also amazing in this. I am using a Nivida GeForce GTX 770 with this game, Ultra, FXAA on, and it is nice looking. From vast mountains, bamboo trees, ponds, old Japanese architecture, huge temples, and towns. Nice lighting, textures and overall design. Only thing that could have had a bit more work is the faces of the people, they look sorta bad but they work. There is also some amazing cinematics, sort of like a visual moving novel. They tie into the story with the characters in it.
The last part I want to go over is the story, its good. Its about a Japanese man named Lo Wang, a bodyguard for a corporation called Zilla Enterprises. Lo Wang is tasked to retrieve a sword called the Nobistura Kage for his boss Orochi Zilla. All hell breaks loose and the sword is taken by a demon like ghost. And demons rain all through Japan and murder everyone. You then are met with a demon entity named Hoji. Which he tells you the end of the world is because of the Nobistura Kage. There is a mix of Japanese spirit world lore in this too, and surprisingly an interesting and captivating story for a shooter like this.
Now should you buy this game? Yeah, if you like hack and slash games with an old/new school fps twist with a good story. There are not very many games that are fps and have hack and slash elements: and its solid. I would even say I enjoyed this game more than a triple A title like Bioshock Infinite.

"For want of a Nail....the kingdom was lost...."
Only you can unlock the mysteries of Hallownest, your Nail to save the kingdom, or not, as you choose.
PROS:
~The soundtrack. It is not only splendid in its own right, but also serves a clear purpose to every aspect of the game. You change areas? Awesome, the music changes. You're near certain enemies/situations? Fantastic, those have unique themes as well.
~The graphics. At a glance, they may not look like much. But the painstaking detail that was put into these hand-rendered scenes and animations. The dedication and adoration that was put into this is clear in every line and curve.
~The gameplay. You want to just hack-n-slash through? You can. You're the type that likes to find those hidden nuggets? Those are here, too. You want to talk to everyone, learn every secret? Cool, you practically can.
~The story. You have to find it, want it, work for it. Every piece of the puzzle. You aren't spoon fed. This isn't your hyper-linear RPG of modern day. This is classic, wanna-learn-gotta-earn lore delivery.
~The bosses. No two boss fights are the same. No two are even really similar (with special exceptions, not spoiling that, however). The mechanics, movements, patterns, attacks, everything is absolutely unique to each BBEG.
~The enemies. There's always a twist. That little challenge, or tweak. That hint of danger even when you think its past.
~The NPCs. Some are obvious, and helpful. Some are hidden, and secretive. Some you have to buy off, some freely give you all they know. Friends? Enemies? You may or may not learn, but none will leave your feelings untouched.
~The world. This map is vast, varied, and beautifully joined. The intermingling of areas, the crossing from A to B to C with a matter of baby steps, while other times may take you half a lifetime to see the next area. There is no shortage of world layout.
CONS:
~The vast world size could be considered cumbersome, if you have to go from one end to the other. (As a note, I did not find it so, but my experiences in Super Metroid have innoculated me against frustrations of these types.)
~The ability spread. There is that early-game-hump. Your money is sparse, and hard to get. Your abilities seem just a touch too weak, and you feel like everywhere you go is somewhere you need to revisit later, for one small section. It passes, but the frustration is justified.
Personal review:
This storyline is one of the most heart wrenching I have experienced, while at the same time housing a kernel of uplift that leaves the whole experience as one of nostalgia, longing, and a strong desire to play again (and again....and again....).
I have had to pause this game to wipe tears. Actually shouted at my screen. Stared in horror, awe, or despair. Genuinely covered my mouth in an attempt to suppress emotions I cannot define.
I love working this out, finding the breadcrumbs and following them. I am enamoured of the need to know still more, and the balance of light and darkness. Balance. Delicate, and wrought with heartache, forged in hope, and etched in loss, this game fulfils everything I have been waiting for for more than two decades....when I didn't even know I was waiting.
Do I recommend this game? ABSOLUTELY. But be warned. Be prepared. Hours, days, weeks. This game deserves them. And replayability is a no-brainer. Steel Soul mode or no, this is my new go-to for its genre, possibly even for my library as a whole. I encourage anyone, everyone, to buy this game. Give it a chance. There's still more to come, and I cannot wait. Join me in giddy anticipation, a journey through the world of Hallownest, down the path of discovery, and beyond the edges of memory.

As silly and fun as this game is, I simply just cannot recommend it.
The Stanely Parable is different. It's core gameplay involves making choices and the hilarious outcomes that result. It has you searching for opportunities and taking new paths as they arise. However, this is the problem. The game is too dang similar every time you play. No matter which ending you take, you end up going down the same path every single time. It gets to the point where you just rush through and ignore all the dialogue, just so you can hear a new line of dialogue. It becomes a chore to play.
The Stanley Parable does have some good parts to it. The narrator is often humorous and witty, and his lines are funny. Some of the endings are very creative, such as the portal and minecraft ending. The game has little easter eggs here and there. In many situations the narrator will react to stanely just sitting around or clicking on everything and comment on it.
At the same time, The Stanley Parable just doesn't come through. Some of the endings are too bland. Hearing the same lines of dialogue, making the same choices, going down the same path, following it, keep going, just to take a left turn right before the end instead of going straight; is it really worth it? No. It isn't. This is the big problem. The game is so repetetive and boring. You WANT to find all the endings, to find all the random differences, but to have to go through it all again just to attempt to find somethin new is too much. I couldn't force myself to do it. It was fun for a bit but it got old fast. This brings me to my one big complaint: the price. Why are they charging 20 bucks for this game for such little content? Seriously, this game deserves to be 15 TOPS. Why buy this game when you could get Garry's mod for you and a friend? I bought this game on sale, but really, I feel bad for people who paid 20 dollars for 4 hours max of legitimate gameplay.
This game is fun at first, but the lack of variety just kills the game. You'll get about 4 hours of fun from this before realizing you should have kept the 20 bucks you spent.
