Arrrrr! And my Assassin's Creed gaming spree has ended (until new AC: Unity and AC: Rogue releases that is) for now and I can honestly say that I haven't had that much fun since AC 2. Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag offers lots and lots of stuff to do. Just the seafaring on your Jackdaw ship while listening to the sea shanties of your crew truly imerse you into the pirate theme this game went into. And as a pirate themed game, I haven't played a realy good one ever since Sid Meier's Pirates Gold!... and that was close to ten years ago!
Naturally, this game has its ups and downs but compared to AC3, it is a huge step in the right direction. Black Flag has a bigger focus on "simply having fun", gameplay speaking. Storywise, the pirate-Animus setting delivers, while you progress your pirate career as Edward Kenway and seek help from other known pirates like Charles Vane, Blackbeard, Anne Bonny, James Kidd, etc. You have many lost treasures on maps to search in this game, which unlocks elite upgrades for your ship and I would say mandatory if you want to have a chance against the legendary Man-o-War battleships. You got the whaling minigame that opens up Edward's crafting abilities and unlocks better gear, similar to Far Cry 3. The Templar vs Assassin theme is still there in this game but not as omnipresent as previous AC games.
My biggest deception in this game was the pointless "modern setting". Walking around, finding sticky notes and hacking collegues computers only to have a pseudo continuation from the events of AC 3. Another big irritant of Black Flag was the many many many eavesdropping and tailing missions. Way too annoying and very frustrating as you are forced to play these missions as how the developer has intended for you, which is don't be seen, don't do this/that... "oh you did! DESYNCH and repeat mission! ENJOY! :D"
Aside from these irritants, the rest could be pretty much discarded but I'll still elaborate on the Pros and Cons.
PROS:
+Killer visuals! A gorgeous, vibrant world full of reasons to go exploring!
+Outstanding naval combat. (Picks up from AC3 naval combat but improved in every ways).
+Progression systems are profoundly rewarding (crafting, upgrading Edward and the Jackdaw, etc).
+Terrific pirate story that depicts how they lived and also, shows you the pirates in a human light.
+Seafaring and on-foot exploration complement each other in a perfect mix.
+Gameplay mechanics delivers but hopefully, they'll be more refined in the new AC games. Although the moves are more fluid compared to AC3. (Played with Xbox One controller).
+Decent soundtrack from composer Brian Tyler. Also the sea shanties arrrrrr good!
CONS:
-I haven't experienced any bugs or gamecrashing glitches but read that Black Flag has nasty issues at launch, until it was properly patched that is! I did had a few glitches and were all fixed by reloading a checkpoint!
-Just too many eavesdropping and tailing missions... I mean c'mon, couldn't you have done something different here? I just hate those missions badly!
-Bland and boring modern setting. Now that Desmond Miles is out of the portrait, this new unknown guy you play as in the Abstergo Entertainment Montreal studios has little to offer in the main Templar vs Assassin everlasting confict. That setting felt forced and I do hope on the future AC games, the modern setting will be much more developed, just like the other AC games.
-I would've liked to see the other main countries in this game, like the French and the Dutch, who were colonizing the Americas of that time too and also, at war against Spain and England. More countries at war, the merrier! Might happen on AC Rogue, who knows!
-If the multiplayer is your reason to play AC games, you'll find nothing new here... same old same old and not my cup of tea!
OVERALL:
Fantastic game! I really enjoyed this game which you have tons and tons of stuff to do. Ubisoft have redeemed themselves with Black Flag since AC3 was beyond disappointing in every possible way. Black Flag delivers and whether you're new to the Assassin's Creed franchise or not, this game takes a big pause in the main modern theme of Templar vs Assassin from previous games and enables you to just jump into this fun pirate theme and well, just have fun plundering other ships!
RECOMMENDATION:
Yes, absolutely! AC fan or not, play this game... as long as you dig the pirate theme!
BLACK FLAG RATING:
9.0 / 10
AVELINE DLC:
Short straightforward DLC that doesn't add much in Aveline de Grandpré's storyline. It picks up at the end of AC Liberation and whether you played or not that game doesn't matter for this DLC. You just start somewhere and after you've done climbing the side of a Fort, you have to liberate someone inside and the end... Very below-average! Sad because Aveline could have been a decent main character to play, aside from AC Liberation but is quite under-developed. Overall, if it comes with your Black Flag game, give it a shot since it is very short... 45 minutes max! If you only have Black Flag game, discard this DLC! You won't miss much!
AVELINE RATING:
6.0 / 10.
FREEDOM CRY DLC:
You play as Edward Kenway's quartermaster, Adéwalé. This DLC picks up at the end of Black Flag. It doesn't give you any info about Edward's and Black Flag storyline so you can always play this DLC in any way you seek as it doesn't impede BF main plot. Adéwalé is a great character. His involvement into liberating the slaves of Port-au-Prince felt rewarding each time I got to massacre the slavers. You do have some seafaring missions as you do steal a ship and roam the West-Indies. You have about ten or so locations to explore. Freedom Cry has a good mix of side missions and main ones. The story is solely focused on liberating Port-au-Prince from the French slavers and there is little to no mention of the Templars. You have about a good ten hours of playtime in FC DLC. My main gripes are like Black Flag, way too many eavesdropping and tailing missions! I'd actually recommend this DLC if you get around to it. Freedom Cry is fun and straightforward while having the fun parts of Black Flag like seafaring, in the DLC.
FREEDOM CRY RATING:
7.5 / 10.

Sailing along in the dead of night, the seas are calm, but the air is still. "A ship behind us Captain," shouts a crew member "Possibly a scout or merchant," we all turn to look only to see another ship right behind it, "that aint no scouting party," I announce; suddenly they open fire; luckly were but a small ship so the shots to the stern all missed; "Turn hard to port," exclaims the captain, "Ready the cannons!" The captain skillfully runs us parallel with the enemy ship "Fire!" our cannons rip several holes in the enemy ship instantly setting it ablaze but they also shoot back damaging our sails and putting a few holes in the deck and igniting the gunpowder barrels "Put those flames out you maggots" "the captain shouts while pushing a crewmate and I towards the open flame. Then as quick as the attack a man, donned in blue with a hood over his a head and a blade fixed to his wrist, hops on board and kills the captain and then puts his sights on me. "I have no weapons and not much fighting experience, what do I do?" I think to myself as I step back, suddenly the gunpowder barrels explode, launching both the mysterious assailant and I into the waters.
I managed to get to the shore of a nearby island but so does the mysterious assailant, holding his hand to a wound possibly shrapnel from the explosion, he beckons to me; offering me a job take him to Havana or something, claims he will pay me. Pffft as if, a pirate would just take the gold he will pay me with and thats what im going to do but the assailant isnt as crippled as he lets on, he raises a flintlock startling me to my knees "damned pirates" he mumbles, he tosses the empty flintlock aside and scurries off.

Shadow Warrior is a action packed single player that offers the best katana gameplay I experienced. Wang is the protagonist, a bodyguard of Zilla Enterprises, looking to collect parts of a sword and assemble it to create a very powerful weapon. Unravel the mystery of the demons who are invading the human world. The sirens who protect the sword from the demons, and the guardians who protect the sword pieces from being gathered.
The companion that follows you around is actually pretty amusing and the dynamic between him and Wang work well. Constantly making jabs at you throughout the game really adds humor that actually works with the game rather than against since it doesn’t feel out of place. An example of this is on chapter 12, you teleport into a new area, nearly fell off the mountain and lived by grasping onto a broken bridge.
Wang: You suck!
Wang: Do you enjoy dropping me like that?
Companion: Just trying to land you in the air, it beats materializing a couple of feet underground
Wang: Your logic is sound
The katana and powers are far more effective against enemies than guns except in some instances where having distance between you and a mini-boss is beneficial. Guns are mostly used for bosses even though they could be used for interesting combos to get a higher score during fights for more karma and better position in the leaderboard. I highly recommend using the crossbow, rocket launcher, and shotgun throughout the game.
Be constantly on the move or you are going to take quite a bit of damage. The game has enough enemy variations and threats to make you constantly have to be on the move to avoid being hit.
The jumping in this game is pretty average which in case you're wondering means its bad. The dashing is far superior in this game which you will always use in combat since its far more effective for getting away from enemy attacks. The jumping I found was only useful when i used explosives near me to blow up groups of enemies i threw down when using the tiger skill. Overall movement in this game is a big step up from the previous game this engine was used for Hard Reset.
The level design itself is not as complex as others would like however there are many areas to explore which rewards you with money. There are also secrets that have a retro graphic theme style to it which pays tribute to the game the remake is based on. The only issue I have with the level design itself is that certain maps have elements which can be incredibly annoying like the platforming level where you can fall if you are not precise about where you jump.
The variety of enemies mixes up the gameplay and allows the player to come up with interesting ways to deal with multiple enemies at once or certain types that would otherwise kill you. What makes the enemies really stick out is their ability to rage. Their rage ability makes them go much faster and hit for more which means you need to either take them out fast or calm them down before they strike you down.
People tend to use the Divider of Heaven for most enemies seeing as how you can kill enemies in a row with its  piercing effects while being in constant movement.
The bosses are towering impressive looking monsters of death with nice animations and environments that you fight them in. Ultimately the bosses feel boring as a result of their ability to regenerate armor back on the weakness spots exposed. It really becomes a chore to constantly take down the armor off bosses just to hit the crystal which has a iffy hitbox.
Heroic mode offered a great challenge of having to clear a whole level without dying once, or you would be reset to the start of that level. It was quite hard at times considering that the staircases could kill you if you dashed down them too fast. The chapter 12 was particularly bad since there were many gimmicks like limiting your vision and spamming tons of suicidal monsters to attempt to kill you while you were limited in movement since you were stuck on a train.
If you are a fan of games that are like quake,painkiller,serious sam, look no further for another dose of crazy action just don't expect the bosses to be climatic...

I want to preface this by saying two things: one, Hollow Knight is the first game I've ever felt compelled to write a review for and two, I just completed my first playthrough. I wanted to write this while my hands were still shaking.
Hollow Knight tells the tale of the fallen kingdom of Hallownest, once a beacon of civilization for bugs, now a ruin ripe for plundering. You, the protagonist with a mysterious background, come to the kingdom with intentions unknown. Like From Software's
series (
included), much of the story is up to you to determine, typically through exploration--and
, there's a lot of exploration to be had in Hallownest. In true Metroidvania fashion, as you progress deeper and deeper into the kingdom, you'll acquire new abilities which open up new pathways and new areas. Each new section of Hallownest feels connected, like a living, breathing world, and it's a thing of beauty to watch how your map begins to grow and fill out, how you begin to discover the connections between areas--I promise you, there is no shortage of places to explore or things to discover in this game.
Stemming from the exploration and world-building, combat in Hollow Knight is fantastic as well. It's simple at first--press this button to attack, press this button to jump--and indeed, the combat is based on simple hack-and-slash gameplay. As you progress, however, enemies get harder, bosses get smarter, and frankly, sometimes it's hard to catch a breath between all the frantic, fast-paced dodging and swiping. Several bosses (who I won't name--if you want spoilers, you can find them elsewhere) are absolutely exhilarating to fight, and even those that aren't are still pretty damn good. The platforming elements are mostly tame, with a few exceptions (you can bounce off spikes by hitting them with your weapon! Gah, that's
) and one very skill-intensive area. The core gameplay is very,
solid.
Last but absolutely not least, the art direction is gorgeous and the soundtrack is stunning. From vivid groves to Gothic architecture, from musical bombast to somber silence, Hollow Knight delivers on all fronts. Each area is unique and unforgettable, and that signature "quaint but epic, cute but creepy" style has wormed its way into my heart and burrowed into the hard tissue there.
I cannot praise this game enough. Buy it. Experience it. I promise you, it will not disappoint.

Shadow Warrior ina  nutshell: Arcadey
I use that adjective as a Postitive, i've wanted arcade games like this to see a resurgance for a long time. However, the problem with arcadey games is that harder difficulty doesn't make the AI better at killing, or increase the number of enemies, or simply make you less tanky. No, Arcade games ramp up the difficulty by making the game LONGER. The hardest difficutly in this game barely amps enemy damage and almost DOUBLES enemy health. THis isn't an issue really, because it takes two sword swings instead of one, or a Chi Power, or 30 Uzi Bullets instead of 15. The issue comes from the bosses. You literally cannot kill the first boss on the hardest difficulty unless you ahve two hours to kill and are INCREDIBLY patient, because the bosses all have the same returning mechanic. Break the armor plate by throwing lots of bullets at it, and then break the crystals underneath to take out a chunk of health. Great mechanic, don't get me wrong, until you double enemy health. Because at that point, you have to empty almost three clips of Uzi Ammo (that's with the dual weilding skill so 360 bullets) into an armor plate to break it, wait for him to use his "Oh no, i'm stuck in place now" attack, and then pour more ammo into the chi lines, which take even more poundings than the armor! This ^ needs to be fixed. If it were, it'd make the game freaking AMAZING. Make the hardest difficulty something like "No Checkpoints, insta-death if hit, enemies are faster" don't make it "Enemies do slightly mroe damage and you'll finish the game in about...... 134 hours."

Well, that's much better, guys. Ubisoft redeemed itself with this after the horible failure that was AC 3. It looks like they managed to iron out many of the problems that were in AC3. This title runs better (After some tweaking of the settings), has many more graphics options for setting up your own personal optimal performance and visual balance. They are a bit confusing compared to most graphical options thanks to Nvidia optimizing the game, but when you figure out what they all are and their impact on performance, you can quite easily set it up to run the way you want it.
A tip for other AMD users like myself, disable V sync in game, and use Radeon Pro for your V sync. Create a profile in it, set V sync to always on in the tweaks tab, set triple buffering on, and enter your monitors refresh rate in the box next to the triple buffering check box. Make sure Radeon Pro is running in the backround so the profile is applied. This lifted the annoying 30 FPS cap in cities, allowing for variable FPS up to a max of 60, and got rid of screen tearing. Ubi's V sync is the main issue with AMD cards in this title (Thanks, Nvidia). After doing this I was able to crank almost everything up to max including environment detail with a minimum of 35 smooth FPS on the busiest of streets and most dense of forests. I am using an R9 280X.
On to the gameplay. This game was genuinely fun to play. It seemed a little too easy at times, but at least it was not frusterating like AC 3 was. The sailing is awesome, and the controls were revamped from the awkward ones in AC 3. It doesn't annoy the hell out of me like AC 3 did. The fighting controls work much better as do the free running controls. Just much better all around. Upgraded weapons actually increase your effectivness in combat unlike AC 3, you can craft useful items once again, you can make money more effectively, and the list of improvements go on. The characters are also much more interesting and likable. The story is interesting and makes you actually want to complete the game, much like AC 2 through Revelations were. Very good game, definitely recommended!

I spent about 40 hours playing this game.  Gameplay wise, it's great.  The gameplay is the same engine as AC3.  Edward Kenway controls the same as Haytham & Connor Kenway.  The ship traveling is the same mechanic but improved greatly.  Sailing island to island, ship combat, boarding an enemy ship & plundering all their loot is a lot of fun & something I did probably over 50 times.
The gameplay is perfect, no complaints here.  I wouldn't spend 40 hours if the gameplay was flawed.
The big part of every AC game is the story, and I have kind of mixed feelings about the story here.  On one hand, it's a great story with great characters that takes place in the Assassin's Creed universe, but the whole assassins vs templars thing isn't necessarily the main plot going on.  All of the supporting characters are interesting, but I have these complaints with it:
1) The main villain of the story is barely seen only a few times through out the entire game, we really don't get to know much about him which is a major contrast to how well we got to know previous AC villains, especially the villains in AC3 which we knew quite well, only Revelations had a villain we knew less about.
2) For that matter, pretty much all of the antagonists don't really get much screen time.  While some characters become good guys & others become bad guys, very little time is devoted to developing any of the other characters that aren't one of the main 5 or so characters.
3) The motive is kind of hard to understand.  It starts out simple: "I want booty, gotta get rich or die trying" and it progresses into something more complicated, but it skips a lot of steps that explain why Edward has a change of heart and develops into a more mature character.
At one point in the end of the game, one of the villains makes a comment that he's lost everyone in his life thanks to him & the other villains, but that's not true.  He was already divorced/separated from his wife before the game started.  A few of his friends died or betrayed him, but it wasn't necessarily due to anything the villains or Edward did.  It was the villain taking credit for what wasn't his to take credit for.  At some points, Edward shows that he cares about people in his life and at other points, acts like nobody matters to him but himself.
And I'm trying to not spoil anything, but come on AC games always have plot twists and characters dying.
Having gotten these flaws out of the way, it's still a very fun game.  I'm actually curious where they're going with the modern day 2013 storyline again, where as the 2012 storyline in AC3 was pretty boring.  Ubisoft has said they've thought of an ending that will be final & ultimate, but I have a feeling they're going to keep milking out yearly AC titles until the cash cow runs dry, ala Call of Duty.  At any rate, AC Unity looks pretty damn good, I'll be getting it probably around Christmas.
Final verdict: 8.4/10  Better than AC1 & AC3, but the Ezio trilogy still reigns supreme.

I have one, and only one, complaint about this game.
The controls are what I would describe as overly sensitive. Essentialy, what the game needs you to do, control wise, combined with the speed at which your character responds, I find myself often fighting against the speed of my character to achieve the precision the game wants. I think it would be better if it had analog movement, or if it were not seemingly built for a 360 controller which has a terrible D pad. I also think it would be much better if the game had an "attack downwards" button instead of requriing you to hold down, as doing that again conflicts with the extremely sensitive horizontal control of your character and using an analog stick.
With that out of the way, the game is absolutely beautiful, utterly gorgeous artistically and frankly very enjoyable to play. I wholly recommend it for anybody who enjoys 2d platformers of any stripe, and if you particularly like metroidvanias I would argue it is an extremely good example of the form. It also, if you will forgive the cliche comparison, is reminiscent of a Dark Souls game in both difficulty, some of the mechanics, and general atmosphere. If you enjoyed the thematic setting of DS1 I think you will find an awful lot to enjoy in this game too. As I said my only frustration is the way the game handles its controls which are very sensitive because your character responds very quickly and is highly mobile, and the game has quite a bit of pretty precise platforming required from you. There's no weight to your character, you press a direction and they move, and this may be a feature if you're fond of games like that, though I find it more of a hindrance coming from games with characters having more inertia.
I strongly recommend the game anyway and I would say if you have a controller with a properly positioned and good quality D pad this game would be much better as I have yet to find any part of it that even notices analog control, much less makes functional use of it. If you are using a 360 controller and can't get away with the D pad on it, you may find sections of the game a little frustrating, but the rest of the game is still excellent, so I would still say the game is easily worth the asking price and especially if it is on sale. Design wise it's a really fun 2d platformer/metroidvania and especially if you like exploring and sequence breaking, you'll get a lot of mileage out of this game.

This game was probably the most value for money purchase I have ever made. I have sunk countless hours into this game (I lied.. steam counted 737..) and it has provided me with hours of fun, a great community and a lot of interesting gameplay. The game itself is a 3rd person tower defence game with an rpg element to it. Your hero levels up and gets new items that drop from the monsters you kill. The loot is randomly generated which in itself has a good and a bad side. The good side being BAJILLIONS of armor/weapon variants. The down side is that getting good quality loot and more importantly loot that you need and are looking for is very difficult, especially when you get to the higher rarity armor and weapon types. This can make the game very grindy and if doing levels over and over again, perfecting your layout and gameplan isn't for you then Dungeon Defenders isn't for you, at least not if you want to be the very best like no one ever was..
That being said there are a lot of levels, challenges, maps and various modes to play giving the game enough variety and interesting gameplay to warrent anyone playing it for the price. There are some big flaws with the game. The prime of these boil down to two things; There is a lot of DLC, and I do mean a lot of it, and the game is very easy to hack. Now the DLC aspect of the game isn't too terrible. There is a lot of it but a lot of it is cosmetic and almost all of them are cheap. Now the hacking is an actual problem. The game is very easy to hack and hence hackers are prominent in the community, even in the online play. Trendy tries to monitor and ban hackers but it is a bit out of their control. If you are the kind of person who likes to play by themselves (which you totally can) then this won't affect you at all. If you want to play online with others then I suggest using the forums and getting to know a few people who play the game (or get your friends to play with you). Having people you regularly play with ensures a nicer experience then trying to adapt to pub games and risk having your experience ruined by hackers.
With all this in mind I still feel like Dungeon Defenders was a great purchase and a great experience. I would recommend it to anyone if for nothing else just to play through the story and see the interesting gameplay it provides. This game is old however and the sequal is on its way so perhaps holding off for that may be a better idea if you don't plan on getting into this game hardcore.

Shadow Warrior is good mindless fun that fits under a pick up and play kind of game. Technically a FPS, but you'll spend most of your time using a sword since it's the most effective weapon overall and requires no ammo. Which is fine, because hacking demons into pieces never gets old. So it's first person melee and a shooter. You can upgrade your abilities using Karma (essentially experience you get from killing enemies) and crystals which you find in the levels. You can use these to upgrade your health and healing abilities, learn new sword techniques, learn new combat techniques, improve how much money and ammo you find, etc. You upgrade weapons from good old fashioned money which is dropped all over.
While I generally had fun with the game it does have some flaws. For the most part, the combat is just trash mob after trash mob. The same lowly crawlers you fight in the first level will still show up in the last level, there's just more and more of them as you go along. There's few enemy types in the game, they just increase in numbers as you progress further. It's one of those games where at the end of an early level a big baddie comes out and you fight him solo, and then in later levels that big baddie is in the middle of every other trash mob.
The game has secrets to find, basically just ways to get more karma/crystals/money. Which is fine, but looking for it makes the levels drag on. Towards the end the levels just way overstay their welcome. If you just focus on what you need to do the game will go by a lot quicker but the only way to get ammo and money is to find them in the level as enemies don't drop money or ammo. So searching for it slows you down. Also, the game does a horrible job of showing you where to go next. Objectives are general, usually something that just lasts the whole level so you get no guidance on what to do next when you're looking for a specific door or switch to open a door. Several times I spent several minutes searching for where to go next. Also no map in the game.
Official bosses are scarce, and when they do show up it's attack a weak point until they kneel over and expose and another new weak point you need to wail away on but do it quickly because they only kneel over for a short time.
The story is decent and there are plenty of one liners around so if immature♥♥♥♥♥♥and fart jokes are fine by you the dialogue will make you crack a smile every now and then. Totally cheesy, but in a good way as long as you don't mind that.
All in all I enjoyed my time with it, but by the time I got to the end I was ready for it to be over. I give it a recommend, not the deepest game, but the core gameplay is solid fun and it's always enjoyable to hack up demons after the end of a long day.

I feel a little bad for developer Flying Wild Hog, remaking or "rebooting" Shadow Warrior is just not something I would expect any modern game company to do willingly. While I played and enjoyed the original Shadow Warrior, and even the recent "redux" version, it is not a game that could be made today by any legitimate company. The terrible racism present in the original that comes from a time in which that level of ignorance was the norm, would cripple any modern company's public image. That being said, it is that same racism and offensive humor that made the original so funny. So what is Flying Wild Hog left with?
Humor: 7/10
Not surprisingly, Shadow Warrior 2013 is not as funny as the original. There are some genuine laugh-out-loud moments, but they are few. The humor overall is cheesy (which I like, to be honest, but is isn't for everyone), and the writing is pretty lame. While I did enjoy the game's sense of humor, it was nowhere near the original.
Story: 7/10
The story in this game is also pretty mediocre. Your demon sidekick, Hoji, is very entertaining and later you meet a couple ladies who spice things up a bit, but overall Lo Wang himself is kind of an idiot and you don't really find yourself attached to him by the end of the game. The plot begins as a riveting plot about a demon apocalypse and devolves into a family squabble gone wrong, that no one seems to understand.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
The combat is where this game really shines. It is definitely an "old-school shooter," and a lot like the Serious Sam games. Your run speed is blazing fast and you have a dash move that makes you even faster, so mobility is your primary way to avoid taking damage. While there isn't a large variety of weapons, all of the weapons in the game are really fun and you could easily play this game with just guns and have a blast. However, where the combat really shines, and is unique from almost ALL other FPS games, is with the sword fighting. You will probably end up using the sword 90% of the time, which is awesone because you feel like a superpowered ninja when you do.
In addition to the weapons, there are numerous upgrades. You can buy weapon upgrades for your guns with money that you find, and many of them add a secondary fire mode that opens up new play styles and tactics. You unlock skills- which include health and stamina upgrades, weapons skills, and passive abilities- using karma, which you earn during battles by using a variety of weapons and attacks. And finally, you also upgrade your Ki powers, using crystals that you find on each level. These powers allow you to heal, stun, and protect yourself from damage.
The result is a fast-paced hectic arena filled with demons rushing towards you as you dash, stab, slice, blast, and basically just destroy everything around you. In a word, it's awesome!
I do have a few minor complaints though: there isn't much demon variety. Old school shooters often had upwards of 15 different enemy types, this game has about 12 in total. The maps are mostly boring too, while the first one is really cool and there are a few other interesting ones, you will still spend many hours in metal corridors and boring industrial maps. Finally, two of the powers you can upgrade are essentially the same: one knocks enemies down, and the other lifts them in the air, so both essentially stun enemies. It would have been better if devs removed one of the powers and gave you something offensive, like a health-sapping poison, or a short attack-damage boost with a cooldown after.
Overall, it is a great game that I think will surprise you with how fun it is. I highly recommend it!

I really enjoyed this game. It is one of my favorites.
You are a little hero like an apprentice, knight monk or huntress and have to defend the Eternia Crystals from the evil force in level-based towerdeffense roleplay. The mechanics and uniqueness of each hero and the combination of all are the key to victory. For example, the kobolds are running straight to your crystal and you have an apprentice and your friend a monk. With killing enemies and winning levels you can earn weapons or armor, which ups the damage of your electric aura or the durabilty of your spike blockades. Also your character can level up to become stronger. To make it a solo game too, you have before every wave a build phase, where you can build your towers and change to other characters, but the game is best played with a friend. My biggest problem with the game is the fact, that the game can not played that good without DLCs. While some DLCs just add new characters and levels, some of them are needed to get some levels, so i would buy just the original game or directly all DLCs, so you really know, that you do not buy something you cannot reach without annother DLC. Another good fact about the producer studio is, that EVERY dlc is free for the fist 2 weaks after publication and that is definitly a thing you should support with buying this game.
All in all I really recommend this game to all RPG and Towerdeffense fans, because it combines both genres perfectly in an awesome comic style game with a nice community and a modding system.

I am absolutely loving this game! Metroidvanias are some of my favorite games and this one is definitely one of the best out there. Before buying, I read some of the negative reviews to see where some of the pitfalls may be. Some people feel the game is unnecessarily difficult because it makes you pay for your maps and in a sense, even to see where you are on that map. I disagree and actually enjoy this part of the game. I have fun looking for the map maker in each area and currency is not hard to come by. I have also read that some people feel the areas are "too samey," which I don't agree with. The areas are similar in that they are cohesive in portraying an environment that is gloomy, decaying, forgotten about and yet wholly beautiful at the same time. Music changes by area as do all the enemy types.
I have read comparisons to Dark Souls and feel this is mostly accurate, but I would say it more closely resembles Bloodborne, which I prefer over DS. Combat is fluid, fast and rewards an aggressive playstyle. There isn't a health regeneration commodity but you inherently have the capability of healing yourself from the onset using Focus. Focus is earned through combat, which reminds me of the health take-back mechanic in Bloodborne.
In addition to excellent combat, the soundtrack is phenomenal and haunting, the narrative is compelling, exploration is rewarded in a way that doesn't feel frivolous (I'm pointing the finger at devs that use game art as a reward) and the characters are quirky and interesting. This is my dream game in a nut-shell: a Bloodborne-esque metroidvania.

This game is is special. It's not often something like this comes around. A perfect mix of a Metroidvania with a Dark Souls-esque game.
Exploration feels rewarding and there is a wide variety of locations, all with a different look and feel. Enemies are amazingly designed, and from basic grunt enemies to bosses, they all present their own level of difficuly/strategy to defeat. There are also more enemies than SotN, so...a lot. Map layout is perfect, with enemies strategically placed to make the area difficult, but not to the point of rage inducing.
The game also presents an amazing atmosphere, creating a sense of hopelessnes and despair for the residents of Hollownest, and you truly feel like your character is special amongst the world. The hand drawn enemies and environment look absolutely fantastic. This combined with the music, creates one of the best worlds I've ever seen in a game.
Combat feels rewarding, and each upgrade to your attacks/moves make you really feel like you are on the way to becoming a bad♥♥♥♥♥ I've read a lot of complaints about backtracking...which if you know anything about a Metroidvania game...that's kind of par for the course, so not sure the reason for the complaints unless you've literally never heard of Metroid or SoTN...The difficulty never feels cheap, and each hit/death is a mistake on your part. The game really rewards patience (study enemy movement, look at your surrounding before jumping off a cliff into straight up death.
The lore is also something to be in awe of. You aren't required to dive into it much if you don't want, but if you do choose to, you will begin to put pieces together that really craft a mysterious and deep world, with a lot open to interpretation in a way. It really furthers the sense hopelessness and straight up sadness in the world.
If you enjoy difficult games with a true sense of accomplishment, but this game, I promise you won't be disappointed. If you are even on the fence of buying it, try it out for a bit and refund it, but I swear to you it is worth investing your money and time.
One more thing; getting the White Palace...relic, becomes a bit easier if you've grown up playing Mario games.
And Zote...♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

I picked this game up after watching a bit of the TFS Let's Play. The charming, somewhat cute art style paired with visceral, fast-paced combat and platforming was enough to instantly sieze my attention and make me crave a first-hand experience.
A modest sum of fifteen bucks and some fifty hours later, I finished my first play through, having somehow stumbled my way into a 100% completion run and gotten several times my money's worth in entertainment. Capturing the essence of the Metroidvania franchise better than any game I've played in recent years, Hollow Knight goes a bit further beyond by telling a compelling story, taking a Souls-like approach to its lore that draws you in on another level as you troll endless levels of homicidal bug men.
From a rotating cast of unique, engaging characters, you slowly piece together the story of Hallownest and your own place within it, culminating in some of the most delightfully challenging boss fights and intense platforming sections I've played in some time. The combat is fluid and rapidly paced, the environments you navigate through beautifully realized with a wonderfully orchestrated back drop, excellent art, and dozens of secrets that can only be found after combing through most of the areas multiple times at different points in the game.
I didn't expect to get so much entertainment value for the price I paid, and with more on the way in the form of Extras still in the works, I look forward to starting another playthrough soon. Needless to say, I'll also be keeping an eye on Team Cherry's work going forward.

I feel a little bad for developer Flying Wild Hog, remaking or "rebooting" Shadow Warrior is just not something I would expect any modern game company to do willingly. While I played and enjoyed the original Shadow Warrior, and even the recent "redux" version, it is not a game that could be made today by any legitimate company. The terrible racism present in the original that comes from a time in which that level of ignorance was the norm, would cripple any modern company's public image. That being said, it is that same racism and offensive humor that made the original so funny. So what is Flying Wild Hog left with?
Humor: 7/10
Not surprisingly, Shadow Warrior 2013 is not as funny as the original. There are some genuine laugh-out-loud moments, but they are few. The humor overall is cheesy (which I like, to be honest, but is isn't for everyone), and the writing is pretty lame. While I did enjoy the game's sense of humor, it was nowhere near the original.
Story: 7/10
The story in this game is also pretty mediocre. Your demon sidekick, Hoji, is very entertaining and later you meet a couple ladies who spice things up a bit, but overall Lo Wang himself is kind of an idiot and you don't really find yourself attached to him by the end of the game. The plot begins as a riveting plot about a demon apocalypse and devolves into a family squabble gone wrong, that no one seems to understand.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
The combat is where this game really shines. It is definitely an "old-school shooter," and a lot like the Serious Sam games. Your run speed is blazing fast and you have a dash move that makes you even faster, so mobility is your primary way to avoid taking damage. While there isn't a large variety of weapons, all of the weapons in the game are really fun and you could easily play this game with just guns and have a blast. However, where the combat really shines, and is unique from almost ALL other FPS games, is with the sword fighting. You will probably end up using the sword 90% of the time, which is awesone because you feel like a superpowered ninja when you do.
In addition to the weapons, there are numerous upgrades. You can buy weapon upgrades for your guns with money that you find, and many of them add a secondary fire mode that opens up new play styles and tactics. You unlock skills- which include health and stamina upgrades, weapons skills, and passive abilities- using karma, which you earn during battles by using a variety of weapons and attacks. And finally, you also upgrade your Ki powers, using crystals that you find on each level. These powers allow you to heal, stun, and protect yourself from damage.
The result is a fast-paced hectic arena filled with demons rushing towards you as you dash, stab, slice, blast, and basically just destroy everything around you. In a word, it's awesome!
I do have a few minor complaints though: there isn't much demon variety. Old school shooters often had upwards of 15 different enemy types, this game has about 12 in total. The maps are mostly boring too, while the first one is really cool and there are a few other interesting ones, you will still spend many hours in metal corridors and boring industrial maps. Finally, two of the powers you can upgrade are essentially the same: one knocks enemies down, and the other lifts them in the air, so both essentially stun enemies. It would have been better if devs removed one of the powers and gave you something offensive, like a health-sapping poison, or a short attack-damage boost with a cooldown after.
Overall, it is a great game that I think will surprise you with how fun it is. I highly recommend it!

I have one, and only one, complaint about this game.
The controls are what I would describe as overly sensitive. Essentialy, what the game needs you to do, control wise, combined with the speed at which your character responds, I find myself often fighting against the speed of my character to achieve the precision the game wants. I think it would be better if it had analog movement, or if it were not seemingly built for a 360 controller which has a terrible D pad. I also think it would be much better if the game had an "attack downwards" button instead of requriing you to hold down, as doing that again conflicts with the extremely sensitive horizontal control of your character and using an analog stick.
With that out of the way, the game is absolutely beautiful, utterly gorgeous artistically and frankly very enjoyable to play. I wholly recommend it for anybody who enjoys 2d platformers of any stripe, and if you particularly like metroidvanias I would argue it is an extremely good example of the form. It also, if you will forgive the cliche comparison, is reminiscent of a Dark Souls game in both difficulty, some of the mechanics, and general atmosphere. If you enjoyed the thematic setting of DS1 I think you will find an awful lot to enjoy in this game too. As I said my only frustration is the way the game handles its controls which are very sensitive because your character responds very quickly and is highly mobile, and the game has quite a bit of pretty precise platforming required from you. There's no weight to your character, you press a direction and they move, and this may be a feature if you're fond of games like that, though I find it more of a hindrance coming from games with characters having more inertia.
I strongly recommend the game anyway and I would say if you have a controller with a properly positioned and good quality D pad this game would be much better as I have yet to find any part of it that even notices analog control, much less makes functional use of it. If you are using a 360 controller and can't get away with the D pad on it, you may find sections of the game a little frustrating, but the rest of the game is still excellent, so I would still say the game is easily worth the asking price and especially if it is on sale. Design wise it's a really fun 2d platformer/metroidvania and especially if you like exploring and sequence breaking, you'll get a lot of mileage out of this game.

Now that I've sunk more than 20 hours into this, I feel it's time to expand why I think this game is not that good, or at least not worth the asking price.
I do understand it's early access and so some of the faults are to be forgiven and will probably be smoothed out for the complete realease. I would however like to point out the biggest flaw in the system for now - If you do not have a friend or two to play with, your victory or loss will depend on the luck of the draw - whoever gets a better "composition", has vastly increased chances, and there is nothing to be done once the match starts. Even if everyone in the match has comperable level of skill, all you can do is suck it up.
Now, why I think the whole premise is not very good in general. Despite it clearly being a MOBA, it lacks ANY strategy aspect of the genre and contains next to no tactics. It is possible to form a semblence of a functioning team with divided tasks, but that's pretty much where all planning apart ends. You can't outmaneuver or outsmart the enemy team, lure them into a trap or misdirect their efforts - you can only outplay them.
To do so effectively you must practice the same character extensively to know the cooldowns and range by muscle memory, so the short duration of the match doesn't matter, it's just the same thing over and over again, especially with a very limited character pool players can pick from and balancing issues which make some of them the only viable option if you want to climb in rating. This means you face the same matchups game after game.
In my opinion the formula simply doesn't work. You have a MOBA version of Unreal Tournament, but it's neither this fast paced nor easy to just jump in and play. I am not saying it can't be fun, I had some good times playing with friends for a little while, but it just gets really stale. It begs for something added to the gameplay to flesh it out, but that would also ruin the quick 10-minute match aspect, so I see no win-win situation for it.
To sum it up, I would advise you to wait for it to be f2p, or just pick from a huge number of other available MOBA's. I am having much better time with them than battlerite and so should you.

This is a highly recommended and fun game, though it is very gory. If lots of blood is not your thing, then you should probably avoid this title. That aside, Shadow Warrior ticks many boxes and has impressed me. First of all is the story. While many FPS games do not necessarily require a good story in order to give you some enemies to shoot or melee for a few hours, Shadow Warrior includes a very nice campaign, with some quite memorable characters and dialogue fleshing out the surprisingly high quality plot. With your protagonist named Lo Wang, one should expect some crude humour, and Flying Wild Hog do not disappoint. The cutscenes are also very nice,while also giving you the option to skip them if you so desire.
The art style, particularly the basic enemies you fight, may look a little... crude? That's fine though, the dismemberment or other assorted violence will soon put that out of your mind. But the graphics of this game are quite brilliant, and the environments are truly spectacular - be they urban, forest, or snow. This also extends to the design of the weapons, which you can get a close up view of when you upgrade them with in-game cash you can find scattered all over the various levels. With a large variety, all of which you can carry at the same time if you are up to that point of the story, the weapons all look incredibly interesting, and play well too - bonuses for the visible changes in the weapons as you upgrade them, be it a laser pointer, or a larger tank, or the ability to fire multiple missiles at the same time...
The levels all look impressive, and are very vast, although they are essentially linear. Not all of the secrets are incredibly well hidden, but they can be challenging to find them all. And the nod back to the original game and other old-school shooters in the form of secret retro areas is a very nice touch. Especially when Lo Wang breaks the fourth wall. One of the few complaints I have with this game is that the large nature of the maps means that sometimes you will be forced to double back, and sometimes it can become quite difficult to find out where you actually have to go to progress.
That said, where this game truly shines is in the combat. Visceral, brutal, and with a variety of enemies to keep you on your toes, from standard humans with weapons, to demons with claws, wings, enemies who can teleport or turn invisible, to mention nothing of the mini-bosses or bosses in the game. This is not a truly realistic game, where cover is irrelevant, and you can tank damage by just healing it up again with one of your abilities, but it's fine and fun because you can just smash face first into enemies.
The game revolves around finding a legendary katana, and so swordplay is a central point of the game, with skills to improve your character and the ability to hack and slash quite satisfying - dismemberment and decapitations galore. The ability to acquire both skills and other passive bonuses, as well as upgrading your weapons also gets a tick. The guns are also quite special, from more standard revolver and shotgun to the more esoteric quad-barrel shotgun and crossbow, each with 3 upgrades, and the ability to purchase extra ammo if you're in a pinch. This is complemented by the completely insane, but incredibly fun possibilities of using demon parts as one of your demon extermination tools...
EDIT: The other problem I've found with this game is the boss fights: they become quite repetitive, and the same strategy is used to beat all 3. In addition, some of the "mini-bosses", especially the Berserker, can be annoying and time consuming to kill.
Huge fun, with good replayability too. +1 recommendation.

Dungeon Defenders is an original hybrid of two hot genres: Tower Defense and cooperative online Action-RPG!
The game puts players in the role of one of four distinctive hero classes, tasked with fending off hordes of invading beasties by strategically summoning a variety of Defenses & Traps throughout their castle. But as much more than just a strategy game, players directly participate in the action-packed combat with their hero characters, while upgrading their statistics, gathering tons of loot and inventory items, customizing & upgrading equipment, and developing unique class abilities. All of this can be enjoyed in seamless online and split-screen local multiplayer, as players cooperate and compete through the story campaign and challenge missions to build the strongest heroes and achieve the highest scores in the kingdom.
Combining the depth of strategic gaming with the satisfying action of RPG character building, in a beautifully stylized ‘toon fantasy setting, Dungeon Defenders is designed to be a distinctly addictive, easy-to-play experience for casual and hardcore gamers alike!

A bold reimagining of 1997's Shadow Warrior. Everything about this game respects the old school aspects of early FPS gems adding a thin layer of modern upgrade and weapon customization. The game is genuinely fun and has a great sense of humor, fighting with a demon sidekick while delivering one liners feels just like a buddy cop action flick done right.
There are LOTS of secrets to be found, and I do mean LOTS. I've spent 17 hours in my first run while OCCASSIONALLY looking for secrets and yet I haven't unlocked half of them. And as far the game lenght goes it is HUGE, expect a 10+ hours in your first playthrough at normal difficulty. The level design is pretty good, while you won't be entirely lost because mission objects glow, you'll certainly take a time to figure the level layout, no point A and B, corridor bullsh*t.
I only hold one complaint against this game: I feel that the way you're forced to kill enemies in some kind of arena, exhausting the "enter arena, lock doors, kill enemies, unlock doors, proceed" formula. The game should have let the player proceed at his own pace.
Huge replaybility since the game can get pretty harsh at max level.
The graphics are ok at best, but since this is an old school fps game I wasn't expecting jaw dropping graphics.
This game plays and controls like a dream.
If Duke Nukem Forever let you down, Shadow Warrior will lift you up to the heavens with a certain sense of nostalgia. 8.5/10

This game plays like 2d Dark Souls with a metroidvania twist, exploring a dark, dead kingdom, and yet while it doesn't advertise itself as a Dark Souls clone for a quick buck, it is infinitely closer in theme and atmosphere than any of the other Souls-like wannabes that do (I'm looking at you, Salt & Sanctuary and Lords of the Fallen). Hollow Knight is full of genuine surprises, and great detail was put into both the design of the world and its inhabitants, as well as the order you complete parts of the game - talking to my friends, we'd accidentally discover differences between each others' runs, including whether an NPC was or wasn't in a given location, whether they ever found certain zones or charms (there are many optional locations), or even beating the game without a few mechanics I would've thought were mandatory. There are many secret locations, bosses, and storylines you can find in this game, and playing it just once isn't enough to uncover all the twists the developers penned down.
I can't recommend this game enough. Graphically it isn't as impressive as Ori and the Blind Forest but it has a much richer world, lore and atmosphere.

Initially I was quite worried (but still enthusiastic) about a new Assassins Creed as the events that took place at the end of the last game effectivly tied up the existing series. The power of the AC franchise is having the flexibility to move forward and develop a new game that can tell a self contained story within the Universe. They don't HAVE to rely specifically on Desmond as they can tell a story using an interesting Character from any point in history...and they delivered!
The game tells the story of Edward Kenway, a privateer turned pirate out to seek his fortune in the Caribbean. I found the characters to be very likeable and the game told an interesting story with Edward trapped between the conflict of the Assassins and Templars of which he is neither. I prehaps would have preferred if Edward truly belonged to a side as the game leaned more towards a 'Pirate Simulator' with an AC theme rather than a true AC game because of it. HOWEVER it is still the best damn pirate simulator I have ever played! I genuinly enjoyed all the mechanics the game had to offer, especially the Naval combat.
Practically the game runs on a new engine (Anvil) and Ubisoft have taken great strides to make this a much more cinematic offerring than previous titles. The camera is lower and closer during combat (which is visceral and gory) and small things like running and jumping now have camera effects and motion blur. I found during my playthrough that the engine sometimes struggled to keep up with the effects (which made me a sad panda) as they made the game much more immersive. The game has also had a graphical overhaul and is just STUNNING. It is amazingly pretty with vibrant colours and fantastic textures.
I am not sure whether I should take points off for this or not but whilst I played for 52 hours, the story only lasted for about 8. I do this with every AC and knock everything optional over early (100% every single collectible) so I can just focus on the story and I found it to be a little on the shorter side. The sheer amount of collectibles in this game is staggering and I am not 100% sure they added anything to the game. They add hours to your playthrough yes... but is this value for money? Debatable. I just found it a little over the top...
So anyway, I better wrap this up! The game and the story (although short) are fantastic and Ubisoft have put a lot of love into this title. They set out to prove that they could do something new and they succeeded!
8/10.

If Studio Ghibli made Metroid Souls
is how I would describe this gem. The art and music are phenomenal, and at the same time, stark, painting the picture of big ambitions gone horribly wrong. Impressive still, is that this intricate detail doesn't come at the price of quantity - the game world is massive, and every bit of it seems to have its own unique, hand-drawn artwork. Populating it are numerous charming characters, that serve as a delightful contrast to the overall grim tone.
Gameplay doesn't take a backseat either. The controls are crisp, the combat feels weighty and satisfying thanks to excellent feedback, the enemies are varied and well animated, and the plentiful boss fights make for memorable encounters.
Beware, though. I did not add "Souls" to that description without reason. This game likes to kill you. A lot. And it doesn't shy away from throwing ridiculous difficulty spikes at you if you chose to go off the beaten path, or from letting you into areas you shouldn't be in yet. If something proves too difficult at first, take another route and come back later with better gear.
10/10 would play again

I was never one to play the original Shadow Warrior, but I think this game captures the spirit of old school fps games with some neat twists. I would love for Flying Wild Hog to expand on the game a bit more, maybe create a more polished sequel, as I feel there were some bits and pieces of this game that felt unrealized or primarily unfinished. And the plot takes a surprising turn near the end. But in the grand scheme of it all these are minor gripes.
Where the game truly shines is in the combat. Not quite Serious Sam level, but still more than enough to keep things tense and exciting. The environments have some nice touches, and although the secrets aren't necessarily well hidden, it's more than enough for anyone who wants to take the time to look for them. Unlike other franchises that have rebooted, while forgetting what made them so enjoyable (looking at you Painkiller and Duke Nukem), Flying Wild Hog has not only revived an aging series, but they've done so with good design sensibility, and an explosion filled, blood soaked shoot fest that also happens to have some very satisfying swordplay. 8.5/10.

Anyone who believes video games can't be considered a form of art should play this. The Stanley Parable is more of an experience than it is a game. There are no rules, there are no winners, and there is no fourth wall. The game really feels like a fluid experience between you and the narrator, even occasionally spanning multiple playthroughs. Every path you take has a unique philosophical message for the player's interpretation, and every one of them makes you reconsider what is real, what makes sense, and even how you perceive the world around you.
Whether you think of art as a creative medium for individuals to express themselves, or as something for each individual to experience and interpret on their own, The Stanley Parable fits the bill.

I can say with all certainty that The Stanley Parable is the strangest game I have ever played.
There is no true objective to speak of; You play as the titular Stanley who has, up to now, lived a completely content life performing his job of pressing buttons. However, one day, he discovers that all of his fellow coworkers have suddenly vanished. Stanley is free to investigate this disappearance however he choses, while accompanied by the musings of a helpful (though, not always friendly) narrator.
Sadly, this is all I can divulge without spoiling what makes this game so unique, intriguing, and most of all, enjoyable. Much (if not all) of this is due to your relationship with the narrator. Very rarely do I see any work of fiction pull off having the narrator as his/her own character in the story well. Yet, The Stanley Parable somehow manages to make the narrator consistantly funny, but also a relatable character. It's difficult to describe without playing the game for yourself.
That's actually a very accurate summary of this experience: It's difficult to truly describe what makes The Stanley Parable a worthwhile experience without playing it for yourself.
If you're looking for a more concrete example of what makes this game enjoyable, then know that the various endings to this game range from following an out-of-control quest arrow pointing you towards your goal, all the way to playing the first stage of Portal.
I have absolutely no regrets about purchasing this title.

This is a game that has some extremely high points and extremely low points.
Let's start with the good: Sailing. After the first hour or two of faffing about, the game gives you a pirate ship and sets you loose on the seas. Most of the fun times you'll have in the game will be sailing around and getting into incredibly dramatic ship battles on the high seas. If you've ever played Sid Meier's 'Pirates!' then you'll be pleased to know that sailing in Black Flag is basically a modernized version of that. You have to manuever your ship to bring cannons to bear while staying out of their firing zone by managing your ship's speed and manuevers.
In one memorable moment, I assaulted a British fortress in the middle of a storm, riding waves and dodging artillery as a British Man O War and a pair of Frigates bore down on me. Using a wave to barrel out of the way of an artillery barrage before delivering a round of heavy guns onto a Man O War's backside is absolutely thrilling stuff. The sailing alone is enough to make me recommend the game. It's incredibly fun and incredibly fresh.
The story (ignoring the modern day headache that the game insists on vomiting onto you now and again) is alright, if fairly predicatable. One problem I had is telling apart the male pirates. It seemed like I killed about 8 pirate guys that betrayed me somehow and I had some sort of beef with. But I didn't really care about the details of the templar/assassin nonsense anyhow, so I'll give the story a pass. I liked James Kidd quite a bit after all.
The problems with the game are basically everything else.
Let me discuss the major points:
First:
Whenever you go back to land to take an assassination mission, the first thing you'll be asked to do is tail and/or eavesdrop on someone. This involves jumping on a rooftop as they walk along town (and needless to say every town in the Caribbean has a good five or six guards inexplicably guarding rooftops) or hiding in a bush as they walk along. If you fall behind, mission failed, start again. Not fun.
Second:
The land combat is ridiculously easy.
I did some early assassination missions, made some gold and then bought the Wheellock Pistols, which have massive range but do less damage. Unfortunately for every Spanish soldier in the Caribbean, pistol damage means♥♥♥♥♥♥when a headshot is an instant kill no matter what. For when I did do melee, I had a pair of swords that I bought in the first hour of the game that let me jump around going for a stabathon on all the bad guys without much trouble.
But honestly, that wasn't even the problem. There are three points in the game where your weapons get arbitrarily taken away in an attempt to get you to use stealth, but even with just your wrist knives you can kill infinite guards with parry and break defense.
Sure it's fun at a visceral level to walk up to a fortress of British soldiers and kill everyone inside, but Dark Souls this ain't.
Third:
The game wastes time with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
There's this entire diving minigame with unique mechanics where you've got to dive underwater for some treasure while using air bubbles and dodging sharks. It's a terrible minigame that no one in the right mind would want to play and Ubisoft seemed to recognize this, because you only have to do it once. You can explore ship wrecks as an optional thing on your own, but it's such a tedious busywork section that no one in the right mind would want to do it.
Which brings us to the central point, which is that Ubisoft has no idea how to tell a good idea from a bad one.
Instead of underwater travel or tailing (and I'm not even going to talk in any detail about the stupid ♥♥♥♥ing modern day office/hacking crap), they could've given the sailing a bit more depth and made more things to do at sea.
As it stands, the game is great fun up until the point where you've got your ship upgraded to the point where you can take on two Man O Wars with ease. At that point, the game sort of peters out and you'll fast travel from story mission to mission to wrap the thing up.
Just goes to show that while a team behind a game might have talent, you still need a director with a coherent vision to make a game great. Without that vision, you end up with a scatterbrain game like AC: Black Flag.
Still, cool that a brother is heading a big video game project. Keep improving, Ashraf Ismail.

So, you know when you are playing a game, and it seems SUPER promising? But there are things that just fall flat? You keep playing the game because there is just something you really enjoy, but those little grievances always at the back of your head. Hollow Knight, at least for me, had none of these. Each and every part just kept hitting its mark. Each and every part kept giving me things I didn't even know I wanted.
I went into it expecting a decent Metroidvania with some Souls-like aspects. What I got was a *fantastic* Metroidvania with Souls-like aspects that NO OTHER SOULS-LIKE GAME has grasped, even Dark Souls 2 and 3. One of my favorite parts of Dark Souls 1 is how you find characters throughout your journey that are all on their own journeys. Each of them has their own personalites and quests that are shaped by your actions. I really haven't encountered any other game to do that, until Hollow Knight. You meet so many other characters throughout the game that are just like the ones in Dark Souls 1.
The gameplay is very solid. The Metroidvania-style progresion is spot on. The platforming would have been perfect all on its own. The combat is simple, but well executed. The handle both platforming and combat difficulty very well, too. You can get through the required stuff without too much difficulty, but there is definitely enough extra stuff that REALLY challenges you.
The exploration is amazing. This game is chalk-full of hidden areas, items, characters, and quests. There are always at least 3 things at the back of your mind that you want to go check out.
Which brings me to my favorite part and the thing that cemented this as one of my all time favorite games: The World, and how it's presented. I can scarcely communicate the feelings I feel about this. First off, this game is just ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous. Some of the best art, just plain old art, I have ever seen. The soundtrack is fantastic as well, each piece fits so well with what is happen, great music design. The area design is just absoutely masterful. Each area is unique and well thought out. You can tell just walking through them that they have a story. It does a great job of really making you feel like you are walking through this once majestic kingdom. Some of the areas were just sooo damn good I had to stop and stare. I wish I could walk into the City of Tears for the first time again. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥
All in all, this game is just so incredibly dense with tiny, amazing pieces that all fuse together to make this resplendent diamond of a game.

I got this game expecting a fun time sink because I love the metroidvania genre, and got so much more than I could have hoped for.
Overall I'd give this game a 9/10
The beginning was a little rough for me, as not having an automatic map combined with the huge world they give you got me lost quite a few times, and the game doesn't tell you where to go for the majority of the midgame.  This made the story feel a little slow for me, but had I known what to do it probably would have felt different.  That being said, I like that it doesn't help you.  I helps immerse you more in the world and you go only where you decide you want to explore.  More often than not, that turns into another whole adventure.  As you travel you will notice areas that seem suspicous and when you get items that deal with those locations most of them are fairly easy to remember, but it can be confusing at times.
The npcs that you get introduced you get their own lives, their own stories, and without giving away any spoilers as you gain access to new mechanics the backstory on character you can get goes up exponentially.  I truly felt invested in the fall of this ancient city, and how it related to what was happening in the present.
The combat is fairly intuitive.  I am actively trying to avoid comparing this game to dark souls but the combat is similar in that you have to learn enemy mechanics or you will have trouble with the basic enemies in new areas, but once you know their patterns it becomes more of a puzzle, especially the bosses, but that doesn't make it any less hectic (looking at you failed champion, soul tryant, and lost kin).
The game is atmospherically very dark.  Each zone has a color that it is focused around but overall the color tones are very muted and dark besides red infections/projectiles, and that pairs very well with the way they designed the characters and the music they chose to bring you much deeper into the game than you might expect.
I beat the game in roughly 8-9 hours, but there is still so much more i need to do, so many more bosses to find, and more endings to see.  In terms of completion I am probably around 40% there with 14-15 hours in game, which is a lot more than I expected for 15$
tl;dr:  This game is easily worth its price, and will likely go on sale soon or be part of the humble monthly.  With tons of exploring, great visuals and soundtrack [Marissa ):  ],  and the promise of upcoming DLC to play as hornet (rumored to be free),  this game is definitely work a pickup.  This game is a top contender for my game of the year (currently its between this and Nier: automata).

I think that in general it is rare to get into a game with little prior knowledge about it these days. People like to follow a game's development or press for obvious reasons: they're excited, they want to make an informed decision, they want to talk about it beforehand, etc. Wanting to go into a game "blind" is a common goal but not one that is easy to execute in a world where information is coming in whether you like it or not. It also can easily be a bad thing! It only takes one bamboozle and you tell yourself "Welp never doing that again," and when there are so many games out these days its easy to get that bad experience. However this post is about my experience with Hollow Knight and how going into a game blind can still be an incredible experience that I believe we should all try more often (and just to gush about Hollow Knight).
I purchased Hollow Knight on impulse. I am not a die-hard Metroidvania fan - I've actually never played a Castlevania game or some of Metroid's derivatives, but I did enjoy the Metroid games I played! I knew what the genre was and what I was getting into at least judging from its description on the Steam store page. I actually did not know this was a Kickstarter game until some time after I had purchased it, which makes going into the game blind all the more amazing. Kickstarters tend to drip-feed updates, progress, ideas, art, etc. constantly if they are doing it right, and I had managed to avoid all of that going in. Now that I have completed the game I looked back at the Kickstarter updates and the game's related media, and they gave all sorts of surprises away! I was blown away by some things in the game that would have had a great deal of their magic taken away if I had done as much as watch even a second trailer. Mechanics, number of bosses or areas, characters you meet - they all ended up as a bullet point somewhere. It makes me wonder how we can balance enjoying the adventure of a game, while still being able to make an informed decision on it. Below I'll list some examples of what surprised me about the game and gush about it for a bit in an effort to convince you to try it, while trying to leave out as much as possible in order to try and keep that experience for others.
The game's aesthetic is very interesting. I went into this thinking it was a game set in a world of bug-people, but they managed to do it without giving you that squick-y feeling a lot of people get around insects (except for one zone that is absolutely 100% that and is awful) due to an art style that is just charming and cartoony enough. I also didn't expect how well Team Cherry took that idea and created an entire setting that could surround such a thing. They didn't just make some lamps that are fireflies for instance, but also took into account why an area would look a certain way in given with the culture and history that they have created. Sure its a world of bugs, but no two given areas look the same if the bugs that lived there would lead different lives. Its also a very bleak world - its a cliche at this point to compare a game to Dark Souls but in this case it must be done because they were clearly heavily influenced by it with their art direction. The world is depicted as old and decaying, with heavy hints to things far more ancient than yourself or even the civilizations you see. There are a lot of blues and greys, black and white, and you think all you'll see is some rocky tunnels and spikes.
But before a skeptic can roll their eyes at yet another grimdark indie Dark Souls clone the world soon explodes into life and color in places that show how far the hand-drawn art style can go into detail. Even in a world that is supposed to be mostly underground you rarely feel claustrophobic (except for that one area), just like I felt the Metroid games accomplished.
I thought of a similar game in Salt and Sanctuary, but while the two are both 2D and influenced by Dark Souls, SnS is quite...ugly. Its ugly enough to turn me off more than a game about bugs would, and the difference in art between the two is vast. Its also important how well its animated considering the metroidvania aspect of it. Everything moves around the screen a great deal - your character, the enemies, the background, the foreground, projectiles, effects - and its all very smooth and well done. Lots of little touches make the world charm you that much more.
The biggest surprise to me however was the story, lore, and characters of the game. I mentioned the Dark Souls influence before, but I did not expect the story to be as deep and rich as that other series can be, almost as if simply taking the best aspects of it. Like Dark Souls, the plot of the game and the history of the world must be put together piecemeal from item descriptions, cryptic NPC dialogue, and environmental clues. Unlike Dark Souls, this one can actually be put together without writing a peer-reviewed journal, provides some actual closure to those who piece it all together, and it includes a very helpful bestiary to flesh out the world more. It is incredibly deep and evocative for a $15 cartoony indie title, with some heavy themes and a lot of mystery that leaves you wanting to explore for more. Keep in mind this is not an RPG, but I finished the game after feeling I got everything I wanted out of it purely story-wise in about 20 hours. I did not get 100% completion (that's more mechanic-collectey wise anyway). There is a key mechanic in the game that is mostly used for just lore, and its enjoyable to play around with it. The game gives a perfect feeling of adventure since around every corner you can find something new. Heading down a new tunnel you missed before doesn't simply reward you with an upgrade, but instead you'll often find a completely new zone, another encounter with a character, a new mystery, or you'll just panic in a "where am I NOW its been like an hour since the last save bench and found yet another entirely new zone." The game's world keeps expanding. This is actually one of the most liked pictures on the Hollow Knight artwork page:
This doesn't mean the game is without flaws. The first and largest is that if you want to get the most out of the game and see all the story it gets frustratingly hard. I don't just mean the combat either, since the game has a bizarre section that completely switches genres from metroidvania to Super Meat Boy/Dustforce so completely that its like it was running on an emulator within the game. I feel confident in saying that there has to be a large number of players, especially after the Switch release, that will buy this game and not be able to complete all of it. Is that fine? I'm not sure. While it in my opinion is also a breath of fresh air, for those who play a lot of metroid-vanias there is not a lot new mechanic-wise. You will get to a gap and instantly know you will get a double-jump ability to cross it since that's just what happens in metroidvanias and its true here, as well as other similar abilities. You can also expect a great deal of backtracking in the huge world, and even with all the mobility you can get it can be tedious.
So while all of this was mostly to gush about my positive experience with Hollow Knight, I also hope that others can find their own positive experiences going into a game without knowing much about it. I was recently unpleasantly surprised by ME: Andromeda and we could all use a little pick me up from time to time.
