An outstanding game. Fairly heavy on PC requirements but it looks good even on low settings with many features turned off. Free running is stream-lined and only requires the use of one button to run. It is also much faster and while targeting your jumps still suffers in accuracy, it works better than ever before. There are also new run animations such as moving around objects and swinging from object to object (monkey bars). In other words the free running has reached what the designers had planned for the first game. The world feels populated and unlike other Assassins Creed games it is one that you will want to explore. Cities are smaller but personally I prefer that to big maps such as Brotherhood's Rome which consisted of largly empty space and similar buildings. In other words the new cities are exciting, alive, and easier to traverse. The addition of fast travel also helps. Fast travel is not exclusive to the big map, it is also avaliable within cities. All viewpoints are now fast travel locations, which more often then not are placed relatively close to missions and side activites. Side activites are better than in past games. I have yet to encounter anything such as races, which I welcome as I often found them infuriating in past games due to the inaccuracy during free running. In fact the only side activity I have encountered so far is assassination contracts. Assassination contracts no longer have cutscenes or really add to the story in any way. Some may take issue with this but I found that it made them easier to jump into. Side activites are a bit quicker and in my opinion feel more like actual side activites, quick breaks from the main game. To make up for the lack of the old side activities there are more collectibles. There are animus scraps, chest, viewpoints, treasure maps, messages in bottles, and sea shanties. Sea shanties could be considered the new race system. When you approach one it will start to fly away and you must chase after it and catch it before it disappears, though if you position yourself right it will fly straight into you as soon as it starts moving. There is a new crafting system that requires you to hunt animals in order to make health upgrades, weapons, and pouches. While this isnt terribly exciting, it isn't bad either and adds some more gameplay. Your pirate ship now functions as your base, meaning that you can upgrade it and change its appearance. I have yet to come across any sort of money accumulation system such as in Brotherhood or AC 2 so money carries more value and decisions require more thought.There are Mayan artifacts that serve as the new hidden puzzles. I have found one so far and it was not very difficult. I liked how I was able to do it in the game though as opposed to past games where I would have to find something hidden in a painting to watch a video. This one only required that I match a shape with nearby objects. The sailing is great and the game makes you feel like a real pirate. Naval battles are fun and dangerous. Enemy ships often travel in groups, so fighting one ship often turns into fighting two or three ships. You really feel like a pirate attacking a convoy. The new combat system is a little tougher but in a good way. I found it harder to win fights than in Brotherhood where I could kill 56 enemies without being touched. Fights seem to pose more of a threat now but that may also be due to my game lagging during these. I am running this game on a basic laptop so I do suffer a small amount of frame rate drop on rare occasion. The final thing I should mention is that health is now regenerative. I have seen people complain about this but I enjoy it. I got tired of always having to run to a doctor in Brotherhood especially when my character jumping off the side of a building and hurt himself, against my best efforts to guide him to the adjacent roof. I enjoy the regerative health because I found the old system tedioius. I also feel that the more menus that I am required to jump through the less immersed I am in the game. Upon this, I am reminded to mention that I have yet to leave the animus. So far it  seems that leave the animus is not a requirement at all. This feels good, unlike in past games where you were taken out right when the action was picking up and reminded that it is just a simulation. Also, regarding combat, you can no longer kill civilians unless you go into free target and shoot them. I don't know why it took this long to remove that feature, as in past games killing civilians would result in a "game over". As a result targeting is easier and you will take out that enemy you were aiming at instead of a civilian. I run this game on an unmodified Dell Inspiron laptop and while I have to use low settings the game still looks nice and plays well. Anyone reading this review should bear in mind that the last Assassins Creed game I played was Brotherhood on Xbox 360. So some of the improvements I have mentioned may have been made already in Assassins Creed 3. Overall AC IV is a great game 10/10, it is my favorite Assassins Creed game and I would recommend it.
P.S. If you are worried about the controls with mouse and keyboard I can tell you that they are smooth and function well. I honestly don't feel like I am suffering because I do not have a gamepad. I think that a gamepad is still (I imagine) the best way to play this game but it is equally enjoyable and easy to play without one.
If you like tower defense and strategy, you'll like this game. If you hate tower defense and strategy, you'll still like this game.

This game has a lot of features that you rarely see, and sometimes make a game worse but somehow work in this one.
Pros:
Essentially a walking simulator that doesn't suck (never thought I'd say that.)
The antagonist is largely the narrator as he tries to convince you to follow his commands.
One ending requires you play an immensely boring game about pressing 2 buttons to save cardboard cutouts for 4 freaking hours. (Look it up online cause yeah....)
Great comedy that has self referencing, breaking the 4th wall, etc...
The game changes at random like loading a different office to start, or having papers on the floor, or even just having different dialog play so you can't tell if the game is new or if your restart triggered some new strange events.
Cons:
Basically the only point is the achievements, jokes, and endings all of which can be look up online to see what they entail.
Not much replay once you've done all the endings.
It has the full spectrum of ridiculous events in it. The game is about an office employee Stanley whos job is to mindlessly follow commands, the game then proceeds to have the narrator cough up commands for you to blindly follow. It has multiple endings and the "True ending" (the one you get the achievment for beating the game) is the one where you do as he says. That said it doesn't so much have multiple endings as the game IS multiple endings. They vary depending on when/if you disobey the narrators instructions, and the journey to the endings is often crazy enough to involve false game resets, slightly altered areas (Though the areas and dialog alter slightly at random times too just so you can never tell if it's part of the ending from last time.), and self referencing commentary.
The game also has crazy achievements, some as easy as turning the ability to earn achievments on or spamming 8 on the numberpad in the bosses office. To insane request, like not playing the game for 5 years (or just changing your computers date) and one that has a list of randomly generated requirements to unlock.
It's worth a buy but definitely wait for a sale I'm not sure it's worth the $15.

That may not tell you much about the game, unless you know about my gaming life and tastes. What I can tell you is that I
like "metroidvanias" in general, and this is one of the best out there.
Hollow Knight does many things in the way I consider the most fun in this type of games: It lets you explore its world the way you want, it gives you choices on how you build your character, it tells its story in creative and non-traditional ways, it strikes you with astonishing visuals and soundtrack, and it does all of that with simplicity and elegance.
Hallownest, the world of Hollow Knight, is
. For this kind of game, I wasn't expecting such a large world to explore. And I certainly didn't notice how open ended it was when I started playing. Then, I went to see other players and their routes, and I realised that I followed a path that was very different than the other. And this is beautiful: to be able to trace your own route, without feeling like you're doing it too right or too wrong. The way everything connects is wonderful and the environment is always surprising you.
The combat mechanics are also very thight and well done. You don't have a plethora of different equipment or combos - instead, you must rely on mastering your technique with your sword, I mean, nail, with a handfull of skills and abillities. But these dynamics offer more depth than one might think, and the added system of Charms add a lot of tactical and customizable flavour - with many different charms to find and little room to use all at once, you must choose the right combination to fit your needs, be it survivalbility, strength, magic, mobility...
Artistically, I find this game incredibly appealing. The first thing that comes to fruition is its gorgeous, hand drawn visuals, and as you progress through the game you will be delighted with amazing music and sounds. But the artistic endeavors don't end here - I like how the game tells its story with a nonlinear, somewhat abstract narrative, that leave many things to the player's interpretation. I did not understand everything, and that's a good sign for me - it means it was not digested for me, and I'll probably have to play again and pay more attention on what's going on. Also, the way the characters are built and depicted is very charming, and many people might like the fact that many characters are bugs with no defined genre (many others are clearly 'girls' or 'boys' but it really doesn't matter).
In general, Hollow Knight does a great job at mixing the classic "metroidvania" feel with added Legend of Zelda flavours (the way you unlock character upgrades is very Zelda-ish, and also the characters feel like they could be around Hyrule), with some platforming and combat reminiscent of Megaman X/ Zero, and of course, the obligatory Souls-esque death/currency dynamics. And yes, this game can be brutally hard sometimes. I also could draw a parallel to Hyper Light Drifter, in that both games took a step beyond in their respective "retro" genres, and came with something completely new.
tl;dr just buy at full price.

+Hollow Knight is awesome, definitely not what I expected from watching the previews and reading some of the reviews. The games takes you on a Dark Souls-esque journey of being a lone wanderer with no apparently purpose in the beginning, blindly feeling your way out through a once proud kingdom brought down to nothing but memories and dust. When I say Dark Souls-esque, I really only mean the story.
+The game feels more like a classic metroidvania much in the way Ori and the Blind Forest had it's great exploration. There's tons of unlocks to discovers, collectables galore, the map is enormous and there's little secrets strewn through out the entire game including different endings. I've seen a lot of complaints about the game's difficulty but for the parts that really beat you down and take you by surprise, the game is very VERY forgiving and provides you a second chance without any backtracking or fighting your way to the boss. Even for normal boss fights and events, there's checkpoints throughout the game in convenient locations if you explore and find those little nooks and crannies they're hiding in.
+The characters of Hollow Knight have a lot of heart, be them money grubbing merchants or would-be warriors looking for glory and fortune while the story ranges from cute light-hearted comedy to dark and even disturbing moments that might make your skin crawl (when you get to Deepnest, you 'll know what I mean). Don't be fooled by the simple art style of Hollow Knight, there's a lot of depth strewn through out the game that will make you ask 'Wow, what happened here? I wonder what that is?'. The locales and atmosphere of the game tell a story in itself.
+The sound design of Hollow Knight is pretty fantastic, I found myself looking up the OST ever since I arrived to the first area. The music for the zones is usually very somber for the most part, but the beat picks up quick when something is just about to go down. The ambient noise in a lot of a zones really sets the mood for what you're going to expect, from the rustling of trees and chirpy creatures in the foresty zones to the click-clack of unseen creepy crawlies all around you in some dark abyss. You can tell they put a lot of love into immersing you into the area you're exploring and just loved it.
-Some places have a couple of unfair pitfalls that you wouldn't know to avoid before getting hit blindsided by them which I found to be kind of annoying. Hollow Knight does a good job for the most part of sampling you what kind of challenges to expect before plunging into a new area but occasionally it throws you a curve ball and you pay for it. Most of these are pitfalls that you accidently fall into, not really fatal (spikes and falls only take one health point and then set you somewhere safe) but it was more irritating than challenging.
-There were a few mechanical problems with the game, I would experience slowdowns and even stumbled onto a bug that made a boss invincible until I reset the game but these slow downs were few and far between and everything seemed to resolve itself once things got rebooted.
Overall, I'd give Hollow Knight a solid 8.5 to 9.0 out of 10.0. I'd highly recommend you try it out for yourself, I put well over 20 hours into it my first couple of days and got hooked instantly. If you love dark and somber metroidvanias, you'll love Hollow Knight.

Originally I hesitated in purchasing this game due to the disappointment that was AC III.  It seemed like the culmination of everything I hated about the previous franchises, which was in fact, sailing ships around and a lack of grand old cities.  As a fan of the Ezio storyline, entering a world where you primarily sailed a ship around and explored small outposts on small islands seemed like a dramatic turn for the worse.  I could not have been more wrong.
The ship mechanics and execution are incredible.  Whether your simply sailing around listening to your crew sing sea shanties or engaging enemy ships in combat in an effort to board them and steal their supplies for your own gain, you are never bored while on your ship.  The ocean and all weather patterns, including hurricanes, are rendered beautifully.  The combat noises and graphical effects are downright immersive.  Never before did I think ship sailing could be more fun.  If you were looking for nothing more than a fun pirate game I can whole heartedly recommend this title.
The storyline and voice acting is another strong point of this game.  Not only is the animation done really well, but the tasks they have for you and characters you meet make this game top notch when it comes to single player experience.  Could some of the missions use improvement?  Of course.  Not every game is going to offer a completely perfect experience.  But those few missions with tedious exercises are made up for with the rest of the story.
This game has great value and I would recommend it to anybody looking for a new, good single player story, even at the full price.  But if you see this game go on sale for less than $20 like it did in the 2014 summer sale, jump on it immediately.

I hadn't played a metroidvania in a very long time, after playing Momodora: Reviere Under the moonlight a little over a month before I was looking for another game with a similar mood and story delivery.
This game delivered and it delivered everything;
The controls and tight and responsive which is important as the combat requires being active and striking openings at the right time. The combat difficulty is medium to high. Regular enemies can catch you off guard but if you learn to read their tells it becomes easy to keep them at bay.
Boss fights are more about reading tells and less about strick patterns and some bosses require a bit of learning to find the way to full take advantage of their openings.
I am not too big on jumping puzzles but the ones in this have been good for the most part, even the area deemed the hardest in the game I found very enjoyable but still very challenging.
The game does a very good job of painting the mood with very good music that carries the tone well all the way through. The story is told by peicing together bits of lore and NPC dialgoue which I find is very well done expesically for a game that encourages you to explore the world. The way maps are handled I think also gives you a clear objective each time you enter a new area and along the way you will run into hiddne secrets and interesting bits of story.
The characters are very good and while not all may have massive impacts they all feel like they are people just living within the world.
The art is one of the strongest parts of this game the unque style and the choice of using bugs I think was a great direction in crafting this game's own unique visual and audio style.
This is a definite recommendation especially if you like games with some exploration, metroidvania and abstract story telling that leads you into it slowly at your own pace.

Challenging, intuitive and absolutely gorgeous, this game puts a Dark Souls-style spin on the metroidvania genre in terms of atmosphere, style and oftentimes difficulty. Don't let the cute bugs deceive you; this game is pretty hardcore.
Aside from the backtracking and areas being unreachable without certain upgrades (it is true to the genre, after all), gameplay is fresh and deeply engrossing. Do I wish there were more benches after dying to the same boss several times and having to hack and slash my way back? Yes. Am I bad at these kinds of games and shouldn't really complain? Debatable, since I keep blaming myself for dying and not the game—which is probably the intended effect. At any rate the controls feel nice (albeit wonky at first) and you generally have a good feel for where to direct yourself. Takes some getting used to but it pays off.
Outside of the gameplay itself, the sound design is flawless and the music gradually progresses from oppressively dark ambient chillers to lush ballads and melodies that are at once similar to each other and altogether fresh and new between areas.
This is an incredibly solid and satifying game, and I highly recommend it.

Graphics are awesome, soundtrack is excellent, story is intriguing. But I'm mad at the game, because I'm being childish. After visiting a place called "White Palace", I throw my controller away, no kidding. Now trying to continue with my back-up controller. If you don't mind me being childish, I'd like to whine about it a little bit, before proceeding further.
Seriously though, that place, the "White Palace" turned the whole experience to a sour one for me. All the good feelings I had about the game suddenly vanished. Maybe it's the purpose of that place? Drain you of your soul and hope? Anyway enough rambling about that part of the game, but be warned. I mean I'm not great at these games, but not too bad either. I played and finished Super Meat Boy, and didn't have this much frustration. Because SMB is designed like that; you accept death as a part of the game. It is somewhat the same over here, but as you are progressing through the game, you encounter a few jumping puzzles here, and timing puzzles there, and sometimes a combination of both. But the "White Palace"?... I avoided stuff like IWBTG (I Wanna Be The Guy) and alike, and this "White Palace" feels like it was designed by developers from those games. Pure frustration (for me anyway, maybe you'll find it easy when you arrive there).
Now that the whining is over, as I've said, graphics are awesome. Game kept surprising me by throwing more and more areas, with new enemies and such. Everything is drawn nicely, and some of the effects are used cleverly. Soundtrack gets a prize from me, because it has been a long while I've enjoyed OST of a game this much. It is so good, I'd recommend you to get it with OST, in fact, if you are one of those people who gets good game OSTs. Some places are very creepy even for a 2D game, with sound effects, sounds, and graphics all working together... just amazing.
Story is... well you are thrown into the game with no explanation. You get information bit by bit, and even though what you get is so little, the atmosphere created by the graphics and soundtrack kinda get you into a mood where even a small bit is enough for you to keep looking for more. So far I haven't finished the game, and depending on how you play (if you are worse than me) you'll still have a good amount of 20h+ of playtime I think. Some NPCs you get to care for some reason... I don't know why.
Right now, even though a controller is recommended, my controller (the one that hasn't turned into two seperate HTC Vive controllers "magically" after hitting a wall) is not properly recognized. As far as any game goes, this controller acts like an XBox controller (I think), it is a Logitech F710 Wireless Gamepad, and triggers are not working. Additionally, left and right thumb buttons register as left and right shoulder buttons. I don't know what's up with that, but it is seriously annoying. BUT, good thing is, you can remap some of your Gamepad buttons. That's so cool, being able to remap your Gamepad buttons, and a bit surprising as well. More games need to do this. Anyway, gamepad, shoulder, trigger, bla bla... you get the point. Didn't try Keyboard, but I think I'll get a hand-cramp trying to play this game with a Keyboard I think. Not sure though.
Now, the gameplay... Why do I put this at the end? Because I think it is the least important part of the game, funnily enough. The other parts of the game is just excellent (apart from "White Palace"), so even a passable rating on gameplay would suffice. However, it is more than a passable rating. You get currency to buy stuff, get stronger, equip "traits", etc... there is a good amount of character customization in my opinion, and a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of movement skills. This is a metroidvania in a way, the last good one I played was called "Axiom Verge". So you see something that you cannot reach way too often, because backtracking is a natural part of games like these. That's why I hate the "White Palace" that much, the entire game turns into a death trap in there, which is so alien to what you've been playing so far. Lots of places to explore, ♥♥♥♥♥on of hidden stuff to find. I'm kinda amazed with the amount of content to be honest.
Back to the gameplay topic, the movement is... well I'm not great at these games, I'm mediocore at best. It is very responsive, but attacking can get a little bit tedious, Even after this many hours, I keep swinging towards the wrong direction way too often. Maybe I'm very used to a setting like "Binding of Isaac". If I could, I'd use a setting where 4 buttons on the right or the other stick was used for attack direction to be honest (but I'd need to grow another finger or two to use the other functions, if that was the case...). Also, boss battles are epic. There are some hard-mode fights as well (as I call them) and those can get a little bit... annoying though. One mistake and all goes to hell. I've never played a "platformer" like this where boss battles can get this hard to be honest. But still as epic as ♥♥♥♥.
Overall... You like games like Metroid, and perhaps even heard of and played a recent game called Axiom Verge as well? As far as exploration goes, the game feels like those. Story is intriguing, Graphics and soundtrack are enchanting. Gameplay is solid. Boss battles are epic. If this is a genre you enjoy, you MUST get this. But seriously, ♥♥♥♥ that "White Palace".

I only played this game for 2 hours, and it was only survival mode.
But I don't need to play it any further to know that this game is ♥♥♥♥ing fun and akin to Serious Sam and other classic titles of the 90's. It's real effin colorful too and forgoes the realistic black and brown plague of recent ''trouble in a Middle-Eastern town'' shooters. Or, god forbid, the blue hue of Battlefield 3, which I just don't get.
Actually, I'll update this later when I fully get to the game, but I already know it's gonna be awesome. I'm excited enough for it that I'll recommend it based on first impressions alone.
------
edit- I was right. It pretty much IS ''Serious Sam with Lo Wang'', the basic level progression is moving forward, encountering several enemies you have to take out, and proceeding with story scenes thrown here and there in the middle or towards the end of the level. Story scenes are kept succinct, obviously.
One thing this game has that Serious Sam (or any other FPS title) doesn't have is fleshed out melee mechanics. Any other title and the melee weapon is merely a last resort for when you run out of ammo; ♥♥♥♥♥♥, slow, low damage output, and unwanted. Shadow Warrior made it so that your melee is versatile and preferable to long-range weapons. Don't get me wrong, sticky bombs on a crossbow and firing off 6 shotgun shells simultaneously is fun, but you have a dash that lets you get up to your enemies really quickly. You also have a sword technique to impale, to spin 360 degrees and clear out people around you, and to release a long range energy burst. Coupled with your healing technique you'll be dashing into enemies and clearing out waves, pulling back to heal (4 second heal time) and quickly rushing back in.
In fact, I think its fair to say that the developers wanted you to mainly stick to your sword, since theres a level-up system that requires cash, and you might wanna forego buying ammo for weapons to scrougne up the funds to add bombs to your crossbow or to have auto-fire on your revolver. Which means that you'll only ever use your guns when you have the ammo to spare, to take out those annoying flying enemies, or when facing the larger enemies that really damage you if you stay close to them for long.
Hell, I'll call this a first person hack and slash, or a FPS title-First Person Slicer. Witty, I know. There's nothing wrong with the guns, and the upgrades are REALLY worth it and make them incredibly fun. But the attention paid to melee makes this game really unique, and there's something satisfying about having your screen fill with blood and seeing a crowd of ghoulish faces up close rather than taking them out from afar. Your slashes and dashes are arguably more enjoyable than killing people from 15 feet away.
I guess there are some downsides. Weapons are found as you progress with the game, rather than pickups in levels. So you don't get to enjoy the flamethrower until you're deeper into the game. Also, some enemy variety in attack patterns would make combat a little more tactical and less of a 'mow♥♥♥♥♥♥down' fest. There's the aformentioned bomb enemy, and those flying dudes that become a target range. But it still feels like there could've been more. Let me see...the environments and enemies look good, but some of the character models in cut scenes look a little low-tier, but its an FPS title so who cares. When I'm finding myself trying to pick negatives rather than them coming immediately to mind that means its a good game.

I went into Hollow Knight without many expectations. I assumed it was just going to be an average indie metroidvania and that I would probably get some mild enjoyment out of playing it. However, I'm very happy to admit how wrong I was in my first assumptions about this game. I can confidently say Hollow Knight is one of the best games I've played in years, and maybe one of the best I've ever played in general.
Hollow Knight is a beautiful, sprawling metroidvania that draws you in as soon as you begin with its difficulty and atmosphere that is truly unique. It is painstakingly hand-drawn with meticulous detail in every single area, along with a beautiful musical composition to boot, and it only gets better from zone to zone. From the very beginning you can quickly tell just how much love, time, and work went into making sure that every bit of the game is nearly flawless.
The story of Hollow Knight is told in a similar way to Dark Souls. Much of the lore of the world is hidden and obscured in item and equippables text with only occasional dialogue prompts. If you're looking for something very rich in story, this game definitely has it, but be prepared to work for it.
For the majority of people though, the factor to draw you in will be the gameplay itself. Prepare to be lost, prepare to die, prepare to adventure, and prepare to learn the world like the back of your hand. I have not played a game that ever compares to this in regards to just how vast and daunting the entire world feels. I would even go as far as to say it emulates that feeling and execution of what a metroidvania is as a whole better than either Metroid or Castlevania ever did. It is easily the best metroidvania I have ever played and I can't stress that enough. Whether you just enjoy boss slaying, adventuring and exploring, trying to find every secret (and there is a LOT of secrets in this game), or taking your time and learning every piece of lore to do with the world, this game is a master in it all.
Prepare to recieve your value for your money as well, because Hollow Knight is absolutely filled to the brim with content to complete. My first playthrough in which I 100% completed the game without any guide was 36 hours, to put it into perspective. Every single minute you spend will feel worth it too since there's always more to complete. Nothing at all in Hollow Knight feels like it's padded out content either; every single thing you do in this game will have a purpose. You can easily expect to get a minimum of about 20 hours worth of content for your money even if you did not set out to collect every item or defeat every boss.
If you want something that feels truly unique, has stunningly beautiful art and music, has tight controls, will give you a minimum of 20 hours of play time to complete, and so much more, buy Hollow Knight right now. This is a game that is an instant classic and one of the best I've ever played. My only regret in purchasing this game is that I can't play it all over again for the very first time, and I can guarantee you'll feel the same.

"No mind to think. No will to break. No voice to cry suffering. Born of god and Void."
Quite possibly my most favorite game of the year so far, Hollow Knight is simutaneously a lovely and hideous game that demands no prisoner but only souls. For a game that has the same cryptic writing and story delivering style of From Software's Souls series, it managed to break my heart not once but at least four times thanks to the ugly conclusions of various sidequests that made me feel like a hero at first. If you need to cut deep to open a path, so be it, just don't forget that you're not alone in this hellhole, and always expect the worst if you happen to care about... someone particularly.
Contributing to the emotional impact is the lovely hand drawn artstyle where even the most hideous creatures can look fluffy and cute while the divine ones can turn into monsters in a blink of an eye. Okay that's probably an exaggaration but the diversity and quality here is phenomenal, every single area in Hollow Knight has a distinct theme that makes the game itself a treat to look at and traverse through, from the fascinating greenhouse of death in Greenpath, the cold heart of royal ♥♥♥♥ery in City of Tears, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t claustrophobic "WHY IS THIS PLACE SO NARROW AND WHERE'S THE ♥♥♥♥ING LIGHT" feeling in Deepnest, or... yeah, that White Palace. Visual cues make sure you're never lost, from pieces of paper that lead you to the mapmaker, directional signs with an image of a bench or tram on it, or even some paths suddenly have visual distinct from other areas grow near it. Hollow Knight also doesn't lack melancholic tunes that sometimes make you feel hopeless and furious, but my most favorite moments must be that relief feeling when I hear Cornifer's humming across an area: We're heading the right way! We don't need to wander aimlessly anymore!
Smartly interconnected levels make backtracking less a chore and more meaningful, since you can easily pass on any path that you can't quite reach yet and come back later with any mobility ability. Any unexplored path, any unopened door, any dark deep hole can always contain something that's worth risking our lives for, even discovering a shortcut back to previous ares feels like a true accomplishment. Hollow Knight encourages you to explore as much as you want, how quick and far you progress throughout the game really depends on your own pace. Of course, there are some definitive narrative structure that needs you to be in a specific place to trigger and can feel scripted, but the rest of the game allows you to go wherever you want, do what you feel like you want to first, Metroidvania and Souls-style.
Control can be iffy at times with overly sensitive strafing but it doesn't take much time to get used to it. Combat relies on the visceral feel rather than stylish combos, the charms make up for lack of equipments by giving you different utility, defensive or offensive effects. The game's difficulty is on par with your typical Dark Souls game, you don't have heath bar and your "health mask" depletes as the amount of damage taken, every weak monster can kill you if you're not careful, every boss can make you bang your head against wall, but they all have telegraphed moves that can be used against themselves.
I still believe that Radiance was designed by Satan.
Overall if you don't mind a lot of bugs (( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)), don't mind to be heartbroken, don't hate the map system, don't mind backtracking, and deeply a masochist, then you would be foolish to pass on Hollow Knight. Science hasn't proved that playing this game will turn you hollow or not, but I can guarantee that 22 hours into the game made my skin thicker and controller grew some scars that I didn't regret giving it.

By far the most gripping game of 2017 for me. This metroidvania gets everything right (apart from 1 small gripe), and it trully a masterpiece and then accomplished by such a small team is a great accomplishment of its own. Well done!
I'm a sucker for great platformers, metroidvanias especially, and this one foots the bill perfectly. Let me bring out some of the key points on why you should own this game and spend 30+ hours on it:
- Extremely responsive and smooth controls. Movements are fluid, jumping precise and allows you to master the controls. Combat is a joy, no matter at which point, just starting or by the time you are a seasoned pro. Any misses, failures trully feel like your own mistakes and not the fault of the game.
- Gradual introduction even without hand holding. I love how the game slowly ramps up at the start, giving you a chance to pick up all the essentials, spikes the difficulty at times to challange you and make you improve youreslf, but remains fair at all stages of the game. It also flows naturally, and instructions are not shoved down your throat but allowed to be discovered on your own if you explore.
- Git gud factor is extremely fair. Sure you will hit obstacles that will whoop your♥♥♥♥♥ That's great! You will come back analyze the patterns, learn to be more evasive, make progress, almost make it next time. Be encouraged as you progress and feel more confident in your skills. Sometimes you'll be super outclassed. That's ok too! You'll come back when your skills and abilities are a better match for the boss that's a thorn in your butt.
- Exploration is an experience of its own. Discovery is extremely rewarding, weather it be the tracing the map while getting to know the new area, finding out the secret nooks to find items you can sell for much needed cash or new abilities. In a classic metroidvania style you will see many paths you can't yet take and know new movement abilities will open up those for you later.
- Backtracking does not feel a chore (at least not to me). Sure, you will be doing those a lot at times, but they don't feel too cumbersome. If anything I felt excited retracing the steps back to reach the spot I couldn't take before but now I know I would be able to. And you'll be pleasently surprised how you will simply breeze through the areas given how much more powerful you are by then.
- Hand drawn arts, attention to detail and accompanied music are astounding. The world comes to life, and it's worthy of desktop backgrounds on many occasions. If you stop for a breather you can notice a lot of interesting details and little quirks which are a great escape from the otherwise gloomy world. I bought the OST separately because I enjoyed the music so much, it perfectly fits the game and many of its sections, especially boss fights.
- Abilities you can acquire are varied and well thought of. None of them feel super novel, but they all fit right into a metroidvania game. Aside from movement abilities and power upgrades, you also get to use utility charms that you wear to give you abilities that have pros and cons, which introduce an element of strategies that is extremely fun to discover. Certain charms makes your exploration easier, while others help deal with particular bosses, give you health padding, extend your reach etc.
- The game is huge. I did not expect this much content at all. And I want more. Any DLCs they release on this I'd just go shut up and take my money. None of the areas feel repetitive, and they all provide unique challanges in their own, styled for the theme of the area. None of them detract from the experience IMHO, only enhance it.
- Story is shrouded in a bit of mystery with letting you the player fill in the gaps. If you are keen on exploring you can pick up a lot of lore to learn the background of it all. Even if you are not, it won't leave you disappointed. However, this game is not like Ori in a sense that the story is first and foremost element of the game.
- Speaking of Ori, this game has a great combination of combat and platforming, leaning more on combat, where Ori was mostly focused on platforming with some combat mixed in but not nearly as refined as here.
Ok sure, you love the game so much, are there any negatives? Flaws?
A few. The difficulty can be offputting at times, especially for new comers to the genre. It is supposed to be a challange. As you get better you get further motivated to go back and try again. When you see how close you got to actually winning it can be a great confidence boost.
There are two particular areas in late game that are extremely unforgiving. One in terms of platforming the other is just sheer insanity (you'll know what I'm talking about when you reach them). My jaw dropped when I saw them and will wavered. I thought it was impossible. I'll just say that after enough git gud (about 83h total of game play) I finished the game including those 2 sections in steel heart mode (you can't die not even once all game and need to complete 100% of the game). You will get better you will triumph, you will feel invincible once you beat them. Could they have relaxed the difficulty on those? Probably just a tad bit. But they are completely optional (unless you are after 100% but then again if you are you should have a challange) so I don't consider it a flaw really.
There are a few bugs here and there. They range from super rare minor annoyance to still super rare pain in the butt. None of them are worth mentioning in particular, and all are solvable by just restarting if they do happen. The devs are super supportive and working hard to fix all of them as they are identified.
The performance issues were never really a problem for me, but others have reported them. Also judging by the forums most of them are resolved now so even if you don't have a top rig (mine is about 2 years old) you shouldn't have any concerns.
Edit: I've revisited the game with the new content in and oh boy I had a blast. Again... And all the content updates fit in the game really well, and best of all free?! I'd gladly pay for all of them (within reason), but this is just icing on the cake.

I'm going to start this review by saying this game is amazing.
It's like Dark Souls and Metroid had a baby and its baby was successful.
What this game does superbly:
+Combat. It is top tier, you can reflect sword strikes and other attacks, it sounds amazing when you do this.
+Hitboxes. These are actually fair and close. This is Dark Souls 3 level of hitbox pronz.
+Exploration. They don't hand feed you the map, you actually have to go out, discover and explore all the areas.
+Non-Linear. After you beat the 1st required area, they let you run loose and go wherever you want. Since it is Metroidvania you will need to backtrack in order to get to places you could not earlier.
+Powerups. There are a wide variety of powerups. Sword skills, "soul skills", abilities, and charms are delivered to you at regular intervals throughout the game.
+Charms. These augment your character in various ways. While 4 are similiar, this still leaves 32 distinct charms to augment your character with.
+Story. This is one of the best stories I've encountered in a game in a long time. This is up there with Bastion/Transistor/Undertale.
+Art. The art is fantastic in this game. For the most part, every section, every room, every hallways all is individual and distinctly different art. There appears to be little to no copy-pasting of the enviornment.
+Runs Efficiently. My computer is a potato and this game ran fantastic on it. The only minor drops occurred in the "City of Tears" due to the raining particle effects. The game is aware that you may face drops in this area, so places you fight bosses/large amounts of enemies have reduced particle effects which cuts out frame drops. This is good design.
+Soundtrack. Usually I have youtube or podcasts open in the background when I play games. Not this game, the greatness of the soundtrack forced me to keep my ears open while playing.
+Content. This game gives you more content for $15 than most new $60 titles give you nowadays. Why is it that Indie Studios are delivering more on content for less money than AAA titles do with AAA studio budgets. I'm at nearly 40 hours in this game and I've 100% it. And I'm going in for a second run. And they're releasing a new playable character with new story in the coming months. How can this studio be so good?
Common Criticisms:
-The game is a "walking simulator". Taking this complaint with any grain of salt is silly considering this is a Metroidvania game. The entire point is having to backtrack to get to places you couldn't reach before. The game is even considerate and gives you fast travel stations.
-The game is "2hard5me". Considering this is a game that has taken ideas from such titles as the Dark Souls series, of course it is going to be hard. Maybe I'm just good at the game but the only parts that gave me trouble were the optional "Dream Bosses" and the optional "White Palace". Both of these were the hardest parts of the game, however they were optional.
You're reading this review when you should be buying this masterpiece of a game, hurry up.

Tower Defense is a divisive genre. On one hand there is strategy involved in the placement of towers and proper management of limited resources; on the other, the gameplay aspects are usually boring.  Dungeon Defenders attempts to take the formula and mix in more RPG elements such as leveling, buying/finding/equipping gear, having multiple unique character types, and actually being able to fight in the game while you're managing towers. It makes Tower Defense more engaging and addictive, but can easily cause issues with balance. Beating a level will not always be dependent on skill, but on stats as well. This leads to the eventual grinding for gear or levels in order to tackle the toughest of stages.
However, that is hardly a true downside because ultimately that end-game content is meant for time-wasting for those who desire it (and paid for it). For the average gamer with a passing interest, I'm sure hours of fun can still be had at a rather cheap price, especially with friends or strangers in multiplayer.

+Story. This is one of the best stories I've encountered in a game in a long time. This is up there with Bastion/Transistor/Undertale.
+Art. The art is fantastic in this game. For the most part, every section, every room, every hallways all is individual and distinctly different art. There appears to be little to no copy-pasting of the enviornment.
+Runs Efficiently. My computer is a potato and this game ran fantastic on it. The only minor drops occurred in the "City of Tears" due to the raining particle effects. The game is aware that you may face drops in this area, so places you fight bosses/large amounts of enemies have reduced particle effects which cuts out frame drops. This is good design.
+Soundtrack. Usually I have youtube or podcasts open in the background when I play games. Not this game, the greatness of the soundtrack forced me to keep my ears open while playing.
+Content. This game gives you more content for $15 than most new $60 titles give you nowadays. Why is it that Indie Studios are delivering more on content for less money than AAA titles do with AAA studio budgets. I'm at nearly 40 hours in this game and I've 100% it. And I'm going in for a second run. And they're releasing a new playable character with new story in the coming months. How can this studio be so good?
Common Criticisms:
-The game is a "walking simulator". Taking this complaint with any grain of salt is silly considering this is a Metroidvania game. The entire point is having to backtrack to get to places you couldn't reach before. The game is even considerate and gives you fast travel stations.
-The game is "2hard5me". Considering this is a game that has taken ideas from such titles as the Dark Souls series, of course it is going to be hard. Maybe I'm just good at the game but the only parts that gave me trouble were the optional "Dream Bosses" and the optional "White Palace". Both of these were the hardest parts of the game, however they were optional.
You're reading this review when you should be buying this masterpiece of a game, hurry up.

So, it controls much like any first person exploration game, WASD to move, mouse to look around, click to interact, everything checks out so far. But here's the twist. Anything the narrator says you to do is all up to you. I won't spoil too much, but basically it's all up to you. The game has many endings to discover.

I bought this expecting an entertaining but shallow FPS. Instead, I got a surprisingly solid storyline with GREAT action.
The swordplay is so satisfying that I ended up using the sword 95 percent of the time, except during boss fights and when fighting certain monsters. There are a bunch of different moves you can do. They are executed via easy-to-remember combos which involve hitting two directional keys and then the left or right mouse button.
Another thing which makes the sword fighting even better is the variation in enemy types. Each requires a different tactic to kill them. Once you get the hang of it, the battles in the game become very fluid as you dart around killing demons with all of these different moves.
There are slight RPG elements present. They allow you to customize Lo Wang's different powers, skills and abilities.
This game would be worth playing even if the sword fighting was the only good thing about it. But you also get a good plot and excellent level design. There was not one area in the game which became tedious or annoying. I was not stuck trying to progress at any point.
The game is quite long for a modern FPS. It took me 13 hours on normal difficulty. I only died maybe ten to fifteen times, and like I said before I was not stuck or lost at any point.
Lo Wang isn't nearly as over the top in this game. Given the presence of an actual good plot, I prefer it that way. That being said, there is still a good amount of humor in the game.
There are a lot of secrets in the game too. Keep and eye out for fortune cookies and retro areas!

It's good. Would be an even more fun game if it could be played as intended. Instead, you have all manner of hackers and cheats running rampant on the Ranked servers (the Open servers don't even pretend to enforce the rules) to the point that you literally can't have a game without someone tainted by illegitimate play joining, be it someone who hacks or has been given items/mana by someone who does.
In addition, individual hosts can kick (read: ban) players from their game at any time, which they can and will do frequently and without warning, reason, or provocation. You can reasonably expect to be kicked from games multiple times per play session, and never know why.
That said, both issues do not exist if you play primarily solo, with friends, or as a host. It's a pretty solid game that is still supported by a dev team, has community events on a regular basis, and generally pretty fun to play. There are a large variety of maps, heroes, and ways to play. Early, mid, and late game progression all play completely differently from one another, and they're all worth experiencing in my opinion.
I've been told the DLC system is not great, but I personally picked it up with all DLC from the Humble Bundle. Many maps and the "Nightmare" difficulty require DLC to start from your own Tavern, but all of them (except the Eternia Shards maps) can be played without owning the DLC. All of the most recent updates (and all future updates) are free, and you don't need any DLC to fully enjoy the game if you play with a friend who has it (except the Eternia Shards maps).
All heroes besides the base four are DLC. Summoner and EV are best for players who enjoy building, while Jester and Barbarian are best for players who enjoy fighting. EV can also be an extremely effective fighter if properly equipped, and Jester can be an exceedingly potent (albeit clumsy) builder. Summoner is worthless for fighting (although he can be very useful mid-wave), and Barbarian literally cannot build. The gender-swapped heroes are minor side-grades - none of them are must-have, although they can be useful if available. Builders are more useful for people playing solo (because the maps quickly become too big to handle without significant defenses), whereas fighters are more useful for people playing in groups (because the number of useful builders is limited, but fighters are always useful).

Stanley has been sitting in his office for quiet some time, deliberately and patienlty pressing specific buttons for the review of this game called The Stanley Parable. S-t-a-n-l-e-y. What a ridiculous name, especially for a videogame! Suddenly a realisation came - Steam was empty. Not a single of Stanley's many friends was online, the whole community hub thing was dead. "Number of players in games - 0", declared the main page. At that very moment, Stanley feld something was very wrong here... But the buttons kept appearing on the screen, review had to be finished, Stanley was neither in position nor in right to oppose the demand. Who was he, after all? Stanley, a simple man, playing this videogame and writing a review about it afterwards in order to show his friends he's not a primitive dungeon dweller, silly achievement hunter, oh no! He, Stanley, perceives videogames as art, reflects upon choices made within and bravely faces any consequences. His friends, they always liked that about him... But were there any friends after all? Emptiness. Buttons were still on the screen. Who needs this review, who's even going to read it? Stanley leapt out of his chair, puzzled, desperate, looking back at all the years of sitting in this thrice damned room, pressing these countless buttons for reviews no one read, of games no one played. Did they ever exist? Perhaps only an illusion of a videogame, a reflection of the starry sky in the surface of a pond.
He already knew what was happening when a soft, painfully familiar voice whispered out of the darkness:
"This is a story of a man named Stanley."
Stanley clumsily collapsed.

Don't look at the metascore for this one. This  is an old-school shooter with tight controls, satisfying gameplay, and a fantastic-looking environment. It's also full of crude humor and general oldschool machoness. Think Serious Sam or Duke Nukem, but with a lot more melee options. The gameplay is tight, you move fast, the enemies strafe and dodge your fire. The environments are detailed and feel realistic (as opposed to Seriouis Sam, where alleys look like football stadiums). The game is linear, but there are plenty of hidden gems and secrets to be found. It's also full of references to old school shooters.
This game is gorgeous, even on low settings. But if you want higher fidelity you'd have to add a bit of heat to your graphics cards.
Sometimes the enemies feel a bit repetitive or even bullet-spongey. The characters are maybe a bit too macho to be likeable, the same way that Bulletstorm's characters didn't really appeal to me.

I highly recommend this game. Before it came out I was pretty worried about it. Mainly the price and the lack of 3D realms plus they didn't exactly lead an encouraging ad campaign. But the price was sorted out by good deals everywhere within a month of its release. I picked it up for 20 bucks on the humble store and it came with a DRM free copy. And after i got to play through it turned out to be one of my favorite games of 2013.
To start off. This is NOT a straight reboot like Serious Sam 3 or the new Rise of the Triad. Flying Wild Hog (Dev) really put their own spin on the game. The game has the sort of FPS\RPG aspect going on. With abilities and powers. as well you can upgrade your weapons to give them more damage output and if you have a bit of cash stored up you can upgrade them to have a secondary fire which can really change the way you use that weapon.
The thing that really caught me off guard about the game and what really made it stand out to me were the characters and story. Hoji was funny and likeable and Lo Wang was a real character now instead of a joke like in the original. (Not to bag on Shadow Warrior.)
The story that you follow is actually prety interesting too. As far as video games go at least. without being 'spoilery', I must say. The way the story goes toward the end will suprise you. They break off from the silly part of the game at the end there to bring you a real conclusion to the story. And I think the ending alone will always make this game stand out to me.
To wrap things up. The gameplay itself is as fun and challenging as you would want and with the skills, powers and upgrades you can take many different approaches to the game and play your own way.
Incredibly funny game which will also challenge your perception on what video games are in general. I used it in part to explain to a friend the art of compromise with authority.

A nice blend of the classic fast-paced FPS formula (taking inspiration from Serious Sam and Quake in equal measure) with modern touches like checkpointing (quicksaving is still an option!) and weapon upgrades. What sets this game apart is its unique melee/combo-based combat system--the katana is probably the most effective weapon in the game thanks to its unlockable special attacks. However, this leads to the various guns in the game feeling rather underpowered, particularly on the higher difficulty levels where enemies almost become bullet-sponges.
Aside from that quibble, however, it's tough not to recommend this game for ~20 hours of freewheeling fun. Excellent production values and an above-average story with genuinely entertaining characters are icing on the cake. Also check out Hard Reset, from the same developer, for a different "modern classic FPS" experience with less of a melee focus.

Before I start my review, I would like to say that I'm a fanboy of the AC series so I may overlook issues with the game.
Story:
- Likeable personality for the protagonist
- Interesting and fleshed out side characters that you will get attached to.
Mechanics:
- Ship-Ship fighting mechanics are very enjoyable and sometimes actually quite challenging
- Melee fighting mechanics were slightly changed in this game and were not as enjoyable as it was in AC3 (not as satisfying combos)
- Range fighting is much better with the use of multiple pistols, berserk/sleep/rope darts.
- The guards AI is not very much different from the previous games (I do like the introduction of guards with a long range rifle on guard towers).
- Stealth is much improved by the addition of stalking zones.
Conclusion:
I am enjoying this game quite a lot and would definitely recommend it to fans of the series as well as players who are new to the franchise.

This is the first time in which I've wished I could leave just an "OK" review. This game does not deserve an overwhelmingly positive score, but I do not think I'd necassarily say the game is
. I think it lies just in the middle. The game is and isn't a MOBA. By definition a MOBA is a MULTIPLAYER ONLINE BATTLE ARENA, which sums up what this game is to a tee. However, this game is more of a compilation of DotA, LoL, and HotS with many apsects of those
games stripped away.
The game very blatantly takes things from the afforementioned games, but reuses those things in a new and unique, easy-to-learn way. But perhaps the things stripped away to make this game was just too much. I feel like I'm playing just another MOBA but it's way too simple. You just go into a circle and cast abilities on each other. There is no real learning curve, no skill builds, no items... It's just learn what your characters do, and go lay the smackdown on some fools.
And that's fun the first few times, but gets old really fast, especially since all of the characters are kind of just rebrands of each other. Your left mouse click is an attack. Your right click is a stronger attack that might have some casting time. Your Q is a counter attack. Your space bar is for mobilty or a shield depending on if you're playing a support or core role. Your E is generally the most diverse and unique ability. And that's that. Each of the heroes has that kind of general foundation.
One thing I didn't mention though about part of the abilties is the way they handle ultimates, they give you a strong abilty and a stronger ability. Each of the abilities uses up some energy that you gain over time from either hitting things or picking stuff up around the map and you get to make the choice of whether to use your strong ability to get an advantage over the enemy, or wait for your stronger ability and win the fight that way.
You might notice that I give this game points for being unique every time they do it, because I think being unique is good, but this game just isn't that unique. Like I said before, this game copies. This game even copies the bad♥♥♥♥♥♥that doesn't need to be in the game, such as loot crates. Hearthstone really started some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and I have had enough of it. It works for a goddamn digital card game, but now the loot crate system is in literally every ♥♥♥♥ing game and it needs to stop. IT'S TIME TO STOP. I don't need having microtransactions in your game be the norm. I don't need that to be the gimmick that keeps a game afloat. I want a game's content to be what keeps it going, not its ♥♥♥♥ing skins and that false sense of luck when you open something LEGENDARY. The♥♥♥♥♥♥is worthless and has no place being in the game. And especially not in this game in which all of the skins look exactly the same except legendaries have an epileptic glow. To me, it really feels like this game has skins just to have skins, which is exactly the thing I knew would happen right when I saw Todd Howard present his new Fallout game for iOS featuring loot crates with the same exact rarity rating from WoW.
Somehow this game managed to diversify itself by adding a pricetag, putting itself on a pedastal to look down on MOBA's and say "I'm not like you." No, this game is just like those games, but for people looking to get the bare minimum of the MOBA experience. If this game was free, I'd probably be more inclined to give it a positive review, because it would be just another MOBA clone, but with a unique twist just unique enough to be refreshing yet nostalgic. But if this game was free, it likely would not have any recognition. It's like that old wondorous age-old question. Would you rather have Harambe live, but be forgotten, or have him killed only to be the most famous gorilla of all time?

Stanley has been sitting in his office for quiet some time, deliberately and patienlty pressing specific buttons for the review of this game called The Stanley Parable. S-t-a-n-l-e-y. What a ridiculous name, especially for a videogame! Suddenly a realisation came - Steam was empty. Not a single of Stanley's many friends was online, the whole community hub thing was dead. "Number of players in games - 0", declared the main page. At that very moment, Stanley feld something was very wrong here... But the buttons kept appearing on the screen, review had to be finished, Stanley was neither in position nor in right to oppose the demand. Who was he, after all? Stanley, a simple man, playing this videogame and writing a review about it afterwards in order to show his friends he's not a primitive dungeon dweller, silly achievement hunter, oh no! He, Stanley, perceives videogames as art, reflects upon choices made within and bravely faces any consequences. His friends, they always liked that about him... But were there any friends after all? Emptiness. Buttons were still on the screen. Who needs this review, who's even going to read it? Stanley leapt out of his chair, puzzled, desperate, looking back at all the years of sitting in this thrice damned room, pressing these countless buttons for reviews no one read, of games no one played. Did they ever exist? Perhaps only an illusion of a videogame, a reflection of the starry sky in the surface of a pond.
He already knew what was happening when a soft, painfully familiar voice whispered out of the darkness:
"This is a story of a man named Stanley."
Stanley clumsily collapsed.

Well it's not as good as the trailers would tell you, but it's certainly not bad at all.
As usual the game looks great. I guess there's not much to add if you're familiar with the rest of the series.
Well, the combat. It's hasn't improved, infact, it changed a little bit for the worse; it's not as spectacular as it used to be and feels kind of clumsy to control. The good part is you can have up to 4 preloaded pistols, so at least thát helps. Either way, you really should use all your tools in this game, they're totally OP compared to the lack of fighting skills.
I guess it's because you play some stinking peasant turned pirate, rather than a trained assassin. Which is actually a nice change; being no part of either templar or assassin but getting in too deep to avoid the crossfire. The story does unfold quite nicely.
The new things in this game are obviously the ship battles, gimmick from the last game. Well, not too surprising since they went with a pirate theme. Most of the game is either at sea, or in ports. A lovely addition to the sea travel are the shanties; a few drunks singing a song makes the trip more enjoyable, so it pays off to search for a few.
The fun and yet frustrating part is boarding a ship to capture it. Somehow the controls suddenly go more wonky than usual when climbing the sails. Especially when there's a few waves moving the ship. And the decks always feel way too small with the amount of people getting in your way.
But most of the boardings look really cool and are fun to do for a while.
Then there's a whole new creature to hunt for; the Great White, and his nautical buddies.
Although whaling is basically just chucking spears at the beast untill it stops flopping, it's pretty cool.  And the sharks do put up quite a fight.
Oh, and another wonderful thing they added is; underwater levels. Because we all know how much people love underwater levels. They actually looks quite magical.
Outside of the Animus there's a few computers to hack, and obviously a less action-packed part of the story going on. Strangely enough you seem to be an Abstergo employeé this time around...
Although they really should've included all the DLC's if they wanted to ask such a high price for it, oh well, I bought it anyway when it was on a sale, I blame the pirate theme, ARRR.
I guess I can't complain, all'n all, it's an entertaining game, pretty much worth what I paid for it. This damn franchise tricks me into buying it anyway.

Hollow Knight is a free game. By "Free" I mean that the game promotes free thinking and free exploration. Aside form the beautiful art and music (as come to be expected of games like these) the level design is superb. Many times did I find myself in a spot where I was able to figure out a way around an obstacle clearly designed for a powerup I did not have yet, or an ability not yet unlocked.
The game is hard. Like, pretty hard. I mean that. People don't compare to dark souls just because of the revive mechanic. Lots of trial and error here. The game even has its own little optional "Star Road" type area where the platforming difficulty ramps up pretty hard.
I do not understand the negative reviews complaining about sloppy controls. The controls are as tight as you'd expect, with its own little mechanics peppered in. Jump height is measured by how long you hold the jump button, trajectory can be changed and halted instantly, etc.
All in all, this 15 dollar game gave me a 25 hour experience in ONE RUN and only with 92% completion. It's pretty great, and you shouldn't skip this gem. Hollow Knight is a wonderful game and you should definately buy it if you can.

Matthew then remembered he had played the Stanley Parable last night. The Stanley Parable had been played through in two hours, but it felt like eight. Matthew pondered the disturbing exposition of the narrator- the very narrator that was now speaking in his head.
Matthew became aware of the narrator speaking this dialogue and became very frightened.
"Am I going insane?" Matthew asked himself.
No, Matthew, you were always insane. And you can never escape this voice in your head, for I have always been here. The Stanley Parable simply gave me a voice, a definite form in your mind. But to avoid thinking about that, Matthew began writing a review of The Stanley Parable.
Ironically, the review took the same format as the narration in his head, and Matthew dutifully inscribed it all down as he had heard it. In fact, the text and inflection was the same, too. Perhaps Matthew really was going insane, or perhaps, since he and I are intrisically combined, his fear of insanity could be a sign a part of his foolish mind was holding on. Perhaps Matthew is not insane, perhaps he is simply infected- Infected by The Stanley Parable, such a unique and twisting game.
Matthew finally decided to not recommend the game.

Hollow Knight is a masterclass in both world and character design. The game starts out slowly but quickly unravels into a sprawling world full of diverse environments and unique characters. The bug motif leads to a lot of imaginative enemies and creatures packed full of personality, while even non-essential NPC characters with only a few lines of dialogue are a joy to interact with. I felt like I was being pulled in five directions at once while exploring Hollownest, constantly finding paths leading to entirely new areas of the world. Exploration comes naturally and even backtracking through areas with new abilities is a pleasure as the map starts to connect together in unexpected ways. It's a testament to the concise world design that even so many disparate themes can fit together so well. The game is absolutely packed full of content and there are secrets to find everywhere too.
The biggest compliment I can give to this game is that after playing for 37 hours, achieving 100% and completing the alternate ending I still wanted to keep going. This game came out of nowhere and I bought it on a whim, but I was rewarded with one of the finest games I have ever played. If you are at all interested in Metroidvania games or just really good games in general, don't hesitate to pick this up. It is absolutely worth it.
I can't recommend it enough.

Maybe one of the biggest surprises in the year 2013. Most people didn't had this on their plan. Shadow Warrior is a complete breath of fresh air in the shooter genre and thank god it proves that the shooter genre on the PC is not dead yet, but let's start from the beginning.
What is good:
Shadow Warrior is Flying Wild Hogs interpretation of the original Shadow Warrior. I must admit those guys are perfect when it comes to shooters on PC (they proved their awesome work with Hard Reset earlier). Just when you think there is no more hope for shooters FWH releases the second piece of software to show the world what shooters are made of.
Positive to mention is that the difficulty is more moderate than in Hard Reset which was really challenging. The dialogs are very good and fun to listen to. Maybe not everyone's taste but definitely funny.
Secrets are placed across the levels which are fun to find since they are kept in retro look.
What is great:
- The engine is amazing. Playing this game on ultra settings making the game a blast. IMO the engine seems to be scaleable and seems pretty good optimized since I'm able to run the game on lower settings on an older PC.
- It's the first game where a melee weapon can be so much fun to fight with. While in other games melee weapons have a limited range and low damage values. the Katana in Shadow Warrior is very powerfull and fun to fight with and gets upgraded with special abilities which makes it a blast to use.
What is awesome:
the complete game is very well balanced. Sometimes I have the feeling that the Katana is a bit too powerfull compared with the other weapons what makes the game more fun to play instead of destroying anything. The great engine, the funny character(s) with its amusing dialogs, the very good level design and non-stop action make this game a great FPS in a genre where "looking through an irogn sight" dominate.

No, but seriously, Hollow Knight is amazing and it burrowed its way into my heart as one of my favorite games of all time. Here's what I love about it:
It's incredibly atmospheric. The gorgeous artwork that looks like a comic book come to life sets simple, often times cute characters against rich backgrounds full of intricate details, whether that's lush forests or gothic architecture. This contrast isn't just a wonderful way to distinguish important visual information for the player, but it also serves to underline the game's challenging, harsh nature. You're just a small bug, in a vast and threatening world.
And, oh my, it truly is vast. Even if you may catch a glimpse of the game map in the trailer, actually playing and forging your path through Hollownest you'll constantly be surprised and in awe of how much there is to discover. There's a lot of secrets, and a lot of optional areas to be found, and if you love exploring game worlds, this is as immersive and exciting as it gets, even if it's only presented in 2D. The artwork with its elaborate parallax effects creates a strong sense of depth and just pulls you in. Though the game has a very distinct, desaturated visual style, each new area feels unique. This is in part due to three factors. One, carefully picked color palettes bringing variety while working within the constraints of the art style. Two, the absolutely gorgeous, orchestral soundtrack that just can't be praised enough and the immersive sound design working together to infuse the world with life (or absence thereof).
And three, all the bugs you encounter in each area. Every creature (there's an impressive amount of 146 enemies and bosses, as well as a whole bunch more NPCs) is lovingly and skillfully animated and just feels alive. They feel at home in their surroundings, which makes them (and their environments) feel believable and real. Don't assume this means that you'll be able to predict what you'll run into next, however. On multiple occasions, encounters with enemies actually left me with my mouth agape, because of their surprising behaviors. Especially when you're starting out and still very, very vulnerable being very, very careful is the only way to survive. A new enemy acting unexpectedly is exciting and terrifying and you'll need to figure out the best way to approach their unique moves and attacks.
You have a lot of options to approach the challenges in the game. You'll collect charms and are able to equip a limited amount of them (different charms taking up varying amounts of slots), gaining various benefits. You'll also amass a large amount of moves and abilities. One thing that stood out very positively to me about Hollow Knight is that despite often running into obstacles in the early game, only rarely was it obvious to me that, hey, you're gonna get an ability later that'll help you with that (something that can easily make games of this genre feel like just going through a shopping list of cut and paste abilities). I think this is in part due to the original and fresh setting of Hollow Knight, but also the clever level design not forcing you down a set path, but enabling many different routes through the game. There are almost no puzzles here, but figuring out how to traverse the environment will still make you feel clever.
The open-ended nature of the exploration may be frustating to some players. In addition to it sometimes not being clear where to go next, maps in new areas need to be found and bought, and markers for special locations also only are added once you've bought them. Purchasing a map doesn't lay everything out for you either. No, you'll need to explore, and then rest at a bench. This will let you regain health and save the game (however, not to worry -
in the game is saved automatically, and benches only dictate where you'll end up again if you die or exit the game) and the parts of the map that you explored will be filled in. Personally, I loved that approach. It really increases the sense of exploration and discovery. And trust me, the game world is alive and full of things. Any time I wasn't sure where to go, I just went to one part of the map that I hadn't been to yet. It never disappointed. Even if I ran into what seemed like a dead end, another path often easily presented itself. Even when backtracking later in the game (a few optional sidequests will have you running around longer routes and searching for things), I often still ran into little secrets I'd previously missed.
Another potential source of frustration may be the difficulty. Hollow Knight isn't easy. If you like a challenge, it absolutely presents that. But even then, it remains fair. For one, the game lets you regain health at your own pace. Every time you hit an enemy, you gain soul. You can focus soul to gain health back, but this leaves you immobile and vulnerable. It's an exciting risk-and-reward system and forces you to be strategic about its usage, especially during boss fights. These are all (with maybe the exception of one) really amazing. There's a lot of bosses that feel like your equals, presenting satisfying fights that escalate wonderfully. But to return to the game being fair: you will die a lot. Especially in the optional boss fights, which present some of the hardest challenges. While usually, when you die in the game, you will leave behind a "shade" of yourself that you need to return to if you want to gather your previously collected money again, these optional bosses skip that. So the game acknowledges that these challenges are hard and minimizes backtracking for them, which makes it fair to me. Even for regular bosses, you usually don't have to make a huge trek from one bench to another boss, and if you feel like you do, there probably is a shortcut you haven't discovered yet.
There is also an area featuring challenging platforming later in the game which, again, is optional. It feels rather Super Meat Boy-ish, but with a generous placement of benches inbetween the different sections and the ability to exit and re-enter the area at your leisure, it struck a wonderful balance of keeping frustration low and the challenge high. I will admit that I got frustrated sometimes, especially when I'd lose my money due to not managing to return to my shade. But I think that games allowing themselves to be frustrating at times is something important. It creates a mood and a narrative, and facing these frustrating moments can eventually result in a much bigger sense of achievement and satisfaction. It's a fine line to tread, of course, but I think Hollow Knight's balancing manages to handle it pretty well.
The one aspect of the game I haven't talked about yet is the writing. It's kind of obscure and it isn't very clear what's going on in the game or what your goal is when you start out. But the writing is intriguing and pulls you in despite it. The vague nature of it keeps the mystery alive. As you progress, things do get clearer. But you never feel like you know everything there is to know about the world and about why things are the way they are. I think that's great in an exploration-focused game like this. Another wonderful aspect of the writing is that all the different and bizarre critters you come across have distinct voices and characteristics. Their dialogue is often clever and funny and had me laughing out loud, which really gave the game a wonderful sense of charm.
To sum it up, Hollow Knight is an enormous game that feels way bigger and more polished than what you'd expect of a four person development team and its humble 15€ price tag. It's an incredible accomplishment in visuals, audio, writing and gameplay, and features an incredible sense of exploration, exciting combat and an original world that truly pulls you in and constantly surprises and challenges you.
