I'm 27 years old. I own a Super Nintendo to USB adapter (the real stuff, not cheap plastic remakes that don't use the original controllers). Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night weren't internet icons when they sat on top of my "favorite game" list. As far as 'Metroidvania' titles were concerned- I peaked in my childhood. I've tried to dethrone those games multiple times without success. Hollowknight nearly slipped past me, I asked a Steam friend if it was worth the effort and his confirmation sealed the deal.
Bottom Line- As a "Vet" of the genre- this is the best 'Metroidvania' I have played, no question about that. I won't spoil anything about the title, i'll simple give you a snapshot of my experience.
• 26 hours into my first run and I'm still discovering. New areas, new items, new considerations
• Death is fair, you made mistakes, you pay for mistakes, no artificial difficulty here.
• "The Fool" was the most difficult and at the same time, the most considerate 2D challenge I've ever faced (Again, no guides through storyline to instruct me- it was a learning process.)
• The ambience is beautiful, the music and atmosphere illustrates the world well enough to get me reading into its Lore, I was hooked in minutes.
• The Story took some time to develop- now, I can't wait to see how it ends.
• Controls are perfect. It takes time to master what you're doing- when you fight a challenging boss and handle it flawlessly- you'll feel rewarded
• $14.99 isn't even a consideration. I'll likely double my time with this game throughout the years- I'm excited to revisit it when I need a good sidescroller.
• I'm excited to play again- that is something I rarely say in Singleplayer titles.
Honestly, if you're still reading this and you're a fan of 'Metroidvania' titles- you need to stop looking over reviews and purchase it. Avoid guides and spoilers, write notes about places you can't visit yet, get lost in a world and find your path again. Pay for your mistakes, criticise your situation and consider alternate routes when you're stuck. retrace your steps and discover something new. Most of all- Enjoy an incredibly solid title. I've gifted this and convinced a few others to buy and I'm watching their hours stack up- It's my favorite title 2017 has brought this year and it's set the bar significantly high- because video games still keep my wife and I up past reasonable hours, and it's nice to be reminded why.

Black Flag does three monitors right. Menus are kept on the central screen, exactly how they should be. (Far too many PC games aren't optimized for this at all. Crysis 3, for example, puts your minimap and ammo indicators on the far left and far right corners of the side monitors, making them nearly useless. Titanfall just gets rid of the entire UI completely.) Even during menus where nothing is really going on, the side screens are made to just show an "animus" animation that's continuous with the background animation going on behind the normal menu.
During cutscenes and such, the view cuts down to the single central monitor; I guess that's just how they designed the cutscene. But whenever this happens, the view on the side monitors is replaced by black screens that slide in, from the left and right, narrowing the view with an animation. When the cutscene is over, the larger view expands back into existence almost seamlessly. The side screens don't just pop in and out of existence. It's strange; I wouldn't have thought that would make such a difference, but it really does.
Going back to playing the game at 1080p feels weird during the on-foot segments, just because of the significantly decreased view of what's around you, but it plays well enough. However, playing the ship segments at 1080p feels incredibly constrained, now. I feel like I can barely see what's going on around me.
This is probably my best experience with triple monitor gaming so far.  I highly recommend this game.

Possibly the best entry in the series so far, and a huge improvement over 3. The main storyline quests are still a fairly linear experience without much freedom to deviate from the scripted manner you're supposed to complete missions in, but in terms of sidequests the game opens up incredibly early, and apart from a handful of storyline-specific locations that don't unlock until later in the game you're free to explore more or less wherever you want. Ship-to-ship combat is a big part of the open world experience, and it's very well designed and satisfying with a huge number of upgrades available to improve your ship's capabilities, and the option to capture enemy ships for bonus loot and put them to work in your fleet.
Unfortunately the melee combat is kind of a mess - especially in large encounters where it can be almost impossible to attack a specific enemy reliably, which is doubly infuriating when faced with a combination of enemies that are immune to different types of attacks. And the free running still has a mind of its own sometimes, resulting in Edward being really, really interested in running up and down a wall continually instead of going around corners. But apart from a few minor control issues, the overall game experience is a huge improvement on the previous instalment, and the number and variety of side activities provides plenty to keep you playing beyond completing the main storyline.

No hero levels, no minions, no lanes, no items. Just one open arena and a slug fest to the death. Take the boring grind out of your moba / hero brawler. You know you only play for the team-fights anyways, and that's what Battleright is.
In this online battle arena you play in either 2v2 or 3v3 team comps; solo or with friends In a first to 3 wins best of 5 rounds format. Each round lasts at most 2:00 minutes and often times is over well before that limit. This makes the games incredibly fast paced and quick, most games are over in 3 to 5 minutes.
The control scheme is twitch based and pretty standard. WASD for movement, left-click / right-click for main attacks, and Q,E,R,F, and Space-bar for various hero abilities which I describe below. Overall this control scheme takes a few games to get used to but overall feels very good.
There are currently 15 unique heros to play which are easy to pick up and fun to play. You have your standard ADC, support, tank champions each with their own unique abilities, skill-shots and learning-curve. Each hero has a basic attack (left-click), alt attack (right-click), jump / evasion (space bar), counter (Q), special attack (E), and ultimate abilities (F or R respectively)
At the beginning of each round each player starts by choosing a "battlerite" which is a trait that modifies a specific ability for your champion. Depending on the hero you're playing these traits give you cool-down reduction, increased ability damage, cool-down reduction, increased healing.. ect. I find this system is very similar to Heros of the Storm's talent system.
The battle arenas all share a similar layout but are all very different aesthetically which keeps things fresh. The arenas are mostly open with several small walls and obstacles throughout to help you avoid your enemies and their attacks. Periodically a buff will spawn in the center of the map which teams can fight over; additionally, health orbs and ultimate charge orbs will occasionally spawn for players to pick up.
Battlerite is easy to pick up, fast paced, and incredibly fun.

The Stanley Parable is a game of unique thought processes, a game of thorough and well-worked out commentary and game physics.
This, however, does not mean you'll get a great time out of it for very long.
The game is based around the principle that your character's background and purpose is a total mystery. Don't let this make you think that the object of the game is to somehow look around for clues to solve this mystery, it's not quite as exciting as that. The Stanley Parable is like playing a narrative where the only story you hear is ten different readings of the same introduction.
The pessimism isn't aside just yet, it is more just a game where you are a character that wanders around an office. The narrator will tell you what to do, and you can either listen to him or ignore him. With every decision, there are new things. However, these 'new things' aren't always particularly exciting and cause the game to restart instantly, making you look for a new ending. This, I suppose, is the catch to the game.
On the plus side, that little catch is exactly what makes it entertaining for the first few hours. It provokes intruige about how the game is so unique, and after you have finished being disappointed that it's a bit different to your expectations of a 'narrative', you can explore the routes that the developers have implemented, albeit the routes are fairly close-ended.
On the whole, an entertaining game that challenges what makes a game popular, and destroys expectations on your typical video game narrative. A good one for the philosophers, too. Worth the money? Quite possibly, but it's one of those games you can't decide if you wasted your money until you have adapted your own take on the game. It doesn't follow any genre stereotypes as such and so it is like marmite in the video game world. Buy full price at your own risk, but it's a game probably best left until Steam sales.

In
, the player takes on the role of a man simply named Stanley. Stanley’s job is just as simple as his name: an average everyday office worker. The only thing that sounds more boring than Stanley’s job and name, are his job requirements: press certain buttons as directed by a computer monitor. But don’t let this boring premise deter you from this game, it’s brilliant beyond measure.
Despite sounding mindless, Stanley has a passion for his boring office job. Such a mindless passion, that when the orders stop coming in for him to press buttons from the monitor, he waits an entire hour beginning to question the lack of instruction. It’s this lack of instruction that causes Stanley to become self aware for the first time in his career (and possibly his life), and drives the beginning of the game. It also helps him notice other strange occurrences around the office and makes him ask questions. Where did my co-workers go? Did I miss a memo? Stanley finally has to make his own choices. He has to speak up. He has to think on his own. Where to I walk? What do I interact with? Stanley had been shielded from independent thinking his entire life it appears, all thanks to a computer monitor always telling him what to do. The choices and the independent thinking are where the finally player comes in, and where the excitement of the game is found. Or more accurately, the lack of choice is where the amusement is found. Mwahahahah. Ahem, carrying on.
Choices (and the lack of) are undoubtedly the cause of entertainment and humor in this game, but it’s the way these choices go hand-in-hand with the witty commentary that makes this game truly amusing. Wait, commentary? What commentary? I think it's a point of emphasis that I mention this a narration-driven game. When Stanley finally gains awareness, a narrator begins to narrate Stanley’s story audibly, remarking his thoughts and actions. The narrator is the one who woke up Stanley from his mindless slumber in the first place. He decides of what happens in the story just as much as the player does. Scratch that-- the narrator is an all powerful omnipotent being who limits the player in every thinkable way possible. That’s the point of the game in a nutshell.
The thrill of the game is toying with the soothing narrator, who comments on every action and choice the player makes, or for that matter, refuses to make. The narrator not only makes comments, but directs and eventually commands Stanley to go down certain passageways and up certain staircases. He wants to control Stanley as much as you yearn to rebel against him. The true amusement is resisting and compromising with the narrator when he directs you to go down a hallway or through a door. In essence, that is the idea of the game. The struggle for control between the narrator of you and you-- No, not this door, I’ll go through this hallway instead. The narrator’s frustration and responses with his own character is hilarious and the most thought out part of this game.
The game has very little visual feedback and reinforcement, which can be it’s downfall and it’s strength depending on the person. In most cases, I’d call it a strength. The player can only interact with a handful of objects, which are limited to doors, computers and buttons. This is what makes
a breath of fresh air. For the first time in my gaming experience, a game relies on the majority of it’s feedback being audible instead of visual. That’s a strikingly new concept despite how simple it is to implement and carry out.
If you like the
franchise or puzzle games like
,
is comparable to a good mix of both, while still maintaining it’s own personality as a video game. The witty commentary and it’s amusement that comes with it draws an easy parallel between
and
. If you like GLaDOS’s company, the game will do a excellent job of keeping you entertained. This game best caters to those who are willing to question everything in the room, and have an eye for patterns and details. The game has a total of 18 different endings depending on how you and the narrator get along, and how well you can think for yourself despite having limited alternatives to what the narrator says.
So what is this game lacking? Choice. Despite the fact lack of choice is one of the key features of the game, it’s nonetheless a bit too limited. The vast majority of doors go unlocked and sometimes the player feels very forced into complying with the narrator. Of course, it’s worth noting the game itself is a analysis on the state of choice in video games. In video games as a medium, we are often more limited with our choices than we care to admit.
makes light of this. We tend to accept the premise prematurely often too much. We blindly accept the number of choices that are presented, are the number of choices there are. Even with that being the case, the game needs more endings. 18 endings is great, but I feel there is a perfect threshold for this game to capture so it can still make it’s point about the lack of choice, and have more choice. Perhaps I’m sour I’ve completed the game and found all the endings, but hey, who wouldn’t want to rebel against an omnipotent soothing narrator a little more?
Currently,
goes for a decent $15 on Steam. At best, it will give you 7 hours of gameplay if you’re sure to analyze every detail. For the average player however, 3 hours is what’s expected. Due to the nature of the game, it’s a rainy day experience. And while it has brilliant commentary and thought-provoking critique on the nature of choice in video games, $15 is a bit much for a day’s worth of entertainment. I’d strongly recommend waiting for a sale, but if you love Portal and soothing voices, I can empathize if you can’t.

This is the first time in which I've wished I could leave just an "OK" review. This game does not deserve an overwhelmingly positive score, but I do not think I'd necassarily say the game is
. I think it lies just in the middle. The game is and isn't a MOBA. By definition a MOBA is a MULTIPLAYER ONLINE BATTLE ARENA, which sums up what this game is to a tee. However, this game is more of a compilation of DotA, LoL, and HotS with many apsects of those
games stripped away.
The game very blatantly takes things from the afforementioned games, but reuses those things in a new and unique, easy-to-learn way. But perhaps the things stripped away to make this game was just too much. I feel like I'm playing just another MOBA but it's way too simple. You just go into a circle and cast abilities on each other. There is no real learning curve, no skill builds, no items... It's just learn what your characters do, and go lay the smackdown on some fools.
And that's fun the first few times, but gets old really fast, especially since all of the characters are kind of just rebrands of each other. Your left mouse click is an attack. Your right click is a stronger attack that might have some casting time. Your Q is a counter attack. Your space bar is for mobilty or a shield depending on if you're playing a support or core role. Your E is generally the most diverse and unique ability. And that's that. Each of the heroes has that kind of general foundation.
One thing I didn't mention though about part of the abilties is the way they handle ultimates, they give you a strong abilty and a stronger ability. Each of the abilities uses up some energy that you gain over time from either hitting things or picking stuff up around the map and you get to make the choice of whether to use your strong ability to get an advantage over the enemy, or wait for your stronger ability and win the fight that way.
You might notice that I give this game points for being unique every time they do it, because I think being unique is good, but this game just isn't that unique. Like I said before, this game copies. This game even copies the bad♥♥♥♥♥♥that doesn't need to be in the game, such as loot crates. Hearthstone really started some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and I have had enough of it. It works for a goddamn digital card game, but now the loot crate system is in literally every ♥♥♥♥ing game and it needs to stop. IT'S TIME TO STOP. I don't need having microtransactions in your game be the norm. I don't need that to be the gimmick that keeps a game afloat. I want a game's content to be what keeps it going, not its ♥♥♥♥ing skins and that false sense of luck when you open something LEGENDARY. The♥♥♥♥♥♥is worthless and has no place being in the game. And especially not in this game in which all of the skins look exactly the same except legendaries have an epileptic glow. To me, it really feels like this game has skins just to have skins, which is exactly the thing I knew would happen right when I saw Todd Howard present his new Fallout game for iOS featuring loot crates with the same exact rarity rating from WoW.
Somehow this game managed to diversify itself by adding a pricetag, putting itself on a pedastal to look down on MOBA's and say "I'm not like you." No, this game is just like those games, but for people looking to get the bare minimum of the MOBA experience. If this game was free, I'd probably be more inclined to give it a positive review, because it would be just another MOBA clone, but with a unique twist just unique enough to be refreshing yet nostalgic. But if this game was free, it likely would not have any recognition. It's like that old wondorous age-old question. Would you rather have Harambe live, but be forgotten, or have him killed only to be the most famous gorilla of all time?

A remake of the classic Shadow Warrior featuring still the character Lo Wang. It is easy to see that much effort went into blending modern and classic FPS styles. Medkits still litter the levels yet you have the ability to heal yourself at will with a Chi spell unlocked early in the game.
Many people will remember the humour of the first game and it is still here, although at a toned down level. Much of the hilarious one liners and jokes are gone or purposefully changed to lower potentional insult certain people might feel and make vocal.
Secret areas do exist and are done up in the classic Shadow Warrior pixel graphics. Areas from old levels and pixel-based girls await your discovery!
Much of the combat focuses on the use of your sword, which I found to be a huge plus. There is an assortment of weapons as one would expect in classic FPS titles with three different upgrades each. Different Chi-based abilities help you fight your foes. Two skills knock down or suspend foes in the air, various katana abilities help you fight at range or slay foes in a circle around you.
All in all I was highly impressed and surprised at how good the overall game was in both quality and length. If you can pick it up on sale for $19.99 or less it's definitely worth it!

For someone who honestly hasn't played many Metroidvanias, this is a game that caught my attention as soon as I saw it on Youtube from the gameplay and art just from being a fan of Rogue-likes.
Here's my impressions of the game after having played through and unlocked basically everything:
The artwork looks great, from the characters and enemies to the maps themselves. Its a treat to look at.
The writing is . . . mostly non-existent, but implicit. People who've played Dark Souls know exactly what I mean by this. Except in Dark Souls you at least get an intro to explain the setting. Here, you don't even get much of that other than a couple bits of information. You're never given any reason WHY you're in Hallownest to begin with, nor are you actually given much direction besides "Go explore". Characters like Hornet and a few others may give you plot points, but you won't understand what the hell they're referring to until much later, if at all as you pass more time exploring. That being said, to those willing to delve and search for lore in all the nooks and cranies of Hallownest, it is fairly interesting, but its not going to be handed to you, you have to do the delving yourself.
Combat and gameplay is pretty simple, but can be complex to master as the game steadily becomes tougher as you gain more abilities and go further. Having said that, I'm willing to say that 80% of the game is relatively easy to beat once you get the hang of the controls, this is not a game of Dark Souls style difficulty for the most part. The remaining 20% can be CRUSHINGLY DIFFICULT though, and can feel like you switched to playing Super Meat Boy or actual Dark Souls at times. Having said that, that 20% is optional to beating the game, and there are exploits to most of the problems that difficulty poses a lot of it lies in proper preparation.
Music is very nice and atmospheric. I don't really have any complaints about this.
Overall, the game was very addictive to play, I couldn't set this down for hours on hours of gameplay to just keep going further and explore more stuff.
Plus, the amount of gameplay, despite being able to be speedrun in less than 5 hours as an achievement, is well worth the price tag.
Definately reccomend buying it.

"Hollow Knight draws out the inner explorer and tryhard in everybody, through the magic that it is"
Hollow Knight is an amazing, difficult, 2-Dimensional traditional platforming game that at first seems like it would be ok, but not worth the money. Ignore any hate this game gets (which I wouldn't excpect it to get any in the first place), because after playing it through twice (once for fun, and then even a second time as a 100% playthrough for another ending, each obviously worth the hours of enjoyment and childlike wonder), I realised that I just spent about 45 hours playing a platformer, a genre that a multiplayer die-hard would usually not play often, and only spent $15 for it! I would have spent $20-$30 for this incredible expirience!
So let's talk about the technical aspects of the game.
For supposedly a hand drawn game, the graphics are appealing and eye-catching, just as they should be. The diverse environments always bring a surprise before you reach the point at which you are tired of the area (may I add that this never happend to me). Although, before the vibrant colors appear, the player has to explore nearly monochromatic scenery.
The platforming and combat in the game shocks me, because the momentum at which it opens up to your control and freedom, is perfect! The minimal tutorial helps the player to interact and learn at their own pace. Team Cherry nailed this obviously essential piece to the game.
Ranging from calm, relaxing, and soothing tunes, to fast-paced, epic, boss fight tracks, Hollow Knight doesn't forget anybody's taste in video game music.
You have to have a lot of patience and time to complete Hollow Knight, but just as any good video game should do, it distracts you from the the world for much longer than you may expect, due to the magnificant storyline! Beating the game normally should take about 25-30 hours, completing it 100% will take roughly 40 hours, and exhausting the game of all content (which I havn't done yet) looks like it will take around 55 hours.
Consider that you will be embarking on one of the most amazing adventures, if not the most amazing adventure in any 2D platformer! Consider that the adventure will not only bring you closer to its end, but the amazing community it has spawned! Consider that all of the above is my opinion.
But most of all... consider that if you buy Hollow Knight, you will put zero effort into making it an enjoyable expirience, because of the simple fact that you don't need to, since it has already sucked you in. Why would you be reading this review in the first place if you didn't care, thus, proving my point that Hollow Knight is magical. Absorbing the souls from even its audience, and replacing them with life (a pun that you will only understand if you play the game).

Man, yeah, this game is... it's great, no question about it. Where to begin.
Okay, this game's best strength is easily its atmosphere and worldbuilding. The game is dark and lonely most of the time. But you have moments where you meet up with some familiar faces, or find a character not yet lost to the madness. The recurring characters are pretty nicely fleshed out and have their own character arcs throughout the length of the game - which is really long for a metroidvania, for the record - and it's interesting to see them grow... or perish, sometimes. The overarching story is not directly told in large chunks but spread throughout the land and you have to dig deep to put all the pieces together and reach the true conclusion. Without really saying too much it's a satisfying story with a satisfying conclusion.
And while a lot of the game is dark, each area has its own distinct atmosphere. Lush, green areas, structured, rigid cities, surreal dreamscapes, dark, horrifying depths, it really feels quite varied. It would've been easy for the atmosphere to get monotonous but they do a good job of keeping each area feeling unique.
Now then, gameplay. Hollow knight himself is great to control, the only weird quirk is the jump mechanic but after an hour of playing I never really noticed how weird it was ever again and it gets feeling quite natural. It's not a "fluid" game in the traditional sense but you move precise and swiftly, the way I like it. It makes both the combat and platforming feel satisfying, and I especially love the downward slash attack that has many a use in many places. On top of that you leard some slower but more powerful attacks along the way that can also have utility outside of combat as well. The skills you learn generally bolster both combat and platforming to interesting degrees & make the game all that more fun to play. Simply put, it's a blast.
And the size. There's over a dozen areas and most of them are pretty meaty in size, coming together for probably the largest metroidvania world I've ever seen. With loads upon loads of secrets to find leading to a great sense of exploration; in fact, just to complete the game through the normal ending would require a fair bit of exploration, even discounting going for the true ending and, should you dare, 100% completion. And with the atmosphere being as good as it is it keeps me interested in exploring, to find new little bits of flavor or some other gorgeous side area.
Oh yeah, let's mention. The game is just gorgeous on all fronts. Beautiful scenery, fluid animation on all the characters and enemies, lovely and atmospheric soundtrack. Crystal peak's track is a favorite of mine especially. It's a joy to look at and play without ever really feeling too cluttered or hard to follow.
The game isn't perfect, mind you. There are a few challenges I'm not a fan of (the coliseum, delicate flower) and the weapon upgrades become almost mandatory as later-game bosses tend to have lots and lots of HP and thus feel really tanky and long to fight if you don't get weapon upgrades. And the healing mechanic feels too slow to mesh well with the fast-paced combat. These are things that occasionally frustrated me but were never enough to really sour my opinion on the game and as a whole it's still a great experience.
Certainly an early contender for game of the year despite its slight imperfections, but as a whole I'd highly recommend this game, and at $15 it's absolutely a steal for the price.

Are you tired of being presented with one bland un-inspired military shooter after another? Tired of playing the brave American soldier blowing the bejeebus out of Russians or developing countries full of brown people because "TERRISM" ? Tired of re-living the same stupid cold war fantasies over and over? Do you enjoy the occasional wang-joke while beheading a demon with your katana? If you long for the days shooters featured over the top action heroes who carried 9 weapons and a bandolier full of one-liners then this game is for you.
Meet Lo Wang, a lovable assassin with a big sword and an even bigger ego who gets caught up in a demon apocalypse.
Shadow Warrior is a game that sits very comfortably inbetween modern shooters and classic ones. You can aim down sights, but you don't have to. There are med-kits and you can regenerate your own health, though not by sitting in a corner sucking your thumbs for 10 seconds. Beyond that you can upgrade your guns, learn new abilities to help you cut through the demon hordes as well as gain access to dark powers which can heal or protect you, and allow you to control the battlefield.
This is NOT a cover-based shooter, why take cover when you can charge in with your sword and become a tornado of death?
As Lo Wang himself says: "come for the shoot-outs, stay for the sword fights"
It should be noted that Shadow Warrior revels in its over the top gore and violence, though this is mostly directed at demons, but occasionaly also at humans. The game also has a lot of secret areas for you to find, often containing resources that allow you to upgrade and improve your guns and abilities. The down-side to this is that there are a lot of these in every level, and if you miss them, you'll miss a big chunk of upgrades and abilities.
Is Shadow Warrior the shooter messiah? Our saviour from the endless parade of military shooters? Sadly, it is not. The game isn't perfect, it has its flaws. But it's a fun ride, the sword-play aspect in particular is enough reason to buy this game.

This is the first time in which I've wished I could leave just an "OK" review. This game does not deserve an overwhelmingly positive score, but I do not think I'd necassarily say the game is
. I think it lies just in the middle. The game is and isn't a MOBA. By definition a MOBA is a MULTIPLAYER ONLINE BATTLE ARENA, which sums up what this game is to a tee. However, this game is more of a compilation of DotA, LoL, and HotS with many apsects of those
games stripped away.
The game very blatantly takes things from the afforementioned games, but reuses those things in a new and unique, easy-to-learn way. But perhaps the things stripped away to make this game was just too much. I feel like I'm playing just another MOBA but it's way too simple. You just go into a circle and cast abilities on each other. There is no real learning curve, no skill builds, no items... It's just learn what your characters do, and go lay the smackdown on some fools.
And that's fun the first few times, but gets old really fast, especially since all of the characters are kind of just rebrands of each other. Your left mouse click is an attack. Your right click is a stronger attack that might have some casting time. Your Q is a counter attack. Your space bar is for mobilty or a shield depending on if you're playing a support or core role. Your E is generally the most diverse and unique ability. And that's that. Each of the heroes has that kind of general foundation.
One thing I didn't mention though about part of the abilties is the way they handle ultimates, they give you a strong abilty and a stronger ability. Each of the abilities uses up some energy that you gain over time from either hitting things or picking stuff up around the map and you get to make the choice of whether to use your strong ability to get an advantage over the enemy, or wait for your stronger ability and win the fight that way.
You might notice that I give this game points for being unique every time they do it, because I think being unique is good, but this game just isn't that unique. Like I said before, this game copies. This game even copies the bad♥♥♥♥♥♥that doesn't need to be in the game, such as loot crates. Hearthstone really started some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and I have had enough of it. It works for a goddamn digital card game, but now the loot crate system is in literally every ♥♥♥♥ing game and it needs to stop. IT'S TIME TO STOP. I don't need having microtransactions in your game be the norm. I don't need that to be the gimmick that keeps a game afloat. I want a game's content to be what keeps it going, not its ♥♥♥♥ing skins and that false sense of luck when you open something LEGENDARY. The♥♥♥♥♥♥is worthless and has no place being in the game. And especially not in this game in which all of the skins look exactly the same except legendaries have an epileptic glow. To me, it really feels like this game has skins just to have skins, which is exactly the thing I knew would happen right when I saw Todd Howard present his new Fallout game for iOS featuring loot crates with the same exact rarity rating from WoW.
Somehow this game managed to diversify itself by adding a pricetag, putting itself on a pedastal to look down on MOBA's and say "I'm not like you." No, this game is just like those games, but for people looking to get the bare minimum of the MOBA experience. If this game was free, I'd probably be more inclined to give it a positive review, because it would be just another MOBA clone, but with a unique twist just unique enough to be refreshing yet nostalgic. But if this game was free, it likely would not have any recognition. It's like that old wondorous age-old question. Hollow Knight carries the dramatic feel and harsh learning curve of the Souls-Borne universe (I'm sure they're getting a bit tired of that comparison) expertly into a 2D world, the gameplay is amplified by the beautiful art direction and wonderfully fitted soundtrack! I understand that the not very "adult" art style could draw you in but, this is not a kids game, don't expect it to be forgiving to your controller or to your feelings. The story is removed enough from the main gameplay elements were it could be ignored if you don't pay attention so please do as it is a tragic and well woven tale that you have to dig deep to find the truth in. The only concession I'll make is that it did not run smoothly upon initial release but Team Cherry has been hard at work releasing patches and updates to resolve issues quickly and I for one am excited for anything they add to this game in the future, and to see what's next from this small group of developers!

Stanley saw a game that had his name in the title and so he proceeded to download it. He knew no one told him to do this but the thought that he had the choice excited him extremely.
So Stanley did what he knew best and he started clicking buttons. After a stimulating walk through a bizzarely empty office space, Stanley had to make a choice.
Left or right? Left or right? Left or right? Left or right? Left or right? Left or right? Left or right?
Stanley's brain was on overload. The instructions told him left, but the right just seemed so appealing. What if he finally did something on his own?
So Stanley went his own way and eventually 'beat' the game,' or did he?
Nontheless, Stanley went to sleep that day rather peacefully.
But as the weeks went on Stanley began to wonder if there was something more, something he didn't see.
It couldn't possibly be however, games are quite limited.
Night passed night as Stanley began having nightmares, twisting in his sleep, waking up in the middle of the night sweating profusely, screaming! He couldn't take it he had to.... he had to....
Stanley knew what he had to do.
So Stanley went to his computer and played. And he played so more. And he played so more.
And then he finally found every ending in the game, or so he thought.
How could the internet possibly know EVERY ending?
And so he searched, and searched, and searched for hours.
This is the story of Stanley: an ordinary office worker driven to insanity in his search for another ending to a game that probably doesn't have another.
But he will continue even after finishing this review because, well, he was happy he could make his own decisions in a game, or could he?
What if this game was actually linear?
NO.
NO.
NO.
NO.
NO.
NO.
It couldn't be.
Stanley needed help.
He took pills.
He didn't sleep.
He quit work.
He didn't eat or drink.
In fact Stanley played so hard his computer exploded.
Stanley stared at the dead computer for another few hours.
Stanley was finished.
But the game wasn't.
There was only one way to end the game.
The police found his body early the next morning with warning post-it reading: "Don't play the Stanley Parable"
But of course, they did.
And so the cycle continued with player 2.
And so I must tell you, don't play this game!
The seduction of the choice to play is getting to you isn't it?
Go ahead, play.
Play like Stanley.
I don't care.
Either way, it's all part of the plan.

Let me be pretty sincere here: this is the best Assassin's Creed so far. I'm a huge fan of the series and had always played all of the games right on the launch. It was not different with Black Flag.
AC IV represents the final move into the pure sandbox experience. Although since AC Brotherhood the series invested in more and more quests and things to do out there in the open world, which has been improved in each instalment of the series, Black Flag has so many things to do, and so much different from each other, that it feels a completely fresh experience.
I saw some criticism about the Creed part of the story being left aside, but for me it isn't too much of a big deal... AC is always about a historical representation, and it truly brings to us the end of the Caribbean Piracy Era. And the plot around Edward Kenway is a pure metaphore for it. Play it, pay attention to the details and you'll clearly see it. Plus, the life of captain Edward is the most emotional of all the series, the character is the most humanized of them all.
As for the gameplay, it feels really great to navigate from island to island, famous port to famous port, engage in battle and in piracy actions. The core gameplay revolves around your ship, but the mechanics of climbing and acting stealth still makes presence.
One good thing is that the stealth part has been greatly improved. The level design is thought to be stealth, differently from the AC III, which had a broken level design for the stealth gameplay, specially for doing 100% of the achievements.
Sure, Edward's drive is the same as the other AC games and sometimes he'll end up doing things you don't want to. Ubisoft must look at this and make it better in AC Unity I believe, it's something that is frustrating sometimes.
The music is great but not that memorable as the AC II or III were, but you can still enjoy and the game has great voice acting. As for the graphics, videos and screenshots speak for themselves: the game is gorgeous, specially on the PC, with many effects and a high resolution.
Do not be affraid: Black Flag is the best Assassin's Creed to date, and one of the best historical games ever made.

The Stanley Parable is a first person exploration game developed by Galactic Cafe on the source engine. It follows a regular office worker named "Stanley" (whose job it is to push buttons on a keyboard) after all of his co-workers mysteriously disappear, and he starts to hear the voice of a mysterious narrator in his head.
The Stanley Parable is at it's core an expermiment in player choice and how that effects gaming as a story-telling medium. It doesn't have any fancy butterfly effects it actually plays out more like a choose-your-own adventure book with preset paths and endings. With the player activating triggers by making choices that lead down branching paths toward one of a variety of endings.
Beyond that core is a commentary on gaming and the medium that games present to a player, involving a main character with no personality beyond literally being the player, and a narrator (voiced by Kevan Brighting) who acts as a standin for the video game's developers. One of the most unique metrodvania games I've ever played. The sheer amount of exploration and non-linear progression has never been matched in this genre with such high caliber. It's cute, creepy, mysterious, jovial, haunting, mystical, and sucks you right into this one of a kind environment with an awe-inspiring sense of wonder.

The pinpoint platforming and combat never gets dull, and kept me entertained to even go for 100% completion. There is no leveling up in this game, it takes a more complex approach to utilize money for upgrades and other various skills. If you die, you have to retrieve your currency or risk losing it for good. You can also choose and experiement with several different combination of skills to fit your play style.
This bug universe they've developed is truly remarkable and really set the bar for creativity. A great blend of old school and modern gameplay elements. I hope they make a sequel to build upon this world they've constructed. If you're a fan of metroidvania games or even something with a Dark Souls-esque feel to it, then there's no excuse why you shouldn't play this.
Hollow Knight is a classic, and I consider it to be the magnum opus of metroidvania games.

This game has done the impossible, it uncrowned Super Metroid, this is the best metroidvania ever made.
I have to thank easy allies for spotlighting this game, i would have just placed this game into my wishlist and waited for the next steam sale, this is gem, a game that can go toe to toe with titans like the new zelda or horizon.
Even if this was a kickstarter don't treat it like it,  because this has AAA quantity and quality, it's a bucket full of great ideas, it takes the best things about the original dark souls and adapts them into the metroidvania style, it's never too similar to dark souls like salt and sanctuary, it knows were its best to drop the souls formula, get back to metroidvania, to just get back to souls when its necessary.
The implementation of the mapping system is fantastic, a 2d game needs a map to be explored fully because you don't have many points of reference in two dimensions, the clever thing here is that the first time you enter a new area you actually have to go blind, without a map, later if you manage to find the map of the area you can look at it but it's not complete, you have to explore and draw it, and the only way to draw it is by getting to a save point, this may sound confusing but it works marvelously, you feel like you are actually exploring and you have to choose if keep going blind looking for a new save point or getting back after a while to save and draw the locations you've been into. The areas to explore are really big and they are amazingly made, with paths interconnecting the zones, and areas that can be discovered the first time in multiple ways, a la dark souls 1, a thing that has never been made in metroidvania before and it works exquisetly.
The controls are so fluid and responsive, bosses are really different and well designed, the game is challenging and it makes every mistake feel like its your fault, animations and artstyle are top quality with a dark malinconic atmosphere that is the stage of a sad but great plot.
I want to reiterate, don't think about this as "the next good kickstarter", this is not another guacamelee or axiom verge, games that were good 10-20$ metroidvania, the content here is 30h+ for the true ending with more than 140 unique enemies and many different locations to explore. Don't skip this.

Reviews for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
With regard to accessibility for deaf/hoh gamers, I give Dungeon Defenders an 8/10.
Gameplay
There appear to be visual cues to most (if not all) events in the game. The screen does get very cluttered, though, and it can become easy to miss a key visual such as your crystal being attacked, which can lead to losing a game. This event is accompanied by a sound for HOH gamers.
Subtitles/Text
Dungeon Defenders has a storyline that plays in cutscenes. When you turn captions on, the cutscenes will be the only time that you see the subtitles, as the gameplay does not require them.
Chatting/Communicating
Dungeon Defenders has voice chat. In my experience so far, most people do not seem to use it, though, and prefer to type. There are no key combinations or voice binds to convey messages quickly, so you will need to type if you cannot hear/speak.

With that said: This game will be released on an F2P model, where you will have a weekly rotation of heroes (think league or brawlhalla) and you can purchase them with in game currency (slower) or buy them outright for real money. *However* Early Access members will receive some special items, AND all heroes for free, forever. Not typically into platformers but I bought this almost on a whim and have so far really enjoyed it. It's difficult and can get frustrating at times but that seems the story of most platforming games. The world is very weird and wacky, it's also incredibly beautiful, you can tell the massive amounts of work that has been put into the world, characters and dialogue.
In terms of the gameplay, it's very open and this might put some people off, I was unsure at first. After the first 10 or 15 minutes, you're not told where to go or who to kill, the game very much encourages you to just wander and see what you can find. It does quietly guide you as you're unable to progress past certain areas without specific powers but outside of that, the maps/levels are large and it's easy to get lost. You are also not provided with a map, you must find the explorer dude somewhere in the level who then gives you the map, so you can be exploring blindly for a while. This isn't a bad thing, the game really wants you to explore of your own free will and you spend a lot of time doing exactly that.
It also has a Souls esque death system whereby you collect currency and then drop it on death, you must then make it back to your death point to get the money back, if you die again, you loose it all. It can be a bit merciless at times, especially when you're just struggling with a boss while also trying to save up for that new cool looking item, but it definitely adds a certain 'tension' to the game.
Definitely recommend it. If you're into platformers this'll be a real favourite, if not, you'll still enjoy it.
tldr; Beautiful game. Very open and doesn't like holding your hand. Merciless and tricky at times, but tense and rewarding.

Hollow Knight carries the dramatic feel and harsh learning curve of the Souls-Borne universe (I'm sure they're getting a bit tired of that comparison) expertly into a 2D world, the gameplay is amplified by the beautiful art direction and wonderfully fitted soundtrack! As someone that grew up playing Metroid, Megaman, and other NES-SNES sidescrollers, this game brought me back to all the wonder of exploring a new area and finding it's secrets, raging out from dying on that boss fight AGAIN, the joy of finally understanding the mechanics of a fight, and most of all just sitting there taking in the sounds and the scenery! I understand that the not very "adult" art style could draw you in but, this is not a kids game, don't expect it to be forgiving to your controller or to your feelings. The story is removed enough from the main gameplay elements were it could be ignored if you don't pay attention so please do as it is a tragic and well woven tale that you have to dig deep to find the truth in. The only concession I'll make is that it did not run smoothly upon initial release but Team Cherry has been hard at work releasing patches and updates to resolve issues quickly and I for one am excited for anything they add to this game in the future, and to see what's next from this small group of developers!

The game is gorgeous and atmospheric, and I couldn't believe how big the game was. My first run was nearly %100 and took around 40 hours, but that is because I was playing slowly. From what i've read elsewhere ~30 hours seems like average time to complete. It is polished with satisfying movement and combat, essential for the genre.
The game is something like Dark Souls meets Metroid, where you'll be exploring a vast 2D world of connected rooms separated into distinct areas, much like a metroid game. And like both metroid and souls, a lot of the value comes from the exploration of this world and figuring out just what happened to the bleak kingdom you're exploring. The game is challenging though, and will test your reflexes both in the combat and occasionally the platforming.
Supposedly the devs are working on more content for this game, including additionally playable characters and a proper NG+ mode, both of which I look forward too.
A strong reccomendation: please challenge yourself, explore this sombre world, discover its secrets, defeat its nightmares.

Shadow Warrior is an awesome game. Period. I believe it is rare to find a game that is so tailored for an immersed and thoroughly entertaining experience. The setting and environments are top notch, the music is engaging and mood-defining. The gameplay is very gratifying and tactically versatile. The game is very challenging. I think what I like most about it is that they don't baby you into the game. You figure it out on your own. The game is a powerful homage to old school hardcore games. Secrets are not easy to find, high scores are not always simple, and you'll be damned if the game is lacking testosterone.
If you're wondering, I played through on normal difficulty and the campaign lasted me 13 hours. That's fairly impressive for games nowadays. I died about 9 times, 5 of which occurred on the final stages. There is no multiplayer and I'd say the replay value is considerably low once you've beaten it once. But I can't say the content of the game is lacking. It didn't feel that way. And I gotta say, I can't wait for more. The game is absolutely beautiful (and demanding) and a memorable experience. I hope more games follow this trend.

Not typically into platformers but I bought this almost on a whim and have so far really enjoyed it. It's difficult and can get frustrating at times but that seems the story of most platforming games. The world is very weird and wacky, it's also incredibly beautiful, you can tell the massive amounts of work that has been put into the world, characters and dialogue.
In terms of the gameplay, it's very open and this might put some people off, I was unsure at first. After the first 10 or 15 minutes, you're not told where to go or who to kill, the game very much encourages you to just wander and see what you can find. It does quietly guide you as you're unable to progress past certain areas without specific powers but outside of that, the maps/levels are large and it's easy to get lost. You are also not provided with a map, you must find the explorer dude somewhere in the level who then gives you the map, so you can be exploring blindly for a while. This isn't a bad thing, the game really wants you to explore of your own free will and you spend a lot of time doing exactly that.
It also has a Souls esque death system whereby you collect currency and then drop it on death, you must then make it back to your death point to get the money back, if you die again, you loose it all. It can be a bit merciless at times, especially when you're just struggling with a boss while also trying to save up for that new cool looking item, but it definitely adds a certain 'tension' to the game.
Definitely recommend it. If you're into platformers this'll be a real favourite, if not, you'll still enjoy it.
tldr; Beautiful game. Very open and doesn't like holding your hand. Merciless and tricky at times, but tense and rewarding.

Assassin's Creed black flag, A game hyped by many for venturing into an area many games avoid focusing on and rather have them as a passing thing while also using the open world system. I agree I am very happy that a free roaming pirate game exists as its one of my dream games, unfortunately this failed to reach my expectations. It is NOT a bad game, in fact I quite enjoyed it however it does have some issues people need to be warned about.
First, You are not a pirate, you are an assassin who sails ships. At no point did I feel like a pirate on foot. The ship to ship battle felt great but yes this is an assassin's creed game, You will feel like an assassin not a pirate while on foot. Not a big issue and probably adds to the combat system that would be rather dull without it. You also get two swords....not a big issue for some but i always felt pirates should only use 1 sword, multiple pistols and possibly a knife. this is nitpicking but whatever my review
*SPOILER WARNING*
Second issue I felt needed to be addressed was the story, It starts off strong you are not the center of the world, you are just a regular pirate who gets ship wrecked with an assassin, you eventually steal his outfit so that you can collect the reward he was supposed to. now this part makes you feel like you are playing a pirate game, as you are doing this to get money, your character even demonstrates this by tossing away the dead assassin's wrist blades. however it just goes down after a while. Characters die and you dont really care even for the big bad♥♥♥♥♥pirates like Black Beard because you never do anything with them. Each character that is supposed to be this big important character goes on one trip with you and thats about it, other than that they just kinda bark at each other then ask you to fix it. I mean if a pirate game cant get me to care even a little bit when Black Beard dies why the hell should i care about the others?! How about you remove some of the boring quests where i go and stab a dude because he slapped a ♥♥♥♥♥ who laughed at his♥♥♥♥♥♥size and give these characters some quests?! Let me do a repeat quest with Black Beard where me and him sail out to capture a large fleet and sink them, or something i mean Jesus these characters are so boring the parts where I should be sad for them is dull because none of them did anything other than stand next to me on a ship and say "shoot at dat ting over der" or "follow de shipz"
*END OF SPOILERS*
Third is the equpment, While this game does have a large variety of equipment to use it sadly falls kinda flat, you typically will only use 3 weapons, your wrist blades, your pistols and your beserker darts. the wrists blades act like swords lettting you block attacks and kill people this is a huge flaw as it means your swords are pointless, in fact several times you lose your swords and have to use only the wrist blades, they could have fixed this by removing the ability to block with them. Your pistols can one shot anyone but a captian and brutes, however they can be fired rapidly and have large stores of ammo, this means weaker enemies quickly get shot down to peices, this isnt an issue really but honestly you wont really wanna use anything else because you can just skip down the road killing anything and everyone in your path the second they try to do something. And finally the Beserker darts, these things start off seemingly harmless till you realize when you need to kill someone you can easily just shoot them with one, and boom they go off and start trying to punch armed guards to death with results in them dying from battle Or if there are no guards left it starts a simple like 5 second timer where they isntantly die when its over. Because they have about the same range as the pistols and are totally silent you end up using them as distractions and to thin guards numbers with ease. Eventually you can have an entire fort fighting itself to death while you quietly wittle another dark in the brush, this weapon is almost game breaking, it would be easily fixed by not working on assassination targets but even then you could just shoot all his buddies and watch them kill each other.
Lastly is just the overall feel to the game, It does feel like a pirate game sometimes but most of the time you just feel like you are driving a big lumbering taxi to your next assassination location so you can then run around and get ♥♥♥♥ing stuck on every little corner ledge while you are trying to follow someone. (btw the controls are....assassin's creed. I need not say more for others who have played these games on pc) The crew feels lifeless and dead if not useless, they rarely help in a fight other than to distract enemies, the first ship i took i didnt realize i could dock so i jumped onto it then killed everyone myself as it was a small ship, then i realized i could dock and took it without issue. They dont explore the ports you visit, they just sit on the ship and rub the cannons...it gets creepy if you watch them do it for a few minutes. It also is quickly ruined by the fact you are still not just In the past exploring, You are some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who repeatedly has to get out of the pirate world to walk around and play boring minigames so some grumpy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the other end of your ipad or whatever will stfu and let you get back to cutting open the bellies of guards. Seriously Ubisoft, no one gives 2 flying ♥♥♥♥♥ about this boring office slavery fetish you got going on, we dont play your games to listen to modern people flap their exposition lips about stuff that Does NOT affect the stuff that happens in the virtual DNA ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t machine. Sadly VooDoo is not present, i mean clearly the Ancient alien's guy is more interesting and plausible than say just having one or two witch doctor characters who can help add to the atmosphere of the game. Also really irked I cant switch ships, i mean the one you give me is fine, but I would love to be able to sail other ships around or at least be able to upgrade my ship to a galleon after i fully upgraded it.
Let me be clear, I do like this game, I am recommending it to Assassin's creed fans and pirate fans who understand its not a full fledge pirate game, Its an assassin's creed game before its a pirate game. Overall I'd give it a 7/10 with 5 being average, its a great game but its not what I was looking for.

This game is just something else. A fun, cute but menacing metroidvania that doesn't hold back in its difficulty. A twisted Dark Souls 2D crossover, which definitely punches above its weight considering its small budget (a ~$45,000USD kickstarter), and very small team of three developers. With a unique and charming hand drawn art style, along an almost Lovecraftian vibe, the atmosphere is something unlike any other game. Its exploration, secrets, map, and combat are all very well constructed. Creating an amazing world for an equally incredible story to take place in. Again, it is very Dark Souls-esque in its storytelling, much of it implied by the environment and the short interactions with the various NPC's. The writing is fantasic, with characters changing and evolving as the game progresses, creating connections and interest in everyone you meet. Its accompaning soundtrack is nothing short of its previous successes either, soft orchestral music giving off an aesthetic not unlike a Studio Ghibli movie in the cities, intense drums in the midst of a boss battle, and beautiful ambient sounds when traversing the world.
With an incredible story, amazing soundtrack, beatiful art design, fluid combat, and a deep world to explore, this game is a must play and is definitely on my personal Game of the Year shortlist.

I don't usually leave any review after buying a game. However, I felt this game deserves one and I'd actually like to let people know of this game. I don't really know why but it seems this game is not getting enough attention.
So, let's begin. Before telling anything to you, I'd like to let you know my progression through the game. I finished the game with 100% completion. Took about 30 hours for me to archieve such thing but I believe for those who never look up on internet about the game, it is going to take more than 30 hours of playtime for beating the game.
Something to note : I played the game on Xbox One controller.
First of all, this game has great amount of contents for its price.
I was expecting the game to be about 10~20 hours long, but the game is much much longer and during the playtime, I never felt boring, since there was nothing repetitive.
Second, It has good amount of mixture between platfomer and action.
Most people compare this to Ori and the Blind forest, which is a solid platformer too, but I don't think it's like Ori at all. Since this game has more of fighting sequence and less puzzle to solve so if you didn't like Ori but liked games like metrovania or even Megaman, You might want to try this game too.
Third, Great graphics and Music.
What you are seeing through those trailers up there, is there. This might be a personal topic to discuss but I think no one would disagree how beutiful this game is.
Lastly, Great combat and boss fight.
As someone who had good amount of boss fights on other good action games, I can definitlely say this game has good amount and good quality boss fights. Few feels a little difficult to overcome, but I thinks it gives good amount of challenge to you. Combat feels really smooth and I liked the pace of combat too. Not to quick, not too long. Just good. Also there are many different types of monster to fight so it does not get easily repetitive.
Game's not guiding everything to you.
I really liked this part of it. However I know there are people who'd prefer to game to tell you what to do. Like press A for jump on certain sequence, you can check map on somewhere or by some button.... This game tells you what button does what but does not tell you when or how to use it right. You will need to figure out yourself.
No quest marker or objective journal thing.
Another thing I liked but some would hate. This game won't tell you where to go at all. This makes you to venture through everything you see and waste good amount of time and effort of yours. Though, it will give you true feeling of adventuring.
There's no way to lower or raise difficulty level.
I do not think the game is unfair or too hard to beat. However this is just an opinion of mine and I played lots of difficult games. [ like Souls series, Super meat boy ] And I see some people saying the game's too hard for them. I'd say challenging but it's your call. I'd recommend watching few bossfight if you are worried about difficulty.

This game is the definition of funky... In a good way, of course.
I never did like the MOBA genre of games, and this at first glance looked like another cookie cutter MOBA. One of my biggest gripes with DOTA and LoL is the click-to-move style of control. I never found it fun, kinda a personal issue. As someone with 1000+ hours in Spiral Knights, this WASD click-to-attack hacky-n-slashy style was a really welcome concept.
Alongside that, you can choose Battlerites during the game to further funkify stuff. It reminds me a lot of the mutation system in Nuclear Throne.
Aaaaaaand, on top of it all, there is no way to change character/champion/hero/god/battledude once you enter a game. Therefore, there is no real "rock paper scissors" aspect this game, and as such, you can feel free to main whatever character you like, without people complaining that you aren't "countering" someone.
Games are short and sweet, or short and sour. If you're reking the enemy, you'll win quick. If they're reking you, it's over quick. It's great because you're not locked into a 50+ minute game with completely incompetent dweeberonis.
But, as much as I like this game, I'll highlight some flaws/cons:
-Some abilities feel a bit off, such as Croak(my main)'s swords/daggers having a bit shorter of a range than I feel they should. It's almost like the swords are longer than the actual attack radius. This is more of a quality of life thing, all things considered.
-Maps are very same-y. Pretty much all maps have the exact same layout, the only difference being the way you enter. I'm sure they'll add more variety in the future, however.
-Game mode restricted. So far I've only really found the head-to-head arena gamemode, which makes me think it's the only one in the game. While it is perfectly fine, and definitely fun, I feel like the game could use some more variety.

Shadow Warrior is everything I've expected from DNF, but without Duke Nukem. It has great (and witty, not purely childish) humor, a good gameplay (although some attacks need to be boosted/nerfed and the player should encounter a little less invisible walls), incredible easter eggs (8 bit zones taken from the original game, extremely satisfying to find and rather well hidden), and an extremely satisfying lifespan (around 25h for a single playthrough without searching for all the secrets).
As for the story, it is delightfully poetic and somehow managed to surprise me. Usually, every game I play lets me guess what's going to happen way before it does, but Shadow Warrior didn't let me.
Apart from a few bugs and such that could be polished faster by a bigger company, Shadow Warrior represents everything that an AAA game should be: the cream of the crop.
Sadly, today, AAA means Advertised Asmuchaspossible Andallthetime, so I won't call SW an AAA game. It simply is a great game, and it deserves to be bought and played extensively by anyone who calls themselves a gamer or an FPS fan. It is the perfectly successful revival of an old character, and I can't thank Flying Wild Hog enough for that.
Gearbox ruined Duke Nukem and it really saddened me, but SW made up for all the disappointment that DNF brought me.

Game is ♥♥♥♥ing bananas.  This was the first shooter I played in a long time where I had so much ♥♥♥♥ing FUN.  The game makes you feel like a badass samurai slicing enemies up.  Gameplay is incredibly fast paced - reminiscent of the Serious Sam type of gameplay where enemies come at you in an open arena nonstop.  This is one of the few FPSes out there where the melee is far better than the gunplay.  The guns are great, don't get me wrong, but you really feel like you're tearing things up once you get skills to allow you to use special moves with your katana.
The story's pretty good.  Uses characters based off of Chinese and Japanese mythology.  The character interaction between Lo Wang and Hoji (an exiled demon who helps you out) is awesome - lots of banter but in a good sort of way.  You almost get the "buddy cop" feeling as Hoji initially starts off as an irritating sidekick and the story progresses to a point where you start enjoying his company.
The level design is still somewhat linear - there's "off the beaten path" options you can take to get extra ammo and secrets.  It's actually very important to find as many of these as possible - skipping over them can limit the upgrades you get.  But it's nothing along the lines of the original where you have to jump into hidden walls or break open hard-to-see cracks in the wall to get to them.  Usually it's some sort of fork that leads to these.
Tons of references to different aspects of pop culture, lots of throwbacks to the classic Shadow Warrior, and incredibly intense battles.  The bossfights are actually a bit of a weak point, but they do the job.
I finished this game in about 15 hours.  That is UNHEARD of for a modern shooter game.  Each chapter is incredibly long, and just like old school Shadow Warrior, you have the luxury of being able to save at any time.  Very convenient when you can only play this game in spurts, and probably a necessity considering some levels take over an hour to fully complete.
If you can find this game on sale, GET IT.

Fantastic looking game with some amazing boss fights. It's challenging but fair most of the time. The level design and soundtrack are fantastic.
- Let's start with the biggest problem: the tons of running. You will spend half of your time backtracking to the boss or your lost points. It`s normal to backtrack 4 minutes just for a 2 minute boss fight over and over again. Wanna go back to the city? 5 - 10 min. Lost right before a savepoint? Theres no running past enemies most of the time so better do the whole 20 min area again. Wanna retry a jumping challenge? 5-10 min backtracking. Go to the Bank? 5 min. Oh, and don't forget farming. Never seen a game treating the players time with such disrespect.
- The way the game is designed you have a strange difficulty curve. It starts of perfectly fine and turns quite hard one third trough. After that it only gets easier. I even killed the last 5 bosses by facetanking them. The last endgame content is difficult again. Those mid game weapon upgrades are way too overpowered. Such open worlds need some sort of scaling or weaker upgrades. Otherwise some content has to get too easy near the end. But never dying removed the backtracking which made the game extremly enjoyable.
- They have put an unaccessible secret into nearly every room. There are dozens of places you need to remeber but no map marker feature. I can't think of any game needing this more than this one.
- Shops are all over the place without any reason other than to let the player backtrack even more. This is really cheap playtime inflation.

- I finished the games story and i have to disagree with most reviews. They praise the story way above what it actually is. Sure, it's good and sometimes really charming but not the holy once in a lifetime revelation some describe it as.

- Having no save point near Crystallised Mound is stupid. Acient basin and Deepnest could use some more save points and stag stations too. Crystal cave needs a stag station, the Hive or Kingdom`s Edge too.
They actually added one new stag station in the acient basin. A step in the right direction. The new teleport ability helps a bit too but is given way to late into the game. Hope these weren´t the last backtracking fixes. At least two more patches to go.
- Steam forums are always more or less bad but HK forum takes the crown. 95% of all responses are pure garbage. Look at the subreddit if you need help.
Honestly, all negative points could be forgiven if it wasn´t for the insane amount of backtracking. Imagine having to stare at a blank wall for 20 minutes after every fight in street fighter. That`s what this game feels like. If you don`t mind that at all, go ahead and buy it. It`s a really good game otherwise.
More benches and bench teleporting (or just more stag stations). Bam 10/10 game of the year.
Since a comment showed that people don`t get my review heres some clarification. I have no personal problem with the difficulty. I love frustrating boss fights. Some parts of the game are just unfair which is bad game design but i don`t mind it that much. I`ve spend most of my time playing with mindless boring running. No challenge, no skill, just mundane and stale running. Originally this was done mostly in old games as a way to strech game time. This outdated design decision should be buried and forgotten.

Better late then never!  Dungeon Defenders is honestly one of the best Indie games I have ever played.   The fusion of RPG elements and progressive leveling with tower defense is refreshing and fun.  On the surface the game feels offers a story, albeit weak one, to complete and many different challenges; however, the game has much more to offer than just this.   Going out and challenging maps on harder difficulties, completing harder challenges for rewards and titles, and even the collecting of higher level equipment as you go through survival runs all await anyone that is willing to welcome the challenge.
The game does have its flaws.  Be prepared to get DLC'd out of the gym.  While there are welcomed additions, there is just a glut of content here that is being bundled and sold.  Secondly, be prepared for disconnects.  Occasionally, when steam loses connectivity, you will also be booted out of your game with no way of saving your progression midway.  This can be very frustrating when you are doing the longer survival runs.  Lastly, progression through harder content can be a little difficult for most.  This is mainly due to no real explaination on HOW to progress.  It is very much possible to progress your characters after the storyline, but if solo, be prepared to fight for inches.
Despite all of this, the game is one of the BEST games you can play for the investment.  It has the depth of a MMO and the ease of access like your casual IOS game.  I highly recommend the game.

While each gun you can use is wildly different from each other and satisfying to shoot, it's the swordplay that really takes the cake here. Each swing brutally decapitates lesser demons in a convincing way and the special Ki attacks are equally satisfying and cleverly implemented. Even with the fun weapon variety, I still find myself going back to the blade for most of my murdering needs. Each level is quite varied from each other with a fairly wide color pallete and if you appreciate a nice cringe-worthy pun, you'll really enjoy the humor in this game as well. I only have a couple complaints about the game, those being the somewhat bullet spongy larger demons (which become more manageable once you get some upgrades) and the lack of direction some of the game gives you (there was more than one occasion where I had to circle around an area multiple times in order to find the tiny gold button or keycard that would let me progress). These complaints are fairly minor and shouldn't take away from my recommendation overall.
8.5/10 - Easily worth your time and the price of admission with only a couple minor annoyances that are quickly forgotton as soon as you behead another demon with a ki blast swung from your sword.

Better late then never!  Dungeon Defenders is honestly one of the best Indie games I have ever played.   The fusion of RPG elements and progressive leveling with tower defense is refreshing and fun.  On the surface the game feels offers a story, albeit weak one, to complete and many different challenges; however, the game has much more to offer than just this.   Going out and challenging maps on harder difficulties, completing harder challenges for rewards and titles, and even the collecting of higher level equipment as you go through survival runs all await anyone that is willing to welcome the challenge.
The game does have its flaws.  Be prepared to get DLC'd out of the gym.  While there are welcomed additions, there is just a glut of content here that is being bundled and sold.  Secondly, be prepared for disconnects.  Occasionally, when steam loses connectivity, you will also be booted out of your game with no way of saving your progression midway.  This can be very frustrating when you are doing the longer survival runs.  Lastly, progression through harder content can be a little difficult for most.  This is mainly due to no real explaination on HOW to progress.  It is very much possible to progress your characters after the storyline, but if solo, be prepared to fight for inches.
Despite all of this, the game is one of the BEST games you can play for the investment.  It has the depth of a MMO and the ease of access like your casual IOS game.  I highly recommend the game.

On my radar, there are currently only three major FPS/Tower Defense games out. The first one I experienced was 'Sanctum' (thanks, Stormy!). It was a crazy tower-building game that put you in the middle of all the action-packed craziness, which became even more fun in multiplayer (and I'm one of those that usually likes to play solo). However, it had one major flaw; it seriously lacked content. Though the weapons were interesting enough, the number of maps simply were not. Combined with a limited story, this one ultimately felt a little unfinished. [note: there were several DLC packs including more maps and/or weapons and a comic online somewhere]
The next one I tried was 'Orcs Must Die!' (thanks again, Stormy!), a lighthearted and funny game, with plenty of weapons and traps. The sequel was more of the same with more of everything, including an option for having a second player, which the original did not have. This one was more of a "trap-defense" than tower defense though, since it had a predefined maze system.
'Dungeon Defenders' is similar to OMD, consisting of a trivial story and being a trap-defense game with predefined mazes for enemies to travel. However, there isn't a real "grid", so things do not simply "snap" into place. The main aspect that sets this title ahead of the other two is that there's some "investment" into the character/characters (you can swap toons on the fly during the game between waves) you play. I really like the dash of action-RPG thrown into the mix, with leveling and picking the best gear. OMD also had some investment with the skulls/weapon upgrades, but anyone could get the maximum number of upgrades on weapons and traps if they put in enough time to earn the skulls. DD takes a step further to add uniqueness in customizing your character. Leveling your character takes care of the traps, but luck and personal comparing gear choices is what makes your character different from everyone else's. [note: lots of DLC for this one... maybe too much, but at least some of it's free]
Now, I'm really looking forward to playing the upcoming sequels for Sanctum and Dungeon Defenders.

Not typically into platformers but I bought this almost on a whim and have so far really enjoyed it. It's difficult and can get frustrating at times but that seems the story of most platforming games. The world is very weird and wacky, it's also incredibly beautiful, you can tell the massive amounts of work that has been put into the world, characters and dialogue.
In terms of the gameplay, it's very open and this might put some people off, I was unsure at first. After the first 10 or 15 minutes, you're not told where to go or who to kill, the game very much encourages you to just wander and see what you can find. It does quietly guide you as you're unable to progress past certain areas without specific powers but outside of that, the maps/levels are large and it's easy to get lost. You are also not provided with a map, you must find the explorer dude somewhere in the level who then gives you the map, so you can be exploring blindly for a while. This isn't a bad thing, the game really wants you to explore of your own free will and you spend a lot of time doing exactly that.
It also has a Souls esque death system whereby you collect currency and then drop it on death, you must then make it back to your death point to get the money back, if you die again, you loose it all. It can be a bit merciless at times, especially when you're just struggling with a boss while also trying to save up for that new cool looking item, but it definitely adds a certain 'tension' to the game.
Definitely recommend it. If you're into platformers this'll be a real favourite, if not, you'll still enjoy it.
