Going into Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag, I was expecting fun. Reviews of the ship gameplay had been favourable, and that seemed like the selling point of the whole thing. Despite the often repetitive gameplay of the sidequests, it was indeed fun. I found myself lost exploring the oceans, firing off cannons at ships twice the size of mine just to scrape together the metal needed to make myself an even more menacing pirate. With sugar and rum exploding out of my sleeves, I really did feel like a freedom fighter of the 18th century. Even when I was ashore I felt like a true badarse, firing off my four pistols while simultaenously fighting off guards with swords and knives.
That being said, the game as it stands isn't hard. There's certainly enough challenge to be had in the side quests and optional objectives within the storyline, but if you want to just charge in with no concern for the silent approach (probably closer to a true pirate), then so be it. And I love that. Optional difficulty that isn't a menu option is really what makes me want to keep playing.
Sure there's not much replayability, but it was certainly a game I enjoyed. I'll definitely be watching Ubisoft closely for the new Assassin's Creed release and most likely continuing my adventure in Black Flag, squeezing every bit of gameplay I can out of it.

Overall, I really like this AC, and I hope the next one will have a similar "do whatever you want" philosophy.

While this title has near universal public praise, I will focus on the 'cons' for those on the fence. Typically in games that take over 10 hours to complete, small issues in the begining become really annoying in late game.
As far as I can see, save for the universe setting, there is not a single idea that is fresh here. That's not a horrible thing - because it is all done
well. You will be treading over the entire map many, many times. You get permanent upgrades that allow you to access areas that you couldn't before. You collect badges of sorts, that give you different powers. For example some extend your swing, some get you more money per kill, and others give you armor buffs. You crawl through a level, kill a boss, and collect rewards along the way.
+Remarkable artwork and soundtrack - I can't emphasize this enough.
+Super tight controls that are awesome with a controller from the couch.
+There is a ton of game to be had with a 10-15 hour main game, and I hear there is NG+.
+Awesome universe where it is just a pleasure to experience all the different worlds.
+Yeah, it is addicting. I put in 10 hours with about a two day period, which is rare for me.
-
I know this is a point of contention, but after 10 hours, I am 100% certain that this is the biggest problem with this title. When you die (lets say in a boss fight), you will respawn at the last bench (save point) you sat at. Sometimes its like two rooms away, but a majority of the time its a slightly longer trek. This really adds up unless you can kill a boss in two trys, or so. It's a difficult game, lets be honest. Sometimes I had to fight a boss more than five times, which translates to a
of walking. Some gamers claim that people with this problem are not finding the bench rooms, but I assure you - I am. I know some are hidden and I actively look. I think the people that don't find this to be a problem are just great at twitch-style gaming. For the amount of time I game, I'm decidedly
.
-
This was my main point with
, too. When I find myself rage-quitting and coming up with new swear words, I generally am having a bad time. While
more tested ones platforming skills,
is more testing combat reflexes - so I am doing a bit better in this case. I do fear end-game skill requirements, though. The difficulty is right on the fence for me, where I am always balancing when I will decide it has gotten too difficult.
-
There is not a single new idea in here as far as I am concerned. This would usually be a deal-breaker for me, but the unique universe setting and just overall great gameplay makes up for it.
-
There is dialogue, but after a bunch of hours you realize its more-or-less meaningless filler. The town hub had me thinking there would be a story, but nope. I think this is a major 'con', honestly. It needs legs to stand on for how long it takes to complete.

So, after i played some hours, i can say that i really enjoyed playing Battlerite.
The abilities feel good, the characters show great diversity, the fights are fun and intense, the rounds are quick.
Battlerite is very competitive and with every game you are trying to improve your skills more and more, dodge more attacks and ultis, support your teammates, play mind games with the ennemies. A Match takes about 5 to 15 minutes (my experience). You are able to chose between 2 vs 2 games or 3 vs 3 games. It's pure PvP. "Feeding" an ennemy is impossible, there's no ingame shop to buy better items during the match. After every round every player is able to chose one upgrade for his character, so you can adjust your character in every new game.
I know that Battlerite is Early Acess, but i still wanna write down the negative things. I hope those will be patched in the future.
- There's no option to lower or higher your mouse sensitivity. This option should be very important in such a fast game, because some people prefer lower or higher mouse sensitivity. You really need to "aim" in Battlerite.
- AFK's. I saw that there is a report button after every match. I just hope that the developers deal with this problem. I'm having an AFK like every 5th game. Why? Because it's very easy to just click the join button and idle a whole match. People are doing this to level up there characters (for each level you get ingame money to buy cosmetics or chests. at some levels you get chests right away. You can open those chests to get some new cosmetics or Avatars. You don't need to buy keys for real money to open those chests, like we know from other games). Players abuse the possibility to idle whole matches. I just hope they are getting banned for some days for doing this.
- Adding a possibilty to enable "Instant-Casts" in the options would be great too, but it's not one of the most important things for this game. It would be still a nice feature to add this.
Nontheless it's a great game for this Early Stage, i hope to see a lot more Characters and Arenas in the future.

*Updated Review after playing The Grimm Troupe:*
This is still by far the best metroidvania I've played in recent years, and this definitely comes from the multiple aspects that make a game great.
Hollow Knight is a game in which you take control of "The Knight" and explore the vast, ruined kingdom of Hallownest. On this journey you'll learn about the kingdom's history, why you've come to this kingdom, and how the fall of this once tremendous empire even occured.
-The art direction is absolutely superb, which always made me excited to find the next area.
-Every area has unique enemies that make you consider how to go about attacking/avoiding them.
-The NPCs you meet are all unique and most are actually voiced which really helps makes the characters feel alive.
-A sprawling underground kingdom for you to explore, which also includes fast travel points that you unlock for easier/faster travel.
-A multitude of bosses, each of which are just as fun as the last.
-A soundtrack filled with amazing songs that each fit the tone of their respective area.
-There's so much more I can't even put it into words
-There's also a charm system that gives you abitlies/slight combat changes and allows for too many combinations to count.
The Hidden Dreams and The Grimm Troupe DLCs have also been released which are completely free, and add more bosses, items, as well as secrets to the ever mysterious kingdom of Hallownest.
I couldn't recommend this game enough its easily one of the best games of its time and should be considered an industry standard for future metroidvanias.

I wanna start out by saying i really love this game!
Really fluid gameplay, good depth and varied champions.
But as this game is 100% competitive (No unranked queues) i have some major gripes with it.
- To start with you are not guaranted to get a support in 2v2, which means if the one team doesnt get one and the other does you are in a major disadvantage (Yes i do think that certain supports are really strong in this game).
- The balancing is questionable at best. Let me give you an example: Support hero Lucie has no inherent dodge (She has an ex one but really you dont want to spend ultimate charge on it) nor counter making her an extremely easy target. Support hero Sirius however has a dodge and a counter that even teleports him to a new place, oh did i mention he has an AOE petrify that lasts for 3.4 secs? Also his standard attack can infilct weaken which reduces healing and DAMAGE for 50% over 2.5 secs (Up to 3.5 secs). While Lucie on the other hand has a knockback and cleanse potion with terrible travel time. I'm not gonna bother with the rest of her abilities, they are all very lackluster except for the shield.
Also do you love seeing the same characters over and over? Because you're gonna see a lot of: Poloma, Sirius, Varesh to mention the most popular ones. (In my experience).
Poloma is by far the worst designed support i've ever seen, not that she's bad but rather that she is nearly unkillable (While still healing mind you) since she can not only make herself invulnerable for nearly 2 secs and also has an interrupt that causes panic. Dont even bother ignoring her, she is just as good standing in the backline.
Sirius i've already talked about.
And Varesh is crazy good even more so with experienced people, double counter's, constant debuffs that he can shatter for healing and an ultimate that makes him invulnerable during the channel. Do you like constantly teleporting heroes because this guy is all over the place.
I hope that these champions will be changed in the recent future as i love the concept of most of the current ones, but it's just so boring when these three curbstomp any competition. Though if you play this casually like i do then it's fine i guess ^^ But i dont bother with ranked when basically only 3 champions are viable in my opinion.

Pick a hero and fight in an arena against other players.  That's the main premise of Battlerite, and while that might not sound that exciting the game's core mechanics and balance is well done.
You pick a hero (15 total at the moment), choose 3v3 or 2v2, and jump almost instantly into a game.  At the start of each round you pick a Battlerite (which is a buff for your abilities that lasts in each concurrent round).  You spawn on the left side of the arena and head straight to the middle and fight over middle control. Each game is a bo5, and each round doesn't last too long.  Games are quick so it's easy to fix and understand your mistakes.
The mechanics of Battlerite are neat, and play like a fighting game. You have energy and health, and as you get hit you lose some of your max health.  Poking is very important in Battlerite.  In the middle of the arena is an orb which when burst open gives energy and some lost max health back. Energy is used for your ultimate (which cost 100%), and a lesser ability that is pretty strong (which cost 25%).  Each hero also has two EX abilities, similar to a fighting game.   These 2 upgraded abilities cost a varying amount of energy and make a skill stronger. Each hero also has a mount + mount speedbost.  The mount has a small channel time, so you can use it to get around the arena and get straight into the action at the start of each round.
Overall, Battlerite feels and plays like a completed game.  The game's future looks bright, and I'd gladly recommend it to anyone who enjoys PVP battles.  Even if you are casual as hell, the game offers a lot of fun and is easy to understand.   With only more content to come, it's a great purchase.

Possibly the best metroidvania on Steam. There is SO MUCH content in one playthrough, it will blow your mind. If you like to take your time and explore every little section of the map like I do, it will take you over 20 hours to beat the game. That itself is a selling point for some people, but the real selling points are in all of the fine details.
The tight controls. The way they made the platforming and the combat equally meaningful. Rewarding exploration. A beautiful and unique hand drawn aesthetic. A world that feels alive with all sorts of unique locations, NPC's, unique enemies, spirits, destructible scenery, and enough backstory / lore to give you an emotional connection to the world. The epic and challenging boss battles that will test all of your skill. The gigantic map. The tasteful use of limited charms to unlock new combat potential. The classic staple of unlocking new areas by acquiring new abilities. THE SOUND DESIGN that will give you the chills. The sparse voice acting that gives each NPC so much character!
Everything about this game feels deliberate. Everything about it feels fair. You can feel the love put into every detail. The game is a damn masterpiece. Buy it.

Shadow Warrior is an old school 90s-style shooter that is a spiritual successor to the 90s FPS of the same name, only with modern graphics and sound, RPG-style upgrades and effects.  The original Shadow Warrior used the same "Build" engine as Duke Nukem and was released in 1997.  I haven't been able to stop playing this game since I got it.  Features include smart♥♥♥♥♥protagonists, over the top violence, numerous enemies, and large maps with SECRETS.  Yes, exploring is encouraged in an FPS once again!  The maps include power ups, money, weapons, and secret rooms and areas - very old school and awesome.  Each level is linear but not in a CoD way, since you need to find keys and switches to access different parts of each level, requiring backtracking - yes, that 90s FPS trope, BACKTRACKING.  It's not overdone and never boring, however.  You have upgradable guns, skills and powers - including a kitana sword (my personal favorite) - and you'll need them all to fight the hoardes of baddies and the BOSSES.  Bosses!  No regenerating health in this game, though, so you'll have to look for ammo and health packs, but I haven't been at a loss for either outside of big boss battles (I'm at level 8 of the game).  I got it on sale for $9.99 which is a steal - this modernized Shadow Warrior is highly recommended!

Amazing game.
Positives:
Controls are tight, progression feels incredibly open and the game poses a decent challenge overall. It's incredible to see how much you can improve throughout the game, and the game lets you by offering a wide variety of simple moves that blend well together.
The map is surprisingly expansive and intricate, and there are lots of things to discover. The upgrades especially feel really natural, and not just like "red keycard, blue keycard".
And I love the art. Seriously, bugs as knights? They already wear armor, it's perfect!
Criticism:
It assumes players are familiar with the basics of Metroidvanias and Souls-like games. Most of the game is self-explanatory, but specific mechanics, like how only one shade can exist at a time, are straight from other games, and while they work well here too, aren't fully explained.
Still, if you keep your eyes open, you'll be fine, and it does enough unique things to not feel too derivative either.
All in all, fantastic little game, but beginners might have a tough time with later areas.

This game is amazing. It will be the game that kills League, mark my words. Already 2k overwhelmingly positive steam reviews within 3 days of Early Access? Wow.
Anyway, after spending thousands of hours in League and getting tired of it, I decided to try this game after getting hyped by the trailer.
For everyone who's been frustrated lately by certain things about League and other MOBAs, this game most likely has what you're looking for. First off, everything is based purely on skill, there is no luck factor in this game. There is a 2v2 and 3v3 ranked mode, and it is definitely possible for you to carry yourself if you are good enough. It's basically a fast paced League style combat with 100% skillshots and is all about outplaying your opponents. There's no farming creeps for 30 minutes and in fact a full game only lasts 10-15 minutes. It's also got a Co-op vs AI mode for practicing. The heroes I've tried so far seem unique and fairly well balanced.
Overall the game is just fun, the graphics are great, and you can unlock tons of cool stuff through in game currency. It's a competitive player's wet dream.

Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is the usual Assassin's Creed game, with open world exploration, free running, epic combat and a historical setting. This time, however, the setting is 18th century Caribbean and that means pirates. Assassin's Creed and pirates, need I say more? :P
While the modern arc of the storyline is really weird, I found that the historical arc was very interesting and engaging. Definitely a major improvement over Assassin's Creed III. The combat system is even more advanced that ever, with the usual counter-kills and assassination moves, but now including even more pistol usage and interaction with the world around you. Naval combat, being the main focus of the game, has been revamped and upgraded since the previous title. One thing I did notice was that compared to previous Assassin's Creed games, makng money (in order to buy new weapons, outfits and upgrade your ship and mansion) was a lot more difficult.
Black Flag was a really fun game to play and I highly recommend getting it, especially if you're a fan of the Assassin's Creed series. Or pirates. :P

It's been a while since I last played a videogame that made me want to fling my controller through a brick wall out of frustration. Welcome to


Hollow Knight. But that's selling it short.
Hollow Knight is a beautiful hand drawn 2D action/adventure game with a good heaping helping of Dark Souls influence thrown in there. The story unfolds very slowly and it is entirely up to you whether it unfolds at all. You need to discover the story as you wander through the hallowed halls of, heh, Hallownest. Along the way, you'll find plenty of different monsters to keep you company, some eccentric and some disturbing NPCs and of course, so much loot that you won't know what to do with it all.
The only downsides for me are the sometime finicky platforming which can lead to some grey hair as you mess up and land in spikes, or acid, for the fifteenth time in a row - and the combat. In Hollow Knight, you are filled with feathers and as you connect with a hit on a monster, it knocks you back which I find completely stupid but not a dealbreaker. That, and there's a Charm that'll fix that for ya.
For 14,99€, the game has a ridiculous amount of content in it and I don't regret buying it at all.

I was waiting for optimization updates before giving a positive rating.  The low FPS really frustrated me when I played the beta - I didn't expect a 2D game built for PC to be running at like 10-15 frames.  Now I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to people like me who want a fun, different type of adventure, but don't want to spend money on high-end computers.
Edit (4/20/2017):  I lied, optimization only moderately improved (like five-to-seven frames in general), which was not enough for this type of game.  Did not consider it a problem in the first hours of gameplay, tried to tolerate it for the majority of it, but now at the point of harder platforming and combat where low framerates lead to really frustrating deaths and delays in progress.  It's at the point where I can't tell if the input lag for jumping (especially wall jumping) was intended or not because all the areas I really need precise, fluid-feeling controls are too laggy to let me tell.  There are certainly some neat graphical details that take some rendering, but I find it hard to believe that a game that overall looks about as detailed as like Megaman X4, even after lowering the particle settings, could still run so slow.
I probably should've seen this coming when the only iteration of the beta I saw pretty much demanded you use higher-end computers... for a 2D indie game.  As a Kickstarter backer, it's disappointing since I had really high hopes for this game as an option for people like me on a hardware budget.  Part of the consideration for supporting indie games is because they're supposed to be the interesting games you can still play even when you can't run something like Skyrim or Overwatch at decent frames.  Games like Darkest Dungeon, Undertale, Banner Saga, or their more active counterparts like Risk of Rain, Fez, Papo & Yo - they all (probably) run better.  If the closest game to Hollow Knight in terms of graphical density and genre, Ori in the Blind Forest, only runs just as well as Hollow Knight, then disregard what I'm saying (even though my system isn't even that old), but I doubt that's the case.
In its current state, I can't recommend Hollow Knight anymore to people with lower-end machines.  Well, if there's a sale go for it, but barring that it won't be worth the frustration of dropping down a stage for the fifth time because your wall jump didn't input, falling down onto spikes after being hit because the lag makes it that much harder to remanuveur yourself onto a platform, etc.  I hope Team Cherry will continue to optimize the PC version of this game so I can give it a thumbs-up.
Edit (6/22/2017):  When Team Cherry first listed Hollow Knight on Kickstarter, their golden standard for gameplay was Megaman 2.  After the latest patch, I can comfortably say that low-end users like me who appreciated the ambition that Team Cherry showed off years ago can now (probably) appreciate the actual game itself.  Where wall jumps used to have hitches in moderately intense particle areas, there are none, and framerate in high intensity particle stages now feels mangeable.  I hope Team Cherry continues to pursue the indie game spirit and strives to make their games accessible to all types of users.

Possibly the best metroidvania on Steam. There is SO MUCH content in one playthrough, it will blow your mind. If you like to take your time and explore every little section of the map like I do, it will take you over 20 hours to beat the game. That itself is a selling point for some people, but the real selling points are in all of the fine details.
The tight controls. The way they made the platforming and the combat equally meaningful. Rewarding exploration. A beautiful and unique hand drawn aesthetic. A world that feels alive with all sorts of unique locations, NPC's, unique enemies, spirits, destructible scenery, and enough backstory / lore to give you an emotional connection to the world. The epic and challenging boss battles that will test all of your skill. The gigantic map. The tasteful use of limited charms to unlock new combat potential. The classic staple of unlocking new areas by acquiring new abilities. THE SOUND DESIGN that will give you the chills. The sparse voice acting that gives each NPC so much character!
Everything about this game feels deliberate. Everything about it feels fair. You can feel the love put into every detail. The game is a damn masterpiece. Buy it.

While I slightly despise the recent trend of rebooting old franchises with their original names while often not being half as satisfying as the original this one obviously has been done very well. The joy, the action, the massacre is actually comparable to the 1997 Shadow Warrior. The game is fast, smooth and feels perfect. Some great weapon and character upgrades (and also some less interesting), good looking graphics and fun character models. So the following nitpicks are far from game-breaking, but noticeable.
When talking about fast paced FPS games from the 90's I don't care about cut-scenes and storylines in general (unless they would be very original and compelling, or really fun) and I'm not exactly in need of a snarky companion while killing bad guys. Both story and characters have been well executed and everything is fully skippable if you so desire, but the story itself hasn't got a lot of depth or originality to offer, really. Still, I guess you could have a much much worse companion than Hoji.
The biggest con though would be the level design, when compared to the original. It's much more linear and not as huge and maze-like, and consequently there's not as much sense of freedom. I want to be able to backtrack from start to the end and back again, but the game explicitly does not let you do so. Also there are tons of locations where it clearly looks like you can go somewhere, except for those infamous invisible walls. There's still quite some explorational fun to be had, just not as complicated or with as much freedom as the original.
But man, does the game look good and man are that sword and its powers satisfying to use. Nothing of the points of criticism takes away any of that and neither did it stop me from grinning like a maniac most of the time. This is by far one of my favorite modern FPS games and I would heartily recommend it to anyone and everyone. As long as they enjoy flying limbs and tons of blood.

Dungeon Defenders is the first game to combine hardcore tower defense with hack-and-slash RPG elements to make a truly unique experience, and a massive replay value to boot! There's always a score to beat, whether it's someone else's or your own.
Easy to learn, hard to master: With difficulty levels ranging from Easy to the ultimate difficuly, Nightmare, you'll always find a challenge no matter how powerful or skilled you become.
Item drops are generated using a RNG akin to that of Diablo's for a seemingly infinite variety of loot. The maps are wonderfully done, and enjoyable to build on, as well as simply explore.
Each DLC Trendy Entertainment conceives is usually free within the first week of its release, and the game itself goes on sale relatively frequently.
The main downsides I've noticed are that you will probably get bored of the game once you've tackled all the content and challenges, and later drops can vary greatly in quality giving you the feeling you might be stuck in a sort of 'limbo'.
Due to the division of tower and character stats, you will probably end up having "builder" and "combat" characters, so you will end up having to switch out during different phases.
Personally I would have preferred stats and their parallel counterparts to be the same, as well as giving each player their own fraction of a stage's total build units, which would keep every character relevant and allow every player to contribute to and be involved in both aspects of the game.
Overall though, Dungeon Defenders is an even greater value than its price denotes, and with this much content, I can promise time well spent too.
I look forward to seeing the improvements Dungeon Defenders 2 will likely make to this experience.

What do you get if you combine Dark Souls with Castlevania, push the difficulty to the limit, and turn everyone into bugs? Hollow Knight may give you an answer to this question, but leave you with many others. This is a game that revels in mystery, from the moment you enter its mesmerizing world to striking the killing blow on its final boss. You're never really told what's going on, exactly. You can figure it out if you pay attention! All the information is there, but you'll have to reach out for it.
Hollow Knight came out of nowhere for me, though I understand that it is a kickstarter game, due to the presence of backer characters in some locations. It's clearly inspired by classic titles of the genre, but the invertebrate motif is what really caught my interest. Rarely do you see a concept so fully realized: they take the "what if everyone was bugs" thing and ride it as far as they possibly can, replacing conventional weaponry with nails and shells and inventing a background story concerning the transformation of unthinking insect towards personhood and eventual undeath.
That's not to say there aren't some controversial aspects of the game, to be sure. Some may disagree with its punishing approach to exploration: players can only update their map whenever they make their way back to a save point, where they may rest and take out their quill to draw the relevant details and mark any important objects with pins. You also cannot draw a map until you have something to draw it on: a traveling merchant will sell you the canvas, but you have to find him in each new area first, and until then you are exploring the place without any sort of guidance. Take this and the possibility of visiting those areas in pretty much any order you please and you have a recipe for truly getting lost in some obscure corner of Hallownest.
A notable departure from similar titles is that the powerups of the game follow a conservative approach with only small increases in strength compared to what your character starts out with. The result of this is that enemies and traps continue to be threatening for a much longer time than you would expect, and you'd be wise to keep your wits about you even during travels through previously explored territory. You may find "charms" which can be equipped to strengthen your character in significant ways, but only a few of them can be worn at a time, so you will start looking for particularly strong "builds" of charms that work well together, for example by combining the charms that improve your weapon or the ones that improve defense.
I assumed this would be quite similar to Ori and the Blind Forest, but I couldn't have been more wrong - this is a massive, sprawling world unlike anything I've seen and you will be repeatedly surprised by some new detail of things, as if Billy Mays popped his head up to say "But wait, there's more!" It may not have the killer pacing of Ori but it certainly comes out on top in the sheer volume of fantastic content packaged into one game.

I did not expect a remake for a classic such as Shadow Warrior. But after their cyberpunk FPS, Hard Reset, Flying Wild Hog decided to keep the old school shooter formula and use a more recognisable name. I like how the game does not take itself seriously - while the story is somewhat serious (suddenly demons appear out of nowhere) it does not stop our protagonist, Lo Wang, from delivering one-liners here and there (usually, after a successful slicing up of an enemy). Even the conversations he has with his companion make you smile and some of the references to other products of the entertainment industry can be hilarious.
In the golden era of FPS games melee combat was uninteresting. In fact, after a level or two the melee weapon was never used again. Shadow Warrior used an equally weak weapon in the form of a katana and this is what the remake keeps; in fact, with the abilities and upgrades the player can acquire later on this weapon becomes even more useful. Also, while the rest of the arsenal consists of the usual firearms (submachine guns, shotgun, grenade launcher etc.) this array of weapons is also upgradable so here you also have some nice surprises - in order to have all upgrades and skills in place you need to finish the game once more in new game plus mode.
Hard Reset was rather repetitive. Both the environment and the tasks you needed to carry out remained pretty much the same throughout the story. Shadow Warrior employs different surroundings each time and with the scripted events and various tasks you have the desired variety at hand throughout your quest. And while the game was not developed as an AAA title some of the levels can be jaw-dropping. The music accompanying your missions is equally good. Then of course you have a lot of collectibles and dozens of achievements.
Shadow Warrior is one of the best old school style FPS games out there. The developer support is also commendable - they do listen to you and ever since its release date last September they have kept upgrading the game and constantly fixing any issues players encounter. Thumbs-up!

As much as I enjoyed the gunplay - shredding demons into bloody gibs is very satifying indeed I was totally frustrated by ridiculous hand-holding and invisible walls as well as inability to backtrack to explore. This is just infuriating.
Pros:
+ Really satisfying gunplay
+ Somewhat funny one liners
+ More or less not-a-bad story
+ Graphics is also good
Cons:
- Inability to backtrack (doors are closed not only in front of you, but behind you. Doors you should be able to open, but for some reason you can't)
- Invisible walls EVERYWHERE
- Ridiculous skill spikes. I think the most hard battle was not a boss fight, but a fight with mere two Berserkers.
- Finding secrets is not very satisfying as they are "hidden" in plain view. But you miss some of them because finding them sometimes implies checking where there is an Invisible wall and where there is not. It's just boring.
- Complex system of skills/powers/upgrades is not very useful. I predict healing from Ki and katana strikes. Demons die faster just from WW-M1. Stamina is useful though. I have troubles with deciding what to pick for Kis and Karma beginning from chapters 7-8 because I equally DON'T need everything I don't have.
- Same goes with weapons. I found the Shotty and Flamer to be quite redundant.
All in all, it might be fine for someone who is looking for a shooty-blowy shooter and does not feel the urge to search every level through. If you like to rummage areas for loot I think you will be as much frustrated as I am right now.
But at least it's not as bad as Duke Nukem Forever, so I guess that counts.

I was waiting for optimization updates before giving a positive rating.  The low FPS really frustrated me when I played the beta - I didn't expect a 2D game built for PC to be running at like 10-15 frames.  Now I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to people like me who want a fun, different type of adventure, but don't want to spend money on high-end computers.
Edit (4/20/2017):  I lied, optimization only moderately improved (like five-to-seven frames in general), which was not enough for this type of game.  Did not consider it a problem in the first hours of gameplay, tried to tolerate it for the majority of it, but now at the point of harder platforming and combat where low framerates lead to really frustrating deaths and delays in progress.  It's at the point where I can't tell if the input lag for jumping (especially wall jumping) was intended or not because all the areas I really need precise, fluid-feeling controls are too laggy to let me tell.  There are certainly some neat graphical details that take some rendering, but I find it hard to believe that a game that overall looks about as detailed as like Megaman X4, even after lowering the particle settings, could still run so slow.
I probably should've seen this coming when the only iteration of the beta I saw pretty much demanded you use higher-end computers... for a 2D indie game.  As a Kickstarter backer, it's disappointing since I had really high hopes for this game as an option for people like me on a hardware budget.  Part of the consideration for supporting indie games is because they're supposed to be the interesting games you can still play even when you can't run something like Skyrim or Overwatch at decent frames.  Games like Darkest Dungeon, Undertale, Banner Saga, or their more active counterparts like Risk of Rain, Fez, Papo & Yo - they all (probably) run better.  If the closest game to Hollow Knight in terms of graphical density and genre, Ori in the Blind Forest, only runs just as well as Hollow Knight, then disregard what I'm saying (even though my system isn't even that old), but I doubt that's the case.
In its current state, I can't recommend Hollow Knight anymore to people with lower-end machines.  Well, if there's a sale go for it, but barring that it won't be worth the frustration of dropping down a stage for the fifth time because your wall jump didn't input, falling down onto spikes after being hit because the lag makes it that much harder to remanuveur yourself onto a platform, etc.  I hope Team Cherry will continue to optimize the PC version of this game so I can give it a thumbs-up.
Edit (6/22/2017):  When Team Cherry first listed Hollow Knight on Kickstarter, their golden standard for gameplay was Megaman 2.  After the latest patch, I can comfortably say that low-end users like me who appreciated the ambition that Team Cherry showed off years ago can now (probably) appreciate the actual game itself.  Where wall jumps used to have hitches in moderately intense particle areas, there are none, and framerate in high intensity particle stages now feels mangeable.  I hope Team Cherry continues to pursue the indie game spirit and strives to make their games accessible to all types of users.

Possibly the best metroidvania on Steam. There is SO MUCH content in one playthrough, it will blow your mind. If you like to take your time and explore every little section of the map like I do, it will take you over 20 hours to beat the game. That itself is a selling point for some people, but the real selling points are in all of the fine details.
The tight controls. The way they made the platforming and the combat equally meaningful. Rewarding exploration. A beautiful and unique hand drawn aesthetic. A world that feels alive with all sorts of unique locations, NPC's, unique enemies, spirits, destructible scenery, and enough backstory / lore to give you an emotional connection to the world. The epic and challenging boss battles that will test all of your skill. The gigantic map. The tasteful use of limited charms to unlock new combat potential. The classic staple of unlocking new areas by acquiring new abilities. THE SOUND DESIGN that will give you the chills. The sparse voice acting that gives each NPC so much character!
Everything about this game feels deliberate. Everything about it feels fair. You can feel the love put into every detail. The game is a damn masterpiece. Buy it.

Amazing game.
Positives:
Controls are tight, progression feels incredibly open and the game poses a decent challenge overall. It's incredible to see how much you can improve throughout the game, and the game lets you by offering a wide variety of simple moves that blend well together.
The map is surprisingly expansive and intricate, and there are lots of things to discover. The upgrades especially feel really natural, and not just like "red keycard, blue keycard".
And I love the art. Seriously, bugs as knights? They already wear armor, it's perfect!
Criticism:
It assumes players are familiar with the basics of Metroidvanias and Souls-like games. Most of the game is self-explanatory, but specific mechanics, like how only one shade can exist at a time, are straight from other games, and while they work well here too, aren't fully explained.
Still, if you keep your eyes open, you'll be fine, and it does enough unique things to not feel too derivative either.
All in all, fantastic little game, but beginners might have a tough time with later areas.

Alright, here is the deal. I've read a lot of the reviews both posative and negative; the way I see it is that both sides are mostly right in their views / reasoning. I very much enjoyed the game and I feel that it is a bit short. I would love to see a second game or even an expansion. Sadly it looks like that will not happen any time soon. The Stanley Parable is very clever and at times quite funny. I purchased the game on release at full price. While I do think that anything over $10 USD is pushing it as a reasonable price for what you get here, I -personally- don't mind that I payed full price. My reasoning is that TSP is something semi unique, a fresh new concept, and an over all enjoyable experience; this is something I'm willing to pay extra to support. What do you get if you combine Dark Souls with Castlevania, push the difficulty to the limit, and turn everyone into bugs? Hollow Knight may give you an answer to this question, but leave you with many others. This is a game that revels in mystery, from the moment you enter its mesmerizing world to striking the killing blow on its final boss. You're never really told what's going on, exactly. You can figure it out if you pay attention! All the information is there, but you'll have to reach out for it.
Hollow Knight came out of nowhere for me, though I understand that it is a kickstarter game, due to the presence of backer characters in some locations. It's clearly inspired by classic titles of the genre, but the invertebrate motif is what really caught my interest. Rarely do you see a concept so fully realized: they take the "what if everyone was bugs" thing and ride it as far as they possibly can, replacing conventional weaponry with nails and shells and inventing a background story concerning the transformation of unthinking insect towards personhood and eventual undeath.
That's not to say there aren't some controversial aspects of the game, to be sure. Some may disagree with its punishing approach to exploration: players can only update their map whenever they make their way back to a save point, where they may rest and take out their quill to draw the relevant details and mark any important objects with pins. You also cannot draw a map until you have something to draw it on: a traveling merchant will sell you the canvas, but you have to find him in each new area first, and until then you are exploring the place without any sort of guidance. Take this and the possibility of visiting those areas in pretty much any order you please and you have a recipe for truly getting lost in some obscure corner of Hallownest.
A notable departure from similar titles is that the powerups of the game follow a conservative approach with only small increases in strength compared to what your character starts out with. The result of this is that enemies and traps continue to be threatening for a much longer time than you would expect, and you'd be wise to keep your wits about you even during travels through previously explored territory. You may find "charms" which can be equipped to strengthen your character in significant ways, but only a few of them can be worn at a time, so you will start looking for particularly strong "builds" of charms that work well together, for example by combining the charms that improve your weapon or the ones that improve defense.
I assumed this would be quite similar to Ori and the Blind Forest, but I couldn't have been more wrong - this is a massive, sprawling world unlike anything I've seen and you will be repeatedly surprised by some new detail of things, as if Billy Mays popped his head up to say "But wait, there's more!" It may not have the killer pacing of Ori but it certainly comes out on top in the sheer volume of fantastic content packaged into one game.

Some people love to complain about the amount of DLC this game has, but early buyers get a lot of the DLC for free and the game frequently goes 75% off with a complete pack for late comers.  Others will complain about the number of updates it receives.  I say it's nice to have such a well-supported game for a change.  And for value, it's unmatched.  I've gotten way more playtime and enjoyment out of this cheap game than many others that cost much more.
At its core, Dungeon Defenders is a tower defense game, but also an RPG.  You play tower defense, but your character can also fight and the enemies drop loot for you to upgrade your character with.  There's a massive range of difficulty through a good sized campaign, tons of challenges, and bonus maps.  Stepping up to nightmare mode can be difficult, but if you get a higher level player to help you with that hurdle, you can do most of it on your own.  Very high level play requires multiple players, however.
While there are a few outstanding bugs here and there, Trendy has done a great job updating the game and keeping fresh content rolling out regularly.  The game is still being updated more than a year after release which is pretty rare these days outside of highly successful MMOs and F2P games.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes tower defense, especially if you have some friends to play with.  But if you don't like towers, you can just run around shooting everything while your friends handle the towers.

Heyyo, wow! So much to love and enjoy about this game. It's definitely refreshing how they mixed the ship combat & boarding with the solid Assassin's Creed foundation. Side missions / activities are pretty good and varied... Deep sea diving, Animal hunting on land and at sea, Assassin Missions, Trader Missions, searching for Mayan puzzle pieces, Templar key hunts... Lots to do.
One of my favorite little side activities is collecting "Shanties" which is songs the Pirates sing... and each Shanty you collect? Your crew learns a new song! A game where collecting things adds more fun to the game indirectly and in a good way!? Awesome. :P
On PC it was optimized incredibly well compared to even Skyrim even with packing more detail on screen. :)
The only poor part is the controls when diving underwater and a current carries you... can't spin the camera and know what Edward's skull is about to bounce off of lol... only other control issue? Parcour. The classic controls of Right click enables parcour and Shift increases the running speed is sorely missed here. Sometimes it's hard to tell Edward which way you wish for him to move with just WASD, that and if you're trying to make a tight manuver (ie, Climbing the masts to cut down a Ship's flag) Edward will think you meant leaping somewhere else instead of 90 degree turn and climb the Mast some more. :(
Overall? Even with a few control flaws? It's still my favorite Assassin's Creed game to date... Definitely worth the money, especially if it's on sale. :)

I’m going to describe my gaming process of Hollow Knight with Kubler-Ross model.
“The game seemed really great at first, surely there can be some directions somewhere where I can understand what the plot is about and why am I going where I’m going?”
“I bought all the items from map vendor, I even have ink, why do I have to find a bloody npc to buy a map for this specific location? This is terrible, my character can’t even create a map and I need to equip a special item for my location to be shown. Why do I have to move a huge distance to get to the boss after dying? If only I could find a bench nearby. That’s right, I can’t, because there’s no clear map.”
“Maybe if I look the map online – it won’t be that bad? It might get better, right? What if I try looking it up no more than once in an hour, the process won’t be spoiled, right?”
“What? I’ve missed the mantis boss at the beginning of the game and still progressed further? It’s all meaningless, I can’t operate with so much data missing and obscure directions. Screw it, let me just write something on the review and then go on to the next game.”
“Alright, the community is really helpful and the game is actually enjoyable once you know what you need to do. There’s lots of content, so I’m not bored. As I play more, the game starts to be fun. The content is great and the art style is really immersive.”
Further review video, if you'd rather watch:
Seriously though,
I’ve played the game for about 16 hours and that’s a brief description of my experience so far. The community is split into two parts: those, who like the lack of direction and those who don’t. I can understand both sides: there are not many metroidvanias with such obscure sense of purpose but also heightened sense of exploration. The lack of directions when you traverse the game map (with lots of mazes) can build an excitement but it can also take it away when you are going through the dungeon for the twentieth time (I wish I was exaggerating – maybe I suck at this game, but I’ve honestly tried to play without googling stuff for the first 10 hours) because you don’t know where you should be.
Rock Paper Shotgun
calls this a worse version of “Ori and the Blind forest.” I cannot agree to that: while Ori offered a great steamlined experience (let’s be honest, you always knew where you had to go) with mostly ups and some downs (water flooding level, anyone?), Hollow Knight offers a mix of emotions, from deep frustrations to overwhelming joy. The difficulty level of hollow knight is also considerably higher, but the game is totally skill-based. There’s no random factor: if you win – it’s because you did great. If you lost – that’s your fault entirely.
•	Challenging, skill-based gameplay
•	Lots of content: levels, enemies, items
•	Amazing art style, really immersive surroundings: the feeling of the abandoned world that changes as you change.
•	Responsive controls (except for the “ground slam” move, it’s really hard to pull that one off because the timeframe when you have to press jump button is so small).
•	Awesome sounds and music
•	Boss fights are amazing – really hard, but really rewarding once you complete them
•	The map system is horrible: even if you buy the items necessary to update your map, you still need to find the npc that sells you the map of the current location. A lot of times, you cannot do this easily.
•	^ Because you have no map, it’s hard to find resting places. Since you cannot find resting place, you have to restart at your last resting place (which is usually very far). If you die the second time when you move towards your death – you lose your coins. Sure, you can put coins in the bank, but then you’d have to return to the bank every time you want to put something else there.
•	Lack of direction: if you like tightly knitted plots and someone telling you what needs to be done – this game is not for you. You really have to explore that underground city, return to the locations you’ve previously been to in case you missed something. You won’t even understand that you missed something until there’s nowhere else to go and you’re out of options.
The game does not lead you by the hand (which is great), but it sometime feels that it gives too much freedom, which might be a disappointment if you are looking for something with a straightforward plot and at least some vague directions where you need to be.
Overall, the Hollow Knight to me was a bittersweet experience. I could not play it for more than 1-2 hours a day, because it can easily get frustrating. Still, don’t let that discourage you: that’s the game that actually gives you a bouquet of different emotions. Because you feel frustrations, the emotional reward of completing something here also feels greater than great. And because you experience so much, the game begins to feel great. Due to that, the game captivates you. This magical feeling of wanting to overcome the difficulties will drive you forward once you pass the initial resistance.
The lack of decent mapping might hurt, but overall it adds the sense of unknown when you are trying to explore new location. If you lose patience easily – this game is not for you. 100%. Otherwise – highly recommended, a great _experience_ that will take you from frustration to the joy of solving problems and overcoming challenging foes. Definitely grab this one right away if you are a fan of metroidvanias.

The came is PURELY skillbased. No autoaim, it's controlled with WASD and the dodging and aiming is performed by -you- the player. This gives you as the player a gratuitous satisfaction when you succeed besting that one enemy that had given you an incredibly hard time, just to later fall at your feet because you had finally learned their tactics, their techniques. Dear lord where to start with this behemoth of a game! I suppose we could start by addressing that this game is no where near as mind numbing and vomit inducing and its predecessor Assassins Creed 3. Ubisoft has seen there mistakes and absolutely capitalized on the strongest point that AC3 made, and that my fellow gamers is navel combat. Oh yes! I was very much impressed with the ship combat of AC3 and what they have brought to the table with AC4 is something I am going to remember for a very long time.
We join Edward Kenway, the grandfather of AC3's Connor Kenway, as he makes a name for himself in the Caribbean islands in the early 18th century. He first leaves England for the new world as a privateer, but soon turns to piracy realizing that it is far more profitable. What I like most about Edward Kenway here is they have decided to go back to the witty assassin reminiscent of the young Ezio Auditore. I won't lie. While the story of Connor Kenway is a sad one, he is far too much of a whining ♥♥♥♥♥ and never listens to those with experience. Even in the end he neglects his mentor Achilles. Although Edward is a pirate, he has his band of pirate vagabonds to crack jokes with. Instead of complaining and belittling the man who taught him everything.
I'm sure what everyone is most interested in is the focus of the game being on the vast, blue, and very much alive, Caribbean Sea. The ship operates much the same way that a character would in the Assassins Creeds since the second one, in that weapons, armor and special ammunition can all be bought. Of course you must plunder the materials from enemy ships to build said upgrades. The ship, The Jackdaw, is commanded by Edward and is manned by a crew who actively keeps your ship, erm... ship shape. They will run about tying down masts, preparing/cleaning the cannons and yes, of course, swabbing the poop deck. The transition from ship to land in most instances is literally a matter of jumping off your ship and swimming to shore. There are a few larger areas and 3 cities that require a load in order to reach. Aside from those areas the Sea is the limit. If you see a small island, feel free to drop anchor and swim ashore to check for any treasure (which you will find plenty of). When on land you can acquire treasure maps that lead you to plunders of gold or plans for new weapons for you to equip and use. Ship combat is also something to drop your jaw and drool all over. Once you "incapacitate" a ship you can pull yours up alongside it and choose to board. Your crew will then toss over the grappling hooks and pull the ships together. Once on board you have to complete certain objectives like "kill 10 crew members" or "kill the captain" and even setting off the powder reserves is a fine objective and swift manner of clearing the deck. There is forts for you to assault, whales and sharks to hunt (don't feel bad they aren't real and can't go extinct) animals on land to hunt, assassin missions, and some other side quests I won't go into too much detail about.
The fighting mechanic of the game has you with dual cutlasses, smoke bombs, your hidden blades, rope darts, a few miscellaneous items and I will say again, oh yes, four flintlock pistols. Nothing feels more piratey than swinging over on a rope from your ship to an enemies, slashing down the captain with two cutlasses, and then blasting away four crewmembers with your pistols. The counter attack and sneak attacks are your best weapons as always and now instead of the poison blade we have a poison blow-dart gun. Extremely useful for knocking an enemy musketeer down or sending a brute into a full blown rage on his comrades. The game feels swift and smooth when in combat.
I could go all day praising this game. I really could. 10 out of 10. Really. Not lying. A full 100%. It quickly rose to my top 10 favorite games of all time and I know that anyone seeking a true pirate adventure would fall head over heels in love with this game. It has really done proper justice to the pirate theme of movies and games. It is an absolute masterpiece and any person could enjoy this game. Even those not familiar with the series. Pick this up!

I've played through almost the whole game and I'm absolutely in love with it! Here's my Pros and Cons as a casual player.
Pros:
The controls are really tight. You can move left and right while in air and it responds very well for me (Wired Xbox 360 Controller)
The charms. They give you a lot of flexibility and build options that really round out the combat.
The story. I love games that give you bits and pieces of story as you go along rather than being vague and then getting an exposition dump at the end or something.
The NPCs. Even if a lot of NPC dialogue is short, you can usually revisit them at a later time and get more dialogue, and the characters are all (usually) really lovable. Favorite is Salubra.
The art design. I'm a sucker for cute-art-darker-story games like this and Ori and the Blind Forest.
Cons:
The maps. I'm not completely against how the maps work. I understand why you can only update your map when you sit at checkpoints (can't draw and fight at same time), but functionality wise, it's extremely hard as someone with a kinda bad memory to know where I am without finding the map of the area.
The lack of upgrades early. You won't get any weapon upgrades until about 1/3rd through the game, and if you don't know where to go already, there are about 2 or 3 bosses that you would fight without knowing where to get that upgrade that are extremely hard without it. I was one of the people who didn't know you could upgrade, and I suffered about 3 hours on 1 boss fight because I kept dying after not doing enough damage.
Other than those two things, I love this game to death and would definitely recommend it to anyone who asks

This game is an incredible Metroidvania/Dark Souls hybrid, and is very much worth your time if you enjoy either of those games.
The game is pretty hard, but it rarely feels cheap. A few bosses move around a bit sporadically, and with the combination of your very short attack range and how any kind of collision will damage you, it feels a bit unforgiving when learning some of these fights, but nothing else about them is at all cheap. You will die a good bit in this game, but you'll also get better, and the game rewards you very well. After figuring out how to dodge a boss' attacks, you will artfully weave around them slashing them to bits.
The atmosphere is dense, accentuated by a hauntingly soothing soundtrack. The environments are as varied as you can get, at least for a giant underground cave anyway. There are tons of unique enemies and the bosses are fun as hell to fight.
There is an absolute ton of collectibles in this game. Like, a stupid amount of collectibles. The game can be completed fairly quickly if you are skilled, but collecting everything is going to take a really long time your first run. You'll get a lot of mileage if you are a completionist, because while the game really only has a couple of areas it NEEDS you to go to, you are well rewarded for wandering around and seeing everything.
Performance is not always steady though. In some areas, the game takes a noticeable dip in fps, and it isn't like my machine is weak or anything. It's not top of the line, but it's far from poor, which makes some areas a bit awkward to go through because the mechanics of the game demand a lot of precision. This is pretty rare though, 90% of the game plays fine.
My chief complaint is that the map system is significantly weaker than other Metroidvania titles, despite the map being a tool as essential to completion of the game as your primary weapon. It's a bit annoying that not only when you enter an area you have to find a NPC to *buy* a map from, but you also need to buy everything that you can mark the map with, and the map only updates when you reach a save area. Honestly, 2 of these things in tandem would be fine if a bit mildly annoying, but all 3 start to grate on you as you try to decipher where the hell you are and how you got there.
All around though, the game is absolutely fantastic and well worth your money if you like a challenging action/platformer.
If you have every wanted to be a Pirate this is the game for you.

First things first, this is probably the best FPS you are gonna play this year.
The gameplay is fast, old-school fast. Maybe not Quake fast (This is in the Rise of the Triad remake), but "enough" fast to remember the good old times of circle strafing everyone. There are medkits (wohoo!) and armors, a proper arsenal with different upgradeable weapons and the best melee/magic combat I've seen in a "gun" FPS in my life.
There is a nice story to fill the reasons for what you are killing everyone with nice moment (Not the best plot ever, but good enough) filled with funny dialoges and one liners from the new Lo-Wang, lot of references (To both other games from Devolver Digital and the classic (and better) Shadow Warrior), all in a BEAUTIFULL, colorful (although in some times it has the EVERYTHING IS A SHADE OF THE SAME COLOUR illness) and vibrant maps full of things that go boom and things that make you go "wow". Just look at my screenshots. Is ♥♥♥♥ing impressive.
But...
...it is not an "Old school shooter". Yeah, there are circle strafing. And medkits. And loads of weapons. Then what happens?
If you played Hard Reset, you already know what happens, as Shadow Warrior is "the same game", longer and with improvements in how the combat works and in enemy design. If you don't know how Hard Reset played, let me explain you: You walk into a big room, all the access closes, and the monsters start to spawn until you kill them all.
Walk again, repeat.
Until the end.
Serious Sam invented the "Arena Shooter" and Painkiller made it more similar to what Hard Reset did. Shadow Warrior repeats this mechanic and gets you into arena after arena until you end up fighting a boss that works EXACTLY AS THE BOSSES IN HARD RESET. All of them are the same. Repeat, repeat, repeat, repeat.
It is still funny killing monsters in arenas, but it gets old REALLY fast. You will still firing up the game over and over just to get into two arenas of the story, kill everyone, and save right after you walk into the next one because you are already bored of "doing the same" again. And to be honest, is not "really" hard to beat the game, having a "magic" to heal yourself.
I sincerely hope that the guys at Flying Wild Hog move away from this mechanics and start going into a more "open" shooters. A man can dream, ain't it?

Capitalizing on the interest in all things pirates, AC4 moves us to the early 1700's.  What is different is your character isn't actually an Assassin, but rather you kill one in the early moments of the game and take his uniform.  Motivated by money instead of the Creed, this gives Edward a unique (and fresh) personality to the AC lore.
Those that played Far Cry 3 will see the same sanbox style progression.   While in FC3 you had bases that you'd take to increase control in an area, AC4 gives you forts that function the same.  Capture a fort not only gives you a quick travel location but reveals nearby points of interest on the map.  The hunting side missions in FC3 are replaced with harpooning here.  This harpooning is more tense, as you're up close and person with Great White Sharks and Whales.
The biggest draw (for me) is the open world sailing.  You can simply hop on your ship and sail the seas plundering as you see fit.  Weather is dynamic, so it's not always sunny and calm.  It was quite the sight when you see a water spout barreling down on you.  You can choose to capture instead of sink boats for greater rewards.
While many games tend to get stale (or downright fail) as the sequels pile up, AC4 is not only a great sequel but probably the best in the series.

I’m going to describe my gaming process of Hollow Knight with Kubler-Ross model.
“The game seemed really great at first, surely there can be some directions somewhere where I can understand what the plot is about and why am I going where I’m going?”
“I bought all the items from map vendor, I even have ink, why do I have to find a bloody npc to buy a map for this specific location? This is terrible, my character can’t even create a map and I need to equip a special item for my location to be shown. Why do I have to move a huge distance to get to the boss after dying? If only I could find a bench nearby. That’s right, I can’t, because there’s no clear map.”
“Maybe if I look the map online – it won’t be that bad? It might get better, right? What if I try looking it up no more than once in an hour, the process won’t be spoiled, right?”
“What? I’ve missed the mantis boss at the beginning of the game and still progressed further? It’s all meaningless, I can’t operate with so much data missing and obscure directions. Screw it, let me just write something on the review and then go on to the next game.”
“Alright, the community is really helpful and the game is actually enjoyable once you know what you need to do. There’s lots of content, so I’m not bored. As I play more, the game starts to be fun. The content is great and the art style is really immersive.”
Further review video, if you'd rather watch:
Seriously though,
I’ve played the game for about 16 hours and that’s a brief description of my experience so far. The community is split into two parts: those, who like the lack of direction and those who don’t. I can understand both sides: there are not many metroidvanias with such obscure sense of purpose but also heightened sense of exploration. The lack of directions when you traverse the game map (with lots of mazes) can build an excitement but it can also take it away when you are going through the dungeon for the twentieth time (I wish I was exaggerating – maybe I suck at this game, but I’ve honestly tried to play without googling stuff for the first 10 hours) because you don’t know where you should be.
Rock Paper Shotgun
calls this a worse version of “Ori and the Blind forest.” I cannot agree to that: while Ori offered a great steamlined experience (let’s be honest, you always knew where you had to go) with mostly ups and some downs (water flooding level, anyone?), Hollow Knight offers a mix of emotions, from deep frustrations to overwhelming joy. The difficulty level of hollow knight is also considerably higher, but the game is totally skill-based. There’s no random factor: if you win – it’s because you did great. If you lost – that’s your fault entirely.
•	Challenging, skill-based gameplay
•	Lots of content: levels, enemies, items
•	Amazing art style, really immersive surroundings: the feeling of the abandoned world that changes as you change.
•	Responsive controls (except for the “ground slam” move, it’s really hard to pull that one off because the timeframe when you have to press jump button is so small).
•	Awesome sounds and music
•	Boss fights are amazing – really hard, but really rewarding once you complete them
•	The map system is horrible: even if you buy the items necessary to update your map, you still need to find the npc that sells you the map of the current location. A lot of times, you cannot do this easily.
•	^ Because you have no map, it’s hard to find resting places. Since you cannot find resting place, you have to restart at your last resting place (which is usually very far). If you die the second time when you move towards your death – you lose your coins. Sure, you can put coins in the bank, but then you’d have to return to the bank every time you want to put something else there.
•	Lack of direction: if you like tightly knitted plots and someone telling you what needs to be done – this game is not for you. You really have to explore that underground city, return to the locations you’ve previously been to in case you missed something. You won’t even understand that you missed something until there’s nowhere else to go and you’re out of options.
The game does not lead you by the hand (which is great), but it sometime feels that it gives too much freedom, which might be a disappointment if you are looking for something with a straightforward plot and at least some vague directions where you need to be.
Overall, the Hollow Knight to me was a bittersweet experience. I could not play it for more than 1-2 hours a day, because it can easily get frustrating. Still, don’t let that discourage you: that’s the game that actually gives you a bouquet of different emotions. Because you feel frustrations, the emotional reward of completing something here also feels greater than great. And because you experience so much, the game begins to feel great. Due to that, the game captivates you. This magical feeling of wanting to overcome the difficulties will drive you forward once you pass the initial resistance.
The lack of decent mapping might hurt, but overall it adds the sense of unknown when you are trying to explore new location. If you lose patience easily – this game is not for you. 100%. Otherwise – highly recommended, a great _experience_ that will take you from frustration to the joy of solving problems and overcoming challenging foes. Definitely grab this one right away if you are a fan of metroidvanias.

Played Dayz Epoch: Panthera map.
Dayz is an unforgiving game. At first the game feel very open ended, you walk around alone in a big map dotted with small villages, one or 2 bigger towns, a couple airfields, a lot of vehicles and a couple of loot spawns. Also you can participate in missions to obtain bigger stashes of differing (gold, weapons, medical supplies or building materials) materials which you can then stockpile or put to use.
The main goal for a lot of players will be to build their own base. To get a base youll need to stockpile a lot of items, so youll probably will want a safe first and before that a car to taxi between your pile and the lootspots. This will prove to be a timeconsuming occupation as it quickly turns out you need to have so many materials to actually build a base that looting is a disheartening grind. For all the time ive spent in the game +-60hours with three persons weve been able to get enough loot to pay for 2 stone walls, we need another 2 a floor and a roof to get a house so go figure.
The main tension in the game stems from other players who might try to interfere with your plan or kill you and take all your possesions. People who try to become a bandit usually kill you on sight so meeting other players in the field can be quite dangerous.
This the main selling point of the mod, if you die you will lose everything and have to start again. This can be circumvented somewhat by the use of vaults but there will still be a lot of moments your carrying around more gear then you are willing to lose.
So the game in the end boils down to either or both of 2 goals, killing others or looting for gold. The game in itself functions sort of like the goverment due to the large amounts of bugs in the game you will lose A LOT of items, weapons, vehicles and gold. Of everything you earn the game takes a portion via bugs and disconnects. Today and yesterday ive lost a total of 6 vehicles, which were worth about 62gold, due to server crashes and bugs.
It can happen that you drop your backpack all the sudden, your backpack might be empty after a reconnect, the keys of your car can dissappear, your car can die to all sort of random stuff, you might reconnect inside of a car and die, you might reconnect in the ocean and die of undercooling, you can break your leg if a door opens into you or if you get up a staircase. A zombie might hit you trough the ground or a wall, you can kill a buddy by driving past him, you gunsight might not load correctly or you might not be able to sell things. The list could continue on but I think the point is clear.
This game has to few goals (looting players, or looting terrain) and to many bugs (gazzilions) to worth your time. You might be interested in the concept, then wait for the standalone to be finished but dont spend money on arma 2 and arrowhead for this mod.
Do you enjoy life? Then buy this game.

First of all: holy guacamoly was this a good game.
I've seen a bunch of people commenting stuff like "well it's k but too similar to other games". Congrats, you just discovered the meaning of "genre".
Not all games are genre-defining games. You have the Dark Souls, you have the Smash games, you have the goddamn Call of Duty. But you also have those games that just like to walk a path already marked, and maybe explore all the sideroads that the big dude with the torch didn't bother to visit. Games like Hollow Knight.
And damn do they walk good.
Hollow Knight was an amazing experience. I won't talk about the amazing art style, the super creative mob list, the compelling need for exploration it litterally injects into the player (I had surprisingly fun looking for the worms in the jars); instead, the thing I liked most about this game was its simplicity. Many games of the genre like to make bosses hard by gifting them nearly-invincibility states (for example, some bossess will require you to hit them in the head to damage them, or hit them with a specific weapon, or in a limited time-frame), but this does NOT happen in Hollow Knight.
The combat system can be summed in: hit them with the pointy end; and dodge (optional).
This does not mean that boss battles lack complexity, but rather that they set the "hard" part in such a way that it is immediate to understand and react. You don't have to fight a boss 15 times before understanding its ♥♥♥♥ing weak point (which then makes the whole thing a piece of cake): it's all about understanding the patterns, and how to counter them, and preparing for the fight through the use of the many charms the game offers.
"Should I use the all-blue-life thingy? Or does the boss offer safespots to heal? Do I wanna invest in 2 offensive charms, or are the avaiable slots too tight?"
I really enjoyed when the game put me through this kind of reasoning, expecially because my intuitions worked 99% of the time (not thanks to me, again, but to the intuitivity of the game).
Props to Team Cherry for this one, I'll be on the lookout for your following works!
P.S: if you rage because the game loses 10 frames once in 2 hours, causing you to land on a spike and lose 1 out of 6 healable healthpoints, you are a ♥♥♥♥ing crybaby.

Man, this is a tough one.
Shadow Warrior is a game that has a lot of things going for it.  The main gameplay mechanic is the swordfighting, which is incredibly satisfying and enjoyable.  The shooting is fun as well, and the game mixes up enemy types in a way where it encourages variety.  Considering these developers have worked on games like Hard Reset and Painkiller, it's not surprising that the game throws tons of enemies at you at any given minute and keeps up a breakneck pace.
However, the problem is that the game is 4 hours too long.  It gets to a point where the game runs out of enemy types, and every encounter feels the same.  In addition, a decent amount of the later levels involve a lot of backtracking that feels incredibly unnecessary, like the developers wanted to make a longer game for some reason but didn't have the time or budget to do so.  It got to the point where most encounters just felt like a slog and I just wanted to get it over with.  If this game were 7 or 8 hours long instead of 12, the pacing wouldn't have felt nearly as sloppy.
So, having said that, I would recommend this game when it's on sale (I got it for $10), because it CAN be a lot of fun and the developers seem like really cool dudes who care about their fans, but be warned that it really loses steam in the last third of the game.

I played a shit♥♥♥♥ worth of this game(over 1000 hrs) and honestly the game is broke by design and only if you are dedicated to the game will you really ever notice most of this.
The game was designed to be more strategic and had a max upgrade of 20 on armor and like 32 on weapons. As such a lot of the elements were coded with this in mind. When the super loot update came it changed the game completely and added megalomania in the stats and they have ballooned to the point where armor can have 350 upgrade vs the 20 when the game started.
They also increased the level cap from 70 to 100 and as such you can feel how the game was designed for the 70 cap and then again forced to the 100. You can join some of the higher difficulty maps that other people are playing and go from 1-70+ in 1-3 waves. I mean this is not even all that horrible in design, but still was a tacked on thing. For level 100 it's over 1.1 billion xp vs 70 which is 3,279,707 xp.
The points I made about the loot also have another big issue which leaks out being that stats will rollover the maximum and ruin loot that should have been good but instead are now useless. The worst part of this is that it creates a grind for gear. The other issue with this is that the bridge between godly gear and mythical+ gear is very high and hard to get past without buying gear from people who are much further, joining friends who are willing to drag you up or grind hoping to find something useful.
Another loot issue is the sheer volume of it that is dumped in each game and how most of the stuff will disappear and even good loot can disappear or be stuck in a place you can't loot it(inside spawns)which also add's to the grind when you can't gain all the gear that is even dropped.
The shop system they added was one of worst aspects of the game, but I understand some of the reasons they had to do it in such a way. It was a web based site made by the community and lacked in some key intergration methods like figuring out if the person is online, ingame, running an afk shop or even plays the game anymore.

The art of the game is the best thing about the game. The levels all look beautiful when post processing is on.
There is many things about the game which could have been improved from custom loot filters so you could pick what gear you wanted to see, fixing the random number generator so the stats don't rollover and ruin loot, fixing the gap between the base game and the dlc, fixing the multiplayer so it would not get knocked out when steam goes down, securing the game from most forms of hacking, fixing the trading bugs, making a better system for a auction house or a more useful web based trading spot and many other issues I have found that are lost in the recesses of my mind.
