This is my first review ever for a game. Don't be discouraged by that fact, though; I'll be sure to provide with all the information whomever reads this will ever need.
I'll split this review in three parts, the first is combat/a bit of how the game works.
If you just came down into the reviews instead of looking at the screenshots and gameplay, then let me tell you that Hollow Knight is 2D action/exploration game, where you WILL die a lot of times, and that's a main part of how you get better and better until you master how to get past your obstacles. If you die, you're sent back to the last checkpoint (in this case, bench) you rested at, losing all the currency (called Geo) and leaving behind a Shade that you must fight to recover your lost Geo and soul capacity (another way to say mana, or an extra pool that serves as fuel to cast a variety of spells) because a Shade takes a third of your starting capacity with you. There's ways around this, but I won't spoil it for the players. Anyhow, the fights are simple, you traverse the screen, dodging and swinging attacks at the bosses/normal monsters until they die. There's no "block", you can only evade and memorize attack patterns if a boss or regular monster gets too hard for you. If you get hit, you lose a tick of health and you have a short moment of invulnerability until you can get damaged again. Naturally, this game has progression so you never feel like you're consistently behind everything else and at the same time, you know that there's some X place you should be going to, or some X boss you should be beating. However, nothing about this game is forgiving. Usually, you'll find yourself very far away from a checkpoint, or frustrated about not being able to beat a boss. Depending on how you explore, some fights will be brutally hard, and others will be a breeze. But don't underestimate anything, because if not, you'll often find yourself getting damaged by even the most easiest of monsters or obstacles.
And now we have exploration. This game is a gem for people who love to explore, to surpass obstacles and to discover a plethora of secrets. Hollow Knight brings everything to the table. Trust me, I said there was nothing forgiving about this game and I was right. Exploring takes up time but you'll find VERY useful stuff that'll help you with even more exploring or with combat. And exploration in this game is much more than walking around, but I'll avoid spoiling that. A very important thing to note is that Hollow Knight does NOT hold your hand and point where to go, you have to fight enemies and explore locations to advance in both the plot and the game. Often times you'll find yourself milling about already explored areas trying to figure out what you missed, or re-exploring the area because now you have the means to explore an important bit that you couldn't explore before. Personally, there was only one time during this game that I found myself frustrated trying to find out where to go, because everything was inaccessible. And I was wrong. I just had to get creative, and it was so satisfying to get past an obstacle that didn't need any help, just a little imagination.
All in all, this game is amazing. It's the first thing that I've personally seen come out of Kickstarter that's just completely worth it. I discovered this by myself and I won't ever regret delving into Hollownest. Hollow Knight is full of action, exploration, feels and naturally, frustration. Try it out, and don't give up if things get hard. Master the game and beat the stacked odds or just grow stronger and come back to plow through whatever you thought was unbeatable at one point.
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
With that out of the way, what comes next is my personal rant and this probably encompasses many other players as well. I don't know if the devs will ever see this but.. They must've gotten together at some point and thought "we need to break the will of our players, we need to engrave in their minds what a legendary difficulty is" and lo and behold, White Palace was born. I'm sure that anyone that reaches up until this point will cry tears of blood, will curse their own ancestors until none remain pure, and will want to beg the devs to nerf this stage of the game to an early grave.
No number of boss fights, even the most impossible ones that made me realize that I was just too weak or incompetent, were able to instill the sense of helplessness that White Palace engraved in my mind. If I ever have grandchildren, I'll tell them that this game left a deeper mark than the King's Brand in my soul. I just hope the new players have a patience as deep and profound as the sea, so that they can weather that stage on their own.

What a superb adventure!
I was in the kickstarter for this so it was great enough to see the project finished and released, but (not paying too much attention during development) I'd somehow expected the game to be a shortish 5-8 hour experience, and was wholly unprepared for the 40 hour epic it turned out to be.
This is a magnificent, vast, thoughtful Metroidvania, that takes influence from the way the Souls games do narrative. So the game is filled with numerous haunting, mysterious and memorable moments and NPCs, plenty you are bound to miss on a regular playthrough. The main story is simple, the background lore and world building is rich and fascinating.
The visuals are resplendent, with some breathtaking painted backgrounds and character animation, making for an absolutely stunning looking world. It's a fairly tough game too at times, so be prepared for a fair challenge, with a few precision platforming gauntlets and hard bosses.
If you enjoy Metroid games and especially their atmosphere and feeling of isolation and environmental storytelling, if you like the underlying tragedy and melancholy of the Souls games, as well as the exploration and unearthing of secrets and hidden layers to the world and story, then definitely give Hollow Knight a try. It's been a very pleasant, atmospheric 40 hours I've spent with it and I can't be the only one.

I don't really write reviews but I felt like writing one for this game. I saw gameplay of this on a stream and thought wow this looks fun but it looks like another game I've seen before and after doing some research, I found out it was the successor to Bloodline Champions. To be honest, I wasn't the biggest fan of BLC and I tried out that game for an hour or two and just wasn't as interested as I thought I was.
Fastforward to now, having played for a good 16 hours of Battlerite (I'm hooked), at 2.3k mmr, the game offers fun and exciting gameplay - although similar to BLC but has enough tweaks to improve the game. It's filled with unique feeling champions that all feel very different but share similar skills (ex. counter q, escape/shield spacebar, etc.), the graphics and effects are pleasing to look at, and games are quick and can be intense at times. If I had to describe Battlerite, it would be a combination of Dota and Smash Brothers to make a team-based arena brawler type game!
The game right now is good but it can definitely be improved into something greater:
- More options for people with more than 3 friends to play together (As of now, private game is the only option that yields no battle rewards).
- There should be a 3v3 Ai mode, not sure why there isn't tbh (Only in private game but this has no reward value for playing except for pure practice).
- Implement a different type of que - a ranked draft mode with the possibility of banning certain heroes? Instead of just picking your champs and jumping straight into battle.
- The ranking system is definitely weird and probably needs a tweak. (This happend a couple of times, I qued for 2v2 with my friend, we were up against rank 9/10 people, my friend and I were rank 3/5, yea we got stomped 0-3 most of the time, that wasn't enjoyable.)
All in all, Battlerite is definitely an action-packed game which I would see myself playing reguarly. Games are quick and last about 8-10 minutes. Be warned, it's a very skill based game and I'd give it 8.5/10! Yes, I recommend this game :)

Un juego que se basa pura y exclusivamente en la habilidad que tenga uno para usar los variados heroes.
Es casual y está en early access, por lo que comprarlo deja en claro el inminente encuentro de bugs o cheaters (que por cierto yo no encontré ninguno a simple vista). Los requisitos mínimos para jugarlo son bastante simples y su estética es linda. Por ahora la comunidad es una de las mejores cosas, y principalmente porque tiene algo que muchos juegos online no tienen: PERDER es divertido también. Y uno se da cuenta de que perdió porque el otro es mejor.
Los tiempos de espera para matchmaking 2vs2 no superan el minuto como mucho, y para 3vs3 se hace mas tedioso pero tampoco busca por tanto tiempo. Hay muchísimas regiones e inclusive Sudamérica tiene servidores para Peru y creo que Chile también.
Buenos diseños y buen concepto. Es un juego que mas allá de por ahora no tener un modo casual (si, desde el primer juego te calibra el MMR) se mantiene como se presenta: simple y divertido. En caso de querer llevarlo mas al extremo, uno puede jugar con 2 amigos y perfeccionarse en los diversos heroes que nunca dejan de sorprender a medida que uno se vuelve mejor con ellos.
9.5/10 solo porque creo que la perfección no existe.

I LOVE this game. It's a tactical shooter/military simulator that has singleplayer, coop, and PvP. There are hundreds of vehicles, weapons, and player models for you to use, so each time you play, you try something new. However the game also has some parts that bring it down. I will list all the good/bad points.
The good:
Emphasis on realism
Emphasis on multiplayer
Wide array of equipment, all usable in-game
Small but active, mature and helpful community
Good graphics
Good atmosphere
Easy to learn, difficult to master
Large map, open world. Able to travel over entire country
Good inventory system
Fun custom missions
Replayability
The bad:
Bad voice acting. Every time you order people around, it feels like all the words are spliced. For example: "team RED. go to that TANK"
Clumsy infantry movement. While sprinting around for kilometers in open areas feels fine, moving around in buildings is slow, clumsy, and innefecient. You will notice that you either move too fast or slow for CQB, and that your gun won't fit through doors unless you're holding it down.
Large amount of HDD space taken up. This game can take up around 15 gigs on your hard drive.
No low-spec computer support. While you can turn graphics options down, you will find it hard to target enemies over 1 kilomenter away when everyone's texture is just a blur and there's a great big wall of fog right where they are.
The engine. There are no ragdoll physics at all, object collision doesn't always work, shadows take up much processing power
All in all, if you can get past the poor engine, you will find this game extremely addictive and fun. 8/10

If you're the type of dude who plays overwatch or LoL and love the high of making the occasional 1v3 play I would check this out. This game is pure unadulterated PvP action. I would not call it a moba as it has no npc's nor objectives- if anything I would compare it to Arena PvP in World of Warcraft, but with an Isometric view- also note its way faster paced, and I would say more skill based as there are very few auto-targeted abilities in this game, almost everything is a "skillshot" using Moba Terminology.
I want to repeat, if you love making those "Did you see that!?" plays definitely try this game out. The game does not have a "play of the game" system like overwatch, but every game is recorded and allows you to cut a recording (so say you only show the part of the match where you 1v3'd) and then post it on your profile to share with friends and other players.
Now, a quick mention that this is essentially an overhaul of Stunlock Studio's Previous Game, Bloodline Champions. Now that game was phenomenal, but it had several underlying issues (cough funcom cough)- this game however has addressed many of them while making it more accessable without hurting the depth of the game. I talk about these toward the bottom in the "differences between this and BLC" part of the review.
Lets talk about how long it takes to play a match. A match plays in a best of 5 round system, with a timer at the start of the match counting down to an "overtime" where a painful fog circles the map to make sure slippery characters can't just stall the match out for too long- it creeps up into a small circle toward the center of the map and ~30 seconds after that it will just begin closing onto the whole map. With that being said you will usually finish a match within 10 minutes, with 20 minutes being an extreme outlier. So this pairs up against Overwatch's time to play pretty well and beats out hard Moba's for sure.
The player population has only gone up since it launched, starting at 5k concurrent players on launch day and is almost at 10k concurrent players- considering how niche of a game this is thats awesome as matchmaking is actually pretty solid now that they've made sure that players in placement games aren't getting put into high rated matches. Finding a match is pretty quick- I usually get into a game within ~15 seconds and haven't waited more than 2 minutes yet.
For those who have played BLC and are curious about the changes, here they are.
1) Battlerites- instead of the medallion system to customize your character we have a non-grind based system that works more like Heroes of the Storm talents- at the start of each round you pick one out of three perks to add to your character- some characters have more "clearly best/worst" options, but for some it works very well, for example I love Bakko (Vanguard) round 1 choices are a) next auto attack deals double damage after using his leap, b) bulwark can be cancelled early to melee an opponent and apply a weaken (-50% damage/healing output) on them, or c) his short dash now Incapitates a target if they get knocked into a wall. All 3 are pretty solid options although I usually lean toward the third.
2) Characters are actually talkitive- this was something I always brought up as a downside to Bloodline Champions- the characters didn't have much character outside of their appearance, in this day and age characters need to be talkative to appeal to more casual players, and hell, even as a guy who likes playing games very seriously/competitively I notice that a game that isn't very talkative doesn't seem to have the same grab on me. The voice lines are pretty limited, but its still far better than BLC was.
3) Changes to general kit layout- tanks are no longer an archtype, you definitely have more beefy characters in the archtype, but tanks are no longer a full on archtype, the old tanks have been retooled to be supportive damage dealers (more emphasis on damage dealer) than in BLC. For example Rook (Glutton in BLC) lost his rock shield, eat (its now an exe ability) and his dust cloud. He instead gained a trance move that procs his attack speed buff. Also worth noting is that characters have a third ex only ability now- they changed the R button to be a move that is only useable with Ex energy (25% usually) For example Shifu's(Spearmaster) Incapitate swipe is an ex ability- although a third round perk causes it to refund its cost.
What this change overall means is that its easier for new players to hop in as there's one less regular ability to keep track of its cooldown, without really removing skill cap as it means experienced players now have more options on how to use their ex energy.
4) Smaller Maps
This is a big one, the maps are smaller and this helps out tremendously with keeping the game feeling fast paced. They're not "tiny" but the scale is definitely a bit smaller (I'd say ~20%) and there is no Bridges map, thank god.
Also, for those wondering what characters are currently in, 13 of the 15 characters in game are "ports" of the original 16 characters in bloodlines minus Harbinger, Herald of Insight, and Thorns. I use Port lightly as they've been tweaked to fit the new battlerite system, removal of tank archtype, and addition of an ex only move. The two "new" characters are Pearl and Oldur, who are both supports- I don't think Herald will be coming back as Oldur is a heavily reworked Herald- but if you watched the trailer you probably noticed Seeker/Harbinger are in a mostly complete state and will probably be added soon enough.
Either way, this got a bit disorganized/ranty but I would highly recommend the game, Definitely more approachable than Bloodline champions and I feel it has much more longetivity. Stunlock Studios has definitely learned from Bloodline Champions and has made a superior product.

At first, I was reluctant to recommend this game.
One of the biggest flaws of this game is that, at high levels, everything becomes just numbers. A lot of the time, high level'ed players can sit AFK and do extremely well. It also uses the ol' Skinner Box mechanic quite heavily.
However, after playing the game more in-depth, this game simply has so much to offer that it honestly is one of the best value-for-money games out there. There are tons of maps and countless challenges to play with, so there's always something to do.

I've played through almost the whole game and I'm absolutely in love with it! Here's my Pros and Cons as a casual player.
Pros:
The controls are really tight. You can move left and right while in air and it responds very well for me (Wired Xbox 360 Controller)
The charms. They give you a lot of flexibility and build options that really round out the combat.
The story. I love games that give you bits and pieces of story as you go along rather than being vague and then getting an exposition dump at the end or something.
The NPCs. Even if a lot of NPC dialogue is short, you can usually revisit them at a later time and get more dialogue, and the characters are all (usually) really lovable. Favorite is Salubra.
The art design. I'm a sucker for cute-art-darker-story games like this and Ori and the Blind Forest.
Cons:
The maps. I'm not completely against how the maps work. I understand why you can only update your map when you sit at checkpoints (can't draw and fight at same time), but functionality wise, it's extremely hard as someone with a kinda bad memory to know where I am without finding the map of the area.
The lack of upgrades early. You won't get any weapon upgrades until about 1/3rd through the game, and if you don't know where to go already, there are about 2 or 3 bosses that you would fight without knowing where to get that upgrade that are extremely hard without it. I was one of the people who didn't know you could upgrade, and I suffered about 3 hours on 1 boss fight because I kept dying after not doing enough damage.
Other than those two things, I love this game to death and would definitely recommend it to anyone who asks

Really fun game if you don't try and pretend it's a sequel/prequel or in any way related to the first game. It does it entirely differently, which I and a lot of people didn't like, but it is seriously fun.
The graphics are amazingly good but also not too taxing, the gunplay is exceptional, especially later on when you get more interesting guns and starts getting particularly interesting after you get the shotgun. The weapons can be upgraded in a fairly linear manner but the fully upgraded version is most definitely a lot better than the plain gun, and it also looks different too, instead of just being a statistical upgrade with no visual difference. There are also other upgrades which improve your combat with the sword and just your general combat effectiveness, and healing abilities, which can be overpowered early on in the game.
I didn't like the linearity of the game, however. It used to be a giant labyrinth of keycards and danger. Now it's just a story driven linear shooter, though a fun one at least. You can divert from the path and go exploring, though not much, sort of Crysis 2 level of exploration, but it is very easy to get lost if you don't know what you're doing.
Overall, I recommend it if you're not a big fan of the original and were expecting it to be more of the same. If you are though, you won't get the same so if you wanted more of the same, this is not the game for you.

I just want to say that I was initially frustrated by this game, but I gave it a second chance.  I cleared my mind of the bad habits that modern shooters had instilled in me:  Being Cautious, Conserving Resources, Fearing Death.  And suddenly it was 12 hours later and I was exhausted and oh hey the sun is coming up how did that happen.  The combat system in this game is amazingly engrossing.  I probably didn't take nearly as much advantage as I could have of some of the crowd control sword moves, but honestly, that would have sullied the Zen I had achieved while wading through the hip deep pools of blood I created mowing down everything that wasn't me.  The Sword is Useful, Effective, and provides the right amount of Feedback to make melee exceptionally satisfying.  You will want to use it.  Most of the guns are not immediately wonderful but if you invest in their upgrades nearly all of them BECOME wonderful.
Bottom line, if you've been burned by previous "Reimaginings" of classic franchises, I implore you to give the concept one more chance.  Shadow Warrior does it right.

I recommend this game because it's a thoughful strategical and tactical army simulator. It distinguishes itself from other shooters where it has far more community capabilities in very large worlds to allow a very realistic army simulation, and community generated mods, gamemodes, scenarios and campaigns just provide a non-stop gaming experience whether singleplayer or multiplayer.
Pros:
- Realistic weapon stats
- Realistic environment with good graphics
- Great modding community
- A lot of community-made gamemodes
- Mature community
- Challenging AI
Cons:
- Glitchy at times
- Hard to find European realism units (EST dominant)
- Mods are a must
- Mostly multiplayer
The game is great stand-alone but mods are almost a must, which isn't neccessarily a big deal, but depending on what you aim for you're going to need mods to better the experience. You can find a lot of different gamemodes, scenarios and campaigns all deviating from each other, from realism simulations to mexican drug cartel hunting and zombie survival.
The community is mature although very US dominant, so it's hard to actually find an active realism unit in a European timezone, which I have been looking for myself a lot but was just unable to find 'good' communities that sort of fit in my time schedule. Scenarios were done very late in the evening.
Mods are great as is the modding community. I advise mods such as ACRE (if you multiplayer) and ACE to better the realism of your experience. The game is extremely immersive. You sort of just feel like you're an actual soldier, excluding the action-man part which Battlefield and Call of Duty pick up on like you're playing in a live Rambo movie.
Sometimes the game is a bit glitchy and animations sometimes don't look smooth, as does the driving overall. I miss how you see yourself steering, which is although there in ARMA 3. In ARMA 2 you only see the wheel spin and you have a static animation. The game isn't really glitch-free in terms of obstacles but that's just the engine the game is running on.

Dungeon Defenders is a tower defense game with RPG elements. Level and equipment progression allows a sense of elevation as player characters become stronger over time. Each class has five 'tower' type abilities, and a character can be built to have extremely effective defenses, be an extremely effective fighter, or a hybrid of the two.
For starting players it is recommended to start with an apprentice or squire and develop one's abilities toward a monk or huntress, as the former two have much sturdier and easier to manage tower defenses, which are crucial for managing the mobs of monsters heading your way. But, the ability to switch out heroes even during a single match allows one player to place defense types from all the classes to counter the weaknesses of each class, meaning that there is great benefit to having a character of every class type. This game is also incredibly fun for team play, and I highly suggest it if one seeks strategic play with equipment/level progression!

A solid game, though repetitive.  I've been a huge AC fan from the beginning, and while graphically and musically beautiful, I found myself disappointed in the story compared to the great stories in AC2 and Brotherhood.  This game's main focus is on naval combat and sailing, which is a nice break from the gameplay of the past installments, and it becomes quite the (enjoyable) grind to get your ship upgraded.  Main story missions suffered the most in this game, as 90% of your objectives are Eavesdropping and Tailing, with a small chance you'll actually kill your target.  90% of the optional objectives are Avoiding Combat or killing your target in a specific way (no surprise there, though).
I really fell in love with the story of this series after AC2 (as the original AC left me a little confused and curious).  This game left me feeling the same as I did at the end of the original AC.  I'm not sure what the point was of a lot of what I did, what degree the characters really mattered, and whether or not my actions in this game will make sense in the next.  The continuity of the Ezio storyline was absolutely brilliant in my opinion, and I think I may be one of the rare people that genuinely liked the story in AC3 as well.  My hope is that my utter confusion at the end of this game is because this installment will be a launching platform for an entirely new, immersive story (as the original AC was).
This game is certainly a change of pace from previous installments, and while I had many "This is awesome!" moments, I had just as many "Meh" moments.  It's odd going from Assassin's Creed that's heavy on the "assassin" aspect to an Assassin's Creed that focuses less on being an assassin and more on being a ship captain.  It could just be the purist in me, but ship battles and beautiful graphics really weren't enough to sell me on the (what seemed to be) thrown-together-in-less-time-than-it-should-have-been storyline and character development.
All this being said, I still highly recommend the game.  It, like all other installments is worth a play.  The multiplayer is still just as fun as the previous installments, and this game has ample amounts of side activities to focus on when you're not in the mood to continue with any missions.  The game really is beautiful, and if you've ever wanted to feel like a feared pirate sailing a bada** ship, then you will definitely like this game.  I've played many games where I've been mad about an ending, only to realize later how great of a game it was regardless.  This will probably be another one of those games.  Prepare for some possible frustration, but give the game a go.  It's worth it.

The Gulf War (2 August 1990 – 28 February 1991), codenamed Operation Desert Storm (17 January 1991 – 28 February 1991) was a war waged by coalition forces from 34 nations led by the United States against Iraq in response to Iraq's invasion and annexation of Kuwait.The war is also known under other names, such as the Persian Gulf War, First Gulf War, Gulf War I, Kuwait War, or the First Iraq War, before the term "Iraq War" became identified instead with the 2003 Iraq War (also referred to in the U.S. as "Operation Iraqi Freedom").[18] Kuwait's invasion by Iraqi troops that began 2 August 1990 was met with international condemnation, and brought immediate economic sanctions against Iraq by members of the U.N. Security Council. U.S. President George H. W. Bush deployed U.S. forces into Saudi Arabia, and urged other countries to send their own forces to the scene. An array of nations joined the Coalition, the biggest coalition since World War II. The great majority of the Coalition's military forces were from the U.S., with Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and Egypt as leading contributors, in that order. Saudi Arabia paid around US$36 billion of the US$60 billion cost.The war was marked by the beginning of live news on the front lines of the fight, with the primacy of the U.S. network CNN. The war has also earned the nickname Video Game War after the daily broadcast images on board the U.S. bombers during Operation Desert Storm.The initial conflict to expel Iraqi troops from Kuwait began with an aerial bombardment on 17 January 1991. This was followed by a ground assault on 24 February. This was a decisive victory for the Coalition forces, who liberated Kuwait and advanced into Iraqi territory. The Coalition ceased its advance, and declared a cease-fire 100 hours after the ground campaign started. Aerial and ground combat was confined to Iraq, Kuwait, and areas on Saudi Arabia's border. Iraq launched Scud missiles against Coalition military targets in Saudi Arabia and against Israel.United Nations Security Council Resolution 687 passed in April 1991 established formal cease-fire terms. For starters, this game has great combat. Cutting enemies into pieces with your sword is very satisfying and the gunplay isn't half bad, either. Aside from a few tedious enemies and bosses that seem to drag on, fighting in this game stays enjoyable. Lots of blood and gore make kills especially fun. Slicing a demon in half as it tries to crawl away comes to mind. Also, it's worth noting that when executing an enemy via limb chopping or beheading etc. it is done free-form. No QTE-like assassinations in this game. One of my favorite things about this game is the fact that it lets you progress as fast as you can kill your enemies, aside from a very miniscule amount of the compulsary "press E on glowing button or switch" that take about a second. Not a big deal, the game still doesn't hold your hand.
Something this game has over a lot of modern shooters are its colors! Stunning Cherry Blossoms, Fireworks, multicolored magical effects and of course, vibrant red blood. Another way it breaks the modern-shooter-mold is its return to weapon and enemy variety. Knowing what gun to use for what enemy obviously comes in handy, and each weapon has a fair amount of entertaining upgrades. The map design may not be anywhere near as stimulating as something like in DOOM, or other older FPS games it gives homage to, but in my opinion it is a great step towards returning the genre to its original glory.
Bottom line is if you like old shooters, or even modern ones then you will like this game.
However, if you like the idea of claiming a powerful demons head and firing from it a powerful magic stream, thus turning lesser foes into demon stew, then you will REALLY like this game.

I do not hold Metroidvania games in my heart.
There is no special slot where platformers snuggle in the cynical recesses of my psyche.
At no point does an indie, retro-inspired platformer (such as Shovel Knight) interest me.
So why is it that I have fallen so, so deeply in love with Hollow Knight? This game that is a combination of things that I've never looked twice at, never cared for, and never given time to has soared past my expectations. It is one of my favourite games of all time. As a matter of fact, it's probably flat out the best experience I have ever had in gaming.
Put simply, I am in love.
So, why is that? Well, I think I've managed to break it down a little.
-----
What caught me is the soundtrack. Immediately reminiscent of not just the style, but the quality of Final Fantasy and Kingdom Hearts games of yore. It tugged immediately at my heartstrings, and with a little gloss over the trailer, I had it and the soundtrack in my library.
The music in the trailer is not some unique piece that stands out fro mthe crowd. No, the truth is that every piece in the game is of similar quality, if not better in some cases.
From the sombre yet beautiful tones of Dirtmouth, the heart-string pulling chords of the City of Tears, to the grim yet gorgeous organs of the Soul Sanctum. Every piece is fresh and wonderful.
-----
Of course, you're not here for music. If you wanted that, do yourself a favour and just buy the OST. Of course, I recommend buying it and the game! But the OST is worth it in it of itself.
So, to match the gorgeous and varied soundtrack, what better than a gorgeous and varied world?
The level of detail in each piece of each area is mindblowing. The attention to detail at every corner, the way that the NPCs change depending on what's happened since you've been gone.
The variety of areas, each totally unique, which all somehow are happening while underground! Decrepit cities, jungle-like ruins, lost wastelands of toxicity.
And, once again, the City of Tears. A level of beauty I never believe a 2D game come every accomplish.
I could go on and on and on. But I don't want to spoil anything. Simply note that each detail is lovingly hand-crafted, and absolutely beautiful.
-----
So we've got an amazing soundtrack and a gorgeous world. What's next?
The game itself.
The entire map, all of it, is open.
Not from the start, of course. There are shortcuts to open, backpassages to unlock, secrets to be found.
It's a Metroidvania, and to its namesake the game opens up more and more as you find new abilities to traverse it. Places that were once impossible to ascend are done so with ease. But there's more to it than that.
There's a feeling of true progression.
Not just the ability to cast a new spell, or swing that slightly stronger weapon.
No, here you start out as a little bug man who hops from block to block.
Soon you're dashing around the world, like a child in a playground. Once tricky obstacles, now nothing more than wind beneath your feet.
You feel growth in both yourself as a player for navigating this world with expertise, and in the game as a character unlocking new methods of traversal.
The combat is simple, responsive, and very competent. Enemy variety is, so far, excellently done. I've not gone "Oh god, it's this enemy yet again". No, when you meet a similar enemy later in the game it will have some *spice* added to it. That generic flier will have new abilities, and a totally new look. To the point where you won't even recognise it, because it's no longer the same creature. It's not a case of red slime -> blue slime. These  are simply more and more addvanced enemies which you need to use the tricks you've learned to overcome.
On that note, the game as a whole is extremely responsive. And at no part did I feel a death was anything more than my own fault.
The level of polish is absurd for an indie title. Hell, it's absurd for any title.
But, I digress.
The game has a lot to keep you interested. Secrets to find, upgrades to hunt for and purchase. Meaningful upgrades, mind you. Some quality of life, some game changingly powerful. Each requiring you to plan out the slots given, as the strongest upgrades come with the highest slot usage.
-----
I would like to put into perspective how fantastic I think this game is.
My biggest gripe is the map is sometimes annoying to open, and instead of the quickmap you can accidentally pull up the big map. This slightly disrupts the flow of movement every now and again.
Yeah. That right there is my biggest bugbear with this game.

I can't have enough words to describe this game.
It's one of those cases when you can't decide what to start a review with, because you are filled up with emotions. But there needs to be something, so I'll try to be informative now:
+ Graphics are amazing. Every location looks stylish and has a lot of details.
+ Combat feel awesome. It has the good old-school feeling to it. Whether you wield a katana to chop some meat to bloody pieces or just like to shoot baddies from far - it all will feel very intense and satisfying. I really like the presence of alternative modes for shooting weapons. It's something that I missed in shooters long time (screw you, "Press RMB to aim"! Hail to the "Press RMB to kick♥♥♥♥♥").
+ You have 4 magic abilities and 4 sword powers. Those are activated by tapping the movement key twice and pressing LMB or RMB (you can use magic while wielding shooting weapons too). If it doesn't work well for you, you can make timing adjusments in settings, which is nice.
+ Enemies are well varied and have their own strengths and weaknesses. If you use your magic abilities too much, they will become more and more enraged and will attack more swiftly and painfully.
+ The plot is surprisingly good. The dialogues are well-written and characters are likeable. There's a lot of funny lines.
+ Secrets! Lots of secrets and easter eggs! Something that I've missed a lot too!
+ My personal favorite - a lot of interactive, destructable, physical objects (comma before 'physical' is intentional). In latest games I literally HATED the lack of physics, most objects being static pieces of environment (even in action games! that's absurd!). In this game, however, you can let your inner redneck out and smash vases, break tables, ruin the furniture, etc. A decent room may become a total mess after a good fight... or after some fooling around. I loooooove to break stuff.
There are also some downsides though, but nothing big:
- Bosses are very similar in terms of fighting them. You just need to shoot the shiny parts of their armor and then destroy the uncovered crystals. Normal enemies make more challenge at some points.
- A lot of using the "This door is magically sealed! Go destroy 3 statues that are holding the seal!" method. It gives some depth to levels and makes them more varied-less linear (because you have to go search for those statues), but to the game's end it become quite annoying.
- Players with not powerful enough computers may experience sluggishness and low framerate. I've made it through the whole game on max settings and never had a problem (and my system is not a high-end one), but I saw people complaining on forums, so I think this should be stated here. But you know, people always complain. If your system is good, the game should run just fine.
That's all, I guess. I adore this game. An intense, fun, sort of nostalgic experience. If you love lots of blood and gore, if you like good humor, if your eyes are used to nice graphics, if you miss the good old days when shooters were clever and challenging - this game brings it all.

This is a great game.  No grind, no gear, just pure combat.  It is in very good shape considering Early Access, no crashes or issues yet for me.  Graphics are good.  Movement and controls feel smooth and precise.  No downtime either...the game loads quick, matches start quick, queues for both 2v2 and 3v3 pop within 30 seconds most times.   I hate games with 2 loading screens, intro videos and all that junk.
I was a long-time WoW arena player (years ago), and this game captures the same feel, but without any gear differences.  The focus on healing is much less than in WoW, since once your health drops below certain thresholds you can only be healed above the threshold by a health globe.  I find that damage mitigation is much more vital than healing.  The lack of power healing also keeps matches from going on too long.  I had some 45 minute WoW arena matches as Mage/Resto Druid...those stop being fun early on!
Counters/Stuns/Fears/Saps are all important, and very satisfying to lock someone down for a few seconds while you kill the teamate.
The classes feel balanced enough, have not seen anyone crying about OP classes/builds which is very rare for games like this.
If you are a solo player, its still worth a buy.  Lack of voice chat is a little problem, but so far in my solo matches I have run across very few toxic players.  I am sure that will change, but usually the stress of games like this bring out the absolute worst in humanity.  Text chat during pre-match to pick a primary target is usually all the communication you will get.  But that is enough to at least get some teamwork going.
Highly recommended.

With so many games out there that focus so heavily on making intense stories with enough action, puzzles, and mystery in them to keep the player invested, The Stanley Parable does something absolutely different- questioning video games at their very core. The Narrator is possibly one of the most entertaining and interesting characters I've met in my years of gaming. He adds a lot of sarcastic and dark humor that made me chuckle quite a few times. And the story draws you in and makes you really question ideas of freedom, story, and what really makes a good game... good.
The gameplay is minimalistic (as in, you walk and listen), but what the game offers that other games with little gameplay don't do- and I'm specifically pointing at 39 Steps when I say this- is choice. And choice is the most essential part of games. TSP has plenty of choice, and uses those choices to really make you think about what it is you're deciding on, and explore the Narrator and game's every corner and facet until you start to get a real feel for what's going on around you. However, unfortunately I won't be playing this game for another five years... because I want that achievement it offers.

Full review
So i didn' know this game until i got the demo in the Humble monthly. I didn't even tried it because i don't like demos in general, and i'm not a big plateformer player and the visuals of the screenshot of the game didn't appeal me that much.
I saw a short stream of HK at it's release and when i see the things moving i felt in love with the art of the game so i decided to buy it.
And i don't regret it, Hollow Knight is a masterpiece.
Don't juge it on screenshot, you NEED to see this game in action, it's a true gem of animation and the art direction of the game is absolutly well done.  the atmosphere of each biomes are really gorgeous and diverse, and each transition between two areas is stunning.
The mechanics are simples, but deep, the weapon system that might look poor at a first glance is finally really complete and offers a lot of path, with 3 specials techniques (which are more for the end game IMHO, i find it too long to charge it until you get a charm to reduce the cooldown ), and 3 skills. You can wear charms, items that change different things, most of them modify or enhance the combat mechanics (either the defense or the attacks). This greatly improve and add diversity into the gameplay.
The plateforming is quite easy, with some tough parts, but these part are only necessary for optional stuff. One dungeon is a very hard platefroming world, that coul remind super meat boy but it's the only part of the game of it's kind, and it's optional too (you'll need it if you want all endings tho).This part makes me really salty as i'm not that good at this kind of things, it took me several hours just to pass it, but i was really satisfy to beat it.
You start the game with almost not clue on what to do, and how to do it, sometimes you'll wonder what to do, but a look on the map to explore place you've never been always fixes that (you don't see unexplored rooms, you see that there's an open path on the boarder of a visited room leading to somewhere you never been).
The difficulty might appear very hard, but never forget that's it's an open world, if you're stuck at a boss, go ahead and improve your power, your sustain, your skills, once you're fully upgraded the game is really in an easy mode and not a lot of bosses will seems hard. Well it could looks hard the first time, then you look them doing their sh*t, you learn their patterns, and you should be able to beat most of them without much trouble once you find the best way to minimize the threat of their patterns. There's actually one boss that gave me hard times even fully stuffed  (it's optional for 100% but necessary for what people usually call the "true" ending even if i personally find this very subjective since all endings makes sense IMHO).
The real challenge in this game is not to beat it, as i just said, this could be such a simple task, what is hard is to try to finish it quick, or without all the upgrades (see the achievment to get an idea on the difficulty levels ("beat the game in under 10 hours", under 5 hours", "under 20 hours with 100%" etc.) not to mention the Steel Soul mode once you beat the game once, which is basically the real hard way, with perma death and not even shade (when you are killed you can return where you died and kill your shade to recover your stuff, if you die before killing your shade you lose all the money and souls you had).
Talking about this, the death system in the game can be frustrating, so get ready for some salty moments, a lot of money lose, a lot of walking from a save point to some place you are in difficulty. You're warned.
If you aim to 100% the game you'll have to walk a lot across the world, visit places again, and quick travel points are something rare in this game, soooo... It could be annoying if you don't like to return to some known places.
There's a tons of things to do, to collect, to discover, lot of replayability potential (speed run, arena, more playable characters are coming in future updates, in brief, this game might hook you for a while).
Aaaaand last but not least, the story, which is cool (yeah, i won't speak much about it, cuz you know, spoilers and stuff).
As i said at the beginning,  the lore is marked with some kind of melancholy, and gloomy things, this games bring feelings, sometimes i felt sad, sometimes i was smiling or suprised.  Yeah, i'm definitly not the Hollow Knight.
Conclusion:
Fantastic game, it's only $15 for hours and hours of joy. Buy it now support the devs (and hopefolly with the money they will make more things like this (and incidentally, buy food and stuff like that)!

Remember the nineties? Remember those silly shooters you would play, like doom, quake or unreal?
This game channels that era and updates it to the present. It's a shooter that confronts you with many enemies at one time, and there are no cover mechanics. You are free to charge right in and kill them before they kill you, dodging their attacks and limiting the amount that can attack you with natural obstructions. The gameplay features a rather generic selection of guns and a huge sword with fun mechanics! In truth, I felt this was why I liked the game. It brought back some of the gameplay of the excellent jedi knight games. Your sword doesn't feel like a random melee weapon, but like an instrument of murder that can dice up enemies in very gory and bloody ways until nothing but lumps of flesh and bone remain.
If you are looking for a game that brings back some of that feeling of shooters of the nineties, then this is for you. If you liked painkiller or serious sam, then this is for you.

You know, it's wierd. Usually I insist that any game where its purpose can be entirely digested just by watching a full playthrough of all the content is not worthy of being a game. And yet, while The Stanley Parable falls under that categorization, it is not pretentiously so. The Stanley Parable is a well-written comedy experience that uses the medium as a way to enhance the delivery, so one way of looking at it is that buying this game is like buying a DVD of some stand-up (where you're actually in the show and you're in the front row and you keep getting called on so you try heckling except you can only do a finite number of tangents but you get my point). It's also an intelligent commentary; people who did English or Media Studies would be having a field day pulling back all the layers on show here. But, you know, don't let that detract from the fact that this game would DEFINITELY be worse off as anything but a game.
I still did get a little kick out of being able to handle the experience myself even after the jokes were already shown to me, which might have something to do with the game's surreal applications of the source engine coming across like a damn magic show. Is that kick work x amount of money? Well, it's in good faith. We put the bread on the table for this indie dev fellow, and you can still play the demo, which includes none of the content in this paid-for package but instead has its own unique hilarious post-modern/satirical set pieces.
By the way most of this review doesn't apply if you actually HAVEN'T seen the game in action yet. In which case, give the demo a go even if you were going to buy it, it's not a snubbed version of the experience so it won't spoil you to anything, and if the humour clicks well with you do what you want to do with your cash. That's pretty much the best advice.
all in all, this is a pretty darn good game, it did have quite a lot of bugs to start with, but most have been fixed by now

This is an Assassin's Creed game. I am supposedly an assassin in this game. Assassins are supposed to be masters of subtlety and grace and patience and guile. They are shadows in the night, that are barely ripples upon the water, elegant as poetry and deadly as poison. You get the idea.
Edward Kenway is none of those things. Edward Kenway's general solution to most things involves a matchlock pistol and a cutlass. Sea shanties and cannons. Debauching and wenching (kids, go look up wenching on google!), rum and eye patches. In short, ol' Eddie here is the antithesis of the Assassin.
Assassin's what? I'm sorry, I didn't hear you over the fun I was having looting and plundering ships and generally screaming YARR. So, hum. This is really a pirate game, where you nominally are tied into the assassins creed universe with the most perfunctory backstory imaginable (HELLO YOU ARE PERSON BLANK WORKING AT ABSTERGO ON THIS PROJECT WHICH IS CLEARLY SIGNPOSTED BECAUSE WE COULD NOT BE BOTHERED TO THINK OF A REAL PLOT). It tries to shove all that sci-fi nonsense out of the way as quickly as possible because well, frankly, you're a mighty pirate. You have a mighty pirate ship, and the carribean is your canvas to do as many horrible things to the british and spanish navies in equal measure. Go have fun. That's about the measure of it.
There is a story to follow, which unlocks various things, much like previous assassins creed games, but here you'll only be following the story so you can unlock more stuff to do AS A MIGHTY PIRATE, not because you have any real interest in the whole Assassins vs. Templar thing. I mean it's made clear that ol' Eddie is a pirate who just happened to pick up the robe and is a dab hand at stabbing people, he's not even an actual assassin! HE IS A MIGHTY PIRATE. THIS IS A MIGHTY PIRATE GAME.
So. Yeah, get on and get through the story, create merry havoc and unlock the stuff as you go, and enjoy life on the ocean waves, which then leaves the sandbox side and the collection, which really is the meat of it. Life on the ocean waves, and life on the ocean waves is pretty damn good. There's a ton of things to do, the waves are -gorgeous-, the atmosphere is terrific, the shanties are plenty, and there's never a shortage of gorgeous vistas and inviting targets to shoot, loot, and generally investigate. Be the pirate and the explorer, stuff the creed in the rum bottle where it belongs.
As an Assassins Creed game? It's terrible. It's not an Assassins Creed game, it's BARELY an AC game. As a pirate game? Second only to the seminal sid meier's pirates, and only because of the animus sci-fi nonsense. Dear Ubisoft, jettison the sci-fi junk, and make a pure pirate game from what you've got, and people will worship the result. That is all.

Flying Wild Hog has done it again with their re-imagining of Shadow Warrior.
I love the atmosphere they pour into their games.  Both Hard Reset, and Shado Warrior had this in abundance.  The only thing I wish is that you came into contact with a few more stragglers (single enemies or very small groups of them) instead of sections of groups of enemies.  But minor complaint.
The optimization this time around seems slightly improved over Hard Reset.  I mean this because on the same rig, Shadow Warrior Looks noticeably better graphics wise, while the performance may even be slightly more stable than Hard Reset. (at least no worse stable than Hard Reset)
I enjoyed the weaponry, just like in the original Shadow Warrior, (although the nuke upgrade for the Rocket Launcher could be a bit more powerful).  I love the ability to upgrade them, and my abilities.
I don't mind for one second that this game doesn't have any multiplayer. They made a solid single player experience. The levels are pretty big, and most are quite long.  The combat is fun, especially the sword combat.  The movement, and feel of the game is very solid.
This is not a typical short FPS game like we are use to seeing these days.
The music is nice, I especially like the way it added to the atmosphere. Some of the levels are done extremely well on here that make you just stop, and admire the work the devs have done!  Which you can see in some of my screenshots of the game.  The story is nice too, its an interesting telling, and the way its told is pretty nice as well.  I found myself doing a quiet little (non-sarcastic) golfclap at the end of the story, right before the credits started rolling, which were nicely done as well.
I caught this game on sale for like $7.50-$9.99.  I easily got my worth, it was a great game, and I would have got my worth even paying up to $25-$30.  I wouldn't pay any more than that though.
I would love to see Flying Wild Hog do a re-imagining of the 90's build engine FPS called BLOOD! I would buy that in a heart beat. That being said, I have my eyes on anything Flying Wild Hog will be working on.

Oh boy, this game is a treat. Where to even begin? Well, first I should say that Hollow Knight is nothing special. It doesn't iterate upon the genre or push the envelope or anything like that. And that, perhaps, is one of its biggest strengths. Because instead what you've got is just a good, solid game.
So, what Hollow Knight lacks in innovation it makes up for in familiarity, reliability. It's a simple game, nothing more, nothing less. BUT (and that's a big but), with that all said and done, I feel the need to point out HK's strong points; the stunningly gorgeous hand-drawn graphics, the hauntingly beautiful music and sound, the incredibly smooth and tight control and combat.
HK also has a painstakingly realized world and characters. There's so much attention to detail, little bits of lore and story sprinkled throughout. The characters are relatively simple in terms of depth, and yet quite memorable at the same time because of their personalities and the way they're written.
The game itself also has quite the long tail to it. I completed in just under 30 hours, and that was without going for 100% completion.
There's not a whole lot to say about the combat. It's pretty simple, but it has such good game feel to it. Bosses are very challenging, it's not uncommon to need multiple attempts on them, messing with item configurations in-between attempts. Some have complained that the difficulty is too high, but to me it feels like a nice sweet spot. Challenging yet fair. The game itself is also pretty forgiving, nothing ever felt unfair to me. And unlike say, Dark Souls with its limited Estus Flasks, you even have what is essentially infinite healing, as long as you keep building up your Soul Gauge (effectively MP, hit enemies to fill it up). The caveat however is that you have to hold down the button for a good while, and taking damage cancels the charge, so you need to find safe opportunities to heal. It's not just an "I Win The Game" button.
If you're a fan of the Metroidvania genre, you owe it to yourself to play Hollow Knight. It's such an incredible gem of a game.
One quick addendum: There were a few sticking points for me in terms of negatives. So, the map system in this game I feel is utterly atrocious. You don't have a map by default; instead, you have to find the Map NPC tucked away in a specific corner and then buy his map. And it's quite easy to miss him, because there's no sense of direction and exploration in zones is a bit non-linear. Exploring new zones feels treacherous and I was extremely hesitant to do so, largely because I didn't know where I was going or where savepoints were.
Also, the map by default is only filled out a certain amount, and going into new rooms doesn't fill it in until you get to a save point. So, a lot of the time you're fumbling around in the dark. However, this can be circumvented by finding a picture of the full 100% completed map (outside of the game, I mean, that doesn't exist in the game itself). I used that as a reference point for exploring new areas and it felt ten times better. I do realize the way the map system was designed was a conscious design decision, but I hate it all the same. It doesn't feel good.
The other big sticking point for me was that sometimes the game would start hitching and getting these massive slowdowns for a good couple of seconds. This has lead to my death on more than one occasion. However, the optimization patch just came out and hopefully this has all been addressed in that. But I've already completed the game and I have no intentions of replaying it, so it's a bit moot for me personally. But it's good to see that it was (hopefully) addressed regardless.
But anyway, aside from those two things, the rest of the game was very enjoyable. I had no other qualms or complaints otherwise.

Arma 2 Is really an different ''shooter'' Well it's really a Military Sim. But it does have quite a bunch of hilarious bugs that makes it silly as well, it isn't all that serious, so don't be afraid of the ''Simulator'' part. Multiplayer still works despite gamespy's demise, since all the servers are now on Steam. There are lots of players still online and you are guaranteed to find a game for pretty much any mission or mode. There are loads of mission editor and modding possibilities, if you are into that. You can be either a soldier on the field or someone all the way up in the high command, giving orders for a whole army of units. Bullet ballistics are present and I can tell that sniping is satisfying and unforgiving if you happen to miss a shot. Bullet damage is quite high, so except to die fast if you get hit anywhere from the waist up.
The thing I really don't like is the somewhat poor optimization. But you can get the game to run better, if you just modify a couple of text files. Still chernarus and other maps with dense forest are quite heavy on your PC. But maps like Takistan with less trees run very well. Also Desync is sometimes present if the server has been on for a long time. So you can shoot first and still die, if the server has been on for a long time. So you should check the Up Time if possible.
All in all I recommend the game, although the 20€ price tag for both OA and the vanilla game is a tad bit high I think for such a ''old'' game. So perhaps you should wait for a sale, maybe not. It's really your own preference.

You know, it's wierd. Usually I insist that any game where its purpose can be entirely digested just by watching a full playthrough of all the content is not worthy of being a game. And yet, while The Stanley Parable falls under that categorization, it is not pretentiously so. The Stanley Parable is a well-written comedy experience that uses the medium as a way to enhance the delivery, so one way of looking at it is that buying this game is like buying a DVD of some stand-up (where you're actually in the show and you're in the front row and you keep getting called on so you try heckling except you can only do a finite number of tangents but you get my point). It's also an intelligent commentary; people who did English or Media Studies would be having a field day pulling back all the layers on show here. But, you know, don't let that detract from the fact that this game would DEFINITELY be worse off as anything but a game.
I still did get a little kick out of being able to handle the experience myself even after the jokes were already shown to me, which might have something to do with the game's surreal applications of the source engine coming across like a damn magic show. Is that kick work x amount of money? Well, it's in good faith. We put the bread on the table for this indie dev fellow, and you can still play the demo, which includes none of the content in this paid-for package but instead has its own unique hilarious post-modern/satirical set pieces.
By the way most of this review doesn't apply if you actually HAVEN'T seen the game in action yet. In which case, give the demo a go even if you were going to buy it, it's not a snubbed version of the experience so it won't spoil you to anything, and if the humour clicks well with you do what you want to do with your cash. That's pretty much the best advice.

Remember the nineties? Remember those silly shooters you would play, like doom, quake or unreal?
This game channels that era and updates it to the present. It's a shooter that confronts you with many enemies at one time, and there are no cover mechanics. You are free to charge right in and kill them before they kill you, dodging their attacks and limiting the amount that can attack you with natural obstructions. The gameplay features a rather generic selection of guns and a huge sword with fun mechanics! In truth, I felt this was why I liked the game. It brought back some of the gameplay of the excellent jedi knight games. Your sword doesn't feel like a random melee weapon, but like an instrument of murder that can dice up enemies in very gory and bloody ways until nothing but lumps of flesh and bone remain.
If you are looking for a game that brings back some of that feeling of shooters of the nineties, then this is for you. If you liked painkiller or serious sam, then this is for you.

Full review
So i didn' know this game until i got the demo in the Humble monthly. I didn't even tried it because i don't like demos in general, and i'm not a big plateformer player and the visuals of the screenshot of the game didn't appeal me that much.
I saw a short stream of HK at it's release and when i see the things moving i felt in love with the art of the game so i decided to buy it.
And i don't regret it, Hollow Knight is a masterpiece.
Don't juge it on screenshot, you NEED to see this game in action, it's a true gem of animation and the art direction of the game is absolutly well done.  the atmosphere of each biomes are really gorgeous and diverse, and each transition between two areas is stunning.
The mechanics are simples, but deep, the weapon system that might look poor at a first glance is finally really complete and offers a lot of path, with 3 specials techniques (which are more for the end game IMHO, i find it too long to charge it until you get a charm to reduce the cooldown ), and 3 skills. You can wear charms, items that change different things, most of them modify or enhance the combat mechanics (either the defense or the attacks). This greatly improve and add diversity into the gameplay.
The plateforming is quite easy, with some tough parts, but these part are only necessary for optional stuff. One dungeon is a very hard platefroming world, that coul remind super meat boy but it's the only part of the game of it's kind, and it's optional too (you'll need it if you want all endings tho).This part makes me really salty as i'm not that good at this kind of things, it took me several hours just to pass it, but i was really satisfy to beat it.
You start the game with almost not clue on what to do, and how to do it, sometimes you'll wonder what to do, but a look on the map to explore place you've never been always fixes that (you don't see unexplored rooms, you see that there's an open path on the boarder of a visited room leading to somewhere you never been).
The difficulty might appear very hard, but never forget that's it's an open world, if you're stuck at a boss, go ahead and improve your power, your sustain, your skills, once you're fully upgraded the game is really in an easy mode and not a lot of bosses will seems hard. Well it could looks hard the first time, then you look them doing their sh*t, you learn their patterns, and you should be able to beat most of them without much trouble once you find the best way to minimize the threat of their patterns. There's actually one boss that gave me hard times even fully stuffed  (it's optional for 100% but necessary for what people usually call the "true" ending even if i personally find this very subjective since all endings makes sense IMHO).
The real challenge in this game is not to beat it, as i just said, this could be such a simple task, what is hard is to try to finish it quick, or without all the upgrades (see the achievment to get an idea on the difficulty levels ("beat the game in under 10 hours", under 5 hours", "under 20 hours with 100%" etc.) not to mention the Steel Soul mode once you beat the game once, which is basically the real hard way, with perma death and not even shade (when you are killed you can return where you died and kill your shade to recover your stuff, if you die before killing your shade you lose all the money and souls you had).
Talking about this, the death system in the game can be frustrating, so get ready for some salty moments, a lot of money lose, a lot of walking from a save point to some place you are in difficulty. You're warned.
If you aim to 100% the game you'll have to walk a lot across the world, visit places again, and quick travel points are something rare in this game, soooo... It could be annoying if you don't like to return to some known places.
There's a tons of things to do, to collect, to discover, lot of replayability potential (speed run, arena, more playable characters are coming in future updates, in brief, this game might hook you for a while).
Aaaaand last but not least, the story, which is cool (yeah, i won't speak much about it, cuz you know, spoilers and stuff).
As i said at the beginning,  the lore is marked with some kind of melancholy, and gloomy things, this games bring feelings, sometimes i felt sad, sometimes i was smiling or suprised.  Yeah, i'm definitly not the Hollow Knight.
Conclusion:
Fantastic game, it's only $15 for hours and hours of joy. Buy it now support the devs (and hopefolly with the money they will make more things like this (and incidentally, buy food and stuff like that)!

Flying Wild Hog has done it again with their re-imagining of Shadow Warrior.
I love the atmosphere they pour into their games.  Both Hard Reset, and Shado Warrior had this in abundance.  The only thing I wish is that you came into contact with a few more stragglers (single enemies or very small groups of them) instead of sections of groups of enemies.  But minor complaint.
The optimization this time around seems slightly improved over Hard Reset.  I mean this because on the same rig, Shadow Warrior Looks noticeably better graphics wise, while the performance may even be slightly more stable than Hard Reset. (at least no worse stable than Hard Reset)
I enjoyed the weaponry, just like in the original Shadow Warrior, (although the nuke upgrade for the Rocket Launcher could be a bit more powerful).  I love the ability to upgrade them, and my abilities.
I don't mind for one second that this game doesn't have any multiplayer. They made a solid single player experience. The levels are pretty big, and most are quite long.  The combat is fun, especially the sword combat.  The movement, and feel of the game is very solid.
This is not a typical short FPS game like we are use to seeing these days.
The music is nice, I especially like the way it added to the atmosphere. Some of the levels are done extremely well on here that make you just stop, and admire the work the devs have done!  Which you can see in some of my screenshots of the game.  The story is nice too, its an interesting telling, and the way its told is pretty nice as well.  I found myself doing a quiet little (non-sarcastic) golfclap at the end of the story, right before the credits started rolling, which were nicely done as well.
I caught this game on sale for like $7.50-$9.99.  I easily got my worth, it was a great game, and I would have got my worth even paying up to $25-$30.  I wouldn't pay any more than that though.
I would love to see Flying Wild Hog do a re-imagining of the 90's build engine FPS called BLOOD! I would buy that in a heart beat. That being said, I have my eyes on anything Flying Wild Hog will be working on.

Arma 2: OA is a wonderful military simulator, boasting tons of fantastic mods. DayZ has fueled Arma 2, allowing it to rise up into popularity and giving people a look at the sim. Though, sure, you can buy Arma 2 just for the DayZ mod or Wasteland, but Arma 2 can hold itself up on its own, with the mods that base themselves around it being nice little bonuses that keep you from running out of content.
The engine's core issues do detract from this. The game is easy to run on singleplayer, but multiplayer is rather taxing. The engine doesn't utilize your resources that well, which doesn't result in fun. Though I can mess around on anything vanilla Arma 2 at very high with a steady and smooth framerate, modded multiplayer gamemodes appear to completely wreck the FPS even at low, which is what prevented me from playing DayZ. Due to this, I played Arma 2: OA and Arma 2 as Armas instead of modding bases, and still had a lot of fun.
The gunplay is solid, realistic, and tense. The controls are a bit clunky, and the first person view is annoyingly shakey, but third person holds up (but can easily be exploited.) The AI can be rather stupid at times, and singleplayer is rather harsh, forcing you to restart if you meet your death, but it is rather fun to play missions you pick up from the community or just try some of the base ones, or even make your own.

Oh boy, this game is a treat. Where to even begin? Well, first I should say that Hollow Knight is nothing special. It doesn't iterate upon the genre or push the envelope or anything like that. And that, perhaps, is one of its biggest strengths. Because instead what you've got is just a good, solid game.
So, what Hollow Knight lacks in innovation it makes up for in familiarity, reliability. It's a simple game, nothing more, nothing less. BUT (and that's a big but), with that all said and done, I feel the need to point out HK's strong points; the stunningly gorgeous hand-drawn graphics, the hauntingly beautiful music and sound, the incredibly smooth and tight control and combat.
HK also has a painstakingly realized world and characters. There's so much attention to detail, little bits of lore and story sprinkled throughout. The characters are relatively simple in terms of depth, and yet quite memorable at the same time because of their personalities and the way they're written.
The game itself also has quite the long tail to it. I completed in just under 30 hours, and that was without going for 100% completion.
There's not a whole lot to say about the combat. It's pretty simple, but it has such good game feel to it. Bosses are very challenging, it's not uncommon to need multiple attempts on them, messing with item configurations in-between attempts. Some have complained that the difficulty is too high, but to me it feels like a nice sweet spot. Challenging yet fair. The game itself is also pretty forgiving, nothing ever felt unfair to me. And unlike say, Dark Souls with its limited Estus Flasks, you even have what is essentially infinite healing, as long as you keep building up your Soul Gauge (effectively MP, hit enemies to fill it up). The caveat however is that you have to hold down the button for a good while, and taking damage cancels the charge, so you need to find safe opportunities to heal. It's not just an "I Win The Game" button.
If you're a fan of the Metroidvania genre, you owe it to yourself to play Hollow Knight. It's such an incredible gem of a game.
One quick addendum: There were a few sticking points for me in terms of negatives. So, the map system in this game I feel is utterly atrocious. You don't have a map by default; instead, you have to find the Map NPC tucked away in a specific corner and then buy his map. And it's quite easy to miss him, because there's no sense of direction and exploration in zones is a bit non-linear. Exploring new zones feels treacherous and I was extremely hesitant to do so, largely because I didn't know where I was going or where savepoints were.
Also, the map by default is only filled out a certain amount, and going into new rooms doesn't fill it in until you get to a save point. So, a lot of the time you're fumbling around in the dark. However, this can be circumvented by finding a picture of the full 100% completed map (outside of the game, I mean, that doesn't exist in the game itself). I used that as a reference point for exploring new areas and it felt ten times better. I do realize the way the map system was designed was a conscious design decision, but I hate it all the same. It doesn't feel good.
The other big sticking point for me was that sometimes the game would start hitching and getting these massive slowdowns for a good couple of seconds. This has lead to my death on more than one occasion. However, the optimization patch just came out and hopefully this has all been addressed in that. But I've already completed the game and I have no intentions of replaying it, so it's a bit moot for me personally. But it's good to see that it was (hopefully) addressed regardless.
But anyway, aside from those two things, the rest of the game was very enjoyable. I had no other qualms or complaints otherwise.

The naval part was one of the prizewinning features of this video game it was grand.  Legendary ship battles will have you shouting for joy once you defeat these monstrous ships.  Now the other downside to Assassin's Creed: Black Flag was the every so often how you would find the hole in the world and just free falling to your death. Arma 2: OA is a wonderful military simulator, boasting tons of fantastic mods. DayZ has fueled Arma 2, allowing it to rise up into popularity and giving people a look at the sim. Though, sure, you can buy Arma 2 just for the DayZ mod or Wasteland, but Arma 2 can hold itself up on its own, with the mods that base themselves around it being nice little bonuses that keep you from running out of content.
The engine's core issues do detract from this. The game is easy to run on singleplayer, but multiplayer is rather taxing. The engine doesn't utilize your resources that well, which doesn't result in fun. Though I can mess around on anything vanilla Arma 2 at very high with a steady and smooth framerate, modded multiplayer gamemodes appear to completely wreck the FPS even at low, which is what prevented me from playing DayZ. Due to this, I played Arma 2: OA and Arma 2 as Armas instead of modding bases, and still had a lot of fun.
The gunplay is solid, realistic, and tense. The controls are a bit clunky, and the first person view is annoyingly shakey, but third person holds up (but can easily be exploited.) The AI can be rather stupid at times, and singleplayer is rather harsh, forcing you to restart if you meet your death, but it is rather fun to play missions you pick up from the community or just try some of the base ones, or even make your own.

I can now safely say that Hollow Knight is the absolute best modern metroidvania I ever played. The game has a ton of new and cool stuff which is new to this genre and adds A LOT to it, even if it borrows some elements from one well known and respected series and imho, it's a HUGE plus! Also, the world in this game is absolutely massive, extremely well done and interesting to explore. Worldbuilding and lore is also excellent along with many characters you'll encounter during your journey. I can't say enough how much I love and adore this game.
***************************
How so happens that each year we're getting an absolutely incredible metroidvania game (and sometimes even more than one)  each with its own unique world, artstyle, amazing soundtrack and sometimes even new to the genre gameplay mechanics etc.?
Honestly? Hollow Knight is amazing and I absolutely adore this game. Everything from visuals, animations, soundtrack, characters and adorable bug-like creatures is really well done, along with huge interconnected and dangerous world which is really fun to explore, dicover new areas, characters, secrets and so on. You may think that it's another metroidvania game but nope, Hollow Knight has unique gameplay mechanics which I won't spoil and which you won't find in any other game in this genre.
But if there's one or two things to complain about.. it sure as hell be frequent stuttering and overall performance issues which can stand in the way of enjoyment and sometimes even ruin your experience. Also, you can only save the game when you use benches or something like that, not only that but there also not a lot of these benches in each given area, so if you die in the new area and not dicovered a bench there, you'll be backtracking a lot to get your way back and frankly it takes way more time than it should.
It's not that this is a game-breaking issues or anything, but still, they are anoying and I hope it'll be soon fixed. But these issues aside, I can easely recommend this game to absolutely every metroidvania fan out there. Buy it! It's amazing!
