The narrator is telling Stanley's story now.  Stanley did not like his story being told by the narrator and jumps off a cliff in an act of defiance.  Too bad, it was the narrator's story all along and Stanley dies because the narrator had planned to tell the story that way all along.
The Stanley Parable is a unique concept when it comes to gaming, -but isn't actually unique, in the sense where its only gimmic copies the very principles and concepts of exemplary works of post-modern literature.
The Stanley Parable explores the concept of "story telling" in gaming. Where if a character is "controllable" and given free will by the player, but is dominated by an overarching story and narration, is the player actually playing a game? Or is the game playing the player?
To take this into perspective, if a game is open world where you can make infinite number of decisions that could impact the gaming experience but cannot change the overarching story or outcome, are you really make any significant decisions while playing? Are you controlling a character to any significant degree? OR, is the game controlling your experience of the game?
In The Stanley Parable, you will have "choice" at times while at other times the narrator will be a♥♥♥♥♥♥and take away your "choice." The paradox here is, if a story is being dictated by two separate entities, can it be told cohesively?  The answer is no, which is the main premise of the game.
Pros:
+Novel gaming experience
+Not made to cater to lowest common denominator, thank you very much.
+Confusing...-in a good way
+Interesting game concept
Cons:
-The Stanley Parable gets boring pretty fast
-Tongue-in-cheek jokes become fairly predictable after some point.
-Uninteresting soundtrack.
-Short and overpriced (I'd price the game at $5-$8)
-Is it fun? no.
-Are there gameplay mechanics? Not at all.
TL;DR
Go read the City of Glass, by Paul Auster.

I'd like to preface this review by saying that everyone will have a different experience with Dungeon Defenders. Many of them will be positive. However, my own time with this game has shown it to be underwhelming. Allow me to explain my bias.
Dungeon Defenders does well in blending the tower defense and third person action genres. As one of four different classes (more if you've purchased the DLCs), you'll be fending off waves of enemies through a multitude of well designed and colorful levels.
The biggest issue I've noticed is the class imbalance. Some classes will have skills that can easily diminish hordes of enemies. Other classes, even at a higher level, will find enemies resistant to their abilities. Secondly, the combat just isn't engaging. Not only is it a bore repeatedly hitting the attack button, but it's also a bore to watch.
For the majority of its audience, Dungeon Defenders boasts great replay value. For those looking for more excitement, try elsewhere.
Grade: C+

I highly recommend this game, although I've only played 28 hours so far and still haven't nearly completed it, I have had a lot of fun. The primary reason I say this is that it's essentially the old Sid Meier's Pirates game (which I very much enjoyed), except done up with Assassin's Creed's plot and better graphics, as well as much more entertaining ship and boarding combat. On a macro scale it's similar as well; you cruise around the Caribbean at your own free will depending on which way the wind is blowing, and are free to visit towns and cities to repair, rearm and upgrade your ship (and your character - Edward Kenway), you can raid and capture European forts which provide mercenary contracts, insiders whom you may pay off to lower your bounty from either Britain or Spain, and a shipwright, who again can repair, rearm and upgrade your ship - the Jackdaw. The one thing which in my opinion is the heart of the game is the fact that you can simply sail around fighting, boarding and capturing European schooners, galleons, frigates and man'o'wars, all of which have lucrative rewards for those in need of cash. This is highly entertaining and I haven't found myself getting board of this particular mechanic once yet.
I will also add that the creators at Ubisoft have not optimised this game for PC, and in fact stated they simply didn't care to do so for this title. As such, expect it to run quite a bit worse than Assassin's Creed III, even if you played both on the medium graphical preset. All-in-all, and considering it took Ubisoft a rushed year to get this game out (as they will be doing from now on with all subsequent games in the franchise), I'd recommend anyone to buy this game, even if you're not previously a fan of the A.C. series.

The classic 3D Realms humor is still present also. The voice acting is spot on, delivering Wang's one-liners glibly. There's a good balance of tongue-in-cheek and break-the-fourth-wall jokes, keeping the humor from becoming grating.

Absolutely worth buying this, preferably the collector’s edition for the extra skins and soundtrack.

I discovered my love of metroidvanias back in 2015 with the release of Ori and the Blind Forest.  I loved every bit of that game from its gorgeous graphics, emotional tale, to its epic escape sequences.  The game re-introduced me to a genre I thought I didn't care about and now know I absolutely adore and have since consumed most of Steam's offerings for good metroidvanias.
I only bring my love of Ori in this review to highlight that with as much as I love Ori and the Blind Forest, I think Hollow Knight has surpassed it in my place for top metroidvania game.
This game has an amazing art style with hand-drawn animations.  It oozes style and many of the scenes in the game could be right at home just as a wallpaper on your computer.  As most metroidvanias the game starts very simple.  You have access to a small part of the world and your movement/actions are simple, however as you play you gain access to more abilities that opens up the world in ways you didn't think at first.  There is back-tracking (as in most in this genre) as you discover abilities and secret areas. Loadouts in this game come in the form of charms which "modify" your character's abilities or passive stats.  Everyone I've talked about this game has played the game slightly different which is always interesting to read.
The world is reminiscing of Dark Souls in the way the lore is presented.  You are thrust into a dying world and start putting the pieces together as to what happened and what you need to do to save it.  The NPCs are very well crafted I enjoyed seeing familiar faces on newly discovered ground always hoping to glean something from their dialogue or actions. Every area is populated with its own unique set of enemies which makes each very unique from each other.
One strange thing is that the difficulty of the game is pretty well balanced.  It's not extreme on either way (not too easy, not too hard) as long as you're not going for the "true" ending (there is one).  In that case the game's difficulty may have a spike due to a couple of the requirements being way above the difficulty of the rest of the game.  Regardless, getting there was well worth it.
For $15 you really can't go wrong with this game.  There were some performance issues but it seems most if not all of these have been addressed in the last patch.  The game is much longer than I expected as well.  I finished the true ending at around 30 hours and I'm going for the 100% so I'll be playing it for a while still and it seems they'll be adding a second playable character in the future with her own unique skills and attacks.
TL:DR:
* Great art style from the music, to the graphics, to animation
* Evolving combat is fun with the evolving abilities, charms, and enemy variety
* A lot longer than I thought for $15.  Ori took me 9 hours while it took me around 30 for the true ending on this one.  Definitely worth your money
* Interesting lore, though some of it may be cryptic (in the style of Dark Souls)

At this point in time, Hollow Knight is a contender for game of the year for me, and that says something about the game considering its only March. For such a small price tag I went into it expecting to be finished in seven hours or so, what I didn't expect was how much content is packed into this game and just how brutally hard it can be.
After my first five deaths in this, to starter enemies and all, I couldn't help but compare it to the Dark Souls game series because of how easily I had my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me because of a simple mistake. You screw up your timing and jump too late or too early, you lose health, you go to parry but mess up, you lose health, you get the gist. You can't run about hacking and slashing in this, timing is key.
Every boss I fought took me at least a minimum of three tries to beat as I always charged in spamming my attack button, hoping to get in enough hits to stun them. But alas my efforts were vain and all I could do was watch as I lost my hard earned Gio yet again and cursed myself for my foolishness and being made to backtrack there all over again to reclaim them.
Taking a leaf from Dark Souls, there are also optional bosses in this that can and will kick you all the way to hell and back if you're not prepared, a great example being the Mantis Lords. The first time I fought them I went in with the starter weapon and base health, I got in maybe five hits before they annihilated me.
There's quite a variety of enemies, going from your standard husks who mindlessly attack you, to the irritating balloon like enemies who shoot poisonous gas at you, to the even more infuriating teleporting spell-casters who if I had the ability to reach through the screen and punch, I would. Teleportation is one of the cheapest mechanics and turns any fight from a fair and challenging one to an absolutely unfair one that will have you cursing the devs of this game.
But they shouldn't be bought down by this one little fact, because the rest of the game is phenomenal. It boasts some of the best hand-drawn animations I've seen in a game to date, even more so than Jotun. I still have yet to beat the game because I can't help but stop and look at every area in detail and admire it. Musically, the game has an incredible soundtrack and I recommend buying it when it's available, thats all I'll say about it.
The only gripes I really have with this game are the teleporting enemies as mentioned earlier and how easily you can get lost in this. For an indie game, it really is big and although you can buy maps from vendors scattered about, I still got lost a lot. The fact that you get next to no tips on what to do or where to go, also like Dark Souls, adds to this confusion. But the feeling you get when you finally realise where to go and make actual progress is like none other.
Considering that I only heard about this a week before it got released, I absolutely adore this game and cannot recommend it enough. Everything from the visuals to the music to the challenging combat makes this an early contender for game of the year and it deserves it.

After more than 20 years of gaming, Hollow Knight became instantly one of my all-time favourites.
Amazing, how an indie game can have so much content and yet be indistinguishable from AAA games qualitywise. The artistic direction is pure diamond. Visual and musical brilliance results in an exceptionally atmospheric game.
Platforming and combat are fluid and often fast-paced while requiring quick wits. Different charms, spells and nail arts make the combat diverse enough to be interesting and still keep it relatively simple, so skill is a major factor. Challenging, but completely fair. Some parts, especially optional content, are actually pretty hardcore but oh so satisfying. More casual players might not get to complete everything. That is, if they even find it all.
Secrets are all over the vast world and well hidden, so that is not something to be taken for granted. It is funny how you'll find new things even in the very first area throughout the whole game. Hollow Knight has a wonderful feeling of exploration. You need to buy a map for each area, they are not available instantly when entering a new one. Keep an eye out for shortcuts or stag stations.
The game's progression often requires you to revisit areas later, when you have a certain ability or item acquired. ARMA II: Operation Arrowhead is a fatally flawed genius of a game. The way the UAV works in the helicopter mission is never explained and, trying to figure out how to use its targetting takes all the fun out of that mission. To show the user that they really don't understand what we want, one of the missions has an idiotic "puzzle" element added to it you're expected to write down some weird squiggles and punch them into a bomb defusing keypad. The gunplay is smooth and upgrading adds not only significant benefits but also visual flair to each weapon. This Re-interpretation of the classic 1997 shooter actually pleasantly suprised me in several ways in just how good it is.
The combat system for a start is immensely satisfying, The sword combat is implemented so well that along with chivalry it's the most fun i've had doing first person melee combat.
Guns are also really fun to use thanks to the dismemberment of all enemy limbs in the game as well as some of the more unique weapons from the original game such as the enemy heart and head.
The graphics are relatively eye pleasing featuring a lot of colour, rich texture quality and a nice variety of environments to explore in, although monotony does set in at times through either the same type of environment repeating themselves too many times (Enough of the damn Bamboo Forests) or a level going on for too long.
The plot was also somewhat suprising in how intriguing it was and the characters are funny/interesting enough to not be annoying, it's also a decent sized game at around a dozen hours and you can get plenty of replay value maxing out all of the characters abilites and unlocking all of his skills.
So in summary as long as you don't expect a true remake of the original shooter you should have a blast playing this and for me this was one of the best shooters of 2013.

Great metroidvania with a beautiful and a breathtaking world. For me personally, I like games which the world looks organic but also lived in. What Hollow Knight does beautifully is create a world where there is a palpable sense of history in everything you see. You roam through ruined cities and roadways where dead guards still roam with single minded purpose, you tackle overgrown forests with remanants of a lost civilization slowly being taken over by nature and even in a grand palace where retainers still fawn and heap fake praise on the king.
All of the areas are organic, breathtaking and a sense that the world is dying out slowly hangs heavily in the air. The various NPCs throughout the world punctuate the bleak tone with some of them reminising time long past. All the exploration is kept fresh with a stunning soundtrack playing in the background. I am glad I got the soundtrack for this becuase this one is a keeper. The music itself is pretty simplistic but the emotion and the range it conveys are awesome. My favorites are Greenpath, Crystal Peak and Forgotten Crossroads.
Now the areas themselves, all of the are massively interconnected which means each area have a lot of connecting links to other areas. Some of these paths are locked out initially but as you get more abilities these areas open up (it is a metroidvania after all) You will spend a long time in each of the areas exploring and thinking on how to proceed further. This game has no "Go here now" signs so you will be stuck with no direction and only exploration can reveal the way to you.
It helps that the each of the areas are littered with critters and creatures out to get you. From simple, small bugs walking along a set path, to fully armored bug guards who you will more like try to avoid than fight. The combat system is simplistic but with the myriad of movement options, it opens up to become something special. Each of the enemies follow a pattern and a timing window. A flying bug will spit out acid every 4 seconds leaving you with 3 guaranteed seconds to attack. You will need to observe carefully, learn patterns and start exploiting timings to traverse areas because the enemies are numerous and what they lack in ability then make up for in numbers. Make no mistake this is a difficult game but you will progress from throwing tentative pokes in the beginning to confidently jumping and dashing around abusing spacing and timing once you get adept.
Bosses also use pretty much the same formula. Where normal creature have 1 or 2 patterns, bosses have upwards of 4-5 patterns with varying timing windows. If you are like me, you will die over and over until you nail all the patterns and abuse the timing windows while retreating to safety and healing during other times. Suffice to say the bosses are challenging and require your complete attention.
Overall a great game. Took me about 27 hrs to finish and my end game completion report says only 85% complete. There is still much to do and explore in the massive map and still some bosses I havent fought yet. Add to this the promise of a secondary playable character in a future update this is very good value for money. I cannot wait to re-play the whole game again with hte second character whenever its released. Personally I didnt face too many slowdowns tho some ppl seem to face them.
TL:DR One of the best Metroidvanias I have played.

This game. Oh, this game.  When it went $9.99 during the Steam sale, I watched TB's video on it, and you could tell he was having a ridiculous amount of fun with the game, so I picked it up.  Just got around to playing it over the last week.  I'm only about 1/2 way through the game but let me tell you:  BUY THIS GAME RIGHT NOW.  It is worth full price, but I'd say it is an absolute must-buy any time on sale at $20 or less.
First, though, understand what you're getting here.  This is a single-player campaign so you're not going to get endless multiplayer out of it.  It is also a reimagining of 90s FPS games, which I'm sure is why I love it so much.  It moves fast (though not as fast as ROTT - more on that in a minute), and you don't have shields or recharging health per se.  It does emulate more modern FPS games in that you can recharge your health to a certain point with abilities, and you can also buy ammo and weapons upgrades (not unlike Far Cry 3's system, though not in stores and you don't have arbitrary animal skins you need to upgrade).
I mentioned ROTT:  this game doesn't move at light speed like that game did, and it feels more "modern" than ROTT does. It also looks great and doesn't run like hot garbage like ROTT.  I have a core i7 with 8GB RAM and a GTX660.  I can play Shadow Warrior on pretty much max settings and it runs great, and looks terrific.  ROTT, on the other hand, has far worse graphics and runs like crap with frame-rate spikes and drops all over the place.  Shame because ROTT has sweet multiplayer, but this game's campaign is everything I'd hoped to get out of ROTT.
Anyway... you get plenty of graphics and control options here, they definitely didn't skimp.  The game looks terrific.  Like the FPS games of old, there are tons of secrets to find in each level.  There's also no assistance as far as navigating the levels, and backtracking is often required, so you get a bit of that old-school feeling of navigating through some maps repeatedly looking for a specific room or key.  That takes a bit to get used to, as most modern games give you way more assistance, so just be aware of this.
The swordplay in this game is... amazing.  I have no idea how they did it, but this is easily the best FPS melee system I've ever seen.  That isn't to say the gunplay is bad, because it isn't, and the weapons are awesome, but the sword really steals the show here.
I think the one-liners and dialogue are great, and also carry over that 90s feel.  I liked it, but YMMV.
TL;DR   Just buy the game already.  Great graphics, awesome melee system, and easily the most fun I've had in a single player FPS campaign in years.  One of the most fun games of 2013 without a doubt.

Shadow Warrior is an excellent classic arcade-style shooter. There aren't too many around these days, and Shadow Warrior stands head and shoulders above most.
The good:
-The swordplay: Definitely the strong point of the game. Incredible in both visuals and execution. While chopping my way through hordes of demons, I often neglected the rest of the arsenal, simply because it was just so much more satisfying to use the katana. You'd be hard pressed to find a game with better (or at least more spectacular) melee combat.
-The writing and dialogue: A very nice mix between the serious and the silly, with neither side becoming too tedious or too repetitive. Lo Wang's quips are reminiscent of 80's B-movies in both style and delivery. If you enjoyed Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon, you will love this! As for the story, it's surprisingly good for a first person shooter; my expectations were exceeded greatly. The voice acting should also not go unmentioned; Hoji's and Lo Wang's voice actors maintain superb delivery throughout.
-The upgrade system: Simple and integrates with the fast paced combat very well. No skill trees, no minmaxing; just whatever makes you faster and deadlier (or adds more barrels to your gun). The non-sword based powers were also a nice touch, offering just a little extra depth to the combat.
While I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone in search for a fresh take on the FPS genre, I'd be lying if I said it was all good. Some weak points:
-The boss fights: Complely underwhelming, and not anything like the rest of the game (Deus Ex: HR, anyone?). Every single boss fight is your bog standard shoot-the-big-dude-in-the-massive-glowing-spot battle. There are 4 boss battles throughout, and all are nearly identical. The only saving grace is that they are of almost zero challenge, so you won't suffer for long.
-The variety of enemies: However spectacular the combat may be, your targets will be the standard demon most of the time.     Throughout the game, you'll find two more types of the demon, and two bigger, miniboss-esque creatures: the Necromancer and the Warlord. Other than these, there's the odd troop of human gangsters, but overall, there's little difference in the standard enemy units.
To sum up, Shadow Warrior is not without some flaws, but for anyone wishing to try something slightly different, it's an excellent experience. If you're interested in the time taken to complete, it took me 12 hours on normal, so it's definitely longer than most games these days. There's an NG+ for completionists, too.

At this point in time, Hollow Knight is a contender for game of the year for me, and that says something about the game considering its only March. For such a small price tag I went into it expecting to be finished in seven hours or so, what I didn't expect was how much content is packed into this game and just how brutally hard it can be.
After my first five deaths in this, to starter enemies and all, I couldn't help but compare it to the Dark Souls game series because of how easily I had my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me because of a simple mistake. You screw up your timing and jump too late or too early, you lose health, you go to parry but mess up, you lose health, you get the gist. You can't run about hacking and slashing in this, timing is key.
Every boss I fought took me at least a minimum of three tries to beat as I always charged in spamming my attack button, hoping to get in enough hits to stun them. But alas my efforts were vain and all I could do was watch as I lost my hard earned Gio yet again and cursed myself for my foolishness and being made to backtrack there all over again to reclaim them.
Taking a leaf from Dark Souls, there are also optional bosses in this that can and will kick you all the way to hell and back if you're not prepared, a great example being the Mantis Lords. The first time I fought them I went in with the starter weapon and base health, I got in maybe five hits before they annihilated me.
There's quite a variety of enemies, going from your standard husks who mindlessly attack you, to the irritating balloon like enemies who shoot poisonous gas at you, to the even more infuriating teleporting spell-casters who if I had the ability to reach through the screen and punch, I would. Teleportation is one of the cheapest mechanics and turns any fight from a fair and challenging one to an absolutely unfair one that will have you cursing the devs of this game.
But they shouldn't be bought down by this one little fact, because the rest of the game is phenomenal. It boasts some of the best hand-drawn animations I've seen in a game to date, even more so than Jotun. I still have yet to beat the game because I can't help but stop and look at every area in detail and admire it. Musically, the game has an incredible soundtrack and I recommend buying it when it's available, thats all I'll say about it.
The only gripes I really have with this game are the teleporting enemies as mentioned earlier and how easily you can get lost in this. For an indie game, it really is big and although you can buy maps from vendors scattered about, I still got lost a lot. The fact that you get next to no tips on what to do or where to go, also like Dark Souls, adds to this confusion. But the feeling you get when you finally realise where to go and make actual progress is like none other.
Considering that I only heard about this a week before it got released, I absolutely adore this game and cannot recommend it enough. Everything from the visuals to the music to the challenging combat makes this an early contender for game of the year and it deserves it.

When I played Assassin's Creed 3 I said to myself, "I hope they make a whole game centered around this amazing naval combat ".  When Black Flag was announced my excitement and anticipation was highly optimistic.  After playing Black Flag I can honestly say it's by far my favorite Assassin's Creed title, and quite possibly the best game of the entire series.
Ubisoft has hit every nail squarely with their design decisions for AC4, starting with a new badass main character that rivals the charm, toughness, and intriguing story of the Ezio era.  The Connor character from AC3 was likable in few ways compared to Kenway.
The naval system and combat was improved and given a much larger focus in AC4, as to be expected in a game about pirates.  The vast scale of the map will blow you away the first time you zoom out to find your location, and realize how large this open world is.  Once I took to the seas I immediately found myself unable to stop playing.  The atmosphere is amazing.  Storm clouds rolling, whales jumping, ships sailing and battling each other, all while your crew sings the most catchy shanties that will have you singing along.  I seriously loved just casually sailing looking for collectables while listening to my crew sing.
Speaking of collectables they introduced a perfect pirates tie in for collection quests in the form of actual treasure maps.  The maps would give you a general coordinate to search, but to find the treasure you'll have to study the map and your surroundings looking for landmarks to find the X that marks the spot.  Other collectables included animus fragments, sea shanties lyrics, messages in bottles, and money chests.  These aren't hidden collectables, but they are scattered all over the open world and add more story for those completion fans.
Now, it wouldn't be an AC game without assassination missions.  While the games best moments occur on the seas, it's by no means saying the assassin parts are bad.  They are quite excellent.  Granted the games combat mechanics have not changed or evolved much since it's inception, but that's not a bad thing entirely.  They simply want to stick with what works, and are not trying to reinvent the wheel of the AC franchise.   The assassin segments do a great job of adding variety to the environments spanning huge Caribbean cities,  jungle villages, island fishing towns, and underwater caves.
The one definitive thing about Black Flag is you'll never be without something cool to see or do.  I didn't even mention multiplayer yet, which is still the same solid game it's been since Revelations.  My only complaint about Black Flag was they couldn't give a us Pirate Ship multiplayer battle mode.
All I can say is, "I hope they make a whole multiplayer game centered around this amazing naval combat "

At heart, AC IV is a great game. Well, its a great pirate game, anyway. The sailing feels great, and ship battles are fun. Whether is blasting away with cannons or climbing the rigging to assassinate enemy captains as I capture a ship, playing as a pirate is extremely fun, and more than a little satisfying.
And therein lies the problem.
Because AC IV does not want me to play as a pirate. It wants me to play Assassin's Creed. You know, annoying hud, immersion wrecking, failed attempts to create set piece missions, and linear, scripted content constantly interrupting my open world frolicking, the tacked on AC bits are the worst addition to an otherwise fine pirate game ever created.
And they really are bad.
Whether its the twenty or so tailing and eavesdropping missions, or the way in which whole swaths of a town suddenly become hostile territory just to make the mission harder; or the idea that while tailing I have to look at the person I am following literally ever 20 seconds or fail the mission; or the absolutely horrid HUD - the worst I have ever seen, in any game, ever - tacking AC IV onto an otherwise solid pirate experience served to do nothing other than ruin the pirate game this could have been.
And that's before the modern day content. The parts where you are yanked out of the game and forced to walk slowly in first person mode as you perform hacking missions as an errand boy at a Templar run video game development office. Yep, don't see those in the previews or advertising screens, do we? Know why? Its because they suck. Add to that the worst hacking mini games ever invented by man, and the modern day sections are easily the worst of this entire series. And that takes some work indeed.
Ubisoft could have built themselves a fantastic pirate game. By leaving the absolutely dreadful AC IV stuff out. Because adding it in did nothing for the game but drag it down.
Cannot recommend; done with this series forever.

My time with Shadow Warrior probably represents the most fun I've had with a FPS in ages. Well, since Bulletstorm at least. When did that come out? 2011? OK, then since 2011.
As I’m sure any of you remotely interested in playing this game already know, most of the gameplay in Shadow Warrior involves moving from room to room across large, sprawling levels and brutally slaughtering the hundreds of enemies that spawn within. Nothing new there. I’ve been doing that since the Wolfenstein days.
What makes Shadow Warrior so much fun is the variety of weapons and powers at your disposal (the use of all of which is encouraged through a decent upgrade system; the more creative and varied your methods of wiping out enemies, the more experience points … I mean, karma … you get to spend on adding new ways to be creative and varied in wiping out your enemies).
There’s also the sword. Man, using that sword is a blast. Watching demon limbs flying everywhere is a real joy. That makes me sound kind of insane, doesn’t it? So be it.
Alternating among guns and the sword and powers is relatively easy, although there were times when using a power (which, if you’re playing with a controller like I was, involves tapping a direction twice and then hitting a button) was a little clumsier than I would have liked, resulting is a barrage of profanity as I received a pummeling while trying to heal or something.
Shadow Warrior tells a better story than I expected, painting juvenile humor against a backdrop of relatively sombre events. To me, this mostly works well, and the juxtaposition of super-serious mythology and rapid fire♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes concludes in a genuinely bittersweet finale. I imagine this kind of thing won’t be everyone’s cup of tea, but it appealed to me.

I’m not usually one to say this, but Shadow Warrior played a bit too long for me. By the time my 18 hours with the game concluded, I was ready to be done. It was still fun, mind you, and I never felt compelled to leave it unfinished. But I was ready to move on. Most individual levels felt like they could have been trimmed (with the exception of the one-off boss fight chapters, each stage took me around an hour to complete. More if I was really hunting for the secrets tucked away in the corners of each), and after a while, they all kind of blend together.
Should you buy Shadow Warrior? If you enjoy the maze-like level layouts and breakneck combat of classic FPS games, then I’d say your enjoyment is as guaranteed as herpes in a ♥♥♥♥♥house. In other words, yes.

I've played this game for a solid 30 hours, have achieved about 100% completion (Trial of the Fool is something which evades me) and I think i'm ready to leave a review for this diamond in the rough.
Hollow Knight is basically what i'd call "Metroidvania Souls". It retains a lot of elements from both types of games. Metroidvania's world style and ability/item collecting combined with devious difficulty, tough enemies and a dying mechanic very similar to the Dark Souls series.
If you wish to fully complete everything, expect to check every nook and cranny for collectibles, hidden bosses and other assorted things.
So, onto the list of pros and cons.
PROS:
1: Beautiful Animation/Graphics, all hand-animated. Much attention to detail was placed in the world, and it shows. While not comparable to high fidelity games such as Ori and the Blind Forest, it certainly does good work with what it has.
2: Large amount of content. The amount of bosses, secrets and collectables in this game is quite large and diverse. You'll be searching andhitting many walls looking for secrets. Even some bosses are hidden and optional.
3: Tight, responsive controls. Your character will move where you wish them to, and you can adjust the height of your jumps quite easily. Movement is superb in this game, and is something you'll want to master by the end of it.
4: The soundtrack. Solemn melodies with pianos and violins start things off, but can escalate to dramatic crescendos when needed. Christopher Larkin nailed this OST.
5: High skill curve. WHile some might see this as daunting, knowing when or when not to attack or how to use your movement abilities to their maximum extent is quite fun, as you learn many things as you play. For this reason, I may suggest a second playthrough, more as a comparison kind of thing.
------
CONS:
1: Benches/Checkpoints are too far apart from one another: Dark Souls is something which did this right. Levels were usually  designed so when fighting andlosing to a boss, the trip back is usually fast and quick via checkpoints, so there is less downtime when dying.
However, Hollow Knight does not follow this example. You might have to go through half the area to get back to the boss arena if you die, with little to no shortcuts. It can be infuritating to fight a boss then have to go through their difficult area again. (I'm looking at you, Soul Master.)
2: Mapping System: I'm of two minds on this one. On one hand, I love how it's done and is quite immersive. On the other hand, having to equip a charm just to see where you are on the map seems a little backwards.
To summarize, this is how the mapping system works. Let's say you wish to get a map of the first area. You do not start with one. Instead, you must buy one from the mapper in the area. Then you have to buy stamps to mark certain things, like vendors or benches (only one-time purchase, however). To top it off, to update your map, you must buy a quill and can only do so at a bench.
It makes sense from an immersion perspective. Updating your map in the middle of fighting doesn't make much sense, especially with how your character actually holds out their map to look at it. However, from a gameplay perspective it can be a little confusing and inconvenient at times. Especially the charm/compass thing. That was dumb.
3: No late-game money sink: When you start Hollow Knight, there are several vendors with much to buy. However, for the most part, they don't update their stock at all, meaning once you've bought everything from every vendor, there's nothing to spend it on. I ended up wih something close to 20,000 cash/geo simply rattling around in my pocket.
4: Very difficult platforming sections: These are optional, but some of these sections are incredibly tedious to get through, especially the secret area known as the White Palace. Took me three hours of trial and error to get through there. It's very tough, with sometimes no margin for error. But if you like that kind of thing? Good, you'll have fun here.
----
All and all, Hollow Knight is a very good game with great presentation and gameplay. While it doesn't innovate too much, it's still something i'd highly recommend picking up if you are into this sort of thing.

Shadow Warrior is good game, but it is not without its problems, thankfully most of them are superficial.First up is the good, the graphics in Shadow Warrior are quite nice, nothing ground breaking, but the art direction is very strong.Things get a little bloomy here and there, but it works most of the time.Next is the gameplay, and fortunately it's quite good.Being a fan of the original, I was worried about the gameplay, but Devolver Digital did a great job bringing the original to the present.Personally it's one of the best modern shooters that I have played.Last is the sword, which is one of the best melee weapons I've used in a game.What makes it standout is how useful it is, and how well integrated it is, but this also leads to one of the games' faults.Now for the bad, to put it simply, the sword is overpowered.At first it is very balanced, but as you upgrade and unlock,  it slowly becomes your best weapon.The problem with this is that it makes the other weapons feel useless, and they give you a good few.While it doesn't break the game, it does make guns feel like the second option almost all the time.My last issue with the game is the comedy.The original Shadow Warrior was somewhat of a comedic game, they tried to capture some of that in this one, but it often falls flat or feels forced.The game even started to be a little annoying at times, but these aren't real big issues.All in all Shadow Warrior is a great title that I'd recommend to any shooter fan, and I look forward to seeing a sequel.

Probably one of the best 2D Metroidvania game i've played in these past couple years.
In Hollow Knight, you play as a bug-like creature exploring the underground world of Hallownest, from dimly lit caverns to jellyfish-infested jungles. Infested with bug-like npcs and enemies, the bosses in this game are great and their designs are unique for each one of them. Although the environment may be drag and grey, it matches the setting of this game rather well.
In terms of gameplay, this game plays surprising well. The controls are tight even though you are slightly limited to a jump and a strike (and the occasional dash). The "Swapper", one of the unique mechanics in this game involves the use of charms, once you are rested on a bench (the Bonfire of Hollow Knight) you can swap charms to increase your abilities or add new ones.
My main issues for this game is the excessive backtracking, without the compass charm to track where you on the map, the confusing level layout will make you lost very easily. Areas you have not explored before requires the purchase of a map purchased at the vendor in said new area. This forces you to search high and low and look at every nook and cranny until you find the vendor.
Overall this game is excellent in terms of gameplay and art design, if you like the Metroidvania genre, or even like the exploration aspect, this game is a must buy. The only thing I regret is not backing this kickstarter a couple years back.

Hoo, boy. I've been watching this game for its' two years of production. Now that I've played through it and got the True Ending, I guess it's safe for me to give this game my cents.
I have only one 'con' for the game right now, but it's a big one, and can either further make or break your purchase.
The entire map is for you to explore, and at your own pace. You can get maps and things to help you chart your way about the world, but it does not give you definitive missions or objectives. You can play through it how you want.
The world of Hallownest is your oyster.
Which is also a drawback of the game.
I certainly did. For some, this will add more charm. For others, it will stray them away from the game itself. Whether you feel like you can stomach it or not, is all up to you. I can definitely imagine that some people will get angry at the game because of it, or not even like it as a whole because of it.
(I'm not gonna call people babies because of it, though. Time is a pretty precious thing. But, hey. Time enjoyed wasting is not wasted time.)
Now, let's go across the pros.
Whilst playing through the game, you can tell that they've carved out a fleshed-out world in it. Lore can be found throughout the game to discover, and the game itself feels balanced, and well-made. Characters deliver their roles well, and nothing feels out of place. If you allow it to, this game will give you an immersive experience that might just linger.
If you have at least some degree of emotional output, this game will make sure it ticks.
I'm talking Super Meat Boy tight. They've done a good job with making every input feel as precise as possible--and in a game such as Hollow Knight, it pays off and adds to the experience.
Combat feels very clean, and not once in the game have I gone "I shouldn't have died there! That's unfair". Every time you get hit, the game will make it clear to you that you've got hit, but not in an annoying way. The sound and music will numb out, followed by a small crack on the screen and an audible sound to signify it. The game even freezes during that moment to let you mind register it all. With every death in the game, you have the ability to reflect on how that could've gone better.
No revives. One life. Death is permanent. Upon death, the save is wiped.
I've yet to go through that experience(and i actually want to), but I can only imagine that it'll give me a whole new state of mind. Whilst I was playing through the game normally, I had the freedom to be a bit cocky and try my luck with things. But in such a mode, I can only imagine that I'd be careful with a lot of things I'd do.
Eventually I'll get around to playing it. As of writing this, I'm just taking a little break from the game for now.
I shouldn't have to explain this one. All of the tracks are made with orchestra synths, but they all deliver and set the tone for most, if not all of the areas.
The ambient tracks of the game are also just, unf.
It's a Metroidvania that's certainly not for everyone--even some of those who adore Metroidvanias as a genre. But for those who endure and immerse themselves within Hollow Knight, it'll pay off as a powerful, enjoyable experience that'll at least leave some kind of memory in the player.
Infact, if you don't want to use a walkthrough(I don't blame you),
A notepad(both physically and digitally) is always a good idea. I'll be sure to use one myself whilst going through my Steel Soul playthrough.

Black Flag brings the Assassin's Creed series back to the heights of AC II with both a great story and a brilliant and varied cast of characters which AC III fell just a bit short of delivering.
Combat and navigation are solid and little changed from the established formula but are sidelined in this installment by naval combat and navigation which is refreshing as the gameplay threatened to become increasingly tedious as the series progessed.
The only noteworthy faults I can think of are small but can build up to the point of frustration in a long playing session. The freerunning sometimes decides to throw you in a direction in which you weren't pointing or you end up running into something that looks perfectly scaleable but apparantly isn't. As a result the freerunning experience seems slightly less fluid than in the previous installment. Boarding enemy ships is definitely one of the most exciting aspects of the game, however on a deck crowded with allies things get cramped, ruining the fluidity of combat and sometimes making it hard to keep track of where you are. Finally the missions can seem a bit repetative if you've been playing for an hour or so though a controlled progression through the story more or less alleviates this problem.
Overall this is a beautiful game with a gripping story, excellent characters and great gameplay. I would most certainly reccommend.

Recommend Rating: 3.5/5
Good: Beautiful level design, funny dialogues, best katana game ever
Bad: Repetitive enemies, boring boss fight, gets dull after mid-game
Shadow warrior reminds me of the hard old crazy FPS shooters like Painkiller, Duke Nukem. It is a refreshing experience to play this game. This is a very straightforward FPS. It has a very simple plotline, funny dialogues, giant bosses like those in Painkiller. The level design is beautiful, especially in the first part of the game that took place in Japan. The zen-style design is just beautiful. However the next stage in the dock is less amazing to behold, and the place gets boring after some chapters. Other than the level design, the game has a very good melee system - the katana. There are so many ways to fight with a katana in this game, and as game progresses the player will learn more ways to use it. The game has a very simple RPG system, but that simplicty does not make the system dull. You can choose from gaining max HP, higher damage output, better damage endurance or faster movement. These all contribute to your gamestyle. For me, I took the faster movement skills and health regen ability to support my swordfight style.
However, the game sometimes gets repetitive. It always trap you in a hall full of monsters and you can't leave until you slaughter them all. Moreover, throughout the game there are only a dozen of different enemies.  Instead of introducing new monsters in later chapters, the game just spams more and more monsters per wave. Although the swordfight is fun, it get boring in the mid-game. The boss fight is not ountstanding either. It always require you to fight with guns, rather than giving you choices in the two. And the boss fight isn't that special or fun to play, they just get more HP and consumes more time.
Overall, this is still a good game. Although the game might get kind of repetitive and boring after mid-game. It is still worth your money and your time to play. The katana will not disappoint you, I promise.

Danielewski's House of Leaves. Anyway. to put it simply:
This game changed my life.
I've never been the biggest fan of shooters or FPSs or even many RPGs. Recommend Rating: 3.5/5
Good: Beautiful level design, funny dialogues, best katana game ever
Bad: Repetitive enemies, boring boss fight, gets dull after mid-game
Shadow warrior reminds me of the hard old crazy FPS shooters like Painkiller, Duke Nukem. It is a refreshing experience to play this game. This is a very straightforward FPS. It has a very simple plotline, funny dialogues, giant bosses like those in Painkiller. The level design is beautiful, especially in the first part of the game that took place in Japan. The zen-style design is just beautiful. However the next stage in the dock is less amazing to behold, and the place gets boring after some chapters. Other than the level design, the game has a very good melee system - the katana. There are so many ways to fight with a katana in this game, and as game progresses the player will learn more ways to use it. The game has a very simple RPG system, but that simplicty does not make the system dull. You can choose from gaining max HP, higher damage output, better damage endurance or faster movement. These all contribute to your gamestyle. For me, I took the faster movement skills and health regen ability to support my swordfight style.
However, the game sometimes gets repetitive. It always trap you in a hall full of monsters and you can't leave until you slaughter them all. Moreover, throughout the game there are only a dozen of different enemies.  Instead of introducing new monsters in later chapters, the game just spams more and more monsters per wave. Although the swordfight is fun, it get boring in the mid-game. The boss fight is not ountstanding either. It always require you to fight with guns, rather than giving you choices in the two. And the boss fight isn't that special or fun to play, they just get more HP and consumes more time.
Overall, this is still a good game. Although the game might get kind of repetitive and boring after mid-game. It is still worth your money and your time to play. The katana will not disappoint you, I promise.

I've always been a firm believer that a key component to making a great game (not a good game, not a fun game, a great game) is having a solid amount of control over movement and player action. The OG game that did this was Mario 64.
This game is what I like to call, "the melee of mobas".
You have total control over your character. You move with WASD, you turn aim with your mouse. Everything is manual aiming (no click on target and auto hit). This game at its highest level is a pure demonstration of individual skill, reading your opponent, reacting to your opponnent, and teammwork (2v2 and 3v3).
You'll get stomped, you'll almost get a sick 2v1 comeback and make a stupid mistake costing your team the game, and yet it still feels good.
Its arena goodness without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of gear. You get better - not your character.

Hollow Knight is a compentent, charming, content-filled Metroidvania entry. It has echoes of both Dark Souls and Ori both. It also pulls no punches when it comes to difficultly - everything is earned, deaths are punishing, and the game asks a lot of you. For your efforts, you're rewarded with one of the longest Metroidvania games I've ever played - expect to spend well north of 30 hours on your first playthrough if you choose to explore without a guide. Two thumbs very much up - Hollow Knight is in the running for my favorite GOTY, certainly.

Overall I feel that Shadow Warrior was a fun distraction.  Don't go into it expecting anything mind blowing or paradigm shifting, it's just a game where you blow crap up, blow people up, hear a crude joke, go down another hallway, and repeat it all again.
Some of the humor fell flat for me, a few jokes were amusing, but I was a little disappointed that nothing made me laugh out loud, or even chuckle.  I'm sure that if I went back to the orignal game, a game I do remember having me laugh out loud, I'd find the humor crude and not as good as I remember it, but there's still that bar there, even if it was set by a much younger version of me who found more humor in wang jokes.
There's also some enemy types that are horrendously annoying, a necromancer type guy and a blueish bull type thing, and there's a part at the very end that puts multiples of both of these guys in an arena that you must defeat!  This was a bit annoying, and I cringed each time I saw those enemies come up, but most of the enemies weren't too bad to fight, most arenas were very fun to slice and dice through.
Overall if you are looking for a game that is nothing more than a bit of eye candy (there are some great scenes in this game) and a lot of explosions, you could do a lot worse than this game.  Go into it knowing what you are getting into: middle school humor, blood, gore, explosions, and sword play, and you wont be disappointed.

Not so much a sequel, prequel, reimagining, or reboot of the original Shadow Warrior, but some combination of all four. It's surprisingly loyal to the source material, but gives more than enough of its own voice so it doesn't feel like it's needlessly pandering to a niche fanbase. Everything is vibrant and colorful to look at, especially at the beginning, though it falls off in acts two and three as you move to more drab, industrial environments.
The gameplay is simple but fun, mindless violence. If you like blood, this game has it in spades. Enemies don't just drop down dead; they go in pieces and explosions of blood that leaves areas coated in red. The genius of the game is that if you have a favored weapon, you can pretty much go through the entire game with that weapon and never feel like the you're being pressured to use something else. The combat itself is pretty much the same from beginning to end, with new enemies and new weapons and powers added over time, but it's done right so that it's never a chore in order to move on to the next level.
The sword was a fantastic weapon in the original game, and they made it even better in this. The sword feels sharp and powerful when you swing it, and when you cut something apart, the sound and the enemy reactions feels like you're cutting through flesh and bone, not just whacking a guy over the head with a stick until they die.
There are two major downsides, however. The first is that this game is very resource intensive, so if you don't have a powerful computer, forget it. The second is the bosses are the old three hit pattern bosses with glowing weak points. They aren't terrible, but it subtracts from figuring out the best way to kill the new enemy by having their weak points highlighted to you and forcing you to remove their armor in specific patterns.
Other than that, this game does everything right, and is a testament to what Duke Nukem Forever should have been.

The Stanley Parable is a narrative story that stars, you guessed it, Stanley. Stanley works in a dead end job carrying out mindless tasks; and the story is told by one of the best narratives I have ever heard. Graphics isn't an important feature here, but that being said, it looks really nice.

The design of the world is very well done, you are essentially in an office building, but it does a very clever thing where you can sometimes be walking around in a circle, and then all of a sudden the world changes, and you are somewhere else. This made the experience feel more real to me. You can make this game as easy or as difficult as you want. There is fifteen different stories and endings to the Stanley Parable, each of them is amazingly written, probably one of, if not the best story in gaming I've experienced and well worth playing.  It has taken me almost seven hours to play through all of the endings, and do all but one of the achievements. After you have played all of the endings though, there is probably no need to go replay any of the game again.
Is the game worth £9, 99, sure? For about seven hours of gameplay and the amount of fun I had playing it; you cannot miss out on The Stanley Parable. This is now in my top ten favourite games of all time.

The Stanley Parable is a narrative story that stars, you guessed it, Stanley. Stanley works in a dead end job carrying out mindless tasks; and the story is told by one of the best narratives I have ever heard. Graphics isn't an important feature here, but that being said, it looks really nice.

The design of the world is very well done, you are essentially in an office building, but it does a very clever thing where you can sometimes be walking around in a circle, and then all of a sudden the world changes, and you are somewhere else. This made the experience feel more real to me. You can make this game as easy or as difficult as you want. There is fifteen different stories and endings to the Stanley Parable, each of them is amazingly written, probably one of, if not the best story in gaming I've experienced and well worth playing.  It has taken me almost seven hours to play through all of the endings, and do all but one of the achievements. After you have played all of the endings though, there is probably no need to go replay any of the game again.
Is the game worth £9, 99, sure? For about seven hours of gameplay and the amount of fun I had playing it; you cannot miss out on The Stanley Parable. This is now in my top ten favourite games of all time.

Hollow Knight is probably the best modern Metroidvania I've played. The map is really huge, full of secrets and interesting monsters to fight. The combat is very smooth and you can customize your abilities to best fit your playstyle. It's a bit hard, but always fair, you just need to remember that the game is not about button-mashing, but patience and planning. The bosses are all very cool.
The art is gorgeous and the music very distinctive, and they both come together to create a nice, melancholic atmosphere. The story,  much like some of the gameplay elements, takes some hints from Dark Souls, which is never a bad thing. But it also doesn't take itself super seriously, what with all the adorable bugs running around. It's pretty charming.
In short, if you like Super Metroid, Symphony of the Night, Momodora, Axiom Verge, Ori and the Blind Forest or any other Metroidvania game, you really should get Hollow Knight. It's a love letter to the genre, expanding upon its basic gameplay elements while also adding its own spin to them. You shouldn't miss it.

There are some surface level similiarities to Dark Souls that stood out to me, the most obvious one being that you drop your sould upon dying and have to return to that location to retrive them (oh and they're also called souls, and you are a 'hollow' knight). It also has a cryptic feeling story that is revealed through brief dialog snippets and encounters. Eventually you will acquire a way to read peoples thoughts which also reveals more about the world (somewhat simliar to how lore in dark souls is revealed through reading item descriptions)

The Stanley Parable will not merely forever change how you think and feel about games, but it will change how you consider the very concept of choice in daily life as well.
This work of exquisite and powerful art will at first seem strange, and perhaps silly. In time, it will confound and then deeply disturb you - not with gore, or violence or any ordinary video game shock. The Stanley Parable with force you to examine what it is you actually are doing within any game you play - and then what you do in every waking moment of your life.
The Stanley Parable presents your own existential conundrum bare faced and naked before you, and once you have seen your own truth as an acting being within the world - whatever world - you will never be the same.
This is very likely the most dangerous game ever made, it is certainly the most intelligent and powerful work of game art ever created. It deconstructs the very essence of games, and what it shows cannot be escaped by fleeing to daily life.
The Stanley Parable never ends. You don't yet know it, but you truly are playing it, right now, this very minute.
If you dare to understand the conundrum that is choice itself, play The Stanley Parable. You will never play a more deeply affecting game in your life, because once you have finished with The Stanley Parable, and exited to desktop, and put it away never to be run again, you will have only begun to play it, and you will never stop until your dying day.

The Stanley Parable is a narrative story that stars, you guessed it, Stanley. Stanley works in a dead end job carrying out mindless tasks; and the story is told by one of the best narratives I have ever heard. Graphics isn't an important feature here, but that being said, it looks really nice.

The design of the world is very well done, you are essentially in an office building, but it does a very clever thing where you can sometimes be walking around in a circle, and then all of a sudden the world changes, and you are somewhere else. This made the experience feel more real to me. You can make this game as easy or as difficult as you want. There is fifteen different stories and endings to the Stanley Parable, each of them is amazingly written, probably one of, if not the best story in gaming I've experienced and well worth playing.  It has taken me almost seven hours to play through all of the endings, and do all but one of the achievements. After you have played all of the endings though, there is probably no need to go replay any of the game again.
Is the game worth £9, 99, sure? For about seven hours of gameplay and the amount of fun I had playing it; you cannot miss out on The Stanley Parable. This is now in my top ten favourite games of all time.

Shadow Warrior was INCREDIBLE. The visuals were absolutely gorgeous and the gameplay was sharp and precise.  There were a selection of guns you could use, and occasionally I'd be forced to use them.  But nothing spells precision like a katana, and you truly feel like a badass mastering the powers and abilities of the sword in battle.  One would expect that a sword would be something you would revert to when you ran out of ammo, but not in Shadow Warrior.  Nearly 100% of the time it was my weapon of choice.  While Shadow Warrior doesn't have the depth of other first person titles like Borderlands, it does have a remarkable story that keeps you intrigued to keep going to find out how it all ends.  The banter between Lo Wang and Hoji is also entertaining, starting off as dislike and mistrust, finally evolving into mutual friendship and sacrifice.  Ultimately, Shadow Warrior was a fantastic addition to the world of first person shooter/swordsman games.  I thoroughly enjoyed the game, even when wave after wave of enemies would be thrown at me, making me say outloud to the screen, "REALLY!?"  Great, great game. Highly recommended. A+

If you are a fan of the FPS-genre, this game is a must-buy.
Shadow Warrior offers things I've been looking for in FPS games for years. You get many different weapons, which are interesting to use. You have to search for additional ammo, though, which means you *will* have use different weapons. The obvious diamond among these weapons is your katana, which is always a good option - especially because it becomes stronger and stronger throughout the game. Not to mention that the voice actors for Lo Wang and Hoji are brilliant!
It isn't the perfect game, of course. The level design, especially around the end of the game is astonishing. The first few levels are very basic and almost boring, though. Maybe a bit more enemy diversity could have helped, because at the end you'll have slain dozens of dozens of the same enemies. Still, it is the best FPS I have played in a *very* long time, oldschool attitude with a new-age coat and true next-gen graphics.
tl;dr: This game is probably better than Half-Life 3

In my opinion, this is by far the best Assassin's Creed game to date. Yes, the first two Ezio games were great, but this game is entirely different; the open-world is incredibly expansive but not so much so you get overwhelmed, and the diversity of gameplay options is phenomenal. The multitude of ways to deal with situations and enemies is quite refreshing from the monotony of AC3, as there are dozens (or more) ways to kill an enemy or get to your objective. A HUGE aspect to the game is the much-improved open sea gameplay and combat. It is quite easy to get caught up in and distracted by upgrading your ship, plundering resources from ships, taking down the legendaries, capturing all the garrisons, etc. This game is the breath of fresh air the franchise needed after the far-from-stellar previous game. I would even venture to say that this didn't really feel like an Assassin's Creed game at all! It just felt like an awesome pirate game that was kind of similar to Assassin's Creed except for a few plot points here and there. It would still be just as wonderful of a game if there weren't any future-y Abstergo or Animus or Minerva/Juno (or whoever those women are) elements in it and it was completely it's own stand-alone pirate game! A high quality game that has my recommendation!

The demo is a good basis for the emotion and confusion found in the game. Unlike the demo,
has
More accurately, a choice about which ending the game will take. Think of it as a choose-your-own adventure kind of thing, but with the following changes:
- Dialouge between characters
+ Narrator personality
- Constantly flipping pages
+ Confusion and uncertainty
- Sense
Like any other story, people may interpret it diffrently. People who take certain paths first may find the game very intreguing, while others may dismiss it as a waste of time. Even those who take the same path may have diffrent opinions on it. Another large factor is how much prior knowledge you had; those who had no prior knowledge of this game than it's existence will find it much more intresting than those who watched an entire playthrough of all the possible options. The experience does rely on uncerteinty. This is why I asked you to play the demo; so you would know how the main game may reflect on you.
With my personal experience, I played through a total of an hour in 2 seperate play sessions then the rest of the game in 2 hours all at once. I will say this game was meant to be played all at once, with a short amount of playtime anyway the general confusion will be much more effective in one sitting. An issue I found twoards the end was some of the endings were quite cryptic and often needed an outside guide and rarely tools. When all is done, the replayability value isn't that good, however you may still feel tingles of the experience deep inside you. What I would suggest is you have your friends, if you have any, play it and laugh at there confused faces.
Overall, for what it's worth I'd give
an 8/10. If it were cheaper, say, 12$, I would give it a 9.5/10.

When Shadow Warrior first came out, I wasn't sure what to make of it. I thought it was another one of those generic first person shooters. When I picked it up during the Holiday Sale and started playing, however, I was pleasently surprised. I've always had a soft spot for retro shooter types, and this one is no exception to the retro shooter genre.
The whole point of Shadow Warrior is to kick as much♥♥♥♥♥as you can, and look stylish as hell doing it. After each tango, the game even rates you on how well you used all of the things in your arsenal; whether that be your swordplay, use of guns, or efficiency taking down enemies.
If you like Quake or Doom type shooters, then seriously consider picking up Shadow Warrior.

Backtracking, the game!
I haven't been so frustrated over a game for a looong time...
You want to explore? You get punished, You want to face new enemies? You get punished. Want to beat that boss? You get punished!
Seriously, the amount of backtracking and PUNISHMENT you get in this game is insane. And as you progress deeper it gets more and more frustrating. Enemies are impossible to ignore while backtracking since a lot of them fly, teleport around, fire missiles, sometimes homing ones, and execute randoms moves. Making the whole progress a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Especially when you backtrack to the boss for the 10th time. At some point you are bound to die to some random enemy moves before you will get to your "soul" and lose all the coins you been gathering so far.
While in other metroidvania games you feel as though you progress and become stronger, in this game the deeper you go the more you get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you. Some enemies become unbelievably frustrating to deal with, and defeating them has no real value since you are not getting anything outside of credits.
It feels as though the game does not want to be focusing on combat since it provides no upgrades to it whatsoever (at least so far for me). But the combat becomes really intense later on, especially the bosses that require perftect timing and have TONS of hitpoints. You usually have window for 1 attack between their moves, so the fights last forever, with little to no breaks. And guess what, in order to get used to the bosses and defeat them you will have to die, a lot, and then BACKTRACK. And when you reach the boss, you will have to fight your soul along with the boss, leaving you open for 1-2 hits at the beginning of the encounter.
Exploring is a deathtrap. You have to find the map vendor in each area before you can use your map there. Sometimes you even manage to go to another area before even finding the map to the previous one, This can lead you to get trapped in a new territory, with harder enemies, no idea where to go and pretty much doomed. If you die, then you have to go there AGAIN to retrieve your soul and all your credits. So basically you are  forced to backtrack blindly into uknown  territory and then you are stuck there, provided you actually manage to reach your soul and dont die in the proccess. If you die trying to retrieve your soul, you just lost all your credits you gathered by exploring.
This game gives you a lot of options and then punishes you for trying them out, don't get me wrong the game is beautiful and the gameplay is solid. But the rules inside the game contradict and create situations where it simply becomes a pile of frustration.

My Arma 2 review can be seen here:
Before I get onto the review I must mention it's optimization. Arma 2 and by extension Operation Arrowhead is one of if not THE most unoptimized games I have ever played. Arma is the game that time and time again has forced me to upgrade my PC to continue to play it as if it were some sort of bad drug habit. If it weren't for how good it looked tweaking my settings and fiddling with launch options would have turned me off years ago. While I did first start playing Arma with two ductaped potatos (An AMD GPU with an AMD CPU) there's no excuse for a games performance going to♥♥♥♥♥♥the moment more than two players joined back then. I ran it on the lowest settings back in the day but now I just boot up Arma 2 Opeartion Arrowhead for a quick skirmish and to benchmark any PC I get my hands on. Even to this day if anymore then 10 join an online server the frames drop harder than an atom bomb. Here are my settings and a before and after demonstrating some weirdness that comes from cranking up settings even after 10 years:
Here are my current specs:
-Windows 7 (64-Bit)
-GTX 980 SC ACX 2.0
-i7 4790k Devils Canyon
-16 Gigs Dual Channel
-232 Gig SSD dedicated Arma series.
Here are my launch options:
-noBenchmark -noPause -noSplash -maxMem=16384 -maxVRAM=4096 -cpuCount=4 -exThreads=7 -malloc=system -winxp -noLogs very high
With the performance and issues out of the way onto the review:
This was and still is in many respects the Gmod of military simulators. It's worth putting up with a few bugs and clunky mechanics for some truly great unique one of a kind moments. From the get go Arma 2 OA has some great memorable locations (Such as Chernarus if you own Arma 2.) and a wide variety of weaponry. The community makes this worthwhile purchase and there are still a large amount of people playing it even in 2016. So long as you have a decent PC and some patience this is a title no PC gamer should not have least tried.
I reccomend getting the expansions too as they update the visual fidelity and add tons of weapons,clothing,factions and maps.

For a very long time, I have considered Assassin's Creed Brotherhood to be my favorite game in the entire Assassin's Creed franchise. When Assassin's Creed 3 was initially announced, I was very excited, seeing a brand new game engine and character. However, like many others who played the game, I became very disappointed. Because of this, I was not excited about Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag. I decided to try the game out when it was on sale during the holiday sale, and I regret nothing. This game is everything I wanted in an Assassin's Creed game. My problems with other games in the series tends to be that eventually, I feel like I have run out of things to do. I have yet to approach such a wall in this game. From the naval combat to the hunting, there is always more to do. Because of this, I feel like my favorite game in the Assassin's Creed franchise is now Black Flag. It is worth every penny that it costs. The only downside to this game is the Uplay interface. Anyone who has purchased other games from Ubisoft for the PC know how the games require Uplay to be launched, so it tends to be just more crap to deal with. However, it does not negatively affect the actual gameplay.

Backtracking, the game!
I haven't been so frustrated over a game for a looong time...
You want to explore? You get punished, You want to face new enemies? You get punished. Want to beat that boss? You get punished!
Seriously, the amount of backtracking and PUNISHMENT you get in this game is insane. And as you progress deeper it gets more and more frustrating. Enemies are impossible to ignore while backtracking since a lot of them fly, teleport around, fire missiles, sometimes homing ones, and execute randoms moves. Making the whole progress a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Especially when you backtrack to the boss for the 10th time. At some point you are bound to die to some random enemy moves before you will get to your "soul" and lose all the coins you been gathering so far.
While in other metroidvania games you feel as though you progress and become stronger, in this game the deeper you go the more you get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you. Some enemies become unbelievably frustrating to deal with, and defeating them has no real value since you are not getting anything outside of credits.
It feels as though the game does not want to be focusing on combat since it provides no upgrades to it whatsoever (at least so far for me). But the combat becomes really intense later on, especially the bosses that require perftect timing and have TONS of hitpoints. You usually have window for 1 attack between their moves, so the fights last forever, with little to no breaks. And guess what, in order to get used to the bosses and defeat them you will have to die, a lot, and then BACKTRACK. And when you reach the boss, you will have to fight your soul along with the boss, leaving you open for 1-2 hits at the beginning of the encounter.
Exploring is a deathtrap. You have to find the map vendor in each area before you can use your map there. Sometimes you even manage to go to another area before even finding the map to the previous one, This can lead you to get trapped in a new territory, with harder enemies, no idea where to go and pretty much doomed. If you die, then you have to go there AGAIN to retrieve your soul and all your credits. So basically you are  forced to backtrack blindly into uknown  territory and then you are stuck there, provided you actually manage to reach your soul and dont die in the proccess. If you die trying to retrieve your soul, you just lost all your credits you gathered by exploring.
This game gives you a lot of options and then punishes you for trying them out, don't get me wrong the game is beautiful and the gameplay is solid. But the rules inside the game contradict and create situations where it simply becomes a pile of frustration.

So, this game is by Stunlock Studios, the folks behind Bloodline Champions. BLC is (was, I suppose) one of my favorite games of all time. It's one of the only online multiplayer games to actually get me to compete so intensely, to really desire to improve.
BLC was a powerful combination of absolute skill based aiming, (even for melee attacks) fast paced gameplay, varied and pretty well balanced champions to play, and a heaping helping of SKILL CAP. The best BLC players were insanely better than even a pretty good player, but the magic was that they were using the same toolkit as somebody that had just started playing. That last bit wasn't true near the end of BLCs life, but I try to forget those times.
Sorry, this isn't entirely on topic. Battlerite is not BLC, but Battlerite is the spiritual sequel to BLC, and it's my current hope that Battlerite gets popular enough to raise it to heights BLC never reached.
Battlerite continues the charm of Stunlock's weird tribal art, absolute skill based aiming for every attack, and potentially blisteringly fast combat.
They're attempting innovation with the "Battlerite" system, the ability to choose an enhancement for your champion after each round, up to 5 enhancements with 1 out of 3 per turn.
How they balance their new Battlerite system will likely be key to if this game can usurp the glory days of BLC, but rest assured, I'll be there for this games future.
Thanks for reading my disorganized rant! I'm bad at reviews. This game's future is important to me, so even if my writing is scattered, I want to voice my positivity for this game. It really is good, blind nostagia aside. It's extremely polished and fun for an Early Access game, and has managed to scratch that  BLC itch of mine that has been plaguing me for ages.
Oh, and if you play and enjoy the game, please remember to give them feedback, as it is a beta, and remember to spread the word about the game as well. Battlerite is quite unique, so it shouldn't be too hard to sell some people on it.

More accurately, a choice about which ending the game will take. Think of it as a choose-your-own adventure kind of thing, but with the following changes:
- Dialouge between characters
+ Narrator personality
- Constantly flipping pages
+ Confusion and uncertainty
- Sense
Like any other story, people may interpret it diffrently. People who take certain paths first may find the game very intreguing, while others may dismiss it as a waste of time. Even those who take the same path may have diffrent opinions on it. Another large factor is how much prior knowledge you had; those who had no prior knowledge of this game than it's existence will find it much more intresting than those who watched an entire playthrough of all the possible options. The experience does rely on uncerteinty. This is why I asked you to play the demo; so you would know how the main game may reflect on you.
With my personal experience, I played through a total of an hour in 2 seperate play sessions then the rest of the game in 2 hours all at once. I will say this game was meant to be played all at once, with a short amount of playtime anyway the general confusion will be much more effective in one sitting. An issue I found twoards the end was some of the endings were quite cryptic and often needed an outside guide and rarely tools. When all is done, the replayability value isn't that good, however you may still feel tingles of the experience deep inside you. What I would suggest is you have your friends, if you have any, play it and laugh at there confused faces.
Overall, for what it's worth I'd give
an 8/10. If it were cheaper, say, 12$, I would give it a 9.5/10.
