About the story, the game is full of nice npcs well placed along the huge sprawling map and with enough weight to keep you invested in what each has to say, from the tid bits of the cartographer about each area to the book in progress of a bug that falls in love with you, her knight in shining armor and rescuer.
I'm glad I paid for this game, I'd even pay for more content without a doubt.
Seeing my progress and the fact that I haven't even located the first of the main bosses, I'd guess the game might have about 20 more hours of enjoyment for me. A 30ish hour game for this price is golden in my book.
I very much encourage anyone to get it, if you like metroidvania games, this one won't let you down. If you don't like them, this one might steal your heart.

In a nutshell this game is a blend of Ori & The Blind Forest and Dark Souls. It was an amazing game that came to me out of nowhere and I really hope this thing gets more attention.
Art and sound-wise it shares a lot of the same beauty as Ori, but with occasional darker areas ranging from unsettling to downright terrifying. The aesthetics are not quite as godlike as in Ori, but they're still pretty darn good. The focus on platforming is lesser than the focus on combat, but there's still a decent amount of tricky platforming, plus one really challenging optional area if you're into harder platforming.
Combat is spacing and movement heavy, with some mechanical similarities to Shovel Knight such as bounceback on hits and a downswing you can use to bounce up from enemies. Healing leaves you vulnerable, and can be tricky to do during faster-paced bossfights. Some later abilities may allow slightly different approaches to combat, but the core principles never change. For playstyle customization there's collectible charms you can only wear a limited capacity of at a time. I ended up with a pretty static charm layout for most of the time, but I wouldn't be surprised if another player would end up with a different layout.
Combat difficulty starts out on the lower side, but gets gradually more chalenging. Some optional fights felt nigh-impossible at first, but with enough persistence I became sort of proficient enough at them. Also missing some upgrades has apparently given some people issues with some mandatory fights (the main culprit being the first weapon damage upgrade at around when midgame starts). Trying optional endgame fights early can also turn out badly unless you're good (yours truly spent an hour getting slaughtered by an optional superboss with midgame equipment before giving up and returning later).
The main takeaway from the Souls side is a lack of direction, multiple paths through the game, and parts where you can feel truly lost. The map system seems to be a major source of controversy, as while I absolutely love it, some people are really frustrated about it. When you first enter an area, you have absolutely no map until you find a map vendor there. Even after you find one, you can only update your map with new rooms at checkpoints, and seeing where you are on the map is an optional charm ability which takes away from your combat boosts. Thanks to these mechanics, there were situations in the early-midgame where I had very little idea where I am and how to get back. If you don't like to explore blindly and get lost, consider it a point against this game, but if you do, this becomes one of the game's greatest strengths.
Lastly, for a metroidvania this game is surprisingly long. You're looking at 15-20 hours for standard completion, 25-30 for high completion percent and true ending, and even more for 100%. The game has tons of optional secrets, with even easy to miss hidden bosses.
On the performance side, the early launch has had some stuttering issues even on capable machines, and there's still some glitches that haven't been ironed out. One section has been reported as having near unplayable performance for some, although personally I had little issues there. If you're sensitive to performance issues, you may want to wait a bit. Word seems to be that the most glaring issues are getting patched in the near future. This review was written within the first week of the game's release, so if a lot of time has passed, things may have changed.

In a nutshell this game is a blend of Ori & The Blind Forest and Dark Souls. It was an amazing game that came to me out of nowhere and I really hope this thing gets more attention.
Art and sound-wise it shares a lot of the same beauty as Ori, but with occasional darker areas ranging from unsettling to downright terrifying. The aesthetics are not quite as godlike as in Ori, but they're still pretty darn good. The focus on platforming is lesser than the focus on combat, but there's still a decent amount of tricky platforming, plus one really challenging optional area if you're into harder platforming.
Combat is spacing and movement heavy, with some mechanical similarities to Shovel Knight such as bounceback on hits and a downswing you can use to bounce up from enemies. Healing leaves you vulnerable, and can be tricky to do during faster-paced bossfights. Some later abilities may allow slightly different approaches to combat, but the core principles never change. For playstyle customization there's collectible charms you can only wear a limited capacity of at a time. I ended up with a pretty static charm layout for most of the time, but I wouldn't be surprised if another player would end up with a different layout.
Combat difficulty starts out on the lower side, but gets gradually more chalenging. Some optional fights felt nigh-impossible at first, but with enough persistence I became sort of proficient enough at them. Also missing some upgrades has apparently given some people issues with some mandatory fights (the main culprit being the first weapon damage upgrade at around when midgame starts). Trying optional endgame fights early can also turn out badly unless you're good (yours truly spent an hour getting slaughtered by an optional superboss with midgame equipment before giving up and returning later).
The main takeaway from the Souls side is a lack of direction, multiple paths through the game, and parts where you can feel truly lost. The map system seems to be a major source of controversy, as while I absolutely love it, some people are really frustrated about it. When you first enter an area, you have absolutely no map until you find a map vendor there. Even after you find one, you can only update your map with new rooms at checkpoints, and seeing where you are on the map is an optional charm ability which takes away from your combat boosts. Thanks to these mechanics, there were situations in the early-midgame where I had very little idea where I am and how to get back. If you don't like to explore blindly and get lost, consider it a point against this game, but if you do, this becomes one of the game's greatest strengths.
Lastly, for a metroidvania this game is surprisingly long. You're looking at 15-20 hours for standard completion, 25-30 for high completion percent and true ending, and even more for 100%. The game has tons of optional secrets, with even easy to miss hidden bosses.
On the performance side, the early launch has had some stuttering issues even on capable machines, and there's still some glitches that haven't been ironed out. One section has been reported as having near unplayable performance for some, although personally I had little issues there. If you're sensitive to performance issues, you may want to wait a bit. Word seems to be that the most glaring issues are getting patched in the near future. This review was written within the first week of the game's release, so if a lot of time has passed, things may have changed.

When I first heard of Black Flag, I must admit I was a sceptic. A new Assassins Creed only a year after the last one... Bet this is going to be like Call of Duty. I was pretty happy with Assassins Creed (AC) 3 singleplayer. The story was desent, and the maps were pretty good - but like with all other AC games, I never got into collecting or multiplayer.
I desided to go around AC4, 'cause how can it be any good so close to the last one?
I had my birthday just after New years, and desided to try out AC4, due to good reviews.
And boy was i pleasently suprised! First of all, they cut back on all that Animus crap from the other games, so that was a great suprise.
The story is "okay", nothing like AC1 or AC2, but good enough to keep you moving forward.
You play a pirate that engages in navelcombat with a random boat, that has an Assassin onboard. You both end up on the beach, and after abit of learning the movements and combat, you end up killing him and taking his clothes. Turns out he was a traitor, and you use this for personal glory. I wont spoil it all here :)
The big thing in the game is the sailing. And do it deliver big time. I love roaming the sea, having my crew sing different songs, and plundering innocent merchant ships from Spain or Great Britain. The naval combat functions really well, and it is easy to switch between weapons, controling the ship and boarding other vessels.
Its so much fun, that after reaching Act 8 (of 13) i totaly forgot about the story and just went around plundering and upgrading my ship.
After a while I desided to get back to the story, and finished it rather quickly. But the game wouldnt let me go there.
After finishing, I really wanted to collect stuff. You can see on your map, when a location has been depleted of all activity (it turns yellow). And it didnt take long for me to make them all turn yellow!
The most tedious part was the diving missions, because you have very limited movement and time (and no weapons). But ive heard from others they found them to be the most thrilling parts of the game...
Ive now fully upgraded my ship, got a badass Mayan (bulletproof) Armor and almost collected everything in the game. Ive spent 60+ hours, and was very entertained all the way.
And on a end note, may I recommend watching the Black Sails (starz) serie that is currently running in between gameingsessions, just to keep the mood going! :D
TL:DR; Desent singleplayer, great navalcombat and really adictive! A must buy for every Assassins Creed fan!

Originally saw this game on youtube as a part of a first impressions video, but for some reason it didn`t capture my attention enough for it to warrant its cost at the time. Boy do I regret not jumping on it at that time. Apart from a few dull puzzles and platforming sections, It`s definitely one of my favourite FPS game of 2013.
The sheer fun this game offers to someone who is a fan of anything Serious Sam -or Painkiller-esc. is insane. You get to carry up to 9 (if i remember correctly) weapons simultaneously, with slots 8 & 9  being hearts and skulls picked from enemies you encounter. The gunplay feels really visceral and the upgrade system is perfect for a "shoot-em-up" game like this. Do you like killing tons of demons with swords or with tight gunplay? - Then this is the game for you.
But the strongest parts of this game comes in the shape of:
- Art direction - beautiful use of colors and Asian influenced set pieces and nature
- Katana sword-play
- PC features such as FOV slider which goes up to 120 if you so desire, a whole slew of neat    graphics options and no mouse accel. or smoothing. ("Praise the lord!")
I will go out on a limb here and say that I have never been this pleasantly surprised when it comes to the feel and handling of a sword in an FPS setting. The feeling when you slice up demons and execute the katana special moves is unmatched in anything I`ve played earlier. The fast-paced movement system allows for you to feel like an actual ninja in first person view, dashing in and out of combat slicing up demons. It also opens up for you to "kite" enemies around just like in Serious Sam and Painkiller, which is a feature I especially appreciate during battles in the more open arena-style settings the game has to offer.
I really liked the story for what it was, and it takes you on a fun ride through a variety of different locations and offers a good variety in scenery, even if its somewhat stretched through backtracking and puzzles. The characters are fun, and early on you get to meet a really fun and excellently voice acted side character that will follow you throughout the game.
The humor in this game Is something I really enjoy, even if its juvenile. Hearing Lo Wang crack jokes during combat is a nice touch that keeps you coming back for more demon-slicing goodness.
I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Serious Sam -or Painkiller-type games, as its the best in its genre by far.
Lastly, I`d like to add that Shadow Warrior`s opening "cinematic" might be the best to date, in any game ever!

This game is totally enjoyable.
I cannot agree with most of the criticism I've seen in other reviews.
First, this runs at constant 144fps on my computer (with vsync enabled).
I did notice some stuttering once in a while, but it doesn't make the game any less playable.
Yes, there is a risk of loosing all your money if you die twice in a row, before getting back to your soul.
But that's what the game is about too: you need to be a little careful.
If you buy your firt map, the quill, the compass and the map markers soon enough (which you can do before you get to the second level), it's pretty easy to plan your way through.
Also, your soul won't appear right where you died, but usually a little closer to the entrance of the room, most notably in boss rooms. Which means you can go fetch it and turn back, without having to face the boss immediately.
The health system is a bit old school. It forces you to be extra careful.
This and the damage animation are clearly there to stress you out.
Yes, there are very few indications on which is the next way to go.
But it's still pretty easy to guess. You will face impassable gaps, spiky walls and such,
which clearly hint you need a special skill to get through.
Exploration is key, and the fact that the game is not pointing you the way all the time is actually pretty refreshing.
With an up-to-date map and a bit of memory, it shouldn't be too hard.
And you will soon find fast travel points to spare you some walking.
Apart from that, the gameplay is super smooth.
The art is nice, even though it's a bit austere.
The voices and sounds of the creatures add some life to it.
About the story, I can't tell.
There is some lore scattered here and there, but the narrative background doesn't seem very deep.
Well, at least it doesn't build up any false hopes about it (I'm looking at you, AAA studios my♥♥♥♥♥)

After having some time to invest in Battlerite I will attempt to make a review. I dont usually review games but this one definitly deserves it.
Gameplay:
This is a brother of the MOBA type game without lanes , minions , and towers. I would consider it a battle arena game with Heros. There are no objectives to be fought for and as such you jump right into 2v2 , or 3v3 hero battles. This lends itself to quick twitch, fast paced action that only happens occasionaly in games like DOTA 2, and League of legends.
Every skill used in BattleRite is aimed with the mouse and fired as a skill shot. Movement is done with the WASD keys. Gameplay is super crisp and everything feels very fluid for an early access title. I feel this game is superior to the previous titles for pure action. If you are looking for long, strategy filled games then DOTA 2 and League of legends are the games for you. Because BattleRite lacks lanes and objectives the games are much shorter.
The typical game lasts an average of 10 minutes.  There are a variety of heros to choose from ranging from melee to ranged and lastly support. Each hero has its own unique style similar to MOBA games.
Closing thoughts: I have only had this game for 3 days but its the only game I have played since I bought it. BattleRite's constant action, quick games , and its ability to be played at a high level lend itself to being the perfect game for the E-sports scene. I highly recommend this game to almost everyone!

SHORT VERSION: Metroidvania with a very small hint of Dark Souls. Namely the "retrieve your money on death" aspect. If you like Metroidvanias, this game balances the three key aspects of a good one very well. Those being Combat, Exploration, and Platforming.
OKAY, longer version.
I came into this off friends recommending it, as I love me a good Metroidvania. I am not disappointed so far after my initial 7 hours.
The game opens with a surprisingly minimal tutorial for today's standards, but in a good way. It uses the 'learn by doing' approach where you're given very simple jumps to start out, with minially threatening enemies. Tutorials are only used to explain the mechanics unique to Hollow Knight. This is a game that assumes you know how to play a platformer and doesn't insult your intelligence. It respects the player, and I in turn respect that about the game.
What comes after is everything I want in a good Metroidvania. The game doesn't try to prioritize one of the key aspects of a good Metroidvania over others. It's equal parts exploration, combat, and platforming, as I mentioned in the short version. You have a nice responsive character who can easily fight on the move, with just the right amount of floatiness for jumping. Not Super Metroid floaty, but not Metroid Fusion heavy either. New abilities you gain are as good for combat as they are getting around, like your Airdash while lets you quickly get behind enemies, and make longer jumps.
The game also gives you the ability to aim your attacks up or down, so position is less of a burden in combat. On top of this, I was rewarded for experimenting when I discovered ways to reach areas and shortcuts by using my sword in mid air to bounce off an enemy by striking them from above. There's no tutorial that teaches you this technique. I discovered it purely through experimentation, and I think that's a GOOD thing. It's something you'll eventually try when you realize you can do directional attacks, and surely enough you'll eventually land a hit from above and go "Hey...That's interesting...!"
The game also has a fairly non linear approach, as I'm pretty sure at least one of the major story areas can be reached by one of two possible upgrades, or you could get both upgrades and use them together for an even easier time. And this kind of approach is what I want to see in Metroidvanias. Less linear "Get upgrade A, reach area B" approaches, and more openness in how you can reach locations. Like how you could theoretically go to Marida in Super Metroid via The Tube, or the back entrance from the Wrecked Ship.
The game's method of healing is a rather interesting one, but also one I like because it doesn't make you rely on random health drops. You build up Soul (your magic) through landing hits. Soul can be spent on special attacks, or used to focus in place and heal yourself. So basically as you hit/kill enemies, you can heal your wounds, or if you aren't hurt, spend your Soul on powerful attacks to prevent getting hurt in the first place. It's a surprisingly well thought out system.
Like any good Metroidvania, there's plenty of optional stuff to look for via exploration as you find new powers and ways to get around. You're rewarded with various upgrades that can augment your character, and help you find a playstyle you like. Exploration is generously rewarded with shortcuts, upgrades, and the money you'll need to buy other upgrades.
The game's choice of Dark Souls style death is an odd one, but not too frustrating from what I've played so far. Like Dark Souls, you leave behind a 'Shade' when you die that has all your accumulated money. Die again and it's gone. Kill it and you reclaim your lost cash and your maximum Soul meter.
Mapping is the one area I have slightly mixed emotions on. You do not start out with any kind of map, and have to buy maps from a cartographer as you progress through the game's many areas. You also need a Quill to map out areas he hasn't charted (But you still need his maps to do this) and you need a compass to show WHERE on a map you are. Once you have all the pieces, it's not so bad, but early on if you rely heavily on maps you may find yourself getting lost, so I don't recommend going too far until you have gotten the Quill and Compass from the shop so you can get full maps of areas as you find them.
I'm not one when it comes to graphic and music criticism unless they're bad. So I'll keep it simple here.
Graphically, the game has a very cute, handdrawn style that reminds me of something I just can't put my finger on. That said, I like it. Music is a nice mix of ambient and instrumental, working perfectly for this kind of game.
So, if you like a good Metroidvania? Pick this up already.

Pro's: It's a smashing 30-minute action satire with 80's synth music, dinosaurs, viking babes, and Nazi's.
Con's: No nude curvaceous women.
A very well executed, fun 30-minute satire of everything that makes 80's action movies, cartoons, comics, TV heroes like Knight Rider, and gaming so entertaining. You get a rented VHS-tape look to the film, the typical pulsating 80's synthesizer music, and an iconic action hero who looks like he should have been 80's GI Joe figure. Nazi's, dinosaurs, and viking babes with machine guns are all invited to the Kung Fury action party as the movie doesn't forget what's popular now in entertainment and gaming. Just no zombies -- unless you want to count the Nazi's.
The fight scenes almost look like a send up of not just over the top action heroes, but Japanese Tokusatstu TV shows. The arcade machine Kung Fury fights would fit into Kamen Rider's monster of the week formula. Of course, being in this movie, everything has it's own memorable twists to send everything even farther over the top.
The Nazi's have become a popular enemy in movies and games, and it's no wonder they have been given the Kung Fury treatment as well. What's outstanding here more than a comic Kung Fuehrer and his mecha golden eagle is a great little fight scene at the film's climax. The background of stumbling, confused gas-masked Nazi's is just as fun as our hero ripping off his attacker's limbs and using them as weapons, a go-go-Gadget helicopter propeller, or even a skateboard.
As a fan of bad movies and 80's classics like Revenge of the Ninja, I found this very well done. It's a comic tribute to those kinds of things, but it also has some very nice special effects, CGI, visual compositions, and sound design that would be satisfying if you'd paid to see this in a theater. At only 30-minutes it seems about right and has earned a special place in my short list of favorite weird movies. It's one of those little things you just have to tell people about and say, "You have to see it." KITT would be proud of this movie, and probably get a laugh at the Hoff9000.

The first thing I thought when I heard there was going to be a remake of Shadow Warrior was, "It's probably going to suck." Well this new Shadow Warrior game definitely does not suck. Far from it in fact. Not only is it a fun reimagining of the old school 90s shooter, it's also gorgeous and has a fairly lengthy single player campaign (15+ hours). The humor is good too and manages to not go stale, especially considering that Lo Wang is basically a walking ♥♥♥♥ joke. Probably the most shining feature is the swordplay. It's just plain satisfying to kill stuff with the katana and slicing off arms and torsos never gets old.
Despite being a great game there's two minor nitpicks I had. First the lack of significant enemy variation causes the game to get repetitive at times. Second, compared to the katana some of the guns feel like pea shooters, especially the SMG. Fortunately this is mostly alleviated by the upgrades you can purchase for your guns throughout the game but in the early chapters you'll find yourself using the katana almost exclusively. That's not a huge problem because the katana is damn fun to use but it's still a nitpick.
The most important thing here is that this game is fun from beginning to end and if you grew up on 90s shooters like Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior, and Rise of the Triad then you owe it to yourself to play this game.

What can I say to compliment this game in a way that won't be self-evident when you play? This is one of the most beautiful, enjoyable games I've ever seen. Even down to the open sea hunting. I've had the dubious pleasure of swimming with hammerhead sharks IRL, and the designers captured the way they move and swim so realistically, I felt a moment of adrenaline while trying to harpoon one. It moved just like ones in real life. So awesome. Everything is wonderful this way -- the oceans, the combat, the scenery.
I've heard people complain about it lacking the kind of purity of game-play of previous AC instalments, due to the piracy subject matter and the ship-to-ship combat. Those kinds of concerns are plainly laughable; this is classic AC "plus". Nothing you appreciated from earlier versions is missing. On the contrary, the diversity of environments only enhances what might have become repetitive about previous versions. The combat style of the assassin's seem so much more brilliant having to use vehicles and machinery. The same old "find area, climb building, drop down and kill" is dramatically reduced. I can't just walk around holding the counter, waiting to hit the "I win button" in every fight. Some enemies are too hard to counter, and you have to break their defences while being attacked from all sides. I have to be aware of the battlefield, and make use of my shipmates in combat. I can win by boarding the enemy ship and jumping into the fray, or by sneaking across the rigging of my own ship, or by just sniping objectives from my own rigging.
While some things were a bit cheese, like enemy scouts one shotting you down to the deck when you use a lift to reach their platforms, the glitches seemed to cut both ways. In fact, some missions or objectives seemed almost to rely on them as if the dev's wanted you to glitch your way to victory. For example, if you disable a ship, then swim over to it instead of boarding it normally, you can kill the crew without having to fight endlessly spawning enemies. Even the scout snipers behaviour is less aggressive this way, and you can use a lift to reach them and get behind the back kills. Doing it normally, their aggro behaviour would be far more aggressive. All things considered, if you want to sacrifice the extra time to do it this way, it almost seems like a fair trade off. Some Man 'o Wars can be found moored with their rigging up, and can be taken solo long before the Jackdaw is capable of capturing them in battle.
Choices are the spice of life -- coming up with my own way to achieve victory is thrilling! Thank you, Ubisoft, for having enough respect for my intelligence to let me find my own way to win. You have no idea how refreshing that is these days.
Definitely take your time to enjoy this game the proper way. Don't race through the main storyline. Try to finish all the side missions, go after all the special outfits and armour sets, the pistol rewards from the naval missions, etc., then worry about completing the storyline.
The very best missions, hands down, were the one's that involved elaborate, nail-biting chases. Like Sequence 6, Memory 3 -- if they could make a whole game like that particular memory I'd die of joy. Often, side missions were far more entertaining than main missions, like Templar Hunt 4 mission 3 where you escort a drunk. So hilarious.
Not wanting to sound the gushing fanboy, I do have criticisms. I really appreciated the challenge of the legendary ship battles (even Impoluto, that likes to defy physics and jump out of the water just to teach you your place, petty inferior human AI), but mourned the fact that I have no legendary ships left to use the ram charge ability on. After all the legendary ships are dead, and you can one-shot most man-o-wars with the reward, the ship combat is over. There's nothing to go after at that point, nothing worth upgrading the Jackdaw for unless you feel OCD.
I suppose I do have a complaint in that respect: the best weapons and armour were by no means overpowered enough to have them become available so late in the game. The rope darts for example, why couldn't we enjoy that until the very final sequences of the main storyline? What a shame to have played nearly the entire game, and then get this ability or item, only to have nothing left to use it on. Maybe the devs assumed I would use it to go do the side missions with after the main was done, but what point is there in doing those if the reward of the side missions is the best gear you only have an incentive to acquire to do the main missions with?
You can gather more than enough money and resources to fully upgrade the ship before the final sequences, but get told "prerequisite - this upgrade is available later in the main storyline". I assume this artificial block on abilities is meant to prevent me from becoming so OP that there is no challenge in the later missions. I imagine balancing gear with a challenging main storyline is difficult, and I don't want to complain too much. I will limit my complaint to saying that I actually found grinding to improve my ship enjoyable; I anticipated not liking it so much, but being a pirate is really fun. I just wish their was more chance to choose moving ahead in the game by piracy, rather than being told go "do more ninja now".
Why not write missions where I use piracy to get information, instead of tailing people with cheesy arbitrary ways to fail? I'd rather attack a fort or take down a really hard convoy to get the info the storyline wants me to have.
If I had to limit myself to one major complaint, it would have to be the excessive reliance on "tail this guy" or "eavesdrop on this conversation" style missions. These get obnoxious fast, especially when you realize how limited you are in creatively solving these challenges. It puts drag on the composition of the characters and story too, because it feels like everything is being shoe-horned into a stealth mission "just because". It felt like Deus ex Machina sometimes, being told I will get full synchronization for assassinating the diplomat from a haystack, but the only haystack on his path is in a restricted area between four guards. Somehow, they just magically don't notice this not-so-stealth slaughter, but catch whiff of me from a football field away if I try anything else. We just jump to a cutscene, and magically I'm standing at the gate of a party. Didn't have to kill the guy for his clothes then successfully escape. It feels unnatural for a game so focused on combat and stealth, to just shuffle me along a storyline and rewarding me for not fighting or for only being stealthy to a point then abandoning that emphasis. Even punishing me for these things.
If the point here is to minimize combat, or make players think outside the box, running fights are definitely the better way to go than boilerplate "tail someone without being noticed" drudgery. There's just as much reliance on timing and spacial awareness during a fighting chase as during a "tail someone without being seen", and feels more believable. Its more fun being able to recover from being detected than it is to have to wait through loading screens because I didn't use some boring sniper trick or environment exploit to kill or tail a guy without been noticed.
Introduce stealth, brute force, piracy as options, but leave it to the player to decide which way to skin the cat imho.
Overall 9/10. Buy this game. You won't regret it. Cheers.

I can't express to you how PERFECT this game is. Everyone's always looked at Assassin's Creed with fascination, or scorn. AC1 was the first step for a new type of action-adventure genre. It looked to cinematic storytelling with historic significance to immerse the player in the highest precision-crafted historical setting since the cultural tie-backs of Prince of Persia. Add photo-realistic graphics and a overarching theme involving Assassins and Templars and you've got yourself a five-star game. AC2 completely revamped the gameplay mechanics and style, making it more fluid, more immersive and expanded the genre to a new setting, new Assassin and easily had the best cliffhanger of the year. AC Brotherhood and Revelations kept progressing the story, the game, and the mechanics, experimenting with a variety of tactics, additions and modifications whilst retaining the historical significance and incredibly fun gameplay that defined the series. Assassin's Creed III took a new direction, with updated graphics, a new gaming/physics engine and a powerful conclusion to the Desmond Trilogy. While critically acclaimed for its technological marvel, it wasn't received as the strongest in the series. Here to bring the crown back  is Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag.
This game has EVERYTHING. Magnificent storytelling, cinematic fluidity, the historical accuracy penned by world-class game developers and writers, immersion from the studded soundtrack (Brian Tyler) to the fauna of the time period, all whilst maintained the absolute best of each Assassin's Creed game that preceded it. Naval combat, stealth tactics, long-range weaponry, political and emotional upheaval, grounded and gritty dramatizations of caricatures that we've come to define as legends (Ed Thatch, Charles Vane, Calico Jack, etc) set during the one brief moment in human history where people were truly free: The Golden Age of Piracy. Play as a pirate, play as an assassin, play as a privateer caught between two ancient wars between order and freedom, fight your way through friend and foe establishing your own priorities, securing artifacts and ledgers too precious to be exposed. Live in the 18th century, defying empires and forging alliances to the Creed, Order or the Republic.
If you haven't played this game, you're doing yourself the most incredible disservice. This is easily the BEST Assassin's Creed game made yet, titled with Game of the Year for 2013. Worth every penny.

For me this is the Diablo 3 PvP arena with matchmaking that the con artists at Blizzard advertised but never actually implemented.
It's also kind of like MOBA combat without the tedious grind.
As of this writing you can do matchmaking with 2v2, 3v3, 2vAI, where the first team to win 3 rounds wins the game, and private matches where you can use custom match settings. In private game you can also play solo with all bots. There is also a practice mode and a tutorial.
So far there are 15 champions with a good mix of melee, ranged, support, and some which are kind of hybrid but they will add more. Each character has at least 7 abilities plus 'hidden' versions of 2 of your abilities (tutorial doesn't tell you about them) that you can see if you hold shift and consume 1 bar of energy.
'Battlerite' refers to talents you can pick from at the beginning of each round that give your abilities an aditional property.  In a close game that lasts for more rounds, characters will accumulate more battlerites which makes everyone more powerful and make skill interactions between abilities and between characters more complex.  You can see what battlerites everyone else has (your team and enemy).
Game runs on dedicated servers and there are 11 regions to choose from (or you can have it auto select) so lag is not a problem.
Movement is WASD and you aim with the mouse which works really well for this game.
When a character dies, time slows down for a second for everyone to react.

SHORT VERSION: Metroidvania with a very small hint of Dark Souls. Namely the "retrieve your money on death" aspect. If you like Metroidvanias, this game balances the three key aspects of a good one very well. Those being Combat, Exploration, and Platforming.
OKAY, longer version.
I came into this off friends recommending it, as I love me a good Metroidvania. I am not disappointed so far after my initial 7 hours.
The game opens with a surprisingly minimal tutorial for today's standards, but in a good way. It uses the 'learn by doing' approach where you're given very simple jumps to start out, with minially threatening enemies. Tutorials are only used to explain the mechanics unique to Hollow Knight. This is a game that assumes you know how to play a platformer and doesn't insult your intelligence. It respects the player, and I in turn respect that about the game.
What comes after is everything I want in a good Metroidvania. The game doesn't try to prioritize one of the key aspects of a good Metroidvania over others. It's equal parts exploration, combat, and platforming, as I mentioned in the short version. You have a nice responsive character who can easily fight on the move, with just the right amount of floatiness for jumping. Not Super Metroid floaty, but not Metroid Fusion heavy either. New abilities you gain are as good for combat as they are getting around, like your Airdash while lets you quickly get behind enemies, and make longer jumps.
The game also gives you the ability to aim your attacks up or down, so position is less of a burden in combat. On top of this, I was rewarded for experimenting when I discovered ways to reach areas and shortcuts by using my sword in mid air to bounce off an enemy by striking them from above. There's no tutorial that teaches you this technique. I discovered it purely through experimentation, and I think that's a GOOD thing. It's something you'll eventually try when you realize you can do directional attacks, and surely enough you'll eventually land a hit from above and go "Hey...That's interesting...!"
The game also has a fairly non linear approach, as I'm pretty sure at least one of the major story areas can be reached by one of two possible upgrades, or you could get both upgrades and use them together for an even easier time. And this kind of approach is what I want to see in Metroidvanias. Less linear "Get upgrade A, reach area B" approaches, and more openness in how you can reach locations. Like how you could theoretically go to Marida in Super Metroid via The Tube, or the back entrance from the Wrecked Ship.
The game's method of healing is a rather interesting one, but also one I like because it doesn't make you rely on random health drops. You build up Soul (your magic) through landing hits. Soul can be spent on special attacks, or used to focus in place and heal yourself. So basically as you hit/kill enemies, you can heal your wounds, or if you aren't hurt, spend your Soul on powerful attacks to prevent getting hurt in the first place. It's a surprisingly well thought out system.
Like any good Metroidvania, there's plenty of optional stuff to look for via exploration as you find new powers and ways to get around. You're rewarded with various upgrades that can augment your character, and help you find a playstyle you like. Exploration is generously rewarded with shortcuts, upgrades, and the money you'll need to buy other upgrades.
The game's choice of Dark Souls style death is an odd one, but not too frustrating from what I've played so far. Like Dark Souls, you leave behind a 'Shade' when you die that has all your accumulated money. Die again and it's gone. Kill it and you reclaim your lost cash and your maximum Soul meter.
Mapping is the one area I have slightly mixed emotions on. You do not start out with any kind of map, and have to buy maps from a cartographer as you progress through the game's many areas. You also need a Quill to map out areas he hasn't charted (But you still need his maps to do this) and you need a compass to show WHERE on a map you are. Once you have all the pieces, it's not so bad, but early on if you rely heavily on maps you may find yourself getting lost, so I don't recommend going too far until you have gotten the Quill and Compass from the shop so you can get full maps of areas as you find them.
I'm not one when it comes to graphic and music criticism unless they're bad. So I'll keep it simple here.
Graphically, the game has a very cute, handdrawn style that reminds me of something I just can't put my finger on. That said, I like it. Music is a nice mix of ambient and instrumental, working perfectly for this kind of game.
So, if you like a good Metroidvania? Pick this up already.

Extremely good game. As of this review I have almost 100% it. I still lack more than a couple challenges that will take yet more hours to complete. And I've loved every hour I've spent playing this game. It's a phenominal game, the best Metroid like I've played since Super Metroid.
The map is extremely open ended. If you're good enough and know what to look for you can access most of the map within a couple hours of play. It's not "optimal" to do so, but it's possible. Which speaks a lot about how well designed the map is. The game re treads a lot of old ground, but does so extremely well, and the entire game feels very fresh and unique.
It's hard to believe such a small team made such a big game. The sound design is stellar, the enemy design very consistent, the map itself a joy to explore. There are so many secrets, I still haven't found all of them. I cannot emphasize how much I love the map in this game. Bosses as well, they're all very fun to fight and very rewarding to beat, save a couple of the more ridiculous bosses which border on frustration.
Now, it's not a perfect game, there are a few flaws. Mostly technical issues such as bad framedrops and a couple major bugs I've encountered, but the game is great in spite of them. Hopefully the issues will be resolved soon, but in the meantime, be aware.
As for non technical related issues I have, the map system itself can be somewhat annoying. You have to buy a map for each area, until then you're going in blind, and the map maker is somewhere in the new area. If you beat the boss without meeting him then you can return to the village to buy a more expensive map. Those are the only two ways to gain the map, buy it sooner or later. Generally he is easy to find, but in the Fog Canyon which you can access early, you cannot reach him until you get a late game mobility item. He's simply hidden extremely well in the Kingdom's Edge. I doubt I would have ever found him if someone hadn't told me where he was.
A few secrets end up being rather cryptic, or at the very least, require extreme attention to detail to find. The game gives hints about basically everything, but how useful they are varies.
Sometimes the movement feels a little funny. Generally it controls very well. Jumping is responsive and context sensitive, dashes are rapid, when it works it works. Edges, especially when jumping from below to above, can sometimes behave a tad funny however. At times my character seems to get knocked under a ledge, usually leading to falling into spikes, when I hit an edge with a jump. Could be user error, but it's fairly irregular which is the most annoying part.

Combat is good, it's solid, it works, it's reliable. It's a bit one dimensional. Well, two dimensional to be technical, so while it does feel nice especially once you get the Great Slash art, it's never really mind blowing. Which is okay, the boss fights end up being as much a test of jumping and dashing skill as they are a test of combat, and I wouldn't say I ever got bored with the combat either, but the combat also never stood out for me. The platforming during fights was always more interesting and dynamic than the slashing.
Two of the upgrades, a Dash Slash and a Cyclone Slash, are also not very. Good? There's just very little reason to use them, especially because the Dash Slash doesn't give you invulnerability frames, so if you don't kill or knock the enemy back while doing it you'll take damage. Cyclone Slash has the opposite problem, where it will knock most enemies away and they end up not taking much damage at all.
The spells are a bit more interesting, but because they draw from the same reserve as the resource you use to heal with (soul, which you gain from founts in the world or by striking enemies) I often find myself using my limited reserve to heal rather than cast offensive magic. It covers all the bases, a ranged bolt, an upward explosion of magic, and a downward pound (which is also used to navigate the world by breaking certain floors), but at the end of the day your sword is more than enough. Even with the spell related trinkets they can't take out any bosses on their own, and because you don't gain soul from killing enemies with magic attacks, it's usually not smart or worth it to use magic on regular enemies.
Some normally invulnerable (crystal bugs) or exceedingly tough enemies exist that magic is worth using on, but they're not the norm.
Aside from those complaints I can find no other faults with the game. Some bugs, it's got Metroidvania combat (which is less of a complaint and more a don't expect 2D Ninja Gaiden Black), and the map system can be annoying at times.
Despite that it's an outstandingly good game. I'd give it a 9/10 if it weren't so buggy, so for now 8/10 until the bugs are fixed. If you like Symphony of the Night, Metroid, La Mulana, exploration in general, or just want to get imerssed in an incredibly well thought out and unique story, get this game. It's worth every single penny.

Team Cherry's Hollow Knight was one of my most anticipated releases of 2017.  It's an adventure platformer that sports a gorgeous art style and has a heavy emphasis on exploration.  I'm a fan of the genre and have played through quite a few of them.  Perhaps predictably, I had very high hopes for this game.  Although the game currently has significant flaws, I'm happy to report that Hollow Knight has met my expectations.
You take the role of a character that has recently arrived in a small town and is now setting off to adventure in the ruins below.  It's difficult to write too much about the story, because of the nature in which it slowly unfolds as you  play.  They clearly put significant effort into crafting the lore, but you'll have to put some work into uncovering it and interpreting it.  Hollow Knight is a game that is best played knowing as little about it as possible.  Before it was released, I remember reading that the development team's goal was to create the largest world a game of this style has ever seen.  The statement reeked so strongly of marketing speak that I immediately wrote it off.  It turns out there is actually some truth to it.
The world feels huge, so huge in fact that I struggle to think any other games of this genre with comparable world sizes.  The exploration aspect of Hollow Knight is where the game truly shines.  Due to the nature of the map system, it isn't uncommon to wander through areas blindly.  When you combine this fact with the nonlinear nature of the game, you can end up running around for hours without any sort of idea where you're supposed to be going.  Some may be frustrated by this, but I felt it allowed me to become lost in the world both literally and figuratively.  Just when I thought there couldn't be any more areas left, I'd find another one, and then another one.   It's also worth mentioning that when you die, your money remains at your place of death and you temporarily lose a portion of your magic power.  This creates a level of tension while exploring unknown dangerous areas, because if you die it may be difficult to collect your belongings.  Each and every area is gorgeous, unique, and offers information about how the world was before being ruined.
Aside from being pretty and containing story related content, the areas also contain plenty of items and upgrades.  There are the standard mobility upgrades you would expect in a game like this, as well as a handful of combat skills.  Most notable are the charm items which allow a level of character customization.  They function as pieces of equipment and provide a wide variety of boons.  I only used a handful of them during my playthrough, but after learning more about them I'd probably equip and unequip them more frequently on a second run through the game.
As much as I might enjoy playing a second time, I'm not sure I'll be doing it any time soon.  The game has so many small bugs and typos that I found myself wondering why they didn't beta test it more than they did.  Most of them weren't particularly difficult to find either.  Fortunately, the majority of them are minor.  The biggest problem is sadly much larger.  To be straightforward about it, the game seems to be very poorly optimized.  Some people don't experience any issues, but for others the game is completely unplayable.  Personally, my experience was somewhere inbetween.  Overall the game isn't particularly difficult, but there are a few challenging boss fights and tricky platforming sections.  I took damage numerous times due to sudden random frame drops.  Understandably, some may find this to be very irritating.  I'd write this off as being an issue unique to my hardware, but the reports are so numerous that it's unlikely to be just my machine.
It's sad to see such a great game blemished by performance issues.  Under normal circumstances I would recommend Hollow Knight without a second thought.  It's an enjoyable adventure platformer that provides a feeling of exploration that I haven't found in any other games recently.  There is a considerable amount of content too, it took me nearly 40 hours for a blind 100% completion run of the game.  At its price, it's almost too good to be true.  I'd recommend this game to fans of the genre that want to immerse themselves and become lost in a beautiful well crafted world.  Even with the stuttering I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Hollow Knight, but others may not be able to ignore it so easily.  It might be worth waiting for a patch, or trying the game out within Steam's refund window to see whether or not the level of performance is tolerable for you.  Some lucky users evidently don't experience any performance issues at all.

The 2013 remake of Shadow Warrior is a throwback to classic first-person shooters of yesteryear, and it makes me appreciate how far the genre has developed over the last two decades.
Channeling games more like Chaser or Chrome than Quake or Duke Nukem 3D, the game does have some impressive technical chops. Its engine pumps out some impressive graphics and wide-open levels while maintaining a silky-smooth frame rate. Gorgeous textures and lighting effects make for some scenic vistas. The combat is wonderfully gory, and the voice-acting and characters make for an interesting and somewhat tongue-in-cheek story.
Where it fails is, well, everywhere else. The levels are impressively large but greatly lack in variety. Those same props you see in the first five minutes of the game? You'll be seeing them right through to the end as well. The levels greatly overstay their welcome (each one takes close to an hour to complete), and - when you get right down to it - there isn't significant difference between the different levels anyway. Each level itself is broken down into micro-levels (similar to the levels in Half Life 2) so every time you open a door there is a brief - but noticeably disrupting - pause as it loads up the next arena. There is a deficiency in monsters and weapons as well; by the halfway point, you'll have met everything the game has to offer, meaning the last ten or so hours will just be a repetitive mowing down of the same enemies.
The gameplay is disappointingly old school as well. Maps are essentially just large arenas separated by twisty corridors; gates to the next arena does not unlock until you either hunt down all the monsters or find all the hidden statues that serve as the Shadow Warrior equivalent of key-cards. Too often the gates are not clearly marked, and I wasted too much time looking for the glowing door that would let me progress to the next section of the game. The combat itself was fun - although many of the early weapons lacked enough punch, and some monsters were overpowered bullet-sinks that overstayed their welcome - but in between the combat the levels were -with a handful of exceptions - dry and uninteresting slogs through repetitive scenery.
It had its moments, but overall this Shadow Warrior remake was more chore than fun.

After having some time to invest in Battlerite I will attempt to make a review. I dont usually review games but this one definitly deserves it.
Gameplay:
This is a brother of the MOBA type game without lanes , minions , and towers. I would consider it a battle arena game with Heros. There are no objectives to be fought for and as such you jump right into 2v2 , or 3v3 hero battles. This lends itself to quick twitch, fast paced action that only happens occasionaly in games like DOTA 2, and League of legends.
Every skill used in BattleRite is aimed with the mouse and fired as a skill shot. Movement is done with the WASD keys. Gameplay is super crisp and everything feels very fluid for an early access title. I feel this game is superior to the previous titles for pure action. If you are looking for long, strategy filled games then DOTA 2 and League of legends are the games for you. Because BattleRite lacks lanes and objectives the games are much shorter.
The typical game lasts an average of 10 minutes.  There are a variety of heros to choose from ranging from melee to ranged and lastly support. Each hero has its own unique style similar to MOBA games.
Closing thoughts: I have only had this game for 3 days but its the only game I have played since I bought it. BattleRite's constant action, quick games , and its ability to be played at a high level lend itself to being the perfect game for the E-sports scene. I highly recommend this game to almost everyone!

I hope that my review doesen't contain any SPOILER but if it does i'm really sorry. It's very hard to review a game like this without speaking a little bit of its essence.
That said, it's very difficult for me to give a bad review to a well-packed game like The Stanley Parable. But in this case I will. Let me explain: I hate games that try to make me feel stupid, sad and, basically an helpless human case of nerdiness and empty life behind a desk.
A lot of people will say that i haven't understood the game true meaning and its deep essence. But this is exactly the problem. I understood them very well.
This game tries to bypass the boundaries of the videogame media and make your experience an... experience. As i said the game is really good packed with a nice use of the Source and a wonderful voice acting. But.... it's simply not fun at all.
You're Stanley (or if you want the push-one-button-for-eight-hours-every-day guy), and your quest is to find your missing colleagues. A few minutes in the game and you realize that the meta-message that the devs wanted to put in this piece of software is, effectively, the point of it all. You wander between sliding doors of choices, obeying or not the narrator voice and experiencing multiple endings.
But...it's boring, boring, boring. Sometimes I have to admit that the devs tried hard to dig deep in the game design mechanics and meta-language stuff but..seriously? You want me to say "whoa! so that's the truth behind it all? i'm really throwing my life away? i need to stop listening to the common sense? is this the secret of happiness (and game design)?
Thanks, The Stanley Parable, i'm 34 YO, happy and with a wonderful job. I play games since i was 3 and i know that I mustn't waste the time I have left so...I'm uninstalling you, sorry. And thanks for the irony too.

I will say it again, Shadow Warrior is THE shooter of 2013 and you will be doing yourself a disservice by not playing this game!

If you were wondering about buying this game and have spare time, stop reading now and buy this game. If you are that kind of person and are intrested in a complete review, read on!
OK. I'm going to write a complete review with PROS and CONS of this game. Before that let me say that Assassin's Creed is a game where you play as an assassin. You have your main mission but there is nothing saying that you can't wander off and cause trouble with the guards and what not. There are always side missions and the map is HUGE!
PROS:
Easy to pick up and play.
Combat is simple with the attack+counter keys. You can also break an enemies defense or throw them. Why not?
Free running is insane fun. Run up buildings or climb all the way to the top of the ship and plummit down to your death! Or if your precise you can land in the water! Why not?
The main missions are always fun, but if you somehow get tired of that you can go and travel+explore, or go try an assassination mission.
Graphics are beautiful.
Gameplay is smooth and fun. You will never find yourself in a dull moment. Even the parts where you just stalk someone while listening in to their conversations sometimes lay in restricted zones and always are intense.
SWORD FIGHTING!!!!!!!!! BLADE FIGHTING!!!!!!!!!!!! MUSKETS AND GUNS!!!!!!!!!!!!! WEAPONRY IS AMAZING!!!!!!!!!!!!
The ocean is a vast place! Take your boat anywere! Enter a restricted zone? Why not? Need crew or supplies? Raid an ememy boat and take their supplies! Take over a fort? Who says no!!!
YOUR NOT JUST AN ASSASSINS. YOUR A FREAKING PIRATE!
There are so many more PROS in this game, that I recommend just buying it and finding out for yourself!
CONS:
The multiplayer isn't the absolute best, although it is fun.
The game runs and feels like assassin's creed 3, but this should not stop you from buying this.
You can replay missions, but you have to replay the whole entire mission. For example. Say you want to replay the mission where you steal your first boat, then escape in bad weather with rouge waves and tornadoes. Before getting to the part where you drive the boat, you have to spend 30 minutes before hand finding your crew, and this can get annoying if you just want to drive the boat. (INSANE FUN IN THAT KIND OF WEATHER)
I know that this has been going on for every game, but I think that you should be able to at least harm civillians. They are technically impervious to everything. It can get a little annoying not being able to just stab them. lol.
You can control all the cannons on either side of the boat when you drive it, but I think it would have also been cool if you could have controlled one cannon specifically. That option could have made the boat funner.
This took me a long time to write because this game is so much fun that I was having difficulty coming up with cons for the review :D
So go buy this game now.

First things first: This game is pretty awesome!
I have one big issue with it tho:
Checkpoint (Bonfire) system with combination of level design and map system is punishing in really frustrating way. Don't get me wrong. I love hard games, especially Souls like games, so I am used to to certain amount of desperation ;) But Hollow Knight does not simply seem fair...
Here is a example: I cleared 2 areas and I have huge amount of Geo (basically equivalent of souls) with me. Like in any other Souls like game, if you die, you lose all your Geo and you have to get to place where you died to retrieve them. If you die on your way there, you lose everything for good. And here is my big issue. I simply did not get opportunity to spend my Geo. I really wanted to but I could not... I was so looking forward for buying items which allow you to explore new area, but again - I was not allowed to do that for fairly large amount of time.
Even tho that I found few checkpoints, none of them had fast travel which is needed to get back to area with merchants. In the end I got to the end of next area where I was force to fight a boss. Also last checkpoint was pretty fair away from this boss and getting to him was not easy. Ofc after few attempts I ♥♥♥♥ed up on my way back and I lost all my geo. Level of frustration was over 9000... (And after 6 hours of playing first playthrough, I immediately deleted this save).
Basically every souls game gives you opportunity to spend your souls before boss fight or when you reach a checkpoint. If you do not, it is a risk which you are willingly taking. Hollow Knight sometimes does not give you a choice and I do not really like that. Game creates weird contradiction when you are getting more and more anxious going forward because of increasing amount of Geo which you have, but on the other hand game forces you to explore more if you want to find a checkpoint and a way to spend of your geo.
It might be possible that I overlooked something or I was simply unlucky, but how I alrdy mentioned - this flaw is because of combination of multiple aspects.
1. It is pretty easy to miss checkpoint
2. Not all checkpoints have fast travel, actually very few of them do
3. Levels are quite large and sometimes do not offer shortcut system to reach areas where you czme from
4. You have chance to get a map for levels but again, you can miss the guy who is selling them. And even then, map is not complete
5. You do not get enough opportunities to spend your Geo
6. Checkpoints are not placed well sometimes
I think few of those aspects should be improved and game will feel much more rewarding, instead of punishing player for not really doing anything wrong and wanted to explore more...

I hope that my review doesen't contain any SPOILER but if it does i'm really sorry. It's very hard to review a game like this without speaking a little bit of its essence.
That said, it's very difficult for me to give a bad review to a well-packed game like The Stanley Parable. But in this case I will. Let me explain: I hate games that try to make me feel stupid, sad and, basically an helpless human case of nerdiness and empty life behind a desk.
A lot of people will say that i haven't understood the game true meaning and its deep essence. But this is exactly the problem. I understood them very well.
This game tries to bypass the boundaries of the videogame media and make your experience an... experience. As i said the game is really good packed with a nice use of the Source and a wonderful voice acting. But.... it's simply not fun at all.
You're Stanley (or if you want the push-one-button-for-eight-hours-every-day guy), and your quest is to find your missing colleagues. A few minutes in the game and you realize that the meta-message that the devs wanted to put in this piece of software is, effectively, the point of it all. You wander between sliding doors of choices, obeying or not the narrator voice and experiencing multiple endings.
But...it's boring, boring, boring. Sometimes I have to admit that the devs tried hard to dig deep in the game design mechanics and meta-language stuff but..seriously? You want me to say "whoa! so that's the truth behind it all? i'm really throwing my life away? i need to stop listening to the common sense? is this the secret of happiness (and game design)?
Thanks, The Stanley Parable, i'm 34 YO, happy and with a wonderful job. I play games since i was 3 and i know that I mustn't waste the time I have left so...I'm uninstalling you, sorry. And thanks for the irony too.

I went into this one very optimistic after watching a few videos, and I was not disappointed.
You've got your typical AC-style gameplay here, with cities to explore, buildings to climb, and plenty of ways to kill or escape your enemies.  There's a big multi-arc story which, as with AC and AC2, kept me interested from start to finish, with a solid and surprisingly emotional ending.  There's plenty to see, find and do afterwards or in between the story missions as well.  And of course, top-notch visuals, both technically and asthetically.
But the real treat here is the ship and the sea.  I've been looking for a good sailing game for ages, and of all the places to find one, it's the Assassin's Creed series!  Solid controls and mechanics mix with varying degrees of challenge depending on where in the Carribean you choose to sail, and it makes for a very enjoyable gameplay experience.  The sound and visuals really shine here, too- pristine waves, singing sailors, thundering guns and billowing sheets.  It all kept me yearning to get back out on the sea every time I came into harbor.
There's some blemishes on this gem, tho.  A few graphical glitches mar the pristine scenery- glowing eyes during cutscenes, and some lighting glitches during the out-of-Animus sequences (as of 1/24/2014... hoping for a patch!).  But these were localized, and don't detract much from the regular gameplay.  Some of the ground missions have annoyingly high guard counts, which can make for slow going as you sneak or slice your way through the story, tho some may find the chance for more fights enjoyable.  There are also some spoilers for those who haven't played the earlier games, so if you wan't the full AC experience, I don't recommend starting here.
But if you really wanna be a pirate, then by all means, climb on board!  All in all, a good installment in a brilliant series.

Level of frustration was over 9000... (And after 6 hours of playing first playthrough, I immediately deleted this save).
Basically every souls game gives you opportunity to spend your souls before boss fight or when you reach a checkpoint. If you do not, it is a risk which you are willingly taking. Hollow Knight sometimes does not give you a choice and I do not really like that. Game creates weird contradiction when you are getting more and more anxious going forward because of increasing amount of Geo which you have, but on the other hand game forces you to explore more if you want to find a checkpoint and a way to spend of your geo.
It might be possible that I overlooked something or I was simply unlucky, but how I alrdy mentioned - this flaw is because of combination of multiple aspects.
1. It is pretty easy to miss checkpoint
2. Not all checkpoints have fast travel, actually very few of them do
3. Levels are quite large and sometimes do not offer shortcut system to reach areas where you czme from
4. You have chance to get a map for levels but again, you can miss the guy who is selling them. And even then, map is not complete
5. You do not get enough opportunities to spend your Geo
6. Checkpoints are not placed well sometimes
I think few of those aspects should be improved and game will feel much more rewarding, instead of punishing player for not really doing anything wrong and wanted to explore more...

After having some time to invest in Battlerite I will attempt to make a review. I dont usually review games but this one definitly deserves it.
Gameplay:
This is a brother of the MOBA type game without lanes , minions , and towers. I would consider it a battle arena game with Heros. There are no objectives to be fought for and as such you jump right into 2v2 , or 3v3 hero battles. This lends itself to quick twitch, fast paced action that only happens occasionaly in games like DOTA 2, and League of legends.
Every skill used in BattleRite is aimed with the mouse and fired as a skill shot. Movement is done with the WASD keys. Gameplay is super crisp and everything feels very fluid for an early access title. I feel this game is superior to the previous titles for pure action. If you are looking for long, strategy filled games then DOTA 2 and League of legends are the games for you. Because BattleRite lacks lanes and objectives the games are much shorter.
The typical game lasts an average of 10 minutes.  There are a variety of heros to choose from ranging from melee to ranged and lastly support. Each hero has its own unique style similar to MOBA games.
Closing thoughts: I have only had this game for 3 days but its the only game I have played since I bought it. BattleRite's constant action, quick games , and its ability to be played at a high level lend itself to being the perfect game for the E-sports scene. I highly recommend this game to almost everyone!

This is what I used to think of this game:
"This game is a lot of fun. The graphical style is intense, exciting, and varied, due to the very different locations that the game places you in. The characters' abilities are unique, and synergize well together. My only real complaint is that there's so much DLC and it all costs money. It's hard to do anything without running into it because the DLC adds other characters, maps, and an entire difficulty level and loot tier."
And then Nightmare Mode happened.
If you must play this game, don't buy most of the DLC. Just get the swapped-gender heroes if you really want. Everything beyond the base game is poorly designed, poorly balanced, and a horrible, unrewarding, boring grindfest. If I'm angry at this game for anything, it's for wasting my time.
At the beginning, and all the way through the hardest non-Nightmare maps, the game felt fun. It felt like a fair challenge, while being able to cooperate with my friends in a way that was good. Even Nightmare Mode seemed like a fair challenge at first, but it quickly descended into nothing but grinding. It was so hard to even get into Nightmare that the best way involved surviving for one wave over and over in the hopes that the next tier of loot would drop, which compared to the fair curve of the rest of the game was immensely frustrating.
What was once trying a variety of heroes, towers, and strategies immediately became half of your towers being obsolete, the player's own damage being incredibly important because of how dumb the targeting was, and requiring DLC heroes to get anywhere in Nightmare because they were just better. Somehow they messed up the loot generation so that pets dropped in the PREVIOUS difficulty level could actually be better than Nightmare pets because their stats overflowed and became terrible. The developers resorted to static drops upon achieving certain things.
Players can swap characters while keeping towers they've already built in play, meaning that you can easily cherry-pick the best towers of all your characters if you've spent the boring time to grind them all up to legendary levels and equip them with gear that you spent boring time to grind. Alternately, you could trade one of your static-drop pets for billions of mana crystals, allowing you to buy the best gear available. Eventually I did this myself because good drops were getting harder and harder to come by. I'm glad I did that when I did, because a pet released after that was better with no downsides, immediately ruining the economy.
In the end, Dungeon Defenders just left me with frustration. The levels were interesting with good, varied layouts and a few gimmicks in there. It's clear that they understood how to make a tower defense game, but... It's a shame that they ruined all that with incompetence in almost every other area.

There are a lot of pretenders out there who claim to be metroidvanias but more often than not they're thoroughly linear affairs with occasional backtracking for minor power ups.
Hollow Knight is the real deal! Every time I find a new power or key  my mind reels with all the new routes each opens up. Frequently I find myself expecting a to find a minor puzzle holding a trinket only to find myself lost in a newly discovered labyrinth brimming with unique enemies and hazards.
Before purchase I was worried that Hollow Knight might be annoyingly difficult, that has not been the case. The game is often challenging but seldom unfairly so, and on the rare occasion I got in over my head I found that I was always successful retrieving the goodies from my corpse. Although I must admit I could have done without the semi-mandatory corpse runs.
Everything in this game is beautiful and beautifully animated. All the environments look unique and evocative, whether they be lavish overgrown gardens, strange fields of floating jellyfish, eerie abandoned mines, or The City of Tears. There's a large cast of strange and/or endearing characters. And enemies in addition to covering a huge variety of looks within a consistent theme have subtle tells that give away their oncoming attacks.
I haven't finished yet (I think I'm 3/4s through), so it could fall apart at the end, but even if the game ended right where I last left it Hollow Knight would still be worth twice the $15 they're charging for it!

So this game has pretty graphics, nice art style, awesome melancholic music, crisp controls, interesting quirky foes, challenging bosses and some strange pleasant characters.
Why thumbs down then?
Well, there're fundamentall differences in approach to gameplay between what is acceptable for me and what the developers thought would be a good idea.
The main reason I had to drop it is the placement of savepoints. The save system here is akin to the one in Dark Souls - if you die, you get resurrected at a checkpoint, and you have to get to the place of your death again without dying to recover all your money. The levels in the game are pretty big, with a lot of dangerous places and a boss or several waiting for your somewhere. The problem is, the savepoints are pretty far away from your boss battles, and if you, say, don't have perfect reflexes, and can't beat the boss within the first three attempts, but rather ten or fifteen, the mere necessity to traverse half a level for several minutes and possibly fight off lesser enemies before facing the boss again and again is really frustrating. It's hard, sure, but not in a good way, and not in a fair way. And I'm not even that far into the story - judging by the trailer the things will really kick off later, with harder bosses and platforming that would make Super Meat Boy cry and bite its elbows out of jealousy.
Another questionable mechanic is the necessity to purchase the maps for each level to, well, get an access to a map. The problem is, the map merchant is hidden within that level somewhere, and often not at its beginning. So you have to explore half a level or possibly more to find him, and only then do your exploration properly. Is it doable? Sure. Obviously, I can get by without a map or draw my own if needed. Does it add something fun to the gameplay, though? Definitely not for me.
So there. If you can live with these artificial complications, you're facing a lot of hours of pure distilled fun. If not, however, do ride past this frustration station. Sure, there're not so many metroidvanias on the market, but let's face it, if you're a fan of the genre, you've probably bought it and beaten it at least ten times already. If you, however, are looking for something pleasant to spend a reasonable amount of time with while keeping your controller intact, be warned. This game is not for you.

I pretty much got what I expected with this title - good old school PC FPS, and lots of it!
The developers seemingly didn't wanna leave any boxes unchecked, and went all-in with powers (double tab a direction keys and press LMB or RMB), skills (permanent stat upgrade like more max health) and upgradeable weapons. Each category has its own resource - Money, KI crystals and karma. Lots of stuff is borrowed from other titles, but all things good imo. This is a lot like the "Darksiders" of FPS'es - a compilation of everthing that has proven to work in other titles.
The basic FPS mechanics feel fairly solid and rewarding, but there's a certain undefinable something missing. I don't know if it's the visual/sonic feedback from hitting your target that's a bit "off" - but it simply didn't feel as tight as I've come to expect from the best FPS'es.
I did experience some annoyances with the physics - dash while running down a flight of stairs and you just instantly die, and terrain climbing is awfully unintuitive - luckily you hardly have to do any, unless you're searching for secrets.
The presentation is a hit and miss - The narration/dialogue is witty, and the voice acting fairly good. The sound effects decent, but some of the weapon sounds lacked personality. My biggest gripe was with the graphics - the textures and 3d models were at times pretty lackluster. Fortunately the graphics engine is feature rich, and with all the bells and whistles acivated, you essentially apply enough makeup to make it all seem passable.
But whoever drew and layered the 2d comic book style "cutscenes" absolutely nailed it - suberb stuff!
Sadly the 3d engine performs somewhat poorly, and the latest WHQL nvidia drivers didn't even have a working SLI profile for this game, so I spent the first couple of hours with very poor framerates until I learned that it was fixed in the latest beta drivers. Stuff like this really has to be sorted at release date.
I spent 12 hours on the SP campaign which is the longest I can remember in a FPS, and even though there were some recycled parts, I enjoyed the entire game a great deal. If anything the first couple of hours was the least fun, as you hardly have any weapons or skills. Not that you REALLY need the weapons anyways, as the Katana melee weapon with it's shuriken partner is plenty powerful for most of what the game has to throw at you (too powerful perhaps).
My verdict is 80%
