So the Assassin’s Creed series is one that I believed hit its peak by♥♥♥♥♥Creed 2. Then the other 1000 titles that came after followed suit on a winning formula, bled it dry and then proceeded to repeatedly pound at its lifeless chest with defibrillators hoping that just maybe they –could- continue this longwinded substance-less yawn of a game series.
Casual gamers, just chill. I know many people, the majority of which 10 – 12 years old, would be up in arms and savagely beating back my opinion, BUT….fear not! As I am decidedly very pleased with the latest game in the series.
Assassins Creed: Black Flag is an amazingly fun experience. Everything, from sailing briskly across the sea to an island in promise of treasure to opening fire upon a hulking Man ‘o War engaging in firey hellish combat, feels rich and rewarding in its function. Many times just simply sailing vast distances to reach your next objective can be pleasantly rewarded with the feeling of that epic adventure on the high seas, whilst your men sing an oh so piratey chanty and give you that “Hell yeah ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥” feeling that I assume real pirates had (?).
So unlike many other♥♥♥♥♥creed games where the protagonist awkwardly throws you into the role of obligation to the creed and becoming and assassin of outspoken cause and purpose, Edward Kenway is a man who just wants to make some solid coin. Most of us can more readily relate to this character and his very cool and piratey lifestyle. He’s a man quite down trodden and defeated to begin with, realising at some point he’s run out of ♥♥♥♥s to give so he pounds the rum and turns pirate. Awesome.
Now where this game really shines is in its scope of possibility and huge selection of activities whilst sailing the deep blue waters of the Caribbean…but unfortunately, this is still very much and assassins creed game in regard to combat, climbing/free running and stealth mechanic. I say that in the sense that Assassins Creed has been around for a long time, with many sequels to iron out the problems in their consistently flawed mechanics. I’m sorry to say that they still HAVE NOT figured it out.
Many a time whilst I ran across the roof tops and directed my camera, character and used all the right controller input to do something as simple as jump from one building to the next…he’ll just decide “NOPE. MUAHAHAHA” and jump right the ♥♥♥♥ off, three stories down and consequently blowing my silent tail as I land breaking my ankles right in front of my target. Many many times, the free running felt clunkier and ever more possible in breaking immersion than any other♥♥♥♥♥creed title I’ve played to be honest.
The stealth system is okay, but emphasis on the ‘okay’. Some times, but mostly on an important mission you’re just about to complete…if you do something outside the invisible ‘guideline’ of the games intended path, you may just glitch out the guards warning system…leaving you feeling cheating and thinking “wtf did I do….???”
With so many rich and interesting stories on which the campaigns in assassins creed have been based before, it seems now the integrity is lacking a bit. The main missions in this game are just…..very much a chore. The biggest annoyance? TAILING….MISSIONS. That and eavesdropping just pisses me off in how they expect you to follow your target  It does something to try and get you attached to the different characters along the way, but falls flat on its face when it tries to keep too many of those characters involved in a plot for more than two missions before they’re forgotten about and then reintroduced somewhere down the line.
So it seems I’ve gone on a jolly fine rant more so about the things that hold this game back. But I mean…they reeeeally hold it back. Despite much of my dismay I was mostly very very impressed with this game. Every moment I was on the sea raiding ships, islands for treasure, shipwrecks for long lost gold chests, fighting back sharks, sea eels and all sorts of nasties down in the deep trying to ruin your life, was an absolute riot. This by far is the best pirate game to date.

I pretty much got what I expected with this title - good old school PC FPS, and lots of it!
The developers seemingly didn't wanna leave any boxes unchecked, and went all-in with powers (double tab a direction keys and press LMB or RMB), skills (permanent stat upgrade like more max health) and upgradeable weapons. Each category has its own resource - Money, KI crystals and karma. Lots of stuff is borrowed from other titles, but all things good imo. This is a lot like the "Darksiders" of FPS'es - a compilation of everthing that has proven to work in other titles.
The basic FPS mechanics feel fairly solid and rewarding, but there's a certain undefinable something missing. I don't know if it's the visual/sonic feedback from hitting your target that's a bit "off" - but it simply didn't feel as tight as I've come to expect from the best FPS'es.
I did experience some annoyances with the physics - dash while running down a flight of stairs and you just instantly die, and terrain climbing is awfully unintuitive - luckily you hardly have to do any, unless you're searching for secrets.
The presentation is a hit and miss - The narration/dialogue is witty, and the voice acting fairly good. The sound effects decent, but some of the weapon sounds lacked personality. My biggest gripe was with the graphics - the textures and 3d models were at times pretty lackluster. Fortunately the graphics engine is feature rich, and with all the bells and whistles acivated, you essentially apply enough makeup to make it all seem passable.
But whoever drew and layered the 2d comic book style "cutscenes" absolutely nailed it - suberb stuff!
Sadly the 3d engine performs somewhat poorly, and the latest WHQL nvidia drivers didn't even have a working SLI profile for this game, so I spent the first couple of hours with very poor framerates until I learned that it was fixed in the latest beta drivers. Stuff like this really has to be sorted at release date.
I spent 12 hours on the SP campaign which is the longest I can remember in a FPS, and even though there were some recycled parts, I enjoyed the entire game a great deal. If anything the first couple of hours was the least fun, as you hardly have any weapons or skills. Not that you REALLY need the weapons anyways, as the Katana melee weapon with it's shuriken partner is plenty powerful for most of what the game has to throw at you (too powerful perhaps).
My verdict is 80%

Just completed this game, took me a little more than 11 hours so I definitely got my moneys worth. Based on the original Shadow Warrior, which was made in 1997 by 3D Realms (responsible for classics such as Duke Nukem 3D, Blood and Rise of the Triad), it's not really an re-make... more like a re-imagination, a re-boot.
Playing as Lo Wang, hired by Zilla Enterprise to help it's owner find the legendary Nobitsura Kage, a mystical katana connected to ancient demons. Aided by a spirit named Hoji, the player travels back and forth between the real world and the shadow realm to find the three parts of the sword and... yeah, that's about it when it comes to story.
The weapon of choice in this game is the katana, it's so satisfying to run around and chop all the different enemies to small pieces with the sharp katana. Sure, you've got some standard weapons like revolver, machine gun and rocket launcher and to make it all complete you even get to upgrade Lo Wang with different abilites and powers, which comes in handy while fighting wave after wave of demons.
It's GREAT fun and I think this is one of the best FPS games released in some years, it's not like Call of Duty and Battlefield and all that other stuff, it does its own thing and that's why everyone who enjoys the FPS genre should buy it and gives this a chance.

Shadow Warrior takes a lot of elements from all previous People Can Fly and Flying Wild Hog games (Painkiller, Bulletstorm, Hard Reset) as well as adding its own unique twists to the whole. The engine and general feel of the game is reminiscent of the previous FWH product, Hard Reset, with the rather nice looking environs, somewhat quirky movement as well as the fact 90% of the environment explodes in very gratuitous manners. Take these factors and the skill shot system from Bulletstorm being blended into the mix and there is a nice recipe for total ott carnage. I guess there are best methods of killing stuff just to get through the game, but with the incentive to cause wanton madness its possibly a good idea to muck about as much as possible. Also using special moves with the sword is a great way to rack up the kills effectively.
DID I MENTION THE MELEE? THE MELEE! etc...
Shadow warrior is one of the few games that started me out with a sword and I ended up using the sword as the main weapon of choice all the way right up to the end. It may have been something to do with the fact most guns feel very gimpish when first picked up, but these eventually upgrade (Hard Reset style) to be mass killing machines,  but given the choice between shooting enemies with a mildly satisfactory SMG at a distance while racking up a low score, or barging in to the centre of them all, cutting down a few to get to the heart of the battle before spinning like a tornado and hurling limbs and heads everywhere... a bit of a no brainer.
Level design is somewhat hit and miss. It makes good use of good old secrets and nicely placed destructibles in arenas, but like Serious Sam it is largely a number of wide arenas linked by a short corridor for Wang to deliver some one-liners. The later levels from the docks onward can also drag on, with one science lab section an almost Halo degree of annoyance in repetitive and confusing passages, leaving things feeling largely inconsistent like Hard Reset before it.
If there is any strong criticism it comes in some of the cheesy referential humour, with some jokes bordering on blatantly racist. Also the game feels far too long considering the content it has. The levels would not have felt as repetitive if there were more environments to traverse or there was some interesting FPS platforming (Yes I said it. The original Shadow Warrior had some great levels on top of mountains) but the engine may have got in the way, especially with Mr Wang's bounce.
All in all, advised. Not an old, old school shooter like some make it out to be (it is very 1999 - 2003) but a great dollop of fun if you can endure the over long and repetitive levels.

is what some would call the ultimate version of the ARMA series, it's the most well built and content filled version of all the game in the series, even more so if you own the original ARMA 2 since you can easily combined the two into ARMA 2: Combined Ops, letting you play with all the maps, weapons and vehicles from both games. On top of that, there's a big community behind this game with mods, missions and custom campaigns adding even more content or enhances the core gameplay.
The ARMA series is what I would call the ultimate footsoldier simulation, even though the game features tanks, cars, helicopters, armored fighting vehicles and even jets, it's still within the basic footworks of a soldier where the game shines the most as you can play with a varying range of rifles ranging from M4's, M16's to AK's, G36 rifles and even Czech Vz.58.
The ARMA series started with the original ARMA: Cold War Assault, or Operation Flashpoint for us Veterans where the setting is the cold war gone hot. Today, the so called "Armaverse" has rbought us to Takistan where political unrest and civil war has brought the American taskforce to try and overthrow the military leader that rules the Takistan government forces.
You will get to play as several different roles, from the basic grunt to a tank commander.
The Campaign itself is rather short, but it does a good job of showing you the many different aspects of ARMA and on top of that, it is co-operable with three other friends, letting you all do different tasks in each missions, which has an affect on how the missions play other for the other members.
The multiplayer is where the game really shines, which it always has, here you can find a lot of fun missions, like Takistani life,  a kind of a roleplaying mission where civilians can do what they want, live a law abiding life to become a criminal or even a rebel while police officers try to keep the order.
Then you've got missions like standard PvP, like team deathmatch or co-operation missions to large scale PvP or PvE missions where you have to capture towns randomly allocated on the map.
ARMA also comes with the easy to use mission maker where you yourself can create simple to advanced mission which you can play alone or with friends. This is where the game can become really fun as you can make missions like, infiltrate the enemy base, sabotage missions to large scale battles spanning across the entire map. Or you can make a mission where you and your friends are all farmer with dirtbikes and have to escape the enemy chopper that relentlessly tries to murder you in the most horrific way it can.
The game does have it's kinks and problems though. It can be very taxing on your system and many dislike how you handle your soldier, calling it clunky and slow to respond. In my opinion, I've never had any bigger issues with it, but the way how it can be rather slow at turning around and such, especially while standing still can be annoying.
This is mostly something you'll learn after a few hours and will become more effective in using it, so don't let it turn you off, learn it, and I'm sure you'll be pleased with ARMA 2: Operation Arrowhead.

Hollow Knight is simply an amazing Metroidvania game. To be more precise, I think this is as important a game as Super Metroid (genre defining) and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night (genre expanding). Hollow Knight expands the genre like SotN did, but this time with Demon/Dark Souls inspired mechanics, and does it in style.
The game is beautifully drawn and animated. The 2D graphics are hi-res, not retro inspired as many other indie games tend to be right now. The soundtrack is haunting and somber. The level design is absolutely fantastic. The interconnectedness of the map (very important feature in Metroidvanias) is very high, and features many openable shortcuts reminiscent of the Souls games, which fits right into the Metroidvania exploration gameplay.
The world is also very fully developed, with plenty of lore scattered and hidden around the map, in the form of characters to talk with and ancient tablets to read, waiting for the player to piece together. Your character's motiviations and origins you get to discover slowly through the gameplay (if you wish to), and there are multiple endings depending on how thoroughly you explore. Thankfully also the game provides a save before the final boss so you can always go back and achieve better endings without doing another replay, which is needed as a full playthrough will take around 30-50 hours.
Be aware the game is somewhat difficult- the Souls inspired mechanics include Benches which act as a respawn point and restore your health when used, but which will also respawn all non-trivial enemies (trivial enemies constantly respawn on screen change). In 'the field', so to speak, health can be regained standing still and using 'Soul'. Your character only holds a limited amount of Soul, and it must be earned by hitting enemies. When you die, your capacity for Soul is reduced by 1/3 until you return to the scene of your death to recover your Shade (or by one other method eventually unlocked in game).
It's just that great. If you love cheesy 80's movies and TV shows and loved Farcry3: Blood Dragon or Double DFragon: Neon, this is the perfect film to watch! Plus,
Excellent game. If you have the time to explore your way around, it's definitely worth it.

I had fun with this game for a couple of hours, then I suffered through a couple more hours that were exactly the same as the first couple, hoping this was just a minor pacing issue and something would eventually happen to break the monotony. It did not. As far as I can tell this game is a hack-and-slash through and through, and the way you're going to play it is by executing the same special move over and over to kill all of the incredibly non-threatening enemies, and occasionally shoot at the flying ones when they don't for whatever reason fly down low enough to be stabbed in the throat.
Oh, wait, no. There is SOMETHING that breaks up the monotony, from time to time. Unfortunately that something is overly time consuming boss fights that just boil down to "move in circles to avoid his attacks while shooting at his weak points for MASSIVE DAMAGE". Sadly, there is not even a giant enemy crab to make this seem like a parody. It's just the actual way the boss fights work. They are the ultimate low point of the game even though they're the only time you ever really shoot anything.
I have nothing against the developers, I think they set out to make a good game here, and they've been supporting it. I don't even REALLY have anything against the game... but it's another nail in the coffin for old school shooters. Calling this game an old school shooter is glaringly inaccurate for one simple reason - you don't actually shoot anything. The guns are pitifully ineffective while the sword will dispatch most enemy types in a single special attack. The whole melee component of this isn't even challenging because you have a superman dash to clear the distance of an entire room in a split second and, failing that, most of the enemies are melee anyway.
The secrets are also not very secretive, and a lot of the places I thought to look for them turned out to be totally inaccessible thanks to some invisible barrier. Not very old school. The highest difficulty level has managed to not kill me once despite extremely reckless melee only play. Not very old school. In fact, I don't even find myself using my healing spell (healing on demand in an old school shooter?) because not only are health pickups numerous, you eventually get an ability that simply heals an absurd amount of damage whenever you hit something with your sword, which is to say, whenever you hit something because you always use your sword.
Overall I would give this game something like a 6/10 as a hack-and-slash with some guns and minor RPG elements, which is what it is. As an old school shooter I would give it a 0. Buy it if you're not at all looking for what it's advertised as.

This game is a flashback to the 90s, before FPS games started taking themselves seriously. Shadow Warrior gives you a lot of weapons, and then throws wave after ridiculous wave of the same five enemies at you.

The game encourages you to mix things up by giving you a score after each battle based on the variety and effectiveness of your attacks, rewarding you with bonus Karma points (and unlike on Reddit, these Karma points actually matter).
The story, told through a series of beautiful animated cutscenes, is surprisingly not bad. Obviously, story is not the game's primary focus; the pacing is terrible and the somber tone is mismatched to the rest of the game, which is all absurd machismo and silly one-liners. But it is interesting enough that you won't want to skip the interludes.
I'm glad games like this are still being made. It's a refreshing break from the serious, gritty, big-money FPSs that dominate today.

Disclaimer: this is a long review, and I may have spent a bit too much time on the negative side of things. Hang in there.
I came into Assassins Creed 4 with a few fears, as I was mildly dissapointed with Assassins Creed 3. My qualms with that game include the reliance on a sub-par stealth system, and a combat system that is just ridculously easy.
To be honest, none of that has really changed with Assassins Creed 4. It definitely has problems. It is still a game that has an incredibly flawed stealth system. Edward is incapable of crouching, unless of course, he is in a bush. Enemies will sometimes be completely clueless, watching complacently as you stab a man 10 feet in front of him and throw him into a haybale. Somtimes, they'll be ruthless, like they have magic sonar and can spot you from huge distances. And of course, there's always everybody's favorite: Trailing Missions! Oh yeah, they're in full swing here! One detection and instant failure state! I understand that these are sometimes necessary sequences in the story, but, please! For the love of god, please just give us this exposition some other way. These trailing missions are infuriating! Also: Boat Stealth! Yep, not kidding. It's also broken. Lookouts on enemy ships are apparently worthless, or blind, in this game. They only are capable of looking for only 30 feet IN FRONT of the ship, not behind AT ALL. Honestly, how in the world can you not notice a hulking brig lurking around in the water in clear daylight? Boat stealth sections really took me out of the moment, and they just seem ridiculous.
Since AC3, the combat system has largely stayed the same. Don't get me wrong, it is fun to rack up the combo kills, but it just feels so easy. Prolonged fights are nearly impossible, unless you're trying to prolong them. Fights that are supposed to have weight end up falling short because of this. Honestly, the fight with the Assassin at the beginning of this game is extremely anticlimactic. There's a long, dramatic chase sequence that leads up to a dramatic confrontation on the beach. This is an assassin, a legendary killer. How will you defeat him?!! And then he dies in one swing.
This may seem insignificant, but it just seemed steange to me
Like I said, this game has problems. But, If you can look past them, this game is the best Assassins Creed game in the series. But, to me, this really isn't even an Assassin's Creed game anymore. It's a pirate game, up there with Pirates of the Carribean and Sid Meier's Pirates. When you play this game, you feel like a
. Once you get through the opening story missions and get released into the world, at the helm of the Jackdaw, with a crew of fearsome men ready to take on the world, this game shines. You can do whatever you want. Attack ships at random, racking up notoriety until you are wanted dead. Sailing to parts unknown, discovering mayan artifacts and hidden treasure. Hunting island animals and fearsome beasts of the sea, and crafting items from their skins and bones to further your character's abilities. Diving underwater and exploring shipwrecks, while avoiding the fearsome jaws of a shark {Speaking of which, these underwater shark-stealth sequences are tense, and honestly scary. They are the only stealth in this game that I enjoy}. Upgrading your ship into a vessel to be reckoned with, and engaging in epic naval battles with legendary ships. All of these side activites are a welcome distraction from the usual sneaking and stabbing of an Assassin's Creed game, and they work extremely well, because they are always enjoyable. Not to mention the fact that all this is being realized in stunning graphics. This game has an unbeleivable amount of content, and it has never felt like a grind. I have spent close to 80 hours in this game, and I still haven't completed the main story, because I didn't have to. I was busy being a pirate, not an Assassin.
TL;DR: At the end of the day, this is a good game. It has its problems, and they are numerous. But if you think of this as a pirate game and play it like a pirate game, giving marginal attention to the story missions, you will love it.

After finishing every Assassin’s Creed game since the original as an obsessive completionist, Assassin’s Creed IV Black Flag is my favorite by far.  Playing as a pirate, exploring the beautiful seas and islands, made me feel like a kid again.  The thrill of stalking an enemy fleet, launching a surprise attack with heavy mortars and a broadside fusillade of cannon fire, and boarding the crippled ships to seize them in hand-to-hand combat never got old.  I felt like the heroic Errol Flynn in his legendary pirate movies!
AC4’s story wasn’t fantastic, but it was the best one in this franchise after the original AC2.  The protagonist in AC4 is eminently likeable, a charismatic and tough-but-caring rogue far more like AC2’s flamboyant Ezio than AC3’s boringly stoic Connor.  The characters in AC4, particularly some of history’s most-famous pirates, were generally a lot of fun.  And the modern-day Animus hokum that rips you out of the meat of Assassin’s Creed games was thankfully kept to a minimum.  Most of the out-of-Animus activities, which were actually the most entertaining of the series, were fully optional in AC4.  I’m glad the developers are hearing us that the modern-day stuff in Assassin’s Creed is a jarring waste of time.
The missions are classic Assassin’s Creed, with lots of tailing, stalking, assassinating, and escaping after the deed.  The optional objectives in missions were much more manageable than some in AC3, generally achievable without excessive retries.  There is also the option to restart missions at checkpoints within them, rather than at the beginning.  That made the game a lot less frustrating for people like me who want to get all objectives but don’t have tons of time to play games.  Tailing sections in some missions were used to advance the dialogue, which I enjoyed much more than just watching a static cut-scene.  Using stealth-craft to tail targets unseen was often a fun challenge.
The hand-to-hand combat is excellent, easily the best of the series yet.  The animations of our hero and his enemies are exquisitely fluid, with natural transitions between different moves and when switching between enemies.  Unfortunately the weapon options were dramatically reduced from AC3, to essentially just hidden blades, dual swords, and pistols.  The explanation given was pirates prefer a sword in each hand, but it would have been nice to have the larger weapon set from previous games.  You could still disarm enemies to take different kinds of weapons, but they got dropped soon after combat.  The combat isn’t up to Batman Arkham’s stellar standards, but it is still a lot of fun.  Particularly in ship situations, swinging from ropes on the masts to jump into the middle of a scrum and massacre all.
The ship-to-ship combat was utterly amazing, AC4 is easily the best pirate game I’ve ever played and this is coming from a lifelong gamer born in 1974 who started gaming on an Apple ][.  The seas are absolutely beautifully rendered, with the ships acting realistically on the waves with the exception of faster responses than possible in the real world.  The tactics of naval combat can actually be quite deep, such as approaching enemies from the stern to deny them a broadside shot at you.  Blasting enemy ships to splinters with cannons just never gets old, and boarding them to steal their cargoes to upgrade your own ship is very satisfying.  The seas are lousy with ships, so there are always plenty to fight, board, and loot at every turn.
The open-world exploration aspect of AC4 dramatically expands on AC3, and was very addictive.  Between missions you can sail wherever you want whenever you want with virtually no restrictions, discovering new villages, smugglers’ coves, and even underwater shipwrecks.  There are many local assassination missions, which are short and sweet and fun if you like remaining undetected until the killing stroke.  There are tons of collectibles that unlock everything from ship upgrades to new weapons and armor to cheats to multiplayer customization options, and I was surprised how compelled I felt to get absolutely all of them.  That isn’t hard, as after conquering naval forts commanding the open seas or scaling traditional viewpoints in cities the collectibles all appear on the map.  Most are easy to get, and satisfying to collect.

Shadow Warrior initially tries really hard to make you think it's less wonderful than it is, but the conviction that the developers and voice artists exhibit in delivering such a crazy product allows it to pull off the lame jokes, pop culture references and mindless action with panache. And after you're convinced that you're playing a superficial action game with another vapid set of cliche characters, somewhere along the line after all the fan service and wisecracks and gore, you realise that you're invested in the story and you care about the characters, and suddenly you become aware of how shockingly well-made this game is.
Given the patchy success-rate of recent nostalgic reboots and reimaginings (I'm looking at you, ROTT), Shadow Warrior suprised the hell out of me with it's smooth and responsive controls, entertaining gameplay, beautiful visuals, and well-cast voice actors. It understands exactly what it wants to be at any given moment, and excels at both the early tongue-in-cheek schlock, as well as the later more serious character development. This is clearly a game in which all the talent behind the scenes really shines through, and I can't recommend it highly enough.

I think this is a cute fun game, I haven't played for too long yet, but I can't recommend it at this point in time, and I'll explain why.
I find the save mechanism for this game **extremely** frustrating. The game uses save points, so you can't just save and exit when you need to, you either have to pause the game until you can return to it, or loose your progress. I THOUGHT that this was the worst thing in this game, but it's not. The WORST part about this game is that if you die before you reach a save point it takes you alllll the way back to the last save point. That's pretty normal, right? Wrong. It deletes all of the power-ups that were available to you in your first run through. All of the same monsters are still there, none of your progress was saved, but for some reason they decided that if you died then the game should be even harder for your second run through. So not only did it not save your progress, you have to repeat the entire "level" since your previous save in an even harder way.
DON'T BOTHER PLAYING WITH A KEYBOARD.
I have tried remapping the keys so that it wasn't abysmally frustrating and clunky to play on my computer, I really did. Unfortunately both the games native key bindings and any combination of more normal key bindings that I could come up with were all terrible. The game is next to impossible to play with a keyboard, so don't even bother.
YOU CAN'T USE ALL CONTROLLERS
This has already been reported in forums, but a lot of people are finding that they can't use their third party controllers with this game. I spent an infuriating 2 hours trying to get an 8bitdo controller to use this game. My computer sees the controller, the game even says that it's mapped the buttons, but the game refuses to accept imput from the controller AT ALL. After two hours of hitting the internet I've concluded that the developers seem to have only mapped for the bigger named controllers, so if you've got something like an 8bitdo I wish you luck - but I eventually gave up on it.
With a controller that actually freaking works with this game I imagine it could be quite fun, despite the really irritating and stupid save logistics. But since I can't use the controllers I already own, and using a keyboard with this particular game style is just really the most irritating thing I've ever done in a game, I'll most likely be refunding this game.

Hollow Knight is one of the the first indie gems of this year, blending a beautiful aesthetic with solid mechanics and an interesting world.
The game follows a trend in recent gaming that mirrors similar movements in the art and literature world that is referred to as 're-visioning'. What the term means is that rather than directly copying its predecessors and inspirations, Hollow Knight re-visions them entirely, taking the metroidvania style of mechanics and combat and bringing them up to a modern standard of fluidity and visual spectacle.
The hand-drawn aesthetic that they have managed to create is both enticing and organic, breathing life ino the gameplay and environments they create and enticing the player, immersing them deeper into the world. You explore a diverse array of environments, from overgrown jungles to desolate ruins, and each area provides new challenges, interesting new enemies to fight, and its own unique visuals. Your constant need to explore keeps the game fresh and interesting as you navigate the quirky, bug-themed world around you, and the game rewards your exploration with plenty of secrets and loot to uncover. The soundtrack is the perfect backdrop for all of these feelings of immersion, accenting each environment with appropriately curious, wonderful, or somber music depending on the mood.
As far as the challenge level, the game presents a healthy amount of difficulty. Although the learning curve can be steep at certain points, each enemy can be conquered with the tools the game gives you, even if it takes a few tries. The enemies in each area will often train you on the mechanics that you will eventually need to face the larger bosses within each area, so you aren't taken aback when you finally encounter them. I've haven't seen everything the game has to offer just yet, but so far, everything has been fairly well balanced an enjoyable.
There is one major downside. I should mention that the game does seem to be poorly optimized. If you have a modern rig or something relatively new you should be totally fine, and it runs on my mid-tier gaming PC like butter, but it also runs terribly on my 2012 laptop, which admittedly does not have great specs, but if you are looking at this game thinking that the visuals probably make it an easy pickup for a low performance system, I would reconsider.
All in all, this is an absolute must play for any indie game fan and is most likely already a contender for many people's game of the year in 2017.

Hollow Souls.
All right, I made that stupid joke in another review but I be damned if it's not a close comparison. Even if I don't really like comparing games that are just a bit more challenging then usual to the Souls series, the similarities between the two games goes beyond the theme and boss fights.
As an exemple, the story itself is pretty vague. You don't even know who or what the character you play is. The story bares resemblace to the Souls series in the sense that's vague but present, and one needs only to take it slow, interact with the enviroment, NPCs, and later on in the game's life, make heavy use of a very special item you'll be given. If you enjoyed discovering the tales of Lordran, you'll enjoy discovering the ones of Hollownest. A deviation from the more straight forward Metroid-vania style games, the most recent and prominent of which I playd was Ori and the Blind Forest. Another apt comparison.
Along the way you'll find plenty of zones to explore, challeging boss battles and dead ends. Lots of dead ends. In classic metroid style, you'll be able to access these zones only after you acquire a movement skill, which will more often then not lead to either a challenge or a new zones.
Tehcnicaly speaking, you require to do a rather limited amount of exploration to find the tools to progress and reach the final boss, but you'll probably miss a good 50% to 60% of the game and it's story if you do just that. But the option is there alongside the achivements if you wish to go for speed runs.
Alongside an Hardcore mode later on and Charms to make it even harder on top of that.
Charms will be your only option when it comes to customisation, there are no stats increases outside of weapon, healt and "Mana". Each charm has an effect that can drastically change your play style, and finding the ones that suit you best is key. Once again, you'll find more of these exploring.
However, there's something that may be the cause of frustation for some. You see, you don't have a map at the beginning. You start off with just your sword and a simple jump button. To find the maps of the area you'll have to look for a carthographer that will be hidden around the zone you've just entered, untill you can find him, your map is empty and you'll be left to wonder almost blindly, with the exepction of a few signs occasionaly found in the area, but those are resting places and things like that.
Should you complete a zone before finding the person, you'll find a note where he was supposed to be telling you to buy the map from the shop. And considering that the zone aesthetic can be very similar, or even labyrinthian, you'll need the map.
Over all, I'm personaly hooked to this game like I've never been for a while now. It strikes the same cords as the Souls series did at the beginning, the sad tunes of Hollownest combined with the game's art have pushed me towards the end boss in hope to understand what happend to this place. And the challenge of the boss battles was a welcome addition. The design of some of these bosses them self convey much more then what the game tells at times, outside of the inevitable stress after failing multiple times that is.
I can't stress this enough, the game is hard. The bosses are challenging, the maps are hazardus and the jumping challenges required for some of the extras are sometimes rage inducing. If you have problems with jumping, navigating and fighting in a 2D scenario then this game could not be for you. It doesn't hold your hand.
But if you welcome a challenge and are as curious as I am, give the game a try 25 - 30 hours backtracing and exploration included. I scored up to 28 hours with a 66% completition. And for 15€, considering the enjoyment I had from it, it's a bargain.

I think its title and description speak for itself, but anyway it's basically a 30 minute short film that gratuitously celebrates the 1980's & B-movies with over-the-top visuals, a synthesizer heavy soundtrack, and your run of the mill ninjas, lasers, time travel, vikings, & martial arts. It falls into "So bad it's good", like recent releases such as: Far Cry Blood Dragon, Manborg, Machete, Planet Terror. It's fairly well done and accomplishes its goals as outlined by the director in the 2013 trailer and Kickstarter.
The film revolves around a character named Kung Fury, a typical 80's action hero, traveling back in time to fight a fictionalized version of Adolf Hitler, capable of killing cops in the future and trained in martial arts. The acting is pretty decent for a film of this type, but the movie relies a bit too much on CGI & greenscreen; however it looks fine considering the budget ($630k) and what visuals+style the film aims for. The film could be considered too brazen about what it pays homage to e.g. Miami Connection, Tron, Heavy Metal magazine, Mortal Kombat, G.I. Joe, etc. falling into more of a parody & tribute to the 80's & B-movies than merely subtly imitating the style and feel of the era and those films.
I think it's pretty obvious from a minimal amount of information whether or not the film is for you, but if this sort of nostalgia exploitation/celebration of gratuitousness appeals to you, I highly recommend it.

You find out about the Lore by reading item descriptions and talking with NPCs you find or your way down Dirtmouth, "à la Dark Souls". The game has little to no tutorial so you'll have to figure out what to do with your habilities. Sound and music design are top-notch, and that's a huge quality in this game.
Controls are really responsive and it feels great to play. So far I've found my little indie gem from 2017 and I'm waiting to see even more in my playthrough.
The only con i've seen so far is the stuttering. It stutters at random places or random actions you do, making it harder to play. Compelling witty dialogue makes you want to explore every nook and cranny of this game. Highly entertaining especially for a game that best fits into the genre of "walking simulator"

TL;DR
Pirates + Cannons + Assassins + Treasure - Limits = Amazing Game
This game blew me out of the water (pun intended).
The biggest thing I loved about the game is the sheer amount of exploration in it. No other Assassins' Creed game has really touched on this before. You can travel all around the carribean either on land or by the ocean, all the while passing ships, fleets, sharks, whales, sunken treasure, pirates, bounty hunters, etc. This game has alligator fights! It has privateering! It has shanties! And the best thing about it is: you aren't forced into focusing on the story the whole game! Probably around 90% of the game is NON story...
The shipfaring is a big part of the game which is well thought out. You really feel like you're controlling your crew through an epic battle and the struggle feels real. Boarding ships is easy and the game does a great part of transitioning into a boarding from a fight. It never gets old! Probably half of my played time is sailing around and plundering ships.
One bad thing about the game is that it doesn't have a lot of assassinations... but honestly who cares? The least fun parts in the game in my opinion were when I was forced to sneak around in the shadows instead of staggering up to my foes and shooting them in the face like a proper pirate.
Caveat: I haven't played an Assassin's Creed game since Assassin's Creed II. So I wouldn't call myself a die hard fan.

I must admit that I went into this one with low expectations. I loved this game. It's not mind blowing in innovation by any means, but it knows that and even makes fun of itself as it comically references classic FPS icons like Duke Nukem 3D, Serious Sam and many more.
This game is linear and has repetitive combat with a leveling and upgrading system that is is fairly rewarding - unlock new attacks and weapon attacks mostly (at least that's the highlights in that category). The over-the-top blood and slicing makes the sword the all time favorite weapon 90% of the time, though it's very fun to mix it up with duel wielding machine guns, flamethrower & crossbow bombs, cowboy style pistol shooting, 4 barrel shotgunning, and of course the classic rocket launcher.
The story starts with you (Lo Wang), and super cocky arrogant badass that you don't really like or hate, meeting a equally cocky and synically quick witted demon that you illogically partner up with. The dialogue between these two is a big highlight in the game as they constantly make fun of each other and in a way that is actually funny. I imagine a shallow plot that would be slightly engaging, and though it was not extremely amazing it was a lot better than I thought it was going to be, and both the main characters (you and the demon dude) develop to become much more interesting than the original childish versions you meet in the beginning.
If you enjoy a good FPS and have been playing them for years I'd say this one's a must.

This is a great example of a great game that has been utterly mutilated by a terrible and overbearing storyline. This game by it's very nature gives you free reign to do as you please throughout most of the Carribbian however this massively contrasts to the super linear and monotonous story missions, this means that you'll dread doing them as you'd rather swashbuckle on your own adventure. The story missions will often involve "go from point A to Point B without being spotted" while throwing arbitrary objectives at you in the process, hardly the freedom that a game about piracy deseves right? Moreso the parts where you're not in the Animus are even worse, Ubisoft thought that it would be clever to this a first person meta-game plot where you work for a gaming company making the game that you're playing, however these parts are even more boring, sluggish and contain no challenge whatsoever as they entirely consist of "go to A, listen to B, Hack C" or variations on that, the worst part being that these parts will often come after completing a story mission and all you will want to do is get back to the pirateering.
The gameplay is the best out of any AC game yet, the naval combat is by far the best bit of the game and there is a lot of it and it'll often leave you feeling like a badass pirate captain after a hard fight. The land aspect is more of the same if you're an AC veteran, freerunning through densly packed environments and dodging guards ect... the combat is as dull as ever, standing a circle of guards murdering them intern and they all try to 1 on 1 you.
The game is very poorly optimised for a PC port, this isn't surprising considering that the devs had to make the game for 6 platforms and that AC3 was even more poorly optimised. The game runs at a poor framerate on reasonably good hardware, I easily surpass all the recommended sysreqs and I still have to turn the resolution down to achieve even 30fps consistantly, Ubisoft has done nothing to change this since release and have only made the performance worse with the Physx update. That being said, the game does look fantastic none the less with great attention to detail in the environment and the animation quality, however the islands do look very underdetailed from the sea with many islands just being several sets of poorly detailed trees on a mountain when viewed from upclose, this does somewhat ruin the immersion as a result but for the most part the graphics are what you'd expect from a "next gen" title.
The game's difficulty varies between easy and outright unfair. As said before the melee combat is easy and involves countering and button mashing for most enemies with the exceptions of some of the special enemies which require filling with a substantial amount of lead. The stealth aspect can be very frustating with much of the Ai having a hivemind e.g. if one guard sees you, the hoard comes running, this can often lead to multiple mission restarts especially if you're going for full sync. The naval battles are where the game can get particularly difficult, while the light ships present less than no challenge, the heavier frigates and manowars can lead to some terrifying confrontations especially in the late game as sometimes you'll fight a heavy ship and then another will come into the frey and then another ect.. especially if you have a "hunter ship" on you. In the later missions and areas, there are frequetly very much contrived storms which will cause serious damage to your ship unless you are careful, this is made worse by the fact that these tornados in storms will actually aim for you, however can rather comically decimate enemy ships too if properly manipulated leading to a big oppotunity for free booty on occasion.
In conclusion AC4:Black Flag is mixed booty, it is without a doubt the best naval combat "simulator" in gaming, the game provides many tens of hours in side missions and exploration which is where most of the game's entertainment value come from. However the game is comprehensively hindered by it being an AC game, in that it is bound by the series various plot points and themes as a result the plot is weak and the story missions do much to discredit the game as a whole. The scourge of the story would be so bad if it wasn't required for progress in the awsome free roam aspect of the game e.g. to explore the game you need to play the story.

I picked up Shadow Warrior, expecting yet another casual slash 'em up.
But by God, I did NOT expect anything this awesome.
This reboot of the classic Shadow Warrior game puts that horrible remake of Duke Nukem to shame, by being both visually stunning and psychotically amusing. As with the first game, you play the legendary 'Mr. Two Million Dollars' himself, Lo Wang: Mercenary Ninja Warrior for hire. He's sent to buy a legendary Katana for his corporation, Zilla Enterprises, and within the first few minutes of entering the Temple where the seller is keeping it, you get your first fight with sword-wielding Yakuza gang members. This is where the main selling point of the game comes; the violent, bloody swordplay we all love in games like this.
If you think he's dead, best to make sure; even an enemy in the process of falling to the floor can be put into an even worse way with another well-placed swing, decapitating and dismembering your victim. Later on in the game, you get to do even worse when you're granted Chi powers and have a demonic companion following you around as a disembodied voice. And best of all, you get given guns.
Glorious,
guns.
These allow you to get even more immersed in the bloodshed, ripping off legs and heads from a distance. The upgrading system is simple, and shows exactly what's needed to unlock that secondary firing mode for your weapon. While this game may be very strenuous on lesser PCs, those with higher grades of computing are in for a real treat.

Yeah, it's got guns and they're pretty cool and effective, but you wanna use that sword.  Make it PERSONAL.  Not to compare it to a totally different genre game like Skyrim, but killing a Dregr in that game with a sword isn't all that satisfying when compared to the SHEER BRUTAL MUTILATION you're capable of in Shadow Warrior.  "If you should encounter God on your journey...GOD WILL BE CUT."
All that said and duely noted, it IS rather generic, and not many people enjoy the classic gameplay that this FPS offers.  It's very linear, and after you have a certain amount of skills, unless you raise the difficulty level, you can burn through enemies with too much ease. I picked up Shadow Warrior, expecting yet another casual slash 'em up.
But by God, I did NOT expect anything this awesome.
This reboot of the classic Shadow Warrior game puts that horrible remake of Duke Nukem to shame, by being both visually stunning and psychotically amusing. As with the first game, you play the legendary 'Mr. Two Million Dollars' himself, Lo Wang: Mercenary Ninja Warrior for hire. He's sent to buy a legendary Katana for his corporation, Zilla Enterprises, and within the first few minutes of entering the Temple where the seller is keeping it, you get your first fight with sword-wielding Yakuza gang members. This is where the main selling point of the game comes; the violent, bloody swordplay we all love in games like this.
If you think he's dead, best to make sure; even an enemy in the process of falling to the floor can be put into an even worse way with another well-placed swing, decapitating and dismembering your victim. Later on in the game, you get to do even worse when you're granted Chi powers and have a demonic companion following you around as a disembodied voice. And best of all, you get given guns.
Glorious,
guns.
These allow you to get even more immersed in the bloodshed, ripping off legs and heads from a distance. The upgrading system is simple, and shows exactly what's needed to unlock that secondary firing mode for your weapon. While this game may be very strenuous on lesser PCs, those with higher grades of computing are in for a real treat.

Currently: 6/10
Definitely worth $14.99, but with some major hangups that may or may not be objective.
So just to get some things out of the way, this game is masterfully made. There's something about the control of your character that really just feels great-immediately. The art is so beautiful in it's simplicity. It's bleak and vivid at the same time. I want to buy posters. On top of that, I want to buy the haunting soundtrack to this. Together they make a beautiful peace of art at least worth experiencing-please do.
The level design plays nicely off my last point here. Everything loops into itself in a true Metroid fashion. There are branching paths off branching paths and you can normally create some pretty sweet shortcuts with some decent exploration-it's never a gimmie. You're going to have to work for all of them. The enemies scattered across each map are relevant to their area and always a treat to experience (except for where I'm at now).
The problem that I have with this game at this point is that it feels like I got toooooo much map to start, and not much direction. I love being able to explore, but I'm not sure where I'm headed or why. I've spent 8.7 hours in the game and most of that has been running back and forth to figure out where I should be trying to progress. Generally that wouldn't be a problem, but this game leans heavily on some of the principals of games like Nioh, Bloodborne, and Dark Souls. Your currency is called Geo, and when you die you find yourself waking at the last Bench (read bonfire/lamplight/shrine) where you have to hoof it back to your... I don't know what to call it. Your Hollow? It's an all-black version of yourself that you have to hit a couple times to get your resources back. There's no traveling between benches, just the "Stag Network" that has one point of insertion per area that generally feels like it was almost intentionally placed in a lopsided manner, rather than gated off in a central location.
I wasn't dying all that much until I made it to the Soul Sanctum, maybe the 6th mapped area from what I can tell, where suddenly I'm quite perturbed about having enemies that teleport when I get anywhere near them and fire homing magic. Unless I catch them in a hallway they've proven to make my experience in this area grating. It doesn't feel like a challenge, it feels like a hamstring, but I've endured. I'm starting to feel like I have a strategy for them now. Lo and behold, the bosses are starting to do the same thing. Ugh. I'll keep at it it, but as of right now it feels like an exponential ramp up in difficulty.
Lastly, there's a sort of upgrade system available in the game by way of Charms and Notches. You can collect a large number of Charms and equip a number of them based off of how many Notches you have. They range from things like a Charm for you to see where you're at on your map, to lengthening your "Nail" (your sword), and so on. I have mixed feelings about this. At first I thought it was neat that you could just have a map reference without a big blinking pointer on it. But now that I'm hitting a genuine challenge I'm finding myself frustrated that I can't use more than one useful charm at a time because I need to keep that on there. I guess I could switch them out, but I can only do that at a bench. That's probably where my hangup is. Benches are scarce, so I end up doing MORE running.
It's almost there. Like many things, this has been a mostly pleasant experience, and I've definitely gotten $15 of entertainment out of so far. I'm going to keep at this and see if it starts to build calouses. I feel like I haven't gotten as far as I should yet-stay tuned.

As others have said, fluid gameplay and extremely responsive controls make this game a delight to play. There is a good balance between exploring and progressing the story that many other games seem to lack. Be warned, however, that this isn't the type of game you can just cruise right through, at least not the first time around. Bosses are fair but can be extremely challenging - even some of the mini-bosses have killed me multiple times. If you're the type of person that likes to explore and doesn't mind spending time to learn how to kill specific enemies rather than just mashing a button over and over again, this game is definitely for you.
As for complaints: so far, only two big ones come to mind:
1. The game discourages exploring in areas you're not supposed to be in yet. What I mean by this is that the map salesman only shows up in the current area of the game you're meant to be exploring. This mechanic struck me as odd because even *with* a map, there are places in each area that you literally can't progress past without certain items/abilities. As a player this just made no sense to me.
2. The game is mostly stable on my machine but I still experience small fps drops and visual lag from time to time. It's not a game-breaking issue by any means, but it happens enough to be noticable after a few hours of playing. If this is happening on my i5-7600k/R9 390 machine, I can't imagine what kind of issues people with less beefy rigs must be having.
The map thing was clearly a conscious choice made by the devs, which is fine, it's their game and we are experiencing it as they intended us to, even if it's hard to find maps for each area. The fps/lag issue is supposedly being worked on as I post this review.
As of the moment I post this, I would give this game an 8.5/10. Great game overall, but a few small flaws that (in my opinion) hold it back from being one of the best. When and if the fps/lag issues get fixed, I'd rate it a 9. Either way, however, I would definitely reccommend this game to anyone looking for a good time waster as well as a good challenge.

This game seems odd to me.
For starters, it is nothing like the original Shadow Warrior whatsoever. Yes, I know what a reboot is, but if your game is unrecognizable as being set in the same universe aside from characters and some weapons, you've strayed too far from the original. The combat is smooth, polished and enjoyable but that's all the game has going for it.
In a lot of ways, Shadow Warrior feels like a downgrade from the original (obviously, minus the graphics). The original's combat wasn't as refined or sensitive as this one's, but it was definitely faster-paced. In the original, you blasted your way through levels. In this, you progress slowly through linear arenas, trying to kill the demons as stylishly as possible before moving onto the next generic arena.
Oh yeah, demons. Those are pretty much the only enemies in the game. There's about five different types, all similar, three of which are melee only, plus three greater demons (Necromancer, Minotaur, Annoying Armoured ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) and three crappy boss battles. In a game of this size, the limited enemy variety feels repetitive. The original had baboons, different kinds of ninjas, invisble super ninjas, coolies, spirits, bees, sumos, snake demons... there's just so much variety there.
The story of this game is alright. It's not too bad. The dialogue that explains it though, is awful. I can confidently say this game has the worst dialogue I've ever heard. It's so tryhard and cliched. The game's humour is terribad too. Only once did I find myself amused, and that was at the opening cutscene where Lo Wang is jamming out in his car. Really, this is where the game falls flat on its face. Without funny jokes and taunts, without having a likeable Lo Wang, the game has no charm or appeal whatsoever. This young Lo Wang is an emotional, Justin Bieber-like crybaby. The old Lo Wang is a crazy, old, stereotypical asian man with more firepower than the North Korea Army. I know which Wang I prefer.
If you haven't played the original, buy it. It's cheap as chips and a classic, way better than this.

Are you an experienced gamer?  Have you played enough games that you instinctively recognize the tropes and common things that all games do, but can't quite put a finger on them?  Would you like a game that points them all out, and makes it amusing at the same time?  Good.  The Stanley Parable does that.
Well, I mean, that's where it starts.  First it puts its finger right on those tropes, pointing them out, having a chuckle.  Then the whole hand.  Then it shoves its hand through the tropes and the wall behind them, shattering a hole into a Escher-like dimension of allegory and humor spiraling endlessly around a story that deliberately falls afoul of the same tropes it works so hard to identify and undermine.
Then the game restarts, or maybe it doesn't restart.  Maybe you restarted it, but did you restart it because you wanted to, or because the game wanted you to?  And is this really a game anymore?
To perhaps make that rambling a bit more clear, The Stanley Parable is a game about a man, which is really allegory about games, which in turn is a metaphor about life and choice and free will and about a billion other things.  There are so many layers to the story you could get lost in it all, but the beauty is that you don't have to.  You can be philisophical about what it all means, or you can simply laugh hysterically at the spot on narration describing, bemoaning, and sometimes belittling you, the story, and who knows what else.
In short, The Stanley Parable is a beautiful mix of humor, philosophy, allegory, and self-aware commentary on video games, requiring almost no skill to understand and enjoy.  It is a masterpiece that blurs the line between game, story, commentary, and art.

After the disappointment that was Assassin's Creed III, Black Flag is a step in the right direction for the premier run-jump-kill franchise. There's still a lot of annoying elements, such as the outdated combat system and clearly-not-fit-for-purpose control scheme, but the majority of the game is actually a whole lot of fun.
The much-touted naval system is an improvement on AC3's, but I feel like they're putting too much emphasis on it. It's almost like they'd rather distract you than fix the obvious problems with the core gameplay mechanics. Nevertheless, it's a feature and a mighty impressive one at that.
If you weren't a fan of the real-life side of the AC storyline, then you'll be disappointed that it's back, though it seemed a bit less pretentious than in previous outings. It's always been one of those love it or hate it scenarios, but I felt they did a better job this time.
It's not a difficult game, either, which can be good or bad depending on your preference, but the lack of difficulty actually seemed to make it more fun to play, as you could set up awesome air assassinations much more easily. The stealth sections are much more forgiving than in previous titles, but still can be frustrating if you're going for undetected objectives.
Outside of those issues above, the game is a gem and legitimately fun to play. Kenway has swag much like Ezio did in AC2, which filters down through the story and into the game itself, as every action he takes is saturated in swashbuckling cool. A highly enjoyable game with minor issues that don't really detract too much from the game experience.

Very solid cookie cutter platformer rpg game. 7/10. At $15usd, thats pretty good. Basically another Dark Souls-esque styled platformer.
The game itself is pretty generic, jump on platforms, hit progressively difficult enemies with a sword or spell, gain new ability and equip the latest thing to change your playstyle by 1%. The controls are really tight with solid animations, hit boxes are well defined and the sword knockback is an interesting evolving mechanic. By that I mean a player can learn to use the sword in different ways to get around the map.
While alot of reviews will probably say that the art style is AMAZING and the music FABULOUS, theyre really just OK to be honest. The gothic bug theming is a nice twist but is barely enough to carry the game, and the music while pleasant to listen as background filter, is neither memorable or enough to evoke any sort of emotion.
Take a look at games like Dust: An Elysian Tail / Shovel Knight / Shantae or even Bleed, and you can see the protagonists will inform the player on how the world is sort of built around them, instead of Hollow Knight, in which the protagonist really has no influence in that world and can be just a generic guy with weapon. And when the title of the game is the protagonist, you really want them to be interesting.
Closing point: If its your first entry into platform rpg's, then go for it, its got very tight controls and cool bug NPCS (The caterpillars are adorable as ♥♥♥♥) and is relatively cheap. Good job for first time indie dev's.

Currency is important to collect, as often you need to purchase maps, fast travel hot spots, open doors and buy items, but nothing is too expensive that you need to grind for. This is only my second negative review ever, and it's a very conditional "not recommended".
There are plenty of positive review with all the good points so I won't repeat them here. If you like Dark Souls type games stop reading this and go buy it. It really is an excellent game.
If you are like me and are a huge fan of Metroidvanias, but don't care for DS-type games, here is what you should know.
1) The game is very slow-paced. I am 8 hours in and have found 3 skills
2) You will probably spend the first hour grinding to get money to buy the map functionality that is standard in virtually all Metroidvanias. You can't even see your current position on the map without buying the ability.
3) You will spend most of your time in areas with no map. You often don't get a map until you are almost done with an area. This is useful to see what you missed, but means you will be spending a lot of time aimlessly wandering around similar-looking screens, trying to find a map merchant or checkpoint.
4) Even when you get a map for an area,  it doesn't update with any new screens you visit until you rest at a checkpoint.
5) Speaking of checkpoints, they are *very* few and far-betwen. There is not always a checkpoint close to a boss.
6) If you die, you will have to run back from the last checkpoint and face not only what killed you, but your dead soul as well. Your souls only takes two hits to kill but if you die before you kill it, you lose all the geos (money) it had on it.
7) You will sometimes be locked in a room with no warning to fight a mini-boss, or at least a large enemy you've never seen before. If you die, your only choice is to run back (sometimes with a complete respawn), get to the same boss with the same HP, possibly die and lose all your geos. Repeat until you beat it, but now you are broke.
8) The game quickly become a desperate search for the next checkpoint, hanging on with 2 HP. At least once, I finally found the next checkpoint, a long series of elevators and tough mobs later, only to find out it costs geos to activate it (which I lost to a lock-in room a few screens before).
If you are ok with all of the above notes, there are few games better than this one. For me, they make it more frustrating than fun. I may finish it at some point, but  it has simply ceased to be enjoyable.

This game will likely be big in a months time. It's like Rocket League for MOBA players. It's an absolute blast, I can clearly see what they set out to accomplish here. Polished 2v2 and 3v3 combat with extremely high tier rule sets.
Having a lot of experience with team based PvP games, I will say this. There are Ranged, Melee, and Support characters. The Ranged are largely capable of the best damage, the Melee are largely capable of being the most sticky and toughest, and the Support can perform their role at a team carrying level.
Here's where things get good at a mechanical level.
Good supports are nearly unstoppable, unless you know how to take advantage of setting up combos against your target. Health bars, once reduced, lose maximum capacity. This may not seem like much, but suddenly the healer that is capable of fully healing their target is less potent. That is where a lot of frustration gets taken out of the game.
If you are a solo player, I suggest sticking to the 2v2 arena. Have fun!

This game is Bloodline Champions reborn. A "reboot" if you will. If you are familiar with BLC, you will see the core gameplay is the same. The game play is slowed down a tad, perspective changed slightly from BLC, but overall makes it feel like a better game and more accessable. I was only a casual BLC player, but I can already tell playing Battlerite was much easier to get into.
To summerize the gameplay, it feels like the core meta game of Arena in World of Warcraft, with action twin-stick shooter mechanics. Everything is a skill shot and there are many cooldowns to manage. With counters, shields, teleports, CC, etc. It makes the game very skill based with lots of room to grow and improve just by landing the shots alone, nevermind cooldown management and timings.
One major feature changed from BLC was the new "Battlerite" system. Each match is a best of 5. At the begining of each round you choose a "Battlerite". Which is essentially a talent that will buff or add effects to your abilities. Much like leveling up in "Heroes of the Storm." It adds a little sense of progression and just ramps up the action.
You play these matches in a 2v2 or 3v3 format. Overall it becomes a very satisfying experience. One round you can get totally destroyed, and turn it all around the next by playing better and smarter. There is great satisfaction to taking a round away from an opposing team who was obviously dominating the first two.
While some BLC fanatics might be off put by some of the changes they made, I feel the overall experience is better for players new to this style of game, and BLC fans will just be happy to have it back in some form or another.
Currently it is in Early Access, but definitely feels like a complete game. Just missing some of the social features and game modes from their orignal game, Bloodline Champions. Early Access will pretty much be mostly for getting these missing features ready, more champions to add, and of course balance feedback. It will launch with what we are assuming a traditional F2P model, with free champion rotations that you have to unlock with money or ingame currency. Buying into Early Access now essentially gives you a MASSIVE pre-order bonus. All Champions free, forever! Pretty sweet deal for having faith in Stunlock studios. I reccomend this game for anyone who is a fan for high skill based competative mulitplayer games.

Dungeon Defenders is not so much a tower defense as it is an RPG, although building towers, walls and traps IS part of the fun.
Pick a class from Wizard, Warrior, Huntress or Monk (or others if you have DLC's) and develop that characters abilities and equipment to suit your gaming style.
That was the RPG part. The tower defence part lies in the abilities each character class has. A wizard for example can create tower that fire numerous kind of bolts. The huntress has other abilities, like traps with poison or plain explosives for example.
And then there is the 1st/3rd person shooter element, depending on how far you zoom in. Most melee players tend to 3rd person whereas most ranged players lean towards 3rd, it's all in your own hands in this puppy.

By far my favourite game of 2013 and easily the best Assassin's Creed game yet. There was always something "not fun" about them. Presentation and story was always top notch, but far too many irritations crept in for my liking. Black Flag changed all that and presents a world that is beautiful and fun to traverse. It's games like this that spur on the gaming industry to create more graphically real worlds and for us to upgrade our PC's to play in them on ultra settings. The water simulation is simply incredible, from calm ocean to raging storms and everything in between, underwater realms and caves..the gfx are jaw dropping. It seems no expense has been spared to create it, with every facet made to immerse the player in the pirate world. Weather and rain effects complete the simulation and kudos to the developers for not constantly reminding the player that it's "just a simulation" by dragging you out of the gorgeous world into reality at every opportunity. We get that when we turn the game off thanks.
The direction, acting and story are of course brilliantly done, though with so many side activities to pursue whilest playing through it, my attention wasn't so much on the story, but more on completion of areas and adventuring, thus the story was difficult to follow at times.
My only complaints would be the, what seemed like 20 or 30 odd "follow" missions and timed ones that went against the freedom the game doles out so well. One particular one wants the player to stick to the script so much i thought i was playing Call of Duty - but i don't normally do COD missions over and over like this trying to figure out how the game wants me to play. These are small things though and their frustrations are heavily outweighed by the sheer fun and addictive qualities the game contains with it's parkour and combat mechanics, not to mention naval combat, which can be fun, if the outcomes weren't so repetitive.
For the next game..i want the same, but a more interesting mission and story structure that utilises more locations on the map, NO follow missions, a far better stealth mechanic that doesn't require waiting waiting waiting and finding bushes and stalks to "hide" in..a crouch option would have been great.
Not interested in multiplayer, though it was fun for an hour.

Amazing game, there's nothing else really like it. If you are a fan of completely skill-based arena games, here you are. All skills are skill-shots meaning you have to aim them. There's no boring laning/item buying/level up phases, just pure PvP. Each round you are granted a choice of 3 Battlerites which basically help customise your champion to allow you and your team to shape themselves in the best way for who you are playing against. There's an abundance of server locations including the oft-neglected Australia(Thank you Stunlock!) and SEA countries.
There are lots of unlockables which are all cosmetic, from skins to weapons and poses. They are granted via chests which you earn through playing the game but can also be bought with the currency you acquire. There's 2v2, 3v3 and AI to play against currently, with daily quests given to help earn more chests and also give you a reason to branch out and try other champions.
So far the community has been great with people understanding that it's a new game and that people have to play to learn. Very refreshing compared to MOBAs which are known for the most toxic communities in existence.
Buying Early-Access gives you every champion that will be ever released for free. Although the game will be Free-to-Play on release, I think it's totally worth it and I'm more than happy to support developers who give us Australian servers. The major reason I instantly purchased this though is because it's been the years of waiting for something like Bloodline Champions to be released(their previous game) and here it is, in a much more user-friendly package.
Definitely pick this up if you like fast-paced, skill-based arena PvP. You won't regret it.

Very solid cookie cutter platformer rpg game. 7/10. At $15usd, thats pretty good. Basically another Dark Souls-esque styled platformer.
The game itself is pretty generic, jump on platforms, hit progressively difficult enemies with a sword or spell, gain new ability and equip the latest thing to change your playstyle by 1%. The controls are really tight with solid animations, hit boxes are well defined and the sword knockback is an interesting evolving mechanic. By that I mean a player can learn to use the sword in different ways to get around the map.
While alot of reviews will probably say that the art style is AMAZING and the music FABULOUS, theyre really just OK to be honest. The gothic bug theming is a nice twist but is barely enough to carry the game, and the music while pleasant to listen as background filter, is neither memorable or enough to evoke any sort of emotion.
Take a look at games like Dust: An Elysian Tail / Shovel Knight / Shantae or even Bleed, and you can see the protagonists will inform the player on how the world is sort of built around them, instead of Hollow Knight, in which the protagonist really has no influence in that world and can be just a generic guy with weapon. And when the title of the game is the protagonist, you really want them to be interesting.
Closing point: If its your first entry into platform rpg's, then go for it, its got very tight controls and cool bug NPCS (The caterpillars are adorable as ♥♥♥♥) and is relatively cheap. Good job for first time indie dev's.

Hollow Knight is a metroidvania that ticks all the boxes of great game design with its high polish. You can tell the developer put a lot of care in each level and encounter with enemies.
Despite being a standard metroidvania, it does feature inspirations from other games, which makes Hollow Knight unique in its own way. One such is the soul power which fills up each time you hit an enemy, which can be used to cast magic or heal yourself as there are no health items throughout levels like in Metroid.
Currency is important to collect, as often you need to purchase maps, fast travel hot spots, open doors and buy items, but nothing is too expensive that you need to grind for. However when you die, you do lose your money and half your soul meter, but you can get it back if you defeat your ghost where you last died, adding that risk/reward mechanic from the Souls series.
The game has an awesome art style, with all NPCs and enemies being a form of an insect which is unique and charming.
