+ Great Soundtrack
+ Art Design
+ Stability (on a ROG - G750JM, i7 2.4ghz processor, NVIDIA m860GTX)
+ Size (map is huge. You think you've found all the regions, and then you discover a new one. Impressive)
+ Customization (equippable effect charms, upgrades, spells, health/mana relics, unique objects)
+ Diverse enemy population and unique bosses and sub-bosses (a surprising amount)
+ Price ( at $15, the game is underpriced for the sheer scale and quality of content. Plus, the developers have been very proactive about communicating with the community to discover and fix bugs and performance problems).
+/- Controller support* (I don't use a controller, so I can't vouch for how well it performs with one)
+/- Story/Setting/Lore/Gameplay presents itself much like Dark Souls, which can be a good thing or a bad thing depending on your tastes. Very inclined to nickname this game "Bug Souls." Personally, really enjoy the similarity. Hollow Knight is more forthcoming with information, but it also implies a lot as well. Overall, it's very satisfying.
+/- Controls are very precise, with no momentum in movements. Stop pressing a movement key, the character stops dead in his tracks (with exception to some abilities, which do have momentum). Might take some getting used to, and I only mention it because some people might have to adapt to it. Personally, did not have an issue.
- Poor Mouse Support (standard 3-button mouse cannot be command-bound. Was able to bind commands to alternate buttons on my Logitech G502. Still, not ideal for a PC game). Devs are apparently considering adding mouse support.
- Minor hitches in frame rate, impact varies. It barely causes me any real grief, others state they're having a worse time of it.
Opinion: This game is great, despite a few, minor issues. Though the game is only ~$15, nothing about it feels cheap. A lot of talent went into producing Hollow Knight, and it shows. If you liked Ori & the Blind Forest, or would like a metroidvania comparable to Dark Souls, stop reading this and buy it.

This is an amazing game. I have to admit, I had low expectations for this game because I confused it with Rise of the Triad. I could not have been more wrong.  Shadow Warrior was one of very few FPS games in which I actually cared enough about the story to push on  to the end. That, combined with nonstop swordplay, gunmanship, and cheesy one liners sprinkled at key moments kept the action fresh and hilarious.
The swordplay in this game is incredible. Not only is it more fun to use than the guns, but the enemy models are sliced apart by your moves and furious slashing,  as pieces and parts fly all over the place. It's very satisfying to use.  The guns start out so/so, but after upgrading become a lot more fun to use, and some are integral to killing some of the later enemies once they are fully upgraded.
The environments are all gorgeous and well thought out. There is some backtracking but it's usually only minor at most and the levels remain fresh throughout. The lighting is pretty damn good and the textures are all high quality hi res textures.
Overall I'd say this has been one of the funnest FPS games I've ever played and I've been playing PC games since the mid 80's.  If you enjoy a good FPS, this is a game you should try out as soon as possible.

I'd love to recommend this game, however there are several issues with the game that make this a '
' currently. I would strongly advise waiting until the developer has had time to address some of the more critical issues that I'll bring up later in my review. If you can get beyond some seemingly frustrating gameplay issues and bugs, you really will enjoy the game.
The game world is presented in an ominous Dark Souls type of atmosphere (clearly a big influence here). The death and rebirth mechanic is pretty much consistent with DS, making you kill your previous self at point of death to regain your geos. Travel is done by way of unlocking stations places in each region of the map, or by foot.
Characters don't really have a whole lot of dialogue, but don't consider that a bad thing. There is a large assortment of characters you will run into on your adventure, each with interesting personalities. Each area has unique NPCs, some of which offer to aid you on your quest. Expect to travel the world looking for each special shop as they are not in a central location.
The game definitely does very little to hold your hand, aside from basic tutorial pop-ups. As you progress in the game, new items unlock all sorts of cool abilities, but mastering them does take some work. Upgrading gear is also essential, expect to grind out geo in order to progress.
The boss fights are fun, some a little too easy. The assortment of different enemies in each area helps give each zone a unique feeling. I'm not sure how I feel about the respawns as sometimes a zone will fully respawn everything and sometimes nothing (might be because you fully cleared the area).
The soundtrack included with this game is wonderful. I've found myself sitting still just to listen to new songs as I transition from area to area. They do a great job setting up the atmosphere (hello Fungal Wastes and City of Tears!). SFX are pretty standard, nothing bad but nothing I'd considering outstanding.
Random freezing - The game looks fantastic, however there are issues with random freezes that can last up to second. I'm on fairly high-end hardware (GTX 1070, 32gb ram) so this appears to be an issue with the game. I can't figure out what exactly is causing the freezes, but they happen during bad moments (wall jumping, boss fights). I've tried to disable the sound to see if that causes the issue, however it still seems to persist with or without sound.
Clunky controls - Ok, this is probably my biggest complaint with the game. Controls are not fluid.. at all. I played with an Xbox One gamepad and also tried my steam controller (the XBO controller works best). I would
recommend playing with a mouse/keyboard. There are several places in this game where you are required to jump over spikes or other obstacles, however if you miss the timing you are forced to reset. Wall riding/jumping seems VERY spotty, half the time it works when I jump, sometimes it pretends I didn't press anything. I've found that the closer you are to the ledge of the wall, the more likely it is to not register a jump (learn to jump, right?). Besides wall jumping, the dash+attack move seems to have issues registering as well. Similar to Castlevania, this is pretty simple to master, or at least I thought it was. Holding the attack and dashing, you have to release the attack button at just the right time, otherwise nothing happens (most of the time). I've found that if I don't time it correctly it sometimes randomly goes off after I start moving again (huh?). I've had several other instances where buttons presses are not registering, but I've become so used to it that I try to ignore it.
Trivial puzzles - Ok so this is just opinion, but I really dislike some of the areas in the game where you are required to avoid traps or obstacles. Since I've had issues with controls not being as fluid as they should and random freezing, it makes doing these sorts of tasks very difficult. To top it off, some of the areas you gain access to are not worth the time invested (really, a geode for all that!?!?).
Overall, the game is great and is definitely worth the asking price. I'd strongly recommend picking this up in the future once the developers have had time to address some of the issues I mentioned above.

Game is a 2D action platformer.  Is it worth playing?  My thoughts after 9 hrs in the game.
Pros:
- Nice 2D art.
Cons:
- Black screen loading from one map to the next.  In 2017.
- Archaic system where if you die you lose your geo (salt/soul equivalent) and you have to go to the place you died and get it back.  Die before you get it back and the previous one disappears.  This system is getting really old and serves no purpose other than to lengthen amount of time spent backtracking and the spawn points are few and far between.  If you died in the middle of a platforming section, next time not only do you have to do the playforming, you also have your dead soul to deal with which will attack you and knock you off, making it literally impossible to recover.  This is really cheap and frustrating.
- No combo system.  No dodge.  No weapon variety.  Bare bones combat.
- Clunky controls.
- Game suffers from stuttering.
- Very short invincibility frames after taking damage.  Damage does not knock you back.  If you get hit once, prepare to get hit lots of times.
Once you get over how good the game looks, you'll be frustrated by the poor mechanics.

Why hello there Stanley! NO no no no NOOOOOO, DON’T scroll down, there’s nothing better down there, I’ve checked. Now I know why you’re here: You want to know if The Stanley Parable is any good. Yes it is, but I’m biased, so I’ll have to prove my case….
What’s that? Your name’s not Stanley? Well you’re going to have to get used to me calling you that if you are at all interested in this...experience. That’s just the name of my character, you know, the protagonist? The “Fill in Your Name Here” Parable just doesn’t have quite the ring to it, does it?
Your name is Stanley? Well well very good, you’ve accepted the inevitable.
No more interruptions, finally? Good. Back to the top. The Stanley Parable is--how am I supposed to explain this to you? You weren’t there with me while I slaved over my typewriter click click click clicking away at all of the different possibilities and endings for Stanley. You couldn't have possibly followed my mind down memory lane as I relived every single video game I’ve played to get all the references and easter eggs just right. And surely you didn’t see my eyes bugging of my head from all the late nights of studying video game history and design so I could craft subtle nuances and jokes for the keen of mind.
You see, ever so many have tried to describe my work, my brainchild, my baby, and have fallen. Hard. Harder than a brick on concrete. That’s why you had no business scrolling by me earlier. There’s absolutely no one better to tell you about it than I, the Narrator. Oh, you want me to enlighten you? How delightful! But, well, you’ll have to take my word for it when I say the less you know about it the better it will be for you. You see, that’s where everyone else falls so short. By trying to explain everything they twist it all up like a Boyscout practicing knots. Let me just say...it’s for the observant gamers, those who have been around and played much over the years. I’ve tried to include a lot of jokes for them and easter eggs for those who play a lot of indie games too. And don’t worry there should be plenty for all you other not-so-educated folks to enjoy...You don’t know what an indie game is? Well...let’s just say you’re looking at one, Stanley. No no not me, I mean The Stanley Parable, my work.
Oh, one last thing...if you do decide to become my pawn--I mean, er, guest!--and play The Stanley Parable, could you please suppress whatever primeval urge you have to go into the Broom Closet? It just boggles my mind why so many people have tried to make an endings out of everything little thing. I’m surprised we haven’t had a Staring At The Wall ending yet. I really should knock some sense into the designers, with all the props they made for that closet...it certainly wasn’t my idea! If it was my idea, THERE WOULD BE SOMETHING IN THERE. MEANINGFUL. LIKE A BUTTON.
Well, I’m glad we had this chat Stanley and I hope you will let me guide you through one of the best experiences of your life. And please do let me do the guiding? Bad things tend to happen when players...er...wander. You know, Broom Closet stuff and the like.
Now, Who Likes to Party??
-- The Narrator

Belated review. Dungeon Defenders is one of the best action-tower defense games I have played. The gameplay is much like other games in the genre - progress through a series of levels in which your goal is to defend a crystal. The catch is the crystal is under attack by waves of enemies. Between waves you have the opportunity to set up defenses (different types are available depending on which of the 4 characters you use). Once a wave starts, it's you and your defense versus the horde... rinse and repeat. So what sets DD apart? Well, one cool thing is that you create and play as a personalized character that can be saved. Your character levels up via experience gained and can be equipped with hundreds of different weapons that are found during levels. Add in an excellent online co-op mode, tons of extra challenges and DLC, and you've got a damn near perfect package. Give this a shot, even if you've never tried tower defense before... but don't blame me if you become addicted! :)

Possibly the weakest entry in the series to date.  The entire story feels arbitrary and half-told, and the "climax" was far from satisfying, leading the end of the game to feel abrupt, as if it ended early to accomodate more DLC.  Issues that have dogged the series have only gotten worse, with ground combat being the worst I have seen yet.  I don't think I've ever played a game where I felt simultaneously more powerful and incredibly weak, but they have managed to somehow pull that off.  It also bears, in my opinion, several strong resemblances to Far Cry 3 while failing to capture any of the uniqueness of that game.  Hunting and scrounging for materials to craft upgrades, weird visions where you're forced to walk really slowly by people from your past as they rage at you, taking over enemy forts to give yourself fast travel locations - fans of the tedious parts of FC3 will be very happy with this title.
Despite buying the game in Steam, it plays in Ubisoft's terrible Uplay, which requires a separate account and tracks achievements separately.  Buying a large pack of DLC here on Steam therefore requires manually copy/pasting each individual code over into Uplay, which is cumbersome and unnecessary.
My playthrough was also plagued with lost savegames, which a quick search shows has been an issue known to Ubisoft for several months and has received no attention, resulting in the loss of about two dozen hours of playtime.  Despite Uplay's "always on" cloud syncing of savegames, I was able to lose entire sessions with no real warning on multiple occasions.  Ubisoft forum denizens offer a workaround for this issue in the form of a batch file to back up your savegames (I did not try this), but the fact that Ubisoft has failed to resolve this issue several months after a botched launch reflects extremely poorly on their further involvement in the title.
Gone is the ability to recruit new assassins, replaced by the ability to create a trading fleet managed in a minigame instead (The less said about this new minigame the better).  I suppose this is due to the fact that Edward isn't actually an assassin until the end of the game, and while he occasionally works with them his ends seem mostly at odds with theirs throughout the game.
In the plus column - this game is gorgeous and there is no way to overstate that.  Every sightline falls on something just beatifully done.  This game also has some of the great jumping and climbing puzzles that has made the series great, and collectibles are very liberally sprinkled all over the place, which made for a lot of fun until I lost an entire day of collecting due to a savegame corruption as mentioned above.
The overall impression I felt while playing was less like I was playing AC4, and more like I was playing a reskinned AC3.

I would rather play Dungeon Defenders than Diablo 3. For a $14.99 indie title (at time of purchase), DD is one of the most enjoyable game I have played this year until Saint Rows 3 is released. This unique Tower Defense Action RPG title brings the best of the gameplay seen in Orcs Must Die (or similar TD games), and fused it with an amazing RPG overlay with 4 distinctive classes, each with their own towers/trap to mess around with. The mage makes use of the ranged attacks and towers that deal elemental damage, while the warrior has barricades and other more conventional trap for a man-at-arms. The amount of the content is really the eye catcher here; a challenging campaign, bonus missions with specific goals and contraints, a survival mode and a mix-max mode which is out to get you in terms of difficulty. A game best played with a team, but quite enjoyable solo as long as you take the time to level up properly, upgrade your gear, and proceed carefully from there on. If you like action-rpgs like diablo/torchlight, and TD games like Orc Must Die, this is a must buy!

“The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.” - Albert Einstein
The Stanley Parable is a hard game to compare against. It is an incredibly linear game, but one that allows you to choose which way to wave in and out of the line to see a different result. It is short, but only as short as your imagination allows you to think – what if I turned around and walked back through the other door? Would something change? It is repetitive, but incredibly variable – one branch can lead to a potentially different outcome.
For all The Stanley Parable is (and isn't), it is an incredibly clever take on the adventure game, driven by charm, humor, and a personality that makes waking up worth every trip down the hallway.
Stanley is an ordinary person that works at an office with a specific job: to press the corresponding buttons on his keyboard when the monitor tells him to. Endlessly. One day, The monitor gives no more instruction, and his coworkers have all disappeared, and your goal is to find out why.
Pros:
+ Hilarious. The narrator is the real star of the show, and his writing is always perfect.
+ Always a bit different. Every time you play, something else seems to be a bit different than before. Annoying the narrator over and over with repeated clicks or standing in a room trigger some of the best lines.
Cons:
- Once you've seen it all, it's all done. No real replayability.
Try not to look at guides until you've hit a wall on finding new things. Don't be afraid to walk backwards. And never play this without sound. An awesome game.

Game is a 2D action platformer.  Is it worth playing?  My thoughts after 9 hrs in the game.
Pros:
- Nice 2D art.
Cons:
- Black screen loading from one map to the next.  In 2017.
- Archaic system where if you die you lose your geo (salt/soul equivalent) and you have to go to the place you died and get it back.  Die before you get it back and the previous one disappears.  This system is getting really old and serves no purpose other than to lengthen amount of time spent backtracking and the spawn points are few and far between.  If you died in the middle of a platforming section, next time not only do you have to do the playforming, you also have your dead soul to deal with which will attack you and knock you off, making it literally impossible to recover.  This is really cheap and frustrating.
- No combo system.  No dodge.  No weapon variety.  Bare bones combat.
- Clunky controls.
- Game suffers from stuttering.
- Very short invincibility frames after taking damage.  Damage does not knock you back.  If you get hit once, prepare to get hit lots of times.
Once you get over how good the game looks, you'll be frustrated by the poor mechanics.

The Stanley Parable is a funny, fourth-wall breaking game that can only be truly appreciated by experienced gamers, who know how games are "supposed" to play out.
One of the charming aspects of the game is the rollercoaster-ish like/hate relashonship with the narrator.
A great deal of fun is had in seeing just how much you can tick him off, but in the end, the game is meaningless without him, as is pointed out in the game itself.
Another thing I love about the game is that almost every ending and path contradicts all the others.
There are times when you think you've discovered the true meaning behind the game.
The plot twist, the shell-shocker, the conspiracy behind it all, but in another ending, an entirely different "breakthrough" is discovered. Which is real? Are any of them real? Or is the game just messing with you? ...Probably.
There are only a few problems I have with this game, one being that as I said before, if you're not already fairly familiarized with games and gaming in general, the charm of T.S.P. may go over your head a bit. As it is a game that, to some extent, makes fun of games.
The other problem being that it doesn't have much replayability.
The Stanley Parable is the kind of game that is at it's best when being played blind for the first time.
Once you've found all the endings and heard all the dialogue, there's not much reason to go back and do it over again.
But all in all it's a very enjoyable experience, and I'm happy I bought it. As a side-note, The Stanley Parable has a free demo, I recommend you give it a try first, to see if you like the style, in fact, the demo is a quaint little game all on it's own. I'd recommend you play it even if you've already bought the full game, or don't intend to buy the full game.

First of all, if you read my rantview of AC3, you know a lot of what I thought was wrong about it.
This game basically fixed all of that. It's a much more logical progression of the series than AC3's "here's a bunch of half-baked ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that doesn't matter and will be used as a one-off that we don't ever ♥♥♥♥ing explain". There's actually a reason to do things, and -- holy shitballs -- those things are actually ♥♥♥♥ing explained.
I know that Ubi has different teams working on AC. This is the A team's game. The B team made AC3, and ♥♥♥♥ me does it show. This game is everything AC3 should have been, plus it has ♥♥♥♥ing shanties. SHANTIES. SHANTIES ALL OVER THE PLACE.
Yes, you're a pirate. Yes, you get a ship. Yes, it's fun to board other ships, steal them, send them to your fleet, etc. Yes, you get to run around stabbing mens from the rooftop. Yes, there's still a modern-day storyline included for no particular reason other than to make you really, really appreciate the REAL game. But shanties are the most important thing in this ♥♥♥♥ing game. There are other things to collect, sure, but SHANTIES. Shanties are to 18th century sailing (AND PIRATES) what ♥♥♥♥ing shooting things is to video games. Inseparable. Natural. Right. SHANTIES.
Seriously, though, the shanties are AWESOME and since you spend so much time sailing around the Caribbean you might as well listen to them. If you don't collect all the shanties you are a bad pirate and I don't like you, but you will also get REALLY ♥♥♥♥ING TIRED of hearing the same handful of shanties over and over again. Collect the shanties both to be the piratey-est pirate that ever pirated things, and to save yourself from hearing Sally Brown about 50,000 times. Shanties.
Beyond SHANTIES, there's actually a good game here. There's hunting, but it's not the stupid, unexplained and utterly useless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that it was in AC3. Bonus: it's optional. You can buy the skins needed if you don't want to sail to bumble♥♥♥♥ nowhere to get two monkey hides for whatever the ♥♥♥♥ upgrade you're looking at, when you're just sitting on a pile of ♥♥♥♥ing money. (See, AC3? This♥♥♥♥♥♥isn't hard, you ♥♥♥♥ing waste. Now go back in the ♥♥♥♥ing corner so I can continue pretending that you don't ♥♥♥♥ing exist.)
The ship stuff is pretty awesome. The controls are a refined version of what was in AC3, except now there's actually a ♥♥♥♥ing reason to sail the ♥♥♥♥ing ship, unlike "Assassin's Creed Seriously, who the ♥♥♥♥ developed this? A room full of syphilitic monkeys? 3". You get a crazy armament, as well. The Jackdaw (that's your baby) has to be the heaviest-armed brig in the ♥♥♥♥ing world. You get not just your broadsides (which can ultimately be upgraded to have 23 guns per side), but also mortars, fire barrels, and a ♥♥♥♥ing ram. That's right, you can ♥♥♥♥ing ram ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and then rock out like it's the 3rd century BC. By game's end, your little ship is taking out ♥♥♥♥ing full-sized warships that quite literally dwarf you as if it's no big deal. Such is the power of the shanty. Did I mention you can make it pretty? You can make it pretty. Then you can ram ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s some more, while being pretty.
The only real downside to the ship game is that eventually most of the challenge goes out of it. You can throw money at most of the ship upgrades, but the upper-tier ones are all locked behind a need to find plans scattered throughout the world. Some are found in buried treasure chests -- because what would a pirate game be without buried treasure -- while some come from exploring sunken wrecks. The wreck stuff is, honestly, kind of tedious and occasionally annoying. ♥♥♥♥ sharks, that's all I'm going to say. It's not impossible, and it's not outright bad (*coughAC3huntingcough*), but there's not a hell of a lot to it. The only real variation in the sunken stuff is that you occasionally find a smuggler's cove and then you have to Batman the ♥♥♥♥ out of the bad men in there, because you don't have your full armament. That stuff is pretty cool.
Anyway, back to the ship. Once you gather enough cash, resources (cloth/wood/metal, gained primarily from capturing prizes on the open waves), and plans, your little ship becomes an unstoppable juggernaut that ♥♥♥♥♥ all over every ship on the sea regardless of size or apparent strength. The one exception to this is the "legendary" ships, which are firmly optional. They offer big rewards, but by the time you're strong enough to actually take them on the rewards are utterly meaningless. They exist primarily for bragging rights, and you have to approach each with a particular strategy, so at least there's more depth to them than the standard "poop out doom at the ship until you can board it, then repeat" nature of the naval game later on.
As a quick aside, it's really ♥♥♥♥ing weird that when you stop to board a ship every other hostile ship just stops attacking you and sort of stands by to watch. Understandable from a gameplay standpoint, but still very odd; doubly so when you realize that you can cripple a ship, wait until you're severely damaged, run back to the crippled ship to board and capture her and then use her to repair your ship back to fighting shape WHILE IN THE MIDDLE OF A BATTLE. It's strange and unrealistic, but I'll give it to them because, hey, at least it's not AC3 (no, I'm not going to stop ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on AC3 -- ever).
The story is what it is. I won't spoil anything, other than to say that the protagonist is actually enjoyable and not a huge ♥♥♥♥ing whiny, irrational and wooden ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that anyone with a ♥♥♥♥ing brain would've simply dragged out back and shot in the ♥♥♥♥ing face to save the human race from having to deal with him. Edward is awesome, although his character development, if you don't pay attention to the dates, can seem really oddly paced. Edward is a pirate's pirate. Even the way that he gets involved with the Assassins is awesome, and the completely unnecessary and stupid hours-long intro of AC3 is nowhere to be found. You get some short backstory, then it's PIRATE TIME with PIRATEY PIRATE THE PIRATE as your protagonist. He even ends up seeming human and rational, if self-centered. Dude's a pirate.
All in all, definitely worth your time.
Incidentally, the first real DLC, Freedom Cry, is also pretty damned good. Not exactly the longest thing, but you get to play as Kenway's quatermaster (read: first mate), Adewale, and he uses a ♥♥♥♥ing machete while running about stabbing men. A machete. There's a kill animation where he hacks it into a man's knee and then LEAVES IT THERE while he punches him in the face. So yeah, worth it if you like the main game, but not terribly long (which is probably a good thing, to be honest).

This is probably one of the best games of 2013.
It has an interesting storyline, and because of the nature of the characters, I will remember them. Lo Wang has lots of wisecracks that will make you laugh. There are also lots of things like fortune cookies, and statues that get you money in game that makeyou check every nook and cranny. The sword fighting is fluid and very good. Things also respond how you think they would. There are destructible items and walls get slash marks on them when you hit them with a sword. The blood and gore is also great. It is a lot of fun dashing up to an enemy and using your sword to slice his arm of from the shoulder, then watching him stumble back in agony as he tries to figure out what the hell hit him. Then he will swing his other arm at you, and you slice him in half. Then his guts pour out and there is blood everywhere. The gunplay is also very good (better than COD). When you shoot someone with a revolver you can blow their arms and legs off. Or you can blow their head to little bits and blood.
The graphics are 2011 at best. But I am sure by next year sometime, as this game is still early in it's life, there will be mods and ENB. But it is quite saturated and looks very good. Models are well done and blood looks good. This game can look very good on good computers, but, because of lots of graphics options, it can run smooth on old computers as well. With a loss of quality. There are also 3 different default sword models. The katana, an axe, and a baseball bat called the excalibat. You can switch these in the options menu.
Overall this game is very good and I definitely reccomend it. But don't play it next to your 6 year old son.

Soundwise, it's pretty normal for a game. Somehow you can hear bullets impacting in enemies that are a hundred meters away, and other sounds are nothing special.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of shooters like Serious Sam and anyone who likes games with swords, like Chivalry or even Skyrim. The katana is one of the most fun weapons I've used in any game ever.

A better "2D Dark Souls" than Salt and Sanctuary.  Beautiful artwork and animation (the way wrought-iron fences break apart and bushes explode into leaves are lovely touches) with simple-albeit-clever, tight combat.  The maps feel labyrinthine and getting lost is easy before you have access to the area's map, however, this only adds to the epic scale of the world, as your small character explores and fights.  Death feels impactful and linking the health recovery and special abilities into the same shared pool is brilliant, requiring careful strategy when fighting both a room of regular baddies and a boss.
Its inspirations are apparent (Dark Souls, Shovel Knight, Studio Ghibli movies) but it doesn't come across as derivative or shallow, but instead the opposite: a game with gentle story telling, little handholding, and so much to explore and discover.  Highly recommended.

The game itself is a true tactical simulation game: It's based on survival in an almost life-like warzone. There's no CoD style run-and-gun then spray-and-pray tactics here, you have to carefully plan out attacks and even playing your own custom missions could prove challenging. The controls are difficult to understand, especially coming off of other games like the superb Battlefield series, the movement is clunky at best and it is sometimes incredibly hard to discover where to go during campaigns or missions due to the games open-world areas. The game has it's fair share of glitches, though these are mostly graphical and don't seem to affect gameplay, being only minor and few when they do occur. All in all, it's strengths outweigh it's weaknesses, and this is truly a game worth purchasing for the those who like concept of a military simulation set in an open world enviroment.

For a while I thought that Assassin's Creed 2 was the best of the series, the original was quite repetitive with WAY too many interruptions for getting out of the Animus a lot of the time just to get in bed, I didn't feel that AC: Brotherhood was very different from AC2 (They also made way to big of a deal over controlling the brotherhood mechanic, most of the time it was just to drop out of nowhere and kill somebody, and their missions were just waiting times for money.), AC: Revelations felt like a buffer game, and honestly AC3 was better than ACB and ACR, but didn't feel completely finished. Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is my new ultimate favorite AC game, so much so that it will be very hard to beat. The historical figures felt very human and realistic, and ACTUALLY were important and given good screentime. (If anyones played AC3 you'll remember the Paul Revere mission, ugh.) This is the most emotionally investing Assassin's Creed to date. Everyone gets up and arms about Edward being more pirate than Assassin, but hey, not every single one of Desmond's ancestors are going to be the Batman of their time period, so I'm fine with it. The only gripe I have is with the modern day segments. I don't know why it was in first person, and it was pretty boring most of the time. No matter how suspenseful they tried to make it, you're never worried about being attacked or anything because there is NO combat system at all. But still, do not let the negatives turn you away, this game blows every other AC game out of the water. I have a solid 47 hours in the game, and I enjoyed every minute, give or take. (Except Ubisoft REALLY needs to tone down the amount of tailing missions.) A lot of the scenes that try to be impactful do it really well, and I really felt for Edward, because in my opinion Ezio and Altair are very monotone and don't use a lot of emotion in the things they do. Many people gripe about the story, but I honestly think they're  just trying to find something to pick on. The story was amazing for me and, without spoiling, I think this game had the best ending of 2013. There is a very beautiful piece of music sung by a woman, and matched with what Edward is doing, I actually teared up a bit. This game is prone to completely freezing your computer, though, once it was doing it every ten minutes so I had to reinstall the game. So, overall, minus the technical issues, I would give this game a solid 10/10. The side quests are very fun, the main story is really touching watching Edward grow more humble and thoughtful, the modern day story is mediocre (But these segments take about 10 minutes, so not that bad), and the characters are much more engaging and human than the other entries in the series. The naval combat is the best naval combat I've seen from that era. So, I say again, 10/10.
And when the ending scene comes up, please pay attention. You might get teary-eyed as well.

Shadow Warrior is one of my favourite games of 2013, a First Person Shooter that incorporates all the mechanics that I prefer as a long time fan of the genre, adds some unique twists, and has amazing tactical depth. Above all, it focuses on just being fun.
You are Lo Wang, a sort of modern day samurai, on a quest to recover an ancient sword for your Yakuza-style boss. You soon discover that the sword is also wanted by a race of demons who live in a shadow realm.
The combat is outstanding, fast paced and intense. There are several types of demons, each with different abilities, and they attack in large waves, usually a dozen or more at a time. Thankfully you have access to a wide variety of weapons, and you can carry all of them simultaneously, so you can always choose the best weapon for each situation.
Your primary weapon is the katana, and Shadow Warrior has some of the best melee combat of any FPS I've ever played. You have a normal attack, two charged power attacks and a spinning area of effect special move. Add to that a really useful dash move to quickly close the distance, and its surprising just how effective the katana is. Most of the guns are useful as well, when enemies attack from outside melee range, or have powerful melee attacks of their own that you want to avoid.
The health system is fantastic. You can collect medkits. You can use magic. You can collect the souls of fallen enemies. Or, my personal favourite, you can absorb health from any enemies killed by the katana's special moves. So now when you're low on health, a group of demons changes from a threat, to an opportunity. Charge up the spinning attack and dive right into the middle. Glorious, and so much more enjoyable than just hiding behind a wall for a few seconds.
There are three separate types of level up systems in play. Killing enemies gains XP which can be used to unlock passive stat bonuses. Finding crystals allows you to unlock or upgrade magic abilities. And money can be used to buy upgrades for the guns. Each system has lots of different options to choose from, so you can decide which ones best suit your playing style.
The technical points are all positive as well. Level design is like a tree, with lots of branches coming off the main path, to explore and find secrets. Graphics are pretty good, makes good use of the Japanese theme, and I was able to get a solid 60 fps. Keyboard and mouse works perfectly, and all keys are rebindable. You can also customise how much info is shown on the HUD. You can save anywhere, and also enable checkpoints. I didn't experience any significant bugs. It took me 12 hours to complete, which is quite long for a FPS.
I honestly can't find anything to complain about, and therefore Shadow Warrior is an absolutely essential purchase.

Just for future reference for anybody that is searching for answers on how to recover a lost game save:
1) Navigate to C:\Program Files (x86)\Ubisoft

Alright so I've had a long while to play this game and I've got a pretty thorough review now.
First of all, the game is great and definitely is a stunning example of Metroidvania style systems. With that being said, it feels like the devs are also trying to channel Dark Souls style games a bit, which is both successful and unsuccessful at times. The game itself is beautiful with great animations and music, so you're never really wanting more in the visuals department. This is definitely in the running for one of my favorite indie games of the year, so instead of just telling you why I like it, I'm going to point out the things I take issue with. WITH ALL OF THIS BEING SAID, it's fantastic, the price is right from the get go, and it's truly a great action platformer. I have no concerns with my purchase whatsoever.
Overall, my biggest issue with this game is the way that they've addressed difficulty. I'm a huge fan of hard games, but with that being said, I take issue with some of the choices this game makes to get there. There are times when the game goes for a "let's just throw more enemies into this little pit and see how often the player can die," which is more of an obnoxious design choice rather than an actual challenge.
Additionally, there are times when they place checkpoints at really frustrating points, and it's a pain due to the fact that a lot of the most challenging elements of this game are platform related. There are a lot of different systems and various types of shopkeepers all over the place that it becomes a chore just to do really basic tasks (i.e. banking your money or fast traveling). Early on, it seemed like they really had a good mental lock on how this was all going to work out, but I find myself circling around too much just trying to get basic stuff done, which detracts pretty significantly from fun elements.
This game has GREAT character designs and really interesting elements surrounding that, but it feels like they included far too many shopkeepers and NPC functionalities because they liked making characters, which often feels like a disservice to the actual gameplay. At times, I just wish I could fast travel from "benches," which are the checkpoints, but instead you have to find all these strange other NPC locations to do that. In general, it's just a weird philosophy to make things feel like a chore rather than an intuitive part of the gameplay.
A lot of aspects of this game work fantastically well, especially considering that it is by no means linear. With that being said, it could also use a less annoying map system (i.e. having to buy a map just to be able to chart locations you've already visited), and I'm never sure if certain items in the stores are only available there or if they can be earned elsewhere. There have been points where I've literally had no idea what to do, and that's a bit concerning considering my love of the Dark Souls games.

I'm very sorry to not recommend The Stanley Parable. I'm very disappointed with this piece of software.
I say 'piece of software' because I don't think this is a game at all. It is an experiment, a social commentary, a parody, an art piece... but not a game. For me, a game needs to have a purpose. Yes... there can be other routes, additional content, extras, easter eggs, etc. But there should be a clear main purpose for the game. A goal to reach and this software doesn't have it.
Instead of a game, what you get here is an experience in which you actually become the main character of this game, Stanley. I mean, when you're running around trying to trick a narrator without no purpose at all, is there really a point to continue "playing"? You're just like Stanley, pressing keys into a keyboard because that's what they're telling you to do it, directly or indirectly, with no consequence and no purpose.
Seriously, if you want to see what this game has to offer, just go and watch a video showing the different endings. You'll have about the same fun as playing it yourself and you'll save yourself $15.
To paraphrase a line from the game: "The only way to win is press escape and quit". Real life is out there, better games are out there.

There isnt really any other game quite like this one. It's an adventure that changes with each playthrough based on the decisions you make. You are Stanley and you start out in your stale office, in your stale job, in your stale life....or do you? Perhaps your life is amazing, sad, depressed, happy...whatever. The choice is yours.
The gameplay is seamless. Perfect controls for the game. The graphics are also top notch. It actually looks like the Unity engine a bit, but if it was, the developer maximized what he got out of it. Some of the puzzles can be challenging, and deception factors in to some aspects of this game as well.
The narration however is really where this game is at. There are only two other games that I can think of that rivals this one in that regard (Battleblock Theater, Bastion), although their styles couldnt be more different.
I have seen something like 18 different endings with this game. Not sure how many there really are, but there are a lot, and so as you can expect, there is a ton of replay value with this game.
The developer also had some fun with the achievements. One of them is to play all day (24 hours) on a Tuesday, lol. One is to play, and then play again a year later. Etc....
This game is an easy 10/10. It is perfect for what it is trying to be, doesnt force anything, and allows itself to be whatever you want it to be.

Well since i have nothing else to say heres a recipe for Banana cinamon waffles! :3
ingredients:
1 cup all-purpose flour $
1/2 cup whole wheat flour $
1/4 cup buckwheat flour
1/4 cup ground flaxseed
2 tablespoons sugar $
1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/4 teaspoon salt $
1 1/2 cups fat-free milk $
3 tablespoons butter, melted $
2 large eggs, lightly beaten $
1 large ripe banana, mashed $
Cooking spray.
preparing:
Lightly spoon flours into dry measuring cups; level with a knife. Combine flours, flaxseed, and next 4 ingredients (through salt) in a medium bowl, stirring with a whisk.
Combine milk, butter, and eggs, stirring with a whisk; add milk mixture to flour mixture, stirring until blended. Fold in mashed banana.
Preheat a waffle iron. Coat iron with cooking spray. Spoon about 1/4 cup batter per 4-inch waffle onto hot waffle iron, spreading batter to edges. Cook 3 to 4 minutes or until steaming stops; repeat procedure with remaining batter.

Stanley Parable is a very clever game in the sense that something so simple usually doesn’t turn out enjoyable. So, there’s a good idea behind this game. Another question would be if it’s right to call Stanley Parable a game at all because of it’s simple nature. It’s dressed as a game but really it’s more of a walking simulator. The great idea behind Stanley Parable is the narrator who comments on everything you do, even on some small random details. The comments are really funny, you will get to laugh a lot. Also, you get to choose paths so there’s a great replay value. The unlocking of achievements is also embedded to the narration so I highly recommend pursuing them.  It can take you less than 5 minutes to complete the game but in my case I put 1,5 hours into it without repeating anything I previously did.
Verdict: I don’t know weather to call Stanley Parable a game but it will be a time well spent.

Holy mother of mercy, this was an excellent game. I purchased it during the Thanksgiving Steam Sale and I absolutely loved it. Shadow Warrior blends the visual excellence of today's shooters with the old school mechanics and level design of shooters past. The first person swordplay is the best I've ever experienced, surpassing even Dishonored, which in my opinion had the best first person melee mechanic around until this game came out. Other than that, the art style is vibrant and gorgeous, both in terms of the level design and the highly stylistic cutscenes, which look like pages from a graphic novel. Additionally, the goofy humor is genuinely hilarious, especially the fortune cookies scattered throughout the game. The writing is surprisingly good and there's a well develloped and engaging story behind all the crude humor. The voice actors for Lo Wang and Hoji seem to have taken their roles seriously enough to balance out humor with some convincing drama. The only complaint I have about this game is that the enemies do become repetitive after a while. The same few demons crop up over and over, so if you're not sold on the gameplay mechanics, this title will turn into a slog. However, if you enjoy the swordplay and gunplay, the number of ways to approach otherwise repetitive situations will keep you entertained throughout. Overall, this is one of the best shooters of 2013; it's sad that this title didn't get as much attention as some of the bigger name titles of the year.

A better "2D Dark Souls" than Salt and Sanctuary.  Beautiful artwork and animation (the way wrought-iron fences break apart and bushes explode into leaves are lovely touches) with simple-albeit-clever, tight combat.  The maps feel labyrinthine and getting lost is easy before you have access to the area's map, however, this only adds to the epic scale of the world, as your small character explores and fights.  Death feels impactful and linking the health recovery and special abilities into the same shared pool is brilliant, requiring careful strategy when fighting both a room of regular baddies and a boss.
Its inspirations are apparent (Dark Souls, Shovel Knight, Studio Ghibli movies) but it doesn't come across as derivative or shallow, but instead the opposite: a game with gentle story telling, little handholding, and so much to explore and discover.  Highly recommended.

In short AC4: Black Flag is the best Assassins's Creed game there has ever been. The gameplay is typically Assassin's Creed however with the element of being a pirate, the combination of both is a fantastic idea and works great. The game truly makes you feel like a pirate sailing the seas in the caribbean.
The sailing sections of the game are spectacular, boarding ships has never gotten boring. The missions are a lot more structure to previous games. The story is much more enjoyable and interesting.
The character, Edward Kenway is not only a lot more charismatic than Connor Kenway (AC3) he is a badass. The combat is also fantastic and much improved over the last games, the flintlock pistols are my personal favourite. He acts more like a brash and reckless pirate than a typical by the book assassin that we have seen before, he is reckless and we see him fine tuning his skills throughout the game.
The graphics are stunning. Parkouring my way up a gigantic man of war ship to stare at the sun or distant ships battling it out is a great sight, diving underwater and exploring secret caves, waves crashing on my ship all look fantastic not to mention the storms which are a sight to behold, the effects when a storm sets in is not only pretty but proves challenging and the jungles are foggy and feel hot. Ubisoft has really pushed the boat out the AC4 and it was worth it. Whether you are underwater, on land or at sea the caribbean looks stunning from every angle. The world feels alive and populated.
The ship battling element of AC4 plays a big part of the game and it is a really enjoable one, infact I once played for 3 hours solely sailing around, battling ships, boaridng them, taking my loot and then went of to search for another boat to destroy. The ship battling was one of my favourite mechanics of the game.
Previous AC games have suffered from poor framerates etc but AC4 runs perfectly. There is still one or two bugs but nothing major game breaking (personally).
The multiplayer has been tidied up and it is easier to jump into a game and get killing.
One thing I did love about the new game is the general UI it is so much better. Ubisoft has taken the time to design it properly and tidy it all up and no longer do you need to traverse through 5 menus to switch weapons.
Voice acting is as stellar as it can be with all characters having great voice acting.
Overall I think the game is near perfection and I think anyone who plays it will feel the same.
There has only ever been a few games where at the end where I felt lost,  where I wanted to keep playing and urged the game to keep going. Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag is one of those games.
This is not a game, its a conversation. It challenges you not skill, but your mind and changes how you think towards, well, everything.

If you're into PvP, skillshots and mindgames, this game is for you. Bloodline Champions (this game's predecessor) was probably ahead of its time and unfortunately didn't get the exposure it deserved. It also had a pretty bad last few years (with patch 2.0, that brought the game to a sad state with the addition of unnecessary traits, medallions and gems). Battlerite, I hope, will make a comeback with no BS to hinder the experience, streaming to aid its marketing and a generally bigger interest for competitive games. I hope it does well. It's a one of a kind game that offers short and intense matches either 2v2 or 3v3 with a diverse pool of champions to choose from, each with their own abilities. The game requires you to manage your cooldowns, have quick reactions and outplay your opponents. Check it out, it's well worth it. Especially if the words pvp, skillshots and competitive tickle your fancy.

The pacing in the game is incredibly slow. It took me 40 minutes (without a guide) to find the first boss. Killing it allows you to find an NPC that SELLS what are essentially keys for doors you need to unlock to continue you the game. A major problem with this happening so early in the game is that you also have to buy 3 seperate items from a different vendor so you can unlock map functionality. This caused the first 60 minutes of the game to feal like a massive grind. During this first hour there is no gear, armor, weapons, new abilities or anything to mix up the gameplay all you have access to is a single jump and a slash attack.
I also want to say that the boss has a completely BS attack were it charges/rams at you faster than you can avoid it unless both you and the boss are on the complete opposite sides of the very small arena. It wasnt so bad that I lost on the first attempt to it but it felt like a really cheap shot considering theres no dodge mechanic in the game. I dont know if this is a sign of boss battles to come.
I wont be updating this review as I'm asking for a refunding due to the incredibly slow pacing.
Update (Surprise!) In response to some criticism of the review: I've played, comlplete, enjoyed, and loved every Souls game so I'm used to having a game not hold my hand. The biggest problem for me was having nothing new or exciting happen during that hour. A lot of people say that after it, you start to get new abilities but I still stand by my conclusion that that is just awful pacing. You shouldn't have to push yourself through an hour of boring content just to get to crums of something interesting.
Edit: I want to point out that he top negative review says youll spend the first hour grinding for the map functionality.
